sub: Walton writes briefly from the Arctic: the voyage is going well and he is sure he will succeed

o:
To Mrs. Saville, England.
July 7th, 17—.
My dear Sister,

I write a few lines in haste to say that I am safe—and well advanced on my voyage. This letter will reach England by a merchantman now on its homeward voyage from Archangel; more fortunate than I, who may not see my native land, perhaps, for many years. I am, however, in good spirits: my men are bold and apparently firm of purpose, nor do the floating sheets of ice that continually pass us, indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing, appear to dismay them. We have already reached a very high latitude; but it is the height of summer, and although not so warm as in England, the southern gales, which blow us speedily towards those shores which I so ardently desire to attain, breathe a degree of renovating warmth which I had not expected.

No incidents have hitherto befallen us that would make a figure in a letter. One or two stiff gales and the springing of a leak are accidents which experienced navigators scarcely remember to record, and I shall be well content if nothing worse happen to us during our voyage.

Adieu, my dear Margaret. Be assured that for my own sake, as well as yours, I will not rashly encounter danger. I will be cool, persevering, and prudent.

But success shall crown my endeavours. Wherefore not? Thus far I have gone, tracing a secure way over the pathless seas, the very stars themselves being witnesses and testimonies of my triumph. Why not still proceed over the untamed yet obedient element? What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man?

My swelling heart involuntarily pours itself out thus. But I must finish. Heaven bless my beloved sister!

R.W.
b2:
To Mrs Saville, England.
7 July 17—.
My dear Sister,

I am writing a few quick lines to tell you that I am safe and have made good progress on my voyage. This letter will reach England on a merchant ship that is now sailing home from Archangel; it is luckier than I am, since I may not see my native land for many years. However, I am in good spirits. My men are brave and seem firmly determined, and the floating sheets of ice that keep drifting past us, warning of the dangers of the region we are heading for, do not appear to alarm them. We have already reached a very high latitude, but it is the height of summer, and although it is not as warm as in England, the southern winds, which carry us swiftly towards the shores I so eagerly long to reach, bring a refreshing warmth that I had not expected.

So far nothing has happened to us that would be worth describing in a letter. One or two strong gales and a small leak are the kind of accidents that experienced sailors hardly bother to record, and I shall be quite content if nothing worse happens to us during the voyage.

Goodbye, my dear Margaret. You can be sure that, for my own sake as well as yours, I will not rush recklessly into danger. I will stay calm, persistent and sensible.

But success will crown my efforts. Why shouldn't it? I have come this far, finding a safe route across the trackless seas, with the stars themselves as witnesses of my triumph. Why not carry on across the wild yet obedient ocean? What can stop the determined heart and firm will of a man?

My full heart pours itself out like this before I can stop it. But I must finish now. God bless my beloved sister!

R.W.
b1:
To Mrs Saville, England.
7 July 17—.
My dear Sister,

I am writing a few quick lines to tell you that I am safe and my voyage is going well. A merchant ship is now sailing home from Archangel, and it will take this letter to England. The ship is luckier than me, because perhaps I will not see my country for many years. But I am in good spirits. My men are brave, and they seem strong and sure of themselves. Big pieces of ice often float past us and show the dangers of the place where we are going, but my men are not afraid. We are already very far north. But it is the middle of summer. It is not as warm as in England, but the winds from the south are pushing us fast towards the land I want to reach so much, and they bring a pleasant warmth that I did not expect.

Nothing interesting has happened to us yet, nothing worth writing about in a letter. We had one or two strong storms, and once water started coming into the ship, but experienced sailors hardly remember things like that. I will be happy if nothing worse happens to us on this voyage.

Goodbye, my dear Margaret. Don't worry: for my sake and for yours, I will not go into danger without thinking. I will stay calm, patient and careful.

But I will succeed. Why not? I have come this far and found a safe way across seas with no paths, and the stars have seen my success. Why not go further across the wild sea, which still obeys me? What can stop a man with a strong heart who really wants something?

My heart is so full that these words just pour out. But I must finish now. God bless my dear sister!

R.W.
a2:
To Mrs Saville, England.
7 July 17—.
My dear Sister,

I am writing quickly to say that I am safe. My journey is going well. A ship is going home from Archangel, and it will take this letter to England. Maybe I will not see England for many years. But I am happy. My men are brave. We often see big pieces of ice in the sea, but my men are not afraid. We are very far north now. But it is summer, and warm winds are taking us quickly to the land I want to find.
Nothing interesting has happened. We had one or two storms and a small hole in the ship. Good sailors do not think these things are important. I hope nothing worse will happen.

Goodbye, my dear Margaret. Don't worry, I will be careful and calm.

And I am going to win! Why not? I have come this far across the big seas, and the stars saw it. Why not go further? Nothing can stop a strong man who really wants something.

My heart is very full. But I must stop now. God bless my dear sister!

R.W.

o.en: To Mrs. Saville, England.
July 7th, 17—.
My dear Sister,
I write a few lines in haste to say that I am safe—and well advanced on my voyage.
o.ru: Пишу второпях несколько строк, чтобы сообщить, что я цел и невредим — и далеко продвинулся в своём плавании.

o.en: This letter will reach England by a merchantman now on its homeward voyage from Archangel; more fortunate than I, who may not see my native land, perhaps, for many years.
o.ru: Это письмо доставит в Англию торговое судно, которое возвращается сейчас на родину из Архангельска; оно счастливее меня — ведь я, быть может, ещё много лет не увижу родной земли.

o.en: I am, however, in good spirits: my men are bold and apparently firm of purpose, nor do the floating sheets of ice that continually pass us, indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing, appear to dismay them.
o.ru: Тем не менее я бодр духом: мои люди отважны и, по всей видимости, тверды в своих намерениях; и плавучие льдины, то и дело проплывающие мимо нас и возвещающие об опасностях края, к которому мы держим путь, как будто их не пугают.

o.en: We have already reached a very high latitude; but it is the height of summer, and although not so warm as in England, the southern gales, which blow us speedily towards those shores which I so ardently desire to attain, breathe a degree of renovating warmth which I had not expected.
o.ru: Мы уже достигли очень высоких широт; но сейчас разгар лета, и хотя здесь не так тепло, как в Англии, южные ветры, быстро несущие нас к берегам, которых я так пылко жажду достичь, веют живительным теплом, какого я не ожидал.

o.en: No incidents have hitherto befallen us that would make a figure in a letter.
o.ru: До сих пор с нами не случилось ничего такого, что заслуживало бы места в письме.

o.en: One or two stiff gales and the springing of a leak are accidents which experienced navigators scarcely remember to record, and I shall be well content if nothing worse happen to us during our voyage.
o.ru: Один-два сильных шторма да открывшаяся течь — такие происшествия бывалые мореплаватели едва ли удосуживаются записывать, и я буду вполне доволен, если в пути с нами не случится ничего худшего.

o.en: Adieu, my dear Margaret.
Be assured that for my own sake, as well as yours, I will not rashly encounter danger.
o.ru: Будь уверена: ради себя самого, как и ради тебя, я не стану безрассудно искать опасности.

o.en: I will be cool, persevering, and prudent.
o.ru: Я буду хладнокровен, упорен и благоразумен.

o.en: But success shall crown my endeavours.
Wherefore not?
Thus far I have gone, tracing a secure way over the pathless seas, the very stars themselves being witnesses and testimonies of my triumph.
o.ru: Вот как далеко я уже зашёл, прокладывая верный путь по бездорожью морей, и сами звёзды были свидетелями и порукой моего торжества.

o.en: Why not still proceed over the untamed yet obedient element?
o.ru: Почему бы не плыть и дальше по неукротимой, но покорной стихии?

o.en: What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man?
o.ru: Что может остановить решительное сердце и твёрдую волю человека?

o.en: My swelling heart involuntarily pours itself out thus.
o.ru: Так невольно изливается моё переполненное сердце.

o.en: But I must finish.
Heaven bless my beloved sister!
R.W.

o.tip: эпистолярный стиль: год скрыт тире — литературная условность XVIII–XIX вв.
обращение в письме с запятой = «Дорогая сестра!» (в русском — восклицательный знак)
C1 · in haste = второпях (simpler: quickly)
C2/устар. · merchantman = торговое судно (simpler: merchant ship)

o.p: more fortunate than I, who may not see my native land
o.tip: формальное than I (не than me) + who-придаточное к местоимению = счастливее меня, который…
C2 · firm of purpose = твёрдый в намерениях (simpler: determined)

o.p: nor do the floating sheets of ice
o.tip: инверсия после nor: nor do the sheets… appear = и льдины не кажутся…

o.p: indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing
o.tip: причастный оборот + towards which = предлог перед which (simpler: showing the dangers of the place we are going to)
C2 · dismay = пугать, приводить в смятение (simpler: frighten)
C2 · renovating = живительный, обновляющий (simpler: refreshing warmth)
C2/книжн. · hitherto = до сих пор (simpler: so far)
C2/книжн. · befall = случиться с кем-то (simpler: happened to us)

o.p: make a figure in a letter
o.tip: устар. идиома: make a figure = быть заметным, заслуживать упоминания
C1 · spring a leak = дать течь (simpler: a leak started)
C1 · scarcely = едва ли, почти не (simpler: hardly)

o.p: if nothing worse happen to us

sub: Walton’s crew rescue a dying stranger from the ice, who begins to tell his story

o:
To Mrs. Saville, England.
August 5th, 17—.

So strange an accident has happened to us that I cannot forbear recording it, although it is very probable that you will see me before these papers can come into your possession.

Last Monday (July 31st) we were nearly surrounded by ice, which closed in the ship on all sides, scarcely leaving her the sea-room in which she floated. Our situation was somewhat dangerous, especially as we were compassed round by a very thick fog. We accordingly lay to, hoping that some change would take place in the atmosphere and weather.

About two o’clock the mist cleared away, and we beheld, stretched out in every direction, vast and irregular plains of ice, which seemed to have no end. Some of my comrades groaned, and my own mind began to grow watchful with anxious thoughts, when a strange sight suddenly attracted our attention and diverted our solicitude from our own situation. We perceived a low carriage, fixed on a sledge and drawn by dogs, pass on towards the north, at the distance of half a mile; a being which had the shape of a man, but apparently of gigantic stature, sat in the sledge and guided the dogs. We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.

This appearance excited our unqualified wonder. We were, as we believed, many hundred miles from any land; but this apparition seemed to denote that it was not, in reality, so distant as we had supposed. Shut in, however, by ice, it was impossible to follow his track, which we had observed with the greatest attention.

About two hours after this occurrence we heard the ground sea, and before night the ice broke and freed our ship. We, however, lay to until the morning, fearing to encounter in the dark those large loose masses which float about after the breaking up of the ice. I profited of this time to rest for a few hours.

In the morning, however, as soon as it was light, I went upon deck and found all the sailors busy on one side of the vessel, apparently talking to someone in the sea. It was, in fact, a sledge, like that we had seen before, which had drifted towards us in the night on a large fragment of ice. Only one dog remained alive; but there was a human being within it whom the sailors were persuading to enter the vessel. He was not, as the other traveller seemed to be, a savage inhabitant of some undiscovered island, but a European. When I appeared on deck the master said, “Here is our captain, and he will not allow you to perish on the open sea.”

On perceiving me, the stranger addressed me in English, although with a foreign accent. “Before I come on board your vessel,” said he, “will you have the kindness to inform me whither you are bound?”

You may conceive my astonishment on hearing such a question addressed to me from a man on the brink of destruction and to whom I should have supposed that my vessel would have been a resource which he would not have exchanged for the most precious wealth the earth can afford. I replied, however, that we were on a voyage of discovery towards the northern pole.

Upon hearing this he appeared satisfied and consented to come on board. Good God! Margaret, if you had seen the man who thus capitulated for his safety, your surprise would have been boundless. His limbs were nearly frozen, and his body dreadfully emaciated by fatigue and suffering. I never saw a man in so wretched a condition. We attempted to carry him into the cabin, but as soon as he had quitted the fresh air he fainted. We accordingly brought him back to the deck and restored him to animation by rubbing him with brandy and forcing him to swallow a small quantity. As soon as he showed signs of life we wrapped him up in blankets and placed him near the chimney of the kitchen stove. By slow degrees he recovered and ate a little soup, which restored him wonderfully.

Two days passed in this manner before he was able to speak, and I often feared that his sufferings had deprived him of understanding. When he had in some measure recovered, I removed him to my own cabin and attended on him as much as my duty would permit. I never saw a more interesting creature: his eyes have generally an expression of wildness, and even madness, but there are moments when, if anyone performs an act of kindness towards him or does him any the most trifling service, his whole countenance is lighted up, as it were, with a beam of benevolence and sweetness that I never saw equalled. But he is generally melancholy and despairing, and sometimes he gnashes his teeth, as if impatient of the weight of woes that oppresses him.

When my guest was a little recovered I had great trouble to keep off the men, who wished to ask him a thousand questions; but I would not allow him to be tormented by their idle curiosity, in a state of body and mind whose restoration evidently depended upon entire repose. Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had come so far upon the ice in so strange a vehicle.

His countenance instantly assumed an aspect of the deepest gloom, and he replied, “To seek one who fled from me.”

“And did the man whom you pursued travel in the same fashion?”

“Yes.”

“Then I fancy we have seen him, for the day before we picked you up we saw some dogs drawing a sledge, with a man in it, across the ice.”

This aroused the stranger’s attention, and he asked a multitude of questions concerning the route which the dæmon, as he called him, had pursued. Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, “I have, doubtless, excited your curiosity, as well as that of these good people; but you are too considerate to make inquiries.”

“Certainly; it would indeed be very impertinent and inhuman in me to trouble you with any inquisitiveness of mine.”

“And yet you rescued me from a strange and perilous situation; you have benevolently restored me to life.”

Soon after this he inquired if I thought that the breaking up of the ice had destroyed the other sledge. I replied that I could not answer with any degree of certainty, for the ice had not broken until near midnight, and the traveller might have arrived at a place of safety before that time; but of this I could not judge.

From this time a new spirit of life animated the decaying frame of the stranger. He manifested the greatest eagerness to be upon deck to watch for the sledge which had before appeared; but I have persuaded him to remain in the cabin, for he is far too weak to sustain the rawness of the atmosphere. I have promised that someone should watch for him and give him instant notice if any new object should appear in sight.

Such is my journal of what relates to this strange occurrence up to the present day. The stranger has gradually improved in health but is very silent and appears uneasy when anyone except myself enters his cabin. Yet his manners are so conciliating and gentle that the sailors are all interested in him, although they have had very little communication with him. For my own part, I begin to love him as a brother, and his constant and deep grief fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble creature in his better days, being even now in wreck so attractive and amiable.

I said in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I should find no friend on the wide ocean; yet I have found a man who, before his spirit had been broken by misery, I should have been happy to have possessed as the brother of my heart.

I shall continue my journal concerning the stranger at intervals, should I have any fresh incidents to record.

August 13th, 17—.
My affection for my guest increases every day. He excites at once my admiration and my pity to an astonishing degree. How can I see so noble a creature destroyed by misery without feeling the most poignant grief? He is so gentle, yet so wise; his mind is so cultivated, and when he speaks, although his words are culled with the choicest art, yet they flow with rapidity and unparalleled eloquence.

He is now much recovered from his illness and is continually on the deck, apparently watching for the sledge that preceded his own. Yet, although unhappy, he is not so utterly occupied by his own misery but that he interests himself deeply in the projects of others. He has frequently conversed with me on mine, which I have communicated to him without disguise. He entered attentively into all my arguments in favour of my eventual success and into every minute detail of the measures I had taken to secure it.

I was easily led by the sympathy which he evinced to use the language of my heart, to give utterance to the burning ardour of my soul and to say, with all the fervour that warmed me, how gladly I would sacrifice my fortune, my existence, my every hope, to the furtherance of my enterprise. One man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the acquirement of the knowledge which I sought, for the dominion I should acquire and transmit over the elemental foes of our race.

As I spoke, a dark gloom spread over my listener’s countenance. At first I perceived that he tried to suppress his emotion; he placed his hands before his eyes, and my voice quivered and failed me as I beheld tears trickle fast from between his fingers; a groan burst from his heaving breast. I paused; at length he spoke, in broken accents: “Unhappy man! Do you share my madness? Have you drunk also of the intoxicating draught? Hear me; let me reveal my tale, and you will dash the cup from your lips!”

Such words, you may imagine, strongly excited my curiosity; but the paroxysm of grief that had seized the stranger overcame his weakened powers, and many hours of repose and tranquil conversation were necessary to restore his composure.

Having conquered the violence of his feelings, he appeared to despise himself for being the slave of passion; and quelling the dark tyranny of despair, he led me again to converse concerning myself personally. He asked me the history of my earlier years. The tale was quickly told, but it awakened various trains of reflection. I spoke of my desire of finding a friend, of my thirst for a more intimate sympathy with a fellow mind than had ever fallen to my lot, and expressed my conviction that a man could boast of little happiness who did not enjoy this blessing.

“I agree with you,” replied the stranger; “we are unfashioned creatures, but half made up, if one wiser, better, dearer than ourselves—such a friend ought to be—do not lend his aid to perfectionate our weak and faulty natures. I once had a friend, the most noble of human creatures, and am entitled, therefore, to judge respecting friendship. You have hope, and the world before you, and have no cause for despair. But I—I have lost everything and cannot begin life anew.”

As he said this his countenance became expressive of a calm, settled grief that touched me to the heart. But he was silent and presently retired to his cabin.

Even broken in spirit as he is, no one can feel more deeply than he does the beauties of nature. The starry sky, the sea, and every sight afforded by these wonderful regions seem still to have the power of elevating his soul from earth. Such a man has a double existence: he may suffer misery and be overwhelmed by disappointments, yet when he has retired into himself, he will be like a celestial spirit that has a halo around him, within whose circle no grief or folly ventures.

Will you smile at the enthusiasm I express concerning this divine wanderer? You would not if you saw him. You have been tutored and refined by books and retirement from the world, and you are therefore somewhat fastidious; but this only renders you the more fit to appreciate the extraordinary merits of this wonderful man. Sometimes I have endeavoured to discover what quality it is which he possesses that elevates him so immeasurably above any other person I ever knew. I believe it to be an intuitive discernment, a quick but never-failing power of judgment, a penetration into the causes of things, unequalled for clearness and precision; add to this a facility of expression and a voice whose varied intonations are soul-subduing music.

August 19th, 17—.
Yesterday the stranger said to me, “You may easily perceive, Captain Walton, that I have suffered great and unparalleled misfortunes. I had determined at one time that the memory of these evils should die with me, but you have won me to alter my determination. You seek for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did; and I ardently hope that the gratification of your wishes may not be a serpent to sting you, as mine has been. I do not know that the relation of my disasters will be useful to you; yet, when I reflect that you are pursuing the same course, exposing yourself to the same dangers which have rendered me what I am, I imagine that you may deduce an apt moral from my tale, one that may direct you if you succeed in your undertaking and console you in case of failure.

Prepare to hear of occurrences which are usually deemed marvellous. Were we among the tamer scenes of nature I might fear to encounter your unbelief, perhaps your ridicule; but many things will appear possible in these wild and mysterious regions which would provoke the laughter of those unacquainted with the ever-varied powers of nature; nor can I doubt but that my tale conveys in its series internal evidence of the truth of the events of which it is composed.”

You may easily imagine that I was much gratified by the offered communication, yet I could not endure that he should renew his grief by a recital of his misfortunes. I felt the greatest eagerness to hear the promised narrative, partly from curiosity and partly from a strong desire to ameliorate his fate if it were in my power. I expressed these feelings in my answer.

“I thank you,” he replied, “for your sympathy, but it is useless; my fate is nearly fulfilled. I wait but for one event, and then I shall repose in peace. I understand your feeling,” continued he, perceiving that I wished to interrupt him; “but you are mistaken, my friend, if thus you will allow me to name you; nothing can alter my destiny; listen to my history, and you will perceive how irrevocably it is determined.”

He then told me that he would commence his narrative the next day when I should be at leisure. This promise drew from me the warmest thanks. I have resolved every night, when I am not imperatively occupied by my duties, to record, as nearly as possible in his own words, what he has related during the day. If I should be engaged, I will at least make notes.

This manuscript will doubtless afford you the greatest pleasure; but to me, who know him, and who hear it from his own lips—with what interest and sympathy shall I read it in some future day! Even now, as I commence my task, his full-toned voice swells in my ears; his lustrous eyes dwell on me with all their melancholy sweetness; I see his thin hand raised in animation, while the lineaments of his face are irradiated by the soul within. Strange and harrowing must be his story, frightful the storm which embraced the gallant vessel on its course and wrecked it—thus!
b2:
To Mrs. Saville, England.
August 5th, 17—.

Something so strange has happened to us that I cannot resist writing it down, even though you will very probably see me before these pages reach you.

Last Monday (July 31st) we were almost surrounded by ice, which closed in on the ship from every side and left her hardly enough open water to float in. Our position was rather dangerous, especially because a very thick fog had closed around us. So we stopped and waited, hoping that the weather would change.

At about two o’clock the fog lifted, and we saw huge, uneven plains of ice stretching out in every direction, apparently without end. Some of my companions groaned, and I was beginning to feel anxious myself, when a strange sight suddenly caught our attention and took our minds off our own problems. About half a mile away we saw a low carriage, fixed on a sledge and pulled by dogs, moving towards the north; sitting in it and driving the dogs was a creature shaped like a man, but apparently of enormous size. We followed the traveller’s rapid progress through our telescopes until he disappeared among the distant ridges of ice.

This sight filled us with complete amazement. We believed we were many hundreds of miles from any land, but this vision suggested that land was not really as far away as we had thought. Trapped by the ice, however, we could not follow his trail, although we had watched it with the closest attention.

About two hours later we heard the swell of the sea beneath the ice, and before night the ice broke up and set our ship free. However, we stayed where we were until morning, afraid of running into the large loose blocks of ice that drift about after a break-up in the dark. I took advantage of this time to rest for a few hours.

In the morning, as soon as it was light, I went up on deck and found all the sailors gathered on one side of the ship, apparently talking to someone in the sea. It was, in fact, a sledge like the one we had seen before, which had drifted towards us during the night on a large piece of ice. Only one dog was still alive, but there was a man in the sledge, and the sailors were trying to persuade him to come aboard. He was not a wild native of some undiscovered island, as the other traveller had seemed to be, but a European. When I came on deck, the ship’s master said, “Here is our captain, and he won’t let you die on the open sea.”

When he saw me, the stranger spoke to me in English, though with a foreign accent. “Before I come on board your ship,” he said, “would you be kind enough to tell me where you are going?”

You can imagine my astonishment at hearing such a question from a man on the edge of death, a man for whom I would have thought my ship was worth more than all the treasures in the world. Nevertheless, I answered that we were on a voyage of discovery towards the North Pole.

On hearing this, he seemed satisfied and agreed to come on board. Good God, Margaret! If you had seen the man who bargained like this for his own rescue, you would have been astonished beyond words. His arms and legs were almost frozen, and his body was terribly thin from exhaustion and suffering. I have never seen a man in such a pitiful state. We tried to carry him into the cabin, but as soon as he left the fresh air he fainted. So we brought him back on deck and revived him by rubbing him with brandy and making him swallow a little of it. As soon as he showed signs of life, we wrapped him in blankets and put him near the kitchen stove. Little by little he recovered and ate some soup, which did him a great deal of good.

Two days passed like this before he could speak, and I often feared that his suffering had driven him out of his mind. When he had recovered a little, I moved him to my own cabin and looked after him as much as my duties allowed. I have never met a more fascinating person: his eyes usually have a wild, even mad, expression, but there are moments when, if someone does him a kindness or the smallest favour, his whole face lights up with a warmth and gentleness I have never seen equalled. But usually he is gloomy and full of despair, and sometimes he grinds his teeth, as if he can hardly bear the weight of the sorrows that crush him.

When my guest had recovered a little, I had great difficulty keeping away the men, who wanted to ask him a thousand questions. I would not let their idle curiosity torment him, since his body and mind clearly needed complete rest in order to heal. Once, however, the lieutenant asked him why he had travelled so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle.

At once his face took on a look of the deepest gloom, and he replied, “To find someone who ran away from me.”

“And did the man you were chasing travel in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we have seen him, because the day before we picked you up, we saw some dogs pulling a sledge with a man in it across the ice.”

This caught the stranger’s attention, and he asked a great many questions about the route taken by the “demon”, as he called him. Soon afterwards, when we were alone, he said to me, “No doubt I have made you curious, and these good people too, but you are too considerate to ask questions.”

“Of course; it would be very rude and unkind of me to bother you with my own curiosity.”

“And yet you saved me from a strange and dangerous situation; you have kindly brought me back to life.”

Soon after this he asked whether I thought the breaking of the ice had destroyed the other sledge. I replied that I could not say for certain, because the ice had not broken until nearly midnight, and the traveller might have reached a safe place before then; but I really could not judge.

From then on, a new spirit of life filled the stranger’s worn-out body. He was extremely eager to be on deck, watching for the sledge we had seen earlier, but I have persuaded him to stay in the cabin, because he is far too weak to bear the raw, cold air. I have promised that someone will keep watch for him and tell him immediately if anything new comes into view.

That is my record of this strange event up to today. The stranger’s health has gradually improved, but he is very quiet and seems uneasy whenever anyone except me enters his cabin. Yet his manner is so gentle and pleasant that all the sailors are interested in him, even though they have hardly spoken to him. As for me, I am beginning to love him like a brother, and his constant, deep sorrow fills me with sympathy and pity. He must have been a noble person in his better days, since even now, broken as he is, he is so attractive and likeable.

In one of my letters, my dear Margaret, I said that I would find no friend on the wide ocean; yet I have found a man whom I would have been happy to call the brother of my heart, before misery broke his spirit.

I will go on with my journal about the stranger from time to time, if anything new happens that is worth recording.

August 13th, 17—.
My affection for my guest grows every day. He arouses both my admiration and my pity to an astonishing degree. How can I watch such a noble person being destroyed by misery without feeling the sharpest grief? He is so gentle, and yet so wise; his mind is so well educated, and when he speaks, although he chooses his words with the greatest care, they flow quickly and with extraordinary eloquence.

He has now largely recovered from his illness and is constantly on deck, apparently watching for the sledge that went ahead of his own. Yet, although he is unhappy, he is not so completely absorbed in his own misery that he cannot take a deep interest in other people’s plans. He has often talked with me about mine, which I have shared with him openly. He listened carefully to all my reasons for believing that I would succeed, and to every small detail of the steps I had taken to make sure of it.

Encouraged by the sympathy he showed, I began to speak from my heart, to express the burning passion of my soul, and to say, with all the fire I felt, how gladly I would sacrifice my fortune, my life and every hope I had to advance my great undertaking. One man’s life or death would be only a small price to pay for the knowledge I was seeking, and for the power I would win and pass on over the natural forces that are the enemies of our race.

As I spoke, a dark shadow spread over my listener’s face. At first I noticed that he was trying to hide his emotion; he covered his eyes with his hands, and my voice shook and broke off as I saw tears running fast between his fingers; a groan burst from his heaving chest. I stopped; at last he spoke, in a broken voice: “Unhappy man! Do you share my madness? Have you also drunk from that intoxicating cup? Listen to me; let me tell you my story, and you will throw that cup away from your lips!”

As you can imagine, these words made me extremely curious; but the fit of grief that had seized the stranger was too much for his weakened strength, and it took many hours of rest and quiet conversation to calm him again.

Having mastered the violence of his feelings, he seemed to despise himself for being a slave to passion; and, overcoming the dark power of despair, he brought the conversation back to me. He asked me about my earlier life. The story was soon told, but it set off many different thoughts. I spoke of my wish to find a friend, of my longing for a closer understanding with another mind than I had ever known, and said I was convinced that a man who lacked this blessing could claim very little happiness.

“I agree with you,” replied the stranger; “we are unfinished creatures, only half made, if someone wiser, better and dearer than ourselves—as a friend should be—does not help us to improve our weak and faulty natures. I once had a friend, the noblest of human beings, so I have the right to judge what friendship is. You have hope, and the whole world in front of you, and no reason to despair. But I—I have lost everything and cannot start my life again.”

As he said this, his face showed a calm, settled grief that touched me deeply. But he said nothing more and soon went back to his cabin.

Broken in spirit as he is, no one can feel the beauty of nature more deeply than he does. The starry sky, the sea and every sight these wonderful regions offer still seem able to lift his soul above the earth. Such a man lives a double life: he may suffer misery and be overwhelmed by disappointment, yet when he withdraws into himself, he is like a heavenly spirit surrounded by a halo, inside which no grief or foolishness dares to enter.

Will you smile at my enthusiasm for this godlike wanderer? You would not if you saw him. Books and a quiet life away from the world have educated and refined you, so you are rather hard to please; but that only makes you better able to appreciate the extraordinary qualities of this wonderful man. Sometimes I have tried to work out what quality he has that raises him so far above anyone else I have ever known. I believe it is an instinctive insight, a quick but never-failing power of judgment, an understanding of the causes of things that is unequalled in clarity and precision; add to this a gift for expression and a voice whose changing tones are like music that conquers the soul.

August 19th, 17—.
Yesterday the stranger said to me, “You can easily see, Captain Walton, that I have suffered great misfortunes, greater than anyone has known. At one time I had decided that the memory of these evils should die with me, but you have persuaded me to change my mind. You are looking for knowledge and wisdom, as I once was; and I sincerely hope that getting what you wish for will not turn into a snake that bites you, as it did for me. I do not know whether the story of my disasters will be useful to you; yet when I think that you are following the same path and exposing yourself to the same dangers that have made me what I am, I imagine you may learn a useful lesson from my story, one that may guide you if you succeed and comfort you if you fail.

Prepare yourself to hear of events that are usually thought of as marvellous. If we were in some gentler landscape, I might be afraid that you would not believe me, or even that you would laugh at me; but in these wild and mysterious regions many things will seem possible that would make people laugh if they did not know the endless powers of nature. And I have no doubt that the story itself, as it unfolds, will prove that the events in it are true.”

You can easily imagine how pleased I was by his offer, yet I could not bear the thought of him reliving his grief by telling me of his misfortunes. I was extremely eager to hear the story he had promised, partly out of curiosity and partly from a strong wish to improve his fate if I could. I told him how I felt.

“Thank you,” he replied, “for your sympathy, but it is useless; my fate is almost complete. I am waiting for just one more event, and then I shall rest in peace. I understand how you feel,” he went on, seeing that I wanted to interrupt him; “but you are mistaken, my friend, if you will allow me to call you that; nothing can change my destiny; listen to my story, and you will see how finally it has been decided.”

He then told me that he would begin his story the next day, when I had some free time. I thanked him most warmly for this promise. I have decided that every night, when my duties do not keep me busy, I will write down, as closely as possible in his own words, what he has told me during the day. If I am busy, I will at least make notes.

This manuscript will no doubt give you the greatest pleasure; but for me, who know him and hear the story from his own lips—with what interest and sympathy shall I read it some day in the future! Even now, as I begin my task, his deep, rich voice rings in my ears; his shining eyes rest on me with all their sad sweetness; I see his thin hand raised as he speaks, while his features are lit up by the soul within. His story must be strange and terrible, and terrible the storm that caught the brave ship on its way and wrecked it—like this!
b1:
To Mrs. Saville, England.
August 5th, 17—.

Something very strange has happened to us, and I must write about it. You will probably see me before you get these pages, but I still want to tell you.

Last Monday (July 31st) ice almost surrounded us. It closed in on the ship from all sides, and there was very little water left around her. We were in some danger, especially because there was also a very thick fog. So we stopped and waited for the weather to change.

At about two o’clock the fog cleared. We saw huge fields of rough ice all around us, and they seemed to have no end. Some of my men groaned, and I was starting to feel worried too. Then suddenly we saw something strange, and we forgot about our own problems. About half a mile away, a sledge pulled by dogs was moving towards the north. Someone was sitting in it and driving the dogs; he had the shape of a man, but he looked very, very big. We watched him through our telescopes as he travelled fast, until we lost him among the ice far away.

We were all amazed. We thought we were hundreds of miles from any land, but this meant that land was perhaps not so far away. But the ice held our ship, so we could not follow him, although we had watched his path very carefully.

About two hours later we heard the sea moving under the ice, and before night the ice broke and our ship was free. But we waited until the morning, because we were afraid of hitting big pieces of floating ice in the dark. I used this time to rest for a few hours.

In the morning, as soon as it was light, I went up on deck. All the sailors were standing on one side of the ship and talking to someone in the sea. It was a sledge like the one we had seen before; in the night it had come towards us on a large piece of ice. Only one dog was still alive, but there was a man in the sledge, and the sailors were asking him to come onto the ship. He was not a wild man from an unknown island, like the other traveller, but a European. When I came on deck, the ship’s master said, “Here is our captain, and he will not let you die on the open sea.”

When the stranger saw me, he spoke to me in English, but with a foreign accent. “Before I come onto your ship,” he said, “please tell me where you are going.”

Imagine how surprised I was! This man was close to death, and I thought my ship was the most valuable thing in the world for him. But I answered that we were travelling to the North Pole to explore.

When he heard this, he seemed happy and agreed to come on board. Oh, Margaret, if you had seen this man, you would have been so surprised! His arms and legs were almost frozen, and his body was terribly thin because he was so tired and had suffered so much. I have never seen a man in such a bad state. We tried to carry him into the cabin, but when he left the fresh air, he fainted. So we took him back on deck and rubbed him with brandy, and we made him drink a little. When he began to show signs of life, we wrapped him in blankets and put him near the kitchen stove. Slowly he got better and ate a little soup, which helped him a lot.

Two days passed before he could speak, and I often worried that his suffering had made him lose his mind. When he was a little better, I moved him to my own cabin and looked after him when my work allowed. I have never met such an interesting person. Usually his eyes look wild, even mad. But when someone is kind to him or does something small for him, his whole face lights up with a wonderful kindness and sweetness. Most of the time, though, he is sad and hopeless, and sometimes he grinds his teeth, as if his sorrows are too heavy for him.

When my guest was a little better, it was hard to keep the men away from him, because they wanted to ask him a thousand questions. I did not let them trouble him, because he clearly needed complete rest to get well. But once the lieutenant asked him why he had come so far across the ice in such a strange sledge.

Immediately his face became very dark and sad, and he answered, “To find someone who ran away from me.”

“And did the man you were following travel in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we have seen him. The day before we found you, we saw some dogs pulling a sledge with a man in it across the ice.”

This interested the stranger very much, and he asked many questions about which way the “demon”, as he called him, had gone. Later, when we were alone, he said to me, “I am sure that you and these good people are curious about me, but you are too polite to ask.”

“Of course; it would be very rude and unkind of me to trouble you with my questions.”

“And yet you saved me from a strange and dangerous situation; you kindly gave me back my life.”

Soon after that he asked me if the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I said that I could not be sure. The ice did not break until nearly midnight, so the traveller could have reached a safe place before then.

After this, the stranger’s weak body seemed full of new life. He wanted very much to be on deck and look out for the sledge we had seen before. But I have persuaded him to stay in the cabin, because he is much too weak for the cold, wet air. I have promised that someone will watch for him and tell him at once if anything new appears.

That is my story of this strange event until today. The stranger’s health has slowly improved, but he is very quiet, and he seems nervous when anyone except me comes into his cabin. But he is so gentle and polite that all the sailors like him, although they have hardly spoken to him. I am starting to love him like a brother, and his deep, constant sadness fills me with pity. He must have been a wonderful person before his troubles, because even now, in this terrible state, he is so attractive and kind.

My dear Margaret, in one of my letters I said that I would find no friend on the wide ocean. But I have found a man who could have been a true brother to me, if sadness had not broken his spirit.

I will continue my diary about the stranger when there is something new to write.

August 13th, 17—.
I like my guest more every day. I admire him and feel sorry for him at the same time. How can I see such a good man destroyed by sadness and not feel great pain? He is so gentle, but also so wise, and he knows so much. When he speaks, he chooses his words very carefully, but they still come quickly and beautifully.

He is much better now and spends all his time on deck, looking out for the other sledge. He is unhappy, but he is still very interested in other people’s plans. He has often talked with me about my plans, and I have told him everything openly. He listened carefully to all my reasons for thinking I would succeed, and to every small detail of my preparations.

Because he was so sympathetic, I opened my heart to him. With great passion, I told him that I would happily give my money, my life and all my hopes for the success of my journey. The life or death of one man was a small price for the knowledge I wanted, and for power over the forces of nature that are dangerous to all people.

As I spoke, his face became dark. At first he tried to hide his feelings and covered his eyes with his hands. My voice shook and stopped when I saw tears running between his fingers, and a groan came from his chest. I stopped talking. At last he said in a broken voice, “Unhappy man! Are you mad like me? Have you also drunk from that dangerous cup? Listen to me; let me tell you my story, and you will throw the cup away!”

Of course, these words made me very curious. But his sudden grief was too much for his weak body, and he needed many hours of rest and quiet talk to become calm again.

When he had controlled his strong feelings, he seemed ashamed of them. He pushed away his dark despair and started to talk about me again. He asked me about my early life. The story was short, but it made me think about many things. I told him that I wanted to find a friend who could really understand me, and I said that a man without such a friend cannot be very happy.

“I agree with you,” said the stranger. “We are not complete; we are only half made if we do not have a friend who is wiser and better than us and who can help us to become better people. I once had a friend, the best of all people, so I know what friendship is. You have hope, and the whole world is in front of you, so you have no reason to despair. But I—I have lost everything, and I cannot start my life again.”

As he said this, his face showed a quiet, deep sadness that touched my heart. But he did not say any more, and soon he went to his cabin.

Although his spirit is broken, nobody feels the beauty of nature more deeply than he does. The starry sky, the sea and all the wonderful sights of these northern lands still lift his soul up from the earth. A man like this lives two lives: he may suffer and feel disappointed, but when he goes into his own thoughts, he is like an angel with a circle of light around him, where no sadness or foolishness can enter.

Are you smiling because I am so excited about this wonderful traveller? You would not smile if you saw him. Books and a quiet life have made you educated and refined, so you are not easy to please; but that means you can understand his great qualities even better. Sometimes I have tried to understand what makes him so much greater than anyone else I have known. I think it is his natural understanding, his quick and always correct judgment, and his very clear view of why things happen; and he also speaks beautifully, with a voice like music.

August 19th, 17—.
Yesterday the stranger said to me, “Captain Walton, you can easily see that I have had terrible misfortunes, worse than anyone else’s. Once I decided that the memory of them should die with me, but you have made me change my mind. You are looking for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did, and I really hope that your wishes will not hurt you like a snake, as mine hurt me. I do not know if my story will help you. But you are going the same way as I did and facing the same dangers that made me like this, so perhaps you can learn something from my story; it may guide you if you succeed and comfort you if you fail.

Be ready to hear about things that most people think are impossible. If we were somewhere ordinary, I might be afraid that you would not believe me or would laugh at me. But in these wild and mysterious lands, many things seem possible that other people would laugh at, because they do not know the great powers of nature. And I am sure that my story itself will show you that it is true.”

Of course I was very glad that he wanted to tell me his story, but I did not want him to feel his pain again by talking about it. I really wanted to hear it, partly because I was curious and partly because I wanted to help him if I could. I told him this.

“Thank you for your sympathy,” he answered, “but it is no use; my life is almost over. I am waiting for only one more thing, and then I will rest in peace. I understand your feelings,” he went on, because he saw that I wanted to say something; “but you are wrong, my friend—if I may call you that; nothing can change my fate. Listen to my story, and you will see that it cannot be changed.”

Then he told me that he would begin his story the next day, when I was free. I thanked him warmly. I have decided to write down every night what he tells me during the day, using his own words as much as possible, when my work allows it. If I am busy, I will at least make notes.

You will certainly enjoy reading this story. But I know him and hear it from his own mouth, so how interesting it will be for me to read it one day in the future! Even now, as I begin, I can hear his deep voice, and I can see his bright, sad eyes looking at me and his thin hand moving as he speaks. His story must be strange and terrible, like a storm that caught a brave ship on its way and destroyed it—like this!
a2:
To Mrs. Saville, England.
August 5th, 17—.

Something very strange happened to us, and I want to write about it. Maybe you will see me before you get this letter.

Last Monday (July 31st) there was ice all around our ship. There was very little water around us. There was also a thick fog, so it was dangerous. We stopped and waited for better weather.

At about two o’clock the fog went away. We saw big fields of ice everywhere, with no end. We were far from home, and we could not go on. Some of my men were unhappy, and I was worried too. Then we saw something very strange. Half a mile away, some dogs were pulling a sledge to the north. In the sledge there was someone like a man, but very, very big. We watched him through our telescopes until he went away among the ice.
We were all very surprised. We thought that there was no land for hundreds of miles. But maybe land was nearer than we thought. Our ship could not move in the ice, so we could not follow him.

Two hours later we heard the sea under the ice. Before night the ice broke, and our ship was free. But we waited until the morning, because big pieces of ice were moving in the dark water. I slept for a few hours.

In the morning, when it was light, I went up on deck. All the sailors were on one side of the ship, and they were talking to someone in the sea. There was another sledge on a big piece of ice. Only one dog was alive, but there was a man in the sledge. The sailors wanted him to come onto the ship. He was not a wild man; he was a European. One sailor said to him, “Here is our captain. He will not let you die in the sea.”

The stranger saw me and spoke to me in English, but he was not English. “Before I come onto your ship,” he said, “please tell me: where are you going?”

I was very surprised. The man was nearly dead, and he was asking questions! I told him that we were going to the North Pole.

Then he was happy to come onto the ship. Oh, Margaret, you would be so surprised if you saw him! His arms and legs were almost frozen, and he was very thin and tired. I never saw a man in such a bad state. We carried him into the cabin, but he fainted there. So we took him back outside and gave him some brandy. Then we put warm blankets around him and put him near the kitchen fire. Slowly he got better, and he ate some soup.

For two days he could not speak. I was afraid that he was mad. When he was a little better, I took him to my own cabin and looked after him. He is a very interesting man. His eyes often look wild. But when someone is kind to him, his face becomes warm and beautiful. Most of the time he is very sad. Sometimes he makes an angry noise with his teeth, because his pain is too big for him.

The sailors wanted to ask him a lot of questions, but I did not let them. He needed to rest. But one day an officer asked him, “Why did you come so far across the ice?”

His face became very sad, and he answered, “To find someone who ran away from me.”

“Did this man travel on a sledge too?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we saw him the day before we found you.”

The stranger became very interested and asked many questions about the “demon”, as he called him. Later, when we were alone, he said, “You want to know about me, but you are too polite to ask.”

“Yes, it would not be kind to ask you questions.”

“But you saved my life.”

Then he asked me, “Did the ice break the other sledge?” I said that I did not know. The ice broke late at night, so maybe the traveller was safe before that.

After this the stranger felt more alive. He wanted to stay on deck and look for the other sledge. He was very excited about it. But he is too weak for the cold air, so I asked him to stay in the cabin. I said that a sailor will watch for him. If the sailor sees the sledge, he will tell him at once.

That is my story until today. The stranger is better now, but he is very quiet. He does not like people in his cabin, only me. But he is very kind, and all the sailors like him. I am starting to love him like a brother. He is very sad, and I feel sorry for him. He was surely a great man before his troubles.

My dear Margaret, I wrote to you that I will not find a friend on the ocean. But now I have found a man who can be like a brother to me.

I will write more about him later.

August 13th, 17—.
I like my guest more and more every day. I think he is wonderful, and I feel very sorry for him. He is kind and clever, and he speaks very beautifully. It is terrible to see such a good man so unhappy.

Now he is much better, and he is always on deck, looking for the other sledge. He is unhappy, but he is interested in other people. I told him all about my plans. He listened carefully to everything. He wanted to know every small detail of my journey.
He was so kind that I told him about my dreams. I said, “I will give my money and even my life for my journey. One man’s life is not important if we can learn new things about the world.”

Then his face became dark. He put his hands over his eyes, and I saw tears between his fingers. I stopped speaking. At last he said, “Poor man! Are you mad like me? Did you drink from the same dangerous cup? Listen to my story, and you will throw the cup away!”

I wanted to know more, but he was too tired and sad. He needed many hours to be calm again.

Later he asked me about my life. I told him that I always wanted a true friend. I think a man without a friend cannot be really happy.

“I agree,” said the stranger. “We need a good, wise friend to help us become better. I once had a friend, the best man in the world. You have hope and your whole life in front of you. But I have lost everything, and I cannot start again.”

His face was very sad. Then he went to his cabin.

He is very unhappy, but he still loves nature. The stars and the sea make his heart happy. A man like this lives two lives. In one life he is sad and has many problems. But when he thinks quietly, he is like an angel, and no sadness can touch him.

Are you laughing at me, Margaret? You will not laugh when you see him. You read a lot of books, so you will understand what a great man he is. He is cleverer than anyone I know. He understands things very quickly, and he is always right. He speaks well, and his voice is like beautiful music.

August 19th, 17—.
Yesterday the stranger said to me, “Captain Walton, I had terrible troubles in my life. I wanted to keep them secret, but now I will tell you about them. You want to learn and discover new things, like me before. I hope that your dreams will not hurt you, as my dreams hurt me. You are going the same way, and you are in the same danger. Maybe my story will help you on your journey. If you fail, maybe it will make you feel better.
My story is very strange. At home you would not believe me. Maybe you would even laugh at me. But here, in this wild place, you will understand that it is true.”
I was happy that he wanted to tell me his story. But I did not want him to be sad again. I also wanted to help him, and I told him this.
“Thank you,” he answered, “but you cannot help me. I am waiting for only one thing, and then I will die in peace. Nobody can change my life, my friend. Listen to my story, and you will understand.”
He said that he will start his story the next day. I thanked him. Every night I am going to write down his words. If I am busy, I will write short notes.

You will enjoy this story, Margaret. But for me it will be even more interesting, because I hear it from him. Even now I can hear his deep voice and see his sad, bright eyes. I can see his thin hand in the air as he speaks. His story will be strange and terrible, like a storm that breaks a ship!

o.en: To Mrs. Saville, England.
August 5th, 17—.
So strange an accident has happened to us that I cannot forbear recording it, although it is very probable that you will see me before these papers can come into your possession.
o.ru: С нами произошёл столь странный случай, что я не могу не записать его, хотя весьма вероятно, что ты увидишь меня прежде, чем эти листки попадут к тебе в руки.

o.en: Last Monday (July 31st) we were nearly surrounded by ice, which closed in the ship on all sides, scarcely leaving her the sea-room in which she floated.
o.ru: В прошлый понедельник (31 июля) нас почти со всех сторон окружили льды, сомкнувшиеся вокруг корабля и оставившие ему едва ли не только ту полоску воды, на которой он держался.

o.en: Our situation was somewhat dangerous, especially as we were compassed round by a very thick fog.
o.ru: Положение наше было довольно опасным, тем более что нас обступил очень густой туман.

o.en: We accordingly lay to, hoping that some change would take place in the atmosphere and weather.
o.ru: Поэтому мы легли в дрейф, надеясь, что в воздухе и в погоде наступит какая-нибудь перемена.

o.en: About two o’clock the mist cleared away, and we beheld, stretched out in every direction, vast and irregular plains of ice, which seemed to have no end.
o.ru: Около двух часов туман рассеялся, и мы увидели простиравшиеся во все стороны огромные неровные ледяные равнины, которым, казалось, не было конца.

o.en: Some of my comrades groaned, and my own mind began to grow watchful with anxious thoughts, when a strange sight suddenly attracted our attention and diverted our solicitude from our own situation.
o.ru: Некоторые из моих товарищей застонали, да и мой собственный ум начали одолевать тревожные мысли, как вдруг странное зрелище привлекло наше внимание и отвлекло нас от забот о собственном положении.

o.en: We perceived a low carriage, fixed on a sledge and drawn by dogs, pass on towards the north, at the distance of half a mile; a being which had the shape of a man, but apparently of gigantic stature, sat in the sledge and guided the dogs.
o.ru: Мы увидели низкую повозку, поставленную на сани и запряжённую собаками, которая неслась к северу на расстоянии полумили; в санях сидело и правило собаками существо, имевшее облик человека, но, по-видимому, исполинского роста.

o.en: We watched the rapid progress of the traveller with our telescopes until he was lost among the distant inequalities of the ice.
o.ru: Мы следили в подзорные трубы за стремительным движением путника, пока он не затерялся среди далёких неровностей льда.

o.en: This appearance excited our unqualified wonder.
o.ru: Это видение повергло нас в безграничное изумление.

o.en: We were, as we believed, many hundred miles from any land; but this apparition seemed to denote that it was not, in reality, so distant as we had supposed.
o.ru: Мы полагали, что находимся за много сотен миль от какой-либо земли; но это явление, казалось, указывало, что на самом деле она не так далеко, как мы думали.

o.en: Shut in, however, by ice, it was impossible to follow his track, which we had observed with the greatest attention.
o.ru: Однако, запертые льдами, мы не могли последовать за ним, хотя с величайшим вниманием следили за его путём.

o.en: About two hours after this occurrence we heard the ground sea, and before night the ice broke and freed our ship.
o.ru: Часа через два после этого происшествия мы услышали шум донной зыби, и ещё до наступления ночи лёд треснул и освободил наш корабль.

o.en: We, however, lay to until the morning, fearing to encounter in the dark those large loose masses which float about after the breaking up of the ice.
o.ru: Тем не менее мы простояли в дрейфе до утра, опасаясь столкнуться в темноте с большими плавучими глыбами, которые носятся по воде после вскрытия льда.

o.en: I profited of this time to rest for a few hours.
o.ru: Я воспользовался этим временем, чтобы несколько часов отдохнуть.

o.en: In the morning, however, as soon as it was light, I went upon deck and found all the sailors busy on one side of the vessel, apparently talking to someone in the sea.
o.ru: Утром, едва рассвело, я вышел на палубу и увидел, что все матросы столпились у одного борта и, по-видимому, разговаривают с кем-то в море.

o.en: It was, in fact, a sledge, like that we had seen before, which had drifted towards us in the night on a large fragment of ice.
o.ru: Это и в самом деле были сани, подобные тем, что мы видели прежде, — их принесло к нам ночью на большой льдине.

o.en: Only one dog remained alive; but there was a human being within it whom the sailors were persuading to enter the vessel.
o.ru: В живых осталась лишь одна собака; но в санях находился человек, которого матросы уговаривали подняться на корабль.

o.en: He was not, as the other traveller seemed to be, a savage inhabitant of some undiscovered island, but a European.
o.ru: Это был не дикий обитатель какого-то неоткрытого острова, каким казался тот, другой путник, а европеец.

o.en: When I appeared on deck the master said, “Here is our captain, and he will not allow you to perish on the open sea.”
o.ru: Когда я появился на палубе, штурман сказал: «Вот наш капитан, и он не позволит вам погибнуть в открытом море».

o.en: On perceiving me, the stranger addressed me in English, although with a foreign accent.
o.ru: Увидев меня, незнакомец обратился ко мне по-английски, хотя и с иностранным акцентом.

o.en: “Before I come on board your vessel,” said he, “will you have the kindness to inform me whither you are bound?”
o.ru: «Прежде чем я поднимусь на борт вашего судна, — сказал он, — не будете ли вы любезны сообщить мне, куда вы держите путь?»

o.en: You may conceive my astonishment on hearing such a question addressed to me from a man on the brink of destruction and to whom I should have supposed that my vessel would have been a resource which he would not have exchanged for the most precious wealth the earth can afford.
o.ru: Можешь представить себе моё изумление, когда я услышал такой вопрос от человека, стоявшего на краю гибели, для которого, как я полагал, мой корабль должен был быть спасением, какого он не променял бы на величайшие сокровища земли.

o.en: I replied, however, that we were on a voyage of discovery towards the northern pole.
o.ru: Тем не менее я ответил, что мы плывём с целью открытий к Северному полюсу.

o.en: Upon hearing this he appeared satisfied and consented to come on board.
o.ru: Услышав это, он, казалось, успокоился и согласился подняться на борт.

o.en: Good God!
Margaret, if you had seen the man who thus capitulated for his safety, your surprise would have been boundless.
o.ru: Маргарет, если бы ты видела человека, который так торговался о своём спасении, твоему удивлению не было бы границ.

o.en: His limbs were nearly frozen, and his body dreadfully emaciated by fatigue and suffering.
o.ru: Руки и ноги его были почти отморожены, а тело страшно истощено усталостью и страданиями.

o.en: I never saw a man in so wretched a condition.
o.ru: Никогда я не видел человека в столь жалком состоянии.

o.en: We attempted to carry him into the cabin, but as soon as he had quitted the fresh air he fainted.
o.ru: Мы попытались отнести его в каюту, но, едва оказавшись вне свежего воздуха, он лишился чувств.

o.en: We accordingly brought him back to the deck and restored him to animation by rubbing him with brandy and forcing him to swallow a small quantity.
o.ru: Поэтому мы вынесли его обратно на палубу и привели в чувство, растирая его бренди и заставив проглотить немного.

o.en: As soon as he showed signs of life we wrapped him up in blankets and placed him near the chimney of the kitchen stove.
o.ru: Как только он подал признаки жизни, мы закутали его в одеяла и положили возле трубы камбузной печи.

o.en: By slow degrees he recovered and ate a little soup, which restored him wonderfully.
o.ru: Понемногу он оправился и съел немного супа, который чудесным образом восстановил его силы.

o.en: Two days passed in this manner before he was able to speak, and I often feared that his sufferings had deprived him of understanding.
o.ru: Так прошло два дня, прежде чем он смог заговорить, и я часто опасался, что страдания лишили его рассудка.

o.en: When he had in some measure recovered, I removed him to my own cabin and attended on him as much as my duty would permit.
o.ru: Когда он до некоторой степени поправился, я перенёс его в свою каюту и ухаживал за ним, насколько позволяли мои обязанности.

o.en: I never saw a more interesting creature: his eyes have generally an expression of wildness, and even madness, but there are moments when, if anyone performs an act of kindness towards him or does him any the most trifling service, his whole countenance is lighted up, as it were, with a beam of benevolence and sweetness that I never saw equalled.
o.ru: Никогда не встречал я более занимательного существа: в глазах его обычно видна дикость и даже безумие, но бывают мгновения, когда, если кто-нибудь проявит к нему доброту или окажет ему хоть малейшую услугу, всё лицо его словно озаряется лучом такой благожелательности и нежности, какой я нигде больше не видел.

o.en: But he is generally melancholy and despairing, and sometimes he gnashes his teeth, as if impatient of the weight of woes that oppresses him.
o.ru: Но обычно он печален и полон отчаяния, а порой скрежещет зубами, словно не в силах выносить бремя терзающих его горестей.

o.en: When my guest was a little recovered I had great trouble to keep off the men, who wished to ask him a thousand questions; but I would not allow him to be tormented by their idle curiosity, in a state of body and mind whose restoration evidently depended upon entire repose.
o.ru: Когда мой гость немного поправился, мне стоило большого труда удерживать матросов, которым хотелось задать ему тысячу вопросов; но я не мог позволить, чтобы их праздное любопытство терзало его, ведь его телу и душе, очевидно, для выздоровления был нужен полный покой.

o.en: Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had come so far upon the ice in so strange a vehicle.
o.ru: Однажды, однако, лейтенант спросил, зачем он забрался так далеко во льды в столь странной повозке.

o.en: His countenance instantly assumed an aspect of the deepest gloom, and he replied, “To seek one who fled from me.”
o.ru: Лицо его тотчас приняло выражение глубочайшей мрачности, и он ответил: «Чтобы найти того, кто бежал от меня».

o.en: “And did the man whom you pursued travel in the same fashion?”
o.ru: «А тот, кого вы преследовали, ехал так же, как и вы?»

o.en: “Yes.”
“Then I fancy we have seen him, for the day before we picked you up we saw some dogs drawing a sledge, with a man in it, across the ice.”
o.ru: «Тогда, пожалуй, мы его видели: за день до того, как подобрать вас, мы заметили собак, тянувших по льду сани, в которых сидел человек».

o.en: This aroused the stranger’s attention, and he asked a multitude of questions concerning the route which the dæmon, as he called him, had pursued.
o.ru: Это возбудило внимание незнакомца, и он засыпал нас вопросами о том, каким путём направился демон — так он его назвал.

o.en: Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, “I have, doubtless, excited your curiosity, as well as that of these good people; but you are too considerate to make inquiries.”
o.ru: Вскоре, оставшись со мной наедине, он сказал: «Я, несомненно, возбудил ваше любопытство, как и любопытство этих добрых людей; но вы слишком деликатны, чтобы расспрашивать».

o.en: “Certainly; it would indeed be very impertinent and inhuman in me to trouble you with any inquisitiveness of mine.”
o.ru: «Разумеется; с моей стороны было бы в высшей степени дерзко и бесчеловечно докучать вам своими расспросами».

o.en: “And yet you rescued me from a strange and perilous situation; you have benevolently restored me to life.”
o.ru: «И всё же вы спасли меня из странного и опасного положения; вы великодушно вернули меня к жизни».

o.en: Soon after this he inquired if I thought that the breaking up of the ice had destroyed the other sledge.
o.ru: Вскоре после этого он спросил, не думаю ли я, что вскрытие льда погубило другие сани.

o.en: I replied that I could not answer with any degree of certainty, for the ice had not broken until near midnight, and the traveller might have arrived at a place of safety before that time; but of this I could not judge.
o.ru: Я ответил, что не могу сказать ничего определённого, ибо лёд вскрылся лишь около полуночи и путник мог к тому времени добраться до безопасного места; но судить об этом я не мог.

o.en: From this time a new spirit of life animated the decaying frame of the stranger.
o.ru: С этой минуты новый дух жизни оживил угасающее тело незнакомца.

o.en: He manifested the greatest eagerness to be upon deck to watch for the sledge which had before appeared; but I have persuaded him to remain in the cabin, for he is far too weak to sustain the rawness of the atmosphere.
o.ru: Он с величайшим нетерпением рвался на палубу, чтобы высматривать появившиеся прежде сани; но я уговорил его остаться в каюте, ибо он слишком слаб, чтобы выносить суровость здешнего воздуха.

o.en: I have promised that someone should watch for him and give him instant notice if any new object should appear in sight.
o.ru: Я пообещал, что кто-нибудь будет нести дозор вместо него и немедленно известит его, если в поле зрения появится что-то новое.

o.en: Such is my journal of what relates to this strange occurrence up to the present day.
o.ru: Таков мой дневник всего, что касается этого странного происшествия, по сегодняшний день.

o.en: The stranger has gradually improved in health but is very silent and appears uneasy when anyone except myself enters his cabin.
o.ru: Здоровье незнакомца понемногу улучшается, но он очень молчалив и выглядит встревоженным, когда в его каюту входит кто-нибудь, кроме меня.

o.en: Yet his manners are so conciliating and gentle that the sailors are all interested in him, although they have had very little communication with him.
o.ru: И всё же манеры его так приветливы и мягки, что все матросы им заинтересованы, хотя почти не общались с ним.

o.en: For my own part, I begin to love him as a brother, and his constant and deep grief fills me with sympathy and compassion.
o.ru: Что до меня, то я начинаю любить его как брата, и его неизменная глубокая скорбь наполняет меня сочувствием и состраданием.

o.en: He must have been a noble creature in his better days, being even now in wreck so attractive and amiable.
o.ru: В лучшие свои дни он, должно быть, был благородным существом, раз даже теперь, сломленный, он так привлекателен и мил.

o.en: I said in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I should find no friend on the wide ocean; yet I have found a man who, before his spirit had been broken by misery, I should have been happy to have possessed as the brother of my heart.
o.ru: В одном из писем я писал тебе, дорогая Маргарет, что не найду друга на просторах океана; и всё же я нашёл человека, которого, пока несчастья не сломили его дух, я был бы счастлив назвать братом своего сердца.

o.en: I shall continue my journal concerning the stranger at intervals, should I have any fresh incidents to record.
o.ru: Я буду время от времени продолжать свой дневник о незнакомце, если у меня появятся новые события, достойные записи.

o.en: August 13th, 17—.
My affection for my guest increases every day.
o.ru: Моя привязанность к гостю растёт с каждым днём.

o.en: He excites at once my admiration and my pity to an astonishing degree.
o.ru: Он вызывает во мне и восхищение, и жалость в поразительной степени.

o.en: How can I see so noble a creature destroyed by misery without feeling the most poignant grief?
o.ru: Как могу я видеть столь благородное существо, погубленное несчастьем, и не испытывать самой острой скорби?

o.en: He is so gentle, yet so wise; his mind is so cultivated, and when he speaks, although his words are culled with the choicest art, yet they flow with rapidity and unparalleled eloquence.
o.ru: Он так кроток и вместе с тем так мудр; ум его так развит, и когда он говорит, то, хотя слова его подобраны с изысканнейшим искусством, они льются стремительно и с несравненным красноречием.

o.en: He is now much recovered from his illness and is continually on the deck, apparently watching for the sledge that preceded his own.
o.ru: Теперь он в основном оправился от болезни и постоянно находится на палубе, по-видимому высматривая сани, опередившие его собственные.

o.en: Yet, although unhappy, he is not so utterly occupied by his own misery but that he interests himself deeply in the projects of others.
o.ru: Однако, хоть он и несчастен, собственное горе не поглощает его настолько, чтобы он не мог живо интересоваться замыслами других.

o.en: He has frequently conversed with me on mine, which I have communicated to him without disguise.
o.ru: Он часто беседовал со мной о моих замыслах, которые я открыл ему без утайки.

o.en: He entered attentively into all my arguments in favour of my eventual success and into every minute detail of the measures I had taken to secure it.
o.ru: Он внимательно вникал во все мои доводы в пользу моего конечного успеха и в каждую мельчайшую подробность мер, принятых мною для его достижения.

o.en: I was easily led by the sympathy which he evinced to use the language of my heart, to give utterance to the burning ardour of my soul and to say, with all the fervour that warmed me, how gladly I would sacrifice my fortune, my existence, my every hope, to the furtherance of my enterprise.
o.ru: Сочувствие, которое он выказывал, легко побудило меня заговорить языком сердца, излить жгучий пыл своей души и сказать со всем охватившим меня жаром, как охотно я пожертвовал бы своим состоянием, своей жизнью, всеми своими надеждами ради успеха моего предприятия.

o.en: One man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the acquirement of the knowledge which I sought, for the dominion I should acquire and transmit over the elemental foes of our race.
o.ru: Жизнь или смерть одного человека — лишь малая цена за обретение знания, к которому я стремился, за власть, которую я завоюю над стихийными врагами нашего рода и передам потомкам.

o.en: As I spoke, a dark gloom spread over my listener’s countenance.
o.ru: Пока я говорил, лицо моего слушателя омрачилось.

o.en: At first I perceived that he tried to suppress his emotion; he placed his hands before his eyes, and my voice quivered and failed me as I beheld tears trickle fast from between his fingers; a groan burst from his heaving breast.
o.ru: Сперва я заметил, что он пытается подавить волнение; он закрыл глаза руками, и мой голос задрожал и прервался, когда я увидел, как между его пальцами быстро струятся слёзы; из его вздымающейся груди вырвался стон.

o.en: I paused; at length he spoke, in broken accents: “Unhappy man!
o.ru: Я умолк; наконец он заговорил прерывающимся голосом: «Несчастный!

o.en: Do you share my madness?
Have you drunk also of the intoxicating draught?
o.ru: Неужели и вы испили опьяняющего напитка?

o.en: Hear me; let me reveal my tale, and you will dash the cup from your lips!”
o.ru: Выслушайте меня; позвольте мне рассказать мою историю, и вы отшвырнёте чашу от своих губ!»

o.en: Such words, you may imagine, strongly excited my curiosity; but the paroxysm of grief that had seized the stranger overcame his weakened powers, and many hours of repose and tranquil conversation were necessary to restore his composure.
o.ru: Такие слова, как ты можешь представить, сильно разожгли моё любопытство; но приступ горя, охвативший незнакомца, оказался сильнее его ослабевших сил, и понадобилось много часов покоя и тихой беседы, чтобы вернуть ему самообладание.

o.en: Having conquered the violence of his feelings, he appeared to despise himself for being the slave of passion; and quelling the dark tyranny of despair, he led me again to converse concerning myself personally.
o.ru: Совладав с бурей своих чувств, он, казалось, презирал себя за то, что стал рабом страсти; и, подавив мрачную власть отчаяния, он снова завёл разговор обо мне самом.

o.en: He asked me the history of my earlier years.
o.ru: Он попросил рассказать о моих ранних годах.

o.en: The tale was quickly told, but it awakened various trains of reflection.
