a2.ru: Вчера незнакомец сказал мне: «Капитан Уолтон, в моей жизни были ужасные беды.

a2.en: I wanted to keep them secret, but now I will tell you about them.
a2.ru: Я хотел сохранить их в тайне, но теперь расскажу вам о них.

a2.en: You want to learn and discover new things, like me before.
a2.ru: Вы хотите учиться и открывать новое, как когда-то я.

a2.en: I hope that your dreams will not hurt you, as my dreams hurt me.
a2.ru: Я надеюсь, что ваши мечты не причинят вам вреда, как мои причинили вред мне.

a2.en: You are going the same way, and you are in the same danger.
a2.ru: Вы идёте тем же путём, и вам грозит та же опасность.

a2.en: Maybe my story will help you on your journey.
a2.ru: Может быть, моя история поможет вам в вашем путешествии.

a2.en: If you fail, maybe it will make you feel better.
a2.ru: Если у вас ничего не выйдет, может быть, она вас утешит.

a2.en: My story is very strange.
a2.ru: Моя история очень странная.

a2.en: At home you would not believe me.
a2.ru: Дома вы бы мне не поверили.

a2.en: Maybe you would even laugh at me.
a2.ru: Может быть, вы бы даже посмеялись надо мной.

a2.en: But here, in this wild place, you will understand that it is true.”
a2.ru: Но здесь, в этом диком месте, вы поймёте, что она правдива».

a2.en: I was happy that he wanted to tell me his story.
a2.ru: Я был рад, что он хочет рассказать мне свою историю.

a2.en: But I did not want him to be sad again.
a2.ru: Но я не хотел, чтобы ему снова стало грустно.

a2.en: I also wanted to help him, and I told him this.
a2.ru: Ещё я хотел помочь ему и сказал ему об этом.

a2.en: “Thank you,” he answered, “but you cannot help me.
a2.ru: «Спасибо, — ответил он, — но вы не можете мне помочь.

a2.en: I am waiting for only one thing, and then I will die in peace.
a2.ru: Я жду только одного, а потом умру спокойно.

a2.en: Nobody can change my life, my friend.
a2.ru: Никто не может изменить мою жизнь, мой друг.

a2.en: Listen to my story, and you will understand.”
a2.ru: Послушайте мою историю, и вы поймёте».

a2.en: He said that he will start his story the next day.
a2.ru: Он сказал, что начнёт свой рассказ на следующий день.

a2.en: I thanked him.
a2.ru: Я поблагодарил его.

a2.en: Every night I am going to write down his words.
a2.ru: Каждый вечер я буду записывать его слова.

a2.en: If I am busy, I will write short notes.
a2.ru: Если я буду занят, я сделаю короткие заметки.

a2.en: You will enjoy this story, Margaret.
a2.ru: Тебе понравится эта история, Маргарет.

a2.en: But for me it will be even more interesting, because I hear it from him.
a2.ru: Но мне будет ещё интереснее, потому что я слышу её от него самого.

a2.en: Even now I can hear his deep voice and see his sad, bright eyes.
a2.ru: Даже сейчас я слышу его низкий голос и вижу его печальные, яркие глаза.

a2.en: I can see his thin hand in the air as he speaks.
a2.ru: Я вижу его худую руку в воздухе, когда он говорит.

a2.en: His story will be strange and terrible, like a storm that breaks a ship!
a2.ru: Его история будет странной и страшной, как буря, которая разбивает корабль!

o.tip: эпистолярный стиль: адрес письма = Миссис Сэвилл, Англия
год скрыт тире — литературная условность XVIII–XIX вв.
so + прилагательное + a + сущ.: so strange an accident = столь странный случай (обычно: such a strange accident)
C2/книжн. · forbear doing = удержаться от (simpler: cannot help recording it)
формально: come into one's possession = попасть к кому-то в руки
причастный оборот; her = корабль (ship — женский род); sea-room = простор для манёвра
архаизм · compass round = окружать (simpler: surrounded by)
морск. · lie to = лечь в дрейф; accordingly = поэтому, соответственно
книжн. · behold (beheld) = узреть, увидеть (simpler: saw)
причастный оборот, вставленный перед дополнением: we beheld, stretched out…, vast plains = увидели простирающиеся…

o.p: my own mind began to grow watchful with anxious thoughts
o.tip: сложная метафора: ум стал настороженным от тревожных мыслей
C2 · solicitude = тревога, забота; divert = отвлечь (simpler: took our minds off)
perceive + объект + инфинитив без to = увидели, как повозка проехала
C1 · stature = рост; of gigantic stature = исполинского роста

o.p: the distant inequalities of the ice
o.tip: inequalities = неровности (здесь: торосы) (simpler: rough places)
C2 · unqualified = безоговорочный, полный; excite = вызывать
C1 · apparition = видение, призрак; denote = означать, указывать

o.p: not, in reality, so distant as we had supposed
o.tip: not so… as + Past Perfect: не так далеко, как мы полагали
причастный оборот с вставкой however: Shut in by ice = запертые льдом
морск. · ground sea = донная зыбь, волнение под льдом
причастный оборот: fearing to… = опасаясь…; encounter = натолкнуться на
loose masses = плавучие глыбы льда
устар. · profit of (совр. profit from / take advantage of) = воспользоваться
устар. предлог: upon deck (совр. on deck)

o.p: It was, in fact, a sledge, like that we had seen before
o.tip: like that (which) we had seen = как тот, что мы видели; Past Perfect

o.p: whom the sailors were persuading to enter the vessel
o.tip: whom — объектное относительное местоимение; persuade sb to do = уговаривать
savage = дикий, дикарь; inhabitant = житель
морск. · master = шкипер, штурман торгового судна (не хозяин)
C1 · perish = погибнуть (simpler: die)
on + -ing = как только, при: On perceiving me = увидев меня

o.p: will you have the kindness to inform me
o.tip: подчеркнуто вежливая формула: не будете ли вы так любезны сообщить
архаизм · whither = куда; be bound (for) = направляться (simpler: where you are going)
книжн. · conceive = представить себе (simpler: imagine)
on the brink of = на грани, на краю

o.p: I should have supposed that my vessel would have been a resource
o.tip: модальное прошедшее: should have supposed = я бы предположил; would have been = был бы

o.p: the most precious wealth the earth can afford
o.tip: afford (здесь) = дать, предоставить
C2 · capitulate = сдаваться на условиях, договариваться (здесь ирония: выторговывал своё спасение)

sub: Victor describes his parents’ marriage, his happy childhood and how Elizabeth Lavenza came into the family

o: I am by birth a Genevese, and my family is one of the most distinguished of that republic. My ancestors had been for many years counsellors and syndics, and my father had filled several public situations with honour and reputation. He was respected by all who knew him for his integrity and indefatigable attention to public business. He passed his younger days perpetually occupied by the affairs of his country; a variety of circumstances had prevented his marrying early, nor was it until the decline of life that he became a husband and the father of a family.

As the circumstances of his marriage illustrate his character, I cannot refrain from relating them. One of his most intimate friends was a merchant who, from a flourishing state, fell, through numerous mischances, into poverty. This man, whose name was Beaufort, was of a proud and unbending disposition and could not bear to live in poverty and oblivion in the same country where he had formerly been distinguished for his rank and magnificence. Having paid his debts, therefore, in the most honourable manner, he retreated with his daughter to the town of Lucerne, where he lived unknown and in wretchedness.

My father loved Beaufort with the truest friendship and was deeply grieved by his retreat in these unfortunate circumstances. He bitterly deplored the false pride which led his friend to a conduct so little worthy of the affection that united them. He lost no time in endeavouring to seek him out, with the hope of persuading him to begin the world again through his credit and assistance.

Beaufort had taken effectual measures to conceal himself, and it was ten months before my father discovered his abode. Overjoyed at this discovery, he hastened to the house, which was situated in a mean street near the Reuss. But when he entered, misery and despair alone welcomed him. Beaufort had saved but a very small sum of money from the wreck of his fortunes, but it was sufficient to provide him with sustenance for some months, and in the meantime he hoped to procure some respectable employment in a merchant’s house. The interval was, consequently, spent in inaction; his grief only became more deep and rankling when he had leisure for reflection, and at length it took so fast hold of his mind that at the end of three months he lay on a bed of sickness, incapable of any exertion.

His daughter attended him with the greatest tenderness, but she saw with despair that their little fund was rapidly decreasing and that there was no other prospect of support. But Caroline Beaufort possessed a mind of an uncommon mould, and her courage rose to support her in her adversity. She procured plain work; she plaited straw and by various means contrived to earn a pittance scarcely sufficient to support life.

Several months passed in this manner. Her father grew worse; her time was more entirely occupied in attending him; her means of subsistence decreased; and in the tenth month her father died in her arms, leaving her an orphan and a beggar. This last blow overcame her, and she knelt by Beaufort’s coffin weeping bitterly, when my father entered the chamber. He came like a protecting spirit to the poor girl, who committed herself to his care; and after the interment of his friend he conducted her to Geneva and placed her under the protection of a relation. Two years after this event Caroline became his wife.

There was a considerable difference between the ages of my parents, but this circumstance seemed to unite them only closer in bonds of devoted affection. There was a sense of justice in my father’s upright mind which rendered it necessary that he should approve highly to love strongly. Perhaps during former years he had suffered from the late-discovered unworthiness of one beloved and so was disposed to set a greater value on tried worth. There was a show of gratitude and worship in his attachment to my mother, differing wholly from the doting fondness of age, for it was inspired by reverence for her virtues and a desire to be the means of, in some degree, recompensing her for the sorrows she had endured, but which gave inexpressible grace to his behaviour to her.

Everything was made to yield to her wishes and her convenience. He strove to shelter her, as a fair exotic is sheltered by the gardener, from every rougher wind and to surround her with all that could tend to excite pleasurable emotion in her soft and benevolent mind. Her health, and even the tranquillity of her hitherto constant spirit, had been shaken by what she had gone through. During the two years that had elapsed previous to their marriage my father had gradually relinquished all his public functions; and immediately after their union they sought the pleasant climate of Italy, and the change of scene and interest attendant on a tour through that land of wonders, as a restorative for her weakened frame.

From Italy they visited Germany and France. I, their eldest child, was born at Naples, and as an infant accompanied them in their rambles. I remained for several years their only child. Much as they were attached to each other, they seemed to draw inexhaustible stores of affection from a very mine of love to bestow them upon me. My mother’s tender caresses and my father’s smile of benevolent pleasure while regarding me are my first recollections.

I was their plaything and their idol, and something better—their child, the innocent and helpless creature bestowed on them by Heaven, whom to bring up to good, and whose future lot it was in their hands to direct to happiness or misery, according as they fulfilled their duties towards me. With this deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life, added to the active spirit of tenderness that animated both, it may be imagined that while during every hour of my infant life I received a lesson of patience, of charity, and of self-control, I was so guided by a silken cord that all seemed but one train of enjoyment to me.

For a long time I was their only care. My mother had much desired to have a daughter, but I continued their single offspring. When I was about five years old, while making an excursion beyond the frontiers of Italy, they passed a week on the shores of the Lake of Como. Their benevolent disposition often made them enter the cottages of the poor. This, to my mother, was more than a duty; it was a necessity, a passion—remembering what she had suffered, and how she had been relieved—for her to act in her turn the guardian angel to the afflicted.

During one of their walks a poor cot in the foldings of a vale attracted their notice as being singularly disconsolate, while the number of half-clothed children gathered about it spoke of penury in its worst shape. One day, when my father had gone by himself to Milan, my mother, accompanied by me, visited this abode. She found a peasant and his wife, hard working, bent down by care and labour, distributing a scanty meal to five hungry babes. Among these there was one which attracted my mother far above all the rest.

She appeared of a different stock. The four others were dark-eyed, hardy little vagrants; this child was thin and very fair. Her hair was the brightest living gold, and despite the poverty of her clothing, seemed to set a crown of distinction on her head. Her brow was clear and ample, her blue eyes cloudless, and her lips and the moulding of her face so expressive of sensibility and sweetness that none could behold her without looking on her as of a distinct species, a being heaven-sent, and bearing a celestial stamp in all her features.

The peasant woman, perceiving that my mother fixed eyes of wonder and admiration on this lovely girl, eagerly communicated her history. She was not her child, but the daughter of a Milanese nobleman. Her mother was a German and had died on giving her birth. The infant had been placed with these good people to nurse: they were better off then. They had not been long married, and their eldest child was but just born. The father of their charge was one of those Italians nursed in the memory of the antique glory of Italy—one among the schiavi ognor frementi, who exerted himself to obtain the liberty of his country. He became the victim of its weakness. Whether he had died or still lingered in the dungeons of Austria was not known. His property was confiscated; his child became an orphan and a beggar. She continued with her foster parents and bloomed in their rude abode, fairer than a garden rose among dark-leaved brambles.

When my father returned from Milan, he found playing with me in the hall of our villa a child fairer than pictured cherub—a creature who seemed to shed radiance from her looks and whose form and motions were lighter than the chamois of the hills. The apparition was soon explained. With his permission my mother prevailed on her rustic guardians to yield their charge to her. They were fond of the sweet orphan. Her presence had seemed a blessing to them, but it would be unfair to her to keep her in poverty and want when Providence afforded her such powerful protection. They consulted their village priest, and the result was that Elizabeth Lavenza became the inmate of my parents’ house—my more than sister—the beautiful and adored companion of all my occupations and my pleasures.

Everyone loved Elizabeth. The passionate and almost reverential attachment with which all regarded her became, while I shared it, my pride and my delight. On the evening previous to her being brought to my home, my mother had said playfully, “I have a pretty present for my Victor—tomorrow he shall have it.” And when, on the morrow, she presented Elizabeth to me as her promised gift, I, with childish seriousness, interpreted her words literally and looked upon Elizabeth as mine—mine to protect, love, and cherish. All praises bestowed on her I received as made to a possession of my own. We called each other familiarly by the name of cousin. No word, no expression could body forth the kind of relation in which she stood to me—my more than sister, since till death she was to be mine only.
b2: I was born in Geneva, and my family is one of the most distinguished in that republic. For many years my ancestors had been councillors and magistrates, and my father had held several public posts with honour and a good reputation. Everyone who knew him respected him for his honesty and his tireless devotion to public affairs. He spent his youth constantly busy with the affairs of his country; for various reasons he had not married early, and it was only late in life that he became a husband and the father of a family.

The story of his marriage says a great deal about his character, so I cannot resist telling it. One of his closest friends was a merchant who, after a series of misfortunes, fell from prosperity into poverty. This man, whose name was Beaufort, was proud and stubborn, and he could not bear to live poor and forgotten in the same country where he had once been admired for his rank and his splendid way of life. So, having paid his debts in the most honourable way, he withdrew with his daughter to the town of Lucerne, where he lived unknown and in misery.

My father was a true and loyal friend to Beaufort and was deeply upset that he had gone away in such sad circumstances. He bitterly regretted the false pride that had made his friend behave in a way so unworthy of the affection between them. He immediately set out to find him, hoping to persuade him to start his life again with the help of his money and influence.

Beaufort had hidden himself very effectively, and it took my father ten months to discover where he lived. Delighted at the discovery, he hurried to the house, which stood in a poor street near the river Reuss. But when he went in, he was met only by misery and despair. Beaufort had rescued only a very small sum of money from the ruin of his fortune, but it was enough to feed him for a few months, and in the meantime he hoped to find a respectable job with a trading company. As a result, those months were spent doing nothing; with time to think, his grief only grew deeper and more bitter, and in the end it took such a firm hold of his mind that after three months he was lying ill in bed, unable to make any effort at all.

His daughter nursed him with great tenderness, but she saw in despair that their small savings were quickly running out and that there was no other way of supporting themselves. But Caroline Beaufort had an unusually strong character, and her courage grew to meet the hardship. She found simple sewing work; she wove straw and, in one way or another, managed to earn a tiny income that was barely enough to live on.

Several months went by like this. Her father grew worse; looking after him took up more and more of her time; their money dwindled; and in the tenth month her father died in her arms, leaving her an orphan with nothing. This final blow broke her, and she was kneeling by Beaufort’s coffin, crying bitterly, when my father walked into the room. He came to the poor girl like a guardian angel, and she placed herself in his care; after his friend’s funeral he took her to Geneva and left her in the care of a relative. Two years later Caroline became his wife.

There was a large age difference between my parents, but this only seemed to bind them more closely in deep and devoted love. My father was an upright man with a strong sense of justice, so he needed to respect someone deeply before he could love them strongly. Perhaps in earlier years he had been hurt when someone he loved turned out, too late, to be unworthy, and so he valued goodness that had been tested. His love for my mother was full of gratitude and admiration, quite unlike the foolish fondness of an old man, because it came from respect for her virtues and a wish to make up, at least in part, for the sorrows she had suffered, and this gave his behaviour towards her an indescribable grace.

Everything was arranged to suit her wishes and her comfort. He tried to protect her from every harsh wind, as a gardener protects a delicate exotic plant, and to surround her with everything that might bring pleasure to her gentle and kind heart. Her health, and even the calm of her once steady spirit, had been shaken by what she had been through. In the two years before their marriage my father had gradually given up all his public duties; and straight after the wedding they went to the pleasant climate of Italy, hoping that the change of scene and the interest of a journey through that land of wonders would restore her weakened body.

From Italy they went on to Germany and France. I, their eldest child, was born in Naples, and as a baby I went with them on their travels. For several years I remained their only child. Although they loved each other dearly, they seemed to draw endless supplies of affection from a deep well of love and pour them all out on me. My earliest memories are of my mother’s gentle caresses and my father’s kind, delighted smile as he watched me.

I was their toy and their idol, and something better—their child, the innocent, helpless creature given to them by Heaven, whom they had to bring up to be good, and whose future it was in their power to lead towards happiness or misery, depending on how well they did their duty by me. They were deeply aware of what they owed to the being they had brought into the world, and they were both full of active tenderness, so you can imagine that, although every hour of my childhood taught me patience, kindness and self-control, I was guided by such a soft silken thread that it all felt like one long series of pleasures.

For a long time I was all they cared about. My mother had very much wanted a daughter, but I remained their only child. When I was about five, during a trip across the Italian border, they spent a week on the shores of Lake Como. Because they were so kind-hearted, they often visited the cottages of the poor. For my mother this was more than a duty; it was a need, a passion—remembering what she had suffered and how she had been rescued—to be, in her turn, a guardian angel to those in trouble.

On one of their walks they noticed a poor cottage in a fold of the valley that looked especially miserable, while the crowd of half-dressed children around it spoke of poverty at its very worst. One day, when my father had gone to Milan alone, my mother took me with her and visited the house. She found a hard-working peasant and his wife, bent with worry and toil, sharing out a meagre meal among five hungry little children. Among them was one who attracted my mother far more than all the others.

She seemed to come from a different family altogether. The other four were dark-eyed, sturdy little tramps; this child was slim and very fair. Her hair was the brightest gold, and in spite of her poor clothes, it seemed to crown her with a special dignity. Her forehead was clear and broad, her blue eyes cloudless, and her lips and the shape of her face showed such sensitivity and sweetness that nobody could look at her without seeing her as a creature of a different kind, sent from heaven, with a heavenly mark on every feature.

The peasant woman noticed that my mother was gazing at this lovely girl with wonder and admiration, and she eagerly told her the child’s story. She was not her own child, but the daughter of a nobleman from Milan. Her mother had been German and had died giving birth to her. The baby had been given to these good people to look after: they had been better off in those days. They had only recently married, and their first child had just been born. The girl’s father was one of those Italians brought up on memories of Italy’s ancient glory—one of the “ever-restless slaves” who fought for the freedom of their country. He fell victim to its weakness. No one knew whether he had died or was still wasting away in an Austrian prison. His property was seized, and his child became a penniless orphan. She stayed with her foster parents and blossomed in their rough home, lovelier than a garden rose among dark brambles.

When my father came back from Milan, he found a child playing with me in the hall of our villa, more beautiful than a painted angel—a creature whose face seemed to shine and whose figure and movements were lighter than a mountain goat’s. The mystery was soon explained. With his permission, my mother persuaded the girl’s country guardians to give her up to her. They loved the sweet orphan. Having her with them had seemed like a blessing, but it would be unfair to keep her in poverty and need when fate was offering her such powerful protection. They asked the advice of their village priest, and the result was that Elizabeth Lavenza came to live in my parents’ house—more than a sister to me—the beautiful and much-loved companion of all my activities and games.

Everyone loved Elizabeth. The passionate, almost worshipping affection that everyone felt for her became my pride and joy, since I shared it. On the evening before she was brought to our home, my mother had said jokingly, “I have a pretty present for my Victor—he shall have it tomorrow.” And when, the next day, she gave me Elizabeth as the promised present, I took her words literally with childish seriousness and thought of Elizabeth as mine—mine to protect, love and treasure. I accepted all the praise she received as if it were praise for something that belonged to me. We called each other ‘cousin’ in a friendly way. No word or phrase could express what she was to me—more than a sister, because until death she was to be mine alone.
b1: I was born in Geneva, and my family is one of the most important families there. For many years my ancestors worked for the government of the city. My father also had several important jobs, and he did them well. People respected him because he was honest and worked very hard for his country. When he was young, he was always busy, so he did not marry early. He only became a husband and a father when he was quite old.

The story of his marriage shows what kind of man he was, so I want to tell it. One of his best friends was a merchant called Beaufort. Beaufort was once rich, but after many problems he became poor. He was a very proud man. He could not live as a poor man in the same country where everyone had known him as rich and important. So he paid all his debts honestly and went away with his daughter to the town of Lucerne. There he lived in a very poor way, and nobody knew him.

My father loved Beaufort as a true friend and was very sad that he had left like this. He was angry with Beaufort’s false pride, because a good friend should not behave like that. He started looking for him at once. He wanted to give Beaufort money and help him to start a new life.

Beaufort had hidden very well, and my father needed ten months to find his home. My father was very happy and hurried to the house. It was in a poor street near the river Reuss. But when he went in, he found only sadness and poverty. Beaufort had saved only a little money, but it was enough for a few months. He hoped to find a good job with a merchant during that time. But he did nothing, and he just thought about his problems. His sadness grew and grew. After three months he became ill and could not get out of bed.

His daughter looked after him lovingly. But she saw that their money was disappearing fast and that nobody could help them. Caroline Beaufort, however, was an unusual and strong young woman, and she found the courage to fight. She did simple sewing and made things from straw. In this way she earned a little money, but it was hardly enough to live on.

Several months passed like this. Her father became worse, and she spent all her time looking after him. They had less and less money. In the tenth month her father died in her arms, and she was left alone with nothing. She was kneeling by Beaufort’s coffin and crying when my father came into the room. He was like a kind angel to the poor girl, and she trusted him. After the funeral he took her to Geneva and asked a relative to look after her. Two years later Caroline became his wife.

My father was much older than my mother, but this only made their love stronger. He was a very fair and honest man, and he could only love someone if he respected them deeply. Perhaps in the past someone he loved had disappointed him, so now he valued real goodness very much. He loved my mother with gratitude and admiration, not with the silly love of an old man. He respected her goodness, and he wanted to make her happy after all her sadness. This made him very gentle with her.

Everything in the house was done the way she wanted. He protected her like a gardener protects a delicate flower from the wind. He tried to give her everything that could make her kind heart happy. Her difficult life had damaged her health and her calm, strong spirit. Before the wedding my father had slowly left all his public jobs. Right after the wedding they went to Italy, a wonderful country with a pleasant climate. They hoped that the journey and the new places would make her strong again.

From Italy they travelled to Germany and France. I was their first child, and I was born in Naples. When I was a baby, I travelled with them. For several years I was their only child. They loved each other very much, but they still had endless love to give me. My first memories are my mother’s gentle touch and my father’s kind, happy smile when he looked at me.

I was their toy and their idol, but, more importantly, I was their child. I was a small, helpless gift from Heaven, and they had to bring me up to be good. My future happiness depended on them. They understood this very well, and they were both very loving. So every hour of my childhood taught me patience, kindness and self-control. But they guided me so gently that my life felt like one long pleasure.

For a long time I was all they cared about. My mother really wanted a daughter, but I stayed their only child. When I was about five, they went on a trip across the Italian border and spent a week by Lake Como. They were kind people, and they often visited poor families in their homes. For my mother this was more than a duty. She remembered her own suffering and how someone had helped her, so she felt that she must help unhappy people too.

On one of their walks they saw a very sad, poor little house in a valley. There were lots of children around it in old, torn clothes, and they looked terribly poor. One day, when my father went to Milan alone, my mother and I visited this house. She found a peasant and his wife there. They worked hard and looked tired and worried. They were giving a small meal to five hungry children. My mother noticed one of the children much more than the others.

This little girl looked different. The other four children had dark eyes and looked strong and wild. This child was thin and very fair. Her hair was bright gold, and even in her poor clothes she looked like a little princess. She had a clear, wide forehead and blue eyes. Her face was so sweet and gentle that everyone who saw her thought she was special, like an angel sent from heaven.

The peasant woman saw that my mother was looking at the lovely girl with surprise and admiration, and she quickly told her the girl’s story. The girl was not her daughter. Her father was a rich nobleman from Milan, and her mother was German. Her mother died when she was born. The baby was given to this family to look after, and at that time they had more money. They were newly married, and their first child was just born. The girl’s father loved Italy and its great past, and he fought for the freedom of his country. But Italy was weak, and he lost. Nobody knew if he was dead or still in an Austrian prison. His money and house were taken away, and his daughter was left poor and without parents. She stayed with the peasant family and grew up in their poor home, as beautiful as a rose among wild plants.

When my father came back from Milan, he found a child playing with me in our house. She was more beautiful than an angel in a picture, and she moved as lightly as a mountain goat. My mother soon explained everything. With my father’s permission, she asked the peasants to let her take the girl. They loved the sweet orphan, and she was like a blessing to them. But they understood that it was not fair to keep her in poverty when she could have a much better life. They asked the village priest for advice. In the end, Elizabeth Lavenza came to live in my parents’ house. She became more than a sister to me, and she shared all my games and lessons.

Everyone loved Elizabeth. I loved her too, and I was proud that everyone loved her so much. On the evening before she came to our house, my mother said with a smile, “I have a pretty present for my Victor—he will get it tomorrow.” The next day she gave me Elizabeth as my present. I was a serious little boy, and I believed her words. I thought Elizabeth was mine—mine to protect and love. When people praised her, I felt they were praising something of mine. We called each other ‘cousin’. But no word can explain what she was to me. She was more than a sister, because she was going to be mine until death.
