b1.ru: Никогда она не была так прекрасна, как тогда, когда снова начала улыбаться и дарила нам свои улыбки.

b1.en: She tried so hard to help us forget our sadness that she even forgot her own.
b1.ru: Она так старалась помочь нам забыть о печали, что забывала даже о своей.

b1.en: At last the day came for me to leave.
b1.ru: Наконец настал день моего отъезда.

b1.en: Clerval spent the last evening with us.
b1.ru: Клерваль провёл с нами последний вечер.

b1.en: He had asked his father to let him come with me and study with me, but his father said no.
b1.ru: Он просил отца отпустить его со мной, чтобы учиться вместе, но отец отказал.

b1.en: His father was a businessman with narrow ideas.
b1.ru: Его отец был торговцем с узкими взглядами.

b1.en: He thought that his son's dreams would only make him lazy and poor.
b1.ru: Он думал, что мечты сына сделают его только ленивым и бедным.

b1.en: Henry was very unhappy that he could not get a good education.
b1.ru: Анри очень переживал, что не может получить хорошее образование.

b1.en: He did not say much, but I could see in his bright eyes that he was determined not to spend his life in boring business work.
b1.ru: Он говорил мало, но в его ярких глазах я видел твёрдое решение не тратить жизнь на скучную торговлю.

b1.en: We sat up late.
b1.ru: Мы засиделись допоздна.

b1.en: We did not want to leave each other or say "Goodbye!"
b1.ru: Нам не хотелось расставаться или говорить «Прощай!»

b1.en: But at last we said it, and we went to our rooms, and each of us pretended to go to sleep.
b1.ru: Но наконец мы это сказали и разошлись по комнатам, и каждый из нас делал вид, что ложится спать.

b1.en: In the morning, when I went down to the carriage that was going to take me away, they were all there.
b1.ru: Утром, когда я спустился к карете, которая должна была меня увезти, все они были там.

b1.en: My father blessed me again, Clerval shook my hand once more, and my Elizabeth asked me again to write often and looked after me for the last time.
b1.ru: Отец снова благословил меня, Клерваль ещё раз пожал мне руку, а моя Элизабет снова попросила писать почаще и в последний раз позаботилась обо мне.

b1.en: I got into the coach and began to have very sad thoughts.
b1.ru: Я сел в карету, и мне в голову пришли очень грустные мысли.

b1.en: I had always had kind friends around me who tried to make each other happy, but now I was alone.
b1.ru: Меня всегда окружали добрые друзья, которые старались порадовать друг друга, а теперь я был один.

b1.en: At the university I would have to find my own friends and take care of myself.
b1.ru: В университете мне придётся самому находить друзей и заботиться о себе.

b1.en: I had always lived a quiet life at home, so I did not like meeting new people.
b1.ru: Я всегда жил тихой домашней жизнью, поэтому не любил знакомиться с новыми людьми.

b1.en: I loved my brothers, Elizabeth and Clerval, because they were "old familiar faces", but I felt that I could not live among strangers.
b1.ru: Я любил своих братьев, Элизабет и Клерваля, ведь это были «старые знакомые лица», но мне казалось, что я не смогу жить среди чужих.

b1.en: Those were my thoughts at the start of my journey.
b1.ru: Такими были мои мысли в начале пути.

b1.en: But as I travelled on, I began to feel happier and more hopeful.
b1.ru: Но чем дальше я ехал, тем счастливее и увереннее становился.

b1.en: I really wanted to learn.
b1.ru: Мне очень хотелось учиться.

b1.en: At home I had often felt that it was hard to spend my young years in one place, and I had wanted to go out into the world and live among other people.
b1.ru: Дома мне часто казалось, что тяжело провести молодые годы на одном месте, и я хотел выйти в мир и жить среди других людей.

b1.en: Now my wish had come true, and it would be silly to be sorry about it.
b1.ru: Теперь моё желание сбылось, и жалеть об этом было бы глупо.

b1.en: The journey to Ingolstadt was long and tiring, so I had a lot of time to think.
b1.ru: Дорога в Ингольштадт была долгой и утомительной, так что у меня было много времени для размышлений.

b1.en: At last I saw the tall white church tower of the town.
b1.ru: Наконец я увидел высокую белую церковную башню города.

b1.en: I got out and was taken to my room, where I spent the evening alone.
b1.ru: Я вышел, и меня отвели в мою комнату, где я провёл вечер один.

b1.en: The next morning I took my letters of introduction to some of the most important professors.
b1.ru: На следующее утро я отнёс рекомендательные письма нескольким самым важным профессорам.

b1.en: Chance, or perhaps some evil power that controlled me from the moment I left my father's house, took me first to M. Krempe, the professor of natural science.
b1.ru: Случай — или, может быть, какая-то злая сила, которая управляла мной с той минуты, как я покинул отцовский дом, — привёл меня сначала к господину Кремпе, профессору естественных наук.

b1.en: He was a rude man, but he knew a lot about his subject.
b1.ru: Он был грубым человеком, но хорошо знал свой предмет.

b1.en: He asked me some questions about what I had studied in science.
b1.ru: Он задал мне несколько вопросов о том, что я изучал в науке.

b1.en: I answered carelessly and told him the names of my old alchemists, the writers I had read most.
b1.ru: Я отвечал небрежно и назвал ему имена своих старых алхимиков — писателей, которых читал больше всего.

b1.en: The professor stared at me.
b1.ru: Профессор уставился на меня.

b1.en: "Have you really spent your time reading such nonsense?" he asked.
b1.ru: «Вы что, правда тратили время на чтение такой чепухи?» — спросил он.

b1.en: I said yes.
b1.ru: Я ответил, что да.

b1.en: "Every minute that you have spent on those books," M. Krempe said angrily, "is completely lost.
b1.ru: «Каждая минута, которую вы потратили на эти книги, — сердито сказал господин Кремпе, — потеряна полностью.

b1.en: You have filled your head with old ideas that nobody believes any more, and with useless names.
b1.ru: Вы забили голову старыми идеями, в которые больше никто не верит, и бесполезными именами.

b1.en: Good God!
b1.ru: Боже правый!

b1.en: Where have you been living?
b1.ru: Где же вы жили?

b1.en: Did nobody tell you that these ideas are a thousand years old and completely out of date?
b1.ru: Неужели никто не сказал вам, что этим идеям тысяча лет и что они совсем устарели?

b1.en: I did not expect, in our modern scientific age, to meet a student of Albertus Magnus and Paracelsus.
b1.ru: Я не ожидал в наш современный научный век встретить ученика Альберта Великого и Парацельса.

b1.en: My dear sir, you must start your studies again from the beginning."
b1.ru: Дорогой сэр, вам нужно начать учёбу заново».

b1.en: Then he wrote a list of science books for me to buy.
b1.ru: Потом он написал для меня список научных книг, которые нужно купить.

b1.en: He told me that the next week he was going to start a course of lectures on natural science.
b1.ru: Он сказал мне, что на следующей неделе начнёт курс лекций по естественным наукам.

b1.en: He also said that M. Waldman, another professor, would give lectures on chemistry on the other days.
b1.ru: Ещё он сказал, что другой профессор, господин Вальдман, будет читать лекции по химии в остальные дни.

b1.en: Then he sent me away.
b1.ru: Затем он меня отпустил.

b1.en: I went home, but I was not disappointed.
b1.ru: Я пошёл домой, но разочарования не чувствовал.

b1.en: As I have said, I had already decided long ago that those old writers were useless.
b1.ru: Как я уже говорил, я давно решил, что эти старые писатели бесполезны.

b1.en: But I did not want to study science again either.
b1.ru: Но и снова заниматься наукой мне тоже не хотелось.

b1.en: M. Krempe was a short, fat man with a rough voice and an ugly face, so he did not make me like his subject.
b1.ru: Господин Кремпе был невысоким толстым человеком с грубым голосом и некрасивым лицом, так что он не заставил меня полюбить свой предмет.

b1.en: Perhaps I have explained my early ideas about science too clearly and logically.
b1.ru: Пожалуй, я объяснил свои ранние представления о науке слишком ясно и логично.

b1.en: As a child I was not happy with what modern scientists promised.
b1.ru: Ребёнком я не был доволен тем, что обещали современные учёные.

b1.en: I was very young and had no teacher to guide me, so my ideas were confused.
b1.ru: Я был очень молод, и у меня не было учителя, который направлял бы меня, поэтому мысли мои путались.

b1.en: I went back in time and chose the dreams of old, forgotten alchemists instead of the discoveries of modern scientists.
b1.ru: Я вернулся назад во времени и выбрал мечты старых, забытых алхимиков вместо открытий современных учёных.

b1.en: Also, I did not respect the practical uses of modern science.
b1.ru: Кроме того, я не уважал практическое применение современной науки.

b1.en: Long ago, great scientists had tried to find how to live for ever and how to become powerful.
b1.ru: Давным-давно великие учёные пытались узнать, как жить вечно и как стать могущественными.

b1.en: Those dreams were impossible, but they were great.
b1.ru: Эти мечты были несбыточными, но великими.

b1.en: Now everything was different.
b1.ru: Теперь всё было иначе.

b1.en: Modern scientists seemed to want only to destroy the dreams that made me love science.
b1.ru: Современные учёные, казалось, хотели только разрушить те мечты, из-за которых я любил науку.

b1.en: I was asked to give up wonderful dreams for small, dull facts.
b1.ru: От меня требовали отказаться от чудесных мечтаний ради мелких скучных фактов.

b1.en: Those were my thoughts during my first few days in Ingolstadt, when I was getting to know the town and the important people there.
b1.ru: Такими были мои мысли в первые дни в Ингольштадте, когда я знакомился с городом и важными людьми в нём.

b1.en: But when the next week started, I remembered what M. Krempe had said about the lectures.
b1.ru: Но когда началась следующая неделя, я вспомнил, что господин Кремпе говорил о лекциях.

b1.en: I did not want to go and listen to that proud little man.
b1.ru: Мне не хотелось идти слушать этого заносчивого коротышку.

b1.en: But I remembered what he had said about M. Waldman, whom I had not met yet because he had been away.
b1.ru: Но я вспомнил, что он говорил о господине Вальдмане, с которым я ещё не встречался, потому что тот был в отъезде.

b1.en: Partly because I was curious and partly because I had nothing to do, I went into the lecture room, and soon M. Waldman came in.
b1.ru: Отчасти из любопытства, отчасти потому, что мне было нечего делать, я зашёл в аудиторию, и вскоре туда вошёл господин Вальдман.

b1.en: He was very different from M. Krempe.
b1.ru: Он был совсем не похож на господина Кремпе.

b1.en: He was about fifty years old and had a very kind face.
b1.ru: Ему было около пятидесяти лет, и у него было очень доброе лицо.

b1.en: His hair was a little grey at the sides but almost black at the back.
b1.ru: Волосы у него на висках немного поседели, а на затылке были почти чёрными.

b1.en: He was short but stood very straight, and he had the most beautiful voice I had ever heard.
b1.ru: Он был невысоким, но держался очень прямо, и у него был самый красивый голос, какой я когда-либо слышал.

b1.en: He began by telling the history of chemistry and the discoveries of different scientists, and he spoke the names of the greatest ones with feeling.
b1.ru: Он начал с истории химии и открытий разных учёных и с чувством произносил имена величайших из них.

b1.en: Then he talked about chemistry today and explained some of its basic words.
b1.ru: Потом он рассказал о современной химии и объяснил некоторые её основные понятия.

b1.en: After a few simple experiments, he finished with some words about modern chemistry that I will never forget:
b1.ru: После нескольких простых опытов он закончил словами о современной химии, которые я никогда не забуду:

b1.en: "The old teachers of this science," he said, "promised impossible things and did nothing.
b1.ru: «Старые учителя этой науки, — сказал он, — обещали невозможное и ничего не сделали.

b1.en: Modern scientists promise very little.
b1.ru: Современные учёные обещают очень мало.

b1.en: They know that you cannot turn metal into gold and that there is no drink that makes you live for ever.
b1.ru: Они знают, что металл нельзя превратить в золото и что нет напитка, который дарит вечную жизнь.

b1.en: Their hands work in dirt, and their eyes look into microscopes, but they have really done wonderful things.
b1.ru: Их руки работают в грязи, а глаза смотрят в микроскопы, но они действительно совершили чудеса.

b1.en: They look deep into nature and show how she works in her secret places.
b1.ru: Они заглядывают в глубины природы и показывают, как она трудится в своих тайных уголках.

b1.en: They study the sky; they have found out how blood moves around the body and what the air we breathe is made of.
b1.ru: Они изучают небо; они выяснили, как кровь движется по телу и из чего состоит воздух, которым мы дышим.

b1.en: They have new and almost unlimited powers: they can control lightning, copy earthquakes, and even play with the invisible world."
b1.ru: У них новая, почти безграничная власть: они могут управлять молнией, воспроизводить землетрясения и даже играть с невидимым миром».

b1.en: Those were the professor's words — or maybe I should say the words of fate, which were going to destroy me.
b1.ru: Таковы были слова профессора — или, может быть, лучше сказать, слова судьбы, которые должны были меня погубить.

b1.en: As he spoke, I felt that my soul was fighting a real enemy.
b1.ru: Пока он говорил, я чувствовал, что моя душа сражается с настоящим врагом.

b1.en: It was as if someone was playing on me like a piano, touching one key after another, until my mind was filled with one idea and one purpose.
b1.ru: Будто кто-то играл на мне, как на рояле, нажимая клавишу за клавишей, пока мой разум не наполнился одной мыслью и одной целью.

b1.en: "So much has been done," my soul cried, "but I will do more, much more.
b1.ru: «Так много уже сделано, — воскликнула моя душа, — но я сделаю больше, гораздо больше.

b1.en: I will follow their path and then find a new one.
b1.ru: Я пойду по их пути, а потом найду новый.

b1.en: I will discover unknown powers and show the world the deepest secrets of life."
b1.ru: Я открою неведомые силы и покажу миру глубочайшие тайны жизни».

b1.en: I could not sleep that night.
b1.ru: В ту ночь я не мог уснуть.

b1.en: Everything inside me was in confusion.
b1.ru: Внутри у меня всё смешалось.

b1.en: I felt that order would come, but I could not make it happen.
b1.ru: Я чувствовал, что порядок придёт, но не мог его навести.

b1.en: Slowly, after the sun came up, I fell asleep.
b1.ru: Медленно, когда уже взошло солнце, я заснул.

b1.en: When I woke up, my thoughts of the night before felt like a dream.
b1.ru: Когда я проснулся, вчерашние мысли казались сном.

b1.en: Only one decision remained: I would go back to my old studies and give my life to a science that I believed I had a natural talent for.
b1.ru: Осталось лишь одно решение: я вернусь к прежним занятиям и посвящу жизнь науке, к которой, как я верил, у меня был природный талант.

b1.en: That same day I visited M. Waldman.
b1.ru: В тот же день я пришёл к господину Вальдману.

b1.en: At home he was even kinder and friendlier than in the lecture room, where he was a little more serious.
b1.ru: Дома он был ещё добрее и приветливее, чем в аудитории, где держался немного серьёзнее.

b1.en: I told him almost the same things about my past studies as I had told M. Krempe.
b1.ru: Я рассказал ему о своих прошлых занятиях почти то же самое, что и господину Кремпе.

b1.en: He listened carefully and smiled at the names of Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus, but he did not laugh at them like M. Krempe.
b1.ru: Он внимательно слушал и улыбнулся при именах Корнелия Агриппы и Парацельса, но не стал смеяться над ними, как господин Кремпе.

b1.en: He said, "These men worked very hard, and modern scientists owe them most of the basic ideas of their science.
b1.ru: Он сказал: «Эти люди очень много трудились, и современные учёные обязаны им большей частью основных идей своей науки.

b1.en: They discovered many facts, and they left us the easier job of giving those facts new names and putting them in order.
b1.ru: Они открыли множество фактов и оставили нам более лёгкую работу — дать этим фактам новые названия и привести их в порядок.

b1.en: The work of great men, even when it goes in the wrong direction, almost always helps people in the end."
b1.ru: Труды великих людей, даже когда идут по неверному пути, почти всегда в конце концов помогают людям».

b1.en: I listened to him; he spoke simply, without any pride.
b1.ru: Я слушал его; он говорил просто, без всякой гордости.

b1.en: Then I told him that his lecture had changed my opinion of modern chemists.
b1.ru: Потом я сказал ему, что его лекция изменила моё мнение о современных химиках.

b1.en: I spoke modestly and politely, as a young man should speak to his teacher.
b1.ru: Я говорил скромно и вежливо, как юноша должен говорить со своим учителем.

b1.en: I did not show him how excited I was about my future work, because I was young and I would have felt ashamed.
b1.ru: Я не показал ему, как взволнован своей будущей работой, потому что был молод и мне было бы стыдно.

b1.en: I asked him which books I should buy.
b1.ru: Я спросил его, какие книги мне купить.

b1.en: "I am happy to have a new student," said M. Waldman.
b1.ru: «Я рад, что у меня новый ученик», — сказал господин Вальдман.

b1.en: "If you work as hard as you are clever, I am sure you will succeed.
b1.ru: «Если вы будете трудиться так же усердно, как вы умны, я уверен, что вы добьётесь успеха.

b1.en: Chemistry is the part of science where the greatest discoveries have been made and will be made.
b1.ru: Химия — та часть науки, где сделаны и будут сделаны величайшие открытия.

b1.en: That is why I have chosen it as my special subject.
b1.ru: Поэтому я выбрал её своим главным предметом.

b1.en: But I have also studied the other sciences.
b1.ru: Но я изучал и другие науки.

b1.en: A man who studies only chemistry will be a very poor chemist.
b1.ru: Человек, который изучает только химию, будет очень плохим химиком.

b1.en: If you want to be a real scientist, and not just a person who does little experiments, you should study every part of science, and mathematics too."
b1.ru: Если вы хотите стать настоящим учёным, а не просто человеком, который ставит мелкие опыты, вам нужно изучать все области науки, и математику тоже».

b1.en: Then he took me into his laboratory and showed me what his different machines did.
b1.ru: Потом он отвёл меня в свою лабораторию и показал, для чего нужны его разные приборы.

b1.en: He told me what I should buy and promised that I could use his machines when I knew enough not to break them.
b1.ru: Он сказал, что мне нужно купить, и пообещал, что я смогу пользоваться его приборами, когда буду знать достаточно, чтобы их не сломать.

b1.en: He also gave me the list of books I had asked for, and then I left.
b1.ru: Он также дал мне список книг, о котором я просил, и я ушёл.

b1.en: That was a day I will always remember, because it decided my future.
b1.ru: Это был день, который я буду помнить всегда, потому что он решил моё будущее.

a2.en: When I was seventeen, my parents decided to send me to the University of Ingolstadt.
a2.ru: Когда мне было семнадцать, родители решили отправить меня в Ингольштадтский университет.

a2.en: Before that, I went to school in Geneva.
a2.ru: До этого я ходил в школу в Женеве.

a2.en: My father wanted me to see how people live in other countries.
a2.ru: Отец хотел, чтобы я увидел, как живут люди в других странах.

a2.en: We chose a day for me to leave.
a2.ru: Мы выбрали день моего отъезда.

a2.en: But before that day, something very bad happened.
a2.ru: Но ещё до этого дня случилось кое-что очень плохое.

a2.en: It was the first sad event in my life, and it was a sign of more sad things to come.
a2.ru: Это было первое печальное событие в моей жизни, и оно было знаком новых бед.

a2.en: Elizabeth became very ill with scarlet fever.
a2.ru: Элизабет тяжело заболела скарлатиной.

a2.en: She was in great danger.
a2.ru: Она была в большой опасности.

a2.en: We asked my mother not to go near her.
a2.ru: Мы просили мать не подходить к ней.

a2.en: At first my mother listened to us.
a2.ru: Сначала мать нас послушала.

a2.en: But when she heard that Elizabeth could die, she was too worried.
a2.ru: Но когда она узнала, что Элизабет может умереть, она слишком встревожилась.

a2.en: She looked after her day and night, and Elizabeth got better.
a2.ru: Она ухаживала за ней днём и ночью, и Элизабет поправилась.

a2.en: But then my mother became ill too.
a2.ru: Но потом заболела и моя мать.

a2.en: Her fever was very bad, and the doctors looked very worried.
a2.ru: Лихорадка была очень сильной, и врачи выглядели очень встревоженными.

a2.en: My mother was dying, but she was still brave and kind.
a2.ru: Мать умирала, но оставалась храброй и доброй.

a2.en: She put Elizabeth's hand in my hand.
a2.ru: Она вложила руку Элизабет в мою руку.

a2.en: "My children," she said, "I always hoped that you two would get married one day.
a2.ru: «Дети мои, — сказала она, — я всегда надеялась, что однажды вы поженитесь.

a2.en: Now this hope will help your father.
a2.ru: Теперь эта надежда поможет вашему отцу.

a2.en: Elizabeth, my dear, you must look after my younger children for me.
a2.ru: Элизабет, дорогая, ты должна заботиться о моих младших детях вместо меня.

a2.en: I am sad to leave you all, because I was so happy with you.
a2.ru: Мне грустно оставлять вас всех, ведь я была так счастлива с вами.

a2.en: But I will try to be calm, and I hope to see you again in another world."
a2.ru: Но я постараюсь быть спокойной и надеюсь увидеть вас снова в ином мире».

a2.en: She died quietly, and her face was full of love.
a2.ru: Она умерла тихо, и её лицо было полно любви.

a2.en: Everyone knows how it feels when someone you love dies.
a2.ru: Все знают, каково это, когда умирает любимый человек.

a2.en: You feel empty inside.
a2.ru: Внутри становится пусто.

a2.en: For a long time you cannot believe it.
a2.ru: Долгое время ты не можешь в это поверить.

a2.en: We saw her every day.
a2.ru: Мы видели её каждый день.

a2.en: How can she be gone for ever?
a2.ru: Как она может уйти навсегда?

a2.en: How can we never hear her dear voice again?
a2.ru: Как мы можем никогда больше не услышать её милый голос?

a2.en: That is how you feel in the first days.
a2.ru: Так чувствуешь себя в первые дни.

a2.en: Later, you understand that it is really true, and then the pain is even worse.
a2.ru: Позже понимаешь, что это правда, и тогда боль становится ещё сильнее.

a2.en: But all people lose someone they love.
a2.ru: Но все люди теряют любимых.

a2.en: After some time, you can smile again.
a2.ru: Через какое-то время можно снова улыбаться.

a2.en: My mother was dead, but we had to go on living.
a2.ru: Моя мать умерла, но нам нужно было жить дальше.

a2.en: We had to be thankful for the people who were still alive.
a2.ru: Нужно было быть благодарными за тех, кто ещё жив.

a2.en: Now we chose a new day for my journey to Ingolstadt.
a2.ru: Теперь мы выбрали новый день для моей поездки в Ингольштадт.

a2.en: I asked my father to let me stay a few more weeks.
a2.ru: Я попросил отца разрешить мне остаться ещё на несколько недель.

a2.en: I did not want to leave our sad, quiet house so soon.
a2.ru: Мне не хотелось так скоро покидать наш печальный, тихий дом.

a2.en: I did not want to leave my family.
a2.ru: Я не хотел оставлять свою семью.

a2.en: Most of all, I wanted to see Elizabeth a little happier.
a2.ru: Больше всего я хотел увидеть Элизабет хоть немного счастливее.

a2.en: Elizabeth hid her sadness and tried to help us all.
a2.ru: Элизабет скрывала свою печаль и старалась помочь всем нам.

a2.en: She was brave and did all the work in the house.
a2.ru: Она была храброй и делала всю работу по дому.

a2.en: She took care of her uncle and cousins.
a2.ru: Она заботилась о дяде и кузенах.

a2.en: She smiled at us again, and she was more beautiful than ever.
a2.ru: Она снова улыбалась нам и была прекраснее, чем когда-либо.

a2.en: She helped us forget our sadness, and she forgot her own.
a2.ru: Она помогала нам забыть о печали и забывала о своей.

a2.en: At last the day came for me to leave.
a2.ru: Наконец настал день моего отъезда.

a2.en: Clerval spent the last evening with us.
a2.ru: Клерваль провёл с нами последний вечер.

a2.en: He wanted to come to university with me, but his father said no.
a2.ru: Он хотел поехать со мной в университет, но отец ему не разрешил.

a2.en: His father was a businessman, and he thought that studying was a waste of time.
a2.ru: Его отец был торговцем и считал учёбу пустой тратой времени.

a2.en: Henry was very sad about it.
a2.ru: Анри очень из-за этого грустил.

a2.en: He did not say much, but I could see in his eyes that he did not want to spend his life in business.
a2.ru: Он говорил мало, но я видел по его глазам, что он не хочет провести жизнь в торговле.

a2.en: We sat together until late at night.
a2.ru: Мы сидели вместе до поздней ночи.

a2.en: We did not want to say "Goodbye!"
a2.ru: Нам не хотелось говорить «Прощай!»

a2.en: At last we said it and went to bed.
a2.ru: Наконец мы это сказали и пошли спать.

a2.en: Early in the morning I went down to the carriage, and they were all there.
a2.ru: Рано утром я спустился к карете, и все они были там.

a2.en: My father blessed me, Clerval shook my hand, and Elizabeth asked me to write often.
a2.ru: Отец благословил меня, Клерваль пожал мне руку, а Элизабет попросила писать почаще.

a2.en: I sat in the coach and felt very sad.
a2.ru: Я сидел в карете, и мне было очень грустно.

a2.en: All my life I had kind friends around me, but now I was alone.
a2.ru: Всю жизнь меня окружали добрые друзья, а теперь я был один.

a2.en: At university I had to find new friends and take care of myself.
a2.ru: В университете мне нужно было найти новых друзей и заботиться о себе самому.

a2.en: I did not like meeting new people.
a2.ru: Я не любил знакомиться с новыми людьми.

a2.en: I loved my brothers, Elizabeth and Clerval, and I was afraid of strangers.
a2.ru: Я любил своих братьев, Элизабет и Клерваля, и боялся чужих людей.

a2.en: But after some time, I felt better.
a2.ru: Но через некоторое время мне стало лучше.

a2.en: I really wanted to learn new things.
a2.ru: Мне очень хотелось узнавать новое.

a2.en: At home I often wanted to go out and see the world.
a2.ru: Дома мне часто хотелось уехать и увидеть мир.

a2.en: Now I could do it, so I was not sorry.
a2.ru: Теперь я мог это сделать, поэтому ни о чём не жалел.

a2.en: The journey to Ingolstadt was long and tiring.
a2.ru: Дорога в Ингольштадт была долгой и утомительной.

a2.en: At last I saw the tall white church tower of the town.
a2.ru: Наконец я увидел высокую белую церковную башню города.

a2.en: I went to my room and spent the evening alone.
a2.ru: Я пошёл в свою комнату и провёл вечер один.

a2.en: The next morning I went to visit some of the professors.
a2.ru: На следующее утро я пошёл к некоторым профессорам.

a2.en: Maybe it was bad luck, but the first one I met was M. Krempe, the professor of natural science.
a2.ru: Может быть, это была неудача, но первым я встретил господина Кремпе, профессора естественных наук.

a2.en: He was not a polite man, but he knew his subject very well.
a2.ru: Он не был вежливым человеком, но очень хорошо знал свой предмет.

a2.en: He asked me what I had studied.
a2.ru: Он спросил, что я изучал.

a2.en: I told him the names of my old alchemists.
a2.ru: Я назвал ему имена своих старых алхимиков.

a2.en: The professor looked at me in surprise.
a2.ru: Профессор удивлённо посмотрел на меня.

a2.en: "Did you really read that rubbish?" he asked.
a2.ru: «Вы правда читали эту ерунду?» — спросил он.

a2.en: "Yes," I said.
a2.ru: «Да», — сказал я.

a2.en: "You have wasted all your time on those books!" said M. Krempe angrily.
a2.ru: «Вы потратили всё своё время на эти книги впустую!» — сердито сказал господин Кремпе.

a2.en: "Those ideas are a thousand years old, and they are all wrong.
a2.ru: «Этим идеям тысяча лет, и все они ошибочны.

a2.en: Didn't anyone tell you?
a2.ru: Неужели вам никто не сказал?

a2.en: I did not expect to meet a student of Albertus Magnus and Paracelsus today.
a2.ru: Я не ожидал встретить сегодня ученика Альберта Великого и Парацельса.

a2.en: You must start again from the beginning."
a2.ru: Вам придётся начать всё сначала».

a2.en: He wrote a list of books for me to buy.
a2.ru: Он написал мне список книг, которые нужно купить.

a2.en: He said that he was going to start his lectures next week.
a2.ru: Он сказал, что на следующей неделе начнёт свои лекции.

a2.en: Another professor, M. Waldman, was going to teach chemistry on the other days.
a2.ru: Другой профессор, господин Вальдман, должен был преподавать химию в остальные дни.

a2.en: I went home, but I was not unhappy.
a2.ru: Я пошёл домой, но не расстроился.

a2.en: I already knew that those old books were useless.
a2.ru: Я уже знал, что эти старые книги бесполезны.

a2.en: But I did not want to study science again.
a2.ru: Но и снова заниматься наукой мне не хотелось.

a2.en: M. Krempe was short and fat, with a rough voice and an ugly face, and I did not like him.
a2.ru: Господин Кремпе был низким и толстым, с грубым голосом и некрасивым лицом, и он мне не понравился.

a2.en: When I was a child, modern science did not interest me.
a2.ru: Когда я был ребёнком, современная наука меня не интересовала.

a2.en: I was young, and nobody helped me.
a2.ru: Я был молод, и никто мне не помогал.

a2.en: So I read the old alchemists instead of modern scientists.
a2.ru: Поэтому я читал старых алхимиков вместо современных учёных.

a2.en: The old scientists wanted to live for ever and to have great power.
a2.ru: Старые учёные хотели жить вечно и иметь огромную власть.

a2.en: Their dreams were impossible, but they were exciting.
a2.ru: Их мечты были несбыточными, но захватывающими.

a2.en: Modern scientists did not have big dreams like that.
a2.ru: У современных учёных не было таких больших мечтаний.

a2.en: I did not want to change my big dreams for small, boring facts.
a2.ru: Я не хотел менять свои большие мечты на мелкие скучные факты.

a2.en: For the first few days I got to know the town and the people in it.
a2.ru: Первые несколько дней я знакомился с городом и его жителями.

a2.en: Then the next week started, and I remembered the lectures.
a2.ru: Потом началась следующая неделя, и я вспомнил о лекциях.

a2.en: I did not want to listen to M. Krempe.
a2.ru: Мне не хотелось слушать господина Кремпе.

a2.en: But I wanted to see M. Waldman, because I had not met him yet.
a2.ru: Но мне хотелось увидеть господина Вальдмана, ведь я ещё с ним не встречался.

a2.en: I went into the lecture room, and soon M. Waldman came in.
a2.ru: Я вошёл в аудиторию, и вскоре туда вошёл господин Вальдман.

a2.en: He was very different from M. Krempe.
a2.ru: Он был совсем не похож на господина Кремпе.

a2.en: He was about fifty, and he had a very kind face.
a2.ru: Ему было около пятидесяти, и у него было очень доброе лицо.

a2.en: He was short, and he had a beautiful voice.
a2.ru: Он был невысоким, и у него был прекрасный голос.

a2.en: First he told us the history of chemistry and the names of great scientists.
a2.ru: Сначала он рассказал нам историю химии и назвал имена великих учёных.

a2.en: Then he did a few experiments.
a2.ru: Потом он провёл несколько опытов.

a2.en: At the end he said some words that I will never forget:
a2.ru: В конце он произнёс слова, которые я никогда не забуду:

a2.en: "The old scientists promised impossible things, and they did nothing," he said.
a2.ru: «Старые учёные обещали невозможное и ничего не сделали, — сказал он.

a2.en: "Modern scientists promise very little.
a2.ru: — Современные учёные обещают очень мало.

a2.en: They know that you cannot make gold and that you cannot live for ever.
a2.ru: Они знают, что нельзя сделать золото и нельзя жить вечно.

a2.en: But they work hard with their microscopes, and they have done wonderful things.
a2.ru: Но они усердно трудятся со своими микроскопами и совершили чудеса.

a2.en: They understand the secrets of nature.
a2.ru: Они понимают тайны природы.

a2.en: They know how blood moves in our bodies and what air is.
a2.ru: Они знают, как кровь движется в нашем теле и что такое воздух.

a2.en: They have great new powers, and they can even make lightning and earthquakes."
a2.ru: У них есть огромная новая власть, и они могут даже создавать молнии и землетрясения».

a2.en: These words changed my life, and later they destroyed me.
a2.ru: Эти слова изменили мою жизнь, а позже погубили меня.

a2.en: As I listened, I felt a great fight inside me.
a2.ru: Пока я слушал, внутри меня шла большая борьба.

a2.en: Soon I had only one idea in my head.
a2.ru: Вскоре в голове у меня осталась только одна мысль.

a2.en: "People have done so much," I thought, "but I will do more!
a2.ru: «Люди сделали так много, — думал я, — но я сделаю больше!

a2.en: I will find a new way.
a2.ru: Я найду новый путь.

a2.en: I will show the world the biggest secrets of life."
a2.ru: Я покажу миру самые большие тайны жизни».

a2.en: I could not sleep that night.
a2.ru: В ту ночь я не мог уснуть.

a2.en: I was too excited and confused.
a2.ru: Я был слишком взволнован и растерян.

a2.en: I fell asleep in the morning.
a2.ru: Я заснул только утром.

a2.en: When I woke up, my thoughts felt like a dream.
a2.ru: Когда я проснулся, мои мысли казались сном.

a2.en: But I knew one thing: I wanted to study science again, because I had a talent for it.
a2.ru: Но одно я знал точно: я хотел снова заниматься наукой, потому что у меня к ней талант.

a2.en: That day I visited M. Waldman at his house.
a2.ru: В тот день я пришёл к господину Вальдману домой.

a2.en: At home he was even kinder and friendlier.
a2.ru: Дома он был ещё добрее и приветливее.

a2.en: I told him about the books that I had read.
a2.ru: Я рассказал ему о книгах, которые читал.

a2.en: He smiled at the names of Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus, but he did not laugh at me.
a2.ru: Он улыбнулся при именах Корнелия Агриппы и Парацельса, но не стал надо мной смеяться.

a2.en: He said, "These men worked very hard.
a2.ru: Он сказал: «Эти люди очень много трудились.

a2.en: They found many important facts, and modern scientists learned a lot from them.
a2.ru: Они нашли много важных фактов, и современные учёные многому у них научились.

a2.en: The work of great men always helps people in the end."
a2.ru: Труды великих людей всегда в конце концов помогают людям».

a2.en: I listened to him and told him that his lecture had changed my mind.
a2.ru: Я выслушал его и сказал, что его лекция изменила моё мнение.

a2.en: I was polite and quiet, and I did not show how excited I was.
a2.ru: Я был вежлив и сдержан и не показал, как сильно взволнован.

a2.en: Then I asked him which books to buy.
a2.ru: Потом я спросил его, какие книги купить.

a2.en: "I am happy to have a new student," said M. Waldman.
a2.ru: «Я рад, что у меня новый ученик», — сказал господин Вальдман.

a2.en: "If you work hard, you will do well.
a2.ru: «Если вы будете усердно трудиться, у вас всё получится.

a2.en: Chemistry is my favourite science, because there are so many new discoveries in it.
a2.ru: Химия — моя любимая наука, потому что в ней так много новых открытий.

a2.en: But I study other sciences too.
a2.ru: Но я изучаю и другие науки.

a2.en: If you want to be a real scientist, you must study all of them, and mathematics too."
a2.ru: Если вы хотите стать настоящим учёным, вам нужно изучать их все, и математику тоже».

a2.en: Then he showed me his laboratory and his machines.
a2.ru: Потом он показал мне свою лабораторию и приборы.

a2.en: He said that I could use them later, when I knew more.
a2.ru: Он сказал, что я смогу пользоваться ими позже, когда буду знать больше.

a2.en: He gave me a list of books, and I went home.
a2.ru: Он дал мне список книг, и я пошёл домой.

a2.en: I will never forget that day, because it changed my future.
a2.ru: Я никогда не забуду тот день, потому что он изменил моё будущее.

sub: Victor studies science with passion, discovers the secret of life and secretly builds a giant human being

o: From this day natural philosophy, and particularly chemistry, in the most comprehensive sense of the term, became nearly my sole occupation. I read with ardour those works, so full of genius and discrimination, which modern inquirers have written on these subjects. I attended the lectures and cultivated the acquaintance of the men of science of the university, and I found even in M. Krempe a great deal of sound sense and real information, combined, it is true, with a repulsive physiognomy and manners, but not on that account the less valuable.

In M. Waldman I found a true friend. His gentleness was never tinged by dogmatism, and his instructions were given with an air of frankness and good nature that banished every idea of pedantry. In a thousand ways he smoothed for me the path of knowledge and made the most abstruse inquiries clear and facile to my apprehension. My application was at first fluctuating and uncertain; it gained strength as I proceeded and soon became so ardent and eager that the stars often disappeared in the light of morning whilst I was yet engaged in my laboratory.

As I applied so closely, it may be easily conceived that my progress was rapid. My ardour was indeed the astonishment of the students, and my proficiency that of the masters. Professor Krempe often asked me, with a sly smile, how Cornelius Agrippa went on, whilst M. Waldman expressed the most heartfelt exultation in my progress. Two years passed in this manner, during which I paid no visit to Geneva, but was engaged, heart and soul, in the pursuit of some discoveries which I hoped to make. None but those who have experienced them can conceive of the enticements of science.

In other studies you go as far as others have gone before you, and there is nothing more to know; but in a scientific pursuit there is continual food for discovery and wonder. A mind of moderate capacity which closely pursues one study must infallibly arrive at great proficiency in that study; and I, who continually sought the attainment of one object of pursuit and was solely wrapped up in this, improved so rapidly that at the end of two years I made some discoveries in the improvement of some chemical instruments, which procured me great esteem and admiration at the university.

When I had arrived at this point and had become as well acquainted with the theory and practice of natural philosophy as depended on the lessons of any of the professors at Ingolstadt, my residence there being no longer conducive to my improvements, I thought of returning to my friends and my native town, when an incident happened that protracted my stay.

One of the phenomena which had peculiarly attracted my attention was the structure of the human frame, and, indeed, any animal endued with life. Whence, I often asked myself, did the principle of life proceed? It was a bold question, and one which has ever been considered as a mystery; yet with how many things are we upon the brink of becoming acquainted, if cowardice or carelessness did not restrain our inquiries. I revolved these circumstances in my mind and determined thenceforth to apply myself more particularly to those branches of natural philosophy which relate to physiology. Unless I had been animated by an almost supernatural enthusiasm, my application to this study would have been irksome and almost intolerable.

To examine the causes of life, we must first have recourse to death. I became acquainted with the science of anatomy, but this was not sufficient; I must also observe the natural decay and corruption of the human body. In my education my father had taken the greatest precautions that my mind should be impressed with no supernatural horrors. I do not ever remember to have trembled at a tale of superstition or to have feared the apparition of a spirit. Darkness had no effect upon my fancy, and a churchyard was to me merely the receptacle of bodies deprived of life, which, from being the seat of beauty and strength, had become food for the worm.

Now I was led to examine the cause and progress of this decay and forced to spend days and nights in vaults and charnel-houses. My attention was fixed upon every object the most insupportable to the delicacy of the human feelings. I saw how the fine form of man was degraded and wasted; I beheld the corruption of death succeed to the blooming cheek of life; I saw how the worm inherited the wonders of the eye and brain.

I paused, examining and analysing all the minutiae of causation, as exemplified in the change from life to death, and death to life, until from the midst of this darkness a sudden light broke in upon me—a light so brilliant and wondrous, yet so simple, that while I became dizzy with the immensity of the prospect which it illustrated, I was surprised that among so many men of genius who had directed their inquiries towards the same science, that I alone should be reserved to discover so astonishing a secret.

Remember, I am not recording the vision of a madman. The sun does not more certainly shine in the heavens than that which I now affirm is true. Some miracle might have produced it, yet the stages of the discovery were distinct and probable. After days and nights of incredible labour and fatigue, I succeeded in discovering the cause of generation and life; nay, more, I became myself capable of bestowing animation upon lifeless matter.

The astonishment which I had at first experienced on this discovery soon gave place to delight and rapture. After so much time spent in painful labour, to arrive at once at the summit of my desires was the most gratifying consummation of my toils. But this discovery was so great and overwhelming that all the steps by which I had been progressively led to it were obliterated, and I beheld only the result. What had been the study and desire of the wisest men since the creation of the world was now within my grasp.

Not that, like a magic scene, it all opened upon me at once: the information I had obtained was of a nature rather to direct my endeavours so soon as I should point them towards the object of my search than to exhibit that object already accomplished. I was like the Arabian who had been buried with the dead and found a passage to life, aided only by one glimmering and seemingly ineffectual light.

I see by your eagerness and the wonder and hope which your eyes express, my friend, that you expect to be informed of the secret with which I am acquainted; that cannot be; listen patiently until the end of my story, and you will easily perceive why I am reserved upon that subject. I will not lead you on, unguarded and ardent as I then was, to your destruction and infallible misery. Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.

When I found so astonishing a power placed within my hands, I hesitated a long time concerning the manner in which I should employ it. Although I possessed the capacity of bestowing animation, yet to prepare a frame for the reception of it, with all its intricacies of fibres, muscles, and veins, still remained a work of inconceivable difficulty and labour. I doubted at first whether I should attempt the creation of a being like myself, or one of simpler organization; but my imagination was too much exalted by my first success to permit me to doubt of my ability to give life to an animal as complex and wonderful as man.

The materials at present within my command hardly appeared adequate to so arduous an undertaking, but I doubted not that I should ultimately succeed. I prepared myself for a multitude of reverses; my operations might be incessantly baffled, and at last my work be imperfect, yet when I considered the improvement which every day takes place in science and mechanics, I was encouraged to hope my present attempts would at least lay the foundations of future success. Nor could I consider the magnitude and complexity of my plan as any argument of its impracticability.

It was with these feelings that I began the creation of a human being. As the minuteness of the parts formed a great hindrance to my speed, I resolved, contrary to my first intention, to make the being of a gigantic stature, that is to say, about eight feet in height, and proportionably large. After having formed this determination and having spent some months in successfully collecting and arranging my materials, I began.

No one can conceive the variety of feelings which bore me onwards, like a hurricane, in the first enthusiasm of success. Life and death appeared to me ideal bounds, which I should first break through, and pour a torrent of light into our dark world. A new species would bless me as its creator and source; many happy and excellent natures would owe their being to me. No father could claim the gratitude of his child so completely as I should deserve theirs. Pursuing these reflections, I thought that if I could bestow animation upon lifeless matter, I might in process of time (although I now found it impossible) renew life where death had apparently devoted the body to corruption.

These thoughts supported my spirits, while I pursued my undertaking with unremitting ardour. My cheek had grown pale with study, and my person had become emaciated with confinement. Sometimes, on the very brink of certainty, I failed; yet still I clung to the hope which the next day or the next hour might realise. One secret which I alone possessed was the hope to which I had dedicated myself; and the moon gazed on my midnight labours, while, with unrelaxed and breathless eagerness, I pursued nature to her hiding-places.

Who shall conceive the horrors of my secret toil as I dabbled among the unhallowed damps of the grave or tortured the living animal to animate the lifeless clay? My limbs now tremble, and my eyes swim with the remembrance; but then a resistless and almost frantic impulse urged me forward; I seemed to have lost all soul or sensation but for this one pursuit. It was indeed but a passing trance, that only made me feel with renewed acuteness so soon as, the unnatural stimulus ceasing to operate, I had returned to my old habits.

I collected bones from charnel-houses and disturbed, with profane fingers, the tremendous secrets of the human frame. In a solitary chamber, or rather cell, at the top of the house, and separated from all the other apartments by a gallery and staircase, I kept my workshop of filthy creation; my eyeballs were starting from their sockets in attending to the details of my employment. The dissecting room and the slaughter-house furnished many of my materials; and often did my human nature turn with loathing from my occupation, whilst, still urged on by an eagerness which perpetually increased, I brought my work near to a conclusion.

The summer months passed while I was thus engaged, heart and soul, in one pursuit. It was a most beautiful season; never did the fields bestow a more plentiful harvest or the vines yield a more luxuriant vintage, but my eyes were insensible to the charms of nature. And the same feelings which made me neglect the scenes around me caused me also to forget those friends who were so many miles absent, and whom I had not seen for so long a time. I knew my silence disquieted them, and I well remembered the words of my father: “I know that while you are pleased with yourself you will think of us with affection, and we shall hear regularly from you. You must pardon me if I regard any interruption in your correspondence as a proof that your other duties are equally neglected.”

I knew well therefore what would be my father’s feelings, but I could not tear my thoughts from my employment, loathsome in itself, but which had taken an irresistible hold of my imagination. I wished, as it were, to procrastinate all that related to my feelings of affection until the great object, which swallowed up every habit of my nature, should be completed.

I then thought that my father would be unjust if he ascribed my neglect to vice or faultiness on my part, but I am now convinced that he was justified in conceiving that I should not be altogether free from blame. A human being in perfection ought always to preserve a calm and peaceful mind and never to allow passion or a transitory desire to disturb his tranquillity. I do not think that the pursuit of knowledge is an exception to this rule.

If the study to which you apply yourself has a tendency to weaken your affections and to destroy your taste for those simple pleasures in which no alloy can possibly mix, then that study is certainly unlawful, that is to say, not befitting the human mind. If this rule were always observed; if no man allowed any pursuit whatsoever to interfere with the tranquillity of his domestic affections, Greece had not been enslaved, Cæsar would have spared his country, America would have been discovered more gradually, and the empires of Mexico and Peru had not been destroyed.

But I forget that I am moralizing in the most interesting part of my tale, and your looks remind me to proceed.

My father made no reproach in his letters and only took notice of my silence by inquiring into my occupations more particularly than before. Winter, spring, and summer passed away during my labours; but I did not watch the blossom or the expanding leaves—sights which before always yielded me supreme delight—so deeply was I engrossed in my occupation. The leaves of that year had withered before my work drew near to a close, and now every day showed me more plainly how well I had succeeded.

But my enthusiasm was checked by my anxiety, and I appeared rather like one doomed by slavery to toil in the mines, or any other unwholesome trade than an artist occupied by his favourite employment. Every night I was oppressed by a slow fever, and I became nervous to a most painful degree; the fall of a leaf startled me, and I shunned my fellow creatures as if I had been guilty of a crime. Sometimes I grew alarmed at the wreck I perceived that I had become; the energy of my purpose alone sustained me: my labours would soon end, and I believed that exercise and amusement would then drive away incipient disease; and I promised myself both of these when my creation should be complete.
b2: From that day on, natural science, and especially chemistry in the widest sense of the word, became almost my only occupation. I read with passion the brilliant and perceptive books that modern researchers had written on these subjects. I went to lectures and got to know the scientists at the university, and even in Krempe I found a great deal of good sense and real knowledge; it is true that his face and manners were unpleasant, but that did not make him any less useful.

In Waldman I found a true friend. His kindness was never spoiled by a know-it-all attitude, and he taught with such openness and good humour that you could never think of him as a pedant. In countless ways he made the road to knowledge smoother for me and made the most obscure questions clear and easy to understand. At first my effort came and went; but it grew stronger as I went on, and soon I was so eager that the stars often faded in the morning light while I was still working in my laboratory.

Since I worked so hard, you can easily imagine that I made rapid progress. My passion amazed the students, and my skill amazed the teachers. Professor Krempe often asked me with a sly smile how Cornelius Agrippa was getting on, while Waldman was sincerely delighted with my progress. Two years went by like this; I did not visit Geneva once, but was devoted, heart and soul, to the discoveries I hoped to make. Only those who have felt it can understand how tempting science is.

In other subjects you can only go as far as others have gone before you, and then there is nothing more to learn; but in science there is always something new to discover and wonder at. Even an ordinary mind that concentrates on one subject is bound to become an expert in it; and I, who had only one goal and was completely absorbed in it, improved so quickly that after two years I made some discoveries that improved certain chemical instruments, which earned me great respect and admiration at the university.

By this time I had learnt as much about the theory and practice of science as any of the professors at Ingolstadt could teach me, so staying there no longer helped me to improve. I was thinking of going home to my friends and my native town when something happened that kept me there longer.

One of the things that particularly fascinated me was the structure of the human body, and indeed of any living creature. Where, I often asked myself, does life itself come from? It was a bold question, and one that has always been considered a mystery; yet how many things we might be close to understanding if cowardice or carelessness did not hold back our research. I thought about all this and decided from then on to concentrate on the areas of science connected with physiology. If I had not been driven by an almost supernatural enthusiasm, this work would have been tiresome and almost unbearable.

To study the causes of life, we must first turn to death. I learnt anatomy, but that was not enough; I also had to observe how the human body naturally decays and rots. When I was growing up, my father had taken great care that my mind should not be filled with supernatural terrors. I cannot remember ever trembling at a superstitious story or being afraid of seeing a ghost. Darkness did not frighten my imagination, and to me a churchyard was simply a place for dead bodies, which had once been beautiful and strong and had now become food for worms.

Now I had to study the cause and course of this decay, and I was forced to spend days and nights in tombs and burial vaults. I focused on everything that is most unbearable to sensitive human feelings. I saw how the fine human form was spoiled and wasted away; I watched the rot of death replace the rosy cheek of life; I saw how the worm took over the wonders of the eye and the brain.

I stopped to examine and analyse every tiny detail of cause and effect in the change from life to death and from death to life, until suddenly, in the middle of this darkness, a light broke in upon me. It was so bright and wonderful, and yet so simple, that although I felt dizzy at the enormous possibilities it opened up, I was amazed that out of so many brilliant men who had studied the same science, I alone had been chosen to discover such an astonishing secret.

Remember, I am not describing the dreams of a madman. What I am telling you now is as certainly true as the fact that the sun shines in the sky. A miracle might have caused it, but the stages of the discovery were clear and logical. After days and nights of incredible work and exhaustion, I managed to discover the cause of generation and life; more than that, I myself became able to bring lifeless matter to life.

The astonishment I felt at first soon gave way to delight and joy. After so much painful work, reaching the height of my desires all at once was the most satisfying reward for my efforts. But the discovery was so huge and overwhelming that I forgot all the steps that had gradually led me to it, and I could see only the result. What the wisest men had studied and longed for since the creation of the world was now within my reach.

That is not to say that everything appeared to me at once, like a scene in a magic show: what I had learnt would guide my efforts once I aimed them at my goal, rather than show me the goal already achieved. I was like the Arab in the old story who was buried alive with the dead and found a way back to life, guided only by one faint and apparently useless light.

I can see from your eagerness, and from the wonder and hope in your eyes, my friend, that you expect me to tell you the secret I know; that is impossible. Listen patiently to the end of my story, and you will easily understand why I keep silent on that subject. I will not lead you, careless and passionate as I was then, towards your own destruction and certain misery. Learn from me, if not from my advice then at least from my example, how dangerous it is to gain knowledge, and how much happier a man is who thinks his home town is the whole world than one who tries to become greater than his nature allows.

When I found that I had such an astonishing power in my hands, I hesitated for a long time about how to use it. Although I was able to give life, preparing a body to receive it, with all its complicated fibres, muscles and veins, was still an unimaginably difficult and laborious task. At first I was not sure whether to try to create a being like myself or a simpler one; but my first success had made my imagination so bold that I could not doubt my ability to bring to life a creature as complex and wonderful as a human being.

The materials I had at that time hardly seemed good enough for such a difficult task, but I had no doubt that I would succeed in the end. I prepared myself for many setbacks; my experiments might fail again and again, and my work might be imperfect in the end. Yet when I thought about how science and engineering improve every day, I felt hopeful that my present attempts would at least lay the foundations for future success. Nor did I think that the size and complexity of my plan proved that it was impossible.

It was with these feelings that I began to create a human being. Because the tiny parts slowed me down a great deal, I decided, against my original intention, to make the creature gigantic, about eight feet tall, and large in proportion. Having made this decision, and having spent several months successfully collecting and arranging my materials, I began.

No one can imagine the mixture of feelings that swept me forward like a hurricane in the first excitement of success. Life and death seemed to me like imaginary borders, which I would be the first to break through, pouring a flood of light into our dark world. A new species would bless me as its creator and origin; many happy and excellent beings would owe their existence to me. No father could deserve his child's gratitude as completely as I would deserve theirs. Following these thoughts, I imagined that if I could bring lifeless matter to life, I might in time (although I now know it is impossible) bring the dead back to life when their bodies had apparently begun to decay.

These thoughts kept my spirits up while I continued my work with tireless passion. My face had grown pale from study, and my body had become thin from being shut up indoors. Sometimes, just when I was on the point of success, I failed; yet I still held on to the hope that the next day or the next hour might bring. The secret that only I knew was the hope I had devoted myself to; and the moon looked down on my midnight work while I chased nature into her hiding places with tireless, breathless eagerness.

Who can imagine the horror of my secret work as I searched among the unholy dampness of graves, or tortured living animals in order to give life to lifeless clay? My arms and legs tremble now, and my eyes fill with tears at the memory; but at that time an irresistible, almost frantic urge drove me on; it was as if I had lost all soul and feeling except for this one aim. It was really only a passing trance, and as soon as the unnatural excitement stopped working and I went back to my old habits, I felt everything even more sharply.

I collected bones from burial vaults and, with unholy fingers, disturbed the tremendous secrets of the human body. I kept my workshop of disgusting creation in a lonely room, or rather a cell, at the top of the house, separated from all the other rooms by a gallery and a staircase; my eyes nearly popped out of their sockets as I concentrated on the details of my work. The dissecting room and the slaughterhouse supplied many of my materials; and my human nature often turned away from the work in disgust, while, driven by an ever-growing eagerness, I brought it close to completion.

The summer months passed while I was absorbed, heart and soul, in this one task. It was a lovely season; the fields had never given a richer harvest, nor the vines a finer crop of grapes, but I was blind to the beauty of nature. And the same feelings that made me ignore the world around me also made me forget my friends, who were so many miles away and whom I had not seen for so long. I knew that my silence worried them, and I remembered my father's words well: “I know that while you are pleased with yourself you will think of us with love, and we will hear from you regularly. Forgive me, but if your letters stop, I will take it as a sign that you are neglecting your other duties too.”

So I knew very well how my father would feel, but I could not tear my thoughts away from my work, which was disgusting in itself but had taken an irresistible hold on my imagination. It was as if I wanted to put off everything connected with my feelings of love until my great aim, which had swallowed up all my usual habits, was achieved.

At the time I thought my father would be unfair if he blamed my neglect on some vice or fault of mine, but now I am sure he was right to think that I was not completely free from blame. A perfect human being should always keep a calm and peaceful mind and never let passion or a passing desire disturb that calm. I do not think that the search for knowledge is an exception to this rule.

If the work you devote yourself to tends to weaken your love for others and to destroy your taste for simple, pure pleasures, then that work is certainly wrong, that is to say, not suitable for the human mind. If this rule had always been followed, if no one had ever allowed any ambition to disturb the peace of family love, Greece would not have been enslaved, Caesar would have spared his country, America would have been discovered more gradually, and the empires of Mexico and Peru would not have been destroyed.

But I am forgetting that I am lecturing you at the most interesting point of my story, and your face reminds me to go on.

My father did not criticise me in his letters; he only showed that he had noticed my silence by asking about my work in more detail than before. Winter, spring and summer passed while I worked; but I did not notice the blossom or the opening leaves, sights which had always given me the greatest joy, because I was so deeply absorbed in my work. The leaves of that year had withered before my work was nearly finished, and now each day showed me more clearly how well I had succeeded.

But my enthusiasm was held back by anxiety, and I looked more like a slave condemned to work in the mines or some other unhealthy job than an artist busy with the work he loves. Every night I suffered from a slow fever, and I became painfully nervous; a falling leaf made me jump, and I avoided other people as if I were guilty of a crime. Sometimes I was alarmed to see what a wreck I had become; only the strength of my purpose kept me going. My work would soon be over, and I believed that exercise and entertainment would then drive away the illness that was starting; and I promised myself both as soon as my creation was complete.

Because I worked so hard, I learnt very quickly. The students were surprised by my passion, and the teachers were surprised by my knowledge. Professor Krempe often asked me with a sly smile how Cornelius Agrippa was doing, but Waldman was really happy about my progress. Two years passed like this. I did not go back to Geneva even once, because I was completely busy with the discoveries I hoped to make. Only people who have felt it can understand how exciting science is.

In other subjects, you can only learn what other people already know, and then there is nothing more. But in science there is always something new to find and to wonder at. If a person with an ordinary mind studies one subject very carefully, he will certainly become very good at it. I had only one goal and thought about nothing else, so I improved very quickly. After two years I found ways to make some chemical instruments better, and people at the university began to respect and admire me.

By now I knew as much about science as any professor at Ingolstadt could teach me, so there was no reason to stay there. I was thinking about going home to my friends and my town, but then something happened that kept me there.

I was especially interested in the human body and in the bodies of all living animals. I often asked myself: where does life come from? It was a brave question, and people had always thought of it as a mystery. But we could learn so many things if we were not afraid or lazy. I thought about this for a long time, and I decided to study physiology, the science of how living bodies work. It was hard and unpleasant work, and without my huge, almost magical enthusiasm, I could not have done it.

To understand life, we must first study death. I learnt anatomy, but it was not enough. I also had to watch how a dead human body slowly goes bad. When I was a child, my father made sure that I was never afraid of ghosts or other supernatural things. I do not remember ever being frightened by a scary story. Darkness did not frighten me, and for me a churchyard was just a place for dead bodies. These bodies were once beautiful and strong, but now they were food for worms.

Now I had to study why and how bodies decay, so I spent days and nights in tombs and in places where bones were kept. I looked closely at things that most people cannot bear to see. I saw how the beautiful human body was spoiled and destroyed. I saw how death took the place of rosy, living cheeks, and how worms ate the wonderful eyes and brain.

I studied every small detail of the change from life to death and from death to life. Then suddenly, in the middle of all this darkness, a light came to me. It was very bright and wonderful, but also very simple. I felt dizzy when I saw how much it could do. Many clever men had studied the same science, and I was surprised that I was the only one to discover this amazing secret.

Remember, these are not the dreams of a crazy man. What I am telling you is as true as the sun in the sky. Perhaps a miracle helped me, but each step of the discovery was clear and made sense. After many days and nights of very hard work, I discovered where life comes from. And more than that: I could now give life to dead things myself.

At first I was very surprised by my discovery, but soon I felt only great joy. After so much hard work, I suddenly had what I wanted most, and this was the best reward. The discovery was so big that I forgot all the small steps that had brought me to it, and I could only see the result. The wisest people in the world had wanted this knowledge since the beginning of time, and now it was in my hands.

But it was not like magic, where everything appears at once. My new knowledge could show me the way to my goal, but it could not give me the finished result. I was like the Arab in the old story who was buried with the dead. He found his way back to life with only one small, weak light to help him.

My friend, I can see the hope and wonder in your eyes. You want me to tell you my secret, but I cannot do that. Listen patiently to the end of my story, and you will understand why I will not talk about it. You are as careless and excited as I was then, and I will not lead you to destruction and unhappiness. Learn from my example how dangerous knowledge can be. A man who thinks his home town is the whole world is much happier than a man who wants to be greater than nature allows.

Now I had this amazing power, but for a long time I did not know how to use it. I could give life, but it was still extremely hard to prepare a body for it, with all its muscles, veins and other small parts. At first I did not know whether to make a being like me or a simpler animal. But my first success made me feel so confident that I was sure I could give life to a creature as wonderful as a man.

The materials I had were not really good enough for such a difficult job, but I was sure that I would succeed in the end. I knew there would be many problems. My experiments might fail again and again, and my work might not be perfect. But science was getting better every day, so I hoped that my work would at least help future success. And I did not think that my plan was impossible just because it was big and difficult.

So I began to make a human being. The small parts of the body were difficult and slowed me down, so I changed my plan. I decided to make a very big creature, about eight feet tall, with everything large in proportion. I spent several months collecting and preparing my materials, and then I started.

Nobody can imagine all the feelings that pushed me forward like a storm when I first began to succeed. I thought that life and death were only borders, and that I would be the first to break through them and bring light into our dark world. A new kind of being would thank me as its creator, and many happy, good creatures would live because of me. No father would deserve his children's thanks as much as I would deserve theirs. I even thought that one day I might bring dead people back to life, though now I know that this is impossible.

These thoughts gave me strength, and I worked with great passion. I became pale from studying and thin from staying inside all the time. Sometimes, when I was very close to success, I failed. But I still hoped that the next day or the next hour would bring it. Nobody else knew my secret, and it was my only hope. At night the moon watched me work, while I followed nature to her most secret places with endless, breathless eagerness.

Who can imagine the horror of my secret work, when I searched in wet graves or hurt living animals to bring dead matter to life? Now my body shakes and my eyes fill with tears when I remember it. But then a strong, almost crazy feeling pushed me forward. I seemed to have no other feelings except for this one aim. It was like a short dream, and when it ended and I went back to normal life, I felt everything even more strongly.

I collected bones from burial places and touched the terrible secrets of the human body. My workshop was in a lonely little room at the top of the house, away from all the other rooms. There I did my dirty work, and my eyes almost came out of my head because I looked so hard at every detail. I got many of my materials from the dissecting room and the slaughterhouse. Often a part of me hated what I was doing. But my eagerness grew stronger and stronger, and my work was nearly finished.

The summer passed while I worked on this one thing. It was a beautiful summer, with a very rich harvest in the fields and lots of grapes on the vines, but I did not see the beauty of nature. Because of the same feelings, I also forgot my friends, who were far away and whom I had not seen for a long time. I knew that my silence worried them. I remembered my father's words: “I know that when you are happy with yourself, you will think of us with love and write to us often. So if you stop writing, I will think that you are forgetting your other duties too.”

So I knew how my father would feel. But I could not stop thinking about my work. It was horrible, but it had taken control of my imagination. I wanted to leave my feelings for my family and friends until later, until my great work was finished.

At that time I thought it would be unfair of my father to believe I was doing something bad. But now I am sure that he was right to think that I was partly to blame. A good person should always stay calm and should never let strong feelings or sudden wishes destroy his peace. I think this is also true for people who are looking for knowledge.

If your studies make you love people less and stop you enjoying simple, innocent pleasures, then those studies are wrong and bad for the human mind. If people had always followed this rule and never let their ambitions destroy the peace of their families, many bad things would not have happened. Greece would still be free, Caesar would not have attacked his own country, America would have been discovered more slowly, and the empires of Mexico and Peru would still exist.

But I am forgetting my story and giving you lessons at the most interesting part! I can see from your face that you want me to continue.

My father did not say anything angry in his letters. He only asked more questions about my work than before, and in this way he showed that he had noticed my silence. Winter, spring and summer passed while I worked. Before, I always loved to watch the flowers and the new leaves, but now I did not even notice them, because I was so busy. The leaves of that year had died before my work was almost finished. Now every day I could see more clearly how well I had done.

But I was very worried, and I felt less and less excited. I looked more like a slave who has to work in the mines than an artist doing the work he loves. Every night I had a slight fever, and I became terribly nervous. A falling leaf made me jump, and I stayed away from other people as if I had done something criminal. Sometimes I was frightened when I saw how ill and weak I had become. Only my goal kept me going. I thought: “My work will soon be finished, and then exercise and fun will make me well again.” I promised myself both of these when my creation was complete.
a2: From that day, I studied science all the time, and chemistry most of all. I read many books by modern scientists, and I loved them. I went to lectures and met the scientists at the university. Krempe was not a nice man, and his face was ugly, but he knew a lot and he was useful to me.

Waldman was a real friend. He was kind and friendly, and he never thought that he knew everything. He helped me a lot, and he made difficult things easy for me. At first I did not always work hard. But soon I loved my work so much that I often stayed in my laboratory all night, until the morning came.

I worked very hard, so I learnt very fast. The students and the teachers were very surprised. Krempe often smiled and asked me about Cornelius Agrippa, but Waldman was really happy for me. Two years passed, and I did not go home to Geneva once. I only wanted to make new discoveries. Science is very exciting, but you can only understand this if you feel it yourself.

In other subjects, you learn what other people know, and then you stop. But in science there is always something new. When a person studies one thing all the time, he becomes very good at it. I had only one goal, and I thought only about it. After two years I made some chemical instruments better, and people at the university started to respect me.
Now I knew everything the teachers at Ingolstadt could teach me. I was not learning anything new there. I wanted to go home to my friends and my town. But then something happened, and I stayed.

I was very interested in the human body and in all living things. I often asked myself: “Where does life come from?” Nobody knew the answer. But I thought: “We can learn many things if we are not afraid or lazy.” So I decided to study how living bodies work. It was hard and unpleasant work, but I loved it very much.

To understand life, you must first understand death. I studied the human body, but this was not enough. I also had to watch what happens to a dead body. When I was a child, my father did not tell me stories about ghosts, so I was never afraid of them. I was not afraid of the dark. For me, a churchyard was only a place for dead bodies.

Now I spent days and nights in old tombs with dead bodies. It was not a nice place, but I stayed there. I looked at terrible things. I saw how a beautiful body changes after death. I saw how worms eat the eyes and the brain.

I studied every small change from life to death and from death to life. Then one day, in all this darkness, I suddenly understood something. It was like a bright light, and it was wonderful and very simple. Many clever men studied the same science before me, but only I found this great secret.

Please believe me: I am not crazy. This is as true as the sun in the sky. Maybe it was a miracle, but every step was clear. After many days and nights of hard work, I found out where life comes from. And more: now I could give life to dead things!

At first I was very surprised, but then I was very, very happy. I worked so hard, and now I had the thing I wanted most. I forgot all the small steps, and I saw only the great result. The cleverest people in the world wanted this secret for thousands of years, and now I had it.

But it was not like magic. I knew the way now, but I still had a lot of work to do. I was like a man in an old story: he was in a grave with dead people, and he found his way out with only one small light.

My friend, I can see in your eyes that you want to know my secret. But I am not going to tell you. Listen to my story, and you will understand why. Learn from me: knowledge can be very dangerous. A man who loves his home town is happier than a man who wants to be more than a man.

Now I had this great power, but what could I do with it? I could give life, but first I had to make a body, and that was very difficult. Should I make a man or a simple animal? I was very excited after my first success, so I decided to make a man.

I did not have very good materials, but I was sure that I was going to succeed. I knew that I was going to have many problems. My experiments could fail many times. But science was getting better every day, and I hoped my work would help in the future.
So I started to make a man. The small parts were difficult and slow to make, so I decided to make a very big man, about eight feet tall. For some months I collected my materials, and then I began.

I had so many strong feelings at that time! I thought: “I will be the first to win over death, and I will bring light into our dark world.” I dreamed of new, happy people. I was going to be their father, and they were going to thank me. I also thought that one day I could bring dead people back to life. Now I know that this is impossible.

These thoughts made me strong, and I worked and worked. I worked hard every day and every night. I became pale and thin because I never went outside. Sometimes I failed, but I always hoped for success the next day. Nobody knew my secret. At night the moon watched me while I worked.

My secret work was terrible. I went into graves, and I hurt living animals. Now I shake when I remember it. But then I could not stop. I was like a man in a dream. I did not feel anything; I only wanted to finish my work.

I took bones from old graves. My workshop was in a small room at the top of the house, far from the other rooms. I did my horrible work there. I also got things from hospitals and from places where people kill animals for meat. Often I hated my work, but I did not stop, and soon it was nearly finished.
