b2.ru: Рука моя уже лежала на замке, когда я опомнился.

b2.en: I stopped, and a cold shiver ran through me.
b2.ru: Я остановился, и меня пробрала холодная дрожь.

b2.en: I flung the door open, as children do when they expect a ghost to be waiting for them on the other side; but nothing appeared.
b2.ru: Я распахнул дверь, как делают дети, когда ждут, что за ней их подстерегает привидение; но ничего не появилось.

b2.en: I stepped in nervously: the flat was empty, and my bedroom was also free of its hideous guest.
b2.ru: Я робко шагнул внутрь: квартира была пуста, и в спальне тоже не было отвратительного гостя.

b2.en: I could hardly believe that such good luck had come my way, but when I was sure that my enemy really had gone, I clapped my hands with joy and ran down to Clerval.
b2.ru: Я едва мог поверить в такую удачу, но, убедившись, что мой враг и правда ушёл, я захлопал в ладоши от радости и сбежал вниз к Клервалю.

b2.en: We went up to my room, and soon the servant brought breakfast; but I could not control myself.
b2.ru: Мы поднялись ко мне, и вскоре слуга принёс завтрак; но я не мог держать себя в руках.

b2.en: It was not only joy that had taken hold of me; my skin was tingling with over-sensitivity, and my pulse was racing.
b2.ru: Мной овладела не только радость; кожу покалывало от обострённой чувствительности, а пульс бешено стучал.

b2.en: I could not stay in one place for a single moment; I jumped over the chairs, clapped my hands and laughed out loud.
b2.ru: Я ни на секунду не мог усидеть на месте; я перепрыгивал через стулья, хлопал в ладоши и громко смеялся.

b2.en: At first Clerval thought my strange high spirits were due to joy at his arrival, but when he watched me more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes that he could not explain, and my loud, uncontrolled, heartless laughter frightened and amazed him.
b2.ru: Сначала Клерваль решил, что моё странное возбуждение вызвано радостью от его приезда, но, присмотревшись, увидел в моих глазах какую-то дикость, которую не мог объяснить, и мой громкий, безудержный, бездушный смех напугал и поразил его.

b2.en: “My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what is the matter?
b2.ru: «Дорогой Виктор, — воскликнул он, — ради бога, что случилось?

b2.en: Don’t laugh like that.
b2.ru: Не смейся так.

b2.en: How ill you are!
b2.ru: Как ты болен!

b2.en: What is causing all this?”
b2.ru: Отчего всё это?»

b2.en: “Don’t ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, because I thought I saw the dreaded ghost slip into the room; “he can tell you.
b2.ru: «Не спрашивай меня, — вскричал я, закрыв глаза руками, потому что мне показалось, будто в комнату скользнул страшный призрак, — он тебе скажет.

b2.en: Oh, save me!
b2.ru: О, спаси меня!

b2.en: Save me!”
b2.ru: Спаси!»

b2.en: I imagined that the monster had grabbed me; I fought wildly and collapsed in a fit.
b2.ru: Мне почудилось, что чудовище схватило меня; я отчаянно отбивался и рухнул в припадке.

b2.en: Poor Clerval!
b2.ru: Бедный Клерваль!

b2.en: What must he have felt?
b2.ru: Что он должен был почувствовать?

b2.en: A meeting that he had looked forward to with such joy had turned so strangely into bitterness.
b2.ru: Встреча, которой он так радостно ждал, столь странно обернулась горечью.

b2.en: But I did not see his grief, because I was unconscious and did not come to my senses for a long, long time.
b2.ru: Но я не видел его горя, потому что лежал без сознания и очень, очень долго не приходил в себя.

b2.en: This was the beginning of a nervous fever which kept me in bed for several months.
b2.ru: Так началась нервная горячка, которая на несколько месяцев уложила меня в постель.

b2.en: During all that time Henry was my only nurse.
b2.ru: Всё это время Анри был моей единственной сиделкой.

b2.en: I later learned that, knowing that my father was too old to make such a long journey, and how unhappy my illness would make Elizabeth, he spared them this pain by hiding how serious my condition was.
b2.ru: Позже я узнал, что, понимая, что отец слишком стар для такого долгого пути, и как несчастна будет Элизабет из-за моей болезни, он избавил их от этого горя, скрыв, насколько серьёзно я болен.

b2.en: He knew that I could not have a kinder or more attentive nurse than himself; and, firmly believing that I would recover, he was sure that, far from doing them any harm, he was doing them the greatest kindness he could.
b2.ru: Он знал, что у меня не может быть сиделки добрее и внимательнее, чем он сам; и, твёрдо веря, что я поправлюсь, он был уверен, что не только не вредит им, но и оказывает им самую большую услугу, какую может.

b2.en: But in fact I was very ill, and surely nothing but my friend’s endless, tireless care could have brought me back to life.
b2.ru: Но на самом деле я был очень болен, и, конечно, только бесконечная, неутомимая забота друга могла вернуть меня к жизни.

b2.en: The shape of the monster I had given life to was always before my eyes, and I raved about him constantly.
b2.ru: Образ чудовища, которому я дал жизнь, всё время стоял у меня перед глазами, и я постоянно бредил о нём.

b2.en: No doubt my words surprised Henry; at first he thought they were just the ramblings of a troubled mind, but the way I kept returning to the same subject convinced him that my illness really had been caused by some unusual and terrible event.
b2.ru: Несомненно, мои слова удивляли Анри; сначала он решил, что это просто бред больного воображения, но то, как упорно я возвращался к одному и тому же, убедило его, что болезнь и правда вызвана каким-то необычным и страшным событием.

b2.en: Very slowly, and with frequent setbacks that frightened and upset my friend, I got better.
b2.ru: Очень медленно, с частыми ухудшениями, которые пугали и огорчали моего друга, я поправлялся.

b2.en: I remember that the first time I was able to look at the world outside with any pleasure, I noticed that the fallen leaves had gone and that young buds were appearing on the trees that shaded my window.
b2.ru: Помню, что, когда я впервые смог с каким-то удовольствием смотреть на окружающий мир, я заметил, что опавшие листья исчезли, а на деревьях под моим окном появляются молодые почки.

b2.en: It was a glorious spring, and the season did a great deal to help my recovery.
b2.ru: Весна была чудесная, и она очень помогла моему выздоровлению.

b2.en: I also felt feelings of joy and affection coming back to life in my heart; my gloom disappeared, and soon I was as cheerful as I had been before that fatal passion took hold of me.
b2.ru: Я почувствовал, как в сердце моём оживают радость и нежность; мрачность исчезла, и вскоре я стал так же весел, как до того, как мной овладела роковая страсть.

b2.en: “Dearest Clerval,” I exclaimed, “how kind, how very good you are to me.
b2.ru: «Дорогой Клерваль, — воскликнул я, — как ты добр, как ты хорош ко мне.

b2.en: This whole winter, instead of being spent studying, as you had planned, has been used up in my sickroom.
b2.ru: Всю эту зиму, которую ты собирался посвятить учёбе, ты провёл в комнате больного.

b2.en: How will I ever repay you?
b2.ru: Как мне когда-нибудь отплатить тебе?

b2.en: I am deeply sorry for the disappointment I have caused you, but you will forgive me.”
b2.ru: Мне очень жаль, что я так тебя подвёл, но ты меня простишь».

b2.en: “You will repay me completely if you don’t upset yourself but get well as quickly as you can; and since you seem to be in such good spirits, may I talk to you about one subject?”
b2.ru: «Ты отплатишь мне сполна, если не будешь волноваться и поправишься как можно скорее; а раз уж ты в таком хорошем настроении, можно мне поговорить с тобой об одном деле?»

b2.en: I trembled.
b2.ru: Я задрожал.

b2.en: One subject!
b2.ru: Об одном деле!

b2.en: What could it be?
b2.ru: Что бы это могло быть?

b2.en: Could he be hinting at the one being I did not even dare to think about?
b2.ru: Неужели он намекает на того, о ком я не смел даже думать?

b2.en: “Calm down,” said Clerval, who noticed me turn pale, “I won’t mention it if it upsets you; but your father and cousin would be very happy to receive a letter from you in your own handwriting.
b2.ru: «Успокойся, — сказал Клерваль, заметив, что я побледнел, — я не буду об этом говорить, если это тебя тревожит; но твой отец и кузина были бы очень рады получить письмо, написанное твоей рукой.

b2.en: They hardly know how ill you have been, and they are worried by your long silence.”
b2.ru: Они почти не знают, как сильно ты болел, и волнуются из-за твоего долгого молчания».

b2.en: “Is that all, my dear Henry?
b2.ru: «И это всё, дорогой Анри?

b2.en: How could you think that my first thoughts would not fly to those dear, dear friends whom I love and who deserve my love so much?”
b2.ru: Как ты мог подумать, что мои первые мысли не полетят к тем дорогим, самым дорогим людям, которых я люблю и которые так заслуживают моей любви?»

b2.en: “If that’s how you feel now, my friend, you may be glad to see a letter that has been waiting here for you for a few days; I believe it is from your cousin.”
b2.ru: «Если ты сейчас так настроен, друг мой, то, наверное, будешь рад увидеть письмо, которое уже несколько дней ждёт тебя здесь; кажется, оно от твоей кузины».

b1.en: It was a dark, rainy night in November when my work was finally finished.
b1.ru: Была тёмная дождливая ноябрьская ночь, когда моя работа наконец была закончена.

b1.en: I was so anxious that it almost hurt.
b1.ru: Я волновался так сильно, что мне было почти больно.

b1.en: I put my instruments around me because I wanted to give life to the lifeless body on the floor.
b1.ru: Я разложил вокруг себя инструменты, потому что хотел дать жизнь безжизненному телу на полу.

b1.en: It was already one o’clock in the morning, the rain was hitting the windows, and my candle had nearly burnt out.
b1.ru: Был уже час ночи, дождь стучал в окна, и моя свеча почти догорела.

b1.en: Then, in the weak light, I saw the creature’s dull yellow eye open.
b1.ru: И тут в слабом свете я увидел, как открылся тусклый жёлтый глаз существа.

b1.en: It breathed heavily, and its arms and legs moved suddenly.
b1.ru: Оно тяжело задышало, и его руки и ноги резко дёрнулись.

b1.en: How can I describe my feelings at this terrible moment, or the poor creature that I had worked so hard to make?
b1.ru: Как описать мои чувства в эту ужасную минуту или несчастное существо, которое я создавал с таким трудом?

b1.en: His body had the right proportions, and I had chosen beautiful features for him.
b1.ru: Тело его было правильных пропорций, и я выбрал для него красивые черты.

b1.en: Beautiful!
b1.ru: Красивые!

b1.en: Oh God!
b1.ru: Боже!

b1.en: His yellow skin hardly covered the muscles and blood vessels under it.
b1.ru: Жёлтая кожа едва прикрывала мышцы и сосуды под ней.

b1.en: His hair was shiny and black, and his teeth were white like pearls.
b1.ru: Волосы у него были блестящие и чёрные, а зубы белые, как жемчуг.

b1.en: But these things only made his watery eyes, his wrinkled skin and his straight black lips look even more horrible.
b1.ru: Но всё это только делало ещё страшнее его водянистые глаза, морщинистую кожу и прямые чёрные губы.

b1.en: Our feelings can change faster than anything else in life.
b1.ru: Наши чувства меняются быстрее всего на свете.

b1.en: For almost two years I had worked hard with only one aim: to put life into a dead body.
b1.ru: Почти два года я упорно работал ради одной цели — вдохнуть жизнь в мёртвое тело.

b1.en: Because of this, I had lost my rest and my health.
b1.ru: Из-за этого я лишился покоя и здоровья.

b1.en: I had wanted it far too much, but now that it was finished, the beautiful dream disappeared.
b1.ru: Я хотел этого слишком сильно, но теперь, когда всё было закончено, прекрасная мечта исчезла.

b1.en: My heart was full of horror and disgust.
b1.ru: Сердце моё было полно ужаса и отвращения.

b1.en: I could not look at the creature I had made, so I ran out of the room.
b1.ru: Я не мог смотреть на созданное мной существо и выбежал из комнаты.

b1.en: For a long time I walked up and down in my bedroom and could not calm down enough to sleep.
b1.ru: Долго я ходил взад-вперёд по спальне и не мог успокоиться, чтобы уснуть.

b1.en: At last I became very tired, and I lay down on the bed in my clothes, hoping to forget everything for a few minutes.
b1.ru: Наконец я очень устал и лёг на кровать в одежде, надеясь хоть на несколько минут обо всём забыть.

b1.en: But it did not help.
b1.ru: Но это не помогло.

b1.en: I slept, but I had terrible dreams.
b1.ru: Я уснул, но мне снились страшные сны.

b1.en: I dreamt that I saw Elizabeth, looking healthy and happy, in the streets of Ingolstadt.
b1.ru: Мне снилось, что я вижу Элизабет, здоровую и счастливую, на улицах Ингольштадта.

b1.en: I was surprised and happy, and I put my arms around her.
b1.ru: Я удивился и обрадовался и обнял её.

b1.en: But when I kissed her, her lips turned the colour of death.
b1.ru: Но когда я поцеловал её, её губы стали мертвенного цвета.

b1.en: Her face changed, and suddenly I was holding the dead body of my mother.
b1.ru: Её лицо изменилось, и вдруг я держал в руках мёртвое тело моей матери.

b1.en: She was wrapped in a burial cloth, and I saw worms in its folds.
b1.ru: Она была завёрнута в саван, и я видел червей в его складках.

b1.en: I woke up in horror.
b1.ru: Я проснулся в ужасе.

b1.en: My forehead was covered in cold sweat, my teeth were chattering and my whole body was shaking.
b1.ru: Лоб был покрыт холодным потом, зубы стучали, всё тело трясло.

b1.en: Then, in the weak yellow light of the moon that came through the shutters, I saw him—the terrible monster I had made.
b1.ru: И тут в слабом жёлтом свете луны, проникавшем сквозь ставни, я увидел его — страшное чудовище, которое я создал.

b1.en: He was holding up the curtain of my bed, and his eyes, if you can call them eyes, were looking at me.
b1.ru: Он приподнимал полог моей кровати, и его глаза, если их можно так назвать, смотрели на меня.

b1.en: He opened his mouth and made some strange sounds, and a grin appeared on his face.
b1.ru: Он открыл рот и издал какие-то странные звуки, и на его лице появилась ухмылка.

b1.en: Perhaps he said something, but I did not hear it.
b1.ru: Может быть, он что-то сказал, но я не услышал.

b1.en: He put out one hand, maybe to stop me, but I escaped and ran downstairs.
b1.ru: Он протянул руку, может быть, чтобы остановить меня, но я вырвался и сбежал вниз.

b1.en: I hid in the courtyard of my house and stayed there for the rest of the night.
b1.ru: Я спрятался во дворе своего дома и оставался там до конца ночи.

b1.en: I walked up and down, very frightened, listening to every sound.
b1.ru: Я ходил взад-вперёд, очень напуганный, прислушиваясь к каждому звуку.

b1.en: Every sound made me afraid that the terrible living corpse was coming.
b1.ru: Каждый звук заставлял меня бояться, что приближается страшный живой мертвец.

b1.en: Oh!
b1.ru: О!

b1.en: No person could look at that face without horror.
b1.ru: Ни один человек не смог бы смотреть на это лицо без ужаса.

b1.en: Even a mummy that came back to life could not be as ugly as he was.
b1.ru: Даже ожившая мумия не могла бы быть такой уродливой, как он.

b1.en: I had looked at him before he was finished, and he was ugly then too.
b1.ru: Я видел его, пока он был не закончен, и он уже тогда был уродлив.

b1.en: But when his muscles and joints could move, he became something more horrible than even Dante could imagine.
b1.ru: Но когда его мышцы и суставы смогли двигаться, он стал чем-то ужаснее всего, что мог вообразить даже Данте.

b1.en: It was a terrible night.
b1.ru: Это была ужасная ночь.

b1.en: Sometimes my heart beat so fast and so hard that I could feel it everywhere in my body.
b1.ru: Иногда сердце билось так быстро и сильно, что я чувствовал его во всём теле.

b1.en: At other times I was so weak that I nearly fell to the ground.
b1.ru: В другие минуты я был так слаб, что чуть не падал на землю.

b1.en: As well as horror, I felt bitter disappointment.
b1.ru: Кроме ужаса, я чувствовал горькое разочарование.

b1.en: The dreams that had kept me going for so long were now like hell.
b1.ru: Мечты, которые так долго поддерживали меня, теперь стали похожи на ад.

b1.en: Everything had changed so quickly and so completely!
b1.ru: Всё изменилось так быстро и так полностью!

b1.en: At last a dark, wet morning came.
b1.ru: Наконец наступило тёмное, сырое утро.

b1.en: With my tired, painful eyes I saw the church of Ingolstadt, with its white tower and its clock, which showed six o’clock.
b1.ru: Усталыми, больными глазами я увидел церковь Ингольштадта с белой башней и часами, которые показывали шесть.

b1.en: The porter opened the gates of the courtyard, and I went out into the streets.
b1.ru: Привратник открыл ворота двора, и я вышел на улицу.

b1.en: I walked very fast, as if I wanted to escape from the monster, because I was afraid to see him around every corner.
b1.ru: Я шёл очень быстро, будто хотел убежать от чудовища, потому что боялся увидеть его за каждым углом.

b1.en: I did not dare to go back to my rooms, so I hurried on, although the heavy rain from the black sky made me completely wet.
b1.ru: Я не смел вернуться к себе и спешил дальше, хотя сильный дождь с чёрного неба промочил меня насквозь.

b1.en: I walked like this for some time, hoping that the exercise would make my mind feel lighter.
b1.ru: Я шёл так некоторое время, надеясь, что движение облегчит мне душу.

b1.en: I went through the streets without really knowing where I was or what I was doing.
b1.ru: Я шёл по улицам, толком не понимая, где я и что делаю.

b1.en: My heart was beating with fear, and I hurried on without looking around.
b1.ru: Сердце колотилось от страха, и я спешил вперёд, не оглядываясь.

b1.en: I was like the man in Coleridge’s famous poem who walks along a lonely road and never turns his head, because he knows that a terrible devil is walking close behind him.
b1.ru: Я был похож на человека из знаменитой поэмы Кольриджа, который идёт по пустынной дороге и никогда не поворачивает головы, потому что знает, что за ним по пятам идёт страшный дьявол.

b1.en: At last I came to the inn where the coaches usually stopped.
b1.ru: Наконец я подошёл к гостинице, где обычно останавливались дилижансы.

b1.en: I stopped here, but I did not know why.
b1.ru: Здесь я остановился, сам не зная почему.

b1.en: For a few minutes I watched a coach that was coming towards me along the street.
b1.ru: Несколько минут я смотрел на карету, которая ехала ко мне по улице.

b1.en: When it came nearer, I saw that it was the coach from Switzerland.
b1.ru: Когда она подъехала ближе, я увидел, что это дилижанс из Швейцарии.

b1.en: It stopped right next to me, the door opened, and I saw Henry Clerval.
b1.ru: Он остановился прямо возле меня, дверца открылась, и я увидел Анри Клерваля.

b1.en: When he saw me, he jumped out at once.
b1.ru: Увидев меня, он тут же выскочил.

b1.en: “My dear Frankenstein,” he said, “I’m so happy to see you!
b1.ru: «Дорогой Франкенштейн, — сказал он, — я так рад тебя видеть!

b1.en: How lucky that you are here just when I arrive!”
b1.ru: Как удачно, что ты здесь как раз тогда, когда я приехал!»

b1.en: I was so happy to see Clerval.
b1.ru: Я был так рад видеть Клерваля.

b1.en: He made me think of my father, Elizabeth and my dear home.
b1.ru: Он напомнил мне об отце, об Элизабет и о милом доме.

b1.en: I took his hand, and at once I forgot my horror and my problems.
b1.ru: Я взял его за руку и сразу забыл о своём ужасе и бедах.

b1.en: For the first time in many months, I suddenly felt calm and happy.
b1.ru: Впервые за много месяцев я вдруг почувствовал себя спокойным и счастливым.

b1.en: I gave my friend a very warm welcome, and we walked towards my college.
b1.ru: Я очень тепло встретил друга, и мы пошли к моему колледжу.

b1.en: Clerval talked for some time about our friends and about how lucky he was to come to Ingolstadt.
b1.ru: Клерваль долго рассказывал о наших друзьях и о том, как ему повезло приехать в Ингольштадт.

b1.en: “You can imagine,” he said, “how difficult it was to persuade my father that there is more to learn than book-keeping.
b1.ru: «Ты можешь себе представить, — сказал он, — как трудно было убедить отца, что учиться можно не только бухгалтерии.

b1.en: I don’t think he ever really believed me.
b1.ru: Не думаю, что он мне по-настоящему поверил.

b1.en: Every time I asked him, he answered like the Dutch teacher in the book The Vicar of Wakefield: ‘I have ten thousand florins a year without Greek, and I eat well without Greek.’
b1.ru: Каждый раз, когда я его просил, он отвечал, как голландский учитель из книги «Векфильдский священник»: „У меня десять тысяч флоринов в год без греческого, и я хорошо ем без греческого“.

b1.en: But in the end he loved me more than he disliked learning, and he let me come here to study.”
b1.ru: Но в конце концов любовь ко мне оказалась сильнее его нелюбви к учёбе, и он отпустил меня сюда учиться».

b1.en: “I’m very happy to see you, but tell me, how were my father, my brothers and Elizabeth when you left?”
b1.ru: «Я очень рад тебя видеть, но скажи, как поживали отец, братья и Элизабет, когда ты уезжал?»

b1.en: “They were very well and very happy, but a little worried because you write to them so rarely.
b1.ru: «Они были здоровы и счастливы, но немного волнуются, потому что ты так редко им пишешь.

b1.en: By the way, I’m going to tell you off a little about that myself.
b1.ru: Кстати, я и сам собираюсь тебя за это немного отругать.

b1.en: But, my dear Frankenstein,” he continued, stopping and looking closely at my face, “I didn’t notice before how ill you look.
b1.ru: Но, дорогой Франкенштейн, — продолжал он, остановившись и внимательно глядя мне в лицо, — я сразу не заметил, какой у тебя больной вид.

b1.en: You are so thin and pale, as if you haven’t slept for several nights.”
b1.ru: Ты такой худой и бледный, как будто не спал несколько ночей».

b1.en: “You’re right.
b1.ru: «Ты прав.

b1.en: Recently I have been so busy with one piece of work that I haven’t rested enough, as you can see.
b1.ru: В последнее время я был так занят одной работой, что мало отдыхал, как видишь.

b1.en: But I hope, I really hope, that all this work is finished now and that I am free at last.”
b1.ru: Но я надеюсь, очень надеюсь, что вся эта работа теперь закончена и я наконец свободен».

b1.en: I was shaking badly.
b1.ru: Меня сильно трясло.

b1.en: I could not even think about what had happened the night before, and I certainly could not talk about it.
b1.ru: Я не мог даже думать о том, что случилось прошлой ночью, и уж тем более не мог об этом говорить.

b1.en: I walked fast, and soon we arrived at my college.
b1.ru: Я шёл быстро, и вскоре мы пришли к моему колледжу.

b1.en: Then I had a thought that made me shiver: perhaps the creature was still in my rooms, alive and walking around.
b1.ru: Тут мне пришла мысль, от которой я задрожал: может быть, существо всё ещё у меня в комнатах, живое и бродит по ним.

b1.en: I was afraid to see the monster, but I was even more afraid that Henry would see him.
b1.ru: Я боялся увидеть чудовище, но ещё больше боялся, что его увидит Анри.

b1.en: So I asked Henry to wait for a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs, and I ran up to my room.
b1.ru: Поэтому я попросил Анри подождать несколько минут внизу у лестницы и побежал наверх, к себе.

b1.en: My hand was already on the door when I stopped.
b1.ru: Моя рука была уже на двери, когда я остановился.

b1.en: I felt cold and started to shiver.
b1.ru: Мне стало холодно, и меня начало трясти.

b1.en: I threw the door open, like children do when they think a ghost is waiting behind it, but nothing was there.
b1.ru: Я распахнул дверь, как делают дети, когда думают, что за ней ждёт привидение, но там никого не было.

b1.en: I stepped in nervously.
b1.ru: Я робко вошёл.

b1.en: The rooms were empty, and the terrible visitor was not in my bedroom either.
b1.ru: Комнаты были пусты, и в спальне страшного гостя тоже не было.

b1.en: I could hardly believe my good luck.
b1.ru: Я едва мог поверить своему счастью.

b1.en: When I was sure that my enemy had really gone, I clapped my hands with joy and ran down to Clerval.
b1.ru: Когда я убедился, что мой враг действительно ушёл, я захлопал в ладоши от радости и сбежал вниз к Клервалю.

b1.en: We went up to my room, and soon the servant brought breakfast, but I could not control myself.
b1.ru: Мы поднялись ко мне, и вскоре слуга принёс завтрак, но я не мог сдержаться.

b1.en: It was not only joy that I felt.
b1.ru: Я чувствовал не только радость.

b1.en: My skin was tingling, and my heart was beating fast.
b1.ru: Кожу покалывало, а сердце билось быстро.

b1.en: I could not stay still for a moment; I jumped over the chairs, clapped my hands and laughed loudly.
b1.ru: Я ни минуты не мог усидеть на месте: перепрыгивал через стулья, хлопал в ладоши и громко смеялся.

b1.en: At first Clerval thought that I was just happy because he had arrived.
b1.ru: Сначала Клерваль подумал, что я просто рад его приезду.

b1.en: But when he looked at me more carefully, he saw a strange wildness in my eyes, and my loud, crazy laughter frightened him.
b1.ru: Но когда он присмотрелся ко мне внимательнее, он увидел в моих глазах странную дикость, и мой громкий безумный смех напугал его.

b1.en: “My dear Victor,” he cried, “what’s wrong, for God’s sake?
b1.ru: «Дорогой Виктор, — воскликнул он, — ради бога, что с тобой?

b1.en: Don’t laugh like that.
b1.ru: Не смейся так.

b1.en: You are so ill!
b1.ru: Ты так болен!

b1.en: What is the reason for all this?”
b1.ru: В чём причина всего этого?»

b1.en: “Don’t ask me,” I cried, and I covered my eyes with my hands, because I thought I saw the terrible ghost come into the room.
b1.ru: «Не спрашивай меня, — закричал я и закрыл глаза руками, потому что мне показалось, что в комнату вошёл страшный призрак.

b1.en: “He can tell you.
b1.ru: Он может тебе сказать.

b1.en: Oh, save me!
b1.ru: О, спаси меня!

b1.en: Save me!”
b1.ru: Спаси!»

b1.en: I imagined that the monster was holding me; I fought hard and then fell to the floor unconscious.
b1.ru: Мне почудилось, что чудовище держит меня; я изо всех сил отбивался, а потом без сознания упал на пол.

b1.en: Poor Clerval!
b1.ru: Бедный Клерваль!

b1.en: How must he have felt?
b1.ru: Что он должен был чувствовать?

b1.en: He had expected such a happy meeting, and it became so strange and sad.
b1.ru: Он ждал такой радостной встречи, а она стала такой странной и печальной.

b1.en: But I did not see his sadness, because I was unconscious for a very long time.
b1.ru: Но я не видел его печали, потому что очень долго был без сознания.

b1.en: This was the beginning of a nervous illness which kept me in bed for several months.
b1.ru: Так началась нервная болезнь, которая на несколько месяцев уложила меня в постель.

b1.en: During all that time Henry was the only person who looked after me.
b1.ru: Всё это время Анри был единственным, кто ухаживал за мной.

b1.en: Later I learned that he did not tell my family how ill I was.
b1.ru: Позже я узнал, что он не рассказал моей семье, как сильно я болен.

b1.en: He knew that my father was too old for such a long journey and that Elizabeth would be very unhappy.
b1.ru: Он знал, что отец слишком стар для такого долгого пути и что Элизабет будет очень несчастна.

b1.en: He also knew that nobody could look after me better than he could.
b1.ru: Он также знал, что никто не сможет ухаживать за мной лучше, чем он.

b1.en: He believed that I would get better, so he was sure he was doing the kindest thing for them.
b1.ru: Он верил, что я поправлюсь, и поэтому был уверен, что поступает с ними как можно добрее.

b1.en: But really I was very ill, and only my friend’s endless care could have saved my life.
b1.ru: Но на самом деле я был очень болен, и только бесконечная забота друга могла спасти мне жизнь.

b1.en: I could always see the monster in front of my eyes, and I talked about him all the time.
b1.ru: Я всё время видел чудовище перед глазами и постоянно говорил о нём.

b1.en: Of course, my words surprised Henry.
b1.ru: Конечно, мои слова удивляли Анри.

b1.en: At first he thought that they came from my sick mind.
b1.ru: Сначала он думал, что это бред больного.

b1.en: But I talked about the same thing again and again, so he became sure that some strange and terrible event had caused my illness.
b1.ru: Но я снова и снова говорил об одном и том же, и он убедился, что мою болезнь вызвало какое-то странное и ужасное событие.

b1.en: I got better very slowly, and I often became ill again, which worried and upset my friend.
b1.ru: Я поправлялся очень медленно и часто снова заболевал, что тревожило и огорчало моего друга.

b1.en: I remember the first time I could look at things outside with some pleasure.
b1.ru: Я помню, как в первый раз смог с каким-то удовольствием посмотреть на то, что за окном.

b1.en: I saw that the dead leaves had gone and that there were new buds on the trees outside my window.
b1.ru: Я увидел, что сухие листья исчезли, а на деревьях за моим окном появились новые почки.

b1.en: It was a wonderful spring, and it helped me a lot to get well.
b1.ru: Весна была чудесная, и она очень помогла мне выздороветь.

b1.en: I began to feel joy and love again; my sadness disappeared, and soon I was as cheerful as I had been before my terrible passion began.
b1.ru: Я снова начал чувствовать радость и любовь; грусть исчезла, и вскоре я стал так же весел, как до того, как началась моя роковая страсть.

b1.en: “Dear Clerval,” I said, “you are so kind and so good to me.
b1.ru: «Дорогой Клерваль, — сказал я, — ты так добр ко мне.

b1.en: You wanted to study this winter, but instead you spent the whole winter in my sickroom.
b1.ru: Ты хотел учиться этой зимой, а вместо этого провёл всю зиму у постели больного.

b1.en: How can I ever pay you back?
b1.ru: Как мне когда-нибудь тебя отблагодарить?

b1.en: I feel very sorry that I have disappointed you, but I know you will forgive me.”
b1.ru: Мне очень жаль, что я тебя подвёл, но я знаю, что ты меня простишь».

b1.en: “You will pay me back completely if you stay calm and get well as fast as you can.
b1.ru: «Ты полностью отблагодаришь меня, если будешь спокоен и поправишься как можно скорее.

b1.en: And since you seem so cheerful, can I talk to you about one thing?”
b1.ru: А раз уж ты так весел, можно мне поговорить с тобой об одном деле?»

b1.en: I started to shake.
b1.ru: Я задрожал.

b1.en: One thing!
b1.ru: Об одном деле!

b1.en: What could it be?
b1.ru: Что бы это могло быть?

b1.en: Was he going to talk about the creature that I did not even dare to think about?
b1.ru: Неужели он заговорит о существе, о котором я даже думать не смел?

b1.en: “Calm down,” said Clerval, who saw that my face had changed colour.
b1.ru: «Успокойся, — сказал Клерваль, заметив, что я изменился в лице.

b1.en: “I won’t talk about it if it upsets you.
b1.ru: — Я не буду об этом говорить, если это тебя расстраивает.

b1.en: But your father and your cousin would be very happy to get a letter in your own handwriting.
b1.ru: Но твой отец и кузина были бы очень рады получить письмо, написанное твоей рукой.

b1.en: They don’t really know how ill you have been, and they are worried because you haven’t written for so long.”
b1.ru: Они толком не знают, как сильно ты болел, и волнуются, потому что ты так долго не писал».

b1.en: “Is that all, my dear Henry?
b1.ru: «И это всё, дорогой Анри?

b1.en: Of course my first thoughts are about my dear family, whom I love and who deserve my love so much!”
b1.ru: Конечно, мои первые мысли — о моей дорогой семье, которую я люблю и которая так заслуживает моей любви!»

b1.en: “If that is how you feel, my friend, you will probably be happy to see a letter that has been waiting here for you for a few days.
b1.ru: «Если ты так настроен, друг мой, то, наверное, будешь рад увидеть письмо, которое уже несколько дней ждёт тебя здесь.

b1.en: I think it’s from your cousin.”
b1.ru: Кажется, оно от твоей кузины».

a2.en: It was a dark and rainy night in November.
a2.ru: Была тёмная дождливая ноябрьская ночь.

a2.en: My work was finished at last.
a2.ru: Моя работа наконец была закончена.

a2.en: I was very nervous.
a2.ru: Я очень волновался.

a2.en: I wanted to put life into the dead body on the floor.
a2.ru: Я хотел вдохнуть жизнь в мёртвое тело на полу.

a2.en: It was one o’clock in the morning, and my candle was almost finished.
a2.ru: Был час ночи, и моя свеча почти догорела.

a2.en: Then I saw the creature’s yellow eye open.
a2.ru: И тут я увидел, как открылся жёлтый глаз существа.

a2.en: It breathed hard, and its arms and legs moved.
a2.ru: Оно тяжело задышало, и его руки и ноги задвигались.

a2.en: How can I tell you about my feelings at that moment?
a2.ru: Как рассказать тебе о моих чувствах в ту минуту?

a2.en: I worked very hard to make him, and I chose beautiful parts for his face.
a2.ru: Я очень много работал, чтобы создать его, и выбрал для его лица красивые черты.

a2.en: Beautiful!
a2.ru: Красивые!

a2.en: Oh God!
a2.ru: Боже!

a2.en: His yellow skin was very thin.
a2.ru: Его жёлтая кожа была очень тонкой.

a2.en: His hair was black and his teeth were white.
a2.ru: Волосы у него были чёрные, а зубы белые.

a2.en: But his eyes were pale and watery, and his lips were black.
a2.ru: Но глаза были бледные и водянистые, а губы чёрные.

a2.en: He was horrible, not beautiful.
a2.ru: Он был ужасен, а не красив.

a2.en: For almost two years I worked hard to make a dead body live.
a2.ru: Почти два года я упорно работал, чтобы оживить мёртвое тело.

a2.en: I did not rest, and I became ill.
a2.ru: Я не отдыхал и заболел.

a2.en: I wanted it very, very much.
a2.ru: Я очень, очень этого хотел.

a2.en: But now my dream was not beautiful any more.
a2.ru: Но теперь моя мечта больше не была прекрасной.

a2.en: I felt only horror.
a2.ru: Я чувствовал только ужас.

a2.en: I could not look at the creature, so I ran out of the room.
a2.ru: Я не мог смотреть на существо и выбежал из комнаты.

a2.en: I walked up and down in my bedroom for a long time.
a2.ru: Я долго ходил взад-вперёд по спальне.

a2.en: At last I was very tired, and I lay on my bed in my clothes.
a2.ru: Наконец я очень устал и лёг на кровать в одежде.

a2.en: I slept, but I had terrible dreams.
a2.ru: Я уснул, но мне снились страшные сны.

a2.en: In my dream I saw Elizabeth in the streets of Ingolstadt.
a2.ru: Во сне я увидел Элизабет на улицах Ингольштадта.

a2.en: She looked happy and well.
a2.ru: Она выглядела счастливой и здоровой.

a2.en: I kissed her, but her lips became grey, like a dead person’s lips.
a2.ru: Я поцеловал её, но её губы стали серыми, как у мёртвой.

a2.en: Then she changed into my dead mother, and I saw worms in her clothes.
a2.ru: Потом она превратилась в мою умершую мать, и я увидел червей в её одежде.

a2.en: I woke up, and I was very frightened.
a2.ru: Я проснулся, и мне было очень страшно.

a2.en: I was cold, and my body was shaking.
a2.ru: Мне было холодно, и всё тело тряслось.

a2.en: In the yellow light of the moon, I saw the monster.
a2.ru: В жёлтом свете луны я увидел чудовище.

a2.en: He was next to my bed, and his eyes were looking at me.
a2.ru: Он стоял возле кровати, и его глаза смотрели на меня.

a2.en: He opened his mouth and made some sounds.
a2.ru: Он открыл рот и издал какие-то звуки.

a2.en: He smiled.
a2.ru: Он улыбнулся.

a2.en: He put out his hand to stop me, but I ran downstairs.
a2.ru: Он протянул руку, чтобы остановить меня, но я сбежал вниз.

a2.en: I stayed in the yard of my house for the rest of the night.
a2.ru: Я провёл остаток ночи во дворе своего дома.

a2.en: I walked up and down and listened to every sound.
a2.ru: Я ходил взад-вперёд и прислушивался к каждому звуку.

a2.en: I was afraid that the monster was coming.
a2.ru: Я боялся, что чудовище идёт за мной.

a2.en: Oh!
a2.ru: О!

a2.en: Nobody could look at that face.
a2.ru: Никто не смог бы смотреть на это лицо.

a2.en: He was uglier than a mummy.
a2.ru: Он был уродливее мумии.

a2.en: He was ugly before, when he was not finished.
a2.ru: Он был уродлив и раньше, когда был не закончен.

a2.en: But when he could move, he became even more horrible.
a2.ru: Но когда он смог двигаться, он стал ещё ужаснее.

a2.en: It was a terrible night.
a2.ru: Это была ужасная ночь.

a2.en: Sometimes my heart beat very fast.
a2.ru: Иногда сердце билось очень быстро.

a2.en: Sometimes I felt so weak that I almost fell down.
a2.ru: Иногда я чувствовал себя таким слабым, что чуть не падал.

a2.en: I was also very sad.
a2.ru: Мне было и очень грустно.

a2.en: My beautiful dream was now a bad dream.
a2.ru: Моя прекрасная мечта теперь стала страшным сном.

a2.en: Everything changed so quickly!
a2.ru: Всё изменилось так быстро!

a2.en: At last morning came.
a2.ru: Наконец наступило утро.

a2.en: It was grey and wet.
a2.ru: Оно было серым и сырым.

a2.en: The church clock showed six o’clock.
a2.ru: Церковные часы показывали шесть.

a2.en: A man opened the gates, and I went into the street.
a2.ru: Сторож открыл ворота, и я вышел на улицу.

a2.en: I walked very fast.
a2.ru: Я шёл очень быстро.

a2.en: I was afraid to see the monster on every corner.
a2.ru: Я боялся увидеть чудовище на каждом углу.

a2.en: I did not want to go home, so I walked on in the rain.
a2.ru: Я не хотел идти домой и шёл дальше под дождём.

a2.en: I walked for a long time.
a2.ru: Я долго шёл.

a2.en: I did not know where I was going.
a2.ru: Я не знал, куда иду.

a2.en: My heart was beating with fear, and I did not look behind me.
a2.ru: Сердце колотилось от страха, и я не оглядывался.

a2.en: I was like the man in a famous poem who walks on a lonely road.
a2.ru: Я был похож на человека из знаменитой поэмы, который идёт по пустынной дороге.

a2.en: He never looks back, because he knows that a terrible devil is walking behind him.
a2.ru: Он никогда не оглядывается, потому что знает, что за ним идёт страшный дьявол.

a2.en: At last I came to a hotel where the coaches stopped.
a2.ru: Наконец я пришёл к гостинице, где останавливались кареты.

a2.en: I stopped too.
a2.ru: Я тоже остановился.

a2.en: I don’t know why.
a2.ru: Не знаю почему.

a2.en: A coach from Switzerland came along the street and stopped next to me.
a2.ru: По улице подъехала карета из Швейцарии и остановилась рядом со мной.

a2.en: The door opened, and I saw Henry Clerval!
a2.ru: Дверца открылась, и я увидел Анри Клерваля!

a2.en: He jumped out.
a2.ru: Он выпрыгнул из кареты.

a2.en: “My dear Frankenstein!” he said.
a2.ru: «Дорогой Франкенштейн! — сказал он.

a2.en: “I’m so happy to see you!”
a2.ru: — Я так рад тебя видеть!»

a2.en: I was very happy to see Clerval.
a2.ru: Я был очень рад видеть Клерваля.

a2.en: He made me think of my father, Elizabeth and my home.
a2.ru: Он напомнил мне об отце, об Элизабет и о доме.

a2.en: I took his hand and forgot my fear.
a2.ru: Я взял его за руку и забыл свой страх.

a2.en: For the first time in many months, I felt calm and happy.
a2.ru: Впервые за много месяцев я почувствовал себя спокойным и счастливым.

a2.en: We walked to my college together.
a2.ru: Мы вместе пошли к моему колледжу.

a2.en: Clerval talked about our friends.
a2.ru: Клерваль рассказывал о наших друзьях.

a2.en: He was very happy to be in Ingolstadt.
a2.ru: Он был очень рад оказаться в Ингольштадте.

a2.en: “It was difficult to get my father’s permission to come here,” he said.
a2.ru: «Было трудно получить разрешение отца приехать сюда, — сказал он.

a2.en: “He thinks that business is the only important thing to learn.
a2.ru: — Он думает, что учиться важно только торговле.

a2.en: He always says, ‘I don’t need Greek to earn money or to eat well.’
a2.ru: Он всегда говорит: „Мне не нужен греческий, чтобы зарабатывать деньги или хорошо есть“.

a2.en: But he loves me, so in the end he said yes.”
a2.ru: Но он любит меня, и в конце концов он согласился».

a2.en: “I’m very happy to see you, but how are my father, my brothers and Elizabeth?”
a2.ru: «Я очень рад тебя видеть, но как поживают отец, братья и Элизабет?»

a2.en: “They are well and happy, but they are a little worried because you don’t write often.
a2.ru: «Они здоровы и счастливы, но немного волнуются, потому что ты редко пишешь.

a2.en: But, my dear Frankenstein,” he said, and he looked at my face, “you look ill!
a2.ru: Но, дорогой Франкенштейн, — сказал он и посмотрел мне в лицо, — у тебя больной вид!

a2.en: You are very thin and pale.
a2.ru: Ты очень худой и бледный.

a2.en: Did you sleep at all last week?”
a2.ru: Ты вообще спал на прошлой неделе?»

a2.en: “You’re right.
a2.ru: «Ты прав.

a2.en: I was very busy with some work, and I didn’t rest enough.
a2.ru: Я был очень занят одной работой и мало отдыхал.

a2.en: But I hope that the work is finished now and I am free.”
a2.ru: Но я надеюсь, что работа теперь закончена и я свободен».

a2.en: I was shaking.
a2.ru: Меня трясло.

a2.en: I could not think about the night before.
a2.ru: Я не мог думать о прошлой ночи.

a2.en: Soon we arrived at my college.
a2.ru: Вскоре мы пришли к колледжу.

a2.en: Then I had a terrible thought.
a2.ru: Тут мне пришла страшная мысль.

a2.en: Perhaps the monster was still in my rooms!
a2.ru: Может быть, чудовище всё ещё у меня в комнатах!

a2.en: I did not want to see him, and I did not want Henry to see him.
a2.ru: Я не хотел его видеть и не хотел, чтобы его увидел Анри.

a2.en: I asked Henry to wait downstairs, and I ran up to my room.
a2.ru: Я попросил Анри подождать внизу и побежал наверх, к себе.

a2.en: At the door I stopped.
a2.ru: У двери я остановился.

a2.en: I felt cold.
a2.ru: Мне стало холодно.

a2.en: I opened the door quickly, like a child who is afraid of a ghost.
a2.ru: Я быстро открыл дверь, как ребёнок, который боится привидения.

a2.en: But nobody was there.
a2.ru: Но там никого не было.

a2.en: The rooms were empty!
a2.ru: Комнаты были пусты!

a2.en: The monster was gone.
a2.ru: Чудовище ушло.

a2.en: I clapped my hands and ran down to Clerval.
a2.ru: Я захлопал в ладоши и сбежал вниз к Клервалю.

a2.en: We went up to my room, and the servant brought breakfast.
a2.ru: Мы поднялись ко мне, и слуга принёс завтрак.

a2.en: But I could not sit still.
a2.ru: Но я не мог усидеть на месте.

a2.en: My heart was beating fast.
a2.ru: Сердце билось быстро.

a2.en: I jumped over the chairs, clapped my hands and laughed loudly.
a2.ru: Я перепрыгивал через стулья, хлопал в ладоши и громко смеялся.

a2.en: At first Clerval thought that I was happy because he was here.
a2.ru: Сначала Клерваль подумал, что я рад его приезду.

a2.en: Then he saw my wild eyes, and my laugh frightened him.
a2.ru: Потом он увидел мои дикие глаза, и мой смех напугал его.

a2.en: “Victor!” he said.
a2.ru: «Виктор! — сказал он.

a2.en: “What’s wrong?
a2.ru: — Что с тобой?

a2.en: Don’t laugh like that.
a2.ru: Не смейся так.

a2.en: You are very ill!”
a2.ru: Ты очень болен!»

a2.en: “Don’t ask me!” I cried.
a2.ru: «Не спрашивай меня! — закричал я.

a2.en: I covered my eyes, because I thought I saw the monster in the room.
a2.ru: Я закрыл глаза руками, потому что мне показалось, что я вижу чудовище в комнате.

a2.en: “Help me!
a2.ru: «Помоги мне!

a2.en: Help me!”
a2.ru: Помоги!»

a2.en: I thought that the monster was holding me.
a2.ru: Мне казалось, что чудовище держит меня.

a2.en: I fought, and then I fell down.
a2.ru: Я отбивался, а потом упал.

a2.en: Poor Clerval!
a2.ru: Бедный Клерваль!

a2.en: He wanted a happy meeting, but it was a sad one.
a2.ru: Он хотел радостной встречи, а она получилась печальной.

a2.en: I did not wake up for a long, long time.
a2.ru: Я очень, очень долго не приходил в себя.

a2.en: I was ill with a fever for several months.
a2.ru: Несколько месяцев я болел горячкой.

a2.en: Henry looked after me all that time.
a2.ru: Всё это время Анри ухаживал за мной.

a2.en: He did not tell my family that I was very ill.
a2.ru: Он не сказал моей семье, что я очень болен.

a2.en: My father was too old for the long journey, and Elizabeth would be very sad.
a2.ru: Отец был слишком стар для долгого пути, а Элизабет очень бы огорчилась.

a2.en: Henry knew that nobody could look after me better than him.
a2.ru: Анри знал, что никто не позаботится обо мне лучше, чем он.

a2.en: He was sure that I was going to get better.
a2.ru: Он был уверен, что я поправлюсь.

a2.en: I was really very ill.
a2.ru: Я был действительно очень болен.

a2.en: Only my friend’s care saved my life.
a2.ru: Только забота друга спасла мне жизнь.

a2.en: I saw the monster in front of my eyes all the time, and I talked about him.
a2.ru: Я всё время видел чудовище перед глазами и говорил о нём.

a2.en: At first Henry thought that I was just ill in my mind.
a2.ru: Сначала Анри думал, что это просто бред больного.

a2.en: But I talked about the same thing again and again.
a2.ru: Но я снова и снова говорил об одном и том же.

a2.en: So he understood that something terrible had happened to me.
a2.ru: И он понял, что со мной случилось что-то ужасное.

a2.en: Very slowly, I got better.
a2.ru: Очень медленно я поправлялся.

a2.en: Sometimes I was ill again, and my friend was worried.
a2.ru: Иногда мне снова становилось хуже, и мой друг волновался.

a2.en: One day I looked out of the window.
a2.ru: Однажды я выглянул в окно.

a2.en: The old leaves were gone, and there were new leaves on the trees.
a2.ru: Старые листья исчезли, и на деревьях появились новые.

a2.en: It was a beautiful spring, and it helped me.
a2.ru: Весна была прекрасная, и она мне помогла.

a2.en: I felt happy again, and soon I was cheerful, like before.
a2.ru: Я снова почувствовал себя счастливым и вскоре стал весёлым, как раньше.

a2.en: “Dear Clerval,” I said, “you are so kind to me.
a2.ru: «Дорогой Клерваль, — сказал я, — ты так добр ко мне.

a2.en: You wanted to study this winter, but you stayed with me in my room.
a2.ru: Ты хотел учиться этой зимой, но остался со мной в моей комнате.

a2.en: How can I thank you?
a2.ru: Как мне тебя отблагодарить?

a2.en: I’m sorry.”
a2.ru: Прости меня».

a2.en: “Just get well quickly.
a2.ru: «Просто поскорее поправляйся.

a2.en: That is enough for me.
a2.ru: Мне этого достаточно.

a2.en: Now, can I talk to you about one thing?”
a2.ru: А теперь можно мне поговорить с тобой об одном деле?»

a2.en: I started to shake.
a2.ru: Я задрожал.

a2.en: What was it?
a2.ru: О каком?

a2.en: Did he want to talk about the monster?
a2.ru: Неужели он хочет поговорить о чудовище?

a2.en: “Don’t worry,” said Clerval.
a2.ru: «Не волнуйся, — сказал Клерваль.

a2.en: “Your father and your cousin want a letter from you.
a2.ru: — Твой отец и кузина ждут от тебя письма.

a2.en: They are worried because you haven’t written for a long time.”
a2.ru: Они волнуются, потому что ты давно не писал».

a2.en: “Is that all?
a2.ru: «И это всё?

a2.en: Of course I want to write to my dear family!”
a2.ru: Конечно, я хочу написать моей дорогой семье!»

a2.en: “Good.
a2.ru: «Хорошо.

a2.en: There is a letter for you here.
a2.ru: Здесь для тебя есть письмо.

a2.en: I think it is from your cousin.”
a2.ru: Кажется, оно от твоей кузины».

sub: Victor reads a long letter from Elizabeth about home and Justine, recovers, turns away from science and studies oriental languages with Clerval, and regains his joy on a spring walking tour

o:
Clerval then put the following letter into my hands. It was from my own Elizabeth:

“My dearest Cousin,

“You have been ill, very ill, and even the constant letters of dear kind Henry are not sufficient to reassure me on your account. You are forbidden to write—to hold a pen; yet one word from you, dear Victor, is necessary to calm our apprehensions. For a long time I have thought that each post would bring this line, and my persuasions have restrained my uncle from undertaking a journey to Ingolstadt. I have prevented his encountering the inconveniences and perhaps dangers of so long a journey, yet how often have I regretted not being able to perform it myself! I figure to myself that the task of attending on your sickbed has devolved on some mercenary old nurse, who could never guess your wishes nor minister to them with the care and affection of your poor cousin. Yet that is over now: Clerval writes that indeed you are getting better. I eagerly hope that you will confirm this intelligence soon in your own handwriting.

“Get well—and return to us. You will find a happy, cheerful home and friends who love you dearly. Your father’s health is vigorous, and he asks but to see you, but to be assured that you are well; and not a care will ever cloud his benevolent countenance. How pleased you would be to remark the improvement of our Ernest! He is now sixteen and full of activity and spirit.

He is desirous to be a true Swiss and to enter into foreign service, but we cannot part with him, at least until his elder brother returns to us. My uncle is not pleased with the idea of a military career in a distant country, but Ernest never had your powers of application. He looks upon study as an odious fetter; his time is spent in the open air, climbing the hills or rowing on the lake. I fear that he will become an idler unless we yield the point and permit him to enter on the profession which he has selected.

“Little alteration, except the growth of our dear children, has taken place since you left us. The blue lake and snow-clad mountains—they never change; and I think our placid home and our contented hearts are regulated by the same immutable laws. My trifling occupations take up my time and amuse me, and I am rewarded for any exertions by seeing none but happy, kind faces around me.

Since you left us, but one change has taken place in our little household. Do you remember on what occasion Justine Moritz entered our family? Probably you do not; I will relate her history, therefore in a few words. Madame Moritz, her mother, was a widow with four children, of whom Justine was the third. This girl had always been the favourite of her father, but through a strange perversity, her mother could not endure her, and after the death of M. Moritz, treated her very ill. My aunt observed this, and when Justine was twelve years of age, prevailed on her mother to allow her to live at our house.

The republican institutions of our country have produced simpler and happier manners than those which prevail in the great monarchies that surround it. Hence there is less distinction between the several classes of its inhabitants; and the lower orders, being neither so poor nor so despised, their manners are more refined and moral. A servant in Geneva does not mean the same thing as a servant in France and England. Justine, thus received in our family, learned the duties of a servant, a condition which, in our fortunate country, does not include the idea of ignorance and a sacrifice of the dignity of a human being.

“Justine, you may remember, was a great favourite of yours; and I recollect you once remarked that if you were in an ill humour, one glance from Justine could dissipate it, for the same reason that Ariosto gives concerning the beauty of Angelica—she looked so frank-hearted and happy. My aunt conceived a great attachment for her, by which she was induced to give her an education superior to that which she had at first intended. This benefit was fully repaid; Justine was the most grateful little creature in the world: I do not mean that she made any professions I never heard one pass her lips, but you could see by her eyes that she almost adored her protectress. Although her disposition was gay and in many respects inconsiderate, yet she paid the greatest attention to every gesture of my aunt. She thought her the model of all excellence and endeavoured to imitate her phraseology and manners, so that even now she often reminds me of her.

“When my dearest aunt died every one was too much occupied in their own grief to notice poor Justine, who had attended her during her illness with the most anxious affection. Poor Justine was very ill; but other trials were reserved for her.

“One by one, her brothers and sister died; and her mother, with the exception of her neglected daughter, was left childless. The conscience of the woman was troubled; she began to think that the deaths of her favourites was a judgement from heaven to chastise her partiality. She was a Roman Catholic; and I believe her confessor confirmed the idea which she had conceived. Accordingly, a few months after your departure for Ingolstadt, Justine was called home by her repentant mother.

Poor girl! She wept when she quitted our house; she was much altered since the death of my aunt; grief had given softness and a winning mildness to her manners, which had before been remarkable for vivacity. Nor was her residence at her mother’s house of a nature to restore her gaiety. The poor woman was very vacillating in her repentance. She sometimes begged Justine to forgive her unkindness, but much oftener accused her of having caused the deaths of her brothers and sister.

Perpetual fretting at length threw Madame Moritz into a decline, which at first increased her irritability, but she is now at peace for ever. She died on the first approach of cold weather, at the beginning of this last winter. Justine has just returned to us; and I assure you I love her tenderly. She is very clever and gentle, and extremely pretty; as I mentioned before, her mien and her expression continually remind me of my dear aunt.

“I must say also a few words to you, my dear cousin, of little darling William. I wish you could see him; he is very tall of his age, with sweet laughing blue eyes, dark eyelashes, and curling hair. When he smiles, two little dimples appear on each cheek, which are rosy with health. He has already had one or two little wives, but Louisa Biron is his favourite, a pretty little girl of five years of age.

“Now, dear Victor, I dare say you wish to be indulged in a little gossip concerning the good people of Geneva. The pretty Miss Mansfield has already received the congratulatory visits on her approaching marriage with a young Englishman, John Melbourne, Esq. Her ugly sister, Manon, married M. Duvillard, the rich banker, last autumn. Your favourite schoolfellow, Louis Manoir, has suffered several misfortunes since the departure of Clerval from Geneva. But he has already recovered his spirits, and is reported to be on the point of marrying a lively pretty Frenchwoman, Madame Tavernier. She is a widow, and much older than Manoir; but she is very much admired, and a favourite with everybody.

“I have written myself into better spirits, dear cousin; but my anxiety returns upon me as I conclude. Write, dearest Victor,—one line—one word will be a blessing to us. Ten thousand thanks to Henry for his kindness, his affection, and his many letters; we are sincerely grateful. Adieu! my cousin; take care of yourself; and, I entreat you, write!

“Elizabeth Lavenza.

“Geneva, March 18th, 17—.”

“Dear, dear Elizabeth!” I exclaimed, when I had read her letter: “I will write instantly and relieve them from the anxiety they must feel.” I wrote, and this exertion greatly fatigued me; but my convalescence had commenced, and proceeded regularly. In another fortnight I was able to leave my chamber.

One of my first duties on my recovery was to introduce Clerval to the several professors of the university. In doing this, I underwent a kind of rough usage, ill befitting the wounds that my mind had sustained. Ever since the fatal night, the end of my labours, and the beginning of my misfortunes, I had conceived a violent antipathy even to the name of natural philosophy. When I was otherwise quite restored to health, the sight of a chemical instrument would renew all the agony of my nervous symptoms. Henry saw this, and had removed all my apparatus from my view. He had also changed my apartment; for he perceived that I had acquired a dislike for the room which had previously been my laboratory.

But these cares of Clerval were made of no avail when I visited the professors. M. Waldman inflicted torture when he praised, with kindness and warmth, the astonishing progress I had made in the sciences. He soon perceived that I disliked the subject; but not guessing the real cause, he attributed my feelings to modesty, and changed the subject from my improvement, to the science itself, with a desire, as I evidently saw, of drawing me out. What could I do? He meant to please, and he tormented me. I felt as if he had placed carefully, one by one, in my view those instruments which were to be afterwards used in putting me to a slow and cruel death. I writhed under his words, yet dared not exhibit the pain I felt.

Clerval, whose eyes and feelings were always quick in discerning the sensations of others, declined the subject, alleging, in excuse, his total ignorance; and the conversation took a more general turn. I thanked my friend from my heart, but I did not speak. I saw plainly that he was surprised, but he never attempted to draw my secret from me; and although I loved him with a mixture of affection and reverence that knew no bounds, yet I could never persuade myself to confide in him that event which was so often present to my recollection, but which I feared the detail to another would only impress more deeply.

M. Krempe was not equally docile; and in my condition at that time, of almost insupportable sensitiveness, his harsh blunt encomiums gave me even more pain than the benevolent approbation of M. Waldman. “D—n the fellow!” cried he; “why, M. Clerval, I assure you he has outstript us all. Ay, stare if you please; but it is nevertheless true. A youngster who, but a few years ago, believed in Cornelius Agrippa as firmly as in the gospel, has now set himself at the head of the university; and if he is not soon pulled down, we shall all be out of countenance.—Ay, ay,” continued he, observing my face expressive of suffering, “M. Frankenstein is modest; an excellent quality in a young man. Young men should be diffident of themselves, you know, M. Clerval: I was myself when young; but that wears out in a very short time.”

M. Krempe had now commenced an eulogy on himself, which happily turned the conversation from a subject that was so annoying to me.

Clerval had never sympathised in my tastes for natural science; and his literary pursuits differed wholly from those which had occupied me. He came to the university with the design of making himself complete master of the oriental languages, and thus he should open a field for the plan of life he had marked out for himself. Resolved to pursue no inglorious career, he turned his eyes toward the East, as affording scope for his spirit of enterprise. The Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit languages engaged his attention, and I was easily induced to enter on the same studies.

Idleness had ever been irksome to me, and now that I wished to fly from reflection, and hated my former studies, I felt great relief in being the fellow-pupil with my friend, and found not only instruction but consolation in the works of the orientalists. I did not, like him, attempt a critical knowledge of their dialects, for I did not contemplate making any other use of them than temporary amusement. I read merely to understand their meaning, and they well repaid my labours. Their melancholy is soothing, and their joy elevating, to a degree I never experienced in studying the authors of any other country. When you read their writings, life appears to consist in a warm sun and a garden of roses,—in the smiles and frowns of a fair enemy, and the fire that consumes your own heart. How different from the manly and heroical poetry of Greece and Rome!

Summer passed away in these occupations, and my return to Geneva was fixed for the latter end of autumn; but being delayed by several accidents, winter and snow arrived, the roads were deemed impassable, and my journey was retarded until the ensuing spring. I felt this delay very bitterly; for I longed to see my native town and my beloved friends. My return had only been delayed so long, from an unwillingness to leave Clerval in a strange place, before he had become acquainted with any of its inhabitants. The winter, however, was spent cheerfully; and although the spring was uncommonly late, when it came its beauty compensated for its dilatoriness.

The month of May had already commenced, and I expected the letter daily which was to fix the date of my departure, when Henry proposed a pedestrian tour in the environs of Ingolstadt, that I might bid a personal farewell to the country I had so long inhabited. I acceded with pleasure to this proposition: I was fond of exercise, and Clerval had always been my favourite companion in the ramble of this nature that I had taken among the scenes of my native country.

We passed a fortnight in these perambulations: my health and spirits had long been restored, and they gained additional strength from the salubrious air I breathed, the natural incidents of our progress, and the conversation of my friend. Study had before secluded me from the intercourse of my fellow-creatures, and rendered me unsocial; but Clerval called forth the better feelings of my heart; he again taught me to love the aspect of nature, and the cheerful faces of children. Excellent friend! how sincerely you did love me, and endeavour to elevate my mind until it was on a level with your own.

A selfish pursuit had cramped and narrowed me, until your gentleness and affection warmed and opened my senses; I became the same happy creature who, a few years ago, loved and beloved by all, had no sorrow or care. When happy, inanimate nature had the power of bestowing on me the most delightful sensations. A serene sky and verdant fields filled me with ecstasy. The present season was indeed divine; the flowers of spring bloomed in the hedges, while those of summer were already in bud. I was undisturbed by thoughts which during the preceding year had pressed upon me, notwithstanding my endeavours to throw them off, with an invincible burden.

Henry rejoiced in my gaiety, and sincerely sympathised in my feelings: he exerted himself to amuse me, while he expressed the sensations that filled his soul. The resources of his mind on this occasion were truly astonishing: his conversation was full of imagination; and very often, in imitation of the Persian and Arabic writers, he invented tales of wonderful fancy and passion. At other times he repeated my favourite poems, or drew me out into arguments, which he supported with great ingenuity.

We returned to our college on a Sunday afternoon: the peasants were dancing, and every one we met appeared gay and happy. My own spirits were high, and I bounded along with feelings of unbridled joy and hilarity.
b2: Then Clerval handed me the following letter. It was from my own Elizabeth: “My dearest Cousin,

“You have been ill, very ill, and even dear, kind Henry’s frequent letters are not enough to reassure me about you. You are not allowed to write, or even to hold a pen; yet one word from you, dear Victor, is needed to calm our fears. For a long time I have expected every post to bring that line, and only my pleading has stopped my uncle from making the journey to Ingolstadt. I have kept him from the discomforts and perhaps the dangers of such a long journey, yet how often I have wished I could make it myself! I imagine that the job of nursing you has fallen to some mercenary old nurse, who could never guess your wishes or attend to them with the care and affection of your poor cousin. But that is over now: Clerval writes that you really are getting better. I eagerly hope that you will confirm this news soon in your own handwriting.

“Get well, and come back to us. You will find a happy, cheerful home and friends who love you dearly. Your father is in robust health, and all he asks is to see you and to know that you are well; then not a single worry will ever cloud his kindly face. How pleased you would be to see how our Ernest has grown! He is now sixteen and full of energy and spirit.

He longs to be a true Swiss and to serve in a foreign army, but we cannot bear to let him go, at least not until his elder brother comes back to us. My uncle does not like the idea of a military career in a distant country, but Ernest has never had your capacity for hard study. He regards study as a hateful chain; he spends his time in the open air, climbing the hills or rowing on the lake. I fear he will become an idler unless we give in and let him take up the profession he has chosen.

“Little has changed since you left us, apart from the children growing up. The blue lake and the snow-covered mountains never change; and I think our peaceful home and our contented hearts are governed by the same unchanging laws. My small daily tasks fill my time and amuse me, and I am rewarded for any effort by seeing nothing but happy, kind faces around me.

Since you left, only one change has taken place in our little household. Do you remember how Justine Moritz came to join our family? Probably not, so I will tell you her story in a few words. Her mother, Madame Moritz, was a widow with four children, and Justine was the third. This girl had always been her father’s favourite, but by some strange perversity her mother could not stand her, and after Monsieur Moritz died she treated her very badly. My aunt noticed this, and when Justine was twelve she persuaded her mother to let her live in our house.

The republican institutions of our country have produced simpler and happier ways of life than those found in the great monarchies around it. As a result, there is less difference between the social classes; and since the lower classes are neither so poor nor so despised, their manners are more refined and moral. A servant in Geneva is not the same thing as a servant in France or England. So Justine, once taken into our family, learned the duties of a servant, a position which, in our fortunate country, does not imply ignorance or the loss of a person’s dignity.

“You may remember that Justine was a great favourite of yours; I recall you once said that if you were in a bad mood, one glance from Justine could chase it away, for the same reason that Ariosto gives for the beauty of Angelica: she looked so open-hearted and happy. My aunt grew very attached to her, and this led her to give Justine a better education than she had first intended. This kindness was fully repaid; Justine was the most grateful little creature in the world. I do not mean that she ever made speeches of gratitude; I never heard a word of that kind from her, but you could see in her eyes that she almost worshipped her benefactress. Although she was lively by nature and in many ways thoughtless, she paid the closest attention to every gesture of my aunt. She saw her as the model of every virtue and tried to copy her way of speaking and her manners, so that even now she often reminds me of her.

“When my dearest aunt died, everyone was too absorbed in their own grief to notice poor Justine, who had nursed her through her illness with the most anxious devotion. Poor Justine was very ill herself; but further trials were in store for her. “One by one, her brothers and sister died, and her mother was left with no child except the daughter she had neglected. The woman’s conscience was troubled; she began to believe that the deaths of her favourite children were a punishment from heaven for her unfairness. She was a Roman Catholic, and I believe her priest encouraged this idea. So, a few months after you left for Ingolstadt, Justine was called home by her remorseful mother.

Poor girl! She cried when she left our house; she had changed a great deal since my aunt’s death; grief had given a softness and a gentle charm to her manners, which had once been remarkable for their liveliness. Nor was life in her mother’s house likely to bring back her cheerfulness. The poor woman wavered constantly in her repentance. Sometimes she begged Justine to forgive her unkindness, but far more often she accused her of causing the deaths of her brothers and sister.

Constant worry finally brought on a decline in Madame Moritz’s health, which at first made her even more irritable, but she is now at peace for ever. She died when the cold weather first came, at the beginning of this past winter. Justine has just come back to us, and I assure you I love her dearly. She is very clever and gentle, and extremely pretty; as I said before, her bearing and her expression constantly remind me of my dear aunt.

“I must also tell you a little, my dear cousin, about darling little William. I wish you could see him; he is very tall for his age, with sweet, laughing blue eyes, dark eyelashes and curly hair. When he smiles, two little dimples appear in his cheeks, which are rosy with health. He has already had one or two little wives, but his favourite is Louisa Biron, a pretty little girl of five.

“Now, dear Victor, I expect you would like a little gossip about the good people of Geneva. Pretty Miss Mansfield has already received visits of congratulation on her coming marriage to a young Englishman, John Melbourne. Her plain sister, Manon, married Monsieur Duvillard, the rich banker, last autumn. Your favourite schoolfriend, Louis Manoir, has had several misfortunes since Clerval left Geneva. But he has already cheered up, and he is said to be about to marry a lively, pretty Frenchwoman, Madame Tavernier. She is a widow and much older than Manoir, but she is greatly admired and popular with everyone.

“Writing to you has lifted my spirits, dear cousin, but my anxiety comes back as I finish. Write, dearest Victor: one line, one word will be a blessing to us. A thousand thanks to Henry for his kindness, his affection and his many letters; we are truly grateful. Goodbye, my cousin; take care of yourself, and I beg you, write! “Elizabeth Lavenza. “Geneva, 18th March, 17—.”

“Dear, dear Elizabeth!” I exclaimed when I had read her letter, “I will write at once and free them from the anxiety they must be feeling.” I wrote, and the effort exhausted me; but my recovery had begun and went on steadily. Two weeks later I was able to leave my room.

One of my first duties after my recovery was to introduce Clerval to the various professors at the university. In doing this, I went through a kind of rough treatment that was badly suited to the wounds my mind had suffered. Ever since that fatal night, which ended my labours and began my misfortunes, I had felt a violent loathing even for the name of natural philosophy. Even when I was otherwise fully recovered, the sight of a chemical instrument would bring back all the agony of my nervous symptoms. Henry had noticed this and had removed all my equipment from sight. He had also moved me to a different room, because he saw that I had come to dislike the one that had been my laboratory.

But all Clerval’s care was useless when I visited the professors. Professor Waldman tortured me when he praised, kindly and warmly, the astonishing progress I had made in the sciences. He soon noticed that I disliked the subject, but not guessing the real reason, he put my feelings down to modesty and turned from my own progress to the science itself, clearly hoping, as I could see, to draw me out. What could I do? He meant to please me, and he tormented me. I felt as if he were carefully laying out before me, one by one, the instruments that would later be used to put me to a slow and cruel death. I writhed under his words, yet I did not dare to show the pain I felt.

Clerval, whose eyes and heart were always quick to sense what others were feeling, avoided the subject, pleading his complete ignorance of it, and the conversation turned to more general matters. I thanked my friend with all my heart, but I did not speak. I could see clearly that he was surprised, but he never tried to draw my secret out of me; and although I loved him with a boundless mixture of affection and respect, I could never bring myself to confide in him the event that was so often in my thoughts, because I feared that describing it to someone else would only fix it more deeply in my mind.

Professor Krempe was not so gentle; and in my state at that time, when I was almost unbearably sensitive, his harsh, blunt praise hurt me even more than Professor Waldman’s kindly approval. “Damn the fellow!” he cried. “Why, Mr Clerval, I assure you he has outstripped us all. Yes, stare if you like, but it is true all the same. A youngster who only a few years ago believed in Cornelius Agrippa as firmly as in the Gospel has now put himself at the head of the university; and if he is not brought down soon, we shall all be put to shame.” Then, noticing the suffering on my face, he went on: “Ah, yes, Mr Frankenstein is modest; an excellent quality in a young man. Young men should be unsure of themselves, you know, Mr Clerval. I was myself when I was young, but that wears off very quickly.” Krempe then began to praise himself, which, luckily, turned the conversation away from a subject I found so painful.

Clerval had never shared my taste for natural science, and his literary interests were completely different from the ones that had absorbed me. He had come to the university intending to master the oriental languages completely, as this would open a field for the plan of life he had set himself. Determined not to follow an undistinguished career, he looked towards the East, which offered scope for his spirit of enterprise. Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit caught his interest, and I was easily persuaded to take up the same studies.

Idleness had always been tiresome to me, and now that I wanted to escape from my own thoughts and hated my former studies, I felt great relief at being my friend’s fellow student, and I found not only knowledge but comfort in the works of the oriental writers. Unlike him, I did not try to gain a scholarly knowledge of their languages, because I meant to use them only as a passing amusement. I read simply to understand the meaning, and they rewarded my efforts well. Their melancholy is soothing and their joy uplifting to a degree I have never felt when reading the writers of any other country. When you read their works, life seems to consist of a warm sun and a rose garden, of the smiles and frowns of a lovely enemy, and of the fire that burns up your own heart. How different from the manly, heroic poetry of Greece and Rome!

The summer passed in these pursuits, and my return to Geneva was fixed for late autumn; but several mishaps delayed me, then winter and snow arrived, the roads were considered impassable, and my journey was put off until the following spring. I felt this delay very bitterly, because I longed to see my home town and my beloved friends. I had only put off my return for so long because I did not want to leave Clerval in a strange place before he had got to know any of its people. The winter, however, was spent cheerfully; and although spring came unusually late, when it did come its beauty made up for its slowness.

May had already begun, and I was expecting any day the letter that would fix the date of my departure, when Henry suggested a walking tour in the countryside around Ingolstadt, so that I could say a personal farewell to the region where I had lived so long. I gladly agreed: I loved exercise, and Clerval had always been my favourite companion on rambles of this kind among the scenery of my native country.

We spent two weeks on these wanderings: my health and spirits had long been restored, and they grew even stronger thanks to the healthy air I breathed, the small events of our journey and my friend’s conversation. My studies had previously cut me off from contact with other people and made me unsociable; but Clerval brought out the better feelings of my heart; he taught me again to love the face of nature and the cheerful faces of children. Wonderful friend! How sincerely you loved me, and how hard you tried to raise my mind to the level of your own!

A selfish pursuit had cramped and narrowed me, until your gentleness and affection warmed and opened my senses; I became the same happy creature who, a few years before, had been loved by everyone and loving everyone, and had known no sorrow or care. When I was happy, lifeless nature had the power to give me the most delightful sensations. A calm sky and green fields filled me with ecstasy. The season was truly divine; the spring flowers were blooming in the hedges, while the summer ones were already in bud. I was no longer troubled by the thoughts that had weighed on me like an unbearable burden during the previous year, despite all my efforts to throw them off.

Henry was delighted by my cheerfulness and sincerely shared my feelings: he did his best to entertain me, while expressing the feelings that filled his own soul. The resources of his mind at this time were truly astonishing: his conversation was full of imagination, and very often, imitating the Persian and Arabic writers, he made up tales full of wonderful fantasy and passion. At other times he recited my favourite poems or drew me into arguments, which he defended with great ingenuity. We returned to our college on a Sunday afternoon: the peasants were dancing, and everyone we met seemed cheerful and happy. My own spirits were high, and I bounded along, full of unrestrained joy and merriment.
b1: Then Clerval gave me a letter. It was from my dear Elizabeth: “My dearest Cousin,

“You have been very ill, and even Henry’s kind letters cannot stop me worrying about you. You are not allowed to write or even hold a pen, but we need just one word from you, dear Victor, to calm us. For a long time I have hoped that every post would bring this word. I persuaded my uncle not to travel to Ingolstadt, because the journey is long and could be dangerous. But how often I wished I could go myself! I imagine that some old nurse who works only for money is looking after you, and she cannot understand your wishes or care for you as lovingly as your poor cousin would. But that is over now: Clerval writes that you are getting better. I really hope that you will write to tell us this yourself soon.

“Get well and come back to us. You will find a happy home and friends who love you very much. Your father is very healthy, and he only wants to see you and know that you are well. Then nothing will ever make his kind face sad. You would be so pleased to see how much Ernest has changed! He is sixteen now and full of energy.

He wants to be a true Swiss and join a foreign army, but we cannot let him go, at least not before his elder brother comes home. My uncle does not like the idea of a soldier’s life in a faraway country, but Ernest has never been good at studying like you. He thinks that studying is like a prison. He spends his time outside, climbing the hills or rowing on the lake. I am afraid he will become lazy if we do not agree and let him choose the job he wants.

“Not much has changed since you left, except that the children have grown. The blue lake and the snowy mountains never change, and I think our quiet home and our happy hearts follow the same laws. My small jobs fill my days and make me happy, and I see only kind, happy faces around me.

Only one thing has changed in our little home since you left. Do you remember how Justine Moritz came to live with us? Probably not, so I will tell you her story in a few words. Her mother, Madame Moritz, was a widow with four children, and Justine was the third. Her father always loved her most, but for some strange reason her mother could not stand her, and after her husband died she treated Justine very badly. My aunt saw this, and when Justine was twelve, she persuaded her mother to let the girl live in our house.
