a2.ru: Он мог взобраться на такую гору, как Салев!

a2.en: So I decided to say nothing.
a2.ru: Поэтому я решил ничего не говорить.

a2.en: I arrived at my father’s house at five in the morning.
a2.ru: Я приехал в дом отца в пять утра.

a2.en: I told the servants not to wake the family and waited in the library.
a2.ru: Я велел слугам не будить семью и подождал в библиотеке.

a2.en: Six years went by like a dream.
a2.ru: Шесть лет пролетели как сон.

a2.en: I was in the same room where I said goodbye to my father before I went to Ingolstadt.
a2.ru: Я был в той же комнате, где попрощался с отцом перед отъездом в Ингольштадт.

a2.en: My dear father!
a2.ru: Мой дорогой отец!

a2.en: I still had him.
a2.ru: Он у меня ещё был.

a2.en: Over the fireplace there was a picture of my mother, Caroline Beaufort.
a2.ru: Над камином висел портрет моей матери, Каролины Бофор.

a2.en: In it she was kneeling by her dead father, sad but beautiful.
a2.ru: На нём она стояла на коленях у тела умершего отца, печальная, но красивая.

a2.en: Under it there was a small picture of William, and I cried.
a2.ru: Под ним был маленький портрет Уильяма, и я заплакал.

a2.en: Then Ernest came in.
a2.ru: Потом вошёл Эрнест.

a2.en: “Welcome, dear Victor,” he said.
a2.ru: — Добро пожаловать, дорогой Виктор, — сказал он.

a2.en: “Three months ago we were all so happy!
a2.ru: — Три месяца назад мы все были так счастливы!

a2.en: Now everything is sad.
a2.ru: А теперь всё так печально.

a2.en: Please help our father, because he is very unhappy.
a2.ru: Пожалуйста, помоги отцу, потому что он очень несчастен.

a2.en: And please help Elizabeth, because she says it is all her fault.
a2.ru: И, пожалуйста, помоги Элизабет, потому что она говорит, что это всё её вина.

a2.en: Poor William! We loved him so much!”
a2.ru: Бедный Уильям! Мы так его любили!

a2.en: Ernest was crying, and I felt terrible pain.
a2.ru: Эрнест плакал, и мне было ужасно больно.

a2.en: Now I could see how sad my home was.
a2.ru: Теперь я видел, как печально у нас дома.

a2.en: I asked about my father and about Elizabeth.
a2.ru: Я спросил об отце и об Элизабет.

a2.en: “She needs help most of all,” said Ernest.
a2.ru: — Больше всех помощь нужна ей, — сказал Эрнест.

a2.en: “She thought it was her fault.
a2.ru: — Она думала, что это её вина.

a2.en: But now they have found the killer—”
a2.ru: Но теперь убийцу нашли…

a2.en: “Found the killer?
a2.ru: — Нашли убийцу?

a2.en: That’s impossible!
a2.ru: Это невозможно!

a2.en: Nobody can catch him.
a2.ru: Никто не может его поймать.

a2.en: I saw him last night!”
a2.ru: Я видел его вчера ночью!

a2.en: “I don’t understand you,” said Ernest.
a2.ru: — Я тебя не понимаю, — сказал Эрнест.

a2.en: “But it is very sad for us.
a2.ru: — Но для нас это очень грустно.

a2.en: At first nobody believed it, and Elizabeth still does not believe it.
a2.ru: Сначала никто не поверил, и Элизабет до сих пор не верит.

a2.en: Who can believe that Justine Moritz did it?
a2.ru: Кто может поверить, что это сделала Жюстина Мориц?

a2.en: She was so kind and loved us all!”
a2.ru: Она была такой доброй и так нас всех любила!

a2.en: “Justine!
a2.ru: — Жюстина!

a2.en: Poor girl!
a2.ru: Бедная девушка!

a2.en: But it isn’t true, Ernest.
a2.ru: Но это неправда, Эрнест.

a2.en: Nobody believes it, right?”
a2.ru: Никто ведь в это не верит, правда?

a2.en: “Not at first.
a2.ru: — Сначала не верили.

a2.en: But then we found out some things, and she is acting very strangely.
a2.ru: Но потом мы кое-что узнали, и она ведёт себя очень странно.

a2.en: Today she will go to court, and you will hear everything.”
a2.ru: Сегодня её будут судить, и ты всё услышишь.

a2.en: Then he told me the story.
a2.ru: Потом он рассказал мне историю.

a2.en: Justine got ill on the morning after the murder and stayed in bed.
a2.ru: Жюстина заболела наутро после убийства и лежала в постели.

a2.en: A servant looked at the dress that Justine wore that night.
a2.ru: Служанка осмотрела платье, в котором Жюстина была в ту ночь.

a2.en: In the pocket there was the picture of my mother.
a2.ru: В кармане был портрет моей матери.

a2.en: The servants went to a judge, and the police took Justine away.
a2.ru: Слуги пошли к судье, и Жюстину забрали.

a2.en: Justine was very confused, so people thought she was guilty.
a2.ru: Жюстина была очень растеряна, поэтому люди подумали, что она виновна.

a2.en: It was a strange story, but I did not believe it.
a2.ru: Это была странная история, но я не поверил.

a2.en: “You are wrong,” I said. “I know the killer.
a2.ru: — Вы ошибаетесь, — сказал я. — Я знаю убийцу.

a2.en: Justine is innocent.”
a2.ru: Жюстина невиновна.

a2.en: Then my father came in.
a2.ru: Потом вошёл отец.

a2.en: He looked very sad, but he smiled at me.
a2.ru: Он выглядел очень печальным, но улыбнулся мне.

a2.en: He wanted to talk about something else, but Ernest said, “Papa! Victor says he knows the killer.”
a2.ru: Он хотел поговорить о чём-то другом, но Эрнест сказал: — Папа! Виктор говорит, что знает убийцу.

a2.en: “We know him too,” said my father sadly.
a2.ru: — Мы тоже его знаем, — грустно сказал отец.

a2.en: “I wish I didn’t know.
a2.ru: — Лучше бы я не знал.

a2.en: I loved her so much!”
a2.ru: Я её так любил!

a2.en: “Father, you are wrong. Justine is innocent.”
a2.ru: — Отец, вы ошибаетесь. Жюстина невиновна.

a2.en: “I hope so.
a2.ru: — Надеюсь.

a2.en: She will go to court today, and I really hope they will let her go.”
a2.ru: Сегодня её будут судить, и я очень надеюсь, что её отпустят.

a2.en: His words made me calmer.
a2.ru: Его слова меня успокоили.

a2.en: I knew that Justine did not kill William.
a2.ru: Я знал, что Жюстина не убивала Уильяма.

a2.en: No person killed him.
a2.ru: Его не убил ни один человек.

a2.en: So I thought that the judges could not find her guilty.
a2.ru: Поэтому я думал, что судьи не смогут признать её виновной.

a2.en: I could not tell my story, because people would think I was mad.
a2.ru: Я не мог рассказать свою историю, потому что люди подумали бы, что я сошёл с ума.

a2.en: Only I knew about the monster that I let go into the world.
a2.ru: Только я знал о чудовище, которое выпустил в мир.

a2.en: Soon Elizabeth came in.
a2.ru: Вскоре вошла Элизабет.

a2.en: She was even more beautiful now than when she was a child.
a2.ru: Теперь она была ещё красивее, чем в детстве.

a2.en: She was still honest and lively, and she looked clever and kind.
a2.ru: Она была всё такой же искренней и живой и выглядела умной и доброй.

a2.en: She was very happy to see me.
a2.ru: Она очень обрадовалась мне.

a2.en: “Dear cousin,” she said, “now I have hope.
a2.ru: — Дорогой кузен, — сказала она, — теперь у меня есть надежда.

a2.en: Maybe you can help my poor Justine.
a2.ru: Может быть, ты сможешь помочь моей бедной Жюстине.

a2.en: If they say she is guilty, nobody is safe!
a2.ru: Если её признают виновной, никто не в безопасности!

a2.en: I am sure that she is innocent.
a2.ru: Я уверена, что она невиновна.

a2.en: We lost our dear little boy, and now we may lose this poor girl too.
a2.ru: Мы потеряли нашего милого мальчика, а теперь можем потерять и эту бедную девушку.

a2.en: If they punish her, I will never be happy again.
a2.ru: Если её накажут, я никогда больше не буду счастлива.

a2.en: But I am sure they won’t.”
a2.ru: Но я уверена, что не накажут.

a2.en: “She is innocent, Elizabeth,” I said.
a2.ru: — Она невиновна, Элизабет, — сказал я.

a2.en: “Don’t be afraid; they will let her go.”
a2.ru: — Не бойся; её отпустят.

a2.en: “You are so kind!
a2.ru: — Ты такой добрый!

a2.en: Everyone else thinks she is guilty, and that makes me so unhappy.”
a2.ru: Все остальные думают, что она виновна, и от этого мне так плохо.

a2.en: She cried.
a2.ru: Она заплакала.

a2.en: “Dear Elizabeth,” said my father, “don’t cry.
a2.ru: — Дорогая Элизабет, — сказал отец, — не плачь.

a2.en: If she is innocent, our laws will be fair to her, and I will help.”
a2.ru: Если она невиновна, наши законы будут к ней справедливы, а я помогу.

sub: Justine is tried and condemned for William’s murder; Victor, knowing the creature is guilty, stays silent and she is executed

o: We passed a few sad hours until eleven o’clock, when the trial was to commence. My father and the rest of the family being obliged to attend as witnesses, I accompanied them to the court. During the whole of this wretched mockery of justice I suffered living torture. It was to be decided whether the result of my curiosity and lawless devices would cause the death of two of my fellow beings: one a smiling babe full of innocence and joy, the other far more dreadfully murdered, with every aggravation of infamy that could make the murder memorable in horror.

Justine also was a girl of merit and possessed qualities which promised to render her life happy; now all was to be obliterated in an ignominious grave, and I the cause! A thousand times rather would I have confessed myself guilty of the crime ascribed to Justine, but I was absent when it was committed, and such a declaration would have been considered as the ravings of a madman and would not have exculpated her who suffered through me.

The appearance of Justine was calm. She was dressed in mourning, and her countenance, always engaging, was rendered, by the solemnity of her feelings, exquisitely beautiful. Yet she appeared confident in innocence and did not tremble, although gazed on and execrated by thousands, for all the kindness which her beauty might otherwise have excited was obliterated in the minds of the spectators by the imagination of the enormity she was supposed to have committed. She was tranquil, yet her tranquillity was evidently constrained; and as her confusion had before been adduced as a proof of her guilt, she worked up her mind to an appearance of courage. When she entered the court she threw her eyes round it and quickly discovered where we were seated. A tear seemed to dim her eye when she saw us, but she quickly recovered herself, and a look of sorrowful affection seemed to attest her utter guiltlessness.

The trial began, and after the advocate against her had stated the charge, several witnesses were called. Several strange facts combined against her, which might have staggered anyone who had not such proof of her innocence as I had. She had been out the whole of the night on which the murder had been committed and towards morning had been perceived by a market-woman not far from the spot where the body of the murdered child had been afterwards found. The woman asked her what she did there, but she looked very strangely and only returned a confused and unintelligible answer.

She returned to the house about eight o’clock, and when one inquired where she had passed the night, she replied that she had been looking for the child and demanded earnestly if anything had been heard concerning him. When shown the body, she fell into violent hysterics and kept her bed for several days. The picture was then produced which the servant had found in her pocket; and when Elizabeth, in a faltering voice, proved that it was the same which, an hour before the child had been missed, she had placed round his neck, a murmur of horror and indignation filled the court.

Justine was called on for her defence. As the trial had proceeded, her countenance had altered. Surprise, horror, and misery were strongly expressed. Sometimes she struggled with her tears, but when she was desired to plead, she collected her powers and spoke in an audible although variable voice.

“God knows,” she said, “how entirely I am innocent. But I do not pretend that my protestations should acquit me; I rest my innocence on a plain and simple explanation of the facts which have been adduced against me, and I hope the character I have always borne will incline my judges to a favourable interpretation where any circumstance appears doubtful or suspicious.”

She then related that, by the permission of Elizabeth, she had passed the evening of the night on which the murder had been committed at the house of an aunt at Chêne, a village situated at about a league from Geneva. On her return, at about nine o’clock, she met a man who asked her if she had seen anything of the child who was lost. She was alarmed by this account and passed several hours in looking for him, when the gates of Geneva were shut, and she was forced to remain several hours of the night in a barn belonging to a cottage, being unwilling to call up the inhabitants, to whom she was well known.

Most of the night she spent here watching; towards morning she believed that she slept for a few minutes; some steps disturbed her, and she awoke. It was dawn, and she quitted her asylum, that she might again endeavour to find my brother. If she had gone near the spot where his body lay, it was without her knowledge. That she had been bewildered when questioned by the market-woman was not surprising, since she had passed a sleepless night and the fate of poor William was yet uncertain. Concerning the picture she could give no account.

“I know,” continued the unhappy victim, “how heavily and fatally this one circumstance weighs against me, but I have no power of explaining it; and when I have expressed my utter ignorance, I am only left to conjecture concerning the probabilities by which it might have been placed in my pocket. But here also I am checked. I believe that I have no enemy on earth, and none surely would have been so wicked as to destroy me wantonly. Did the murderer place it there? I know of no opportunity afforded him for so doing; or, if I had, why should he have stolen the jewel, to part with it again so soon?

“I commit my cause to the justice of my judges, yet I see no room for hope. I beg permission to have a few witnesses examined concerning my character, and if their testimony shall not overweigh my supposed guilt, I must be condemned, although I would pledge my salvation on my innocence.”

Several witnesses were called who had known her for many years, and they spoke well of her; but fear and hatred of the crime of which they supposed her guilty rendered them timorous and unwilling to come forward. Elizabeth saw even this last resource, her excellent dispositions and irreproachable conduct, about to fail the accused, when, although violently agitated, she desired permission to address the court.

“I am,” said she, “the cousin of the unhappy child who was murdered, or rather his sister, for I was educated by and have lived with his parents ever since and even long before his birth. It may therefore be judged indecent in me to come forward on this occasion, but when I see a fellow creature about to perish through the cowardice of her pretended friends, I wish to be allowed to speak, that I may say what I know of her character. I am well acquainted with the accused. I have lived in the same house with her, at one time for five and at another for nearly two years.

During all that period she appeared to me the most amiable and benevolent of human creatures. She nursed Madame Frankenstein, my aunt, in her last illness, with the greatest affection and care and afterwards attended her own mother during a tedious illness, in a manner that excited the admiration of all who knew her, after which she again lived in my uncle’s house, where she was beloved by all the family. She was warmly attached to the child who is now dead and acted towards him like a most affectionate mother.

For my own part, I do not hesitate to say that, notwithstanding all the evidence produced against her, I believe and rely on her perfect innocence. She had no temptation for such an action; as to the bauble on which the chief proof rests, if she had earnestly desired it, I should have willingly given it to her, so much do I esteem and value her.”

A murmur of approbation followed Elizabeth’s simple and powerful appeal, but it was excited by her generous interference, and not in favour of poor Justine, on whom the public indignation was turned with renewed violence, charging her with the blackest ingratitude. She herself wept as Elizabeth spoke, but she did not answer.

My own agitation and anguish was extreme during the whole trial. I believed in her innocence; I knew it. Could the dæmon who had (I did not for a minute doubt) murdered my brother also in his hellish sport have betrayed the innocent to death and ignominy? I could not sustain the horror of my situation, and when I perceived that the popular voice and the countenances of the judges had already condemned my unhappy victim, I rushed out of the court in agony. The tortures of the accused did not equal mine; she was sustained by innocence, but the fangs of remorse tore my bosom and would not forgo their hold.

I passed a night of unmingled wretchedness. In the morning I went to the court; my lips and throat were parched. I dared not ask the fatal question, but I was known, and the officer guessed the cause of my visit. The ballots had been thrown; they were all black, and Justine was condemned.

I cannot pretend to describe what I then felt. I had before experienced sensations of horror, and I have endeavoured to bestow upon them adequate expressions, but words cannot convey an idea of the heart-sickening despair that I then endured. The person to whom I addressed myself added that Justine had already confessed her guilt. “That evidence,” he observed, “was hardly required in so glaring a case, but I am glad of it, and, indeed, none of our judges like to condemn a criminal upon circumstantial evidence, be it ever so decisive.”

This was strange and unexpected intelligence; what could it mean? Had my eyes deceived me? And was I really as mad as the whole world would believe me to be if I disclosed the object of my suspicions? I hastened to return home, and Elizabeth eagerly demanded the result.

“My cousin,” replied I, “it is decided as you may have expected; all judges had rather that ten innocent should suffer than that one guilty should escape. But she has confessed.”

This was a dire blow to poor Elizabeth, who had relied with firmness upon Justine’s innocence. “Alas!” said she. “How shall I ever again believe in human goodness? Justine, whom I loved and esteemed as my sister, how could she put on those smiles of innocence only to betray? Her mild eyes seemed incapable of any severity or guile, and yet she has committed a murder.”

Soon after we heard that the poor victim had expressed a desire to see my cousin. My father wished her not to go but said that he left it to her own judgment and feelings to decide. “Yes,” said Elizabeth, “I will go, although she is guilty; and you, Victor, shall accompany me; I cannot go alone.” The idea of this visit was torture to me, yet I could not refuse.

We entered the gloomy prison chamber and beheld Justine sitting on some straw at the farther end; her hands were manacled, and her head rested on her knees. She rose on seeing us enter, and when we were left alone with her, she threw herself at the feet of Elizabeth, weeping bitterly. My cousin wept also.

“Oh, Justine!” said she. “Why did you rob me of my last consolation? I relied on your innocence, and although I was then very wretched, I was not so miserable as I am now.”

“And do you also believe that I am so very, very wicked? Do you also join with my enemies to crush me, to condemn me as a murderer?” Her voice was suffocated with sobs.

“Rise, my poor girl,” said Elizabeth; “why do you kneel, if you are innocent? I am not one of your enemies, I believed you guiltless, notwithstanding every evidence, until I heard that you had yourself declared your guilt. That report, you say, is false; and be assured, dear Justine, that nothing can shake my confidence in you for a moment, but your own confession.”

“I did confess, but I confessed a lie. I confessed, that I might obtain absolution; but now that falsehood lies heavier at my heart than all my other sins. The God of heaven forgive me! Ever since I was condemned, my confessor has besieged me; he threatened and menaced, until I almost began to think that I was the monster that he said I was. He threatened excommunication and hell fire in my last moments if I continued obdurate. Dear lady, I had none to support me; all looked on me as a wretch doomed to ignominy and perdition. What could I do? In an evil hour I subscribed to a lie; and now only am I truly miserable.”

She paused, weeping, and then continued, “I thought with horror, my sweet lady, that you should believe your Justine, whom your blessed aunt had so highly honoured, and whom you loved, was a creature capable of a crime which none but the devil himself could have perpetrated. Dear William! dearest blessed child! I soon shall see you again in heaven, where we shall all be happy; and that consoles me, going as I am to suffer ignominy and death.”

“Oh, Justine! Forgive me for having for one moment distrusted you. Why did you confess? But do not mourn, dear girl. Do not fear. I will proclaim, I will prove your innocence. I will melt the stony hearts of your enemies by my tears and prayers. You shall not die! You, my playfellow, my companion, my sister, perish on the scaffold! No! No! I never could survive so horrible a misfortune.”

Justine shook her head mournfully. “I do not fear to die,” she said; “that pang is past. God raises my weakness and gives me courage to endure the worst. I leave a sad and bitter world; and if you remember me and think of me as of one unjustly condemned, I am resigned to the fate awaiting me. Learn from me, dear lady, to submit in patience to the will of heaven!”

During this conversation I had retired to a corner of the prison room, where I could conceal the horrid anguish that possessed me. Despair! Who dared talk of that? The poor victim, who on the morrow was to pass the awful boundary between life and death, felt not, as I did, such deep and bitter agony. I gnashed my teeth and ground them together, uttering a groan that came from my inmost soul. Justine started. When she saw who it was, she approached me and said, “Dear sir, you are very kind to visit me; you, I hope, do not believe that I am guilty?”

I could not answer. “No, Justine,” said Elizabeth; “he is more convinced of your innocence than I was, for even when he heard that you had confessed, he did not credit it.”

“I truly thank him. In these last moments I feel the sincerest gratitude towards those who think of me with kindness. How sweet is the affection of others to such a wretch as I am! It removes more than half my misfortune, and I feel as if I could die in peace now that my innocence is acknowledged by you, dear lady, and your cousin.”

Thus the poor sufferer tried to comfort others and herself. She indeed gained the resignation she desired. But I, the true murderer, felt the never-dying worm alive in my bosom, which allowed of no hope or consolation. Elizabeth also wept and was unhappy, but hers also was the misery of innocence, which, like a cloud that passes over the fair moon, for a while hides but cannot tarnish its brightness. Anguish and despair had penetrated into the core of my heart; I bore a hell within me which nothing could extinguish. We stayed several hours with Justine, and it was with great difficulty that Elizabeth could tear herself away. “I wish,” cried she, “that I were to die with you; I cannot live in this world of misery.”

Justine assumed an air of cheerfulness, while she with difficulty repressed her bitter tears. She embraced Elizabeth and said in a voice of half-suppressed emotion, “Farewell, sweet lady, dearest Elizabeth, my beloved and only friend; may heaven, in its bounty, bless and preserve you; may this be the last misfortune that you will ever suffer! Live, and be happy, and make others so.”

And on the morrow Justine died. Elizabeth’s heart-rending eloquence failed to move the judges from their settled conviction in the criminality of the saintly sufferer. My passionate and indignant appeals were lost upon them. And when I received their cold answers and heard the harsh, unfeeling reasoning of these men, my purposed avowal died away on my lips. Thus I might proclaim myself a madman, but not revoke the sentence passed upon my wretched victim. She perished on the scaffold as a murderess!

From the tortures of my own heart, I turned to contemplate the deep and voiceless grief of my Elizabeth. This also was my doing! And my father’s woe, and the desolation of that late so smiling home all was the work of my thrice-accursed hands! Ye weep, unhappy ones, but these are not your last tears! Again shall you raise the funeral wail, and the sound of your lamentations shall again and again be heard!

Frankenstein, your son, your kinsman, your early, much-loved friend; he who would spend each vital drop of blood for your sakes, who has no thought nor sense of joy except as it is mirrored also in your dear countenances, who would fill the air with blessings and spend his life in serving you—he bids you weep, to shed countless tears; happy beyond his hopes, if thus inexorable fate be satisfied, and if the destruction pause before the peace of the grave have succeeded to your sad torments!

Thus spoke my prophetic soul, as, torn by remorse, horror, and despair, I beheld those I loved spend vain sorrow upon the graves of William and Justine, the first hapless victims to my unhallowed arts.

Justine was called on to defend herself. As the trial had gone on, her expression had changed. Surprise, horror and misery were clearly visible in it. At times she fought back her tears, but when she was asked to speak, she gathered her strength and spoke in a clear, though unsteady, voice. “God knows,” she said, “how completely innocent I am. But I do not claim that my protests alone should set me free; I base my innocence on a plain, simple explanation of the facts that have been brought against me, and I hope that the good name I have always had will persuade my judges to interpret things kindly wherever anything seems doubtful or suspicious.”

She then explained that, with Elizabeth’s permission, she had spent the evening of the night of the murder at her aunt’s house in Chêne, a village about three miles from Geneva. On her way back, at about nine o’clock, she met a man who asked her whether she had seen any sign of the lost child. The news alarmed her, and she spent several hours looking for him, until the gates of Geneva were shut and she had to spend part of the night in a barn belonging to a cottage, since she did not want to wake the people who lived there, who knew her well.

She spent most of the night there awake; towards morning she thought she had slept for a few minutes, until some footsteps disturbed her and she woke up. It was dawn, and she left her shelter to try once more to find my brother. If she had gone near the place where his body lay, she had done so without knowing it. It was hardly surprising that she had seemed bewildered when the market-woman questioned her, since she had had a sleepless night and poor William’s fate was still unknown. About the picture she could offer no explanation.

“I know,” the unhappy victim went on, “how heavily and fatally this one fact weighs against me, but I have no way of explaining it; and having admitted that I know nothing at all, I can only guess at how it might have got into my pocket. But here, too, I am stuck. I believe I have no enemy in the world, and surely nobody would have been so wicked as to ruin me for no reason. Did the murderer put it there? I cannot see when he could have had the chance to do so; and even if he had, why would he steal the jewel only to give it up again so soon?

“I entrust my case to the justice of my judges, although I see no reason to hope. I ask permission for a few witnesses to be questioned about my character, and if their evidence does not outweigh my supposed guilt, then I must be condemned, although I would stake my soul on my innocence.” Several witnesses who had known her for many years were called, and they spoke well of her; but their fear and hatred of the crime they believed she had committed made them timid and reluctant to come forward. Elizabeth saw that even this last hope, Justine’s excellent nature and blameless behaviour, was about to fail her, and so, although she was extremely upset, she asked permission to speak to the court.

“I am,” she said, “the cousin of the unhappy child who was murdered, or rather his sister, because I was brought up by his parents and have lived with them ever since, from long before he was born. So it may be thought improper for me to come forward on this occasion, but when I see a fellow human being about to die because of the cowardice of her so-called friends, I wish to be allowed to speak, so that I can say what I know of her character. I know the accused well. I have lived in the same house as her, once for five years and another time for nearly two.

Throughout that time she seemed to me the kindest and most generous person alive. She nursed Madame Frankenstein, my aunt, through her final illness with the greatest love and care, and afterwards looked after her own mother through a long, wearisome illness in a way that won the admiration of everyone who knew her; after that she came back to live in my uncle’s house, where the whole family loved her. She was deeply attached to the child who is now dead and treated him like the most loving mother.

For my part, I have no hesitation in saying that, despite all the evidence brought against her, I believe in her complete innocence and trust in it. She had no reason to be tempted into such an act; as for the trinket on which the main evidence rests, if she had really wanted it, I would gladly have given it to her, I respect and value her so much.”

A murmur of approval followed Elizabeth’s simple and powerful appeal, but it was prompted by her generous intervention and not by any sympathy for poor Justine, against whom public anger now turned with fresh violence, accusing her of the blackest ingratitude. Justine herself wept while Elizabeth was speaking, but she said nothing.

My own agitation and anguish were extreme throughout the trial. I believed in her innocence; I knew it. Could the demon who had murdered my brother (I did not doubt it for a minute) also, in his hellish game, have betrayed an innocent girl to death and disgrace? I could not bear the horror of my situation, and when I saw that public opinion and the faces of the judges had already condemned my unhappy victim, I rushed out of the court in agony. The torment of the accused was nothing compared with mine; she was supported by her innocence, but the fangs of remorse tore at my heart and would not let go.

I spent a night of pure misery. In the morning I went to the court; my lips and throat were dry. I did not dare to ask the fatal question, but people knew me, and the officer guessed why I had come. The votes had been cast; they were all black, and Justine was condemned.

I cannot even try to describe what I felt then. I had felt horror before, and I have tried to find the right words for it, but no words can express the sickening despair I suffered then. The man I spoke to added that Justine had already confessed. “That evidence,” he remarked, “was hardly needed in such an obvious case, but I am glad of it, and, in fact, none of our judges like to condemn a criminal on circumstantial evidence, however convincing it may be.”

This was strange and unexpected news; what could it mean? Had my eyes deceived me? And was I really as mad as the whole world would think me if I revealed whom I suspected? I hurried home, and Elizabeth eagerly asked me the outcome. “My cousin,” I replied, “it has been decided as you might have expected; all judges would rather see ten innocent people suffer than let one guilty person escape. But she has confessed.”

This was a terrible blow to poor Elizabeth, who had firmly believed in Justine’s innocence. “Oh no!” she said. “How can I ever believe in human goodness again? Justine, whom I loved and respected like a sister — how could she wear that innocent smile only to betray us? Her gentle eyes seemed incapable of any harshness or deceit, and yet she has committed a murder.”

Soon afterwards we heard that the poor victim had asked to see my cousin. My father did not want her to go, but said he would leave it to her own judgement and feelings to decide. “Yes,” said Elizabeth, “I will go, even though she is guilty; and you, Victor, must come with me; I cannot go alone.” The thought of this visit was torture to me, yet I could not refuse.

We entered the gloomy prison cell and saw Justine sitting on some straw at the far end; her hands were chained, and her head was resting on her knees. She stood up when she saw us come in, and when we were left alone with her, she threw herself at Elizabeth’s feet, weeping bitterly. My cousin wept too.

“Oh, Justine!” she said. “Why did you take away my last comfort? I trusted in your innocence, and although I was very unhappy then, I was not as miserable as I am now.” “And do you believe too that I am so very, very wicked? Are you joining my enemies too, to crush me and condemn me as a murderer?” Her voice was choked with sobs.

“Get up, my poor girl,” said Elizabeth; “why are you kneeling, if you are innocent? I am not one of your enemies; I believed you were innocent, in spite of all the evidence, until I heard that you yourself had admitted your guilt. You say that report is false; so rest assured, dear Justine, that nothing could shake my trust in you for a moment, except your own confession.”

“I did confess, but what I confessed was a lie. I confessed so that I could receive absolution; but now that lie weighs more heavily on my heart than all my other sins. May the God of heaven forgive me! Ever since I was condemned, my priest has given me no peace; he threatened and bullied me until I almost began to believe that I really was the monster he said I was. He threatened me with being cast out of the Church and with the fires of hell in my last moments if I remained stubborn. Dear lady, I had nobody to support me; everyone looked on me as a wretch doomed to disgrace and damnation. What could I do? In an evil hour I put my name to a lie; and only now am I truly miserable.”

She stopped, weeping, and then went on, “I was horrified to think, my sweet lady, that you might believe your Justine, whom your blessed aunt had honoured so highly and whom you loved, was capable of a crime that only the devil himself could have committed. Dear William! Dearest, blessed child! I shall soon see you again in heaven, where we shall all be happy; and that comforts me, even though I am going to suffer disgrace and death.”

“Oh, Justine! Forgive me for doubting you, even for a moment. Why did you confess? But do not grieve, dear girl. Do not be afraid. I will declare your innocence publicly; I will prove it. I will soften the stony hearts of your enemies with my tears and prayers. You shall not die! You, my playmate, my companion, my sister, die on the scaffold! No! No! I could never survive such a terrible misfortune.”

Justine shook her head sadly. “I am not afraid to die,” she said; “that pain is over. God lifts me up in my weakness and gives me the courage to face the worst. I am leaving a sad and bitter world; and if you remember me and think of me as someone who was unjustly condemned, I can accept the fate that awaits me. Learn from me, dear lady, to accept the will of heaven with patience!”

During this conversation I had withdrawn to a corner of the cell, where I could hide the dreadful anguish that had taken hold of me. Despair! Who dared to talk of that? The poor victim, who the next day was to cross the terrible border between life and death, did not feel such deep and bitter agony as I did. I gnashed and ground my teeth, letting out a groan that came from the depths of my soul. Justine gave a start. When she saw who it was, she came up to me and said, “Dear sir, it is very kind of you to visit me; I hope you do not believe that I am guilty?”

I could not answer. “No, Justine,” said Elizabeth; “he is even more convinced of your innocence than I was, because even when he heard that you had confessed, he did not believe it.” “I thank him with all my heart. In these last moments I feel the deepest gratitude towards those who think of me kindly. How sweet the love of others is to a wretch like me! It takes away more than half my suffering, and I feel I could die in peace now that you, dear lady, and your cousin recognise my innocence.”

In this way the poor sufferer tried to comfort others and herself. And she did achieve the calm acceptance she longed for. But I, the real murderer, felt the undying worm alive in my heart, leaving no room for hope or comfort. Elizabeth too wept and was unhappy, but hers was the misery of innocence, which, like a cloud passing over the bright moon, hides it for a while but cannot dim its brightness. Anguish and despair had pierced the very core of my heart; I carried within me a hell that nothing could put out. We stayed with Justine for several hours, and Elizabeth could only tear herself away with great difficulty. “I wish,” she cried, “that I could die with you; I cannot live in this world of misery.”

Justine put on a cheerful air, though she could barely hold back her bitter tears. She embraced Elizabeth and said, in a voice full of barely controlled emotion, “Goodbye, sweet lady, dearest Elizabeth, my beloved and only friend; may heaven in its goodness bless and protect you; may this be the last misfortune you ever suffer! Live, and be happy, and make others happy too.”

And the next day Justine died. Elizabeth’s heartbreaking eloquence could not shake the judges’ firm belief that the saintly sufferer was guilty. My passionate, indignant appeals had no effect on them. And when I received their cold replies and heard the harsh, heartless reasoning of these men, the confession I had intended to make died on my lips. I could have declared myself a madman, but I could not have overturned the sentence passed on my wretched victim. She died on the scaffold as a murderess!

From the torments of my own heart I turned to look at the deep and silent grief of my Elizabeth. This, too, was my doing! And my father’s sorrow, and the emptiness of that home which had so recently been so happy — all of it was the work of my thrice-cursed hands! You weep, unhappy ones, but these are not your last tears! Once again you will raise the funeral cry, and the sound of your mourning will be heard again and again!

Frankenstein, your son, your relative, your old and much-loved friend; he who would give every last drop of his blood for you, who has no thought or feeling of joy unless it is reflected in your dear faces too, who would fill the air with blessings and spend his life serving you — he bids you weep and shed countless tears; and he would be happier than he ever hoped if this relentless fate were satisfied, and if the destruction stopped before the peace of the grave replaced your sad torments! So spoke my prophetic soul as, torn by remorse, horror and despair, I watched those I loved pour out useless grief over the graves of William and Justine, the first unfortunate victims of my unholy science.
b1: We waited for a few sad hours until eleven o’clock, when the trial started. My father and the rest of the family had to be witnesses, so I went to the court with them. The whole trial was a terrible joke of justice, and for me it was real torture. Because of my curiosity and my terrible experiments, two people were going to die: a smiling, happy, innocent child, and now a young woman who would die in a far worse way, in shame and horror.

Justine was a good girl, and she could have had a happy life; now she was going to die and lie in a shameful grave, and it was my fault! I would have said a thousand times that I was the murderer, but I was not in Geneva when it happened, so people would think I was mad, and it would not save her.

Justine looked calm. She was wearing black, and her face, which was always sweet, looked especially beautiful because of her serious feelings. She seemed sure of her innocence and did not shake, although thousands of people looked at her and hated her. They could not feel sorry for her, because they were thinking about the terrible crime she had probably done. She was calm, but it was not easy for her; before, people had said that her confusion showed she was guilty, so now she tried hard to look brave. When she came into the court, she looked around and quickly saw where we were sitting. There was a tear in her eye when she saw us, but she soon controlled herself, and her sad, loving look seemed to show that she was completely innocent.

The trial began, and after the lawyer explained the charge against her, several witnesses spoke. Some strange facts were against her, and they could make anyone doubt her — anyone who did not know the truth like I did. She had been out all night on the night of the murder, and early in the morning a woman from the market saw her near the place where the child’s body was found later. The woman asked her what she was doing there, but Justine looked at her very strangely and gave a confused answer.

She came home at about eight o’clock, and when someone asked where she had been, she said she had been looking for the child. She asked again and again if there was any news of him. When they showed her the body, she became hysterical and stayed in bed for several days. Then they showed the court the picture that the servant had found in her pocket. Elizabeth said in a shaking voice that it was the same picture she had put around the child’s neck an hour before he disappeared, and everyone in the court made a sound of horror and anger.

Then Justine had to defend herself. During the trial her face had changed. It showed surprise, horror and pain. Sometimes she tried not to cry, but when they asked her to speak, she found her strength and spoke in a clear but shaking voice. “God knows,” she said, “that I am completely innocent. I know that just saying this will not save me, so I will simply explain the facts against me. I hope that my good name will help my judges to think well of me when something seems strange or suspicious.”

Then she told her story. On the evening of the murder, with Elizabeth’s permission, she had visited her aunt in Chêne, a village about three miles from Geneva. On her way back, at about nine o’clock, she met a man who asked her if she had seen the lost child. She was frightened by this news and looked for him for several hours. Then the gates of Geneva were closed, and she had to spend part of the night in a barn near a small house, because she did not want to wake the people there, who knew her well.

She stayed awake there for most of the night; near morning she slept for a few minutes, but she heard some footsteps and woke up. It was early morning, and she left the barn to look for my brother again. If she went near the place where his body was, she did not know it. It was not surprising that she was confused when the market woman asked her questions, because she had not slept all night and did not know what had happened to poor William. She could not explain the picture.

“I know,” the poor girl went on, “that this one fact is very bad for me, but I cannot explain it. I do not know anything about it, so I can only guess how it got into my pocket. But even here I cannot find an answer. I believe I have no enemies in the world, and surely nobody is so cruel that they would destroy me for no reason. Did the murderer put it there? I do not see when he could do it; and if he did, why did he steal the jewel and then give it away so quickly?

“I trust the fairness of my judges, but I have no hope. Please let a few witnesses talk about my character. If what they say is not enough, I must be condemned, but I promise on my soul that I am innocent.” Several people who had known her for many years spoke, and they said good things about her. But they were afraid, and they hated the crime, so they were shy and did not want to say much. Elizabeth saw that even Justine’s good character was not going to save her, so, although she was very upset, she asked to speak to the court.

“I am the cousin of the poor child who was murdered,” she said, “or really his sister, because his parents brought me up and I have lived with them since long before he was born. Maybe people will think it is wrong for me to speak here. But I can see that a person is going to die because her friends are cowards, so I want to tell you what I know about her. I know Justine well. I have lived in the same house as her, once for five years and once for nearly two years.

All that time she was the kindest and most loving person I knew. When my aunt, Madame Frankenstein, was dying, Justine looked after her with great love and care. Later she looked after her own mother during a long illness, and everyone who knew her admired her. After that she lived in my uncle’s house again, and all the family loved her. She loved the child who is now dead and was like a very loving mother to him.

I am not afraid to say that, in spite of all the evidence, I believe she is completely innocent. She had no reason to do such a thing. And the little jewel which is the main proof — if she had really wanted it, I would have happily given it to her, because I respect and love her so much.”

People in the court made a sound of approval after Elizabeth’s simple and strong speech, but they were praising her kindness, not supporting poor Justine. In fact they were even angrier with Justine now and said she was terribly ungrateful. Justine cried while Elizabeth was speaking, but she said nothing.

During the whole trial I was terribly upset and in great pain. I believed she was innocent; I knew it. I was sure that the demon had killed my brother. Had he also, as a cruel game, sent this innocent girl to death and shame? I could not bear it, and when I saw that the people and the judges had already decided she was guilty, I ran out of the court in agony. Her suffering was less than mine; her innocence gave her strength, but my guilt tore at my heart and would not let me go.

I spent a night of complete misery. In the morning I went to the court; my lips and throat were very dry. I was afraid to ask the terrible question, but the officer knew me and guessed why I was there. The judges had voted; all the votes were black, and Justine was condemned.

I cannot describe what I felt then. I had felt horror before, and I have tried to describe it, but no words can explain the terrible despair I felt at that moment. The man I was talking to also told me that Justine had already confessed. “We did not really need that in such a clear case,” he said, “but I am glad, because our judges do not like to condemn a criminal only on indirect evidence, even when it is very strong.”

This was strange news that I did not expect; what could it mean? Were my eyes wrong? Was I really as mad as everybody would think if I told them who I suspected? I hurried home, and Elizabeth quickly asked me what had happened. “My cousin,” I answered, “it is what you probably expected; judges would prefer to punish ten innocent people than let one guilty person go free. But she has confessed.”

This was a terrible shock for poor Elizabeth, who had believed strongly that Justine was innocent. “Oh no!” she said. “How can I ever believe in people’s goodness again? Justine, who I loved like a sister — how could she smile so innocently and then betray us? Her gentle eyes looked as if they could never be hard or dishonest, and yet she has killed someone.”

Soon after that we heard that Justine wanted to see Elizabeth. My father did not want her to go, but he said she must decide for herself. “Yes,” said Elizabeth, “I will go, although she is guilty; and you, Victor, will come with me; I cannot go alone.” The idea of this visit was torture for me, but I could not say no.

We went into the dark prison room and saw Justine sitting on some straw at the far end. Her hands were in chains, and her head was on her knees. She stood up when she saw us, and when we were alone with her, she fell at Elizabeth’s feet, crying bitterly. Elizabeth cried too.

“Oh, Justine!” she said. “Why did you take away my last hope? I believed you were innocent, and although I was very sad then, I was not as unhappy as I am now.” “So do you also believe that I am very, very bad? Are you also with my enemies, who want to destroy me and call me a murderer?” She could hardly speak because she was crying so much.

“Stand up, my poor girl,” said Elizabeth. “Why are you on your knees if you are innocent? I am not your enemy. I believed you were innocent, in spite of all the evidence, until I heard that you had said you were guilty. You say that is not true; then, dear Justine, nothing can make me doubt you, except your own words.”

“Yes, I confessed, but I told a lie. I confessed so that God would forgive my sins; but now this lie is heavier on my heart than all my other sins. May God in heaven forgive me! Since I was condemned, the priest has visited me again and again. He threatened me and frightened me until I almost began to believe that I really was the monster he said I was. He said the Church would reject me and I would go to hell when I died if I did not confess. Dear lady, nobody was there to help me; everyone thought I was a bad person who would end in shame and in hell. What could I do? At a terrible moment I signed a lie; and only now am I really unhappy.”

She stopped and cried, and then she went on, “My sweet lady, it was horrible to think that you might believe your Justine could do such a crime. Your dear aunt respected me so much, and you loved me, and only the devil himself could do a crime like that. Dear William! Dearest, blessed child! I will soon see you again in heaven, where we will all be happy; that helps me, even though I am going to die in shame.”

“Oh, Justine! Forgive me for doubting you, even for a moment. Why did you confess? But do not be sad, dear girl. Do not be afraid. I will tell everyone, and I will prove that you are innocent. My tears and prayers will make your enemies’ hard hearts soft. You will not die! You, my friend from childhood, my sister, die on the scaffold? No! No! I could never live through something so terrible.”

Justine sadly shook her head. “I am not afraid to die,” she said. “That pain has passed. God makes me strong when I am weak and gives me the courage to face the worst. I am leaving a sad and bitter world; if you remember me and think of me as someone who was punished unfairly, I can accept what is going to happen. Learn from me, dear lady, to accept God’s will patiently!”

During this conversation I had moved into a corner of the prison room, where I could hide my terrible pain. Despair! Who could talk about despair? The poor girl, who was going to die the next day, did not suffer as deeply and bitterly as I did. I pressed my teeth together hard and made a groan that came from deep inside my soul. Justine jumped. When she saw who it was, she came to me and said, “Dear sir, it is very kind of you to visit me; I hope you do not believe that I am guilty?”

I could not answer. “No, Justine,” said Elizabeth. “He is even more sure of your innocence than I was, because even when he heard that you had confessed, he did not believe it.” “Thank him for me with all my heart. In these last moments I am so grateful to the people who think kindly of me. How sweet other people’s love is to a poor wretch like me! It takes away more than half of my pain, and I feel I can die in peace now that you, dear lady, and your cousin know I am innocent.”

So the poor girl tried to comfort other people and herself. And she really found the peace she wanted. But I, the real murderer, felt a worm that never dies eating my heart, and it left no hope or comfort. Elizabeth also cried and was unhappy, but her sadness was the sadness of an innocent person. It was like a cloud that goes across the bright moon: it hides the moon for a while, but it cannot make it less bright. Pain and despair had gone into the centre of my heart; I carried a hell inside me that nothing could stop. We stayed with Justine for several hours, and it was very hard for Elizabeth to leave her. “I wish I could die with you,” she cried. “I cannot live in this world of pain.”

Justine tried to look cheerful, but it was hard for her not to cry. She put her arms around Elizabeth and said, in a voice full of feeling, “Goodbye, sweet lady, dearest Elizabeth, my dear and only friend; may God bless you and keep you safe; may this be the last sad thing that ever happens to you! Live, and be happy, and make other people happy.”

And the next day Justine died. Elizabeth’s beautiful, moving words did not change the judges’ minds; they were sure that the poor, good girl was guilty. My angry, passionate words did not help either. When I heard the cold, hard answers of these men, I could not say what I had planned to say. They would only think I was mad, and they would not change the sentence. She died on the scaffold as a murderer!

I stopped thinking about my own pain and looked at the deep, silent sadness of my Elizabeth. This was my fault too! My father’s sadness, and our home, which had been so happy and was now so empty — all of this was the work of my cursed hands! You are crying, my poor family, but these are not your last tears! You will cry at a funeral again, and people will hear you cry again and again!

I, Frankenstein, your son, your relative and your loving friend, would give all my blood for you. I feel no joy unless I see it in your dear faces, and I want to spend my life serving you. But I am the one who makes you cry so many tears. I will be happier than I can hope if cruel fate is satisfied now, and if the destruction stops before you all find peace in the grave! That is what my soul told me about the future, as I watched, full of guilt, horror and despair, the people I loved crying over the graves of William and Justine, the first poor victims of my terrible science.
a2: We waited for a few sad hours. The trial started at eleven o’clock. My father and the family had to speak in court, so I went with them. For me, the whole trial was terrible pain. Because of my experiments, two people were going to die. One was a happy little boy. The other was a young woman, and her death was going to be even worse. Everyone was going to remember this murder with horror.

Justine was a good girl, and her life could be happy. Now she was going to die in shame, and it was my fault! I wanted to say, “I am the killer.” But I was not in Geneva that night. People would think I was mad, and it would not help her.

Justine looked calm. She wore black clothes, and her face was very beautiful. Thousands of people looked at her and hated her, but she did not shake. They thought she was a killer, so they did not feel sorry for her. Before, people said, “She was confused, so she is guilty.” She tried hard to look brave. When she came in, she looked around and saw us. She almost cried, but then she gave us a sad, loving look.

The trial began, and some people spoke against her. Some strange facts were against her. I knew she was innocent, but other people did not know. She was out all night on the night of the murder. Early in the morning, a woman from the market saw her near the place of the murder. The woman asked her a question, but Justine gave a strange answer.

She came home at eight o’clock. She said, “I was looking for William.” She asked many times, “Is there any news about him?” When she saw his body, she became very ill and stayed in bed for days. Then they showed the picture from her pocket. Elizabeth said, “Yes, I put this picture on William’s neck that evening.” Everyone in the court was angry and afraid.

Then Justine spoke. Her face was full of surprise and pain. She tried not to cry, and she spoke clearly. “God knows that I am innocent,” she said. “I will explain the facts. I hope my judges will remember that I am a good person.”

She told her story. That evening she visited her aunt in a village near Geneva. On her way home, a man asked her about the lost child. She was afraid and looked for William for hours. Then the city gates closed, so she slept in a barn. She did not want to wake the people in the house, because they knew her.

She did not sleep much. In the morning she heard some steps and woke up. Then she went to look for William again. She did not know where his body was. She was tired and worried, so she answered the market woman strangely. She did not sleep all night, and she did not know what happened to William. She could not explain the picture.

“I know that the picture is very bad for me,” she said. “But I cannot explain it. I do not know how it got into my pocket. I have no enemies. Did the killer put it there? But why did he steal it and then give it away?”

“I have no hope. Please listen to people who know me. I am innocent. If the judges do not believe them, I must die.” Some people spoke for her, but they were afraid and did not say much. Elizabeth was very worried, and she asked to speak.

“I am William’s cousin,” she said, “but really I am his sister. I have lived with his family for many years. Maybe it is wrong for me to speak here, but I must. Justine’s friends are afraid to help her, so I want to speak. I know Justine well. I lived with her for many years.
She is a very kind person. When my aunt was dying, Justine took care of her with love. Later she took care of her own sick mother. All our family loved her. She loved William like a mother.
I believe she is innocent. She had no reason to do this. If she wanted the picture, I was happy to give it to her. I love and respect her very much.”
People liked Elizabeth’s words, but they did not change their minds about Justine. Now they were even angrier with her. Justine cried, but she said nothing.

I felt terrible during the whole trial. I knew that Justine was innocent. The monster killed my brother. Did he also want Justine to die? I saw that the judges already thought she was guilty, and I ran out of the court. She was innocent, so she was strong. But I felt guilty, and it hurt me terribly.
I had a terrible night. My mouth was very dry. In the morning I went to the court. I was afraid to ask the question, but the officer understood. All the judges said “guilty”, and Justine had to die.

I cannot describe my feelings. There are no words for my terrible sadness. I had felt horror before, but this was worse. The officer also said, “Justine has told us that she did it. We are glad, because now we are sure.”

I did not understand. Was I wrong? Was I mad? I went home quickly, and Elizabeth asked me about the trial. “Justine must die,” I answered. “Judges are happier to kill ten innocent people than to let one bad person go free. And she has said that she did it.”

This was terrible for Elizabeth. She believed that Justine was innocent. “How can I believe in good people now?” she said. “I loved Justine like a sister. She had such kind eyes, and she killed a child!”

Soon Justine asked to see Elizabeth. My father said, “You can decide.” “I will go,” said Elizabeth. “Victor, please come with me.” My father did not want her to go. I did not want to go, but I could not say no.
We went into the dark prison. Justine was sitting on some straw, with chains on her hands. She stood up, and then she fell at Elizabeth’s feet and cried. Elizabeth cried too.
“Oh, Justine!” said Elizabeth. “Why did you say you did it? Now I am even sadder than before.” “Do you also think I am a bad person?” Justine asked. “Are you my enemy too?” She was crying hard.
“Stand up, my poor girl,” said Elizabeth. “I am not your enemy. I believed you, but then I heard that you said you did it. If that is not true, I will believe you again.”

“Yes, I said it, but it was a lie. Now this lie is very heavy on my heart. The priest came to me every day. He shouted at me and frightened me. He said, ‘You will go to hell if you do not say that you did it.’ Nobody helped me. He said, ‘You are a monster,’ and I almost believed him. What could I do? So I told a lie, and now I am really unhappy.”

She cried and then said, “I was afraid that you believed I was a killer. Your aunt was always good to me, and you loved me. Dear William! I will see you again in heaven soon, and we will be happy there. That helps me.”

“Oh, Justine! I am sorry that I did not believe you. Do not be sad. Do not be afraid. I will tell everyone that you are innocent. My tears will make your enemies’ hearts soft. You will not die! You are my friend and my sister. I cannot live without you!”
Justine shook her head sadly. “I am not afraid to die,” she said. “God makes me strong. I am leaving a sad world. Please remember me as an innocent person. Then I can accept my death.”

I stood in a corner because I wanted to hide my pain. Despair! Who could talk about despair? Justine was going to die the next day, but my pain was worse than hers. I made a loud, terrible sound. Justine was surprised. She came to me and said, “Thank you for coming, sir. You do not think I am guilty, do you?”

I could not answer. “No,” said Elizabeth. “He always believed you were innocent.” “Thank you,” said Justine. “Your love helps me very much. Now I can die in peace, because you both know I am innocent.”

Justine tried to help us and herself, and she felt calmer. But I was the real killer, and I had no hope. She found peace. Elizabeth was sad too, but she was innocent. Her sadness was like a cloud in front of the moon: the moon is still bright behind it. But I carried a terrible pain in my heart. We stayed with Justine for hours. Elizabeth did not want to leave. “I want to die with you,” she cried.

Justine tried to smile and not cry. She put her arms around Elizabeth. “Goodbye, dear Elizabeth, my only friend,” she said. “God bless you! I hope this is the last sad day of your life. Be happy, and make other people happy.”

The next day Justine died. Elizabeth spoke to the judges, but they did not listen. I spoke to them too, but they gave me cold answers. I wanted to tell them the truth, but I did not. The judges were cold, hard men. They would only think I was mad. So Justine died as a murderer!

I looked at Elizabeth’s quiet sadness. This was my fault too! My father was sad, and our happy home was now empty. It was all because of me! My poor family, you are crying, but you will cry again! There will be more deaths!

I love you all, and I want to give my life for you. I would give every drop of my blood for you. But I am the one who makes you cry. I hope that these deaths are the last. I thought this as I watched my family cry at the graves of William and Justine. They were the first victims of my terrible work.

o.en: We passed a few sad hours until eleven o’clock, when the trial was to commence.
o.ru: В тягостном ожидании мы провели несколько часов, до одиннадцати, когда должен был начаться суд.

o.en: My father and the rest of the family being obliged to attend as witnesses, I accompanied them to the court.
o.ru: Отец и остальные члены семьи были обязаны явиться как свидетели, и я сопровождал их в суд.

o.en: During the whole of this wretched mockery of justice I suffered living torture.
o.ru: Всё время, пока длилась эта жалкая насмешка над правосудием, я испытывал живую пытку.

o.en: It was to be decided whether the result of my curiosity and lawless devices would cause the death of two of my fellow beings: one a smiling babe full of innocence and joy, the other far more dreadfully murdered, with every aggravation of infamy that could make the murder memorable in horror.
o.ru: Решалось, станут ли плоды моего любопытства и беззаконных опытов причиной гибели двух моих ближних: одного — улыбающегося младенца, полного невинности и радости, другой — убитой куда страшнее, со всеми отягчающими обстоятельствами позора, какие только могут сделать убийство памятным своим ужасом.

o.en: Justine also was a girl of merit and possessed qualities which promised to render her life happy; now all was to be obliterated in an ignominious grave, and I the cause!
o.ru: Жюстина тоже была девушкой достойной и обладала качествами, которые обещали ей счастливую жизнь; теперь всему этому суждено было исчезнуть в позорной могиле — и причиной тому был я!

o.en: A thousand times rather would I have confessed myself guilty of the crime ascribed to Justine, but I was absent when it was committed, and such a declaration would have been considered as the ravings of a madman and would not have exculpated her who suffered through me.
o.ru: Тысячу раз охотнее я сознался бы в преступлении, которое приписывали Жюстине, но меня не было на месте, когда оно совершилось, и такое признание сочли бы бредом безумца, и оно не оправдало бы ту, что страдала из-за меня.

o.en: The appearance of Justine was calm.
She was dressed in mourning, and her countenance, always engaging, was rendered, by the solemnity of her feelings, exquisitely beautiful.
o.ru: Она была в трауре, и её лицо, всегда милое, благодаря торжественности её чувств стало необыкновенно прекрасным.

o.en: Yet she appeared confident in innocence and did not tremble, although gazed on and execrated by thousands, for all the kindness which her beauty might otherwise have excited was obliterated in the minds of the spectators by the imagination of the enormity she was supposed to have committed.
o.ru: И всё же она, казалось, была уверена в своей невиновности и не дрожала, хотя на неё смотрели и её проклинали тысячи людей: всё сочувствие, которое в иных обстоятельствах могла бы вызвать её красота, стёрлось в умах зрителей мыслью о чудовищном преступлении, которое она будто бы совершила.

o.en: She was tranquil, yet her tranquillity was evidently constrained; and as her confusion had before been adduced as a proof of her guilt, she worked up her mind to an appearance of courage.
o.ru: Она была спокойна, но спокойствие это явно давалось ей с трудом; и поскольку прежде её смятение было приведено как доказательство вины, она заставила себя казаться мужественной.

o.en: When she entered the court she threw her eyes round it and quickly discovered where we were seated.
o.ru: Войдя в зал суда, она обвела его взглядом и быстро нашла, где мы сидим.

o.en: A tear seemed to dim her eye when she saw us, but she quickly recovered herself, and a look of sorrowful affection seemed to attest her utter guiltlessness.
o.ru: Когда она увидела нас, её глаза, казалось, затуманила слеза, но она быстро овладела собой, и взгляд, полный печальной любви, как будто свидетельствовал о её полной невиновности.

o.en: The trial began, and after the advocate against her had stated the charge, several witnesses were called.
o.ru: Суд начался, и после того как обвинитель изложил суть обвинения, вызвали нескольких свидетелей.

o.en: Several strange facts combined against her, which might have staggered anyone who had not such proof of her innocence as I had.
o.ru: Против неё сошлись несколько странных фактов, которые могли бы поколебать любого, у кого не было таких доказательств её невиновности, как у меня.

o.en: She had been out the whole of the night on which the murder had been committed and towards morning had been perceived by a market-woman not far from the spot where the body of the murdered child had been afterwards found.
o.ru: Всю ночь, когда было совершено убийство, её не было дома, а под утро её заметила торговка с рынка неподалёку от того места, где позже нашли тело убитого ребёнка.

o.en: The woman asked her what she did there, but she looked very strangely and only returned a confused and unintelligible answer.
o.ru: Женщина спросила, что она там делает, но та посмотрела очень странно и дала лишь сбивчивый, невнятный ответ.

o.en: She returned to the house about eight o’clock, and when one inquired where she had passed the night, she replied that she had been looking for the child and demanded earnestly if anything had been heard concerning him.
o.ru: Она вернулась домой около восьми часов, и когда её спросили, где она провела ночь, ответила, что искала ребёнка, и настойчиво расспрашивала, не слышно ли о нём чего-нибудь.

o.en: When shown the body, she fell into violent hysterics and kept her bed for several days.
o.ru: Когда ей показали тело, с ней случилась сильнейшая истерика, и она несколько дней не вставала с постели.

o.en: The picture was then produced which the servant had found in her pocket; and when Elizabeth, in a faltering voice, proved that it was the same which, an hour before the child had been missed, she had placed round his neck, a murmur of horror and indignation filled the court.
o.ru: Затем был предъявлен портрет, который служанка нашла у неё в кармане; и когда Элизабет дрожащим голосом подтвердила, что это тот самый медальон, который она надела мальчику на шею за час до того, как он пропал, по залу пронёсся ропот ужаса и негодования.

o.en: Justine was called on for her defence.
o.ru: Жюстине предложили выступить в свою защиту.

o.en: As the trial had proceeded, her countenance had altered.
o.ru: По мере того как шёл суд, лицо её менялось.

o.en: Surprise, horror, and misery were strongly expressed.
o.ru: На нём ясно выражались изумление, ужас и страдание.

o.en: Sometimes she struggled with her tears, but when she was desired to plead, she collected her powers and spoke in an audible although variable voice.
o.ru: Порой она боролась со слезами, но когда ей велели говорить, она собралась с силами и заговорила внятным, хотя и прерывающимся голосом.

o.en: “God knows,” she said, “how entirely I am innocent.
o.ru: «Бог знает, — сказала она, — насколько я невиновна.

o.en: But I do not pretend that my protestations should acquit me; I rest my innocence on a plain and simple explanation of the facts which have been adduced against me, and I hope the character I have always borne will incline my judges to a favourable interpretation where any circumstance appears doubtful or suspicious.”
o.ru: Но я не притязаю на то, чтобы мои уверения оправдали меня; я основываю свою невиновность на простом и ясном объяснении фактов, приведённых против меня, и надеюсь, что доброе имя, которое я всегда носила, склонит моих судей к благоприятному толкованию там, где какое-либо обстоятельство покажется сомнительным или подозрительным».

o.en: She then related that, by the permission of Elizabeth, she had passed the evening of the night on which the murder had been committed at the house of an aunt at Chêne, a village situated at about a league from Geneva.
o.ru: Затем она рассказала, что с позволения Элизабет провела вечер того дня, когда случилось убийство, в доме своей тётки в Шене, деревне примерно в одном лье от Женевы.

o.en: On her return, at about nine o’clock, she met a man who asked her if she had seen anything of the child who was lost.
o.ru: Возвращаясь около девяти часов, она встретила человека, который спросил, не видела ли она пропавшего ребёнка.

o.en: She was alarmed by this account and passed several hours in looking for him, when the gates of Geneva were shut, and she was forced to remain several hours of the night in a barn belonging to a cottage, being unwilling to call up the inhabitants, to whom she was well known.
o.ru: Встревоженная этим известием, она несколько часов искала его, а тем временем ворота Женевы закрыли, и ей пришлось провести часть ночи в сарае при одном домике: будить хозяев, которые её хорошо знали, она не захотела.

o.en: Most of the night she spent here watching; towards morning she believed that she slept for a few minutes; some steps disturbed her, and she awoke.
o.ru: Большую часть ночи она провела здесь без сна; под утро, как ей кажется, она задремала на несколько минут; её разбудили чьи-то шаги.

o.en: It was dawn, and she quitted her asylum, that she might again endeavour to find my brother.
o.ru: Светало, и она покинула своё убежище, чтобы снова попытаться найти моего брата.

o.en: If she had gone near the spot where his body lay, it was without her knowledge.
o.ru: Если она и проходила возле того места, где лежало его тело, то сама того не знала.

o.en: That she had been bewildered when questioned by the market-woman was not surprising, since she had passed a sleepless night and the fate of poor William was yet uncertain.
o.ru: То, что она растерялась, когда её расспрашивала торговка, неудивительно: она провела бессонную ночь, а судьба бедного Уильяма была ещё неизвестна.

o.en: Concerning the picture she could give no account.
o.ru: Насчёт портрета она ничего объяснить не могла.

o.en: “I know,” continued the unhappy victim, “how heavily and fatally this one circumstance weighs against me, but I have no power of explaining it; and when I have expressed my utter ignorance, I am only left to conjecture concerning the probabilities by which it might have been placed in my pocket.
o.ru: «Я знаю, — продолжала несчастная жертва, — как тяжело и роковым образом свидетельствует против меня это обстоятельство, но объяснить его я не в силах; и, признавшись в полном неведении, я могу лишь гадать, каким образом он мог оказаться в моём кармане.

o.en: But here also I am checked.
o.ru: Но и здесь я захожу в тупик.

o.en: I believe that I have no enemy on earth, and none surely would have been so wicked as to destroy me wantonly.
o.ru: Я уверена, что у меня нет на земле врагов, и, конечно, никто не был бы так жесток, чтобы погубить меня просто так.

o.en: Did the murderer place it there?
I know of no opportunity afforded him for so doing; or, if I had, why should he have stolen the jewel, to part with it again so soon?
o.ru: Я не знаю, когда бы у него была такая возможность; а если бы и была, зачем ему было красть драгоценность, чтобы так скоро с ней расстаться?

o.en: “I commit my cause to the justice of my judges, yet I see no room for hope.
o.ru: Я вверяю своё дело справедливости моих судей, хотя и не вижу места для надежды.

o.en: I beg permission to have a few witnesses examined concerning my character, and if their testimony shall not overweigh my supposed guilt, I must be condemned, although I would pledge my salvation on my innocence.”
o.ru: Прошу позволить допросить нескольких свидетелей о моём нраве, и если их показания не перевесят моей мнимой вины, меня придётся осудить, хотя я готова поручиться спасением своей души, что невиновна».

o.en: Several witnesses were called who had known her for many years, and they spoke well of her; but fear and hatred of the crime of which they supposed her guilty rendered them timorous and unwilling to come forward.
o.ru: Вызвали нескольких свидетелей, знавших её много лет, и они отзывались о ней хорошо; но страх и ненависть к преступлению, в котором они её подозревали, сделали их робкими и неохотно выступающими.

o.en: Elizabeth saw even this last resource, her excellent dispositions and irreproachable conduct, about to fail the accused, when, although violently agitated, she desired permission to address the court.
o.ru: Элизабет видела, что и это последнее средство — прекрасный нрав и безупречное поведение обвиняемой — вот-вот её подведёт, и тогда, хотя она была сильно взволнована, попросила позволения обратиться к суду.

o.en: “I am,” said she, “the cousin of the unhappy child who was murdered, or rather his sister, for I was educated by and have lived with his parents ever since and even long before his birth.
o.ru: «Я, — сказала она, — двоюродная сестра убитого несчастного ребёнка, или, вернее, его сестра, потому что я воспитывалась у его родителей и живу с ними с тех пор, задолго до его рождения.

o.en: It may therefore be judged indecent in me to come forward on this occasion, but when I see a fellow creature about to perish through the cowardice of her pretended friends, I wish to be allowed to speak, that I may say what I know of her character.
o.ru: Поэтому, быть может, сочтут неприличным, что я выступаю в этом деле, но когда я вижу, как человек вот-вот погибнет из-за трусости своих мнимых друзей, я прошу позволить мне говорить, чтобы рассказать, что я знаю о её характере.

o.en: I am well acquainted with the accused.
I have lived in the same house with her, at one time for five and at another for nearly two years.
o.ru: Я жила с ней под одной крышей один раз пять лет, а в другой — почти два года.

o.en: During all that period she appeared to me the most amiable and benevolent of human creatures.
o.ru: Всё это время она казалась мне самым милым и добросердечным из людей.

o.en: She nursed Madame Frankenstein, my aunt, in her last illness, with the greatest affection and care and afterwards attended her own mother during a tedious illness, in a manner that excited the admiration of all who knew her, after which she again lived in my uncle’s house, where she was beloved by all the family.
o.ru: Она ухаживала за госпожой Франкенштейн, моей тётей, в её последней болезни с величайшей любовью и заботой, а затем ходила за собственной матерью во время её долгой, изнурительной болезни так, что вызывала восхищение всех, кто её знал; после этого она снова жила в доме моего дяди, где её любила вся семья.

o.en: She was warmly attached to the child who is now dead and acted towards him like a most affectionate mother.
o.ru: Она была горячо привязана к ребёнку, которого теперь нет в живых, и относилась к нему как самая нежная мать.

o.en: For my own part, I do not hesitate to say that, notwithstanding all the evidence produced against her, I believe and rely on her perfect innocence.
o.ru: Что до меня, то я без колебаний скажу, что, несмотря на все улики против неё, я верю в её полную невиновность и полагаюсь на неё.

o.en: She had no temptation for such an action; as to the bauble on which the chief proof rests, if she had earnestly desired it, I should have willingly given it to her, so much do I esteem and value her.”
o.ru: У неё не было никакого соблазна совершить такой поступок; а что до безделушки, на которой держится главное доказательство, — если бы она сильно её пожелала, я охотно отдала бы её ей: так я уважаю и ценю её».

o.en: A murmur of approbation followed Elizabeth’s simple and powerful appeal, but it was excited by her generous interference, and not in favour of poor Justine, on whom the public indignation was turned with renewed violence, charging her with the blackest ingratitude.
o.ru: Простую и сильную речь Элизабет встретил одобрительный гул, но вызвало его её великодушное заступничество, а не сочувствие к бедной Жюстине, на которую общественное негодование обрушилось с новой силой, обвиняя её в чернейшей неблагодарности.

o.en: She herself wept as Elizabeth spoke, but she did not answer.
o.ru: Сама она плакала, пока говорила Элизабет, но ничего не ответила.

o.en: My own agitation and anguish was extreme during the whole trial.
o.ru: Моё собственное волнение и мука были безмерны на протяжении всего суда.

o.en: I believed in her innocence; I knew it.
o.ru: Я верил в её невиновность; я знал о ней.

o.en: Could the dæmon who had (I did not for a minute doubt) murdered my brother also in his hellish sport have betrayed the innocent to death and ignominy?
o.ru: Неужели демон, который (я ни минуты в этом не сомневался) убил моего брата, в своей адской забаве ещё и предал невинную смерти и позору?

o.en: I could not sustain the horror of my situation, and when I perceived that the popular voice and the countenances of the judges had already condemned my unhappy victim, I rushed out of the court in agony.
