b1.en: It takes away more than half of my pain, and I feel I can die in peace now that you, dear lady, and your cousin know I am innocent.”
b1.ru: Она забирает больше половины моей боли, и мне кажется, что я могу умереть спокойно теперь, когда вы, милая госпожа, и ваш кузен знаете, что я невиновна».

b1.en: So the poor girl tried to comfort other people and herself.
b1.ru: Так бедная девушка пыталась утешить других и себя.

b1.en: And she really found the peace she wanted.
b1.ru: И она действительно обрела покой, которого хотела.

b1.en: But I, the real murderer, felt a worm that never dies eating my heart, and it left no hope or comfort.
b1.ru: А я, настоящий убийца, чувствовал, как бессмертный червь грызёт моё сердце, не оставляя ни надежды, ни утешения.

b1.en: Elizabeth also cried and was unhappy, but her sadness was the sadness of an innocent person.
b1.ru: Элизабет тоже плакала и была несчастна, но её грусть была грустью невинного человека.

b1.en: It was like a cloud that goes across the bright moon: it hides the moon for a while, but it cannot make it less bright.
b1.ru: Она была как облако, которое проходит по яркой луне: оно на время закрывает её, но не может сделать её менее яркой.

b1.en: Pain and despair had gone into the centre of my heart; I carried a hell inside me that nothing could stop.
b1.ru: Боль и отчаяние проникли в самую глубину моего сердца; я носил в себе ад, который ничто не могло остановить.

b1.en: We stayed with Justine for several hours, and it was very hard for Elizabeth to leave her.
b1.ru: Мы провели с Жюстиной несколько часов, и Элизабет было очень трудно её оставить.

b1.en: “I wish I could die with you,” she cried. “I cannot live in this world of pain.”
b1.ru: «Лучше бы я умерла вместе с тобой, — воскликнула она. — Я не могу жить в этом мире боли».

b1.en: Justine tried to look cheerful, but it was hard for her not to cry.
b1.ru: Жюстина старалась выглядеть весёлой, но ей было трудно не плакать.

b1.en: She put her arms around Elizabeth and said, in a voice full of feeling, “Goodbye, sweet lady, dearest Elizabeth, my dear and only friend; may God bless you and keep you safe; may this be the last sad thing that ever happens to you!
b1.ru: Она обняла Элизабет и сказала голосом, полным чувств: «Прощайте, милая госпожа, дорогая Элизабет, мой любимый и единственный друг; да благословит и сохранит вас Бог; пусть это будет последнее горе в вашей жизни!

b1.en: Live, and be happy, and make other people happy.”
b1.ru: Живите, будьте счастливы и делайте счастливыми других».

b1.en: And the next day Justine died.
b1.ru: А на следующий день Жюстина умерла.

b1.en: Elizabeth’s beautiful, moving words did not change the judges’ minds; they were sure that the poor, good girl was guilty.
b1.ru: Прекрасные, трогательные слова Элизабет не изменили мнения судей: они были уверены, что бедная добрая девушка виновна.

b1.en: My angry, passionate words did not help either.
b1.ru: Мои гневные, страстные слова тоже не помогли.

b1.en: When I heard the cold, hard answers of these men, I could not say what I had planned to say.
b1.ru: Когда я услышал холодные, жёсткие ответы этих людей, я не смог сказать то, что собирался.

b1.en: They would only think I was mad, and they would not change the sentence.
b1.ru: Они только решили бы, что я сошёл с ума, и не изменили бы приговор.

b1.en: She died on the scaffold as a murderer!
b1.ru: Она умерла на эшафоте как убийца!

b1.en: I stopped thinking about my own pain and looked at the deep, silent sadness of my Elizabeth.
b1.ru: Я перестал думать о собственной боли и посмотрел на глубокую, молчаливую печаль моей Элизабет.

b1.en: This was my fault too!
b1.ru: И в этом тоже был виноват я!

b1.en: My father’s sadness, and our home, which had been so happy and was now so empty — all of this was the work of my cursed hands!
b1.ru: Горе моего отца и наш дом, когда-то такой счастливый, а теперь такой пустой, — всё это было делом моих проклятых рук!

b1.en: You are crying, my poor family, but these are not your last tears!
b1.ru: Вы плачете, моя бедная семья, но это не последние ваши слёзы!

b1.en: You will cry at a funeral again, and people will hear you cry again and again!
b1.ru: Вы снова будете плакать на похоронах, и люди снова и снова будут слышать ваш плач!

b1.en: I, Frankenstein, your son, your relative and your loving friend, would give all my blood for you.
b1.ru: Я, Франкенштейн, ваш сын, ваш родственник и любящий друг, отдал бы за вас всю свою кровь.

b1.en: I feel no joy unless I see it in your dear faces, and I want to spend my life serving you.
b1.ru: Я не чувствую радости, если не вижу её на ваших дорогих лицах, и хочу посвятить жизнь служению вам.

b1.en: But I am the one who makes you cry so many tears.
b1.ru: Но именно я заставляю вас проливать столько слёз.

b1.en: I will be happier than I can hope if cruel fate is satisfied now, and if the destruction stops before you all find peace in the grave!
b1.ru: Я буду счастлив больше, чем смею надеяться, если жестокая судьба теперь успокоится и если гибель остановится прежде, чем вы все найдёте покой в могиле!

b1.en: That is what my soul told me about the future, as I watched, full of guilt, horror and despair, the people I loved crying over the graves of William and Justine, the first poor victims of my terrible science.
b1.ru: Вот что предсказала мне душа, когда я, полный вины, ужаса и отчаяния, смотрел, как любимые мною люди плачут над могилами Уильяма и Жюстины — первых несчастных жертв моей страшной науки.

a2.en: We waited for a few sad hours.
a2.ru: Мы ждали несколько грустных часов.

a2.en: The trial started at eleven o’clock.
a2.ru: Суд начался в одиннадцать часов.

a2.en: My father and the family had to speak in court, so I went with them.
a2.ru: Отец и семья должны были выступать в суде, поэтому я пошёл с ними.

a2.en: For me, the whole trial was terrible pain.
a2.ru: Для меня весь суд был ужасной болью.

a2.en: Because of my experiments, two people were going to die.
a2.ru: Из-за моих опытов должны были умереть два человека.

a2.en: One was a happy little boy.
a2.ru: Один был счастливым маленьким мальчиком.

a2.en: The other was a young woman, and her death was going to be even worse.
a2.ru: Другая была молодой женщиной, и её смерть должна была стать ещё страшнее.

a2.en: Everyone was going to remember this murder with horror.
a2.ru: Все должны были вспоминать это убийство с ужасом.

a2.en: Justine was a good girl, and her life could be happy.
a2.ru: Жюстина была хорошей девушкой, и её жизнь могла быть счастливой.

a2.en: Now she was going to die in shame, and it was my fault!
a2.ru: Теперь она должна была умереть в позоре, и это была моя вина!

a2.en: I wanted to say, “I am the killer.”
a2.ru: Я хотел сказать: «Убийца — я».

a2.en: But I was not in Geneva that night.
a2.ru: Но той ночью меня не было в Женеве.

a2.en: People would think I was mad, and it would not help her.
a2.ru: Люди решили бы, что я сошёл с ума, и ей это не помогло бы.

a2.en: Justine looked calm.
a2.ru: Жюстина выглядела спокойной.

a2.en: She wore black clothes, and her face was very beautiful.
a2.ru: Она была в чёрной одежде, и её лицо было очень красивым.

a2.en: Thousands of people looked at her and hated her, but she did not shake.
a2.ru: Тысячи людей смотрели на неё и ненавидели её, но она не дрожала.

a2.en: They thought she was a killer, so they did not feel sorry for her.
a2.ru: Они думали, что она убийца, поэтому им не было её жаль.

a2.en: Before, people said, “She was confused, so she is guilty.”
a2.ru: Раньше люди говорили: «Она растерялась, значит, она виновна».

a2.en: She tried hard to look brave.
a2.ru: Она изо всех сил старалась выглядеть смелой.

a2.en: When she came in, she looked around and saw us.
a2.ru: Когда она вошла, она огляделась и увидела нас.

a2.en: She almost cried, but then she gave us a sad, loving look.
a2.ru: Она чуть не заплакала, но потом посмотрела на нас грустно и с любовью.

a2.en: The trial began, and some people spoke against her.
a2.ru: Суд начался, и некоторые люди выступили против неё.

a2.en: Some strange facts were against her.
a2.ru: Против неё были странные факты.

a2.en: I knew she was innocent, but other people did not know.
a2.ru: Я знал, что она невиновна, но другие люди этого не знали.

a2.en: She was out all night on the night of the murder.
a2.ru: В ночь убийства её не было дома всю ночь.

a2.en: Early in the morning, a woman from the market saw her near the place of the murder.
a2.ru: Рано утром женщина с рынка увидела её рядом с местом убийства.

a2.en: The woman asked her a question, but Justine gave a strange answer.
a2.ru: Женщина задала ей вопрос, но Жюстина странно ответила.

a2.en: She came home at eight o’clock.
a2.ru: Она пришла домой в восемь часов.

a2.en: She said, “I was looking for William.”
a2.ru: Она сказала: «Я искала Уильяма».

a2.en: She asked many times, “Is there any news about him?”
a2.ru: Она много раз спрашивала: «Есть ли о нём новости?»

a2.en: When she saw his body, she became very ill and stayed in bed for days.
a2.ru: Когда она увидела его тело, ей стало очень плохо, и она несколько дней лежала в постели.

a2.en: Then they showed the picture from her pocket.
a2.ru: Потом показали портрет из её кармана.

a2.en: Elizabeth said, “Yes, I put this picture on William’s neck that evening.”
a2.ru: Элизабет сказала: «Да, я надела этот портрет Уильяму на шею в тот вечер».

a2.en: Everyone in the court was angry and afraid.
a2.ru: Все в зале были рассержены и напуганы.

a2.en: Then Justine spoke.
a2.ru: Потом заговорила Жюстина.

a2.en: Her face was full of surprise and pain.
a2.ru: Её лицо было полно удивления и боли.

a2.en: She tried not to cry, and she spoke clearly.
a2.ru: Она старалась не плакать и говорила ясно.

a2.en: “God knows that I am innocent,” she said.
a2.ru: «Бог знает, что я невиновна», — сказала она.

a2.en: “I will explain the facts.
a2.ru: «Я объясню факты.

a2.en: I hope my judges will remember that I am a good person.”
a2.ru: Надеюсь, судьи вспомнят, что я хороший человек».

a2.en: She told her story.
a2.ru: Она рассказала свою историю.

a2.en: That evening she visited her aunt in a village near Geneva.
a2.ru: В тот вечер она была у тёти в деревне недалеко от Женевы.

a2.en: On her way home, a man asked her about the lost child.
a2.ru: По дороге домой мужчина спросил её о пропавшем ребёнке.

a2.en: She was afraid and looked for William for hours.
a2.ru: Она испугалась и много часов искала Уильяма.

a2.en: Then the city gates closed, so she slept in a barn.
a2.ru: Потом городские ворота закрылись, и она спала в сарае.

a2.en: She did not want to wake the people in the house, because they knew her.
a2.ru: Она не хотела будить людей в доме, потому что они её знали.

a2.en: She did not sleep much.
a2.ru: Она почти не спала.

a2.en: In the morning she heard some steps and woke up.
a2.ru: Утром она услышала шаги и проснулась.

a2.en: Then she went to look for William again.
a2.ru: Потом она снова пошла искать Уильяма.

a2.en: She did not know where his body was.
a2.ru: Она не знала, где его тело.

a2.en: She was tired and worried, so she answered the market woman strangely.
a2.ru: Она устала и волновалась, поэтому странно ответила торговке.

a2.en: She did not sleep all night, and she did not know what happened to William.
a2.ru: Она не спала всю ночь и не знала, что случилось с Уильямом.

a2.en: She could not explain the picture.
a2.ru: Портрет она объяснить не могла.

a2.en: “I know that the picture is very bad for me,” she said.
a2.ru: «Я знаю, что портрет очень плох для меня», — сказала она.

a2.en: “But I cannot explain it.
a2.ru: «Но я не могу его объяснить.

a2.en: I do not know how it got into my pocket.
a2.ru: Я не знаю, как он попал ко мне в карман.

a2.en: I have no enemies.
a2.ru: У меня нет врагов.

a2.en: Did the killer put it there?
a2.ru: Может быть, его положил туда убийца?

a2.en: But why did he steal it and then give it away?”
a2.ru: Но зачем он его украл, а потом отдал?»

a2.en: “I have no hope.
a2.ru: «У меня нет надежды.

a2.en: Please listen to people who know me.
a2.ru: Пожалуйста, выслушайте людей, которые меня знают.

a2.en: I am innocent.
a2.ru: Я невиновна.

a2.en: If the judges do not believe them, I must die.”
a2.ru: Если судьи им не поверят, я должна умереть».

a2.en: Some people spoke for her, but they were afraid and did not say much.
a2.ru: Несколько человек выступили за неё, но они боялись и сказали мало.

a2.en: Elizabeth was very worried, and she asked to speak.
a2.ru: Элизабет очень волновалась и попросила слова.

a2.en: “I am William’s cousin,” she said, “but really I am his sister.
a2.ru: «Я двоюродная сестра Уильяма, — сказала она, — но на самом деле я его сестра.

a2.en: I have lived with his family for many years.
a2.ru: Я много лет живу в его семье.

a2.en: Maybe it is wrong for me to speak here, but I must.
a2.ru: Может быть, мне не следует здесь выступать, но я должна.

a2.en: Justine’s friends are afraid to help her, so I want to speak.
a2.ru: Друзья Жюстины боятся ей помочь, поэтому я хочу выступить.

a2.en: I know Justine well.
a2.ru: Я хорошо знаю Жюстину.

a2.en: I lived with her for many years.
a2.ru: Я жила с ней много лет.

a2.en: She is a very kind person.
a2.ru: Она очень добрый человек.

a2.en: When my aunt was dying, Justine took care of her with love.
a2.ru: Когда моя тётя умирала, Жюстина заботилась о ней с любовью.

a2.en: Later she took care of her own sick mother.
a2.ru: Потом она заботилась о своей больной матери.

a2.en: All our family loved her.
a2.ru: Вся наша семья её любила.

a2.en: She loved William like a mother.
a2.ru: Она любила Уильяма, как мать.

a2.en: I believe she is innocent.
a2.ru: Я верю, что она невиновна.

a2.en: She had no reason to do this.
a2.ru: У неё не было причины это делать.

a2.en: If she wanted the picture, I was happy to give it to her.
a2.ru: Если бы она захотела портрет, я с радостью отдала бы его ей.

a2.en: I love and respect her very much.”
a2.ru: Я очень люблю и уважаю её».

a2.en: People liked Elizabeth’s words, but they did not change their minds about Justine.
a2.ru: Людям понравились слова Элизабет, но своего мнения о Жюстине они не изменили.

a2.en: Now they were even angrier with her.
a2.ru: Теперь они злились на неё ещё больше.

a2.en: Justine cried, but she said nothing.
a2.ru: Жюстина плакала, но ничего не сказала.

a2.en: I felt terrible during the whole trial.
a2.ru: Весь суд я чувствовал себя ужасно.

a2.en: I knew that Justine was innocent.
a2.ru: Я знал, что Жюстина невиновна.

a2.en: The monster killed my brother.
a2.ru: Мой брат был убит чудовищем.

a2.en: Did he also want Justine to die?
a2.ru: Неужели оно хотело, чтобы и Жюстина умерла?

a2.en: I saw that the judges already thought she was guilty, and I ran out of the court.
a2.ru: Я увидел, что судьи уже считают её виновной, и выбежал из зала.

a2.en: She was innocent, so she was strong.
a2.ru: Она была невиновна, поэтому была сильной.

a2.en: But I felt guilty, and it hurt me terribly.
a2.ru: А я чувствовал вину, и мне было ужасно больно.

a2.en: I had a terrible night.
a2.ru: У меня была ужасная ночь.

a2.en: My mouth was very dry.
a2.ru: У меня во рту совсем пересохло.

a2.en: In the morning I went to the court.
a2.ru: Утром я пошёл в суд.

a2.en: I was afraid to ask the question, but the officer understood.
a2.ru: Я боялся задать вопрос, но служитель понял.

a2.en: All the judges said “guilty”, and Justine had to die.
a2.ru: Все судьи сказали «виновна», и Жюстина должна была умереть.

a2.en: I cannot describe my feelings.
a2.ru: Я не могу описать свои чувства.

a2.en: There are no words for my terrible sadness.
a2.ru: Нет слов для моей страшной печали.

a2.en: I had felt horror before, but this was worse.
a2.ru: Я и раньше испытывал ужас, но теперь было хуже.

a2.en: The officer also said, “Justine has told us that she did it.
a2.ru: Служитель ещё сказал: «Жюстина сказала нам, что это сделала она.

a2.en: We are glad, because now we are sure.”
a2.ru: Мы рады, потому что теперь мы уверены».

a2.en: I did not understand.
a2.ru: Я не понимал.

a2.en: Was I wrong?
a2.ru: Неужели я ошибался?

a2.en: Was I mad?
a2.ru: Неужели я сошёл с ума?

a2.en: I went home quickly, and Elizabeth asked me about the trial.
a2.ru: Я быстро пошёл домой, и Элизабет спросила меня о суде.

a2.en: “Justine must die,” I answered.
a2.ru: «Жюстина должна умереть», — ответил я.

a2.en: “Judges are happier to kill ten innocent people than to let one bad person go free.
a2.ru: «Судьи скорее убьют десять невинных, чем отпустят одного преступника.

a2.en: And she has said that she did it.”
a2.ru: И она сказала, что это сделала она».

a2.en: This was terrible for Elizabeth.
a2.ru: Для Элизабет это было ужасно.

a2.en: She believed that Justine was innocent.
a2.ru: Она верила, что Жюстина невиновна.

a2.en: “How can I believe in good people now?” she said.
a2.ru: «Как мне теперь верить в хороших людей?» — сказала она.

a2.en: “I loved Justine like a sister.
a2.ru: «Я любила Жюстину, как сестру.

a2.en: She had such kind eyes, and she killed a child!”
a2.ru: У неё были такие добрые глаза, а она убила ребёнка!»

a2.en: Soon Justine asked to see Elizabeth.
a2.ru: Скоро Жюстина попросила о встрече с Элизабет.

a2.en: My father said, “You can decide.”
a2.ru: Отец сказал: «Решай сама».

a2.en: “I will go,” said Elizabeth.
a2.ru: «Я пойду», — сказала Элизабет.

a2.en: “Victor, please come with me.”
a2.ru: «Виктор, пожалуйста, пойдём со мной».

a2.en: My father did not want her to go.
a2.ru: Отец не хотел, чтобы она шла.

a2.en: I did not want to go, but I could not say no.
a2.ru: Я не хотел идти, но не мог отказаться.

a2.en: We went into the dark prison.
a2.ru: Мы вошли в тёмную тюрьму.

a2.en: Justine was sitting on some straw, with chains on her hands.
a2.ru: Жюстина сидела на соломе, с цепями на руках.

a2.en: She stood up, and then she fell at Elizabeth’s feet and cried.
a2.ru: Она встала, а потом упала к ногам Элизабет и заплакала.

a2.en: Elizabeth cried too.
a2.ru: Элизабет тоже заплакала.

a2.en: “Oh, Justine!” said Elizabeth.
a2.ru: «О Жюстина! — сказала Элизабет.

a2.en: “Why did you say you did it?
a2.ru: — Зачем ты сказала, что это сделала ты?

a2.en: Now I am even sadder than before.”
a2.ru: Теперь мне ещё грустнее, чем раньше».

a2.en: “Do you also think I am a bad person?” Justine asked.
a2.ru: «Вы тоже думаете, что я плохой человек?» — спросила Жюстина.

a2.en: “Are you my enemy too?”
a2.ru: «Вы тоже мой враг?»

a2.en: She was crying hard.
a2.ru: Она сильно плакала.

a2.en: “Stand up, my poor girl,” said Elizabeth.
a2.ru: «Встань, бедная моя девочка», — сказала Элизабет.

a2.en: “I am not your enemy.
a2.ru: «Я тебе не враг.

a2.en: I believed you, but then I heard that you said you did it.
a2.ru: Я верила тебе, но потом услышала, что ты сказала, что это сделала ты.

a2.en: If that is not true, I will believe you again.”
a2.ru: Если это неправда, я снова буду тебе верить».

a2.en: “Yes, I said it, but it was a lie.
a2.ru: «Да, я это сказала, но это была ложь.

a2.en: Now this lie is very heavy on my heart.
a2.ru: Теперь эта ложь очень тяжело лежит у меня на сердце.

a2.en: The priest came to me every day.
a2.ru: Священник приходил ко мне каждый день.

a2.en: He shouted at me and frightened me.
a2.ru: Он кричал на меня и пугал меня.

a2.en: He said, ‘You will go to hell if you do not say that you did it.’
a2.ru: Он говорил: „Ты попадёшь в ад, если не скажешь, что это сделала ты“.

a2.en: Nobody helped me.
a2.ru: Никто мне не помог.

a2.en: He said, ‘You are a monster,’ and I almost believed him.
a2.ru: Он говорил: „Ты чудовище“, — и я почти ему поверила.

a2.en: What could I do?
a2.ru: Что мне было делать?

a2.en: So I told a lie, and now I am really unhappy.”
a2.ru: И я солгала, и теперь я по-настоящему несчастна».

a2.en: She cried and then said, “I was afraid that you believed I was a killer.
a2.ru: Она заплакала, а потом сказала: «Я боялась, что вы поверили, будто я убийца.

a2.en: Your aunt was always good to me, and you loved me.
a2.ru: Ваша тётя всегда была добра ко мне, и вы меня любили.

a2.en: Dear William!
a2.ru: Милый Уильям!

a2.en: I will see you again in heaven soon, and we will be happy there.
a2.ru: Скоро я снова увижу тебя на небесах, и мы будем там счастливы.

a2.en: That helps me.”
a2.ru: Это мне помогает».

a2.en: “Oh, Justine!
a2.ru: «О Жюстина!

a2.en: I am sorry that I did not believe you.
a2.ru: Прости, что я тебе не поверила.

a2.en: Do not be sad.
a2.ru: Не грусти.

a2.en: Do not be afraid.
a2.ru: Не бойся.

a2.en: I will tell everyone that you are innocent.
a2.ru: Я всем скажу, что ты невиновна.

a2.en: My tears will make your enemies’ hearts soft.
a2.ru: Мои слёзы смягчат сердца твоих врагов.

a2.en: You will not die!
a2.ru: Ты не умрёшь!

a2.en: You are my friend and my sister.
a2.ru: Ты моя подруга и моя сестра.

a2.en: I cannot live without you!”
a2.ru: Я не могу жить без тебя!»

a2.en: Justine shook her head sadly.
a2.ru: Жюстина грустно покачала головой.

a2.en: “I am not afraid to die,” she said.
a2.ru: «Я не боюсь умереть», — сказала она.

a2.en: “God makes me strong.
a2.ru: «Бог даёт мне силы.

a2.en: I am leaving a sad world.
a2.ru: Я покидаю печальный мир.

a2.en: Please remember me as an innocent person.
a2.ru: Пожалуйста, помните меня как невиновного человека.

a2.en: Then I can accept my death.”
a2.ru: Тогда я смогу принять свою смерть».

a2.en: I stood in a corner because I wanted to hide my pain.
a2.ru: Я стоял в углу, потому что хотел скрыть свою боль.

a2.en: Despair!
a2.ru: Отчаяние!

a2.en: Who could talk about despair?
a2.ru: Кто мог говорить об отчаянии?

a2.en: Justine was going to die the next day, but my pain was worse than hers.
a2.ru: Жюстина должна была умереть на следующий день, но моя боль была сильнее её боли.

a2.en: I made a loud, terrible sound.
a2.ru: Я издал громкий, страшный звук.

a2.en: Justine was surprised.
a2.ru: Жюстина удивилась.

a2.en: She came to me and said, “Thank you for coming, sir.
a2.ru: Она подошла ко мне и сказала: «Спасибо, что пришли, сударь.

a2.en: You do not think I am guilty, do you?”
a2.ru: Вы ведь не думаете, что я виновна?»

a2.en: I could not answer.
a2.ru: Я не мог ответить.

a2.en: “No,” said Elizabeth.
a2.ru: «Нет, — сказала Элизабет.

a2.en: “He always believed you were innocent.”
a2.ru: — Он всегда верил, что ты невиновна».

a2.en: “Thank you,” said Justine.
a2.ru: «Спасибо», — сказала Жюстина.

a2.en: “Your love helps me very much.
a2.ru: «Ваша любовь мне очень помогает.

a2.en: Now I can die in peace, because you both know I am innocent.”
a2.ru: Теперь я могу умереть спокойно, потому что вы оба знаете, что я невиновна».

a2.en: Justine tried to help us and herself, and she felt calmer.
a2.ru: Жюстина старалась поддержать нас и себя, и ей стало спокойнее.

a2.en: But I was the real killer, and I had no hope.
a2.ru: Но настоящим убийцей был я, и у меня не было надежды.

a2.en: She found peace.
a2.ru: Она обрела покой.

a2.en: Elizabeth was sad too, but she was innocent.
a2.ru: Элизабет тоже было грустно, но она была невиновна.

a2.en: Her sadness was like a cloud in front of the moon: the moon is still bright behind it.
a2.ru: Её печаль была как облако перед луной: за ним луна всё равно яркая.

a2.en: But I carried a terrible pain in my heart.
a2.ru: А я носил в сердце страшную боль.

a2.en: We stayed with Justine for hours.
a2.ru: Мы пробыли с Жюстиной много часов.

a2.en: Elizabeth did not want to leave.
a2.ru: Элизабет не хотела уходить.

a2.en: “I want to die with you,” she cried.
a2.ru: «Я хочу умереть вместе с тобой!» — воскликнула она.

a2.en: Justine tried to smile and not cry.
a2.ru: Жюстина старалась улыбаться и не плакать.

a2.en: She put her arms around Elizabeth.
a2.ru: Она обняла Элизабет.

a2.en: “Goodbye, dear Elizabeth, my only friend,” she said.
a2.ru: «Прощайте, дорогая Элизабет, мой единственный друг», — сказала она.

a2.en: “God bless you!
a2.ru: «Храни вас Бог!

a2.en: I hope this is the last sad day of your life.
a2.ru: Надеюсь, это последний грустный день в вашей жизни.

a2.en: Be happy, and make other people happy.”
a2.ru: Будьте счастливы и делайте счастливыми других».

a2.en: The next day Justine died.
a2.ru: На следующий день Жюстина умерла.

a2.en: Elizabeth spoke to the judges, but they did not listen.
a2.ru: Элизабет говорила с судьями, но они не слушали.

a2.en: I spoke to them too, but they gave me cold answers.
a2.ru: Я тоже говорил с ними, но они холодно мне ответили.

a2.en: I wanted to tell them the truth, but I did not.
a2.ru: Я хотел сказать им правду, но не сказал.

a2.en: The judges were cold, hard men.
a2.ru: Судьи были холодными, жёсткими людьми.

a2.en: They would only think I was mad.
a2.ru: Они бы только решили, что я сошёл с ума.

a2.en: So Justine died as a murderer!
a2.ru: И Жюстина умерла как убийца!

a2.en: I looked at Elizabeth’s quiet sadness.
a2.ru: Я смотрел на тихую печаль Элизабет.

a2.en: This was my fault too!
a2.ru: В этом тоже был виноват я!

a2.en: My father was sad, and our happy home was now empty.
a2.ru: Отец был печален, а наш счастливый дом теперь опустел.

a2.en: It was all because of me!
a2.ru: Всё это было из-за меня!

a2.en: My poor family, you are crying, but you will cry again!
a2.ru: Моя бедная семья, вы плачете, но вы будете плакать снова!

a2.en: There will be more deaths!
a2.ru: Будут ещё смерти!

a2.en: I love you all, and I want to give my life for you.
a2.ru: Я люблю вас всех и хочу отдать за вас жизнь.

a2.en: I would give every drop of my blood for you.
a2.ru: Я отдал бы за вас каждую каплю своей крови.

a2.en: But I am the one who makes you cry.
a2.ru: Но именно я заставляю вас плакать.

a2.en: I hope that these deaths are the last.
a2.ru: Я надеюсь, что эти смерти — последние.

a2.en: I thought this as I watched my family cry at the graves of William and Justine.
a2.ru: Так я думал, глядя, как моя семья плачет у могил Уильяма и Жюстины.

a2.en: They were the first victims of my terrible work.
a2.ru: Они были первыми жертвами моей страшной работы.

sub: Tormented by guilt after Justine's death, Victor withdraws into despair, hears Elizabeth's grief, and escapes to the Alpine valley of Chamounix

o: Nothing is more painful to the human mind than, after the feelings have been worked up by a quick succession of events, the dead calmness of inaction and certainty which follows and deprives the soul both of hope and fear. Justine died, she rested, and I was alive. The blood flowed freely in my veins, but a weight of despair and remorse pressed on my heart which nothing could remove. Sleep fled from my eyes; I wandered like an evil spirit, for I had committed deeds of mischief beyond description horrible, and more, much more (I persuaded myself) was yet behind.

Yet my heart overflowed with kindness and the love of virtue. I had begun life with benevolent intentions and thirsted for the moment when I should put them in practice and make myself useful to my fellow beings. Now all was blasted; instead of that serenity of conscience which allowed me to look back upon the past with self-satisfaction, and from thence to gather promise of new hopes, I was seized by remorse and the sense of guilt, which hurried me away to a hell of intense tortures such as no language can describe.

This state of mind preyed upon my health, which had perhaps never entirely recovered from the first shock it had sustained. I shunned the face of man; all sound of joy or complacency was torture to me; solitude was my only consolation—deep, dark, deathlike solitude.

My father observed with pain the alteration perceptible in my disposition and habits and endeavoured by arguments deduced from the feelings of his serene conscience and guiltless life to inspire me with fortitude and awaken in me the courage to dispel the dark cloud which brooded over me. “Do you think, Victor,” said he, “that I do not suffer also? No one could love a child more than I loved your brother”—tears came into his eyes as he spoke—“but is it not a duty to the survivors that we should refrain from augmenting their unhappiness by an appearance of immoderate grief? It is also a duty owed to yourself, for excessive sorrow prevents improvement or enjoyment, or even the discharge of daily usefulness, without which no man is fit for society.”

This advice, although good, was totally inapplicable to my case; I should have been the first to hide my grief and console my friends if remorse had not mingled its bitterness, and terror its alarm, with my other sensations. Now I could only answer my father with a look of despair and endeavour to hide myself from his view.

About this time we retired to our house at Belrive. This change was particularly agreeable to me. The shutting of the gates regularly at ten o’clock and the impossibility of remaining on the lake after that hour had rendered our residence within the walls of Geneva very irksome to me. I was now free. Often, after the rest of the family had retired for the night, I took the boat and passed many hours upon the water. Sometimes, with my sails set, I was carried by the wind; and sometimes, after rowing into the middle of the lake, I left the boat to pursue its own course and gave way to my own miserable reflections.

I was often tempted, when all was at peace around me, and I the only unquiet thing that wandered restless in a scene so beautiful and heavenly—if I except some bat, or the frogs, whose harsh and interrupted croaking was heard only when I approached the shore—often, I say, I was tempted to plunge into the silent lake, that the waters might close over me and my calamities for ever.

But I was restrained, when I thought of the heroic and suffering Elizabeth, whom I tenderly loved, and whose existence was bound up in mine. I thought also of my father and surviving brother; should I by my base desertion leave them exposed and unprotected to the malice of the fiend whom I had let loose among them?

At these moments I wept bitterly and wished that peace would revisit my mind only that I might afford them consolation and happiness. But that could not be. Remorse extinguished every hope. I had been the author of unalterable evils, and I lived in daily fear lest the monster whom I had created should perpetrate some new wickedness. I had an obscure feeling that all was not over and that he would still commit some signal crime, which by its enormity should almost efface the recollection of the past. There was always scope for fear so long as anything I loved remained behind.

My abhorrence of this fiend cannot be conceived. When I thought of him I gnashed my teeth, my eyes became inflamed, and I ardently wished to extinguish that life which I had so thoughtlessly bestowed. When I reflected on his crimes and malice, my hatred and revenge burst all bounds of moderation. I would have made a pilgrimage to the highest peak of the Andes, could I, when there, have precipitated him to their base. I wished to see him again, that I might wreak the utmost extent of abhorrence on his head and avenge the deaths of William and Justine.

Our house was the house of mourning. My father’s health was deeply shaken by the horror of the recent events. Elizabeth was sad and desponding; she no longer took delight in her ordinary occupations; all pleasure seemed to her sacrilege toward the dead; eternal woe and tears she then thought was the just tribute she should pay to innocence so blasted and destroyed. She was no longer that happy creature who in earlier youth wandered with me on the banks of the lake and talked with ecstasy of our future prospects. The first of those sorrows which are sent to wean us from the earth had visited her, and its dimming influence quenched her dearest smiles.

“When I reflect, my dear cousin,” said she, “on the miserable death of Justine Moritz, I no longer see the world and its works as they before appeared to me. Before, I looked upon the accounts of vice and injustice that I read in books or heard from others as tales of ancient days or imaginary evils; at least they were remote and more familiar to reason than to the imagination; but now misery has come home, and men appear to me as monsters thirsting for each other’s blood. Yet I am certainly unjust. Everybody believed that poor girl to be guilty; and if she could have committed the crime for which she suffered, assuredly she would have been the most depraved of human creatures.

For the sake of a few jewels, to have murdered the son of her benefactor and friend, a child whom she had nursed from its birth, and appeared to love as if it had been her own! I could not consent to the death of any human being, but certainly I should have thought such a creature unfit to remain in the society of men. But she was innocent. I know, I feel she was innocent; you are of the same opinion, and that confirms me.

Alas! Victor, when falsehood can look so like the truth, who can assure themselves of certain happiness? I feel as if I were walking on the edge of a precipice, towards which thousands are crowding and endeavouring to plunge me into the abyss. William and Justine were assassinated, and the murderer escapes; he walks about the world free, and perhaps respected. But even if I were condemned to suffer on the scaffold for the same crimes, I would not change places with such a wretch.”

I listened to this discourse with the extremest agony. I, not in deed, but in effect, was the true murderer. Elizabeth read my anguish in my countenance, and kindly taking my hand, said, “My dearest friend, you must calm yourself. These events have affected me, God knows how deeply; but I am not so wretched as you are. There is an expression of despair, and sometimes of revenge, in your countenance that makes me tremble. Dear Victor, banish these dark passions. Remember the friends around you, who centre all their hopes in you. Have we lost the power of rendering you happy? Ah! While we love, while we are true to each other, here in this land of peace and beauty, your native country, we may reap every tranquil blessing—what can disturb our peace?”

And could not such words from her whom I fondly prized before every other gift of fortune suffice to chase away the fiend that lurked in my heart? Even as she spoke I drew near to her, as if in terror, lest at that very moment the destroyer had been near to rob me of her.

Thus not the tenderness of friendship, nor the beauty of earth, nor of heaven, could redeem my soul from woe; the very accents of love were ineffectual. I was encompassed by a cloud which no beneficial influence could penetrate. The wounded deer dragging its fainting limbs to some untrodden brake, there to gaze upon the arrow which had pierced it, and to die, was but a type of me.

Sometimes I could cope with the sullen despair that overwhelmed me, but sometimes the whirlwind passions of my soul drove me to seek, by bodily exercise and by change of place, some relief from my intolerable sensations. It was during an access of this kind that I suddenly left my home, and bending my steps towards the near Alpine valleys, sought in the magnificence, the eternity of such scenes, to forget myself and my ephemeral, because human, sorrows. My wanderings were directed towards the valley of Chamounix. I had visited it frequently during my boyhood. Six years had passed since then: I was a wreck, but nought had changed in those savage and enduring scenes.

I performed the first part of my journey on horseback. I afterwards hired a mule, as the more sure-footed and least liable to receive injury on these rugged roads. The weather was fine; it was about the middle of the month of August, nearly two months after the death of Justine, that miserable epoch from which I dated all my woe. The weight upon my spirit was sensibly lightened as I plunged yet deeper in the ravine of Arve.

The immense mountains and precipices that overhung me on every side, the sound of the river raging among the rocks, and the dashing of the waterfalls around spoke of a power mighty as Omnipotence—and I ceased to fear or to bend before any being less almighty than that which had created and ruled the elements, here displayed in their most terrific guise. Still, as I ascended higher, the valley assumed a more magnificent and astonishing character. Ruined castles hanging on the precipices of piny mountains, the impetuous Arve, and cottages every here and there peeping forth from among the trees formed a scene of singular beauty. But it was augmented and rendered sublime by the mighty Alps, whose white and shining pyramids and domes towered above all, as belonging to another earth, the habitations of another race of beings.

I passed the bridge of Pélissier, where the ravine, which the river forms, opened before me, and I began to ascend the mountain that overhangs it. Soon after, I entered the valley of Chamounix. This valley is more wonderful and sublime, but not so beautiful and picturesque as that of Servox, through which I had just passed. The high and snowy mountains were its immediate boundaries, but I saw no more ruined castles and fertile fields. Immense glaciers approached the road; I heard the rumbling thunder of the falling avalanche and marked the smoke of its passage. Mont Blanc, the supreme and magnificent Mont Blanc, raised itself from the surrounding aiguilles, and its tremendous dôme overlooked the valley.

A tingling long-lost sense of pleasure often came across me during this journey. Some turn in the road, some new object suddenly perceived and recognised, reminded me of days gone by, and were associated with the lighthearted gaiety of boyhood. The very winds whispered in soothing accents, and maternal Nature bade me weep no more. Then again the kindly influence ceased to act—I found myself fettered again to grief and indulging in all the misery of reflection. Then I spurred on my animal, striving so to forget the world, my fears, and more than all, myself—or, in a more desperate fashion, I alighted and threw myself on the grass, weighed down by horror and despair.

At length I arrived at the village of Chamounix. Exhaustion succeeded to the extreme fatigue both of body and of mind which I had endured. For a short space of time I remained at the window watching the pallid lightnings that played above Mont Blanc and listening to the rushing of the Arve, which pursued its noisy way beneath. The same lulling sounds acted as a lullaby to my too keen sensations; when I placed my head upon my pillow, sleep crept over me; I felt it as it came and blessed the giver of oblivion.
b2: Nothing is more painful to the human mind than the dead calm that comes after a rapid series of events has stirred up the feelings: a calm of inaction and certainty that robs the soul of both hope and fear. Justine was dead and at rest, and I was alive. The blood ran freely through my veins, but my heart was crushed by a weight of despair and remorse that nothing could lift. I could not sleep; I wandered about like an evil spirit, because I had done indescribably horrible harm, and I was convinced that more, much more, was still to come.

And yet my heart was full of kindness and a love of goodness. I had started life with generous intentions and longed for the moment when I could put them into practice and be useful to my fellow human beings. Now everything was ruined; instead of a calm conscience that would have let me look back on the past with satisfaction and draw fresh hope from it, I was gripped by remorse and guilt, which dragged me into a hell of torment beyond anything words can describe.

This state of mind wore down my health, which had perhaps never fully recovered from the first shock it had suffered. I avoided other people; every sound of joy or contentment was torture to me; solitude was my only comfort—deep, dark, deathly solitude.

My father noticed with pain the obvious change in my character and habits, and he tried, with arguments drawn from his own peaceful conscience and blameless life, to give me strength and to rouse in me the courage to drive away the dark cloud that hung over me. “Do you think, Victor,” he said, “that I am not suffering too? No one could love a child more than I loved your brother”—tears came into his eyes as he spoke—“but don’t we have a duty to those who are left not to add to their unhappiness by showing excessive grief? You also owe it to yourself, because too much sorrow stops you from improving, from enjoying life, and even from doing your everyday duties, and without these no one is fit to live among others.”

This advice, though good, did not apply to my case at all; I would have been the first to hide my grief and comfort my friends if remorse had not mixed its bitterness, and terror its alarm, with my other feelings. As it was, I could only answer my father with a look of despair and try to keep out of his sight.

Around this time we moved to our house at Belrive. I was especially glad of this change. Because the city gates were always shut at ten o’clock and it was impossible to stay on the lake after that, I had found living inside the walls of Geneva very tiresome. Now I was free. Often, after the rest of the family had gone to bed, I took the boat out and spent many hours on the water. Sometimes I put up the sails and let the wind carry me; sometimes I rowed into the middle of the lake, let the boat drift where it liked, and gave in to my own miserable thoughts.

When everything around me was at peace, and I was the only restless thing wandering through a scene so beautiful and heavenly—apart from the odd bat, or the frogs, whose harsh, broken croaking I heard only when I came near the shore—I was often tempted to throw myself into the silent lake, so that the water would close over me and my misfortunes for ever.

But I held back when I thought of brave, suffering Elizabeth, whom I loved tenderly and whose life was bound up with mine. I also thought of my father and my surviving brother; should I cowardly abandon them and leave them unprotected against the malice of the fiend I had set loose among them?

At such moments I wept bitterly and wished for peace to return to my mind, if only so that I could give them comfort and happiness. But that was impossible. Remorse put out every hope. I had caused evils that could never be undone, and I lived in daily fear that the monster I had created would commit some new crime. I had a vague feeling that it was not all over, and that he would still commit some terrible crime so enormous that it would almost wipe out the memory of the past. There was always room for fear as long as anything I loved was still alive.

No one can imagine how much I loathed this fiend. When I thought of him I ground my teeth, my eyes burned, and I longed passionately to destroy the life I had so carelessly given. When I reflected on his crimes and his malice, my hatred and desire for revenge knew no limits. I would have made a pilgrimage to the highest peak of the Andes if, once there, I could have hurled him down to the bottom. I wanted to see him again, so that I could pour all my loathing onto his head and avenge the deaths of William and Justine.

Our house was a house of mourning. My father’s health had been badly shaken by the horror of recent events. Elizabeth was sad and dejected; she no longer enjoyed her usual activities; every pleasure seemed to her an insult to the dead; she believed that endless sorrow and tears were the fair tribute she owed to innocence so cruelly destroyed. She was no longer the happy girl who, in her early youth, had wandered with me along the shores of the lake and talked with delight about our future. The first of those sorrows that are sent to loosen our ties to the world had come to her, and its shadow had dimmed her sweetest smiles.

“When I think, my dear cousin,” she said, “about the terrible death of Justine Moritz, I no longer see the world and what happens in it as I used to. Before, I thought of the stories of wickedness and injustice that I read in books or heard from others as tales of long ago or imaginary evils; at least they seemed distant, something for the mind rather than the imagination; but now misery has come into our own home, and people seem to me like monsters thirsting for each other’s blood. And yet I am surely being unfair. Everyone believed that poor girl was guilty; and if she really could have committed the crime she died for, she would certainly have been the most wicked of human beings.

To have murdered the son of her benefactor and friend, all for a few jewels—a child she had looked after since he was born and seemed to love as if he were her own! I could never agree to the death of any human being, but I would certainly have thought such a person unfit to live among other people. But she was innocent. I know it, I feel she was innocent; you think so too, and that makes me sure.

Oh, Victor, when lies can look so much like the truth, who can be sure of any happiness? I feel as if I were walking along the edge of a cliff, with thousands of people pressing towards it and trying to push me into the abyss. William and Justine were murdered, and the killer goes free; he walks about the world at liberty, and perhaps even respected. But even if I were sentenced to die on the scaffold for the same crimes, I would not change places with such a wretch.”

I listened to her words in the most terrible agony. Not by my own hand, but in reality, I was the true murderer. Elizabeth saw the anguish in my face, and, gently taking my hand, she said, “My dearest friend, you must calm down. These events have affected me more deeply than I can say, but I am not as miserable as you are. There is a look of despair, and sometimes of revenge, on your face that makes me tremble. Dear Victor, drive these dark passions away. Remember the friends around you, who place all their hopes in you. Have we lost the power to make you happy? While we love each other and stay true to each other, here in this land of peace and beauty, your own country, we can enjoy every quiet blessing—what could disturb our peace?”

Surely such words from her, whom I valued above every other gift of fortune, should have been enough to drive away the fiend that lurked in my heart? Even as she was speaking I moved closer to her, as if in terror, in case the destroyer was near at that very moment, ready to take her from me.

So neither the tenderness of friendship nor the beauty of earth and sky could rescue my soul from its misery; even the voice of love had no effect. I was wrapped in a cloud that no kindly influence could break through. I was like a wounded deer dragging its weak legs into some untouched thicket, to stare at the arrow that had pierced it, and to die there.

Sometimes I could cope with the gloomy despair that overwhelmed me, but at other times the storm of feeling in my soul drove me to look for some relief from my unbearable sensations through physical exercise and a change of scene. It was during one of these fits that I suddenly left home and, heading for the nearby Alpine valleys, tried to forget myself and my passing, merely human sorrows in the grandeur and timelessness of those landscapes. I made my way towards the valley of Chamounix. I had often been there as a boy. Six years had passed since then: I was a wreck, but nothing had changed in those wild, everlasting landscapes.

I travelled the first part of the way on horseback. Later I hired a mule, since it was more sure-footed and less likely to be hurt on these rough roads. The weather was fine; it was about the middle of August, nearly two months after Justine’s death, that miserable time from which I counted all my misery. The weight on my spirit grew noticeably lighter as I went deeper into the ravine of the Arve.

The huge mountains and cliffs towering over me on every side, the roar of the river raging among the rocks, and the crash of the waterfalls all around spoke of a power as mighty as God himself—and I stopped fearing or bowing before any being less powerful than the one who had created and ruled the elements, displayed here in their most awe-inspiring form. As I climbed higher, the valley became even more magnificent and astonishing. Ruined castles clinging to the cliffs of pine-covered mountains, the rushing Arve, and cottages peeping out here and there from among the trees made a scene of rare beauty. But it was made even greater and more sublime by the mighty Alps, whose white, shining peaks and domes rose above everything, as if they belonged to another world, the home of another race of beings.

I crossed the bridge of Pélissier, where the ravine formed by the river opened up in front of me, and I began to climb the mountain that hangs over it. Soon afterwards I entered the valley of Chamounix. This valley is more wonderful and sublime, but not as beautiful and picturesque as the valley of Servox, which I had just passed through. High, snowy mountains closed it in on every side, but I saw no more ruined castles or fertile fields. Huge glaciers came right down to the road; I heard the rumbling thunder of a falling avalanche and watched the cloud of snow it left behind. Mont Blanc, supreme and magnificent Mont Blanc, rose above the sharp peaks around it, and its enormous dome looked down over the valley.

During this journey I often felt a tingling, long-forgotten sense of pleasure. A bend in the road, or some object I suddenly noticed and recognised, reminded me of days gone by and brought back the carefree happiness of my boyhood. The very winds whispered soothing words, and Mother Nature told me to weep no more. Then the kindly influence would stop working, and I found myself chained to grief again, sinking into all the misery of my thoughts. Then I spurred my mule on, trying to forget the world, my fears, and above all myself—or, more desperately, I got down and threw myself on the grass, crushed by horror and despair.

At last I reached the village of Chamounix. The extreme tiredness of body and mind that I had endured gave way to complete exhaustion. For a short while I stayed at the window, watching the pale lightning that flickered above Mont Blanc and listening to the rushing of the Arve as it went noisily on its way below. Those same soothing sounds were like a lullaby to my over-sensitive feelings; when I laid my head on the pillow, sleep crept over me; I felt it coming and blessed the giver of forgetfulness.
b1: After a lot of exciting and terrible events, the quiet that comes next is the most painful thing for the mind. There is nothing to do and nothing to hope for or fear. Justine was dead and at peace, but I was alive. My body was healthy, but my heart was heavy with despair and guilt. I could not sleep. I walked around like an evil spirit, because I had done terrible things, and I believed that even worse things were still to come.

But my heart was still full of kindness and love of goodness. When I was young, I had good plans, and I wanted to be useful to other people. Now everything was destroyed. I could not look back at my past with a calm conscience. Instead, I felt guilt and regret, and they pulled me into a hell of pain that no words can describe.

This state of mind damaged my health, which had never fully recovered from the first shock. I avoided people. Every sound of happiness was torture to me. My only comfort was to be alone—in deep, dark loneliness, like death.

My father saw the change in me with sadness. He had a calm conscience and an innocent life, and he tried to use his own feelings to give me strength and courage. “Do you think, Victor,” he said, “that I don’t suffer too? No one could love a child more than I loved your brother.” There were tears in his eyes. “But we must not make the others even more unhappy by showing too much grief. You must also think of yourself. Too much sadness stops you from enjoying life and even from doing your daily work, and then you cannot live among other people.”

This was good advice, but it did not help me. I would be the first to hide my sadness and comfort my friends, but my guilt and my terror made that impossible. So I could only look at my father with despair and try to stay away from him.

At about this time, we moved to our house at Belrive. I was very happy about this change. In Geneva, the city gates were closed every night at ten o’clock, and I could not stay on the lake after that. I had hated that. Now I was free. Often, when the family had gone to bed, I took the boat and spent many hours on the water. Sometimes I let the wind carry the boat; sometimes I rowed to the middle of the lake, let the boat go where it wanted, and thought my sad thoughts.

Everything around me was calm and beautiful. I was the only unhappy thing there, except for a bat or the frogs, which I heard only near the shore. At those times I often wanted to jump into the silent lake, so that the water would cover me and my troubles for ever.

But then I thought of brave, suffering Elizabeth, whom I loved so much and whose life was joined to mine, and I stopped. I also thought of my father and my other brother. How could I leave them alone and unprotected against the evil creature I had set free among them?

At these moments I cried bitterly. I wished for peace in my mind, so that I could make them happy. But that was impossible. Guilt killed every hope. I had caused terrible harm that could never be changed. Every day I was afraid that the monster would do something evil again. I had a feeling that it was not finished, and that he would commit a crime so terrible that people would almost forget the past. While anyone I loved was still alive, there was always a reason to be afraid.

No one can imagine how much I hated this creature. When I thought of him, I ground my teeth and my eyes burned. I wanted to destroy the life that I had given him so carelessly. When I thought about his crimes, my hatred had no limits. I would travel to the highest mountain in the Andes if I could throw him down from the top. I wanted to see him again, so that I could punish him and take revenge for William and Justine.

Our house was full of sadness. My father’s health was badly damaged by the horror of these events. Elizabeth was sad and hopeless. She no longer enjoyed her usual activities, and she felt that any pleasure was wrong while the dead were in their graves. She thought that she must cry for ever for the innocent girl. She was no longer the happy girl who walked with me by the lake and talked happily about our future. For the first time, real sorrow had come to her, and it took away her sweetest smiles.

“When I think about Justine’s terrible death, my dear cousin,” she said, “I see the world differently. Before, I thought that the stories of evil and injustice in books were old tales or things that people had imagined. They seemed far away. But now misery has come to our home, and people seem to me like monsters who want each other’s blood. But I am not being fair. Everybody believed that the poor girl was guilty. If she had really done that crime, she would have been the most evil person in the world.

Imagine killing the son of your kind friend and employer for a few jewels—a child she had looked after since he was born, and loved like her own! I could never agree to anyone’s death, but I would think that such a person should not live among other people. But she was innocent. I know it, I feel it; you think the same, and that makes me sure.

Oh, Victor, when lies can look so much like the truth, how can anyone be sure of happiness? I feel as if I am walking on the edge of a cliff, and thousands of people are trying to push me over. William and Justine were killed, and the murderer is free. He walks around the world, and perhaps people even respect him. But even if they killed me for the same crimes, I would never change places with such an evil person.”

I listened to her words in terrible pain. I had not killed them with my own hands, but I was the real murderer. Elizabeth saw the pain in my face. She took my hand kindly and said, “My dearest friend, you must calm down. God knows how deeply these events have hurt me, but I am not as unhappy as you. Sometimes I see despair and even revenge in your face, and it makes me shake. Dear Victor, send away these dark feelings. Remember your friends, who put all their hopes in you. Can we not make you happy any more? While we love each other and stay true to each other, here in your beautiful, peaceful country, we can have a quiet, happy life—what can take our peace away?”

She was more precious to me than anything else in the world. Surely her words were enough to chase away the devil hiding in my heart? But even while she was talking, I moved closer to her in fear, as if the killer was near and ready to take her from me at that very moment.

So nothing—not friendship, not the beauty of the earth or the sky, not even words of love—could save my soul from sadness. I was inside a dark cloud, and nothing good could get through it. I was like a wounded deer that drags itself into the forest, looks at the arrow in its body, and dies.

Sometimes I could fight my dark despair, but sometimes my feelings were like a storm. Then I needed physical activity and a change of place to find some relief. During one of these times, I suddenly left home and went to the Alpine valleys nearby. I hoped that their greatness and their timeless beauty would help me forget myself and my small, human sorrows. I travelled towards the valley of Chamounix. I had often been there as a boy. Six years had passed: I was broken, but nothing had changed in those wild places.

I did the first part of the journey on horseback. Later I hired a mule, because mules are safer on rough mountain roads. The weather was fine. It was the middle of August, almost two months after Justine’s death, the day when all my sorrow began. As I went deeper into the valley of the Arve, I felt a little lighter.

Huge mountains and cliffs rose above me on every side. The river roared among the rocks, and waterfalls crashed all around. All this spoke of the power of God, and I stopped being afraid of any weaker being. As I climbed higher, the valley became even more wonderful. There were ruined castles on the cliffs of pine-covered mountains, the fast river Arve, and little cottages among the trees. It was a very beautiful scene. Above everything rose the great white Alps, shining like the homes of beings from another world.

I crossed the bridge of Pélissier, where the river valley opened in front of me, and I began to climb the mountain above it. Soon I entered the valley of Chamounix. This valley is grander and more wonderful than the valley of Servox, which I had just passed, but not as pretty. High, snowy mountains were all around it, and there were no more ruined castles or green fields. Huge glaciers came down close to the road. I heard the thunder of an avalanche and saw the cloud of snow after it. Great Mont Blanc rose above the sharp peaks around it, and its huge white top looked down on the valley.

During this journey I often felt a pleasure that I had forgotten long ago. A bend in the road or something I suddenly recognised reminded me of the happy days of my boyhood. Even the winds seemed to whisper kind words, and Mother Nature told me not to cry any more. But then the good feeling stopped, and I was a prisoner of my sadness again. Then I made my mule go faster, trying to forget the world, my fears and, most of all, myself. Or, when I felt even worse, I got down and threw myself on the grass, full of horror and despair.

At last I arrived at the village of Chamounix. My body and mind were completely exhausted. For a short time I stood at the window and watched the pale lightning above Mont Blanc and listened to the noisy river Arve below. The sounds were like a lullaby for my tired feelings. When I put my head on the pillow, sleep slowly came, and I felt thankful for it, because it helped me forget.
a2: After many terrible events, everything was suddenly quiet. This quiet was very painful for me. Justine was dead, but I was alive. My heart was heavy with sadness and guilt. I could not sleep. I walked around like an evil spirit, because I had done terrible things, and I thought that worse things were coming. Nothing could take this pain away.

But I still had a kind heart. When I was young, I wanted to help other people. Now everything was broken. I could not think about my past with a quiet heart. I felt only guilt, and it was like living in hell.
I became ill because of these feelings. I did not want to see people. Happy sounds hurt me. I only wanted to be alone. Being alone was my only comfort.

My father saw that I was different now, and he was sad. He tried to make me strong. “Victor,” he said, “do you think that I am not sad too? I loved your brother very much.” He had tears in his eyes. “But we must not make the family sadder. And too much sadness is bad for you. You cannot work or live a normal life.”
It was good advice, but it could not help me. My guilt and my fear were too strong. I only looked at my father sadly and tried to stay away from him.

At this time we moved to our house at Belrive. I was glad. In Geneva, they closed the city gates at ten o’clock every night, and I could not go on the lake. Now I was free. At night, when my family was asleep, I often took the boat onto the lake for many hours. Sometimes the wind carried my boat. Sometimes I sat in the boat and thought sad thoughts.

Everything around me was quiet and beautiful. Only I was unhappy. I heard only a bat or some frogs near the shore. I often wanted to jump into the lake and end my life. I wanted the water to close over me and my troubles for ever.

But then I thought of Elizabeth. I loved her very much, and her life was part of my life. I thought of my father and my brother too. How could I leave them alone with the monster? I had made him, and I let him go free among them.

At these times I cried a lot. I wanted to feel better, so that I could make my family happy. But I could not. I had no hope. Every day I was afraid that the monster would do something bad again. I felt that he was going to do a new, terrible crime. While my family was alive, I was always afraid for them.

I hated the monster very much. When I thought of him, I felt angry and I wanted to kill him. My eyes burned, and I ground my teeth. I gave him life, and now I wanted to take it away. I would climb the highest mountain in the world to throw him down from the top. I wanted to see him again and punish him for William and Justine.

Our house was very sad. My father became ill. Elizabeth was very unhappy too. She did not enjoy anything any more. She thought that she must cry for the innocent girl for ever. She was not the happy girl from our childhood now. She did not smile any more.

“Dear cousin,” she said, “after Justine’s death, I see the world differently. Before, I thought that bad people lived only in old stories. They were far away from me. Now I think that people are like monsters. But that is not fair. Everybody thought that Justine was guilty. If she really did it, she was a very bad person.
She killed a child for some jewels? A child that she loved like her own? She looked after him from the day he was born. But she was innocent. I know it, and you think so too.

Oh, Victor, lies can look like the truth. How can anyone be happy? I feel that I am standing at the edge of a cliff. Thousands of people are trying to push me down. William and Justine are dead, but the murderer walks around free. Maybe people even respect him. But I will never change places with him.”

Her words hurt me terribly. I was the real murderer. I did not kill them with my hands, but I made the monster. Elizabeth saw my face and took my hand. “My dear friend,” she said, “you must be calm. I am sad too, but you are sadder than me. Your face frightens me. Dear Victor, forget these dark feelings. Your friends love you. Can we not make you happy? We love each other, and we live in a beautiful, quiet country. Nothing can hurt us.”
I loved Elizabeth more than anything. Her words were kind, but they could not help me. I moved closer to her because I was afraid that the monster was near.

Nothing could help me—not friendship, not beautiful nature, not love. I lived in a dark cloud. Nothing good could come into it. I was like a deer with an arrow in its body, which goes into the forest to die.

Sometimes I could live with my sadness. But sometimes I needed to move and to go to new places. One day I suddenly left home and went to the mountains, the Alps. I wanted to forget myself there. The mountains were old and great, and my problems seemed small next to them. I went to the valley of Chamounix. I often went there when I was a boy. I was different now, but the mountains were the same.

First I travelled on a horse, and then I hired a mule. Mules are safer on mountain roads. It was the middle of August, two months after Justine’s death. The weather was good. In the valley of the Arve, I felt a little better. The beautiful mountains were helping me.

There were huge mountains all around me. The river was loud, and there were waterfalls everywhere. Only God could make something so strong. I was not afraid any more. Higher up, I saw old castles, the fast river and small houses among the trees. Above everything were the great white Alps. They looked like the homes of people from another world.

I crossed the bridge of Pélissier and climbed the mountain. Soon I was in the valley of Chamounix. It was not as pretty as the valley of Servox, but it was grander. There were high snowy mountains all around. Big glaciers came down to the road, and I heard an avalanche. I saw a cloud of snow after it. Great Mont Blanc stood above the valley.

Sometimes on this journey I felt happy again. Things on the road reminded me of my happy childhood. Nature seemed to tell me, “Don’t cry.” The wind seemed to sing kind songs to me. But then the sadness came back. Then I rode faster to forget everything, or I got down and lay on the grass in despair.

At last I arrived at the village of Chamounix. I was very, very tired. I had a very long and hard journey behind me. I stood at the window for a short time and watched the lightning over Mont Blanc. I listened to the river. Its sound was like a song for a baby. When I went to bed, I fell asleep quickly, and I was thankful for it.

o.en: Nothing is more painful to the human mind than, after the feelings have been worked up by a quick succession of events, the dead calmness of inaction and certainty which follows and deprives the soul both of hope and fear.
o.ru: Ничто так не мучительно для человеческого разума, как мёртвое спокойствие бездействия и определённости, которое наступает после того, как чувства были взвинчены стремительной чередой событий, и лишает душу и надежды, и страха.

o.en: Justine died, she rested, and I was alive.
o.ru: Жюстина умерла, она обрела покой, а я был жив.

o.en: The blood flowed freely in my veins, but a weight of despair and remorse pressed on my heart which nothing could remove.
o.ru: Кровь свободно текла по моим жилам, но на сердце давила тяжесть отчаяния и раскаяния, которую ничто не могло снять.

o.en: Sleep fled from my eyes; I wandered like an evil spirit, for I had committed deeds of mischief beyond description horrible, and more, much more (I persuaded myself) was yet behind.
o.ru: Сон бежал от моих глаз; я бродил, как злой дух, ибо совершил неописуемо ужасные злодеяния, и впереди, как я убеждал себя, было ещё больше, гораздо больше.

o.en: Yet my heart overflowed with kindness and the love of virtue.
o.ru: И всё же сердце моё переполняли доброта и любовь к добродетели.

o.en: I had begun life with benevolent intentions and thirsted for the moment when I should put them in practice and make myself useful to my fellow beings.
o.ru: Я начинал жизнь с благими намерениями и жаждал того мгновения, когда смогу воплотить их и стать полезным своим ближним.

o.en: Now all was blasted; instead of that serenity of conscience which allowed me to look back upon the past with self-satisfaction, and from thence to gather promise of new hopes, I was seized by remorse and the sense of guilt, which hurried me away to a hell of intense tortures such as no language can describe.
o.ru: Теперь всё было погублено; вместо того душевного покоя, который позволял бы мне оглядываться на прошлое с удовлетворением и черпать в нём залог новых надежд, мною овладели раскаяние и чувство вины, увлекавшие меня в ад таких жестоких мук, которых не описать никаким языком.

o.en: This state of mind preyed upon my health, which had perhaps never entirely recovered from the first shock it had sustained.
o.ru: Такое состояние духа подтачивало моё здоровье, которое, быть может, так и не оправилось полностью от первого пережитого потрясения.

o.en: I shunned the face of man; all sound of joy or complacency was torture to me; solitude was my only consolation—deep, dark, deathlike solitude.
o.ru: Я избегал людей; всякий звук радости или довольства был для меня пыткой; одиночество было моим единственным утешением — глубокое, тёмное, мертвенное одиночество.

o.en: My father observed with pain the alteration perceptible in my disposition and habits and endeavoured by arguments deduced from the feelings of his serene conscience and guiltless life to inspire me with fortitude and awaken in me the courage to dispel the dark cloud which brooded over me.
o.ru: Отец с болью замечал явную перемену в моём нраве и привычках и старался доводами, почерпнутыми из чувств его спокойной совести и безупречной жизни, вселить в меня стойкость и пробудить мужество, чтобы рассеять мрачную тучу, нависшую надо мной.

o.en: “Do you think, Victor,” said he, “that I do not suffer also?
o.ru: «Неужели ты думаешь, Виктор, — сказал он, — что я не страдаю?

o.en: No one could love a child more than I loved your brother”—tears came into his eyes as he spoke—“but is it not a duty to the survivors that we should refrain from augmenting their unhappiness by an appearance of immoderate grief?
o.ru: Никто не мог любить ребёнка сильнее, чем я любил твоего брата, — при этих словах на глазах у него выступили слёзы, — но разве не долг наш перед живыми — не умножать их несчастья видом неумеренного горя?

o.en: It is also a duty owed to yourself, for excessive sorrow prevents improvement or enjoyment, or even the discharge of daily usefulness, without which no man is fit for society.”
o.ru: Это также и долг перед самим собой, ибо чрезмерная скорбь мешает совершенствованию, радости и даже исполнению повседневных обязанностей, без чего человек непригоден для общества».

o.en: This advice, although good, was totally inapplicable to my case; I should have been the first to hide my grief and console my friends if remorse had not mingled its bitterness, and terror its alarm, with my other sensations.
o.ru: Этот совет, хоть и добрый, совершенно не подходил к моему случаю; я первым скрыл бы своё горе и утешил друзей, если бы раскаяние не примешало своей горечи, а ужас — своей тревоги к остальным моим чувствам.

o.en: Now I could only answer my father with a look of despair and endeavour to hide myself from his view.
o.ru: Теперь же я мог лишь отвечать отцу взглядом, полным отчаяния, и стараться укрыться от его глаз.

o.en: About this time we retired to our house at Belrive.
o.ru: Примерно в это время мы переехали в наш дом в Бельриве.

o.en: This change was particularly agreeable to me.
o.ru: Эта перемена была мне особенно приятна.

o.en: The shutting of the gates regularly at ten o’clock and the impossibility of remaining on the lake after that hour had rendered our residence within the walls of Geneva very irksome to me.
o.ru: То, что городские ворота неизменно запирались в десять часов и после этого часа нельзя было оставаться на озере, делало жизнь в стенах Женевы очень тягостной для меня.

o.en: I was now free.
Often, after the rest of the family had retired for the night, I took the boat and passed many hours upon the water.
o.ru: Часто, когда остальные члены семьи уже уходили спать, я брал лодку и проводил много часов на воде.

o.en: Sometimes, with my sails set, I was carried by the wind; and sometimes, after rowing into the middle of the lake, I left the boat to pursue its own course and gave way to my own miserable reflections.
o.ru: Иногда, поставив паруса, я отдавался ветру; а иногда, выгребя на середину озера, я предоставлял лодке плыть куда ей вздумается и предавался своим горестным размышлениям.

o.en: I was often tempted, when all was at peace around me, and I the only unquiet thing that wandered restless in a scene so beautiful and heavenly—if I except some bat, or the frogs, whose harsh and interrupted croaking was heard only when I approached the shore—often, I say, I was tempted to plunge into the silent lake, that the waters might close over me and my calamities for ever.
o.ru: Часто, когда вокруг всё было погружено в покой и я один был неспокойным существом, беспокойно блуждавшим среди этой прекрасной, небесной картины, — если не считать какой-нибудь летучей мыши или лягушек, чьё резкое, прерывистое кваканье слышалось, лишь когда я подплывал к берегу, — часто, повторяю, меня искушало желание броситься в безмолвное озеро, чтобы воды навсегда сомкнулись надо мной и моими бедствиями.

o.en: But I was restrained, when I thought of the heroic and suffering Elizabeth, whom I tenderly loved, and whose existence was bound up in mine.
o.ru: Но меня удерживала мысль о героической, страдающей Элизабет, которую я нежно любил и чья жизнь была неразрывно связана с моей.

o.en: I thought also of my father and surviving brother; should I by my base desertion leave them exposed and unprotected to the malice of the fiend whom I had let loose among them?
o.ru: Я думал также об отце и оставшемся в живых брате; неужели своим низким бегством я оставлю их беззащитными перед злобой демона, которого сам выпустил на волю среди них?

o.en: At these moments I wept bitterly and wished that peace would revisit my mind only that I might afford them consolation and happiness.
o.ru: В такие минуты я горько плакал и желал, чтобы мир вернулся в мою душу, лишь затем, чтобы я мог дать им утешение и счастье.

o.en: But that could not be.
o.ru: Но этому не суждено было случиться.

o.en: Remorse extinguished every hope.
I had been the author of unalterable evils, and I lived in daily fear lest the monster whom I had created should perpetrate some new wickedness.
o.ru: Я был виновником непоправимых бед и жил в ежедневном страхе, как бы созданное мною чудовище не совершило нового злодеяния.

o.en: I had an obscure feeling that all was not over and that he would still commit some signal crime, which by its enormity should almost efface the recollection of the past.
o.ru: У меня было смутное чувство, что ещё не всё кончено и что он совершит какое-нибудь небывалое преступление, которое своей чудовищностью почти затмит память о прошлом.

o.en: There was always scope for fear so long as anything I loved remained behind.
o.ru: Для страха всегда оставалось место, пока было живо хоть что-то, что я любил.

o.en: My abhorrence of this fiend cannot be conceived.
o.ru: Моё отвращение к этому демону невозможно себе представить.

o.en: When I thought of him I gnashed my teeth, my eyes became inflamed, and I ardently wished to extinguish that life which I had so thoughtlessly bestowed.
o.ru: Когда я думал о нём, я скрежетал зубами, глаза мои воспалялись, и я страстно желал погасить ту жизнь, которую так бездумно даровал.

o.en: When I reflected on his crimes and malice, my hatred and revenge burst all bounds of moderation.
o.ru: Когда я размышлял о его преступлениях и злобе, моя ненависть и жажда мести выходили за всякие пределы.

o.en: I would have made a pilgrimage to the highest peak of the Andes, could I, when there, have precipitated him to their base.
o.ru: Я совершил бы паломничество на высочайшую вершину Анд, если бы мог, оказавшись там, низвергнуть его к их подножию.

o.en: I wished to see him again, that I might wreak the utmost extent of abhorrence on his head and avenge the deaths of William and Justine.
o.ru: Я хотел снова увидеть его, чтобы обрушить на его голову всю силу своей ненависти и отомстить за смерть Уильяма и Жюстины.

o.en: Our house was the house of mourning.
My father’s health was deeply shaken by the horror of the recent events.
o.ru: Здоровье отца было глубоко подорвано ужасом недавних событий.

o.en: Elizabeth was sad and desponding; she no longer took delight in her ordinary occupations; all pleasure seemed to her sacrilege toward the dead; eternal woe and tears she then thought was the just tribute she should pay to innocence so blasted and destroyed.
o.ru: Элизабет была печальна и подавлена; она больше не находила радости в обычных занятиях; всякое удовольствие казалось ей кощунством по отношению к мёртвым; вечная скорбь и слёзы, думала она тогда, — справедливая дань, которую она должна платить невинности, так погубленной и уничтоженной.

o.en: She was no longer that happy creature who in earlier youth wandered with me on the banks of the lake and talked with ecstasy of our future prospects.
o.ru: Она уже не была тем счастливым созданием, которое в ранней юности бродило со мной по берегам озера и с восторгом говорило о нашем будущем.

o.en: The first of those sorrows which are sent to wean us from the earth had visited her, and its dimming influence quenched her dearest smiles.
o.ru: Её посетила первая из тех скорбей, что посылаются, чтобы отлучить нас от земли, и её омрачающее влияние погасило её милейшие улыбки.

o.en: “When I reflect, my dear cousin,” said she, “on the miserable death of Justine Moritz, I no longer see the world and its works as they before appeared to me.
o.ru: «Когда я думаю, мой милый кузен, — сказала она, — о горестной смерти Жюстины Мориц, я уже не вижу мир и дела его такими, какими они казались мне прежде.

o.en: Before, I looked upon the accounts of vice and injustice that I read in books or heard from others as tales of ancient days or imaginary evils; at least they were remote and more familiar to reason than to the imagination; but now misery has come home, and men appear to me as monsters thirsting for each other’s blood.
o.ru: Прежде я смотрела на рассказы о пороке и несправедливости, которые читала в книгах или слышала от других, как на предания древних времён или вымышленное зло; по крайней мере, они были далеки и понятны скорее рассудку, чем воображению; но теперь беда пришла в наш дом, и люди кажутся мне чудовищами, жаждущими крови друг друга.

o.en: Yet I am certainly unjust.
Everybody believed that poor girl to be guilty; and if she could have committed the crime for which she suffered, assuredly she would have been the most depraved of human creatures.
o.ru: Все считали бедную девушку виновной; и если бы она могла совершить преступление, за которое пострадала, она, несомненно, была бы самым порочным из людей.

o.en: For the sake of a few jewels, to have murdered the son of her benefactor and friend, a child whom she had nursed from its birth, and appeared to love as if it had been her own!
o.ru: Ради нескольких драгоценностей убить сына своего благодетеля и друга, ребёнка, которого она нянчила с самого рождения и, казалось, любила, как родного!

o.en: I could not consent to the death of any human being, but certainly I should have thought such a creature unfit to remain in the society of men.
o.ru: Я не могла бы согласиться на смерть ни одного человеческого существа, но, конечно, сочла бы такое создание недостойным оставаться в обществе людей.

o.en: But she was innocent.
