But I scarcely observed this; rage and hatred had at first deprived me of utterance, and I recovered only to overwhelm him with words expressive of furious detestation and contempt.

“Devil,” I exclaimed, “do you dare approach me? And do not you fear the fierce vengeance of my arm wreaked on your miserable head? Begone, vile insect! Or rather, stay, that I may trample you to dust! And, oh! That I could, with the extinction of your miserable existence, restore those victims whom you have so diabolically murdered!”

“I expected this reception,” said the dæmon. “All men hate the wretched; how, then, must I be hated, who am miserable beyond all living things! Yet you, my creator, detest and spurn me, thy creature, to whom thou art bound by ties only dissoluble by the annihilation of one of us. You purpose to kill me. How dare you sport thus with life? Do your duty towards me, and I will do mine towards you and the rest of mankind. If you will comply with my conditions, I will leave them and you at peace; but if you refuse, I will glut the maw of death, until it be satiated with the blood of your remaining friends.”

“Abhorred monster! Fiend that thou art! The tortures of hell are too mild a vengeance for thy crimes. Wretched devil! You reproach me with your creation, come on, then, that I may extinguish the spark which I so negligently bestowed.”

My rage was without bounds; I sprang on him, impelled by all the feelings which can arm one being against the existence of another.

He easily eluded me and said,

“Be calm! I entreat you to hear me before you give vent to your hatred on my devoted head. Have I not suffered enough, that you seek to increase my misery? Life, although it may only be an accumulation of anguish, is dear to me, and I will defend it. Remember, thou hast made me more powerful than thyself; my height is superior to thine, my joints more supple. But I will not be tempted to set myself in opposition to thee. I am thy creature, and I will be even mild and docile to my natural lord and king if thou wilt also perform thy part, the which thou owest me.

Oh, Frankenstein, be not equitable to every other and trample upon me alone, to whom thy justice, and even thy clemency and affection, is most due. Remember that I am thy creature; I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed. Everywhere I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded. I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.”

“Begone! I will not hear you. There can be no community between you and me; we are enemies. Begone, or let us try our strength in a fight, in which one must fall.”

“How can I move thee? Will no entreaties cause thee to turn a favourable eye upon thy creature, who implores thy goodness and compassion? Believe me, Frankenstein, I was benevolent; my soul glowed with love and humanity; but am I not alone, miserably alone? You, my creator, abhor me; what hope can I gather from your fellow creatures, who owe me nothing? They spurn and hate me. The desert mountains and dreary glaciers are my refuge. I have wandered here many days; the caves of ice, which I only do not fear, are a dwelling to me, and the only one which man does not grudge. These bleak skies I hail, for they are kinder to me than your fellow beings.

If the multitude of mankind knew of my existence, they would do as you do, and arm themselves for my destruction. Shall I not then hate them who abhor me? I will keep no terms with my enemies. I am miserable, and they shall share my wretchedness. Yet it is in your power to recompense me, and deliver them from an evil which it only remains for you to make so great, that not only you and your family, but thousands of others, shall be swallowed up in the whirlwinds of its rage.

Let your compassion be moved, and do not disdain me. Listen to my tale; when you have heard that, abandon or commiserate me, as you shall judge that I deserve. But hear me. The guilty are allowed, by human laws, bloody as they are, to speak in their own defence before they are condemned. Listen to me, Frankenstein. You accuse me of murder, and yet you would, with a satisfied conscience, destroy your own creature. Oh, praise the eternal justice of man! Yet I ask you not to spare me; listen to me, and then, if you can, and if you will, destroy the work of your hands.”

“Why do you call to my remembrance,” I rejoined, “circumstances of which I shudder to reflect, that I have been the miserable origin and author? Cursed be the day, abhorred devil, in which you first saw light! Cursed (although I curse myself) be the hands that formed you! You have made me wretched beyond expression. You have left me no power to consider whether I am just to you or not. Begone! Relieve me from the sight of your detested form.”

“Thus I relieve thee, my creator,” he said, and placed his hated hands before my eyes, which I flung from me with violence; “thus I take from thee a sight which you abhor. Still thou canst listen to me and grant me thy compassion. By the virtues that I once possessed, I demand this from you. Hear my tale; it is long and strange, and the temperature of this place is not fitting to your fine sensations; come to the hut upon the mountain. The sun is yet high in the heavens; before it descends to hide itself behind your snowy precipices and illuminate another world, you will have heard my story and can decide. On you it rests, whether I quit for ever the neighbourhood of man and lead a harmless life, or become the scourge of your fellow creatures and the author of your own speedy ruin.”

As he said this he led the way across the ice; I followed. My heart was full, and I did not answer him, but as I proceeded, I weighed the various arguments that he had used and determined at least to listen to his tale. I was partly urged by curiosity, and compassion confirmed my resolution. I had hitherto supposed him to be the murderer of my brother, and I eagerly sought a confirmation or denial of this opinion.

For the first time, also, I felt what the duties of a creator towards his creature were, and that I ought to render him happy before I complained of his wickedness. These motives urged me to comply with his demand. We crossed the ice, therefore, and ascended the opposite rock. The air was cold, and the rain again began to descend; we entered the hut, the fiend with an air of exultation, I with a heavy heart and depressed spirits. But I consented to listen, and seating myself by the fire which my odious companion had lighted, he thus began his tale.
b2: I spent the next day wandering through the valley. I stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which begin in a glacier that is slowly moving down from the tops of the hills as if to block the valley. The steep sides of huge mountains rose in front of me; the icy wall of the glacier hung over me; a few broken pines were scattered around; and the solemn silence of this glorious throne room of mighty Nature was broken only by the roaring water, the fall of some huge rock, the thunder of an avalanche, or the cracking of the piled-up ice, echoing along the mountains, as the silent working of unchanging laws tore it apart again and again, as if it were only a toy in their hands.

These magnificent, awe-inspiring scenes gave me the greatest comfort I was capable of feeling. They lifted me above all petty feelings, and although they did not take away my grief, they calmed and softened it. To some extent they also distracted my mind from the thoughts it had been brooding over for the past month. At night I went to bed, and my sleep seemed to be watched over and cared for by the grand shapes I had gazed at during the day. They gathered around me – the pure snowy mountain top, the glittering peak, the pine woods, the rugged bare ravine, the eagle soaring among the clouds – they all surrounded me and told me to be at peace.

Where had they gone when I woke up the next morning? All my uplifted spirits had vanished with sleep, and a dark gloom clouded every thought. The rain was pouring down in torrents, and thick mists hid the mountain tops, so that I could not even see the faces of those mighty friends. Still, I was determined to break through their veil of mist and look for them in their cloudy hiding places. What did rain and storms matter to me?

My mule was brought to the door, and I decided to climb to the top of Montanvert. I remembered the effect that the view of the immense, ever-moving glacier had had on me when I first saw it. It had filled me with a sublime ecstasy that gave my soul wings and let it soar out of the dark world into light and joy. The sight of what is awesome and majestic in nature had always made me feel solemn and helped me forget the passing worries of life. I decided to go without a guide, as I knew the path well, and another person’s presence would spoil the lonely grandeur of the scene.

The climb is steep, but the path winds back and forth in short turns, which allow you to overcome the sheer face of the mountain. It is a terribly desolate place. In a thousand spots you can see the marks of winter avalanches, where trees lie broken and scattered on the ground – some completely destroyed, others bent and leaning against the jutting rocks or lying across other trees.

Higher up, the path is cut across by gullies of snow, down which stones keep rolling from above; one of them is particularly dangerous, because the slightest sound, even a raised voice, can shake the air enough to bring destruction down on the speaker’s head. The pines are neither tall nor lush, but they are gloomy and give the scene a stern look. I looked down at the valley below; huge mists were rising from the rivers that ran through it and curling in thick wreaths around the mountains opposite, whose tops were hidden in a grey blanket of cloud, while rain poured from the dark sky and deepened the sad impression that everything around me made.

Alas! Why does man boast that his feelings are finer than an animal’s? It only makes him more dependent. If our impulses were limited to hunger, thirst and desire, we might be almost free; but as it is, we are stirred by every wind that blows, and by any chance word or the picture that word may bring to mind. We rest, and a dream can poison sleep. We get up, and one stray thought can spoil the day. We feel, imagine or reason, laugh or cry, cling to our sorrow or throw our cares away – it makes no difference: whether it is joy or sorrow, it is always free to leave. A man’s yesterday may never be like his tomorrow; nothing lasts except change!

It was almost noon when I reached the top of the climb. For a while I sat on the rock that looks down on the sea of ice. A mist covered both the glacier and the mountains around it. Soon a breeze blew the cloud away, and I went down onto the glacier. The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a stormy sea, dipping low, and broken up by deep cracks. The field of ice is almost a league wide, but it took me nearly two hours to cross it. The mountain on the other side is a bare, sheer rock.

From where I now stood, Montanvert was directly opposite, a league away, and above it rose Mont Blanc in awesome majesty. I stayed in a hollow in the rock, gazing at this wonderful, breathtaking scene. The sea – or rather the vast river – of ice wound among the mountains around it, whose airy summits hung over its hidden bays. Their icy, glittering peaks shone in the sunlight above the clouds. My heart, which had been full of sorrow, now swelled with something like joy, and I cried out, “Wandering spirits, if you really do wander and do not rest in your narrow graves, allow me this faint happiness, or take me away with you from the joys of life.”

As I said this, I suddenly saw the figure of a man some distance away, coming towards me at superhuman speed. He leapt over the cracks in the ice, which I had walked among so carefully, and as he came closer he seemed taller than any man. I was shaken; a mist came over my eyes and I felt faint, but the cold mountain wind quickly brought me round. As the shape drew nearer (a terrible, hateful sight!), I realised that it was the wretch I had created. I trembled with rage and horror, and made up my mind to wait for him and then fight him to the death. He came up to me; his face showed bitter anguish mixed with scorn and malice, while its unearthly ugliness made it almost too horrible for human eyes to look at. But I hardly noticed this; at first rage and hatred left me speechless, and when I found my voice, I poured out words full of furious loathing and contempt.

“Devil,” I cried, “how dare you come near me? Aren’t you afraid that my arm will take fierce revenge on your miserable head? Go away, you vile insect! Or rather, stay, so that I can crush you into dust! Oh, if only I could bring back the victims you have so fiendishly murdered by ending your miserable existence!”

“I expected this welcome,” said the monster. “All men hate the unhappy, so how much must I be hated, when I am more miserable than any living thing! Yet you, my creator, hate and reject me, your own creature, to whom you are bound by ties that only the death of one of us can break. You intend to kill me. How dare you play with life like this? Do your duty towards me, and I will do mine towards you and the rest of mankind. If you agree to my conditions, I will leave them and you in peace; but if you refuse, I will feed the jaws of death until they are full with the blood of your remaining friends.”

“Hateful monster! You fiend! The tortures of hell would be too gentle a punishment for your crimes. Wretched devil! You blame me for creating you – come on, then, and let me put out the spark of life that I gave you so carelessly.” My fury knew no limits; I leapt at him, driven by every feeling that can turn one being against the life of another. He dodged me easily and said,

“Calm down! I beg you to hear me out before you pour your hatred on my doomed head. Haven’t I suffered enough, without you trying to add to my misery? Life, even if it is only a heap of suffering, is precious to me, and I will defend it. Remember, you made me stronger than yourself; I am taller than you, and my joints are more flexible. But I will not let myself be tempted to turn against you. I am your creature, and I will even be gentle and obedient to my natural lord and king, if you will also do your part, which you owe me.

Oh, Frankenstein, do not be fair to everyone else and trample on me alone, when I deserve your justice, and even your mercy and love, more than anyone. Remember that I am your creature; I should be your Adam, but instead I am the fallen angel, whom you drive away from joy though he has done nothing wrong. Everywhere I see happiness, and I alone am shut out from it for ever. I was kind and good; misery turned me into a fiend. Make me happy, and I will be good again.” “Go away! I won’t listen to you. There can be nothing in common between you and me; we are enemies. Go away, or let us test our strength in a fight in which one of us must die.”

“How can I move you? Will no pleading make you look kindly on your creature, who begs for your goodness and compassion? Believe me, Frankenstein, I was kind; my soul glowed with love and humanity; but am I not alone, miserably alone? You, my creator, loathe me; so what hope can I have from your fellow men, who owe me nothing? They reject and hate me. The empty mountains and dreary glaciers are my shelter. I have wandered here for many days; the ice caves, which only I am not afraid of, are my home – the only one that man does not begrudge me. I welcome these bleak skies, because they are kinder to me than your fellow men are.

If the mass of mankind knew that I existed, they would do as you do and arm themselves to destroy me. So shouldn’t I hate those who loathe me? I will make no deals with my enemies. I am miserable, and they will share my misery. Yet you have the power to make it up to me and to save them from an evil which only you can allow to grow so great that not only you and your family, but thousands of others, will be swallowed up in the whirlwind of its fury.

Let your compassion be stirred, and do not look down on me. Listen to my story; when you have heard it, abandon me or pity me, whichever you judge I deserve. But hear me. Even the guilty, however bloody human laws may be, are allowed to speak in their own defence before they are condemned. Listen to me, Frankenstein. You accuse me of murder, and yet you would destroy your own creature with a clear conscience. Oh, how admirable is man’s eternal justice! But I do not ask you to spare me; listen to me, and then, if you can and if you want to, destroy the work of your hands.”

“Why do you remind me,” I replied, “of events that make me shudder to think of, events that I myself was the miserable cause of? Cursed be the day, hateful devil, on which you first saw the light! Cursed be the hands that made you, even though I curse myself by saying it! You have made me more wretched than words can say. You have left me unable even to consider whether I am being fair to you or not. Go away! Spare me the sight of your hateful shape.”

“This is how I spare you, my creator,” he said, and he put his hated hands over my eyes, which I pushed violently away; “this is how I take away a sight you hate. Still, you can listen to me and show me some compassion. In the name of the virtues I once had, I demand this of you. Hear my story; it is long and strange, and the cold of this place does not suit your delicate senses; come to the hut on the mountain. The sun is still high in the sky; before it sinks behind your snowy cliffs to light up another world, you will have heard my story and can make your decision. It depends on you whether I leave the world of men for ever and live a harmless life, or become the scourge of your fellow men and the cause of your own swift ruin.”

As he said this, he led the way across the ice, and I followed. My heart was full, and I did not answer him, but as I walked on, I weighed up the various arguments he had used and decided at least to listen to his story. I was partly driven by curiosity, and compassion strengthened my decision. Until then I had believed that he was my brother’s murderer, and I was eager to have this belief confirmed or disproved.

Also, for the first time, I felt what a creator’s duties towards his creature were, and that I ought to make him happy before I complained about his wickedness. These reasons persuaded me to agree to his demand. So we crossed the ice and climbed the rock on the other side. The air was cold, and it started to rain again; we went into the hut, the fiend looking triumphant, and I with a heavy heart and low spirits. But I had agreed to listen, and when I had sat down by the fire that my hateful companion had lit, he began his story.
b1: The next day I walked around the valley. I stood near the place where the river Arveiron begins, in a glacier that moves slowly down from the hills. Huge mountains rose steeply in front of me, and the icy wall of the glacier hung above me. There were a few broken pine trees around. Everything was silent and grand, like the palace of a great queen called Nature. The only sounds were the rushing water, falling rocks, the thunder of an avalanche and the cracking of the ice, which broke again and again as if it were a toy.

These wonderful views gave me more comfort than anything else could. They lifted me above small feelings, and although they did not take away my sadness, they made it calmer. They also helped me stop thinking about the dark thoughts of the last month. At night I went to bed, and the great shapes I had seen during the day seemed to watch over my sleep. The snowy mountain tops, the shining peaks, the pine woods, the wild valleys and the eagle flying among the clouds all gathered around me and told me to be calm.

But where were they when I woke up the next morning? My good feelings had gone with my sleep, and I felt dark and sad again. It was raining very hard, and thick mist hid the mountain tops, so I could not even see my great friends. But I wanted to go through the mist and find them. Rain and storms did not matter to me.

My mule was brought to the door, and I decided to go up to the top of Montanvert. I remembered how I had felt the first time I saw the huge, moving glacier. It had filled me with a great joy that made my soul feel it could fly up to the light. Great sights in nature always made me feel serious and helped me forget my small, everyday worries. I decided to go without a guide, because I knew the path well and another person would spoil the lonely beauty of the place.

The climb is very steep, but the path goes up in many short turns, so you can get up the mountain. It is a terribly empty and wild place. In many places you can see what the winter avalanches have done. Broken trees lie on the ground; some are completely destroyed, and others are bent and lean against the rocks or across other trees.

Higher up, the path crosses gullies full of snow, and stones often roll down them. One of them is especially dangerous: even a loud voice can shake the air and bring rocks down on the person who spoke. The pine trees are not tall, but they are dark and make the place look hard and serious. I looked down at the valley. Thick mist was rising from the rivers and going around the mountains opposite, and their tops were hidden in clouds. Rain was falling from the dark sky, and everything around me made me feel even sadder.

Oh! Why are people proud that their feelings are finer than an animal’s? It only makes them need more. If we only felt hunger, thirst and desire, we could be almost free; but now every wind and every chance word can change how we feel. As a poem says: a bad dream can spoil our sleep, and one sad thought can spoil our day. We laugh or cry, we hold on to our sadness or throw our worries away, but it is all the same, because joy and sorrow can always leave. Tomorrow may never be like yesterday; nothing stays the same except change!

It was almost midday when I reached the top. For some time I sat on a rock above the sea of ice. Mist covered the ice and the mountains around it. Soon a light wind blew the cloud away, and I went down onto the glacier. The ice is very uneven, like the waves of a stormy sea, and there are deep cracks in it. The field of ice is only about a league wide, but it took me nearly two hours to cross it. The mountain on the other side is a bare, straight wall of rock.

From there I could see Montanvert right opposite me, a league away, and above it stood the great Mont Blanc. I stayed in a hollow in the rock and looked at this wonderful view. The sea of ice, or really the huge river of ice, went round the mountains, and their high tops hung over it. Their icy peaks shone in the sun above the clouds. My sad heart now felt something like joy, and I cried out, “Spirits of the dead, if you really wander and do not rest in your graves, give me this little happiness, or take me away with you from life.”

As I said this, I suddenly saw the figure of a man far away, coming towards me very fast – faster than any man. He jumped over the cracks in the ice that I had walked around so carefully, and as he came closer, he looked taller than a man. I felt weak and my eyes went misty, but the cold mountain wind soon made me feel better. As he came nearer, I saw that it was the creature I had made – a terrible, hateful sight! I shook with anger and horror, and I decided to wait for him and fight him to the death. He came up to me; his face showed deep pain, and also hate and anger, and it was so ugly that it was almost too horrible to look at. But I hardly noticed this; at first I was too angry to speak, and then I shouted angry, hateful words at him.

“Devil,” I shouted, “how dare you come near me? Aren’t you afraid of my anger? Go away, you horrible insect! No – stay, so that I can crush you! Oh, if only killing you could bring back the people you have murdered!”

“I expected you to greet me like this,” said the monster. “Everybody hates unhappy people, so they must hate me very much, because I am the unhappiest creature alive! But you, my creator, hate me too, although I am your creature and we are tied together until one of us dies. You want to kill me. How dare you play with life like this? Do your duty to me, and I will do mine to you and to all people. If you agree to what I ask, I will leave you and them in peace; but if you say no, I will kill and kill until death is full of the blood of your other friends.”

“Hateful monster! Devil! Even hell is not a big enough punishment for your crimes. You blame me for making you – so come here, and I will take away the life that I gave you so carelessly.” I was wild with anger, and I jumped at him with all the hate one creature can feel for another. He moved away from me easily and said,

“Be calm! Please listen to me before you show me your hate. Haven’t I suffered enough? Why do you want to make me more unhappy? My life is full of pain, but it is dear to me, and I will defend it. Remember, you made me stronger than you; I am taller than you, and I can move more easily. But I do not want to fight you. I am your creature, and I will be gentle and obedient to you, my master and king, if you also do what you owe me.

Oh, Frankenstein, you are fair to everyone else, so do not be cruel only to me, when I need your kindness and love more than anyone. Remember that I am your creature; I should be your Adam, but I am more like the fallen angel, whom you send away from happiness though he did nothing wrong. Everywhere I see happiness, but I can never have it. I was kind and good; unhappiness made me a devil. Make me happy, and I will be good again.” “Go away! I will not listen to you. We can have nothing to do with each other; we are enemies. Go away, or let us fight until one of us dies.”

“How can I make you feel for me? Will you not look kindly at your creature, who is begging for your kindness? Believe me, Frankenstein, I was good; my heart was full of love; but I am alone, terribly alone. You, my creator, hate me, so what can I hope for from other people, who owe me nothing? They push me away and hate me. The empty mountains and cold glaciers are my home. I have wandered here for many days; I live in the ice caves, which I alone am not afraid of, and which no man wants to take from me. I love these grey skies, because they are kinder to me than people are.

If all people knew about me, they would do the same as you and take up weapons to kill me. So why shouldn’t I hate them, when they hate me? I will not make peace with my enemies. I am unhappy, and they will be unhappy too. But you can help me and save them. If you do not, the evil will become so great that not only you and your family but thousands of other people will be destroyed by it.

Please feel pity for me, and do not hate me. Listen to my story; when you have heard it, leave me or feel sorry for me – whatever you think I deserve. But listen to me. Even criminals are allowed to speak and defend themselves before a judge decides their punishment. Listen to me, Frankenstein. You say I am a murderer, but you want to kill your own creature and feel no guilt. How fair people are! I am not asking you to save my life; just listen to me, and then, if you can and if you want to, destroy what you have made.”

“Why do you remind me of those terrible events?” I answered. “I shake when I think of them, and I know that I caused them. I curse the day when you first saw the light, you hateful devil! I curse the hands that made you, although they are my own! You have made me more unhappy than I can say. I cannot even think about whether I am fair to you or not. Go away! I cannot bear to look at you.”

“Then I will help you, my creator,” he said, and he put his hands over my eyes, but I pushed them away hard. “Now you cannot see me. But you can still listen to me and feel pity for me. I was good once, and I ask this of you. My story is long and strange, and it is too cold for you here; come to the hut on the mountain. The sun is still high; before it goes down behind the snowy mountains, you will hear my story, and then you can decide. It is your choice: I will either go away from people for ever and live without hurting anyone, or I will bring terrible pain to people and quickly destroy you too.”

After he said this, he walked across the ice, and I followed him. I did not answer him because my heart was too full, but as I walked, I thought about what he had said, and I decided at least to listen to his story. I was curious, and I also felt pity for him. Until then I had thought that he had killed my brother, and I wanted to know if this was true.

Also, for the first time, I understood that a creator has duties to his creature, and that I should make him happy before I complained about his evil actions. For these reasons I agreed to do what he asked. So we crossed the ice and climbed up the rock on the other side. It was cold, and it began to rain again. We went into the hut; the monster looked pleased, but my heart was heavy and sad. But I had agreed to listen, so I sat down by the fire that he had made, and he began his story.
a2: The next day I walked in the valley. I stood near the start of the river Arveiron. The river comes from a glacier, and the glacier moves very slowly down from the hills. Big mountains were in front of me, and a wall of ice was above me. There were a few broken trees. It was very quiet. Sometimes I heard water, falling rocks or the loud noise of ice when it broke. Nature was very big and strong, and the ice was like a toy in its hands.

These beautiful places helped me a lot. I was still sad, but I felt calmer. For some time I stopped thinking about the bad things of the last month. At night I went to bed, and I thought about the things I saw in the day: the snowy mountains, the pine trees and an eagle high in the clouds. They were like friends, and they told me to be calm.
But the next morning my friends were gone. I felt sad again. It was raining hard, and there was thick fog, so I could not see the mountains. But I wanted to find them. I did not care about the rain.

I took my mule and decided to go up the mountain Montanvert. I remembered the first time I saw the big glacier there. The glacier was huge, and it moved all the time. It made me very happy then, and I forgot all my problems. I went alone, without a guide, because I knew the way and I wanted to be alone.
The path up the mountain is very steep, and it turns many times. The place is wild and empty. In winter, snow falls down the mountain and breaks the trees. Many broken trees lie on the ground.

Higher up, stones often fall down. In one place it is very dangerous: if you speak loudly, rocks can fall on your head. The trees are small and dark. I looked down at the valley. There was fog over the rivers and clouds over the mountains, and it was raining. Everything made me feel sad.

Why are people so sensitive? Animals only feel hungry or thirsty, and so they are almost free. But one small word can change how people feel. An old poem says: a bad dream can spoil the night, and one bad thought can spoil the day. Happy or sad, our feelings always go away. Nothing stays the same – only change stays!

At about twelve o’clock I got to the top. I sat on a rock above the sea of ice. There was fog everywhere, but then the wind took it away. I walked down onto the glacier. The ice goes up and down like the waves of the sea, and it has deep holes. It took me almost two hours to cross it.

On the other side I stopped and looked. Montanvert was in front of me, and behind it was the great mountain Mont Blanc. The river of ice went between the mountains, and their tops were shining in the sun. I felt almost happy, and I shouted, “Spirits of the dead, if you are here, give me a little happiness, or take me with you!”

Then I suddenly saw a man. He was coming towards me very fast. He jumped over the holes in the ice, and he was taller than a man. I felt weak, but the cold wind helped me. When he came nearer, I saw who it was: the creature I made! I was angry and afraid, and I wanted to fight him. His face was full of pain and hate, and it was terribly ugly. At first I could not speak, and then I shouted at him.
“Devil!” I shouted. “Don’t come near me! Go away! No – stay, and I will kill you! Oh, I wish I could bring back the people you killed!”

“I knew you would say this,” said the monster. “Everybody hates me because I am unhappy. You made me, but you hate me too. You want to kill me. How can you play with life like this? Be good to me, and I will be good to you and to all people. If you do what I ask, I will leave you and them alone. If you say no, I will kill all your friends.”
“You terrible monster! You are a devil! Hell is not enough punishment for your crimes! I made you, and now I will kill you!” I was very angry, and I jumped at him. He moved away easily and said,

“Be calm! Please listen to me. I am already very unhappy. Haven’t I suffered enough? My life is hard, but I love it, and I will fight for it. You made me bigger and stronger than you. But I don’t want to fight you. You are my master, and I will be kind to you if you help me.

Oh, Frankenstein, you are good to other people – be good to me too! I am your creature. I should be your Adam, but I am like the bad angel who was sent away from heaven. I see happy people everywhere, but I can never be happy. I was good, but people made me bad. Make me happy, and I will be good again.” “Go away! I won’t listen. We are enemies. Go away, or fight me!”

“How can I change your mind? Please be kind to me. I was good, and I loved people, but I am alone, very alone. You made me and you hate me, so other people will hate me too. They push me away. I live in the mountains, in caves of ice. Nobody wants to take them from me. The cold sky is kinder to me than people.

If people knew about me, they would try to kill me. So I hate them too, and I am going to make them unhappy. But you can help me and save them. If you don’t, many people will die – you, your family and thousands of others.

Please feel sorry for me. Listen to my story, and then decide what to do with me. Even bad people can speak before a judge. You say I am a killer, but you want to kill me! Listen to me first, and then kill me if you want.”

“Why do you talk about these terrible things?” I said. “It is my fault that they happened. I hate the day when you were born, and I hate the hands that made you! You have made me very unhappy. Go away! I don’t want to see you.”

He put his big hands over my eyes, but I pushed them away. “Now you can’t see me,” he said, “but you can listen. My story is long. It is also very strange. It is cold here, so come to the hut on the mountain. Before the sun goes down, you will hear everything. Then you can decide: I will go away and hurt nobody, or I will kill people and destroy you too.”

He walked across the ice, and I went after him. I did not say anything, but I thought about his words and decided to listen to him. My heart was full. I wanted to know his story, and I felt sorry for him. I also wanted to know: did he kill my brother?

And for the first time I understood that I had to take care of him and make him happy before I talked about his bad actions. So I said yes. We crossed the ice and went up the rock. It was cold and raining again. We went into the hut; the monster was happy, but I was very sad. I sat by the fire, and he started his story.

o.en: I spent the following day roaming through the valley.
o.ru: Весь следующий день я бродил по долине.

o.en: I stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which take their rise in a glacier, that with slow pace is advancing down from the summit of the hills to barricade the valley.
o.ru: Я стоял у истоков Арверона, берущего начало в леднике, который медленно сползает с горных вершин, словно желая перегородить долину.

o.en: The abrupt sides of vast mountains were before me; the icy wall of the glacier overhung me; a few shattered pines were scattered around; and the solemn silence of this glorious presence-chamber of imperial Nature was broken only by the brawling waves or the fall of some vast fragment, the thunder sound of the avalanche or the cracking, reverberated along the mountains, of the accumulated ice, which, through the silent working of immutable laws, was ever and anon rent and torn, as if it had been but a plaything in their hands.
o.ru: Передо мною высились отвесные склоны огромных гор; ледяная стена ледника нависала надо мной; кругом были разбросаны редкие расщеплённые сосны; и торжественное безмолвие этого великолепного тронного зала царственной Природы нарушалось лишь шумом бурлящих волн или падением какой-нибудь огромной глыбы, громовым раскатом лавины или отдававшимся эхом в горах треском скопившегося льда, который в безмолвном действии неизменных законов то и дело раскалывался и разрывался, словно был лишь игрушкой в их руках.

o.en: These sublime and magnificent scenes afforded me the greatest consolation that I was capable of receiving.
o.ru: Эти возвышенные и величественные картины подарили мне самое большое утешение, какое я способен был принять.

o.en: They elevated me from all littleness of feeling, and although they did not remove my grief, they subdued and tranquillised it.
o.ru: Они возвышали меня над всякой мелочностью чувств, и хотя не избавили от горя, но смягчили и успокоили его.

o.en: In some degree, also, they diverted my mind from the thoughts over which it had brooded for the last month.
o.ru: Отчасти они также отвлекли мой ум от мыслей, над которыми он мрачно размышлял весь последний месяц.

o.en: I retired to rest at night; my slumbers, as it were, waited on and ministered to by the assemblance of grand shapes which I had contemplated during the day.
o.ru: Ночью я отошёл ко сну; мою дремоту словно сторожило и охраняло собрание величественных образов, которые я созерцал днём.

o.en: They congregated round me; the unstained snowy mountain-top, the glittering pinnacle, the pine woods, and ragged bare ravine, the eagle, soaring amidst the clouds—they all gathered round me and bade me be at peace.
o.ru: Они собирались вокруг меня: незапятнанная снежная вершина, сверкающий пик, сосновые леса, голое неровное ущелье, орёл, парящий среди облаков, — все они обступили меня и велели мне обрести покой.

o.en: Where had they fled when the next morning I awoke?
o.ru: Куда же они исчезли, когда я проснулся на следующее утро?

o.en: All of soul-inspiriting fled with sleep, and dark melancholy clouded every thought.
o.ru: Всё, что воодушевляло душу, улетело вместе со сном, и тёмная тоска омрачила каждую мысль.

o.en: The rain was pouring in torrents, and thick mists hid the summits of the mountains, so that I even saw not the faces of those mighty friends.
o.ru: Дождь лил потоками, и густые туманы скрывали горные вершины, так что я даже не видел лиц этих могучих друзей.

o.en: Still I would penetrate their misty veil and seek them in their cloudy retreats.
o.ru: И всё же я хотел проникнуть сквозь их туманный покров и отыскать их в облачных убежищах.

o.en: What were rain and storm to me?
o.ru: Что значили для меня дождь и буря?

o.en: My mule was brought to the door, and I resolved to ascend to the summit of Montanvert.
o.ru: К дверям подвели моего мула, и я решил подняться на вершину Монтанвера.

o.en: I remembered the effect that the view of the tremendous and ever-moving glacier had produced upon my mind when I first saw it.
o.ru: Я вспомнил, какое впечатление произвёл на меня вид грозного, вечно движущегося ледника, когда я впервые его увидел.

o.en: It had then filled me with a sublime ecstasy that gave wings to the soul and allowed it to soar from the obscure world to light and joy.
o.ru: Тогда он наполнил меня возвышенным восторгом, который окрылил душу и позволил ей воспарить из тёмного мира к свету и радости.

o.en: The sight of the awful and majestic in nature had indeed always the effect of solemnising my mind and causing me to forget the passing cares of life.
o.ru: Зрелище грозного и величественного в природе всегда настраивало мой ум на торжественный лад и заставляло забыть мимолётные житейские заботы.

o.en: I determined to go without a guide, for I was well acquainted with the path, and the presence of another would destroy the solitary grandeur of the scene.
o.ru: Я решил идти без проводника, потому что хорошо знал тропу, а присутствие другого человека разрушило бы уединённое величие этой картины.

o.en: The ascent is precipitous, but the path is cut into continual and short windings, which enable you to surmount the perpendicularity of the mountain.
o.ru: Подъём крутой, но тропа вьётся частыми короткими петлями, которые позволяют одолеть отвесность горы.

o.en: It is a scene terrifically desolate.

In a thousand spots the traces of the winter avalanche may be perceived, where trees lie broken and strewed on the ground, some entirely destroyed, others bent, leaning upon the jutting rocks of the mountain or transversely upon other trees.
o.ru: В тысяче мест видны следы зимних лавин: деревья лежат сломанные и разбросанные по земле, одни совсем уничтожены, другие согнуты и опираются на выступающие скалы горы или лежат поперёк других деревьев.

o.en: The path, as you ascend higher, is intersected by ravines of snow, down which stones continually roll from above; one of them is particularly dangerous, as the slightest sound, such as even speaking in a loud voice, produces a concussion of air sufficient to draw destruction upon the head of the speaker.
o.ru: Выше тропу пересекают снежные ущелья, по которым сверху постоянно скатываются камни; одно из них особенно опасно, так как малейший звук, даже громко сказанное слово, вызывает сотрясение воздуха, достаточное, чтобы обрушить гибель на голову говорящего.

o.en: The pines are not tall or luxuriant, but they are sombre and add an air of severity to the scene.
o.ru: Сосны здесь невысокие и не пышные, но они сумрачны и придают картине суровость.

o.en: I looked on the valley beneath; vast mists were rising from the rivers which ran through it and curling in thick wreaths around the opposite mountains, whose summits were hid in the uniform clouds, while rain poured from the dark sky and added to the melancholy impression I received from the objects around me.
o.ru: Я смотрел на долину внизу; от рек, бегущих по ней, поднимались огромные туманы и густыми клубами обвивали противоположные горы, чьи вершины скрывались в сплошных облаках, а с тёмного неба лил дождь и усиливал тоскливое впечатление, которое производило на меня всё вокруг.

o.en: Alas!
Why does man boast of sensibilities superior to those apparent in the brute; it only renders them more necessary beings.
o.ru: Зачем человек хвалится чувствительностью, превосходящей ту, что свойственна животному? Она лишь делает его существом, зависящим от большего.

o.en: If our impulses were confined to hunger, thirst, and desire, we might be nearly free; but now we are moved by every wind that blows and a chance word or scene that that word may convey to us.
o.ru: Если бы наши порывы ограничивались голодом, жаждой и желанием, мы были бы почти свободны; а теперь нас волнует всякий ветер и случайное слово или картина, которую это слово может нам навеять.

o.en: We rest; a dream has power to poison sleep.
o.ru: Мы спим — но сон отравит сновиденье.

o.en: We rise; one wand’ring thought pollutes the day.
o.ru: Встаём — и мысль одна омрачит день.

o.en: We feel, conceive, or reason; laugh or weep, Embrace fond woe, or cast our cares away; It is the same: for, be it joy or sorrow, The path of its departure still is free.
o.ru: Мы чувствуем, мечтаем, рассуждаем, смеёмся, плачем, скорбь к груди прижмём иль сбросим бремя с плеч, — всё то же: радость то или печаль, путь для ухода их всегда открыт.

o.en: Man’s yesterday may ne’er be like his morrow; Nought may endure but mutability!
o.ru: Вчерашний день не схож с грядущим днём; ничто не вечно, кроме перемен!

o.en: It was nearly noon when I arrived at the top of the ascent.
o.ru: Было почти полдень, когда я добрался до конца подъёма.

o.en: For some time I sat upon the rock that overlooks the sea of ice.
o.ru: Некоторое время я сидел на скале, возвышающейся над ледяным морем.

o.en: A mist covered both that and the surrounding mountains.
o.ru: Туман окутывал и его, и окрестные горы.

o.en: Presently a breeze dissipated the cloud, and I descended upon the glacier.
o.ru: Вскоре ветерок рассеял облако, и я спустился на ледник.

o.en: The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a troubled sea, descending low, and interspersed by rifts that sink deep.
o.ru: Поверхность его очень неровная: она вздымается, как волны бурного моря, опускается и изрезана глубокими трещинами.

o.en: The field of ice is almost a league in width, but I spent nearly two hours in crossing it.
o.ru: Ледяное поле шириной почти в лигу, но я потратил почти два часа, чтобы пересечь его.

o.en: The opposite mountain is a bare perpendicular rock.
From the side where I now stood Montanvert was exactly opposite, at the distance of a league; and above it rose Mont Blanc, in awful majesty.
o.ru: С того места, где я теперь стоял, Монтанвер был прямо напротив, на расстоянии лиги, а над ним в грозном величии поднимался Монблан.

o.en: I remained in a recess of the rock, gazing on this wonderful and stupendous scene.
o.ru: Я остановился в углублении скалы, созерцая эту чудесную, изумительную картину.

o.en: The sea, or rather the vast river of ice, wound among its dependent mountains, whose aerial summits hung over its recesses.
o.ru: Море, или, вернее, огромная ледяная река, извивалось среди окружающих гор, чьи воздушные вершины нависали над его заливами.

o.en: Their icy and glittering peaks shone in the sunlight over the clouds.
o.ru: Их ледяные сверкающие пики сияли на солнце над облаками.

o.en: My heart, which was before sorrowful, now swelled with something like joy; I exclaimed, “Wandering spirits, if indeed ye wander, and do not rest in your narrow beds, allow me this faint happiness, or take me, as your companion, away from the joys of life.”
o.ru: Моё сердце, прежде полное печали, теперь переполнилось чем-то похожим на радость, и я воскликнул: «Блуждающие духи, если вы и вправду блуждаете, а не покоитесь в своих тесных ложах, даруйте мне это слабое счастье или возьмите меня к себе в спутники, прочь от радостей жизни».

o.en: As I said this I suddenly beheld the figure of a man, at some distance, advancing towards me with superhuman speed.
o.ru: Едва я сказал это, как вдруг увидел в отдалении фигуру человека, приближавшегося ко мне с нечеловеческой быстротой.

o.en: He bounded over the crevices in the ice, among which I had walked with caution; his stature, also, as he approached, seemed to exceed that of man.
o.ru: Он перепрыгивал через трещины во льду, между которыми я пробирался с осторожностью; и рост его, по мере того как он приближался, казался больше человеческого.

o.en: I was troubled; a mist came over my eyes, and I felt a faintness seize me, but I was quickly restored by the cold gale of the mountains.
o.ru: Я смутился; глаза мои заволокло туманом, и я почувствовал, что теряю сознание, но холодный горный ветер быстро привёл меня в чувство.

o.en: I perceived, as the shape came nearer (sight tremendous and abhorred!) that it was the wretch whom I had created.
o.ru: Когда фигура подошла ближе (ужасное и ненавистное зрелище!), я понял, что это тот негодяй, которого я создал.

o.en: I trembled with rage and horror, resolving to wait his approach and then close with him in mortal combat.
o.ru: Я дрожал от ярости и ужаса и решил дождаться его приближения, а затем вступить с ним в смертельную схватку.

o.en: He approached; his countenance bespoke bitter anguish, combined with disdain and malignity, while its unearthly ugliness rendered it almost too horrible for human eyes.
o.ru: Он приблизился; лицо его выражало горькую муку вместе с презрением и злобой, а его неземное уродство делало его почти невыносимым для человеческих глаз.

o.en: But I scarcely observed this; rage and hatred had at first deprived me of utterance, and I recovered only to overwhelm him with words expressive of furious detestation and contempt.
o.ru: Но я едва заметил это; ярость и ненависть сначала лишили меня дара речи, а придя в себя, я обрушил на него слова, полные бешеного отвращения и презрения.

o.en: “Devil,” I exclaimed, “do you dare approach me?
o.ru: «Дьявол, — воскликнул я, — ты смеешь подходить ко мне?

o.en: And do not you fear the fierce vengeance of my arm wreaked on your miserable head?
o.ru: И ты не боишься, что моя рука обрушит яростную месть на твою жалкую голову?

o.en: Begone, vile insect!
Or rather, stay, that I may trample you to dust!
o.ru: Или нет, останься, чтобы я растоптал тебя в прах!

o.en: And, oh!
That I could, with the extinction of your miserable existence, restore those victims whom you have so diabolically murdered!”
o.ru: Если бы я мог, уничтожив твоё жалкое существование, вернуть к жизни те жертвы, которых ты так дьявольски убил!»

o.en: “I expected this reception,” said the dæmon.
“All men hate the wretched; how, then, must I be hated, who am miserable beyond all living things!
o.ru: — Все люди ненавидят несчастных; как же тогда должны ненавидеть меня, несчастнейшего из всех живых существ!

o.en: Yet you, my creator, detest and spurn me, thy creature, to whom thou art bound by ties only dissoluble by the annihilation of one of us.
o.ru: И всё же ты, мой создатель, ненавидишь и отталкиваешь меня, своё создание, с которым ты связан узами, расторжимыми лишь со смертью одного из нас.

o.en: You purpose to kill me.
How dare you sport thus with life?
o.ru: Как смеешь ты так играть жизнью?

o.en: Do your duty towards me, and I will do mine towards you and the rest of mankind.
o.ru: Исполни свой долг по отношению ко мне, и я исполню свой по отношению к тебе и ко всему остальному человечеству.

o.en: If you will comply with my conditions, I will leave them and you at peace; but if you refuse, I will glut the maw of death, until it be satiated with the blood of your remaining friends.”
o.ru: Если ты примешь мои условия, я оставлю в покое и их, и тебя; но если откажешь, я буду насыщать пасть смерти, пока она не пресытится кровью твоих оставшихся друзей».

o.en: “Abhorred monster!
Fiend that thou art!
The tortures of hell are too mild a vengeance for thy crimes.
o.ru: Адские муки — слишком мягкая кара за твои преступления.

o.en: Wretched devil!
You reproach me with your creation, come on, then, that I may extinguish the spark which I so negligently bestowed.”
o.ru: Ты упрекаешь меня тем, что я тебя создал, — так подойди же, чтобы я погасил искру, которую так легкомысленно зажёг».

o.en: My rage was without bounds; I sprang on him, impelled by all the feelings which can arm one being against the existence of another.
o.ru: Ярость моя не знала границ; я бросился на него, движимый всеми чувствами, которые могут вооружить одно существо против жизни другого.

o.en: He easily eluded me and said,
“Be calm!
I entreat you to hear me before you give vent to your hatred on my devoted head.
o.ru: Умоляю тебя выслушать меня, прежде чем ты обрушишь свою ненависть на мою обречённую голову.

o.en: Have I not suffered enough, that you seek to increase my misery?
o.ru: Разве я не выстрадал довольно, что ты стремишься умножить мои муки?

o.en: Life, although it may only be an accumulation of anguish, is dear to me, and I will defend it.
o.ru: Жизнь, пусть даже она лишь нагромождение страданий, дорога мне, и я буду её защищать.

o.en: Remember, thou hast made me more powerful than thyself; my height is superior to thine, my joints more supple.
o.ru: Помни, ты сделал меня сильнее себя: я выше тебя ростом, и суставы мои гибче.

o.en: But I will not be tempted to set myself in opposition to thee.
o.ru: Но я не поддамся искушению пойти против тебя.

o.en: I am thy creature, and I will be even mild and docile to my natural lord and king if thou wilt also perform thy part, the which thou owest me.
o.ru: Я твоё создание и буду даже кротким и послушным своему природному господину и королю, если и ты исполнишь свою часть, которую ты мне должен.

o.en: Oh, Frankenstein, be not equitable to every other and trample upon me alone, to whom thy justice, and even thy clemency and affection, is most due.
o.ru: О Франкенштейн, не будь справедлив ко всем прочим, попирая одного меня, кому более всех причитаются твоя справедливость и даже твоё милосердие и любовь.

o.en: Remember that I am thy creature; I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.
o.ru: Помни, что я твоё создание; я должен был стать твоим Адамом, а стал скорее падшим ангелом, которого ты без всякой вины изгоняешь из рая радости.

o.en: Everywhere I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded.
o.ru: Повсюду я вижу блаженство, от которого лишь я один навсегда отлучён.

o.en: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.
o.ru: Я был добрым и хорошим; несчастье сделало меня демоном.

o.en: Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.”
o.ru: Сделай меня счастливым, и я снова стану добродетельным».

o.en: “Begone!
I will not hear you.
There can be no community between you and me; we are enemies.
o.ru: Между нами не может быть ничего общего; мы враги.

o.en: Begone, or let us try our strength in a fight, in which one must fall.”
o.ru: Уходи — или померяемся силами в схватке, в которой один из нас должен пасть».

o.en: “How can I move thee?
Will no entreaties cause thee to turn a favourable eye upon thy creature, who implores thy goodness and compassion?
o.ru: Неужели никакие мольбы не заставят тебя благосклонно взглянуть на своё создание, которое взывает к твоей доброте и состраданию?

o.en: Believe me, Frankenstein, I was benevolent; my soul glowed with love and humanity; but am I not alone, miserably alone?
o.ru: Поверь мне, Франкенштейн, я был добр; душа моя пылала любовью и человечностью; но разве я не одинок, горестно одинок?

o.en: You, my creator, abhor me; what hope can I gather from your fellow creatures, who owe me nothing?
o.ru: Ты, мой создатель, питаешь ко мне отвращение; на что же мне надеяться от твоих собратьев, которые мне ничем не обязаны?

o.en: They spurn and hate me.
The desert mountains and dreary glaciers are my refuge.
o.ru: Пустынные горы и унылые ледники — моё убежище.

o.en: I have wandered here many days; the caves of ice, which I only do not fear, are a dwelling to me, and the only one which man does not grudge.
o.ru: Я скитаюсь здесь уже много дней; ледяные пещеры, которых я один не боюсь, служат мне жилищем — единственным, в котором человек мне не отказывает.

o.en: These bleak skies I hail, for they are kinder to me than your fellow beings.
o.ru: Эти суровые небеса я приветствую, ибо они добрее ко мне, чем твои собратья.

o.en: If the multitude of mankind knew of my existence, they would do as you do, and arm themselves for my destruction.
o.ru: Если бы множество людей узнало о моём существовании, они поступили бы так же, как ты, и вооружились бы, чтобы меня уничтожить.

o.en: Shall I not then hate them who abhor me?
o.ru: Как же мне не ненавидеть тех, кто питает ко мне отвращение?

o.en: I will keep no terms with my enemies.
o.ru: Я не пойду ни на какие уступки своим врагам.

o.en: I am miserable, and they shall share my wretchedness.
o.ru: Я несчастен, и они разделят моё горе.

o.en: Yet it is in your power to recompense me, and deliver them from an evil which it only remains for you to make so great, that not only you and your family, but thousands of others, shall be swallowed up in the whirlwinds of its rage.
o.ru: И всё же в твоей власти вознаградить меня и избавить их от зла, которое лишь от тебя зависит сделать столь великим, что не только ты и твоя семья, но и тысячи других будут поглощены вихрями его ярости.

o.en: Let your compassion be moved, and do not disdain me.
o.ru: Пусть в тебе пробудится сострадание, не отвергай меня.

o.en: Listen to my tale; when you have heard that, abandon or commiserate me, as you shall judge that I deserve.
o.ru: Выслушай мою повесть; а когда выслушаешь, отвернись от меня или пожалей — как рассудишь, чего я заслуживаю.

o.en: But hear me.
The guilty are allowed, by human laws, bloody as they are, to speak in their own defence before they are condemned.
o.ru: Даже виновным человеческие законы, как бы кровавы они ни были, позволяют сказать слово в свою защиту, прежде чем их осудят.

o.en: Listen to me, Frankenstein.
You accuse me of murder, and yet you would, with a satisfied conscience, destroy your own creature.
o.ru: Ты обвиняешь меня в убийстве, а сам с чистой совестью готов уничтожить собственное создание.

o.en: Oh, praise the eternal justice of man!
Yet I ask you not to spare me; listen to me, and then, if you can, and if you will, destroy the work of your hands.”
o.ru: Но я не прошу пощадить меня; выслушай меня, а потом, если сможешь и если захочешь, уничтожь творение своих рук».

o.en: “Why do you call to my remembrance,” I rejoined, “circumstances of which I shudder to reflect, that I have been the miserable origin and author?
o.ru: «Зачем ты напоминаешь мне, — возразил я, — о событиях, при мысли о которых я содрогаюсь, о том, что я был их злосчастной причиной и виновником?

o.en: Cursed be the day, abhorred devil, in which you first saw light!
o.ru: Будь проклят день, ненавистный дьявол, когда ты впервые увидел свет!

o.en: Cursed (although I curse myself) be the hands that formed you!
o.ru: Будь прокляты (хотя этим я проклинаю себя) руки, которые тебя создали!

o.en: You have made me wretched beyond expression.
You have left me no power to consider whether I am just to you or not.
o.ru: Ты лишил меня способности рассудить, справедлив я к тебе или нет.

o.en: Begone!
Relieve me from the sight of your detested form.”
o.ru: Избавь меня от вида твоего ненавистного облика».

o.en: “Thus I relieve thee, my creator,” he said, and placed his hated hands before my eyes, which I flung from me with violence; “thus I take from thee a sight which you abhor.
o.ru: «Вот так я избавлю тебя, мой создатель», — сказал он и закрыл мне глаза своими ненавистными руками, которые я с силой отбросил; «так я скрою от тебя вид, который тебе отвратителен.

o.en: Still thou canst listen to me and grant me thy compassion.
o.ru: И всё же ты можешь выслушать меня и подарить мне своё сострадание.

o.en: By the virtues that I once possessed, I demand this from you.
o.ru: Во имя добродетелей, которыми я некогда обладал, я требую этого от тебя.

o.en: Hear my tale; it is long and strange, and the temperature of this place is not fitting to your fine sensations; come to the hut upon the mountain.
o.ru: Выслушай мою повесть; она длинна и необычна, а здешний холод не подходит для твоих тонких чувств; пойдём в хижину на горе.

o.en: The sun is yet high in the heavens; before it descends to hide itself behind your snowy precipices and illuminate another world, you will have heard my story and can decide.
o.ru: Солнце ещё высоко в небе; прежде чем оно опустится, чтобы скрыться за твоими снежными обрывами и осветить другой мир, ты уже услышишь мою историю и сможешь решить.

o.en: On you it rests, whether I quit for ever the neighbourhood of man and lead a harmless life, or become the scourge of your fellow creatures and the author of your own speedy ruin.”
o.ru: От тебя зависит, покину ли я навсегда людские края и буду вести безобидную жизнь или стану бичом твоих собратьев и виновником твоей скорой гибели».

o.en: As he said this he led the way across the ice; I followed.
o.ru: С этими словами он повёл меня через лёд; я последовал за ним.

o.en: My heart was full, and I did not answer him, but as I proceeded, I weighed the various arguments that he had used and determined at least to listen to his tale.
o.ru: Сердце моё было переполнено, и я не отвечал ему, но, идя вперёд, взвешивал все доводы, которые он привёл, и решил хотя бы выслушать его повесть.

o.en: I was partly urged by curiosity, and compassion confirmed my resolution.
o.ru: Отчасти меня побуждало любопытство, а сострадание укрепило моё решение.

o.en: I had hitherto supposed him to be the murderer of my brother, and I eagerly sought a confirmation or denial of this opinion.
o.ru: До сих пор я считал его убийцей моего брата и жадно искал подтверждения или опровержения этого мнения.

o.en: For the first time, also, I felt what the duties of a creator towards his creature were, and that I ought to render him happy before I complained of his wickedness.
o.ru: К тому же я впервые почувствовал, каковы обязанности создателя по отношению к своему созданию и что я должен сделать его счастливым, прежде чем жаловаться на его злобу.

o.en: These motives urged me to comply with his demand.
o.ru: Эти причины заставили меня согласиться на его требование.

o.en: We crossed the ice, therefore, and ascended the opposite rock.
o.ru: Итак, мы пересекли лёд и поднялись на противоположную скалу.

o.en: The air was cold, and the rain again began to descend; we entered the hut, the fiend with an air of exultation, I with a heavy heart and depressed spirits.
o.ru: Воздух был холоден, и снова начался дождь; мы вошли в хижину — демон с видом торжества, я с тяжёлым сердцем и в унынии.

o.en: But I consented to listen, and seating myself by the fire which my odious companion had lighted, he thus began his tale.
o.ru: Но я согласился слушать и, когда я сел у огня, который развёл мой отвратительный спутник, он начал свой рассказ.

b2.en: I spent the next day wandering through the valley.
b2.ru: Весь следующий день я бродил по долине.

b2.en: I stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which begin in a glacier that is slowly moving down from the tops of the hills as if to block the valley.
b2.ru: Я стоял у истоков Арверона, которые начинаются в леднике, медленно сползающем с вершин, словно чтобы перегородить долину.

b2.en: The steep sides of huge mountains rose in front of me; the icy wall of the glacier hung over me; a few broken pines were scattered around; and the solemn silence of this glorious throne room of mighty Nature was broken only by the roaring water, the fall of some huge rock, the thunder of an avalanche, or the cracking of the piled-up ice, echoing along the mountains, as the silent working of unchanging laws tore it apart again and again, as if it were only a toy in their hands.
b2.ru: Передо мной поднимались крутые склоны огромных гор; ледяная стена ледника нависала надо мной; вокруг были разбросаны редкие сломанные сосны; и торжественную тишину этого великолепного тронного зала могучей Природы нарушали лишь рёв воды, падение какой-нибудь огромной скалы, гром лавины или треск нагромождённого льда, отдававшийся эхом в горах, когда безмолвное действие неизменных законов снова и снова разрывало его, словно игрушку.

b2.en: These magnificent, awe-inspiring scenes gave me the greatest comfort I was capable of feeling.
b2.ru: Эти величественные, внушающие трепет картины дали мне самое большое утешение, какое я способен был почувствовать.

b2.en: They lifted me above all petty feelings, and although they did not take away my grief, they calmed and softened it.
b2.ru: Они подняли меня над всеми мелкими чувствами и, хотя не избавили от горя, успокоили и смягчили его.

b2.en: To some extent they also distracted my mind from the thoughts it had been brooding over for the past month.
b2.ru: В какой-то мере они также отвлекли мой ум от мыслей, над которыми он мрачно размышлял весь последний месяц.

b2.en: At night I went to bed, and my sleep seemed to be watched over and cared for by the grand shapes I had gazed at during the day.
b2.ru: Ночью я лёг спать, и мой сон словно охраняли величественные образы, которыми я любовался днём.

b2.en: They gathered around me – the pure snowy mountain top, the glittering peak, the pine woods, the rugged bare ravine, the eagle soaring among the clouds – they all surrounded me and told me to be at peace.
b2.ru: Они собрались вокруг меня — чистая снежная вершина, сверкающий пик, сосновые леса, голое суровое ущелье, орёл, парящий среди облаков, — все они окружили меня и велели мне успокоиться.

b2.en: Where had they gone when I woke up the next morning?
b2.ru: Куда же они исчезли, когда я проснулся на следующее утро?

b2.en: All my uplifted spirits had vanished with sleep, and a dark gloom clouded every thought.
b2.ru: Вся моя приподнятость исчезла вместе со сном, и тёмная тоска омрачила каждую мысль.

b2.en: The rain was pouring down in torrents, and thick mists hid the mountain tops, so that I could not even see the faces of those mighty friends.
b2.ru: Дождь лил потоками, и густые туманы скрывали вершины, так что я не мог даже увидеть лиц этих могучих друзей.

b2.en: Still, I was determined to break through their veil of mist and look for them in their cloudy hiding places.
b2.ru: И всё же я был полон решимости прорваться сквозь их туманную завесу и отыскать их в облачных убежищах.

b2.en: What did rain and storms matter to me?
b2.ru: Что мне были дождь и буря?

b2.en: My mule was brought to the door, and I decided to climb to the top of Montanvert.
b2.ru: К дверям подвели моего мула, и я решил подняться на вершину Монтанвера.

b2.en: I remembered the effect that the view of the immense, ever-moving glacier had had on me when I first saw it.
b2.ru: Я вспомнил, какое впечатление произвёл на меня вид огромного, вечно движущегося ледника, когда я впервые его увидел.

b2.en: It had filled me with a sublime ecstasy that gave my soul wings and let it soar out of the dark world into light and joy.
b2.ru: Он наполнил меня возвышенным восторгом, который окрылил мою душу и позволил ей вознестись из тёмного мира к свету и радости.

b2.en: The sight of what is awesome and majestic in nature had always made me feel solemn and helped me forget the passing worries of life.
b2.ru: Вид грозного и величественного в природе всегда настраивал меня на торжественный лад и помогал забыть мимолётные житейские заботы.

b2.en: I decided to go without a guide, as I knew the path well, and another person’s presence would spoil the lonely grandeur of the scene.
b2.ru: Я решил идти без проводника, потому что хорошо знал тропу, а присутствие другого человека нарушило бы уединённое величие картины.

b2.en: The climb is steep, but the path winds back and forth in short turns, which allow you to overcome the sheer face of the mountain.
b2.ru: Подъём крутой, но тропа идёт короткими петлями, которые позволяют одолеть отвесный склон горы.

b2.en: It is a terribly desolate place.
b2.ru: Это ужасно пустынное место.

b2.en: In a thousand spots you can see the marks of winter avalanches, where trees lie broken and scattered on the ground – some completely destroyed, others bent and leaning against the jutting rocks or lying across other trees.
b2.ru: В тысяче мест видны следы зимних лавин: деревья лежат сломанные и разбросанные по земле — одни совсем уничтожены, другие согнуты и опираются на выступающие скалы или лежат поперёк других деревьев.

b2.en: Higher up, the path is cut across by gullies of snow, down which stones keep rolling from above; one of them is particularly dangerous, because the slightest sound, even a raised voice, can shake the air enough to bring destruction down on the speaker’s head.
b2.ru: Выше тропу пересекают снежные овраги, по которым сверху то и дело катятся камни; один из них особенно опасен, потому что малейший звук, даже громкий голос, может сотрясти воздух настолько, что обрушит гибель на голову говорящего.

b2.en: The pines are neither tall nor lush, but they are gloomy and give the scene a stern look.
b2.ru: Сосны невысокие и не пышные, но они мрачны и придают картине суровый вид.

b2.en: I looked down at the valley below; huge mists were rising from the rivers that ran through it and curling in thick wreaths around the mountains opposite, whose tops were hidden in a grey blanket of cloud, while rain poured from the dark sky and deepened the sad impression that everything around me made.
b2.ru: Я посмотрел вниз, на долину; от рек, бегущих по ней, поднимались огромные туманы и густыми клубами обвивали горы напротив, чьи вершины скрывались под серым покровом облаков, а с тёмного неба лил дождь и усиливал грустное впечатление от всего вокруг.

b2.en: Alas!
b2.ru: Увы!

b2.en: Why does man boast that his feelings are finer than an animal’s? It only makes him more dependent.
b2.ru: Зачем человек хвалится тем, что его чувства тоньше, чем у животного? Это лишь делает его более зависимым.

b2.en: If our impulses were limited to hunger, thirst and desire, we might be almost free; but as it is, we are stirred by every wind that blows, and by any chance word or the picture that word may bring to mind.
b2.ru: Если бы наши порывы ограничивались голодом, жаждой и желанием, мы были бы почти свободны; а так нас волнует всякий ветер и любое случайное слово или картина, которую оно может вызвать в памяти.

b2.en: We rest, and a dream can poison sleep.
b2.ru: Мы отдыхаем — и сон может отравить сновидение.

b2.en: We get up, and one stray thought can spoil the day.
b2.ru: Мы встаём — и одна случайная мысль может испортить день.

b2.en: We feel, imagine or reason, laugh or cry, cling to our sorrow or throw our cares away – it makes no difference: whether it is joy or sorrow, it is always free to leave.
b2.ru: Мы чувствуем, воображаем или рассуждаем, смеёмся или плачем, цепляемся за своё горе или отбрасываем заботы — всё равно: радость это или печаль, она всегда вольна уйти.

b2.en: A man’s yesterday may never be like his tomorrow; nothing lasts except change!
b2.ru: Вчерашний день человека может не походить на завтрашний; ничто не длится, кроме перемен!

b2.en: It was almost noon when I reached the top of the climb.
b2.ru: Было почти полдень, когда я добрался до конца подъёма.

b2.en: For a while I sat on the rock that looks down on the sea of ice.
b2.ru: Некоторое время я сидел на скале, с которой видно ледяное море.

b2.en: A mist covered both the glacier and the mountains around it.
b2.ru: Туман окутывал и ледник, и окрестные горы.

b2.en: Soon a breeze blew the cloud away, and I went down onto the glacier.
b2.ru: Вскоре ветерок разогнал облако, и я спустился на ледник.

b2.en: The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a stormy sea, dipping low, and broken up by deep cracks.
b2.ru: Поверхность очень неровная: она вздымается, как волны бурного моря, опускается и изрезана глубокими трещинами.

b2.en: The field of ice is almost a league wide, but it took me nearly two hours to cross it.
b2.ru: Ледяное поле шириной почти в лигу, но мне понадобилось почти два часа, чтобы пересечь его.

b2.en: The mountain on the other side is a bare, sheer rock.
b2.ru: Гора на другой стороне — голая отвесная скала.

b2.en: From where I now stood, Montanvert was directly opposite, a league away, and above it rose Mont Blanc in awesome majesty.
b2.ru: С того места, где я теперь стоял, Монтанвер был прямо напротив, в лиге от меня, а над ним в грозном величии поднимался Монблан.

b2.en: I stayed in a hollow in the rock, gazing at this wonderful, breathtaking scene.
b2.ru: Я остался в углублении скалы, любуясь этой чудесной, захватывающей дух картиной.

b2.en: The sea – or rather the vast river – of ice wound among the mountains around it, whose airy summits hung over its hidden bays.
b2.ru: Море — или, вернее, огромная река — льда извивалось среди окружающих гор, чьи воздушные вершины нависали над его укромными заливами.

b2.en: Their icy, glittering peaks shone in the sunlight above the clouds.
b2.ru: Их ледяные сверкающие пики сияли на солнце над облаками.

b2.en: My heart, which had been full of sorrow, now swelled with something like joy, and I cried out, “Wandering spirits, if you really do wander and do not rest in your narrow graves, allow me this faint happiness, or take me away with you from the joys of life.”
b2.ru: Моё сердце, прежде полное печали, теперь переполнилось чем-то похожим на радость, и я воскликнул: «Блуждающие духи, если вы и правда блуждаете и не покоитесь в своих тесных могилах, подарите мне это слабое счастье или заберите меня с собой прочь от радостей жизни».

b2.en: As I said this, I suddenly saw the figure of a man some distance away, coming towards me at superhuman speed.
b2.ru: Едва я сказал это, как вдруг увидел вдалеке фигуру человека, приближавшегося ко мне с нечеловеческой скоростью.

b2.en: He leapt over the cracks in the ice, which I had walked among so carefully, and as he came closer he seemed taller than any man.
b2.ru: Он перепрыгивал через трещины во льду, между которыми я шёл так осторожно, и по мере приближения казался выше любого человека.

b2.en: I was shaken; a mist came over my eyes and I felt faint, but the cold mountain wind quickly brought me round.
b2.ru: Я был потрясён; глаза мне заволокло туманом, и мне стало дурно, но холодный горный ветер быстро привёл меня в чувство.

b2.en: As the shape drew nearer (a terrible, hateful sight!), I realised that it was the wretch I had created.
b2.ru: Когда фигура приблизилась (ужасное, ненавистное зрелище!), я понял, что это тот негодяй, которого я создал.

b2.en: I trembled with rage and horror, and made up my mind to wait for him and then fight him to the death.
b2.ru: Я дрожал от ярости и ужаса и решил дождаться его, а затем сразиться с ним насмерть.

b2.en: He came up to me; his face showed bitter anguish mixed with scorn and malice, while its unearthly ugliness made it almost too horrible for human eyes to look at.
b2.ru: Он подошёл ко мне; его лицо выражало горькую муку вместе с презрением и злобой, а неземное уродство делало его почти невыносимым для человеческих глаз.

b2.en: But I hardly noticed this; at first rage and hatred left me speechless, and when I found my voice, I poured out words full of furious loathing and contempt.
b2.ru: Но я почти не заметил этого; сначала ярость и ненависть лишили меня дара речи, а когда голос вернулся, я обрушил на него слова, полные бешеного отвращения и презрения.

b2.en: “Devil,” I cried, “how dare you come near me?
b2.ru: «Дьявол, — закричал я, — как ты смеешь подходить ко мне?

b2.en: Aren’t you afraid that my arm will take fierce revenge on your miserable head?
b2.ru: Разве ты не боишься, что моя рука жестоко отомстит твоей жалкой голове?

b2.en: Go away, you vile insect!
b2.ru: Прочь, мерзкое насекомое!

b2.en: Or rather, stay, so that I can crush you into dust!
b2.ru: Или нет, останься, чтобы я растоптал тебя в прах!

b2.en: Oh, if only I could bring back the victims you have so fiendishly murdered by ending your miserable existence!”
b2.ru: О, если бы я мог, покончив с твоим жалким существованием, вернуть тех, кого ты так дьявольски убил!»

b2.en: “I expected this welcome,” said the monster.
b2.ru: «Я ожидал такого приёма, — сказал чудовище.

b2.en: “All men hate the unhappy, so how much must I be hated, when I am more miserable than any living thing!
b2.ru: — Все люди ненавидят несчастных; как же тогда ненавидят меня, несчастнее которого нет ни одного живого существа!

b2.en: Yet you, my creator, hate and reject me, your own creature, to whom you are bound by ties that only the death of one of us can break.
b2.ru: И всё же ты, мой создатель, ненавидишь и отвергаешь меня, своё создание, с которым ты связан узами, разорвать которые может только смерть одного из нас.

b2.en: You intend to kill me.
b2.ru: Ты собираешься убить меня.

b2.en: How dare you play with life like this?
b2.ru: Как ты смеешь так играть жизнью?

b2.en: Do your duty towards me, and I will do mine towards you and the rest of mankind.
b2.ru: Исполни свой долг по отношению ко мне, и я исполню свой по отношению к тебе и ко всему человечеству.

b2.en: If you agree to my conditions, I will leave them and you in peace; but if you refuse, I will feed the jaws of death until they are full with the blood of your remaining friends.”
b2.ru: Если ты примешь мои условия, я оставлю в покое и их, и тебя; но если откажешь, я буду кормить пасть смерти, пока она не насытится кровью твоих оставшихся друзей».

b2.en: “Hateful monster!
b2.ru: «Ненавистное чудовище!

b2.en: You fiend!
b2.ru: Исчадие ада!

b2.en: The tortures of hell would be too gentle a punishment for your crimes.
b2.ru: Адские муки были бы слишком мягкой карой за твои преступления.

b2.en: Wretched devil!
b2.ru: Жалкий дьявол!

b2.en: You blame me for creating you – come on, then, and let me put out the spark of life that I gave you so carelessly.”
b2.ru: Ты упрекаешь меня в том, что я тебя создал, — так подойди же, и я погашу искру жизни, которую так беспечно тебе дал».

b2.en: My fury knew no limits; I leapt at him, driven by every feeling that can turn one being against the life of another.
b2.ru: Моя ярость не знала границ; я бросился на него, движимый всеми чувствами, которые могут обратить одно существо против жизни другого.

b2.en: He dodged me easily and said,
b2.ru: Он легко увернулся и сказал:

b2.en: “Calm down!
b2.ru: «Успокойся!

b2.en: I beg you to hear me out before you pour your hatred on my doomed head.
b2.ru: Умоляю, выслушай меня, прежде чем обрушить свою ненависть на мою обречённую голову.

b2.en: Haven’t I suffered enough, without you trying to add to my misery?
b2.ru: Разве я мало страдал, чтобы ты ещё пытался усилить мои муки?

b2.en: Life, even if it is only a heap of suffering, is precious to me, and I will defend it.
b2.ru: Жизнь, даже если это лишь груда страданий, дорога мне, и я буду её защищать.

b2.en: Remember, you made me stronger than yourself; I am taller than you, and my joints are more flexible.
b2.ru: Помни, ты сделал меня сильнее себя; я выше тебя, и суставы мои гибче.

b2.en: But I will not let myself be tempted to turn against you.
b2.ru: Но я не позволю себе поддаться искушению и пойти против тебя.

b2.en: I am your creature, and I will even be gentle and obedient to my natural lord and king, if you will also do your part, which you owe me.
b2.ru: Я твоё создание и буду даже кротким и послушным своему природному господину и королю, если и ты исполнишь свою часть, которую ты мне должен.

b2.en: Oh, Frankenstein, do not be fair to everyone else and trample on me alone, when I deserve your justice, and even your mercy and love, more than anyone.
b2.ru: О Франкенштейн, не будь справедлив ко всем остальным, топча одного меня, хотя я больше всех заслуживаю твоей справедливости и даже милосердия и любви.

b2.en: Remember that I am your creature; I should be your Adam, but instead I am the fallen angel, whom you drive away from joy though he has done nothing wrong.
b2.ru: Помни, что я твоё создание; я должен быть твоим Адамом, а вместо этого я падший ангел, которого ты изгоняешь из радости, хотя он ни в чём не виноват.

b2.en: Everywhere I see happiness, and I alone am shut out from it for ever.
b2.ru: Повсюду я вижу счастье, и лишь я один навсегда от него отлучён.

b2.en: I was kind and good; misery turned me into a fiend.
b2.ru: Я был добрым и хорошим; несчастье превратило меня в демона.

b2.en: Make me happy, and I will be good again.”
b2.ru: Сделай меня счастливым, и я снова стану добрым».

b2.en: “Go away!
b2.ru: «Прочь!

b2.en: I won’t listen to you.
b2.ru: Я не стану тебя слушать.

b2.en: There can be nothing in common between you and me; we are enemies.
b2.ru: Между нами не может быть ничего общего; мы враги.

b2.en: Go away, or let us test our strength in a fight in which one of us must die.”
