sub: Rejected by the De Laceys, the creature burns their cottage, travels to Geneva, is shot for saving a girl, kills William and frames Justine, then demands that Victor make him a female companion

o: “Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I live? Why, in that instant, did I not extinguish the spark of existence which you had so wantonly bestowed? I know not; despair had not yet taken possession of me; my feelings were those of rage and revenge. I could with pleasure have destroyed the cottage and its inhabitants and have glutted myself with their shrieks and misery.

“When night came I quitted my retreat and wandered in the wood; and now, no longer restrained by the fear of discovery, I gave vent to my anguish in fearful howlings. I was like a wild beast that had broken the toils, destroying the objects that obstructed me and ranging through the wood with a stag-like swiftness. Oh! What a miserable night I passed! The cold stars shone in mockery, and the bare trees waved their branches above me; now and then the sweet voice of a bird burst forth amidst the universal stillness. All, save I, were at rest or in enjoyment; I, like the arch-fiend, bore a hell within me, and finding myself unsympathised with, wished to tear up the trees, spread havoc and destruction around me, and then to have sat down and enjoyed the ruin.

“But this was a luxury of sensation that could not endure; I became fatigued with excess of bodily exertion and sank on the damp grass in the sick impotence of despair. There was none among the myriads of men that existed who would pity or assist me; and should I feel kindness towards my enemies? No; from that moment I declared everlasting war against the species, and more than all, against him who had formed me and sent me forth to this insupportable misery.

“The sun rose; I heard the voices of men and knew that it was impossible to return to my retreat during that day. Accordingly I hid myself in some thick underwood, determining to devote the ensuing hours to reflection on my situation.

“The pleasant sunshine and the pure air of day restored me to some degree of tranquillity; and when I considered what had passed at the cottage, I could not help believing that I had been too hasty in my conclusions. I had certainly acted imprudently. It was apparent that my conversation had interested the father in my behalf, and I was a fool in having exposed my person to the horror of his children. I ought to have familiarised the old De Lacey to me, and by degrees to have discovered myself to the rest of his family, when they should have been prepared for my approach. But I did not believe my errors to be irretrievable, and after much consideration I resolved to return to the cottage, seek the old man, and by my representations win him to my party.

“These thoughts calmed me, and in the afternoon I sank into a profound sleep; but the fever of my blood did not allow me to be visited by peaceful dreams. The horrible scene of the preceding day was for ever acting before my eyes; the females were flying and the enraged Felix tearing me from his father’s feet. I awoke exhausted, and finding that it was already night, I crept forth from my hiding-place, and went in search of food.

“When my hunger was appeased, I directed my steps towards the well-known path that conducted to the cottage. All there was at peace. I crept into my hovel and remained in silent expectation of the accustomed hour when the family arose. That hour passed, the sun mounted high in the heavens, but the cottagers did not appear. I trembled violently, apprehending some dreadful misfortune. The inside of the cottage was dark, and I heard no motion; I cannot describe the agony of this suspense.

“Presently two countrymen passed by, but pausing near the cottage, they entered into conversation, using violent gesticulations; but I did not understand what they said, as they spoke the language of the country, which differed from that of my protectors. Soon after, however, Felix approached with another man; I was surprised, as I knew that he had not quitted the cottage that morning, and waited anxiously to discover from his discourse the meaning of these unusual appearances.

“‘Do you consider,’ said his companion to him, ‘that you will be obliged to pay three months’ rent and to lose the produce of your garden? I do not wish to take any unfair advantage, and I beg therefore that you will take some days to consider of your determination.’

“‘It is utterly useless,’ replied Felix; ‘we can never again inhabit your cottage. The life of my father is in the greatest danger, owing to the dreadful circumstance that I have related. My wife and my sister will never recover from their horror. I entreat you not to reason with me any more. Take possession of your tenement and let me fly from this place.’
“Felix trembled violently as he said this. He and his companion entered the cottage, in which they remained for a few minutes, and then departed. I never saw any of the family of De Lacey more.

“I continued for the remainder of the day in my hovel in a state of utter and stupid despair. My protectors had departed and had broken the only link that held me to the world. For the first time the feelings of revenge and hatred filled my bosom, and I did not strive to control them, but allowing myself to be borne away by the stream, I bent my mind towards injury and death. When I thought of my friends, of the mild voice of De Lacey, the gentle eyes of Agatha, and the exquisite beauty of the Arabian, these thoughts vanished and a gush of tears somewhat soothed me.

But again when I reflected that they had spurned and deserted me, anger returned, a rage of anger, and unable to injure anything human, I turned my fury towards inanimate objects. As night advanced, I placed a variety of combustibles around the cottage, and after having destroyed every vestige of cultivation in the garden, I waited with forced impatience until the moon had sunk to commence my operations.

“As the night advanced, a fierce wind arose from the woods and quickly dispersed the clouds that had loitered in the heavens; the blast tore along like a mighty avalanche and produced a kind of insanity in my spirits that burst all bounds of reason and reflection. I lighted the dry branch of a tree and danced with fury around the devoted cottage, my eyes still fixed on the western horizon, the edge of which the moon nearly touched. A part of its orb was at length hid, and I waved my brand; it sank, and with a loud scream I fired the straw, and heath, and bushes, which I had collected. The wind fanned the fire, and the cottage was quickly enveloped by the flames, which clung to it and licked it with their forked and destroying tongues.

“As soon as I was convinced that no assistance could save any part of the habitation, I quitted the scene and sought for refuge in the woods.

“And now, with the world before me, whither should I bend my steps? I resolved to fly far from the scene of my misfortunes; but to me, hated and despised, every country must be equally horrible. At length the thought of you crossed my mind. I learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator; and to whom could I apply with more fitness than to him who had given me life? Among the lessons that Felix had bestowed upon Safie, geography had not been omitted; I had learned from these the relative situations of the different countries of the earth. You had mentioned Geneva as the name of your native town, and towards this place I resolved to proceed.

“But how was I to direct myself? I knew that I must travel in a southwesterly direction to reach my destination, but the sun was my only guide. I did not know the names of the towns that I was to pass through, nor could I ask information from a single human being; but I did not despair. From you only could I hope for succour, although towards you I felt no sentiment but that of hatred. Unfeeling, heartless creator! You had endowed me with perceptions and passions and then cast me abroad an object for the scorn and horror of mankind. But on you only had I any claim for pity and redress, and from you I determined to seek that justice which I vainly attempted to gain from any other being that wore the human form.

“My travels were long and the sufferings I endured intense. It was late in autumn when I quitted the district where I had so long resided. I travelled only at night, fearful of encountering the visage of a human being. Nature decayed around me, and the sun became heatless; rain and snow poured around me; mighty rivers were frozen; the surface of the earth was hard and chill, and bare, and I found no shelter. Oh, earth! How often did I imprecate curses on the cause of my being! The mildness of my nature had fled, and all within me was turned to gall and bitterness.

The nearer I approached to your habitation, the more deeply did I feel the spirit of revenge enkindled in my heart. Snow fell, and the waters were hardened, but I rested not. A few incidents now and then directed me, and I possessed a map of the country; but I often wandered wide from my path. The agony of my feelings allowed me no respite; no incident occurred from which my rage and misery could not extract its food; but a circumstance that happened when I arrived on the confines of Switzerland, when the sun had recovered its warmth and the earth again began to look green, confirmed in an especial manner the bitterness and horror of my feelings.

“I generally rested during the day and travelled only when I was secured by night from the view of man. One morning, however, finding that my path lay through a deep wood, I ventured to continue my journey after the sun had risen; the day, which was one of the first of spring, cheered even me by the loveliness of its sunshine and the balminess of the air. I felt emotions of gentleness and pleasure, that had long appeared dead, revive within me. Half surprised by the novelty of these sensations, I allowed myself to be borne away by them, and forgetting my solitude and deformity, dared to be happy. Soft tears again bedewed my cheeks, and I even raised my humid eyes with thankfulness towards the blessed sun, which bestowed such joy upon me.

“I continued to wind among the paths of the wood, until I came to its boundary, which was skirted by a deep and rapid river, into which many of the trees bent their branches, now budding with the fresh spring. Here I paused, not exactly knowing what path to pursue, when I heard the sound of voices, that induced me to conceal myself under the shade of a cypress. I was scarcely hid when a young girl came running towards the spot where I was concealed, laughing, as if she ran from someone in sport. She continued her course along the precipitous sides of the river, when suddenly her foot slipped, and she fell into the rapid stream.

I rushed from my hiding-place and with extreme labour, from the force of the current, saved her and dragged her to shore. She was senseless, and I endeavoured by every means in my power to restore animation, when I was suddenly interrupted by the approach of a rustic, who was probably the person from whom she had playfully fled. On seeing me, he darted towards me, and tearing the girl from my arms, hastened towards the deeper parts of the wood. I followed speedily, I hardly knew why; but when the man saw me draw near, he aimed a gun, which he carried, at my body and fired. I sank to the ground, and my injurer, with increased swiftness, escaped into the wood.

“This was then the reward of my benevolence! I had saved a human being from destruction, and as a recompense I now writhed under the miserable pain of a wound which shattered the flesh and bone. The feelings of kindness and gentleness which I had entertained but a few moments before gave place to hellish rage and gnashing of teeth. Inflamed by pain, I vowed eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind. But the agony of my wound overcame me; my pulses paused, and I fainted.

“For some weeks I led a miserable life in the woods, endeavouring to cure the wound which I had received. The ball had entered my shoulder, and I knew not whether it had remained there or passed through; at any rate I had no means of extracting it. My sufferings were augmented also by the oppressive sense of the injustice and ingratitude of their infliction. My daily vows rose for revenge—a deep and deadly revenge, such as would alone compensate for the outrages and anguish I had endured.

“After some weeks my wound healed, and I continued my journey. The labours I endured were no longer to be alleviated by the bright sun or gentle breezes of spring; all joy was but a mockery which insulted my desolate state and made me feel more painfully that I was not made for the enjoyment of pleasure.

“But my toils now drew near a close, and in two months from this time I reached the environs of Geneva.

“It was evening when I arrived, and I retired to a hiding-place among the fields that surround it to meditate in what manner I should apply to you. I was oppressed by fatigue and hunger and far too unhappy to enjoy the gentle breezes of evening or the prospect of the sun setting behind the stupendous mountains of Jura.

“At this time a slight sleep relieved me from the pain of reflection, which was disturbed by the approach of a beautiful child, who came running into the recess I had chosen, with all the sportiveness of infancy. Suddenly, as I gazed on him, an idea seized me that this little creature was unprejudiced and had lived too short a time to have imbibed a horror of deformity. If, therefore, I could seize him and educate him as my companion and friend, I should not be so desolate in this peopled earth.

“Urged by this impulse, I seized on the boy as he passed and drew him towards me. As soon as he beheld my form, he placed his hands before his eyes and uttered a shrill scream; I drew his hand forcibly from his face and said, ‘Child, what is the meaning of this? I do not intend to hurt you; listen to me.’

“He struggled violently. ‘Let me go,’ he cried; ‘monster! Ugly wretch! You wish to eat me and tear me to pieces. You are an ogre. Let me go, or I will tell my papa.’

“‘Boy, you will never see your father again; you must come with me.’

“‘Hideous monster! Let me go. My papa is a syndic—he is M. Frankenstein—he will punish you. You dare not keep me.’

“‘Frankenstein! you belong then to my enemy—to him towards whom I have sworn eternal revenge; you shall be my first victim.’

“The child still struggled and loaded me with epithets which carried despair to my heart; I grasped his throat to silence him, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet.

“I gazed on my victim, and my heart swelled with exultation and hellish triumph; clapping my hands, I exclaimed, ‘I too can create desolation; my enemy is not invulnerable; this death will carry despair to him, and a thousand other miseries shall torment and destroy him.’

“As I fixed my eyes on the child, I saw something glittering on his breast. I took it; it was a portrait of a most lovely woman. In spite of my malignity, it softened and attracted me. For a few moments I gazed with delight on her dark eyes, fringed by deep lashes, and her lovely lips; but presently my rage returned; I remembered that I was for ever deprived of the delights that such beautiful creatures could bestow and that she whose resemblance I contemplated would, in regarding me, have changed that air of divine benignity to one expressive of disgust and affright.

“Can you wonder that such thoughts transported me with rage? I only wonder that at that moment, instead of venting my sensations in exclamations and agony, I did not rush among mankind and perish in the attempt to destroy them.

“While I was overcome by these feelings, I left the spot where I had committed the murder, and seeking a more secluded hiding-place, I entered a barn which had appeared to me to be empty. A woman was sleeping on some straw; she was young, not indeed so beautiful as her whose portrait I held, but of an agreeable aspect and blooming in the loveliness of youth and health. Here, I thought, is one of those whose joy-imparting smiles are bestowed on all but me. And then I bent over her and whispered, ‘Awake, fairest, thy lover is near—he who would give his life but to obtain one look of affection from thine eyes; my beloved, awake!’

“The sleeper stirred; a thrill of terror ran through me. Should she indeed awake, and see me, and curse me, and denounce the murderer? Thus would she assuredly act if her darkened eyes opened and she beheld me. The thought was madness; it stirred the fiend within me—not I, but she, shall suffer; the murder I have committed because I am for ever robbed of all that she could give me, she shall atone. The crime had its source in her; be hers the punishment! Thanks to the lessons of Felix and the sanguinary laws of man, I had learned now to work mischief. I bent over her and placed the portrait securely in one of the folds of her dress. She moved again, and I fled.

“For some days I haunted the spot where these scenes had taken place, sometimes wishing to see you, sometimes resolved to quit the world and its miseries for ever. At length I wandered towards these mountains, and have ranged through their immense recesses, consumed by a burning passion which you alone can gratify. We may not part until you have promised to comply with my requisition. I am alone and miserable; man will not associate with me; but one as deformed and horrible as myself would not deny herself to me. My companion must be of the same species and have the same defects. This being you must create.”
b2: “Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I go on living? Why, at that very moment, did I not put out the spark of life that you had so carelessly given me? I don’t know; despair had not yet taken hold of me; what I felt was rage and a thirst for revenge. I would gladly have destroyed the cottage and the people in it and feasted on their screams and suffering.

“When night came, I left my shelter and wandered in the forest; and now, no longer held back by the fear of being seen, I let out my anguish in terrible howls. I was like a wild animal that has broken out of a trap, smashing everything that stood in my way and racing through the forest as swiftly as a deer. Oh, what a wretched night I spent! The cold stars seemed to mock me, and the bare trees waved their branches above me; now and then the sweet song of a bird broke the silence all around. Everyone except me was resting or happy; I, like Satan himself, carried a hell inside me, and finding that no one felt for me, I wanted to tear up the trees, spread chaos and destruction all around me, and then sit down and enjoy the ruins.

“But such a wild outburst of feeling could not last; I grew exhausted from so much physical effort and sank down on the damp grass, sick and powerless with despair. Among the millions of people on earth there was not one who would pity or help me; so why should I feel kindness towards my enemies? No; from that moment I declared eternal war on the human race, and above all on the one who had made me and sent me out into this unbearable misery.
“The sun rose; I heard people’s voices and knew that I could not go back to my shelter that day. So I hid in some thick bushes, deciding to spend the next few hours thinking about my situation.

“The pleasant sunshine and the fresh daytime air brought back a certain calm, and when I thought about what had happened at the cottage, I could not help feeling that I had jumped to conclusions too quickly. I had certainly acted unwisely. It was clear that my conversation had won the father over to my side, and I had been foolish to show myself to his horrified children. I should have got old De Lacey used to me first, and then gradually revealed myself to the rest of the family once they had been prepared for my arrival. But I did not believe my mistakes could never be put right, and after thinking it over for a long time, I decided to go back to the cottage, find the old man, and win him over with my arguments.

“These thoughts calmed me, and in the afternoon I fell into a deep sleep; but my blood was too feverish to let peaceful dreams visit me. The terrible scene of the day before kept replaying in front of my eyes: the women were running away and the furious Felix was dragging me away from his father’s feet. I woke up exhausted, and seeing that it was already night, I crept out of my hiding place and went to look for food.

“When I had satisfied my hunger, I made my way along the familiar path that led to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I crept into my shed and waited silently for the usual hour when the family got up. That hour passed, the sun climbed high in the sky, but the cottagers did not appear. I shook violently, fearing some terrible disaster. Inside the cottage it was dark, and I heard no movement; I cannot describe the agony of that suspense.

“Soon two peasants walked by, but they stopped near the cottage and began to talk, waving their arms wildly; I did not understand what they said, because they spoke the local language, which was different from that of my protectors. Shortly afterwards, however, Felix came up with another man; I was surprised, as I knew he had not left the cottage that morning, and I waited anxiously to learn from what he said the meaning of these strange events.

“‘Do you realise,’ his companion said to him, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and lose the crops from your garden? I don’t want to take unfair advantage of you, so I beg you to take a few days to think over your decision.’

“‘It is completely pointless,’ Felix replied; ‘we can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of the terrible event I have told you about. My wife and my sister will never get over their horror. I beg you not to argue with me any more. Take back your property and let me get away from this place.’
“Felix was shaking violently as he said this. He and his companion went into the cottage, stayed there for a few minutes, and then left. I never saw any of the De Lacey family again.

“I stayed in my shed for the rest of the day in a state of complete, numb despair. My protectors had gone and had broken the only link that tied me to the world. For the first time, feelings of revenge and hatred filled my heart, and I did not try to control them; letting myself be carried away by the current, I turned my thoughts to harm and death. When I thought of my friends – of De Lacey’s gentle voice, Agatha’s kind eyes and the exquisite beauty of the Arabian girl – these thoughts faded, and a flood of tears calmed me a little.

But when I remembered again that they had rejected and abandoned me, my anger came back, a furious anger, and since I could not hurt anything human, I turned my rage on lifeless objects. As night came on, I piled all kinds of things that would burn around the cottage, and after destroying every trace of planting in the garden, I forced myself to wait until the moon had set before beginning my work.

“As the night went on, a fierce wind rose from the woods and quickly scattered the clouds that had been lingering in the sky; the gale rushed along like a mighty avalanche and stirred in me a kind of madness that swept away all limits of reason and thought. I set fire to a dry branch and danced furiously around the doomed cottage, my eyes still fixed on the western horizon, whose edge the moon was almost touching. At last part of its disc disappeared, and I waved my torch; the moon sank, and with a loud scream I set fire to the straw, heather and bushes I had gathered. The wind fanned the fire, and the cottage was quickly swallowed up by the flames, which clung to it and licked it with their forked, destructive tongues. “As soon as I was sure that nothing could save any part of the house, I left the scene and took refuge in the woods.

“And now, with the whole world in front of me, where should I go? I decided to flee far away from the place of my misfortunes; but for me, hated and despised as I was, every country was bound to be equally terrible. At last I thought of you. I had learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator; and who could I turn to with more right than the one who had given me life? Geography had been among the lessons Felix had given Safie, and from them I had learned where the different countries of the world lay in relation to one another. You had mentioned Geneva as your home town, and I decided to make my way there.

“But how was I to find the way? I knew that I had to travel south-west to reach my destination, but the sun was my only guide. I did not know the names of the towns I would pass through, nor could I ask a single human being for directions; but I did not give up hope. Only from you could I hope for help, although I felt nothing towards you but hatred. Unfeeling, heartless creator! You had given me senses and passions and then thrown me out into the world as an object of scorn and horror for mankind. But you were the only one I had any right to ask for pity and justice, and I resolved to seek from you the justice I had tried in vain to obtain from every other creature in human shape.

“My journey was long and my sufferings were intense. It was late autumn when I left the area where I had lived for so long. I travelled only at night, afraid of meeting a human face. Nature withered around me and the sun lost its heat; rain and snow poured down on me; great rivers froze; the ground was hard, cold and bare, and I found no shelter. Oh, earth! How often did I call down curses on the one who had brought me into being! My gentle nature had disappeared, and everything inside me had turned to bitterness.

The closer I came to where you lived, the more fiercely I felt the desire for revenge burning in my heart. Snow fell and the waters froze, but I did not rest. Now and then something happened to point me in the right direction, and I had a map of the country; but I often strayed far from my route. My tormented feelings gave me no rest; nothing happened that my rage and misery could not feed on; but one event, which took place when I reached the borders of Switzerland, when the sun was warm again and the earth was turning green once more, confirmed in a particular way the bitterness and horror of my feelings.

“I usually rested during the day and travelled only when darkness hid me from human eyes. One morning, however, finding that my path led through a thick forest, I dared to carry on after sunrise; the day, one of the first days of spring, cheered even me with its lovely sunshine and mild, sweet air. I felt feelings of gentleness and joy, which had seemed dead for a long time, come back to life inside me. Half surprised by how new these sensations were, I let myself be carried away by them, and forgetting my loneliness and ugliness, I dared to be happy. Gentle tears ran down my cheeks again, and I even lifted my wet eyes gratefully towards the blessed sun that gave me such joy.

“I went on winding along the forest paths until I came to its edge, which was bordered by a deep, fast-flowing river; many of the trees leaned their branches over it, now covered in fresh spring buds. Here I stopped, not quite sure which way to go, when I heard voices, which made me hide in the shade of a cypress tree. I had hardly hidden myself when a young girl came running towards the spot where I was concealed, laughing, as if she were playfully running away from someone. She ran on along the steep bank of the river, when suddenly her foot slipped and she fell into the fast-flowing water.

I rushed out of my hiding place and, with enormous effort against the force of the current, saved her and dragged her to the bank. She was unconscious, and I was trying everything I could to bring her round, when I was suddenly interrupted by a peasant, who was probably the person she had been playfully running from. When he saw me, he rushed at me, tore the girl out of my arms and hurried off into the depths of the forest. I quickly followed, hardly knowing why; but when the man saw me coming closer, he aimed the gun he was carrying at me and fired. I fell to the ground, and my attacker ran off even faster into the forest.

“So this was the reward for my kindness! I had saved a human being from death, and in return I was now writhing in the terrible pain of a wound that had shattered flesh and bone. The feelings of kindness and gentleness I had felt only a few moments earlier gave way to hellish rage and the grinding of teeth. Burning with pain, I swore eternal hatred and revenge against all mankind. But the agony of my wound overpowered me; my pulse stopped, and I fainted.

“For several weeks I lived a wretched life in the woods, trying to heal the wound I had received. The bullet had gone into my shoulder, and I did not know whether it had stayed there or passed right through; in any case I had no way of getting it out. My suffering was made even worse by the crushing sense of how unjust and ungrateful it was that it had been inflicted on me. Every day I vowed revenge – a deep and deadly revenge, the only kind that could make up for the outrages and anguish I had suffered.

“After some weeks my wound healed, and I went on with my journey. The hardships I endured could no longer be eased by the bright sun or the gentle spring breezes; all joy was only a mockery that insulted my lonely, miserable state and made me feel more painfully that I was not made to enjoy pleasure. “But my hardships were now coming to an end, and two months later I reached the outskirts of Geneva.

“It was evening when I arrived, and I withdrew to a hiding place in the fields around the city to think about how I should approach you. I was weighed down by tiredness and hunger and far too unhappy to enjoy the soft evening breeze or the sight of the sun setting behind the magnificent Jura mountains.

“At this point a light sleep freed me from the pain of thinking, but it was disturbed by a beautiful child who came running into the hidden corner I had chosen, full of the playfulness of early childhood. Suddenly, as I gazed at him, I was struck by the idea that this little creature had no prejudices and had lived too short a time to have learned to be horrified by ugliness. If, then, I could take hold of him and bring him up as my companion and friend, I would not be so lonely on this crowded earth.

“Driven by this impulse, I grabbed the boy as he ran past and pulled him towards me. As soon as he saw my shape, he covered his eyes with his hands and let out a piercing scream; I pulled his hand forcefully away from his face and said, ‘Child, what does this mean? I don’t mean to hurt you; listen to me.’

“He struggled violently. ‘Let me go,’ he cried, ‘you monster! Ugly wretch! You want to eat me and tear me to pieces. You’re an ogre. Let me go, or I’ll tell my papa.’ “‘Boy, you will never see your father again; you must come with me.’ “‘Horrible monster! Let me go. My papa is a magistrate – he is Monsieur Frankenstein – he will punish you. You wouldn’t dare keep me.’ “‘Frankenstein! So you belong to my enemy – to the man I have sworn eternal revenge on; you will be my first victim.’

“The child kept struggling and shouted insults at me that filled my heart with despair; I seized him by the throat to silence him, and a moment later he lay dead at my feet. “I gazed at my victim, and my heart swelled with glee and hellish triumph; clapping my hands, I cried out, ‘I too can bring destruction; my enemy is not untouchable; this death will fill him with despair, and a thousand other miseries will torment and destroy him.’

“As I stared at the child, I saw something glittering on his chest. I took it; it was a portrait of a very beautiful woman. Despite my hatred, it softened me and drew me to it. For a few moments I gazed with delight at her dark eyes, framed by thick lashes, and her lovely lips; but soon my rage returned: I remembered that I was for ever shut out from the joys that such beautiful creatures could give, and that the woman whose likeness I was looking at would, on seeing me, have changed that expression of heavenly kindness into one of disgust and terror.

“Can you be surprised that such thoughts filled me with rage? I am only surprised that at that moment, instead of letting out my feelings in cries and agony, I did not rush among mankind and die trying to destroy them.

“While I was still overwhelmed by these feelings, I left the place where I had committed the murder, and looking for a more hidden shelter, I went into a barn that seemed to be empty. A woman was asleep on some straw; she was young – not, it is true, as beautiful as the woman whose portrait I was holding, but pleasant to look at and glowing with the beauty of youth and health. Here, I thought, is one of those whose joyful smiles are given to everyone except me. And then I bent over her and whispered, ‘Wake up, loveliest one, your lover is near – he who would give his life just for one loving look from your eyes; my beloved, wake up!’

“The sleeping woman stirred; a shiver of terror ran through me. What if she really did wake up, and see me, and curse me, and expose the murderer? That is certainly what she would do if her sleepy eyes opened and she saw me. The thought was madness; it awoke the devil inside me – not I, but she, would suffer; she would pay for the murder I had committed because I was for ever robbed of everything she could give me. The crime had its source in her; let the punishment be hers! Thanks to Felix’s lessons and the bloodthirsty laws of men, I had now learned how to do harm. I bent over her and slipped the portrait safely into one of the folds of her dress. She moved again, and I ran away.

“For some days I lingered around the place where all this had happened, sometimes wanting to see you, sometimes determined to leave the world and its miseries for ever. In the end I wandered towards these mountains and have roamed through their vast hollows, consumed by a burning passion that only you can satisfy. We must not part until you have promised to do what I ask. I am alone and miserable; humans will have nothing to do with me; but a woman as deformed and horrible as I am would not reject me. My companion must be of the same kind as me and have the same defects. You must create this being.”
b1: “Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I stay alive? Why didn’t I end the life that you gave me so carelessly, right at that moment? I don’t know. “When night came, I left my shelter and wandered in the forest. Now I was not afraid of being seen, so I let out my pain in terrible howls. I was like a wild animal that has escaped from a trap. I broke everything in my way and ran through the forest as fast as a deer. Oh, what a terrible night it was! The cold stars seemed to laugh at me, and the bare trees moved their branches above me. Sometimes a bird sang sweetly in the silence. Everyone except me was resting or happy. I was like the devil – I carried hell inside me. Nobody cared about me, so I wanted to pull up the trees, destroy everything around me, and then sit down and enjoy the ruins.

“But I could not go on like this for long. I became very tired and fell on the wet grass, weak and hopeless. Among all the millions of people in the world, there was not one who would feel sorry for me or help me. So why should I be kind to my enemies? No! From that moment I declared war for ever on all people, and most of all on the man who had made me and sent me into this terrible life.
“The sun came up. I heard people’s voices and knew that I could not go back to my shelter that day. So I hid in some thick bushes and decided to spend the next hours thinking about my situation.

“The warm sun and the fresh air made me a little calmer. When I thought about what had happened at the cottage, I began to believe that I had decided things too quickly. I had certainly acted without thinking. It was clear that the father liked me after our conversation. It was stupid of me to show myself to his children, who were terrified. I should have let old De Lacey get used to me first. Then, little by little, I could have shown myself to the rest of the family, when they were ready. But I did not think my mistakes were impossible to correct. After thinking for a long time, I decided to go back to the cottage, find the old man and persuade him to be my friend.

“These thoughts calmed me, and in the afternoon I fell into a deep sleep. But I was hot and feverish, and I did not have peaceful dreams. I kept seeing the terrible scene of the day before: the women were running away and the angry Felix was pulling me away from his father’s feet. I woke up very tired. It was already night, so I crept out of my hiding place and went to look for food.

“When I had eaten, I walked along the path that I knew so well to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I crept into my little shed and waited silently for the time when the family usually got up. That time passed, and the sun rose high in the sky, but nobody came out of the cottage. I was shaking all over. I was afraid that something terrible had happened. It was dark inside the cottage, and I heard no sound. I cannot describe how painful this waiting was.

“Then two country men walked past. They stopped near the cottage and started talking, waving their arms angrily. I did not understand them, because they spoke the local language, not the language of my friends. Soon after that, Felix came with another man. I was surprised, because I knew he had not left the cottage that morning. I waited nervously to understand from their conversation what was happening.

“‘Do you understand,’ the other man said to him, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and lose all the vegetables in your garden? I don’t want to take advantage of you, so please take a few days to think about your decision.’

“‘There’s no point,’ Felix answered; ‘we can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in great danger because of the terrible thing that happened, as I told you. My wife and my sister will never forget their fear. Please don’t try to change my mind. Take back your house and let me leave this place.’
“Felix was shaking badly as he said this. He and the other man went into the cottage. They stayed there for a few minutes and then left. I never saw anyone from the De Lacey family again.

“I stayed in my shed for the rest of the day in complete, empty despair. My friends had left, and they had broken my only connection with the world. For the first time, my heart was full of hatred and a wish for revenge. I did not try to stop these feelings. I let them carry me away, and I began to think about hurting and killing. When I thought about my friends – De Lacey’s soft voice, Agatha’s kind eyes and the beautiful Arabian girl – these thoughts went away, and I cried, which calmed me a little.

But then I remembered again that they had rejected me and left me, and my anger came back, even stronger. I could not hurt any people, so I turned my anger on things. When it got dark, I put lots of things that could burn around the cottage. I destroyed everything that was growing in the garden, and then I waited impatiently for the moon to go down before I started.

“Later that night, a strong wind came from the woods and quickly blew away the clouds in the sky. The wind rushed along like an avalanche, and it made me feel a kind of madness; I could no longer think clearly. I lit a dry branch and danced wildly around the cottage. All the time I watched the western sky, where the moon was almost touching the horizon. At last part of the moon disappeared, and I waved my burning branch. When the moon went down, I gave a loud scream and set fire to the straw and bushes I had collected. The wind made the fire bigger, and soon the cottage was covered in flames, which held on to it and licked it like long, hungry tongues. “When I was sure that nobody could save any part of the house, I left and hid in the woods.

“And now the whole world was in front of me. Where should I go? I decided to go far away from the place where I had been so unhappy. But everyone hated me, so every country would be just as terrible for me. At last I thought of you. I had learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator. Who could I ask for help, if not the man who had given me life? Felix had taught Safie geography, and from those lessons I had learned where the different countries of the world were. You had written that Geneva was your home town, so I decided to go there.

“But how could I find the way? I knew that I had to go south-west, but I only had the sun to guide me. I did not know the names of the towns on the way, and I could not ask anyone. But I did not lose hope. You were the only one who could help me, although I felt nothing for you but hatred. Cruel, heartless creator! You gave me feelings and desires, and then you threw me out into the world, where all people hated me and were afraid of me. But you were the only one I could ask for pity and help. I decided to ask you for the justice that no other human being had given me.

“My journey was long, and I suffered terribly. It was late autumn when I left the place where I had lived for so long. I travelled only at night, because I was afraid of meeting people. Around me, nature was dying and the sun was cold. It rained and snowed; big rivers froze; the ground was hard, cold and bare, and I found no shelter. Oh, earth! How often I cursed the man who had made me! I was not gentle any more; I was full of bitterness.

The nearer I came to your home, the stronger my wish for revenge became. Snow fell and the rivers froze, but I did not stop. Sometimes things I saw showed me the way, and I had a map of the country, but I often got lost. My pain never left me, and everything that happened only made my anger and misery stronger. But something that happened when I reached the border of Switzerland, when the sun was warm again and the fields were turning green, made my feelings even more bitter and terrible.

“I usually rested during the day and travelled only when it was dark and people could not see me. But one morning my path went through a thick forest, so I decided to go on after the sun came up. It was one of the first days of spring, and even I felt happier because of the lovely sunshine and the soft, warm air. Feelings of gentleness and pleasure, which I thought were dead, came back to life in me. I was surprised by these new feelings, and I let them carry me away. I forgot that I was alone and ugly, and I dared to be happy. Soft tears ran down my face again, and I looked up gratefully at the wonderful sun that gave me so much joy.

“I went on along the forest paths until I came to the edge of the forest. A deep, fast river ran along it, and many trees hung their branches over the water, with new spring leaves on them. I stopped there, because I did not know which way to go. Then I heard voices, so I hid in the shadow of a cypress tree. A moment later, a young girl came running towards the place where I was hiding. She was laughing, as if she was running away from someone in a game. She ran along the steep bank of the river, and suddenly her foot slipped and she fell into the fast water.

I ran out of my hiding place. The current was very strong, but with great effort I saved her and pulled her out onto the bank. She was unconscious, and I was trying everything to wake her up when a country man suddenly came. He was probably the person she had been running away from in the game. When he saw me, he ran at me, pulled the girl out of my arms and hurried away into the forest. I quickly followed him, though I did not really know why. But when the man saw me coming, he pointed his gun at me and fired. I fell to the ground, and the man ran away into the forest even faster.

“So this was my reward for being kind! I had saved a human being from death, and now, in return, I was twisting in terrible pain from a wound that had broken my flesh and bone. A few moments before, I had felt kind and gentle. Now I felt a terrible rage, and I ground my teeth. Burning with pain, I promised to hate all people and to take revenge on them for ever. But the pain of my wound was too strong; my heart seemed to stop, and I fainted.

“For some weeks I lived a miserable life in the woods and tried to cure my wound. The bullet had gone into my shoulder, and I did not know if it was still there or had gone right through. Anyway, I had no way of taking it out. My pain was even worse because I knew how unfair and ungrateful it was. Every day I promised myself revenge – a deep and deadly revenge, the only thing that could pay for all the wrongs and pain I had suffered.

“After some weeks my wound got better, and I continued my journey. The bright sun and the soft spring wind could not make my hard journey easier now. All joy seemed to laugh at my lonely life and made me feel even more strongly that I was not made to be happy. “But my journey was nearly over, and two months later I arrived near Geneva.

“It was evening when I arrived. I hid in the fields around the city to think about how I should talk to you. I was very tired and hungry, and much too unhappy to enjoy the soft evening wind or the sunset behind the great Jura mountains.

“Then I fell into a light sleep, which took away the pain of my thoughts for a while. But a beautiful child woke me when he came running happily into my hiding place, playing like little children do. As I looked at him, I suddenly had an idea. This little boy was too young to judge people. He had not lived long enough to learn to be afraid of ugliness. If I could take him and teach him to be my companion and friend, I would not be so lonely in this world full of people.

“So, as the boy ran past, I caught him and pulled him towards me. As soon as he saw me, he covered his eyes with his hands and screamed loudly. I pulled his hand away from his face and said, ‘Child, why are you doing this? I won’t hurt you. Listen to me.’

“He fought hard to get free. ‘Let me go,’ he cried, ‘you monster! Ugly thing! You want to eat me and tear me into pieces. You’re an ogre. Let me go, or I’ll tell my papa.’ “‘Boy, you will never see your father again. You must come with me.’ “‘Horrible monster! Let me go. My papa is an important man – he is Monsieur Frankenstein – he will punish you. You can’t keep me here.’ “‘Frankenstein! So you belong to my enemy – the man I have promised to take revenge on for ever. You will be my first victim.’

“The child went on fighting and calling me terrible names, and his words filled my heart with despair. I took him by the throat to make him quiet, and a moment later he lay dead at my feet. “I looked at my victim, and my heart was full of wild, evil joy. I clapped my hands and shouted, ‘I can destroy things too! My enemy can be hurt. This death will bring him despair, and a thousand other troubles will torture him and destroy him.’

“As I looked at the child, I saw something shining on his chest. I took it. It was a small picture of a very beautiful woman. Although I was full of hate, the picture made me softer and I liked it. For a few moments I looked happily at her dark eyes, with their long lashes, and her lovely lips. But soon my anger came back. I remembered that I could never have the joy that such beautiful women can give. And I knew that if this woman saw me, her kind, gentle face would change and show only disgust and fear.
“Are you surprised that these thoughts made me so angry? I am only surprised that, instead of just crying out in pain, I did not run at people and die trying to destroy them.

“While I was still full of these feelings, I left the place where I had killed the boy. I looked for a better hiding place and went into a barn that seemed empty. A woman was sleeping on some straw. She was young – not as beautiful as the woman in the picture I was holding, but pretty, and she looked young and healthy. I thought, ‘Here is one of those people who smile happily at everyone except me.’ Then I bent over her and whispered, ‘Wake up, my beautiful one, your lover is here. He would give his life for one loving look from your eyes. My love, wake up!’

“The sleeping woman moved, and I felt a wave of fear. What if she woke up, saw me, cursed me and told everyone about the murderer? She would certainly do that if she opened her eyes and saw me. This thought made me mad; it woke the devil inside me. Not I, but she, would suffer! I had killed because I could never have what she could give me – so she would pay for the murder. She was the reason for the crime, so she should have the punishment! Thanks to Felix’s lessons and the cruel laws of people, I now knew how to do harm. I bent over her and put the picture carefully in one of the folds of her dress. She moved again, and I ran away.

“For some days I stayed near the place where all this had happened. Sometimes I wanted to see you; sometimes I wanted to leave the world and its pain for ever. At last I came to these mountains, and I have wandered through them, burning with a desire that only you can satisfy. We will not part until you promise to do what I ask. I am alone and unhappy. People will not be with me. But a woman who is as ugly and horrible as I am would not say no to me. My companion must be the same kind of creature as me, with the same faults. You must make this creature for me.”
a2: “Oh, creator, I hate you! Why did I not die at that moment? You gave me life, but you did not care about me. I did not feel sad yet. I only felt very angry, and I wanted revenge. I wanted to destroy the cottage and the people in it. I wanted to hear them scream.

“At night I left my hiding place and walked in the forest. Now I was not afraid of people, so I cried out loudly in pain, like an animal. I ran through the forest very fast, like a wild animal, and I broke everything in my way. It was a terrible night! The cold stars shone above me, and the trees moved in the wind. Sometimes a bird sang. Everyone was resting or happy, but not me. I felt like the devil. I wanted to pull up the trees and destroy everything around me.

“But after some time I was very tired. I fell down on the wet grass. There were millions of people in the world, but nobody wanted to help me. So why should I be kind to them? From that moment, I was at war with all people – and most of all with you, because you made me.
“The sun came up. I heard people’s voices, so I could not go back to my hiding place. I hid in some bushes and thought about my situation.

“The sun and the fresh air made me calmer. I thought about the cottage again, and I understood that I was too quick. It was my mistake. The old father liked me, but I showed myself to his children, and they were afraid. I should wait and be friends with old De Lacey first. Then he could tell his family about me. I decided to go back and talk to the old man again.

“After that I felt calmer, and in the afternoon I slept. But I had bad dreams. I saw the terrible scene again: the women were running away, and angry Felix was pulling me away from his father. When I woke up, it was night. I went out and looked for food.

“After I ate, I walked to the cottage. Everything was quiet. I went into my shed and waited for the family to get up. But nobody came out, and the sun went up high in the sky. I was very afraid. It was dark in the cottage, and I heard nothing.

“Then two men walked past the cottage. They stopped and talked and moved their arms a lot. I did not understand them, because they spoke a different language. Soon Felix came with another man. I was surprised, and I listened carefully.
“The man said to Felix, ‘You must pay three months’ money for the house, and you will lose your vegetables. Please think about it for a few days.’

“‘No,’ said Felix; ‘we can never live here again. My father is in danger because of the terrible thing that happened. My wife and my sister are still very afraid. Please take your house back. I want to leave this place.’
“Felix was shaking. The two men went into the cottage for a few minutes, and then they left. I never saw the De Lacey family again.

“I stayed in my shed all day. I felt terrible. My friends were gone. They were the only people in my life. For the first time, I felt hate, and I wanted to hurt people. Then I thought about De Lacey’s kind voice, Agatha’s gentle eyes and beautiful Safie, and I cried.

But then I remembered that they left me, and I was angry again. I could not hurt people, so I decided to hurt things. In the evening I put a lot of dry wood and straw around the cottage. I destroyed the garden, and I waited for the moon to go down.

“Later a strong wind came and blew the clouds away. The wind made me feel crazy. I lit a dry branch and danced around the cottage. I watched the moon in the west. When the moon went down, I screamed and set fire to the straw and the bushes. The wind helped the fire, and soon the cottage was burning. “When I was sure that nobody could save the house, I ran into the woods.

“Now I could go anywhere in the world. But where? People hated me in every country. Then I thought of you. I knew from your papers that you were my father, my creator. You gave me life, so you should help me! Felix taught Safie about the countries of the world, and I learned too. You wrote that you came from Geneva, so I decided to go there.

“But how could I find the way? I knew that I had to go south-west, and I followed the sun. I did not know the names of the towns, and I could not ask people. Only you could help me, but I hated you. You were a cruel creator! You gave me feelings, and then you left me alone in a world where everyone hated me. But you had to help me. Nobody else would.

“It was a long, hard journey. I left in late autumn. I only walked at night, because I did not want to meet people. It was cold. It rained and snowed, and the rivers froze. I had no house to sleep in. Oh, how often I cursed you! I was not gentle any more. I was bitter and angry.

The nearer I came to you, the more I wanted revenge. It snowed, but I did not stop. I had a map, but I often got lost. I was always angry and unhappy. And when I came to Switzerland in the spring, something happened that made me even angrier.

“I usually slept in the day and walked at night. But one morning I was in a big forest, so I walked on in the daytime. It was one of the first days of spring. The sun was warm, and the air was soft. For the first time in a long time, I felt kind and happy. I forgot that I was alone and ugly. I cried a little, and I thanked the sun for this joy.

“I came to the end of the forest. There was a deep, fast river there. Then I heard voices, and I hid behind a tree. A young girl ran towards me. She was laughing and playing a game. She ran near the river, and suddenly she fell into the water.

I ran out and jumped into the river. It was very hard, but I saved her and pulled her out. She was not moving, and I tried to help her. Then a man came. He was her friend in the game. He saw me, took the girl from my arms and ran into the forest. I followed him. But he turned, pointed his gun at me and shot me. I fell down, and the man ran away.

“This was my thank-you for being kind! I saved a girl’s life, and now I was in terrible pain. A few minutes before, I was kind and gentle. Now I was full of hate. I promised to hate all people for ever and to take revenge on them. Then the pain was too strong, and I fainted.

“For some weeks I lived in the woods and tried to make my wound better. The bullet was in my shoulder, and I could not take it out. It was so unfair! This made my pain worse. Every day I promised myself a terrible revenge.
“After some weeks my wound was better, and I walked on. The sun and the spring wind did not make me happy now. I knew that I could never be happy. “Two months later, I arrived near Geneva.
“It was evening. I hid in the fields near the city. I wanted to think about how to speak to you. I was tired, hungry and very unhappy.

“I slept a little. Then a beautiful little boy ran into my hiding place. He was playing. I looked at him, and I had an idea. He was very young. Maybe he was not afraid of ugly people yet. I could take him and teach him. He could be my friend, and I would not be alone.
“When the boy ran past me, I caught him. He saw me, covered his eyes and screamed. I took his hand from his face and said, ‘Child, why are you screaming? I will not hurt you. Listen to me.’

“The boy fought me. ‘Let me go!’ he cried. ‘You are a monster! You want to eat me! Let me go, or I will tell my papa!’ “‘You will never see your father again. You must come with me.’ “‘Let me go, you ugly monster! My papa is Mr Frankenstein, and he will punish you!’ “‘Frankenstein! So your family is my enemy’s family. You will be my first victim.’

“The boy fought and shouted bad names at me. I put my hands on his throat to stop him. A moment later, he was dead. “I looked at him, and I was happy, like a devil. I clapped my hands. I cried, ‘I can destroy too! This will hurt my enemy, and I will bring him many more troubles!’

“Then I saw something shining on the boy’s chest. It was a small picture of a beautiful woman. I liked it, and I felt softer for a moment. I looked at her dark eyes and her lovely face. But then I was angry again. A beautiful woman like this could never love me. If she saw me, she would be afraid and disgusted.
“Are you surprised that I was so angry? I am only surprised that I did not attack all the people in the world then.

“I left the place of the murder and looked for a better hiding place. I went into a barn. I thought it was empty. But a young woman was sleeping there on some straw. She was pretty and healthy. I thought, ‘She smiles at everyone, but never at me.’ I bent over her and whispered, ‘Wake up, my beautiful love!’

“The woman moved, and I was afraid. What if she woke up and saw me? She would scream and tell everyone about the murderer. Then a terrible idea came to me. She, not I, would be punished for the murder! Felix’s lessons and the cruel laws of people taught me how to do this. I put the picture in her dress. She moved again, and I ran away.

“For some days I stayed near that place. Sometimes I wanted to see you, and sometimes I wanted to die. Then I came to these mountains. I want something very much, and only you can give it to me. We will not leave this place until you promise to help me. I am alone and unhappy. People will not be my friends. But a woman as ugly as me will not say no to me. You must make a woman like me.”

o.en: “Cursed, cursed creator!
Why did I live?
Why, in that instant, did I not extinguish the spark of existence which you had so wantonly bestowed?
o.ru: Почему в тот же миг я не погасил искру жизни, которую ты так легкомысленно мне даровал?

o.en: I know not; despair had not yet taken possession of me; my feelings were those of rage and revenge.
o.ru: Не знаю; отчаяние ещё не овладело мною; я испытывал лишь ярость и жажду мести.

o.en: I could with pleasure have destroyed the cottage and its inhabitants and have glutted myself with their shrieks and misery.
o.ru: Я с наслаждением уничтожил бы хижину и её обитателей и упился бы их воплями и страданиями.

o.en: “When night came I quitted my retreat and wandered in the wood; and now, no longer restrained by the fear of discovery, I gave vent to my anguish in fearful howlings.
o.ru: Когда наступила ночь, я покинул своё убежище и бродил по лесу; и теперь, уже не сдерживаемый страхом быть обнаруженным, я изливал свою муку в страшном вое.

o.en: I was like a wild beast that had broken the toils, destroying the objects that obstructed me and ranging through the wood with a stag-like swiftness.
o.ru: Я был подобен дикому зверю, разорвавшему сети: я крушил всё, что стояло у меня на пути, и носился по лесу с быстротой оленя.

o.en: Oh!
What a miserable night I passed!
The cold stars shone in mockery, and the bare trees waved their branches above me; now and then the sweet voice of a bird burst forth amidst the universal stillness.
o.ru: Холодные звёзды светили словно в насмешку, голые деревья качали надо мной ветвями; время от времени среди всеобщей тишины раздавался нежный голос птицы.

o.en: All, save I, were at rest or in enjoyment; I, like the arch-fiend, bore a hell within me, and finding myself unsympathised with, wished to tear up the trees, spread havoc and destruction around me, and then to have sat down and enjoyed the ruin.
o.ru: Все, кроме меня, отдыхали или радовались; я же, подобно Сатане, носил в себе ад и, не находя ни в ком сочувствия, желал вырывать деревья с корнем, сеять вокруг опустошение и разрушение, а потом сесть и любоваться развалинами.

o.en: “But this was a luxury of sensation that could not endure; I became fatigued with excess of bodily exertion and sank on the damp grass in the sick impotence of despair.
o.ru: Но это было наслаждение чувством, которое не могло длиться долго; я выбился из сил от чрезмерного телесного напряжения и опустился на сырую траву в болезненном бессилии отчаяния.

o.en: There was none among the myriads of men that existed who would pity or assist me; and should I feel kindness towards my enemies?
o.ru: Среди мириад живущих людей не было ни одного, кто пожалел бы меня или помог мне; так должен ли я испытывать доброту к своим врагам?

o.en: No; from that moment I declared everlasting war against the species, and more than all, against him who had formed me and sent me forth to this insupportable misery.
o.ru: Нет; с той минуты я объявил вечную войну всему роду людскому и прежде всего тому, кто создал меня и обрёк на эти невыносимые страдания.

o.en: “The sun rose; I heard the voices of men and knew that it was impossible to return to my retreat during that day.
o.ru: Взошло солнце; я услышал голоса людей и понял, что в этот день мне невозможно вернуться в своё убежище.

o.en: Accordingly I hid myself in some thick underwood, determining to devote the ensuing hours to reflection on my situation.
o.ru: Поэтому я спрятался в густом подлеске, решив посвятить ближайшие часы размышлениям о своём положении.

o.en: “The pleasant sunshine and the pure air of day restored me to some degree of tranquillity; and when I considered what had passed at the cottage, I could not help believing that I had been too hasty in my conclusions.
o.ru: Приятное солнце и чистый дневной воздух в какой-то мере вернули мне спокойствие; и, обдумав то, что произошло в хижине, я не мог не прийти к мысли, что слишком поспешил с выводами.

o.en: I had certainly acted imprudently.
It was apparent that my conversation had interested the father in my behalf, and I was a fool in having exposed my person to the horror of his children.
o.ru: Было очевидно, что мой разговор расположил отца в мою пользу, и я глупо поступил, показавшись на глаза его детям, которые пришли в ужас.

o.en: I ought to have familiarised the old De Lacey to me, and by degrees to have discovered myself to the rest of his family, when they should have been prepared for my approach.
o.ru: Мне следовало сначала приучить к себе старого Де Лэси, а затем постепенно открыться остальным членам семьи, когда они были бы подготовлены к моему появлению.

o.en: But I did not believe my errors to be irretrievable, and after much consideration I resolved to return to the cottage, seek the old man, and by my representations win him to my party.
o.ru: Но я не считал свои ошибки непоправимыми и, долго поразмыслив, решил вернуться к хижине, найти старика и своими доводами склонить его на свою сторону.

o.en: “These thoughts calmed me, and in the afternoon I sank into a profound sleep; but the fever of my blood did not allow me to be visited by peaceful dreams.
o.ru: Эти мысли успокоили меня, и после полудня я погрузился в глубокий сон; но лихорадка в крови не позволила мирным сновидениям посетить меня.

o.en: The horrible scene of the preceding day was for ever acting before my eyes; the females were flying and the enraged Felix tearing me from his father’s feet.
o.ru: Ужасная сцена предыдущего дня неотступно разыгрывалась перед моими глазами: женщины убегали, а разъярённый Феликс отрывал меня от ног отца.

o.en: I awoke exhausted, and finding that it was already night, I crept forth from my hiding-place, and went in search of food.
o.ru: Я проснулся обессиленным и, увидев, что уже ночь, выполз из своего укрытия и отправился на поиски пищи.

o.en: “When my hunger was appeased, I directed my steps towards the well-known path that conducted to the cottage.
o.ru: Утолив голод, я направился по хорошо знакомой тропинке, которая вела к хижине.

o.en: All there was at peace.
I crept into my hovel and remained in silent expectation of the accustomed hour when the family arose.
o.ru: Я пробрался в свою лачугу и в молчании стал ждать привычного часа, когда семья вставала.

o.en: That hour passed, the sun mounted high in the heavens, but the cottagers did not appear.
o.ru: Этот час прошёл, солнце поднялось высоко в небе, но обитатели хижины не появлялись.

o.en: I trembled violently, apprehending some dreadful misfortune.
o.ru: Я сильно дрожал, предчувствуя какое-то страшное несчастье.

o.en: The inside of the cottage was dark, and I heard no motion; I cannot describe the agony of this suspense.
o.ru: Внутри хижины было темно, и я не слышал никакого движения; не могу описать мучительность этого ожидания.

o.en: “Presently two countrymen passed by, but pausing near the cottage, they entered into conversation, using violent gesticulations; but I did not understand what they said, as they spoke the language of the country, which differed from that of my protectors.
o.ru: Вскоре мимо прошли двое крестьян; остановившись возле хижины, они завели разговор, бурно жестикулируя; но я не понял, о чём они говорили, потому что они говорили на местном языке, который отличался от языка моих покровителей.

o.en: Soon after, however, Felix approached with another man; I was surprised, as I knew that he had not quitted the cottage that morning, and waited anxiously to discover from his discourse the meaning of these unusual appearances.
o.ru: Однако вскоре после этого подошёл Феликс с другим человеком; я удивился, так как знал, что утром он не выходил из хижины, и с тревогой ждал, чтобы из его слов узнать смысл этих необычных событий.

o.en: “‘Do you consider,’ said his companion to him, ‘that you will be obliged to pay three months’ rent and to lose the produce of your garden?
o.ru: „Подумали ли вы, — сказал ему спутник, — что вам придётся заплатить за три месяца аренды и потерять урожай с огорода?

o.en: I do not wish to take any unfair advantage, and I beg therefore that you will take some days to consider of your determination.’
o.ru: Я не хочу пользоваться вашим положением и потому прошу вас взять несколько дней, чтобы обдумать своё решение“.

o.en: “‘It is utterly useless,’ replied Felix; ‘we can never again inhabit your cottage.
o.ru: „Это совершенно бесполезно, — ответил Феликс, — мы больше никогда не сможем жить в вашем доме.

o.en: The life of my father is in the greatest danger, owing to the dreadful circumstance that I have related.
o.ru: Жизнь моего отца в величайшей опасности из-за того ужасного происшествия, о котором я рассказал.

o.en: My wife and my sister will never recover from their horror.
o.ru: Моя жена и моя сестра никогда не оправятся от пережитого ужаса.

o.en: I entreat you not to reason with me any more.
o.ru: Умоляю вас больше не уговаривать меня.

o.en: Take possession of your tenement and let me fly from this place.’
o.ru: Забирайте своё жильё и позвольте мне бежать из этого места“.

o.en: “Felix trembled violently as he said this.
He and his companion entered the cottage, in which they remained for a few minutes, and then departed.
o.ru: Он и его спутник вошли в хижину, пробыли там несколько минут и ушли.

o.en: I never saw any of the family of De Lacey more.
o.ru: Больше я никогда не видел никого из семьи Де Лэси.

o.en: “I continued for the remainder of the day in my hovel in a state of utter and stupid despair.
o.ru: Остаток дня я провёл в своей лачуге в состоянии полного, тупого отчаяния.

o.en: My protectors had departed and had broken the only link that held me to the world.
o.ru: Мои покровители уехали и порвали единственную нить, связывавшую меня с миром.

o.en: For the first time the feelings of revenge and hatred filled my bosom, and I did not strive to control them, but allowing myself to be borne away by the stream, I bent my mind towards injury and death.
o.ru: Впервые чувства мести и ненависти наполнили мою грудь, и я не пытался их обуздать; позволив потоку увлечь себя, я обратил свои мысли к злу и смерти.

o.en: When I thought of my friends, of the mild voice of De Lacey, the gentle eyes of Agatha, and the exquisite beauty of the Arabian, these thoughts vanished and a gush of tears somewhat soothed me.
o.ru: Когда я думал о своих друзьях, о кротком голосе Де Лэси, о ласковых глазах Агаты и о дивной красоте аравитянки, эти мысли исчезали, и поток слёз несколько успокаивал меня.

o.en: But again when I reflected that they had spurned and deserted me, anger returned, a rage of anger, and unable to injure anything human, I turned my fury towards inanimate objects.
o.ru: Но когда я снова вспоминал, что они отвергли и покинули меня, гнев возвращался — неистовый гнев, и, не имея возможности причинить вред ничему человеческому, я обратил свою ярость на неодушевлённые предметы.

o.en: As night advanced, I placed a variety of combustibles around the cottage, and after having destroyed every vestige of cultivation in the garden, I waited with forced impatience until the moon had sunk to commence my operations.
o.ru: Когда стемнело, я разложил вокруг хижины всё, что могло гореть, и, уничтожив в огороде все следы возделанной земли, с вынужденным нетерпением ждал, пока зайдёт луна, чтобы приступить к делу.

o.en: “As the night advanced, a fierce wind arose from the woods and quickly dispersed the clouds that had loitered in the heavens; the blast tore along like a mighty avalanche and produced a kind of insanity in my spirits that burst all bounds of reason and reflection.
o.ru: С наступлением ночи из лесу поднялся свирепый ветер и быстро разогнал облака, медлившие в небе; вихрь нёсся, как мощная лавина, и вызвал в моей душе какое-то безумие, сокрушившее все границы разума и рассудка.

o.en: I lighted the dry branch of a tree and danced with fury around the devoted cottage, my eyes still fixed on the western horizon, the edge of which the moon nearly touched.
o.ru: Я зажёг сухую ветку и в ярости плясал вокруг обречённой хижины, не сводя глаз с западного горизонта, края которого почти касалась луна.

o.en: A part of its orb was at length hid, and I waved my brand; it sank, and with a loud scream I fired the straw, and heath, and bushes, which I had collected.
o.ru: Наконец часть её диска скрылась, и я взмахнул своим факелом; она зашла, и с громким криком я поджёг солому, вереск и кусты, которые собрал.

o.en: The wind fanned the fire, and the cottage was quickly enveloped by the flames, which clung to it and licked it with their forked and destroying tongues.
o.ru: Ветер раздул огонь, и хижину быстро охватило пламя, которое вцепилось в неё и лизало её своими раздвоенными, губительными языками.

o.en: “As soon as I was convinced that no assistance could save any part of the habitation, I quitted the scene and sought for refuge in the woods.
o.ru: Убедившись, что никакая помощь уже не спасёт ни одной части жилища, я покинул это место и искал убежища в лесах.

o.en: “And now, with the world before me, whither should I bend my steps?
o.ru: И вот теперь, когда передо мною был весь мир, куда мне было направить свои шаги?

o.en: I resolved to fly far from the scene of my misfortunes; but to me, hated and despised, every country must be equally horrible.
o.ru: Я решил бежать подальше от места моих несчастий; но мне, ненавидимому и презираемому, любая страна должна была казаться одинаково ужасной.

o.en: At length the thought of you crossed my mind.
o.ru: Наконец мне пришла на ум мысль о тебе.

o.en: I learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator; and to whom could I apply with more fitness than to him who had given me life?
o.ru: Из твоих бумаг я узнал, что ты мой отец, мой создатель; а к кому мог я обратиться с большим правом, чем к тому, кто дал мне жизнь?

o.en: Among the lessons that Felix had bestowed upon Safie, geography had not been omitted; I had learned from these the relative situations of the different countries of the earth.
o.ru: Среди уроков, которые Феликс давал Сафии, не была забыта и география; из них я узнал, как расположены различные страны земли.

o.en: You had mentioned Geneva as the name of your native town, and towards this place I resolved to proceed.
o.ru: Ты упоминал Женеву как свой родной город, и туда я решил отправиться.

o.en: “But how was I to direct myself?
o.ru: Но как мне было найти дорогу?

o.en: I knew that I must travel in a southwesterly direction to reach my destination, but the sun was my only guide.
o.ru: Я знал, что для того, чтобы достичь цели, мне нужно идти на юго-запад, но единственным моим проводником было солнце.

o.en: I did not know the names of the towns that I was to pass through, nor could I ask information from a single human being; but I did not despair.
o.ru: Я не знал названий городов, через которые мне предстояло пройти, и не мог спросить дорогу ни у одного человека; но я не отчаивался.

o.en: From you only could I hope for succour, although towards you I felt no sentiment but that of hatred.
o.ru: Только от тебя мог я надеяться получить помощь, хотя не испытывал к тебе ничего, кроме ненависти.

o.en: Unfeeling, heartless creator!
You had endowed me with perceptions and passions and then cast me abroad an object for the scorn and horror of mankind.
o.ru: Ты наделил меня восприятием и страстями, а потом выбросил в мир — предметом презрения и ужаса для человечества.

o.en: But on you only had I any claim for pity and redress, and from you I determined to seek that justice which I vainly attempted to gain from any other being that wore the human form.
o.ru: Но только от тебя я вправе был требовать жалости и возмещения, и у тебя я решил искать той справедливости, которой тщетно пытался добиться от любого другого существа в человеческом облике.

o.en: “My travels were long and the sufferings I endured intense.
o.ru: Странствия мои были долгими, а страдания, которые я перенёс, — жестокими.

o.en: It was late in autumn when I quitted the district where I had so long resided.
o.ru: Стояла поздняя осень, когда я покинул край, где так долго жил.

o.en: I travelled only at night, fearful of encountering the visage of a human being.
o.ru: Я шёл только по ночам, боясь встретить человеческое лицо.

o.en: Nature decayed around me, and the sun became heatless; rain and snow poured around me; mighty rivers were frozen; the surface of the earth was hard and chill, and bare, and I found no shelter.
o.ru: Природа вокруг меня увядала, солнце перестало греть; лил дождь и валил снег; могучие реки замёрзли; земля была твёрдой, холодной и голой, и я не находил укрытия.

o.en: Oh, earth!
How often did I imprecate curses on the cause of my being!
o.ru: Как часто я призывал проклятия на виновника моего существования!

o.en: The mildness of my nature had fled, and all within me was turned to gall and bitterness.
o.ru: Кротость моей натуры исчезла, и всё во мне обратилось в желчь и горечь.

o.en: The nearer I approached to your habitation, the more deeply did I feel the spirit of revenge enkindled in my heart.
o.ru: Чем ближе я подходил к твоему жилищу, тем сильнее разгоралась в моём сердце жажда мести.

o.en: Snow fell, and the waters were hardened, but I rested not.
o.ru: Падал снег, воды сковал лёд, но я не отдыхал.

o.en: A few incidents now and then directed me, and I possessed a map of the country; but I often wandered wide from my path.
o.ru: Порой мне помогали найти дорогу какие-нибудь случайности, и у меня была карта страны; но я часто сбивался с пути.

o.en: The agony of my feelings allowed me no respite; no incident occurred from which my rage and misery could not extract its food; but a circumstance that happened when I arrived on the confines of Switzerland, when the sun had recovered its warmth and the earth again began to look green, confirmed in an especial manner the bitterness and horror of my feelings.
o.ru: Мучительность моих чувств не давала мне передышки; не было такого события, из которого мои ярость и горе не извлекли бы себе пищу; но одно происшествие, случившееся, когда я достиг границ Швейцарии, когда солнце вновь стало тёплым, а земля снова зазеленела, особенно укрепило горечь и ужас моих чувств.

o.en: “I generally rested during the day and travelled only when I was secured by night from the view of man.
o.ru: Обычно я отдыхал днём и шёл только тогда, когда ночь скрывала меня от глаз людей.

o.en: One morning, however, finding that my path lay through a deep wood, I ventured to continue my journey after the sun had risen; the day, which was one of the first of spring, cheered even me by the loveliness of its sunshine and the balminess of the air.
o.ru: Однако однажды утром, увидев, что мой путь лежит через густой лес, я осмелился продолжать путь и после восхода солнца; день, один из первых весенних дней, радовал даже меня прелестью солнечного света и благоуханием воздуха.

o.en: I felt emotions of gentleness and pleasure, that had long appeared dead, revive within me.
o.ru: Я почувствовал, как во мне оживают чувства нежности и радости, которые давно казались умершими.

o.en: Half surprised by the novelty of these sensations, I allowed myself to be borne away by them, and forgetting my solitude and deformity, dared to be happy.
o.ru: Полуудивлённый новизной этих ощущений, я позволил им увлечь себя и, забыв о своём одиночестве и уродстве, осмелился быть счастливым.

o.en: Soft tears again bedewed my cheeks, and I even raised my humid eyes with thankfulness towards the blessed sun, which bestowed such joy upon me.
o.ru: Тихие слёзы снова оросили мои щёки, и я даже поднял влажные глаза с благодарностью к благословенному солнцу, дарившему мне такую радость.

o.en: “I continued to wind among the paths of the wood, until I came to its boundary, which was skirted by a deep and rapid river, into which many of the trees bent their branches, now budding with the fresh spring.
o.ru: Я продолжал петлять по лесным тропинкам, пока не дошёл до опушки, вдоль которой текла глубокая и быстрая река; над ней склоняли ветви многие деревья, уже распускавшиеся по-весеннему.

o.en: Here I paused, not exactly knowing what path to pursue, when I heard the sound of voices, that induced me to conceal myself under the shade of a cypress.
o.ru: Здесь я остановился, не зная точно, какой дорогой идти, как вдруг услышал голоса, которые заставили меня спрятаться в тени кипариса.

o.en: I was scarcely hid when a young girl came running towards the spot where I was concealed, laughing, as if she ran from someone in sport.
o.ru: Едва я успел спрятаться, как к тому месту, где я скрывался, прибежала молоденькая девушка; она смеялась, словно убегала от кого-то в шутку.

o.en: She continued her course along the precipitous sides of the river, when suddenly her foot slipped, and she fell into the rapid stream.
o.ru: Она бежала дальше по крутому берегу реки, как вдруг поскользнулась и упала в быстрый поток.
