The duration of my absence was left to my own choice; a few months, or at most a year, was the period contemplated. One paternal kind precaution he had taken to ensure my having a companion. Without previously communicating with me, he had, in concert with Elizabeth, arranged that Clerval should join me at Strasburgh. This interfered with the solitude I coveted for the prosecution of my task; yet at the commencement of my journey the presence of my friend could in no way be an impediment, and truly I rejoiced that thus I should be saved many hours of lonely, maddening reflection. Nay, Henry might stand between me and the intrusion of my foe. If I were alone, would he not at times force his abhorred presence on me to remind me of my task or to contemplate its progress?

To England, therefore, I was bound, and it was understood that my union with Elizabeth should take place immediately on my return. My father’s age rendered him extremely averse to delay. For myself, there was one reward I promised myself from my detested toils—one consolation for my unparalleled sufferings; it was the prospect of that day when, enfranchised from my miserable slavery, I might claim Elizabeth and forget the past in my union with her.

I now made arrangements for my journey, but one feeling haunted me which filled me with fear and agitation. During my absence I should leave my friends unconscious of the existence of their enemy and unprotected from his attacks, exasperated as he might be by my departure. But he had promised to follow me wherever I might go, and would he not accompany me to England? This imagination was dreadful in itself, but soothing inasmuch as it supposed the safety of my friends. I was agonised with the idea of the possibility that the reverse of this might happen. But through the whole period during which I was the slave of my creature I allowed myself to be governed by the impulses of the moment; and my present sensations strongly intimated that the fiend would follow me and exempt my family from the danger of his machinations.

It was in the latter end of September that I again quitted my native country. My journey had been my own suggestion, and Elizabeth therefore acquiesced, but she was filled with disquiet at the idea of my suffering, away from her, the inroads of misery and grief. It had been her care which provided me a companion in Clerval—and yet a man is blind to a thousand minute circumstances which call forth a woman’s sedulous attention. She longed to bid me hasten my return; a thousand conflicting emotions rendered her mute as she bade me a tearful, silent farewell.

I threw myself into the carriage that was to convey me away, hardly knowing whither I was going, and careless of what was passing around. I remembered only, and it was with a bitter anguish that I reflected on it, to order that my chemical instruments should be packed to go with me. Filled with dreary imaginations, I passed through many beautiful and majestic scenes, but my eyes were fixed and unobserving. I could only think of the bourne of my travels and the work which was to occupy me whilst they endured.

After some days spent in listless indolence, during which I traversed many leagues, I arrived at Strasburgh, where I waited two days for Clerval. He came. Alas, how great was the contrast between us! He was alive to every new scene, joyful when he saw the beauties of the setting sun, and more happy when he beheld it rise and recommence a new day.

He pointed out to me the shifting colours of the landscape and the appearances of the sky. “This is what it is to live,” he cried; “now I enjoy existence! But you, my dear Frankenstein, wherefore are you desponding and sorrowful!” In truth, I was occupied by gloomy thoughts and neither saw the descent of the evening star nor the golden sunrise reflected in the Rhine. And you, my friend, would be far more amused with the journal of Clerval, who observed the scenery with an eye of feeling and delight, than in listening to my reflections. I, a miserable wretch, haunted by a curse that shut up every avenue to enjoyment.

We had agreed to descend the Rhine in a boat from Strasburgh to Rotterdam, whence we might take shipping for London. During this voyage we passed many willowy islands and saw several beautiful towns. We stayed a day at Mannheim, and on the fifth from our departure from Strasburgh, arrived at Mainz.

The course of the Rhine below Mainz becomes much more picturesque. The river descends rapidly and winds between hills, not high, but steep, and of beautiful forms. We saw many ruined castles standing on the edges of precipices, surrounded by black woods, high and inaccessible. This part of the Rhine, indeed, presents a singularly variegated landscape. In one spot you view rugged hills, ruined castles overlooking tremendous precipices, with the dark Rhine rushing beneath; and on the sudden turn of a promontory, flourishing vineyards with green sloping banks and a meandering river and populous towns occupy the scene.

We travelled at the time of the vintage and heard the song of the labourers as we glided down the stream. Even I, depressed in mind, and my spirits continually agitated by gloomy feelings, even I was pleased. I lay at the bottom of the boat, and as I gazed on the cloudless blue sky, I seemed to drink in a tranquillity to which I had long been a stranger. And if these were my sensations, who can describe those of Henry? He felt as if he had been transported to Fairy-land and enjoyed a happiness seldom tasted by man.

“I have seen,” he said, “the most beautiful scenes of my own country; I have visited the lakes of Lucerne and Uri, where the snowy mountains descend almost perpendicularly to the water, casting black and impenetrable shades, which would cause a gloomy and mournful appearance were it not for the most verdant islands that relieve the eye by their gay appearance; I have seen this lake agitated by a tempest, when the wind tore up whirlwinds of water and gave you an idea of what the water-spout must be on the great ocean; and the waves dash with fury the base of the mountain, where the priest and his mistress were overwhelmed by an avalanche and where their dying voices are still said to be heard amid the pauses of the nightly wind; I have seen the mountains of La Valais, and the Pays de Vaud; but this country, Victor, pleases me more than all those wonders.

The mountains of Switzerland are more majestic and strange, but there is a charm in the banks of this divine river that I never before saw equalled. Look at that castle which overhangs yon precipice; and that also on the island, almost concealed amongst the foliage of those lovely trees; and now that group of labourers coming from among their vines; and that village half hid in the recess of the mountain. Oh, surely the spirit that inhabits and guards this place has a soul more in harmony with man than those who pile the glacier or retire to the inaccessible peaks of the mountains of our own country.”

Clerval! Beloved friend! Even now it delights me to record your words and to dwell on the praise of which you are so eminently deserving. He was a being formed in the “very poetry of nature.” His wild and enthusiastic imagination was chastened by the sensibility of his heart. His soul overflowed with ardent affections, and his friendship was of that devoted and wondrous nature that the worldly-minded teach us to look for only in the imagination. But even human sympathies were not sufficient to satisfy his eager mind. The scenery of external nature, which others regard only with admiration, he loved with ardour:—

——The sounding cataract Haunted him like a passion: the tall rock, The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood, Their colours and their forms, were then to him An appetite; a feeling, and a love, That had no need of a remoter charm, By thought supplied, or any interest Unborrow’d from the eye.

[Wordsworth’s “Tintern Abbey”.]

And where does he now exist? Is this gentle and lovely being lost for ever? Has this mind, so replete with ideas, imaginations fanciful and magnificent, which formed a world, whose existence depended on the life of its creator;—has this mind perished? Does it now only exist in my memory? No, it is not thus; your form so divinely wrought, and beaming with beauty, has decayed, but your spirit still visits and consoles your unhappy friend.

Pardon this gush of sorrow; these ineffectual words are but a slight tribute to the unexampled worth of Henry, but they soothe my heart, overflowing with the anguish which his remembrance creates. I will proceed with my tale.

Beyond Cologne we descended to the plains of Holland; and we resolved to post the remainder of our way, for the wind was contrary and the stream of the river was too gentle to aid us.

Our journey here lost the interest arising from beautiful scenery, but we arrived in a few days at Rotterdam, whence we proceeded by sea to England. It was on a clear morning, in the latter days of December, that I first saw the white cliffs of Britain. The banks of the Thames presented a new scene; they were flat but fertile, and almost every town was marked by the remembrance of some story. We saw Tilbury Fort and remembered the Spanish Armada, Gravesend, Woolwich, and Greenwich—places which I had heard of even in my country.

At length we saw the numerous steeples of London, St. Paul’s towering above all, and the Tower famed in English history.
b2: Days and weeks slipped by after my return to Geneva, and I could not summon the courage to begin my work again. I dreaded the revenge of the frustrated fiend, yet I could not overcome my disgust at the task that had been forced upon me. I realised that I could not create a female without once again spending several months in deep study and painstaking research. I had heard that an English scientist had made certain discoveries which were essential to my success, and I sometimes considered asking my father’s permission to visit England for this purpose; but I clung to every excuse for delay and shrank from taking the first step in a task that no longer seemed quite so urgent.

Indeed, I had changed: my health, which had been declining until then, was now largely restored, and my spirits rose accordingly whenever the memory of my wretched promise did not hold them back. My father was delighted by this change and began to think how best to root out what remained of my melancholy, which still returned now and then in fits and cast a consuming darkness over the brightening sky. At such moments I sought refuge in complete solitude. I spent whole days alone on the lake in a little boat, watching the clouds and listening to the lapping of the waves, silent and listless. But the fresh air and bright sunshine rarely failed to calm me somewhat, and when I came home I greeted my friends with a readier smile and a lighter heart.

One day, when I had returned from one of these outings, my father took me aside and spoke to me like this: “I am glad to see, my dear son, that you have taken up your old pleasures again and seem to be becoming yourself once more. And yet you are still unhappy and still avoid our company. For some time I could only guess at the reason, but yesterday an idea occurred to me, and if I am right, I beg you to admit it. Keeping silent on such a matter would not only be pointless but would bring three times the misery upon us all.”

I trembled violently at these opening words, and my father went on: “I confess, my son, that I have always looked forward to your marriage with our dear Elizabeth as the bond that would hold our family happiness together and the support of my old age. You have been devoted to each other since early childhood; you studied together and seemed perfectly matched in character and taste. But human experience is so blind that the very things I thought would help my plan may have ruined it completely. Perhaps you think of her as a sister and have no wish for her to become your wife. Indeed, you may have met someone else whom you love, and, feeling bound in honour to Elizabeth, you may be torn by a struggle that causes the bitter misery you seem to feel.”

“My dear father, you need not worry. I love my cousin tenderly and sincerely. I have never met any woman who inspired in me such warm admiration and affection as Elizabeth does. All my hopes and plans for the future are wrapped up in the expectation of our marriage.”

“Hearing you express your feelings on this subject, my dear Victor, gives me more pleasure than I have felt for a long time. If you feel this way, we shall certainly be happy, however much present events may cast a shadow over us. But it is this very shadow, which seems to have taken such a firm hold of your mind, that I wish to drive away. So tell me whether you have any objection to the wedding taking place at once.

We have suffered misfortunes, and recent events have robbed us of the everyday peace that suits my age and frailty. You are younger; yet since you have a comfortable income, I do not imagine that an early marriage would in any way get in the way of whatever honourable and useful plans you may have made. Do not think, however, that I want to impose happiness on you, or that a delay on your part would seriously trouble me. Take my words in the spirit they are meant and answer me, I beg you, openly and honestly.”

I listened to my father in silence and for some time was unable to reply. A crowd of thoughts raced through my mind as I tried to reach some decision. Alas! To me the thought of an immediate marriage to my Elizabeth was filled with horror and dismay. I was bound by a solemn promise which I had not yet kept and did not dare to break; and if I did break it, what countless disasters might fall upon me and my loving family! How could I celebrate a wedding with this deadly weight still hanging round my neck and bending me to the ground? I had to fulfil my agreement and let the monster leave with his mate before I could allow myself the joy of a marriage from which I hoped for peace.

I also remembered that I would have to either travel to England or enter into a long correspondence with the scientists there, whose knowledge and discoveries were essential to my present task. Writing letters would be a slow and unsatisfactory way of getting the information I needed; besides, I felt an overwhelming reluctance to carry out my hateful work in my father’s house, living in close daily contact with the people I loved.

I knew that any number of terrible accidents might happen, and even the smallest of them would reveal a story that would horrify everyone connected with me. I was also aware that I would often lose all self-control and all ability to hide the agonising feelings that would grip me while I carried out my unnatural work. I had to stay away from everyone I loved while I was busy with it. Once begun, it would soon be finished, and I could return to my family in peace and happiness. With my promise kept, the monster would go away for ever. Or (as my foolish imagination pictured it) some accident might destroy him in the meantime and end my slavery for good.

These feelings shaped my answer to my father. I said that I wished to visit England, but I hid the real reasons for the request and dressed up my wishes in a disguise that aroused no suspicion, while I pressed my case so eagerly that my father was easily persuaded to agree. After such a long period of all-consuming gloom, which had been like madness in its intensity and effects, he was glad to see that I could take pleasure in the idea of such a journey, and he hoped that a change of scene and a variety of amusements would restore me completely to myself before I returned.

How long I stayed away was left for me to decide; a few months, or a year at most, was the period we had in mind. My father had taken one kind, fatherly precaution to make sure I had a companion. Without telling me beforehand, he had arranged with Elizabeth that Clerval would join me in Strasburgh. This disturbed the solitude I longed for in order to carry out my task; yet at the start of my journey my friend’s presence could hardly be an obstacle, and I was truly glad that I would be spared many hours of lonely, maddening brooding. Indeed, Henry might even stand between me and any intrusion by my enemy. If I were alone, would he not sometimes force his hateful presence on me to remind me of my task or to check on its progress?

So I was to go to England, and it was agreed that my marriage to Elizabeth would take place as soon as I returned. Because of his age, my father strongly disliked any delay. As for me, there was one reward I promised myself for my hated labours, one comfort for my unequalled sufferings: the thought of the day when, freed from my miserable slavery, I could claim Elizabeth and forget the past in my marriage to her.

I now made preparations for my journey, but one feeling haunted me and filled me with fear and anxiety. While I was away, I would be leaving my friends unaware that their enemy existed and defenceless against his attacks, and my departure might well enrage him. But he had promised to follow me wherever I went, so would he not come with me to England? This thought was terrible in itself, but also comforting, since it meant my friends would be safe. I was tormented by the idea that the opposite might happen. But throughout the whole time I was a slave to my creature, I let myself be ruled by the impulses of the moment, and now my instincts strongly suggested that the fiend would follow me and spare my family the danger of his schemes.

It was at the end of September that I left my native country once again. The journey had been my own idea, so Elizabeth agreed to it, but she was uneasy at the thought of me suffering the attacks of misery and grief far away from her. It was thanks to her care that I had Clerval as a companion, and yet a man is blind to a thousand small things that a woman notices with constant attention. She longed to urge me to come back soon, but a thousand conflicting emotions left her speechless as she said a tearful, silent goodbye.

I flung myself into the carriage that was to take me away, hardly knowing where I was going and paying no attention to what was happening around me. The only thing I remembered, and it was with bitter anguish that I thought of it, was to have my chemical instruments packed to go with me. Full of gloomy fantasies, I passed through many beautiful and majestic landscapes, but my eyes were fixed and saw nothing. I could think only of where my travels would end and of the work that would occupy me while they lasted.

After several days of listless idleness, during which I covered many miles, I reached Strasburgh, where I waited two days for Clerval. He arrived. Alas, how great the contrast between us was! He responded eagerly to every new scene, delighted when he saw the beauty of the setting sun, and happier still when he watched it rise and begin a new day.

He pointed out to me the changing colours of the landscape and the look of the sky. “This is what it means to live,” he cried; “now I am enjoying being alive! But you, my dear Frankenstein, why are you so downcast and sad?” In truth, I was absorbed in gloomy thoughts and saw neither the evening star sinking nor the golden sunrise reflected in the Rhine. And you, my friend, would enjoy reading Clerval’s journal far more, for he looked at the scenery with feeling and delight, than listening to my reflections. As for me, I was a miserable wretch, haunted by a curse that blocked every path to happiness.

We had agreed to travel down the Rhine by boat from Strasburgh to Rotterdam, where we could take a ship to London. On this voyage we passed many islands covered with willows and saw several beautiful towns. We spent a day at Mannheim, and on the fifth day after leaving Strasburgh we arrived at Mainz.

Below Mainz the Rhine becomes far more picturesque. The river descends swiftly and winds between hills that are not high but are steep and beautifully shaped. We saw many ruined castles perched on the edges of cliffs, surrounded by dark woods, tall and impossible to reach. This part of the Rhine, in fact, offers a remarkably varied landscape. In one place you see rugged hills and ruined castles looming over terrifying cliffs, with the dark Rhine rushing below; then, round the sudden bend of a headland, the scene is filled with thriving vineyards, green sloping banks, a winding river and busy towns.

We were travelling at the time of the grape harvest and heard the workers singing as we glided downstream. Even I, low in spirits and constantly troubled by dark feelings, even I was pleased. I lay in the bottom of the boat, and as I gazed at the cloudless blue sky, I seemed to soak up a calm I had not known for a long time. And if I felt like this, who could describe Henry’s feelings? He felt as though he had been carried off to Fairyland and enjoyed a happiness that few people ever taste.

“I have seen,” he said, “the most beautiful places in my own country. I have visited the lakes of Lucerne and Uri, where the snowy mountains plunge almost straight down to the water, casting black, impenetrable shadows that would look gloomy and mournful if it were not for the lush green islands that cheer the eye. I have seen that lake whipped up by a storm, when the wind tore up whirlwinds of water and gave you an idea of what a waterspout must be like on the open ocean, and the waves crashed furiously against the foot of the mountain where a priest and his lover were buried by an avalanche, and where their dying voices are still said to be heard when the night wind falls silent. I have seen the mountains of the Valais and the Pays de Vaud; but this country, Victor, pleases me more than all those wonders.

The Swiss mountains are grander and stranger, but the banks of this heavenly river have a charm I have never seen equalled. Look at that castle hanging over that cliff, and that one on the island, almost hidden among the leaves of those lovely trees; and now that group of workers coming out of their vineyards, and that village half hidden in a fold of the mountain. Oh, surely the spirit that lives here and guards this place has a soul more in tune with humanity than the spirits that pile up the glaciers or withdraw to the unreachable peaks of our own mountains.”

Clerval! Beloved friend! Even now it gives me joy to record your words and to linger over the praise you so richly deserve. He was a being made from “the very poetry of nature.” His wild, passionate imagination was softened by the sensitivity of his heart. His soul overflowed with warm affection, and his friendship was of the devoted, wonderful kind that worldly people tell us exists only in the imagination. But even human affection was not enough to satisfy his eager mind. The natural world, which others merely admire, he loved with passion, as the poet says: “The roaring waterfall haunted him like a passion: the tall rock, the mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood, their colours and their forms, were to him a hunger, a feeling and a love that needed no charm added by thought, nor any interest not borrowed from the eye.” (Wordsworth, “Tintern Abbey”)

And where is he now? Is this gentle and lovely being lost for ever? Has this mind, so full of ideas and of rich, magnificent fantasies, which created a whole world whose existence depended on the life of its creator, has this mind perished? Does it now exist only in my memory? No, it is not so; your body, so divinely made and shining with beauty, has decayed, but your spirit still visits and comforts your unhappy friend. Forgive this outpouring of grief; these feeble words are only a small tribute to Henry’s matchless worth, but they soothe my heart, which overflows with the anguish his memory brings. I will go on with my story.

Beyond Cologne we came down to the plains of Holland, and we decided to travel the rest of the way by post-horses, because the wind was against us and the current was too gentle to help. From here our journey lost the interest that beautiful scenery had given it, but in a few days we reached Rotterdam, from where we continued by sea to England. It was on a clear morning in the last days of December that I first saw the white cliffs of Britain. The banks of the Thames offered a new kind of scenery; they were flat but fertile, and almost every town was linked to the memory of some story. We saw Tilbury Fort and remembered the Spanish Armada, and then Gravesend, Woolwich and Greenwich, places I had heard of even in my own country. At last we saw the many church spires of London, with St. Paul’s towering above them all, and the Tower, famous in English history.
b1: Days and weeks passed after I returned to Geneva, but I could not find the courage to start my work again. I was afraid of the angry monster’s revenge, but I still hated the job he had given me. I knew that I could not make a female without spending several more months on difficult study. I had heard that an English scientist had made some discoveries that I needed. Sometimes I thought of asking my father if I could go to England, but I kept finding reasons to wait, and I was afraid to take the first step.

But I had changed. My health was much better now, and when I did not think about my terrible promise, I felt more cheerful. My father was pleased to see this, and he tried to think of the best way to end my sadness completely. It still came back from time to time, like a dark cloud over the sun. At those times I wanted to be completely alone. I spent whole days alone in a little boat on the lake, watching the clouds and listening to the waves, silent and tired. But the fresh air and the bright sun usually calmed me, and when I came home, I greeted my friends with a smile and a happier heart.

One day, after one of these trips, my father took me aside and spoke to me. “My dear son, I am happy to see that you enjoy your old pleasures again and are becoming yourself once more. But you are still unhappy, and you still avoid us. For a long time I did not understand why, but yesterday I had an idea. If I am right, please tell me. Keeping it secret will not help, and it will make us all even more unhappy.”

I began to shake badly when I heard this, and my father went on. “My son, I have always hoped that you would marry our dear Elizabeth. I thought your marriage would keep our family happy and would be a comfort to me in my old age. You have loved each other since you were small children, you studied together, and you always seemed perfect for each other. But perhaps the things that I thought would help my plan have destroyed it. Perhaps you see her only as a sister and do not want her to be your wife. Or perhaps you have met another woman and love her, but you feel that you must keep your word to Elizabeth, and this is why you are so unhappy.”
“My dear father, do not worry. I love my cousin truly and deeply. I have never met any woman whom I admire and love as much as Elizabeth. All my hopes for the future depend on our marriage.”

“My dear Victor, your words make me happier than I have been for a long time. If you feel like this, we will certainly be happy, even though the things that have happened make us sad now. But this sadness has a strong hold on your mind, and I want to take it away. So tell me: would you agree to have the wedding very soon?

We have had bad luck, and recent events have taken away the quiet life that an old and weak man like me needs. You are young, but you have enough money, so I do not think an early marriage will stop you from doing any good and useful things you are planning. But do not think that I want to tell you how to be happy, or that I will be very upset if you want to wait. Please understand my words in the right way and answer me honestly.”

I listened to my father in silence, and for some time I could not answer. Many thoughts went quickly through my mind, and I tried to decide what to do. The idea of marrying Elizabeth soon filled me with horror. I had made a serious promise that I had not kept yet, and I did not dare to break it. If I broke it, terrible things might happen to me and my loving family! How could I have a happy wedding with this heavy weight still hanging round my neck? First I had to do what I had promised and let the monster go away with his wife. Only then could I enjoy a marriage that would bring me peace.

I also remembered that I had to go to England or write many letters to the scientists there. I needed their knowledge and discoveries for my work. Writing letters would be too slow and not good enough. Also, I hated the idea of doing my terrible work in my father’s house, close to the people I loved every day.

I knew that many things could go wrong, and even a small accident could show everyone my horrible secret. I also knew that I would often lose control and would not be able to hide my terrible feelings while I did this unnatural work. I had to be far away from everyone I loved while I did it. Once I started, I would finish quickly, and then I could come back to my family in peace and happiness. When I had kept my promise, the monster would go away for ever. Or, I hoped, some accident might kill him first and make me free for ever.

These feelings decided my answer to my father. I told him that I wanted to visit England, but I did not tell him the real reasons. I hid my plans so well that he did not suspect anything, and I asked him so eagerly that he easily agreed. I had been sad for so long that it had almost seemed like madness, so he was glad that I could look forward to a journey. He hoped that new places and different amusements would make me completely well again before I came home.

I could decide how long to stay away; we thought of a few months, or a year at most. My father kindly made sure that I would have a companion. Without telling me, he and Elizabeth arranged for Clerval to meet me in Strasburgh. This would stop me from being alone, which I needed for my work. But at the start of the journey my friend would not be a problem, and I was really glad that I would not spend so many lonely hours with my terrible thoughts. Also, Henry might protect me from my enemy. If I were alone, the monster might come to remind me of my task or to see how it was going.

So I was going to England, and we agreed that I would marry Elizabeth as soon as I came back. My father was old, so he did not want to wait long. For me, there was one reward for all my hated work and terrible suffering. It was the hope of the day when I would be free from my slavery and could marry Elizabeth and forget the past.

Now I prepared for my journey, but one fear stayed with me and made me very anxious. While I was away, my friends would not know about their enemy and could not protect themselves from him, and my leaving might make him angry. But he had promised to follow me everywhere, so perhaps he would come with me to England. This idea was terrible, but it also comforted me, because then my friends would be safe. I was very afraid that the opposite might happen. But all the time that I was the slave of my creature, I followed my feelings of the moment. And now my feelings told me that the monster would follow me and leave my family in peace.

At the end of September I left my home country again. The journey was my own idea, so Elizabeth agreed to it. But she was worried that I would be unhappy and sad far away from her. She had helped to make Clerval my companion, but she knew that a man does not notice a thousand small things that a woman always sees. She wanted to ask me to come back soon, but she had so many different feelings that she could not speak. She said goodbye silently, with tears in her eyes.

I threw myself into the carriage that would take me away. I hardly knew where I was going, and I did not care what was happening around me. I remembered only one thing, and it made me feel bitter pain: I told the servants to pack my chemical instruments to take with me. My mind was full of dark thoughts, and I passed through many beautiful places, but I did not see them. I could only think about the end of my journey and the work I would do there.

For several days I travelled a long way, tired and doing nothing, and then I arrived at Strasburgh. There I waited two days for Clerval. Then he came. We were so different! He was interested in every new place. He was happy when he saw the beautiful sunset, and even happier when he watched the sun rise and start a new day.

He showed me the changing colours of the land and the sky. “This is real life!” he cried. “Now I enjoy being alive! But you, my dear Frankenstein, why are you so sad?” The truth is that I was lost in dark thoughts. I did not see the evening star go down or the golden sunrise in the waters of the Rhine. You, my friend, would enjoy Clerval’s diary much more than my thoughts, because he looked at everything with feeling and joy. I was a miserable man, and a curse stopped me from enjoying anything.

We had planned to go down the Rhine by boat from Strasburgh to Rotterdam, and from there to take a ship to London. On the way we passed many islands with willow trees and saw several beautiful towns. We stayed one day in Mannheim, and five days after we left Strasburgh, we arrived in Mainz.

After Mainz the Rhine becomes much more beautiful. The river flows fast and turns between hills that are not high, but steep and beautiful. We saw many old broken castles on the edges of cliffs, with dark, high forests all around them. This part of the Rhine is full of different views. In one place you see wild hills and old castles above frightening cliffs, with the dark river rushing below. Then the river turns, and suddenly you see green vineyards, gentle river banks and busy towns.

We travelled at the time when people picked the grapes, and we heard the workers singing as we moved gently down the river. Even I, with my sad mind and dark feelings, even I was happy. I lay at the bottom of the boat and looked up at the clear blue sky, and I felt a peace that I had not felt for a long time. And if I felt like this, how can I describe Henry’s feelings? He felt as if he were in Fairyland, and he was happier than most people ever are.

“I have seen the most beautiful places in my own country,” he said. “I have visited the lakes of Lucerne and Uri, where the snowy mountains go almost straight down into the water. Their black shadows would look sad and gloomy, but the bright green islands make the view cheerful. I have seen that lake in a storm, when the wind lifted the water into the air and the waves hit the bottom of the mountain. There a priest and the woman he loved died under the snow, and people say that you can still hear their voices in the night wind. I have seen the mountains of the Valais and the Pays de Vaud. But this country, Victor, I like more than all those wonders.

The mountains of Switzerland are greater and stranger, but this wonderful river has a special beauty that I have never seen before. Look at that castle above the cliff, and that one on the island, almost hidden by the lovely trees. And look at those workers coming from their vineyards, and that village half hidden in the mountain. Surely the spirit that lives here and protects this place is closer to people than the spirits that live on the ice and the high, cold mountains of our own country.”

Clerval! My dear friend! Even now I am happy to write down your words and to praise you, because you deserve it so much. He was a person made of “the very poetry of nature.” He had a wild and excited imagination, but his kind heart made it gentle. His soul was full of warm love, and he was a true and wonderful friend, the kind that most people think exists only in stories. But even people were not enough for his eager mind. He loved nature with passion, as the poet Wordsworth wrote: the waterfall, the tall rock, the mountain and the deep dark wood were like food and love to him.

And where is he now? Is this gentle and lovely person lost for ever? His mind was so full of ideas and wonderful dreams that it made a whole world of its own. Has this mind died? Does it live now only in my memory? No, it is not so. Your beautiful body is gone, but your spirit still visits and comforts your unhappy friend. Forgive me for this sudden sadness. These weak words cannot show how good Henry was, but they make my heart feel better when I remember him with pain. I will go on with my story.

After Cologne we came down to the flat land of Holland. We decided to go the rest of the way by coach, because the wind was against us and the river was too slow to help. The journey was not so interesting now, because there were no beautiful views. But in a few days we arrived in Rotterdam, and from there we went by sea to England. On a clear morning at the end of December, I saw the white cliffs of Britain for the first time. The land along the River Thames was flat but rich, and almost every town had its own famous story. We saw Tilbury Fort and remembered the Spanish Armada, and we saw Gravesend, Woolwich and Greenwich, places I had heard about at home. At last we saw the many church towers of London, with St. Paul’s above them all, and the famous Tower of London.
a2: I came back to Geneva, and many weeks passed. I did not start my work again. I was afraid of the monster, but I hated this work. To make a woman, I needed to study hard for many months. An English scientist knew some important things, and I needed his knowledge. I thought about asking my father to let me go to England. But I always found reasons to wait.

But I was changing. I was healthier now, and I often felt happier when I forgot my promise. My father was glad, and he wanted to help me stop being sad. But sometimes the sadness came back like a black cloud. Then I wanted to be alone. I spent whole days in a little boat on the lake. I watched the clouds and listened to the water. The fresh air and the sun usually made me calmer, and I came home with a smile.

One day, after one of these trips, my father spoke to me. “My dear son, I am happy that you are enjoying things again. But you are still unhappy, and you do not want to be with us. I did not know why, but yesterday I had an idea. If I am right, please tell me. A secret will only make us all more unhappy.”

I started to shake, and my father continued. “My son, I always wanted you to marry our dear Elizabeth. I thought it would make our family happy and help me when I am old. You have loved each other since you were children, and you studied together. But perhaps you think of her only as a sister. Or perhaps you love another woman, but you think you must marry Elizabeth. Is that why you are so unhappy?”
“My dear father, do not worry. I love Elizabeth very much. No other woman is as wonderful to me as she is. All my hopes are about our future together.”

“Victor, your words make me very happy. If you love her, we will be happy, even after all the bad things that happened. But you are still very sad, and I want to help you. So tell me: can we have the wedding soon?

Bad things have happened to our family, and I am old and weak now. I need a quiet life. You are young, but you have enough money, so marriage will not stop your plans. But I will not be angry if you want to wait. Please answer me honestly.”

I listened to my father, but for a long time I could not answer. I thought and thought. The idea of a wedding soon was terrible to me. I had made a promise to the monster, and I had not kept it yet. If I broke it, he could hurt me and my family! How could I have a happy wedding with this heavy weight on me? First I had to make the woman and let the monster go away with her. Only then could I marry Elizabeth and live in peace.

I also remembered that I needed help from the scientists in England. I could go there or write them letters. But letters were too slow. And I did not want to do my horrible work in my father’s house, near the people I loved.

Something could go wrong, and then everyone would learn my terrible secret. I also knew that I could not always hide my feelings during this work. So I had to go far away from my family. I would finish the work quickly and come back happy. Then the monster would go away for ever. Or perhaps, I hoped, he would have an accident and die, and I would be free.

So I gave my father my answer. I said that I wanted to visit England, but I did not tell him the real reason. He did not suspect anything, and he agreed. I had been very sad for a long time, almost mad. So my father was glad that I wanted to travel. He hoped that new places would make me well again.

I could stay away for a few months, or for a year at most. My father did not want me to travel alone. He and Elizabeth decided that Clerval would meet me in Strasburgh. I wanted to be alone for my work, so this was a problem. But at the start of the journey I was glad to have my friend with me. I did not want to spend many lonely hours with my dark thoughts. Henry could also protect me from the monster. If I was alone, the monster could come to me and remind me of my work.

So I was going to England. We agreed that I would marry Elizabeth when I came back. My father was old and did not want to wait. I hated my work, and I suffered very much. But I had one hope. One day I would be free, and I would marry Elizabeth and forget the past.

I got ready for the journey, but I was very worried. My family did not know about the monster. What if he attacked them when I was away? But he said that he would follow me everywhere. Perhaps he would come to England with me. This idea was terrible, but it was also good, because then my family would be safe. I was afraid of the opposite. But my feelings told me that the monster would follow me and not hurt my family.

At the end of September I left my country again. The journey was my idea, so Elizabeth agreed. But she was worried that I would be sad without her. She helped to find a friend to go with me, Clerval. But she knew that a man does not see many small things. She wanted to ask me to come back soon, but she could not speak. She said goodbye silently, with tears in her eyes.

I got into the carriage and left. I did not care where I was going or what was around me. I remembered only one thing: to take my chemical instruments with me. This made me feel very bad. We passed many beautiful places, but I did not look at them. I could only think about my terrible work.

After some slow, tired days on the road, I arrived in Strasburgh. I waited two days for Clerval, and then he came. We were very different! He loved every new place. He was happy when he saw the sunset, and even happier when he saw the sunrise.

He showed me the colours of the land and the sky. “This is life!” he said. “I am so happy! But Frankenstein, why are you so sad?” I was full of dark thoughts. I did not see the evening star or the golden sunrise on the Rhine. You, my friend, would like Clerval’s diary more than my story, because he enjoyed everything. I was a very unhappy man, and I could not enjoy anything.

We planned to go down the Rhine by boat to Rotterdam, and then by ship to London. We passed many islands with trees and some beautiful towns. We stayed one day in Mannheim, and after five days we arrived in Mainz.

After Mainz the river is more beautiful. It goes fast between steep hills. We saw many old castles on high rocks, with dark forests around them. In one place there are wild hills and old castles, and the dark river runs fast below. Then the river turns, and you see green fields of grapes and busy towns.

It was the time of the grape harvest, and we heard the workers singing. Even I was happy. I lay in the boat and looked at the blue sky, and I felt calm for the first time in a long time. And Henry was even happier. He felt that he was in a fairy tale.

“I have seen the most beautiful places in my country,” he said. “I have been to the lakes of Lucerne and Uri, where the snowy mountains go down to the water. Their shadows are black, but the green islands are very pretty. I have seen a storm on that lake, with huge waves. People say that a priest and his lover died there under the snow, and you can still hear their voices at night. I have seen many mountains in Switzerland. But I like this country more, Victor.

The mountains of Switzerland are bigger, but this river is more beautiful. Look at that castle on the cliff, and that one on the island, between the trees! Look at the workers and that little village in the mountain! The spirit of this place is kinder to people than the spirits of our cold, icy mountains.”

Clerval! My dear friend! Even now I am happy to write your words. He was like a poem of nature. He had a lot of imagination and a kind heart. He loved people warmly, and he was a wonderful friend. Most people think that friends like that live only in books. He also loved nature very much. A poet, Wordsworth, wrote that the waterfall, the rocks, the mountains and the dark woods were like food and love to him.

And where is he now? Is this kind and lovely man gone for ever? His mind was full of ideas and dreams. Is it dead now? Does it live only in my memory? No! Your body is gone, but your spirit still visits me and helps me. I am sorry for these sad words. They cannot show how good Henry was, but they help my heart. Now I will go on with my story.

After Cologne we came to Holland, where the land is flat. The wind was against us, so we travelled by coach. There were no beautiful views now. In a few days we arrived in Rotterdam, and from there we went to England by sea. On a clear morning at the end of December, I saw the white cliffs of Britain. The land by the River Thames was flat, and every town had a story. We saw Tilbury Fort, Gravesend, Woolwich and Greenwich. At last we saw the churches of London, the great St. Paul’s, and the famous Tower.

o.en: Day after day, week after week, passed away on my return to Geneva; and I could not collect the courage to recommence my work.
o.ru: День за днём, неделя за неделей проходили после моего возвращения в Женеву, а я никак не мог собраться с духом, чтобы вновь приняться за работу.

o.en: I feared the vengeance of the disappointed fiend, yet I was unable to overcome my repugnance to the task which was enjoined me.
o.ru: Я боялся мести обманутого демона, и всё же не мог преодолеть отвращения к задаче, которая была мне поручена.

o.en: I found that I could not compose a female without again devoting several months to profound study and laborious disquisition.
o.ru: Я понял, что не смогу сотворить женщину, не посвятив снова несколько месяцев глубокому изучению и кропотливым исследованиям.

o.en: I had heard of some discoveries having been made by an English philosopher, the knowledge of which was material to my success, and I sometimes thought of obtaining my father’s consent to visit England for this purpose; but I clung to every pretence of delay and shrank from taking the first step in an undertaking whose immediate necessity began to appear less absolute to me.
o.ru: Я слышал о неких открытиях, сделанных одним английским учёным, знание которых было существенно для моего успеха, и порой подумывал испросить у отца согласия на поездку в Англию с этой целью; но я цеплялся за любой предлог для отсрочки и уклонялся от первого шага в предприятии, неотложность которого начинала казаться мне уже не столь безусловной.

o.en: A change indeed had taken place in me; my health, which had hitherto declined, was now much restored; and my spirits, when unchecked by the memory of my unhappy promise, rose proportionably.
o.ru: Во мне и впрямь произошла перемена: моё здоровье, до тех пор слабевшее, теперь во многом восстановилось, и дух мой, когда его не омрачало воспоминание о злосчастном обещании, соответственно поднимался.

o.en: My father saw this change with pleasure, and he turned his thoughts towards the best method of eradicating the remains of my melancholy, which every now and then would return by fits, and with a devouring blackness overcast the approaching sunshine.
o.ru: Отец с радостью видел эту перемену и обратил мысли к тому, как лучше искоренить остатки моей меланхолии, которая время от времени возвращалась приступами и всепоглощающим мраком затмевала наступавший было рассвет.

o.en: At these moments I took refuge in the most perfect solitude.
o.ru: В такие минуты я искал убежища в полнейшем уединении.

o.en: I passed whole days on the lake alone in a little boat, watching the clouds and listening to the rippling of the waves, silent and listless.
o.ru: Я проводил целые дни на озере один в маленькой лодке, глядя на облака и слушая плеск волн, молчаливый и безучастный.

o.en: But the fresh air and bright sun seldom failed to restore me to some degree of composure, and on my return I met the salutations of my friends with a readier smile and a more cheerful heart.
o.ru: Но свежий воздух и яркое солнце редко не возвращали мне хоть некоторого спокойствия, и по возвращении я встречал приветствия друзей с более готовой улыбкой и более весёлым сердцем.

o.en: It was after my return from one of these rambles that my father, calling me aside, thus addressed me,
o.ru: Однажды, когда я вернулся с одной из таких прогулок, отец отозвал меня в сторону и обратился ко мне так:

o.en: “I am happy to remark, my dear son, that you have resumed your former pleasures and seem to be returning to yourself.
o.ru: «Я счастлив заметить, мой дорогой сын, что ты вернулся к прежним удовольствиям и, кажется, снова становишься самим собой.

o.en: And yet you are still unhappy and still avoid our society.
o.ru: И всё же ты по-прежнему несчастлив и по-прежнему избегаешь нашего общества.

o.en: For some time I was lost in conjecture as to the cause of this, but yesterday an idea struck me, and if it is well founded, I conjure you to avow it.
o.ru: Некоторое время я терялся в догадках о причине этого, но вчера мне пришла в голову мысль, и если она верна, заклинаю тебя признаться.

o.en: Reserve on such a point would be not only useless, but draw down treble misery on us all.”
o.ru: Скрытность в таком деле была бы не только бесполезна, но и навлекла бы на всех нас тройное несчастье».

o.en: I trembled violently at his exordium, and my father continued—
o.ru: Я сильно задрожал при этом вступлении, а отец продолжал:

o.en: “I confess, my son, that I have always looked forward to your marriage with our dear Elizabeth as the tie of our domestic comfort and the stay of my declining years.
o.ru: «Признаюсь, сын мой, я всегда ждал твоей свадьбы с нашей дорогой Элизабет как залога нашего семейного покоя и опоры моих преклонных лет.

o.en: You were attached to each other from your earliest infancy; you studied together, and appeared, in dispositions and tastes, entirely suited to one another.
o.ru: Вы были привязаны друг к другу с самого раннего детства; вы вместе учились и казались совершенно подходящими друг другу по нраву и вкусам.

o.en: But so blind is the experience of man that what I conceived to be the best assistants to my plan may have entirely destroyed it.
o.ru: Но так слеп опыт человеческий, что то, что я считал лучшими помощниками моего замысла, могло совершенно его разрушить.

o.en: You, perhaps, regard her as your sister, without any wish that she might become your wife.
o.ru: Возможно, ты видишь в ней сестру и вовсе не желаешь, чтобы она стала твоей женой.

o.en: Nay, you may have met with another whom you may love; and considering yourself as bound in honour to Elizabeth, this struggle may occasion the poignant misery which you appear to feel.”
o.ru: Более того, ты, может быть, встретил другую, которую полюбил, и, считая себя связанным словом чести с Элизабет, терзаешься этой борьбой, что и причиняет тебе ту острую муку, которую ты, по-видимому, испытываешь».

o.en: “My dear father, reassure yourself.
I love my cousin tenderly and sincerely.
o.ru: Я люблю свою кузину нежно и искренне.

o.en: I never saw any woman who excited, as Elizabeth does, my warmest admiration and affection.
o.ru: Я никогда не встречал женщины, которая, подобно Элизабет, вызывала бы во мне столь горячее восхищение и привязанность.

o.en: My future hopes and prospects are entirely bound up in the expectation of our union.”
o.ru: Все мои надежды и виды на будущее целиком связаны с ожиданием нашего союза».

o.en: “The expression of your sentiments of this subject, my dear Victor, gives me more pleasure than I have for some time experienced.
o.ru: «Твои чувства на этот счёт, мой дорогой Виктор, доставляют мне больше радости, чем я испытывал уже долгое время.

o.en: If you feel thus, we shall assuredly be happy, however present events may cast a gloom over us.
o.ru: Если ты так чувствуешь, мы непременно будем счастливы, как бы ни омрачали нас нынешние события.

o.en: But it is this gloom which appears to have taken so strong a hold of your mind that I wish to dissipate.
o.ru: Но именно этот мрак, который, кажется, так сильно завладел твоим разумом, я и хочу рассеять.

o.en: Tell me, therefore, whether you object to an immediate solemnisation of the marriage.
o.ru: Поэтому скажи мне, не возражаешь ли ты против того, чтобы свадьбу сыграли немедленно.

o.en: We have been unfortunate, and recent events have drawn us from that everyday tranquillity befitting my years and infirmities.
o.ru: Нас постигли несчастья, и недавние события лишили нас того повседневного покоя, что подобает моим годам и немощам.

o.en: You are younger; yet I do not suppose, possessed as you are of a competent fortune, that an early marriage would at all interfere with any future plans of honour and utility that you may have formed.
o.ru: Ты моложе; но я не думаю, что при твоём достаточном состоянии ранний брак хоть сколько-нибудь помешает благородным и полезным планам, которые ты, возможно, строишь.

o.en: Do not suppose, however, that I wish to dictate happiness to you or that a delay on your part would cause me any serious uneasiness.
o.ru: Не думай, однако, что я хочу предписывать тебе счастье или что отсрочка с твоей стороны серьёзно меня огорчит.

o.en: Interpret my words with candour and answer me, I conjure you, with confidence and sincerity.”
o.ru: Пойми мои слова без предубеждения и ответь мне, заклинаю тебя, с доверием и искренностью».

o.en: I listened to my father in silence and remained for some time incapable of offering any reply.
o.ru: Я слушал отца молча и некоторое время не в силах был ничего ответить.

o.en: I revolved rapidly in my mind a multitude of thoughts and endeavoured to arrive at some conclusion.
o.ru: Я быстро перебирал в уме множество мыслей и старался прийти к какому-то решению.

o.en: Alas!
To me the idea of an immediate union with my Elizabeth was one of horror and dismay.
o.ru: Мысль о немедленном союзе с моей Элизабет вызывала у меня ужас и смятение.

o.en: I was bound by a solemn promise which I had not yet fulfilled and dared not break, or if I did, what manifold miseries might not impend over me and my devoted family!
o.ru: Я был связан торжественным обещанием, которого ещё не исполнил и которое не смел нарушить, а если бы нарушил — какие бесчисленные беды могли бы обрушиться на меня и мою преданную семью!

o.en: Could I enter into a festival with this deadly weight yet hanging round my neck and bowing me to the ground?
o.ru: Мог ли я вступить в праздник, когда этот смертельный груз всё ещё висел у меня на шее и пригибал меня к земле?

o.en: I must perform my engagement and let the monster depart with his mate before I allowed myself to enjoy the delight of a union from which I expected peace.
o.ru: Я должен был выполнить своё обязательство и позволить чудовищу удалиться со своей подругой, прежде чем разрешить себе наслаждаться союзом, от которого я ждал покоя.

o.en: I remembered also the necessity imposed upon me of either journeying to England or entering into a long correspondence with those philosophers of that country whose knowledge and discoveries were of indispensable use to me in my present undertaking.
o.ru: Я вспомнил также о необходимости либо отправиться в Англию, либо вступить в долгую переписку с тамошними учёными, чьи знания и открытия были мне совершенно необходимы в моём нынешнем предприятии.

o.en: The latter method of obtaining the desired intelligence was dilatory and unsatisfactory; besides, I had an insurmountable aversion to the idea of engaging myself in my loathsome task in my father’s house while in habits of familiar intercourse with those I loved.
o.ru: Второй способ получить нужные сведения был медленным и неудовлетворительным; к тому же я испытывал непреодолимое отвращение к мысли заниматься своим омерзительным делом в доме отца, в постоянном близком общении с теми, кого любил.

o.en: I knew that a thousand fearful accidents might occur, the slightest of which would disclose a tale to thrill all connected with me with horror.
o.ru: Я знал, что может случиться тысяча страшных случайностей, и малейшая из них раскрыла бы историю, от которой все близкие мне содрогнулись бы от ужаса.

o.en: I was aware also that I should often lose all self-command, all capacity of hiding the harrowing sensations that would possess me during the progress of my unearthly occupation.
o.ru: Я сознавал также, что часто буду терять всякое самообладание, всякую способность скрывать мучительные чувства, которые овладеют мной во время моего нечеловеческого занятия.

o.en: I must absent myself from all I loved while thus employed.
o.ru: Пока я занят этим, я должен быть вдали от всех, кого люблю.

o.en: Once commenced, it would quickly be achieved, and I might be restored to my family in peace and happiness.
o.ru: Начав, я быстро завершу дело и смогу вернуться к семье в мире и счастье.

o.en: My promise fulfilled, the monster would depart for ever.
o.ru: Когда обещание будет исполнено, чудовище уйдёт навсегда.

o.en: Or (so my fond fancy imaged) some accident might meanwhile occur to destroy him and put an end to my slavery for ever.
o.ru: Или же (так рисовало мне наивное воображение) тем временем какой-нибудь случай погубит его и навсегда положит конец моему рабству.

o.en: These feelings dictated my answer to my father.
o.ru: Эти чувства и продиктовали мой ответ отцу.

o.en: I expressed a wish to visit England, but concealing the true reasons of this request, I clothed my desires under a guise which excited no suspicion, while I urged my desire with an earnestness that easily induced my father to comply.
o.ru: Я выразил желание посетить Англию, но, скрыв истинные причины этой просьбы, облёк свои намерения в такую форму, которая не вызывала подозрений, и настаивал на своём с такой горячностью, что легко склонил отца к согласию.

o.en: After so long a period of an absorbing melancholy that resembled madness in its intensity and effects, he was glad to find that I was capable of taking pleasure in the idea of such a journey, and he hoped that change of scene and varied amusement would, before my return, have restored me entirely to myself.
o.ru: После столь долгой всепоглощающей меланхолии, походившей на безумие силой и последствиями, он был рад увидеть, что я способен находить удовольствие в мысли о таком путешествии, и надеялся, что перемена обстановки и разнообразные развлечения ещё до моего возвращения полностью вернут меня к самому себе.

o.en: The duration of my absence was left to my own choice; a few months, or at most a year, was the period contemplated.
o.ru: Продолжительность моего отсутствия была оставлена на моё усмотрение; предполагалось несколько месяцев или самое большее год.

o.en: One paternal kind precaution he had taken to ensure my having a companion.
o.ru: Одну заботливую отеческую предосторожность он всё же принял, чтобы у меня был спутник.

o.en: Without previously communicating with me, he had, in concert with Elizabeth, arranged that Clerval should join me at Strasburgh.
o.ru: Не сказав мне заранее ни слова, он договорился с Элизабет, что Клерваль присоединится ко мне в Страсбурге.

o.en: This interfered with the solitude I coveted for the prosecution of my task; yet at the commencement of my journey the presence of my friend could in no way be an impediment, and truly I rejoiced that thus I should be saved many hours of lonely, maddening reflection.
o.ru: Это мешало уединению, которого я жаждал для выполнения своей задачи; однако в начале пути присутствие друга никак не могло быть помехой, и я поистине радовался, что буду избавлен от многих часов одиноких, сводящих с ума раздумий.

o.en: Nay, Henry might stand between me and the intrusion of my foe.
o.ru: Более того, Анри мог бы встать между мною и вторжением моего врага.

o.en: If I were alone, would he not at times force his abhorred presence on me to remind me of my task or to contemplate its progress?
o.ru: Будь я один, разве не являлся бы он порой со своим ненавистным присутствием, чтобы напомнить мне о задаче или взглянуть, как она продвигается?

o.en: To England, therefore, I was bound, and it was understood that my union with Elizabeth should take place immediately on my return.
o.ru: Итак, я отправлялся в Англию, и было условлено, что мой союз с Элизабет состоится сразу по моём возвращении.

o.en: My father’s age rendered him extremely averse to delay.
o.ru: Возраст отца делал его крайне нетерпимым к отсрочкам.

o.en: For myself, there was one reward I promised myself from my detested toils—one consolation for my unparalleled sufferings; it was the prospect of that day when, enfranchised from my miserable slavery, I might claim Elizabeth and forget the past in my union with her.
o.ru: Что до меня, была одна награда, которую я обещал себе за свои ненавистные труды, — одно утешение в моих беспримерных страданиях: надежда на тот день, когда, освободившись от жалкого рабства, я смогу назвать Элизабет своей и забыть прошлое в союзе с ней.

o.en: I now made arrangements for my journey, but one feeling haunted me which filled me with fear and agitation.
o.ru: Я занялся приготовлениями к поездке, но меня преследовало одно чувство, наполнявшее меня страхом и тревогой.

o.en: During my absence I should leave my friends unconscious of the existence of their enemy and unprotected from his attacks, exasperated as he might be by my departure.
o.ru: На время своего отсутствия я оставлял друзей, не подозревающих о существовании их врага и беззащитных перед его нападениями, — а мой отъезд мог привести его в ярость.

o.en: But he had promised to follow me wherever I might go, and would he not accompany me to England?
o.ru: Но он обещал следовать за мной, куда бы я ни пошёл, — так не последует ли он за мной и в Англию?

o.en: This imagination was dreadful in itself, but soothing inasmuch as it supposed the safety of my friends.
o.ru: Эта мысль была ужасна сама по себе, но и утешительна, поскольку предполагала безопасность моих близких.

o.en: I was agonised with the idea of the possibility that the reverse of this might happen.
o.ru: Меня мучила мысль о том, что может произойти обратное.

o.en: But through the whole period during which I was the slave of my creature I allowed myself to be governed by the impulses of the moment; and my present sensations strongly intimated that the fiend would follow me and exempt my family from the danger of his machinations.
o.ru: Но всё то время, пока я был рабом своего создания, я позволял собой управлять порывам минуты; а нынешние мои ощущения настойчиво подсказывали, что демон последует за мной и избавит мою семью от опасности своих козней.

o.en: It was in the latter end of September that I again quitted my native country.
o.ru: В конце сентября я вновь покинул родину.

o.en: My journey had been my own suggestion, and Elizabeth therefore acquiesced, but she was filled with disquiet at the idea of my suffering, away from her, the inroads of misery and grief.
o.ru: Поездка была моей собственной затеей, и потому Элизабет согласилась, но её тревожила мысль о том, что вдали от неё меня станут одолевать тоска и горе.

o.en: It had been her care which provided me a companion in Clerval—and yet a man is blind to a thousand minute circumstances which call forth a woman’s sedulous attention.
o.ru: Именно её заботами у меня появился спутник в лице Клерваля, — и всё же мужчина слеп к тысяче мелочей, которые требуют неусыпного женского внимания.

o.en: She longed to bid me hasten my return; a thousand conflicting emotions rendered her mute as she bade me a tearful, silent farewell.
o.ru: Ей очень хотелось попросить меня поскорее вернуться; тысяча противоречивых чувств лишила её дара речи, когда она со слезами, молча, прощалась со мной.

o.en: I threw myself into the carriage that was to convey me away, hardly knowing whither I was going, and careless of what was passing around.
o.ru: Я бросился в экипаж, который должен был увезти меня, едва зная, куда еду, и не обращая внимания на то, что происходит вокруг.

o.en: I remembered only, and it was with a bitter anguish that I reflected on it, to order that my chemical instruments should be packed to go with me.
o.ru: Я помнил лишь об одном — и думал об этом с горькой мукой — распорядиться, чтобы мои химические инструменты упаковали и взяли с собой.

o.en: Filled with dreary imaginations, I passed through many beautiful and majestic scenes, but my eyes were fixed and unobserving.
o.ru: Полный мрачных фантазий, я проезжал мимо многих прекрасных и величественных видов, но мой взгляд был неподвижен и ничего не замечал.

o.en: I could only think of the bourne of my travels and the work which was to occupy me whilst they endured.
o.ru: Я мог думать лишь о цели моего путешествия и о работе, которая займёт меня, пока оно длится.

o.en: After some days spent in listless indolence, during which I traversed many leagues, I arrived at Strasburgh, where I waited two days for Clerval.
o.ru: Проведя несколько дней в вялом бездействии, за которые я проехал много лиг, я прибыл в Страсбург, где два дня ждал Клерваля.

o.en: He came.
Alas, how great was the contrast between us!
o.ru: Увы, как велика была разница между нами!

o.en: He was alive to every new scene, joyful when he saw the beauties of the setting sun, and more happy when he beheld it rise and recommence a new day.
o.ru: Он живо откликался на каждый новый вид, радовался, видя красоту заходящего солнца, и был ещё счастливее, когда смотрел, как оно восходит и начинает новый день.

o.en: He pointed out to me the shifting colours of the landscape and the appearances of the sky.
o.ru: Он показывал мне меняющиеся краски пейзажа и облик неба.

o.en: “This is what it is to live,” he cried; “now I enjoy existence! But you, my dear Frankenstein, wherefore are you desponding and sorrowful!”
o.ru: «Вот что значит жить! — восклицал он. — Теперь я наслаждаюсь существованием! Но ты, дорогой Франкенштейн, отчего ты так уныл и печален?»

o.en: In truth, I was occupied by gloomy thoughts and neither saw the descent of the evening star nor the golden sunrise reflected in the Rhine.
o.ru: По правде говоря, я был поглощён мрачными мыслями и не видел ни заката вечерней звезды, ни золотого восхода, отражённого в Рейне.

o.en: And you, my friend, would be far more amused with the journal of Clerval, who observed the scenery with an eye of feeling and delight, than in listening to my reflections.
o.ru: И вам, друг мой, было бы куда интереснее читать дневник Клерваля, который смотрел на природу с чувством и восторгом, чем слушать мои размышления.

o.en: I, a miserable wretch, haunted by a curse that shut up every avenue to enjoyment.
o.ru: Я же был несчастным горемыкой, преследуемым проклятием, которое закрывало все пути к радости.

o.en: We had agreed to descend the Rhine in a boat from Strasburgh to Rotterdam, whence we might take shipping for London.
o.ru: Мы договорились спуститься по Рейну на лодке от Страсбурга до Роттердама, откуда могли бы отплыть на корабле в Лондон.

o.en: During this voyage we passed many willowy islands and saw several beautiful towns.
o.ru: Во время этого плавания мы миновали множество островов, поросших ивами, и видели несколько красивых городов.

o.en: We stayed a day at Mannheim, and on the fifth from our departure from Strasburgh, arrived at Mainz.
o.ru: Мы провели день в Мангейме, а на пятый день после отъезда из Страсбурга прибыли в Майнц.

o.en: The course of the Rhine below Mainz becomes much more picturesque.
o.ru: Ниже Майнца течение Рейна становится гораздо живописнее.

o.en: The river descends rapidly and winds between hills, not high, but steep, and of beautiful forms.
o.ru: Река стремительно спускается и петляет между холмами — невысокими, но крутыми и красивых очертаний.

o.en: We saw many ruined castles standing on the edges of precipices, surrounded by black woods, high and inaccessible.
o.ru: Мы видели множество разрушенных замков, стоящих на краю обрывов, в окружении чёрных лесов, высоких и неприступных.

o.en: This part of the Rhine, indeed, presents a singularly variegated landscape.
o.ru: Эта часть Рейна и в самом деле являет необыкновенно разнообразный пейзаж.

o.en: In one spot you view rugged hills, ruined castles overlooking tremendous precipices, with the dark Rhine rushing beneath; and on the sudden turn of a promontory, flourishing vineyards with green sloping banks and a meandering river and populous towns occupy the scene.
o.ru: В одном месте видишь суровые холмы, разрушенные замки над страшными обрывами и тёмный Рейн, мчащийся внизу; а за крутым поворотом мыса — цветущие виноградники с зелёными пологими берегами, извилистую реку и многолюдные города.

o.en: We travelled at the time of the vintage and heard the song of the labourers as we glided down the stream.
o.ru: Мы путешествовали во время сбора винограда и слышали песни работников, скользя вниз по течению.

o.en: Even I, depressed in mind, and my spirits continually agitated by gloomy feelings, even I was pleased.
o.ru: Даже я, подавленный духом, чьё настроение постоянно смущали мрачные чувства, даже я был доволен.

o.en: I lay at the bottom of the boat, and as I gazed on the cloudless blue sky, I seemed to drink in a tranquillity to which I had long been a stranger.
o.ru: Я лежал на дне лодки и, глядя в безоблачное голубое небо, словно впитывал покой, от которого давно отвык.

o.en: And if these were my sensations, who can describe those of Henry?
o.ru: И если таковы были мои ощущения, кто опишет ощущения Анри?

o.en: He felt as if he had been transported to Fairy-land and enjoyed a happiness seldom tasted by man.
o.ru: Он чувствовал себя так, будто перенёсся в волшебную страну, и наслаждался счастьем, какое редко выпадает человеку.

o.en: “I have seen,” he said, “the most beautiful scenes of my own country; I have visited the lakes of Lucerne and Uri, where the snowy mountains descend almost perpendicularly to the water, casting black and impenetrable shades, which would cause a gloomy and mournful appearance were it not for the most verdant islands that relieve the eye by their gay appearance; I have seen this lake agitated by a tempest, when the wind tore up whirlwinds of water and gave you an idea of what the water-spout must be on the great ocean; and the waves dash with fury the base of the mountain, where the priest and his mistress were overwhelmed by an avalanche and where their dying voices are still said to be heard amid the pauses of the nightly wind; I have seen the mountains of La Valais, and the Pays de Vaud; but this country, Victor, pleases me more than all those wonders.
o.ru: «Я видел, — говорил он, — прекраснейшие места моей родины; я бывал на озёрах Люцерн и Ури, где снежные горы почти отвесно спускаются к воде, отбрасывая чёрные непроницаемые тени, которые придавали бы им мрачный и скорбный вид, если бы не пышно-зелёные острова, радующие глаз своим весёлым видом; я видел это озеро взволнованным бурей, когда ветер вздымал водяные вихри и давал представление о том, каким должен быть смерч в открытом океане; и волны яростно бьют в подножие горы, где священника и его возлюбленную погребла лавина и где, говорят, их предсмертные голоса до сих пор слышны в паузах ночного ветра; я видел горы Вале и Во; но эта страна, Виктор, нравится мне больше всех этих чудес.

o.en: The mountains of Switzerland are more majestic and strange, but there is a charm in the banks of this divine river that I never before saw equalled.
o.ru: Горы Швейцарии величественнее и необычнее, но у берегов этой божественной реки есть очарование, равного которому я никогда не видел.

o.en: Look at that castle which overhangs yon precipice; and that also on the island, almost concealed amongst the foliage of those lovely trees; and now that group of labourers coming from among their vines; and that village half hid in the recess of the mountain.
o.ru: Взгляни на тот замок, что нависает над тем обрывом; и на тот, на острове, почти скрытый в листве этих чудесных деревьев; а вот группа работников идёт с виноградников; и та деревня, наполовину спрятанная в расщелине горы.

o.en: Oh, surely the spirit that inhabits and guards this place has a soul more in harmony with man than those who pile the glacier or retire to the inaccessible peaks of the mountains of our own country.”
o.ru: О, конечно, дух, что обитает здесь и охраняет это место, ближе душою к человеку, чем те, что громоздят ледники или удаляются на неприступные вершины гор нашей родины».

o.en: Clerval!
Beloved friend!
Even now it delights me to record your words and to dwell on the praise of which you are so eminently deserving.
o.ru: Даже теперь мне отрадно записывать твои слова и останавливаться на похвалах, которых ты столь в высшей степени заслуживаешь.

o.en: He was a being formed in the “very poetry of nature.”
o.ru: Он был существом, созданным из «самой поэзии природы».

o.en: His wild and enthusiastic imagination was chastened by the sensibility of his heart.
o.ru: Его пылкое, восторженное воображение смягчалось чуткостью сердца.

o.en: His soul overflowed with ardent affections, and his friendship was of that devoted and wondrous nature that the worldly-minded teach us to look for only in the imagination.
o.ru: Душа его была переполнена горячими привязанностями, а дружба его была той преданной и чудесной природы, какую люди практичные учат нас искать лишь в воображении.

o.en: But even human sympathies were not sufficient to satisfy his eager mind.
o.ru: Но даже человеческих привязанностей было недостаточно для его жадного ума.

o.en: The scenery of external nature, which others regard only with admiration, he loved with ardour:—
o.ru: Внешнюю природу, которой другие лишь восхищаются, он любил со страстью:

o.en: ——The sounding cataract Haunted him like a passion: the tall rock, The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood, Their colours and their forms, were then to him An appetite; a feeling, and a love, That had no need of a remoter charm, By thought supplied, or any interest Unborrow’d from the eye.
o.ru: ——Шумящий водопад / Преследовал его, как страсть: высокая скала, / Гора, и глубокий, и сумрачный лес, / Их краски и их формы были для него тогда / Желанием, чувством и любовью, / Которым не нужна была иная прелесть, / Привнесённая мыслью, или интерес, / Не заимствованный у глаза.

o.en: [Wordsworth’s “Tintern Abbey”.]
And where does he now exist?
Is this gentle and lovely being lost for ever?
o.ru: Неужели это кроткое и прекрасное существо потеряно навсегда?

o.en: Has this mind, so replete with ideas, imaginations fanciful and magnificent, which formed a world, whose existence depended on the life of its creator;—has this mind perished?
o.ru: Неужели этот ум, столь полный идей, причудливых и великолепных фантазий, создававший целый мир, существование которого зависело от жизни его творца, — неужели этот ум погиб?

o.en: Does it now only exist in my memory?
o.ru: Неужели он живёт теперь лишь в моей памяти?

o.en: No, it is not thus; your form so divinely wrought, and beaming with beauty, has decayed, but your spirit still visits and consoles your unhappy friend.
o.ru: Нет, это не так; твой облик, так божественно созданный и сиявший красотой, истлел, но твой дух всё ещё навещает и утешает твоего несчастного друга.

o.en: Pardon this gush of sorrow; these ineffectual words are but a slight tribute to the unexampled worth of Henry, but they soothe my heart, overflowing with the anguish which his remembrance creates.
o.ru: Простите этот порыв скорби; эти бессильные слова — лишь слабая дань несравненным достоинствам Анри, но они успокаивают моё сердце, переполненное мукой, которую рождает память о нём.

o.en: I will proceed with my tale.
Beyond Cologne we descended to the plains of Holland; and we resolved to post the remainder of our way, for the wind was contrary and the stream of the river was too gentle to aid us.
o.ru: За Кёльном мы спустились на равнины Голландии и решили оставшуюся часть пути проехать на почтовых, так как ветер был встречный, а течение реки слишком слабым, чтобы помочь нам.

o.en: Our journey here lost the interest arising from beautiful scenery, but we arrived in a few days at Rotterdam, whence we proceeded by sea to England.
o.ru: Здесь наше путешествие утратило интерес, который придавали ему красивые виды, но через несколько дней мы прибыли в Роттердам, откуда морем отправились в Англию.

o.en: It was on a clear morning, in the latter days of December, that I first saw the white cliffs of Britain.
o.ru: Ясным утром, в последние дни декабря, я впервые увидел белые скалы Британии.

o.en: The banks of the Thames presented a new scene; they were flat but fertile, and almost every town was marked by the remembrance of some story.
o.ru: Берега Темзы представили новую картину: они были плоскими, но плодородными, и почти каждый город был отмечен памятью о какой-нибудь истории.

o.en: We saw Tilbury Fort and remembered the Spanish Armada, Gravesend, Woolwich, and Greenwich—places which I had heard of even in my country.
o.ru: Мы видели форт Тилбери и вспомнили Испанскую армаду, Грейвсенд, Вулидж и Гринвич — места, о которых я слышал ещё на родине.

o.en: At length we saw the numerous steeples of London, St. Paul’s towering above all, and the Tower famed in English history.
o.ru: Наконец мы увидели многочисленные шпили Лондона, над которыми возвышался собор Святого Павла, и Тауэр, прославленный в английской истории.

b2.en: Days and weeks slipped by after my return to Geneva, and I could not summon the courage to begin my work again.
b2.ru: Дни и недели ускользали один за другим после моего возвращения в Женеву, а я никак не мог набраться смелости, чтобы снова взяться за работу.

b2.en: I dreaded the revenge of the frustrated fiend, yet I could not overcome my disgust at the task that had been forced upon me.
b2.ru: Я страшился мести обманутого демона, но не мог преодолеть отвращения к задаче, которую мне навязали.

b2.en: I realised that I could not create a female without once again spending several months in deep study and painstaking research.
b2.ru: Я понял, что не смогу создать женщину, не потратив снова несколько месяцев на глубокое изучение и кропотливые исследования.

b2.en: I had heard that an English scientist had made certain discoveries which were essential to my success, and I sometimes considered asking my father’s permission to visit England for this purpose; but I clung to every excuse for delay and shrank from taking the first step in a task that no longer seemed quite so urgent.
