He mentioned the beauties of his native country and asked us if those were not sufficient allurements to induce us to prolong our journey as far north as Perth, where he resided. Clerval eagerly desired to accept this invitation, and I, although I abhorred society, wished to view again mountains and streams and all the wondrous works with which Nature adorns her chosen dwelling-places.

We had arrived in England at the beginning of October, and it was now February. We accordingly determined to commence our journey towards the north at the expiration of another month. In this expedition we did not intend to follow the great road to Edinburgh, but to visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Cumberland lakes, resolving to arrive at the completion of this tour about the end of July. I packed up my chemical instruments and the materials I had collected, resolving to finish my labours in some obscure nook in the northern highlands of Scotland.

We quitted London on the 27th of March and remained a few days at Windsor, rambling in its beautiful forest. This was a new scene to us mountaineers; the majestic oaks, the quantity of game, and the herds of stately deer were all novelties to us.

From thence we proceeded to Oxford. As we entered this city, our minds were filled with the remembrance of the events that had been transacted there more than a century and a half before. It was here that Charles I. had collected his forces. This city had remained faithful to him, after the whole nation had forsaken his cause to join the standard of Parliament and liberty. The memory of that unfortunate king and his companions, the amiable Falkland, the insolent Goring, his queen, and son, gave a peculiar interest to every part of the city which they might be supposed to have inhabited.

The spirit of elder days found a dwelling here, and we delighted to trace its footsteps. If these feelings had not found an imaginary gratification, the appearance of the city had yet in itself sufficient beauty to obtain our admiration. The colleges are ancient and picturesque; the streets are almost magnificent; and the lovely Isis, which flows beside it through meadows of exquisite verdure, is spread forth into a placid expanse of waters, which reflects its majestic assemblage of towers, and spires, and domes, embosomed among aged trees.

I enjoyed this scene, and yet my enjoyment was embittered both by the memory of the past and the anticipation of the future. I was formed for peaceful happiness. During my youthful days discontent never visited my mind, and if I was ever overcome by ennui, the sight of what is beautiful in nature or the study of what is excellent and sublime in the productions of man could always interest my heart and communicate elasticity to my spirits. But I am a blasted tree; the bolt has entered my soul; and I felt then that I should survive to exhibit what I shall soon cease to be—a miserable spectacle of wrecked humanity, pitiable to others and intolerable to myself.

We passed a considerable period at Oxford, rambling among its environs and endeavouring to identify every spot which might relate to the most animating epoch of English history. Our little voyages of discovery were often prolonged by the successive objects that presented themselves. We visited the tomb of the illustrious Hampden and the field on which that patriot fell. For a moment my soul was elevated from its debasing and miserable fears to contemplate the divine ideas of liberty and self-sacrifice of which these sights were the monuments and the remembrancers. For an instant I dared to shake off my chains and look around me with a free and lofty spirit, but the iron had eaten into my flesh, and I sank again, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford with regret and proceeded to Matlock, which was our next place of rest. The country in the neighbourhood of this village resembled, to a greater degree, the scenery of Switzerland; but everything is on a lower scale, and the green hills want the crown of distant white Alps which always attend on the piny mountains of my native country. We visited the wondrous cave and the little cabinets of natural history, where the curiosities are disposed in the same manner as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. The latter name made me tremble when pronounced by Henry, and I hastened to quit Matlock, with which that terrible scene was thus associated.

From Derby, still journeying northwards, we passed two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could now almost fancy myself among the Swiss mountains. The little patches of snow which yet lingered on the northern sides of the mountains, the lakes, and the dashing of the rocky streams were all familiar and dear sights to me. Here also we made some acquaintances, who almost contrived to cheat me into happiness. The delight of Clerval was proportionably greater than mine; his mind expanded in the company of men of talent, and he found in his own nature greater capacities and resources than he could have imagined himself to have possessed while he associated with his inferiors. “I could pass my life here,” said he to me; “and among these mountains I should scarcely regret Switzerland and the Rhine.”

But he found that a traveller’s life is one that includes much pain amidst its enjoyments. His feelings are for ever on the stretch; and when he begins to sink into repose, he finds himself obliged to quit that on which he rests in pleasure for something new, which again engages his attention, and which also he forsakes for other novelties.

We had scarcely visited the various lakes of Cumberland and Westmorland and conceived an affection for some of the inhabitants when the period of our appointment with our Scotch friend approached, and we left them to travel on. For my own part I was not sorry. I had now neglected my promise for some time, and I feared the effects of the dæmon’s disappointment. He might remain in Switzerland and wreak his vengeance on my relatives. This idea pursued me and tormented me at every moment from which I might otherwise have snatched repose and peace.

I waited for my letters with feverish impatience; if they were delayed I was miserable and overcome by a thousand fears; and when they arrived and I saw the superscription of Elizabeth or my father, I hardly dared to read and ascertain my fate. Sometimes I thought that the fiend followed me and might expedite my remissness by murdering my companion. When these thoughts possessed me, I would not quit Henry for a moment, but followed him as his shadow, to protect him from the fancied rage of his destroyer. I felt as if I had committed some great crime, the consciousness of which haunted me. I was guiltless, but I had indeed drawn down a horrible curse upon my head, as mortal as that of crime.

I visited Edinburgh with languid eyes and mind; and yet that city might have interested the most unfortunate being. Clerval did not like it so well as Oxford, for the antiquity of the latter city was more pleasing to him. But the beauty and regularity of the new town of Edinburgh, its romantic castle and its environs, the most delightful in the world, Arthur’s Seat, St. Bernard’s Well, and the Pentland Hills, compensated him for the change and filled him with cheerfulness and admiration. But I was impatient to arrive at the termination of my journey.

We left Edinburgh in a week, passing through Coupar, St. Andrew’s, and along the banks of the Tay, to Perth, where our friend expected us. But I was in no mood to laugh and talk with strangers or enter into their feelings or plans with the good humour expected from a guest; and accordingly I told Clerval that I wished to make the tour of Scotland alone. “Do you,” said I, “enjoy yourself, and let this be our rendezvous. I may be absent a month or two; but do not interfere with my motions, I entreat you; leave me to peace and solitude for a short time; and when I return, I hope it will be with a lighter heart, more congenial to your own temper.”

Henry wished to dissuade me, but seeing me bent on this plan, ceased to remonstrate. He entreated me to write often. “I had rather be with you,” he said, “in your solitary rambles, than with these Scotch people, whom I do not know; hasten, then, my dear friend, to return, that I may again feel myself somewhat at home, which I cannot do in your absence.”

Having parted from my friend, I determined to visit some remote spot of Scotland and finish my work in solitude. I did not doubt but that the monster followed me and would discover himself to me when I should have finished, that he might receive his companion.

With this resolution I traversed the northern highlands and fixed on one of the remotest of the Orkneys as the scene of my labours. It was a place fitted for such a work, being hardly more than a rock whose high sides were continually beaten upon by the waves. The soil was barren, scarcely affording pasture for a few miserable cows, and oatmeal for its inhabitants, which consisted of five persons, whose gaunt and scraggy limbs gave tokens of their miserable fare. Vegetables and bread, when they indulged in such luxuries, and even fresh water, was to be procured from the mainland, which was about five miles distant.

On the whole island there were but three miserable huts, and one of these was vacant when I arrived. This I hired. It contained but two rooms, and these exhibited all the squalidness of the most miserable penury. The thatch had fallen in, the walls were unplastered, and the door was off its hinges. I ordered it to be repaired, bought some furniture, and took possession, an incident which would doubtless have occasioned some surprise had not all the senses of the cottagers been benumbed by want and squalid poverty. As it was, I lived ungazed at and unmolested, hardly thanked for the pittance of food and clothes which I gave, so much does suffering blunt even the coarsest sensations of men.

In this retreat I devoted the morning to labour; but in the evening, when the weather permitted, I walked on the stony beach of the sea to listen to the waves as they roared and dashed at my feet. It was a monotonous yet ever-changing scene. I thought of Switzerland; it was far different from this desolate and appalling landscape. Its hills are covered with vines, and its cottages are scattered thickly in the plains. Its fair lakes reflect a blue and gentle sky, and when troubled by the winds, their tumult is but as the play of a lively infant when compared to the roarings of the giant ocean.

In this manner I distributed my occupations when I first arrived, but as I proceeded in my labour, it became every day more horrible and irksome to me. Sometimes I could not prevail on myself to enter my laboratory for several days, and at other times I toiled day and night in order to complete my work. It was, indeed, a filthy process in which I was engaged. During my first experiment, a kind of enthusiastic frenzy had blinded me to the horror of my employment; my mind was intently fixed on the consummation of my labour, and my eyes were shut to the horror of my proceedings. But now I went to it in cold blood, and my heart often sickened at the work of my hands.

Thus situated, employed in the most detestable occupation, immersed in a solitude where nothing could for an instant call my attention from the actual scene in which I was engaged, my spirits became unequal; I grew restless and nervous. Every moment I feared to meet my persecutor. Sometimes I sat with my eyes fixed on the ground, fearing to raise them lest they should encounter the object which I so much dreaded to behold. I feared to wander from the sight of my fellow creatures lest when alone he should come to claim his companion.

In the mean time I worked on, and my labour was already considerably advanced. I looked towards its completion with a tremulous and eager hope, which I dared not trust myself to question but which was intermixed with obscure forebodings of evil that made my heart sicken in my bosom.
b2: London was where we stopped to rest for now; we decided to stay several months in this wonderful and famous city. Clerval wanted to meet the brilliant and talented men who were flourishing at that time, but for me this was of secondary importance. I was mainly concerned with finding the information I needed to fulfil my promise, and I quickly made use of the letters of introduction I had brought with me, addressed to the most distinguished scientists.

If this journey had taken place in my days of study and happiness, it would have given me indescribable pleasure. But a blight had fallen on my life, and I visited these people only for the information they might give me on the subject that concerned me so terribly deeply. Company was tiresome to me; when I was alone, I could fill my mind with the sights of heaven and earth, and Henry’s voice soothed me, so I could trick myself into a brief peace. But busy, dull, cheerful faces brought despair back into my heart. I saw an impassable barrier between me and other people; it was sealed with the blood of William and Justine, and thinking about the events linked to those names filled my soul with anguish.

But in Clerval I saw the image of my former self; he was curious and eager to gain experience and knowledge. The different customs he observed were an endless source of learning and amusement for him. He was also pursuing a goal he had long had in mind. He planned to go to India, believing that his knowledge of its languages and his understanding of its society would allow him to contribute significantly to the progress of European colonization and trade. Only in Britain could he move his plan forward.

He was always busy, and the only thing that spoiled his enjoyment was my sad and gloomy state of mind. I tried to hide this as much as I could, so as not to deprive him of the pleasures natural to someone starting a new chapter of life, untroubled by any worry or bitter memory. I often refused to go with him, pretending I had another appointment, so that I could stay alone. I also began to gather the materials I needed for my new creation, and this felt like the torture of single drops of water falling endlessly on my head. Every thought I gave to it was extreme agony, and every word I spoke about it made my lips tremble and my heart pound.

After spending some months in London, we received a letter from a man in Scotland who had once visited us in Geneva. He described the beauties of his native country and asked whether they were not tempting enough to persuade us to extend our journey as far north as Perth, where he lived. Clerval was eager to accept the invitation, and although I hated company, I wanted to see mountains and streams again, and all the marvellous works with which Nature decorates her favourite places.

We had arrived in England at the beginning of October, and it was now February. So we decided to set off for the north at the end of another month. We did not intend to take the main road to Edinburgh, but to visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock and the Cumberland lakes, planning to finish this tour around the end of July. I packed up my chemical instruments and the materials I had collected, determined to finish my work in some hidden corner of the Scottish Highlands. We left London on the 27th of March and spent a few days at Windsor, wandering in its beautiful forest. This was a new kind of scenery for us mountain people; the majestic oaks, the abundance of game and the herds of stately deer were all new to us.

From there we went on to Oxford. As we entered the city, our minds were filled with memories of the events that had taken place there more than a hundred and fifty years earlier. It was here that Charles I had gathered his forces. This city had stayed loyal to him after the whole nation had abandoned his cause and joined the side of Parliament and liberty. The memory of that unfortunate king and his companions – the charming Falkland, the arrogant Goring, his queen and his son – gave a special interest to every part of the city where they might have lived.

The spirit of former times seemed to live here, and we loved following in its footsteps. Even if these feelings had not been satisfied by our imagination, the city itself was beautiful enough to win our admiration. The colleges are old and picturesque, the streets are almost magnificent, and the lovely Isis, which flows beside the city through beautifully green meadows, spreads out into a calm stretch of water that reflects its majestic collection of towers, spires and domes, nestled among ancient trees.

I enjoyed this scene, and yet my enjoyment was spoiled both by memories of the past and by fears of the future. I was made for peaceful happiness. In my youth I never felt discontented, and if I was ever overcome by boredom, the beauty of nature or the study of the finest and noblest human achievements could always interest my heart and lift my spirits. But I am a tree struck by lightning; the bolt has entered my soul, and I felt even then that I would live on only to show what I will soon stop being – a miserable picture of ruined humanity, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent quite a long time at Oxford, wandering around the surrounding area and trying to identify every place connected with the most exciting period of English history. Our little journeys of discovery were often extended by the new sights that kept appearing. We visited the tomb of the famous Hampden and the field where that patriot died. For a moment my soul rose above its degrading and miserable fears to think about the noble ideas of liberty and self-sacrifice that these places commemorated. For an instant I dared to throw off my chains and look around with a free and lofty spirit, but the iron had eaten into my flesh, and I sank back, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford with regret and went on to Matlock, our next stop. The countryside around this village looked more like Switzerland, but everything was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the crown of distant white Alps that always rises above the pine-covered mountains of my homeland. We visited the wonderful cave and the little natural history museums, where the curiosities were arranged in the same way as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry mentioned the name Chamounix, I trembled, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which had become connected in my mind with that terrible scene.

From Derby we travelled on northwards and spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. Now I could almost imagine I was among the Swiss mountains. The little patches of snow still lingering on the northern slopes, the lakes and the rushing of the rocky streams were all familiar and dear sights to me. Here, too, we got to know some people who almost managed to trick me into being happy. Clerval’s delight was far greater than mine; his mind grew in the company of talented men, and he discovered in himself greater abilities and resources than he could have imagined while he spent his time with people less gifted than himself. “I could spend my life here,” he said to me, “and among these mountains I would hardly miss Switzerland and the Rhine.”

But he found that a traveller’s life brings a great deal of pain along with its pleasures. A traveller’s feelings are always on edge, and just when he begins to settle into rest, he has to leave what he is enjoying for something new, which captures his attention in turn and which he also abandons for other novelties.

We had hardly visited the various lakes of Cumberland and Westmorland and grown fond of some of the local people when the time of our meeting with our Scottish friend drew near, and we left them to continue our journey. For my part, I was not sorry. I had neglected my promise for some time, and I feared how the daemon would react to his disappointment. He might stay in Switzerland and take his revenge on my family. This thought haunted and tormented me at every moment when I might otherwise have snatched some rest and peace.

I waited for my letters with feverish impatience; if they were late, I was miserable and overwhelmed by a thousand fears, and when they came and I saw Elizabeth’s or my father’s handwriting on them, I hardly dared to read them and find out my fate. Sometimes I thought that the fiend was following me and might punish my delay by murdering my companion. When these thoughts took hold of me, I would not leave Henry for a moment but followed him like his shadow, to protect him from the rage I imagined in his murderer. I felt as if I had committed some great crime and was haunted by the awareness of it. I was innocent, but I had truly brought down on my head a horrible curse, as deadly as that of crime.

I visited Edinburgh with a weary eye and a listless mind, and yet that city might have interested even the unhappiest person. Clerval did not like it as much as Oxford, because he preferred the older city’s antiquity. But the beauty and orderliness of Edinburgh’s new town, its romantic castle and its surroundings, the most delightful in the world – Arthur’s Seat, St. Bernard’s Well and the Pentland Hills – made up for the change and filled him with cheerfulness and admiration. But I was impatient to reach the end of my journey.

We left Edinburgh after a week, passing through Coupar, St. Andrew’s and along the banks of the Tay to Perth, where our friend was expecting us. But I was in no mood to laugh and chat with strangers or to share in their feelings and plans with the good humour expected of a guest, so I told Clerval that I wanted to tour Scotland on my own. “Enjoy yourself,” I said, “and let this be our meeting place. I may be away for a month or two, but please don’t interfere with my movements, I beg you; leave me in peace and solitude for a short while, and when I come back, I hope it will be with a lighter heart, more in tune with your own mood.”

Henry tried to talk me out of it, but when he saw I was set on this plan, he stopped arguing. He begged me to write often. “I would rather be with you on your lonely walks,” he said, “than with these Scottish people I don’t know; so hurry back, my dear friend, so that I can feel a little at home again, which I cannot do while you are away.”

After parting from my friend, I decided to go to some remote part of Scotland and finish my work in solitude. I had no doubt that the monster was following me and would reveal himself to me when I had finished, so that he could receive his companion.

With this aim I crossed the northern Highlands and chose one of the most remote of the Orkney Islands as the place for my work. It was a place well suited to such a task, being little more than a rock whose high sides were constantly battered by the waves. The soil was barren, barely providing grass for a few wretched cows and oats for the inhabitants, who numbered five, and whose thin, bony limbs showed how poor their food was. Vegetables and bread, when they allowed themselves such luxuries, and even fresh water, had to be brought from the mainland, about five miles away.

On the whole island there were only three miserable huts, and one of them was empty when I arrived. I rented it. It had only two rooms, and they showed all the squalor of the most wretched poverty. The thatched roof had collapsed, the walls were bare, and the door had come off its hinges. I had it repaired, bought some furniture and moved in – something that would no doubt have caused some surprise if the islanders’ senses had not been dulled by need and wretched poverty. As it was, I lived without being stared at or disturbed, barely thanked for the small amounts of food and clothes I gave them – so much does suffering blunt even the most basic human feelings.

In this retreat I spent the mornings working, but in the evenings, when the weather allowed, I walked on the stony beach to listen to the waves as they roared and crashed at my feet. It was a monotonous yet constantly changing scene. I thought of Switzerland; it was so different from this bleak and dreadful landscape. Its hills are covered with vines, and its cottages are scattered thickly across the plains. Its beautiful lakes reflect a blue and gentle sky, and when the winds stir them up, their turmoil is like the play of a lively child compared to the roaring of the giant ocean.

This was how I divided my time when I first arrived, but as I went on with my work, it became more horrible and hateful to me every day. Sometimes I could not bring myself to enter my laboratory for several days, and at other times I worked hard day and night to finish my task. It was, indeed, a disgusting process I was involved in. During my first experiment, a kind of passionate frenzy had blinded me to the horror of what I was doing; my mind was fixed on completing my work, and my eyes were closed to the horror of my actions. But now I went to it in cold blood, and my heart often sickened at the work of my hands.

In this situation, busy with the most hateful task and buried in a solitude where nothing could distract me even for a moment from what I was doing, my mood became unstable; I grew restless and nervous. Every moment I was afraid of meeting my persecutor. Sometimes I sat with my eyes fixed on the ground, afraid to raise them in case they met the creature I dreaded seeing so much. I was afraid to wander out of sight of other people in case, when I was alone, he came to claim his companion. Meanwhile I kept working, and my work was already well advanced. I looked forward to finishing it with a trembling and eager hope, which I did not dare to question, but which was mixed with vague forebodings of evil that made my heart sick within me.
b1: We stopped in London and decided to stay several months in this wonderful, famous city. Clerval wanted to meet the clever and talented people who lived there at that time. For me this was not so important. I mainly wanted to find the information I needed to keep my promise. So I quickly used the letters of introduction I had brought with me to meet the best scientists.

If I had made this journey in my happy student days, it would have given me great pleasure. But now my life was ruined, and I visited these people only because of the information they could give me. I did not like being with other people. When I was alone, I could look at the sky and the earth, and Henry’s voice calmed me, so for a short time I could feel almost at peace. But busy, happy faces brought my despair back. I felt there was a wall between me and other people, a wall made with the blood of William and Justine. Thinking about them filled my soul with pain.

But in Clerval I saw the person I used to be. He was curious and wanted to learn and experience new things. The different customs he saw taught him a lot and gave him endless fun. He also had a plan he had been thinking about for a long time. He wanted to go to India, because he believed that his knowledge of its languages and people could help European trade there. Only in Britain could he prepare for this plan.

He was always busy, and the only thing that spoiled his fun was my sadness. I tried to hide it as much as I could, because I did not want to spoil the pleasures of a young man starting a new life without any worries or sad memories. I often said I had another appointment and did not go with him, so that I could be alone. I also started to collect the materials for my new creature. This was like torture, like drops of water falling on my head again and again. Every thought about it gave me terrible pain, and every word about it made my lips shake and my heart beat fast.

After some months in London, we got a letter from a man in Scotland who had once visited us in Geneva. He wrote about the beauty of his country and asked us to travel north to Perth, where he lived. Clerval really wanted to accept. I hated being with people, but I wanted to see mountains, rivers and the wonderful places of nature again.

We had come to England at the beginning of October, and now it was February. So we decided to start our journey north after one more month. We did not want to take the main road to Edinburgh. Instead, we planned to visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock and the Cumberland lakes and to finish the tour at the end of July. I packed my chemical instruments and materials, because I wanted to finish my work in some quiet, hidden place in the north of Scotland. We left London on the 27th of March and stayed a few days at Windsor, walking in its beautiful forest. For us mountain people this was something new: the great oaks, the many wild animals and the groups of beautiful deer.

From there we went to Oxford. As we came into the city, we remembered the events that had happened there more than a hundred and fifty years before. King Charles I had gathered his army here. This city stayed loyal to him when the rest of the country had left him and joined Parliament. We thought about the unlucky king and the people around him – Falkland, Goring, his queen and his son – and every place where they had perhaps lived seemed very interesting to us.

We felt the spirit of old times here, and we loved to follow it. But even without these thoughts, the city was beautiful enough for us to admire it. The colleges are old and very pretty, and the streets are almost grand. The lovely river Isis flows past the city through bright green fields and becomes a wide, calm stretch of water. It reflects the city’s towers, spires and domes among the old trees.

I enjoyed this view, but my memories of the past and my fears about the future spoiled my pleasure. I was made to be happy and peaceful. When I was young, I was never unhappy, and if I ever felt bored, the beauty of nature or great works of art and science always interested me and made me feel better. But now I am like a tree hit by lightning; the lightning has gone into my soul. Even then I felt that I would live only to become a sad picture of a broken man, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent quite a long time in Oxford, walking around the area and looking for places connected with the most exciting time in English history. Our little trips often took longer because we kept finding new things to see. We visited the grave of the famous Hampden and the field where he died. For a moment I forgot my terrible fears and thought about the great ideas of freedom and self-sacrifice that these places remembered. For a moment I tried to break my chains and feel free, but the chains had cut deep into me, and I fell back, shaking and without hope, into my misery.

We left Oxford sadly and went on to Matlock, our next stop. The countryside around this village was more like Switzerland, but everything was smaller. The green hills did not have the white Alps in the distance, which you can always see above the pine-covered mountains of my country. We visited the wonderful cave and the small natural history museums, where things were shown in the same way as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry said the name Chamounix, I trembled, and I quickly left Matlock, because it now reminded me of that terrible scene.

From Derby we continued north and spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. Here I could almost imagine that I was in the Swiss mountains. The small patches of snow on the northern sides of the mountains, the lakes and the fast rocky streams were all familiar and dear to me. We met some people here who almost made me happy. Clerval was much happier than I was. His mind grew in the company of talented men, and he found that he was more able than he had thought when he was with less clever people. “I could spend my whole life here,” he said to me, “and in these mountains I would hardly miss Switzerland and the Rhine.”

But he learned that a traveller’s life has a lot of pain as well as pleasure. A traveller’s feelings are always tense. Just when he starts to relax and enjoy a place, he has to leave it for something new, and then he leaves that too for other new things.

We had only just visited the lakes of Cumberland and Westmorland and started to like some of the local people when it was time to meet our Scottish friend, so we left them and travelled on. I was not sorry. I had not worked on my promise for some time, and I was afraid of what the monster would do when he was disappointed. He might stay in Switzerland and take revenge on my family. This thought followed me and tortured me every moment when I could have had some rest.

I waited for my letters with great impatience. If they were late, I was miserable and full of fears. When they came and I saw the handwriting of Elizabeth or my father, I was almost too afraid to read them and learn what had happened. Sometimes I thought that the monster was following me and might kill my friend to punish me for being slow. At those times I stayed with Henry every moment and followed him like a shadow to protect him. I felt as if I had done some great crime, and this feeling never left me. I was innocent, but I had brought a terrible curse on myself, as deadly as the curse of crime.

I visited Edinburgh with tired eyes and a tired mind, but that city could interest even the unhappiest person. Clerval did not like it as much as Oxford, because he preferred Oxford’s old buildings. But the beautiful new town of Edinburgh, its romantic castle and the lovely places around it – Arthur’s Seat, St. Bernard’s Well and the Pentland Hills – made him cheerful and full of admiration. But I was impatient to get to the end of my journey.

After a week we left Edinburgh and travelled through Coupar, St. Andrew’s and along the river Tay to Perth, where our friend was waiting for us. But I did not want to laugh and talk with strangers or to be a cheerful guest, so I told Clerval that I wanted to travel around Scotland alone. “Have a good time,” I said, “and let’s meet here again. I may be away for a month or two, but please don’t try to stop me. Leave me alone in peace for a short time, and when I come back, I hope my heart will be lighter and I will be better company for you.”

Henry tried to change my mind, but when he saw that I had decided, he stopped. He asked me to write often. “I would prefer to be with you on your lonely walks,” he said, “than with these Scottish people I don’t know. So come back soon, my dear friend, so that I can feel at home again, because I can’t without you.”

After I said goodbye to my friend, I decided to go to some faraway place in Scotland and finish my work alone. I was sure that the monster was following me and would come to me when I finished, to take his companion.

So I travelled across the northern Highlands and chose one of the most distant Orkney Islands as the place for my work. It was a good place for such work, because it was almost just a rock, and the waves beat against its high sides all the time. The soil was poor. There was hardly enough grass for a few thin cows and oats for the people. Only five people lived there, and their thin, bony arms and legs showed how badly they ate. Vegetables, bread and even fresh water had to come from the mainland, about five miles away.

There were only three poor huts on the whole island, and one of them was empty when I arrived. I rented it. It had only two rooms, and they were dirty and very poor. The roof had fallen in, the walls were bare, and the door was broken. I had it repaired, bought some furniture and moved in. This would probably have surprised the islanders, but they were too poor and hungry to notice anything. So nobody looked at me or bothered me, and they hardly thanked me for the little food and clothes I gave them. Suffering makes people feel almost nothing.

On the island I worked in the mornings. In the evenings, if the weather was good, I walked on the stony beach and listened to the waves roaring and crashing at my feet. The scene was always the same and yet always changing. I thought of Switzerland, which was so different from this sad and frightening place. There the hills are covered with vines, and there are many little houses in the valleys. The beautiful lakes reflect a soft blue sky, and even when the wind makes waves on them, they are like a playing child compared to the roaring of the great ocean.

At first I spent my time like this, but as my work went on, I hated it more every day. Sometimes I could not make myself go into my laboratory for several days, and at other times I worked day and night to finish. It really was disgusting work. During my first experiment, a kind of wild excitement had stopped me from seeing how horrible it was. I only thought about finishing my work, and I did not see the horror of what I was doing. But now I did it with a cold mind, and I often felt sick at the work of my hands.

Doing this terrible work, completely alone, with nothing to take my mind off it even for a moment, I lost my calm; I became restless and nervous. Every moment I was afraid of meeting the monster. Sometimes I sat looking at the ground, afraid to raise my eyes because I might see the creature I was so afraid of. I was afraid to go far from other people, in case he came to take his companion when I was alone. Meanwhile, I continued working, and my work was already far along. I looked forward to the end with a trembling, eager hope. I did not dare to ask myself about this hope, and it was mixed with dark feelings that something bad would happen, which made my heart sick.
a2: We stopped in London. It is a big and famous city, and we wanted to stay there for some months. Clerval wanted to meet clever and interesting people. I had a different reason. I needed information for my work, because I had to keep my promise to the monster. I had letters to some famous scientists, and I quickly went to see them.

Once, this journey would make me very happy. But now my life was dark. I only visited these people because I needed their help. I did not like to be with people. When I was alone, I looked at the sky and the earth, and Henry’s voice helped me. Then I felt a little better for a short time. But happy, busy faces made me sad again. I felt that there was a wall between me and other people. The blood of William and Justine was on this wall. When I thought about them, I felt terrible pain.

Clerval was like me in the past. He wanted to learn new things and see the world. He watched how people lived in England, and he learned a lot. He also had a big plan. He wanted to go to India, because he knew its languages and wanted to help European trade there. He could only prepare for this in Britain.

He was always busy and happy, but my sadness worried him. I tried to hide it, because I did not want to spoil his new life. I often told him I had another meeting, and then I stayed alone. I also started to collect things for the new creature. It was like torture. Every thought about it hurt me, and when I spoke about it, my lips shook and my heart beat fast.

After some months in London, a letter came from a man in Scotland. He visited us in Geneva before. He wrote about his beautiful country and invited us to his home in Perth, in the north. Clerval wanted to go. I did not like people, but I wanted to see mountains and rivers again.

We came to England in October, and now it was February. We decided to go north after one more month. We wanted to visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock and the lakes of Cumberland on the way. I packed my things for the work. I wanted to finish it in a quiet place in the north of Scotland. We left London on the 27th of March. We stayed in Windsor for a few days and walked in its beautiful forest. We came from the mountains, so the big old trees and the deer were new for us.

Then we went to Oxford. We thought about its history. About a hundred and fifty years before, King Charles I was here with his army. The rest of the country was against him, but Oxford helped him. We thought about the king and his friends, and every street was interesting for us.

We felt the old times in this place, and we liked it very much. But Oxford is also very beautiful. The colleges are old and pretty, and the streets are nearly grand. The river Isis goes past the city through green fields. The water is quiet, and you can see the towers of the city and the old trees in it.

I liked this place, but I could not forget the past, and I was afraid of the future. I was made to be happy. When I was young, I was never unhappy. Nature and books always made me feel better. But now I am like a tree after lightning hits it. I felt that I was going to be a broken man, sad for others and terrible for myself.

We stayed in Oxford for a long time. We walked around and looked for places from an exciting time in English history. We often found new things, so our walks were long. We saw the grave of Hampden, a famous man, and the field where he died. For a moment I forgot my fears and thought about freedom. I wanted to be free, but my chains were too strong. Soon I was sad and afraid again.

We left Oxford and went to Matlock. The country there looked a little like Switzerland, but the hills were smaller, and there were no white Alps behind them. We visited a wonderful cave and some small museums. They were like the museums at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry said “Chamounix”, I started to shake. I remembered the monster there, so I left Matlock quickly.

Then we travelled north and stayed two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. It was almost like the Swiss mountains. I saw snow on the mountains, lakes and fast rivers, and I loved them. We met some nice people there, and I was almost happy. Clerval was much happier than me. He talked with clever men and learned that he was clever too. “I can live here all my life,” he said. “In these mountains I don’t miss Switzerland.”
But Clerval learned that travelling is not always fun. When you start to like a place, you have to leave it and go somewhere new. Then you leave that place too.

We visited the lakes and made friends there, but soon it was time to meet our friend in Scotland. I was not sorry to go. I was not working on my promise, and I was afraid of the monster. Maybe he was angry. Maybe he was in Switzerland and wanted to hurt my family. I thought about this all the time, and I could not rest.

I waited for letters from home every day. When they were late, I was very afraid. When they came, I was almost afraid to open them. Sometimes I thought that the monster was following me and wanted to kill Henry. Then I stayed near Henry all the time, like his shadow. I felt like a criminal. I did not do anything wrong, but there was a terrible curse on me.

Then we visited Edinburgh. It is an interesting city, but I was too tired and sad to enjoy it. Clerval liked Oxford more because it was older. But he liked the new town, the castle and the beautiful hills, and he was happy again. I only wanted to get to the end of the journey.

After a week we went on to Perth, where our friend was waiting for us. But I did not want to talk and laugh with new people, so I told Clerval that I wanted to travel around Scotland alone. “Stay here and have a good time,” I said. “I will be away for a month or two. Please let me go. When I come back, I hope I will be happier.”

Henry did not want me to go, but he saw that I was not going to change my mind. He asked me to write often. “I want to be with you, not with these people,” he said. “I don’t know them. Please come back soon, my friend. I don’t feel at home without you.”

I said goodbye to my friend. I wanted to find a quiet place in Scotland and finish my work alone. I was sure that the monster was following me. He was going to come when I finished, and take his wife.

I travelled across the north of Scotland and chose a small island in the Orkneys. It was far from everything. It was almost only a big rock, and the sea hit it all the time. Not much grew there. Only five people lived on the island, and they were very thin and poor. They got bread, vegetables and even water from the mainland, five miles away.

There were only three small houses on the island, and one was empty. I took it. It had two dirty rooms. The roof and the door were broken. I repaired the house, bought some furniture and started to live there. The people were too poor and hungry to be surprised. Nobody looked at me or asked me questions. I gave them some food and clothes, but they did not thank me much.

I worked every morning. In the evening, if the weather was good, I walked by the sea and listened to the loud waves. The sea was always the same, but it was always different too. I thought about Switzerland. It was very different from this sad, cold place. In Switzerland there are green hills and pretty houses, and the lakes are blue and quiet. Even in the wind they are like a small child next to the great ocean.

As the work went on, I hated it more and more. Sometimes I did not go into my laboratory for days. At other times I worked day and night. It was horrible, dirty work. When I made the first creature, I was too excited to see how terrible it was. Now I saw everything clearly, and I often felt sick.

I was alone, and I did this terrible work every day. I became nervous. I was always afraid that the monster was going to come. Sometimes I sat and looked at the ground, because I did not want to see him. I did not want to be far from other people. The work was nearly finished. I hoped to finish it soon, but I also felt that something bad was going to happen.

o.en: London was our present point of rest; we determined to remain several months in this wonderful and celebrated city.
o.ru: Лондон стал местом нашего нынешнего отдыха; мы решили провести несколько месяцев в этом чудесном и прославленном городе.

o.en: Clerval desired the intercourse of the men of genius and talent who flourished at this time, but this was with me a secondary object; I was principally occupied with the means of obtaining the information necessary for the completion of my promise and quickly availed myself of the letters of introduction that I had brought with me, addressed to the most distinguished natural philosophers.
o.ru: Клерваль жаждал общения с людьми гения и таланта, процветавшими в ту пору, но для меня это была цель второстепенная; я был главным образом занят поисками средств получить сведения, необходимые для исполнения моего обещания, и поспешил воспользоваться рекомендательными письмами, привезёнными с собой и адресованными самым выдающимся естествоиспытателям.

o.en: If this journey had taken place during my days of study and happiness, it would have afforded me inexpressible pleasure.
o.ru: Если бы это путешествие состоялось в дни моих занятий и счастья, оно доставило бы мне невыразимое наслаждение.

o.en: But a blight had come over my existence, and I only visited these people for the sake of the information they might give me on the subject in which my interest was so terribly profound.
o.ru: Но на моё существование легла порча, и я посещал этих людей лишь ради сведений, которые они могли дать мне о предмете, к которому я питал столь страшно глубокий интерес.

o.en: Company was irksome to me; when alone, I could fill my mind with the sights of heaven and earth; the voice of Henry soothed me, and I could thus cheat myself into a transitory peace.
o.ru: Общество было мне в тягость; оставшись один, я мог наполнить ум картинами неба и земли; голос Анри успокаивал меня, и так я мог обманом погрузить себя в мимолётный покой.

o.en: But busy, uninteresting, joyous faces brought back despair to my heart.
o.ru: Но деловитые, неинтересные, радостные лица возвращали отчаяние в моё сердце.

o.en: I saw an insurmountable barrier placed between me and my fellow men; this barrier was sealed with the blood of William and Justine, and to reflect on the events connected with those names filled my soul with anguish.
o.ru: Я видел непреодолимую преграду, воздвигнутую между мною и моими ближними; эта преграда была скреплена кровью Уильяма и Жюстины, и размышления о событиях, связанных с этими именами, наполняли мою душу мукой.

o.en: But in Clerval I saw the image of my former self; he was inquisitive and anxious to gain experience and instruction.
o.ru: Но в Клервале я видел образ себя прежнего; он был любознателен и жаждал приобрести опыт и знания.

o.en: The difference of manners which he observed was to him an inexhaustible source of instruction and amusement.
o.ru: Различие нравов, которое он наблюдал, было для него неиссякаемым источником познания и развлечения.

o.en: He was also pursuing an object he had long had in view.
o.ru: Кроме того, он преследовал цель, которую давно имел в виду.

o.en: His design was to visit India, in the belief that he had in his knowledge of its various languages, and in the views he had taken of its society, the means of materially assisting the progress of European colonization and trade.
o.ru: Он намеревался посетить Индию, полагая, что в знании её разнообразных языков и во взглядах, составленных им на её общество, он обладает средствами существенно способствовать успехам европейской колонизации и торговли.

o.en: In Britain only could he further the execution of his plan.
o.ru: Лишь в Британии мог он продвинуть исполнение своего замысла.

o.en: He was for ever busy, and the only check to his enjoyments was my sorrowful and dejected mind.
o.ru: Он был вечно занят, и единственной помехой его удовольствиям было моё печальное и подавленное состояние духа.

o.en: I tried to conceal this as much as possible, that I might not debar him from the pleasures natural to one who was entering on a new scene of life, undisturbed by any care or bitter recollection.
o.ru: Я старался по возможности скрывать это, чтобы не лишать его радостей, естественных для того, кто вступает на новое поприще жизни, не омрачённое ни заботой, ни горьким воспоминанием.

o.en: I often refused to accompany him, alleging another engagement, that I might remain alone.
o.ru: Я часто отказывался сопровождать его, ссылаясь на другое приглашение, чтобы остаться одному.

o.en: I now also began to collect the materials necessary for my new creation, and this was to me like the torture of single drops of water continually falling on the head.
o.ru: Теперь я также начал собирать материалы, необходимые для моего нового создания, и это было для меня подобно пытке, когда капли воды одна за другой беспрестанно падают на голову.

o.en: Every thought that was devoted to it was an extreme anguish, and every word that I spoke in allusion to it caused my lips to quiver, and my heart to palpitate.
o.ru: Каждая мысль, посвящённая этому, была нестерпимой мукой, и каждое слово, произнесённое мною с намёком на это, заставляло мои губы дрожать, а сердце трепетать.

o.en: After passing some months in London, we received a letter from a person in Scotland who had formerly been our visitor at Geneva.
o.ru: Проведя несколько месяцев в Лондоне, мы получили письмо от одного человека из Шотландии, который прежде гостил у нас в Женеве.

o.en: He mentioned the beauties of his native country and asked us if those were not sufficient allurements to induce us to prolong our journey as far north as Perth, where he resided.
o.ru: Он упоминал о красотах своей родины и спрашивал, не достаточно ли они соблазнительны, чтобы побудить нас продлить путешествие на север, до самого Перта, где он жил.

o.en: Clerval eagerly desired to accept this invitation, and I, although I abhorred society, wished to view again mountains and streams and all the wondrous works with which Nature adorns her chosen dwelling-places.
o.ru: Клерваль горячо желал принять это приглашение, и я, хотя питал отвращение к обществу, хотел снова увидеть горы и потоки и все дивные творения, которыми Природа украшает избранные ею обители.

o.en: We had arrived in England at the beginning of October, and it was now February.
o.ru: Мы прибыли в Англию в начале октября, а теперь был февраль.

o.en: We accordingly determined to commence our journey towards the north at the expiration of another month.
o.ru: Соответственно, мы решили начать путь на север по истечении ещё одного месяца.

o.en: In this expedition we did not intend to follow the great road to Edinburgh, but to visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Cumberland lakes, resolving to arrive at the completion of this tour about the end of July.
o.ru: В этой поездке мы не намеревались следовать большой дорогой на Эдинбург, а хотели посетить Виндзор, Оксфорд, Матлок и Камберлендские озёра, рассчитывая завершить это путешествие к концу июля.

o.en: I packed up my chemical instruments and the materials I had collected, resolving to finish my labours in some obscure nook in the northern highlands of Scotland.
o.ru: Я упаковал свои химические приборы и собранные материалы, решив закончить свои труды в каком-нибудь глухом уголке северного нагорья Шотландии.

o.en: We quitted London on the 27th of March and remained a few days at Windsor, rambling in its beautiful forest.
o.ru: Мы покинули Лондон 27 марта и провели несколько дней в Виндзоре, бродя по его прекрасному лесу.

o.en: This was a new scene to us mountaineers; the majestic oaks, the quantity of game, and the herds of stately deer were all novelties to us.
o.ru: Для нас, горцев, это было новое зрелище; величественные дубы, обилие дичи и стада статных оленей — всё было для нас в диковинку.

o.en: From thence we proceeded to Oxford.
As we entered this city, our minds were filled with the remembrance of the events that had been transacted there more than a century and a half before.
o.ru: Когда мы въезжали в этот город, наши умы наполнились воспоминаниями о событиях, свершившихся здесь более полутора столетий назад.

o.en: It was here that Charles I. had collected his forces.
o.ru: Именно здесь Карл I собирал свои силы.

o.en: This city had remained faithful to him, after the whole nation had forsaken his cause to join the standard of Parliament and liberty.
o.ru: Этот город оставался верен ему после того, как весь народ отрёкся от его дела и встал под знамя Парламента и свободы.

o.en: The memory of that unfortunate king and his companions, the amiable Falkland, the insolent Goring, his queen, and son, gave a peculiar interest to every part of the city which they might be supposed to have inhabited.
o.ru: Память об этом злосчастном короле и его соратниках — любезном Фолкленде, надменном Горинге, его королеве и сыне — придавала особый интерес каждому уголку города, где, как можно было предположить, они обитали.

o.en: The spirit of elder days found a dwelling here, and we delighted to trace its footsteps.
o.ru: Дух былых дней нашёл здесь пристанище, и мы с восторгом шли по его следам.

o.en: If these feelings had not found an imaginary gratification, the appearance of the city had yet in itself sufficient beauty to obtain our admiration.
o.ru: Даже если бы эти чувства не нашли воображаемого удовлетворения, облик города сам по себе был достаточно прекрасен, чтобы вызвать наше восхищение.

o.en: The colleges are ancient and picturesque; the streets are almost magnificent; and the lovely Isis, which flows beside it through meadows of exquisite verdure, is spread forth into a placid expanse of waters, which reflects its majestic assemblage of towers, and spires, and domes, embosomed among aged trees.
o.ru: Колледжи древние и живописные; улицы почти великолепны; а прелестная Айсис, что течёт рядом с ним среди лугов изысканной зелени, разливается безмятежной гладью вод, в которой отражается величественное собрание башен, шпилей и куполов, укрытых среди старых деревьев.

o.en: I enjoyed this scene, and yet my enjoyment was embittered both by the memory of the past and the anticipation of the future.
o.ru: Я наслаждался этой картиной, и всё же моё наслаждение было отравлено и памятью о прошлом, и предвидением будущего.

o.en: I was formed for peaceful happiness.
o.ru: Я был создан для мирного счастья.

o.en: During my youthful days discontent never visited my mind, and if I was ever overcome by ennui, the sight of what is beautiful in nature or the study of what is excellent and sublime in the productions of man could always interest my heart and communicate elasticity to my spirits.
o.ru: В дни моей юности недовольство никогда не посещало мой ум, а если меня и одолевала скука, то зрелище прекрасного в природе или изучение превосходного и возвышенного в творениях человека всегда могли увлечь моё сердце и придать бодрость моему духу.

o.en: But I am a blasted tree; the bolt has entered my soul; and I felt then that I should survive to exhibit what I shall soon cease to be—a miserable spectacle of wrecked humanity, pitiable to others and intolerable to myself.
o.ru: Но я — дерево, сражённое молнией; удар проник в мою душу; и уже тогда я чувствовал, что переживу себя лишь затем, чтобы являть собою то, чем скоро перестану быть, — жалкое зрелище разрушенной человеческой природы, достойное жалости других и невыносимое для меня самого.

o.en: We passed a considerable period at Oxford, rambling among its environs and endeavouring to identify every spot which might relate to the most animating epoch of English history.
o.ru: Мы провели немалое время в Оксфорде, бродя по его окрестностям и стараясь отыскать каждое место, которое могло быть связано с самой вдохновляющей эпохой английской истории.

o.en: Our little voyages of discovery were often prolonged by the successive objects that presented themselves.
o.ru: Наши маленькие путешествия-открытия часто затягивались из-за всё новых предметов, представавших перед нами.

o.en: We visited the tomb of the illustrious Hampden and the field on which that patriot fell.
o.ru: Мы посетили гробницу прославленного Хэмпдена и поле, на котором пал этот патриот.

o.en: For a moment my soul was elevated from its debasing and miserable fears to contemplate the divine ideas of liberty and self-sacrifice of which these sights were the monuments and the remembrancers.
o.ru: На миг моя душа возвысилась над своими унизительными и жалкими страхами, чтобы созерцать божественные идеи свободы и самопожертвования, памятниками и напоминаниями о которых служили эти места.

o.en: For an instant I dared to shake off my chains and look around me with a free and lofty spirit, but the iron had eaten into my flesh, and I sank again, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.
o.ru: На мгновение я осмелился стряхнуть свои цепи и оглядеться вокруг свободным и возвышенным духом, но железо въелось в мою плоть, и я снова погрузился, дрожащий и безнадёжный, в своё жалкое «я».

o.en: We left Oxford with regret and proceeded to Matlock, which was our next place of rest.
o.ru: Мы с сожалением покинули Оксфорд и направились в Матлок, где была наша следующая остановка.

o.en: The country in the neighbourhood of this village resembled, to a greater degree, the scenery of Switzerland; but everything is on a lower scale, and the green hills want the crown of distant white Alps which always attend on the piny mountains of my native country.
o.ru: Местность в окрестностях этой деревни в большей степени напоминала пейзажи Швейцарии; но всё здесь в меньшем масштабе, и зелёным холмам недостаёт венца далёких белых Альп, который неизменно сопутствует сосновым горам моей родины.

o.en: We visited the wondrous cave and the little cabinets of natural history, where the curiosities are disposed in the same manner as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix.
o.ru: Мы посетили дивную пещеру и маленькие кабинеты естественной истории, где диковины расположены так же, как в собраниях Сервоза и Шамони.

o.en: The latter name made me tremble when pronounced by Henry, and I hastened to quit Matlock, with which that terrible scene was thus associated.
o.ru: Последнее название, произнесённое Анри, заставило меня задрожать, и я поспешил покинуть Матлок, с которым теперь связалась та ужасная сцена.

o.en: From Derby, still journeying northwards, we passed two months in Cumberland and Westmorland.
o.ru: Из Дерби, продолжая путь на север, мы провели два месяца в Камберленде и Уэстморленде.

o.en: I could now almost fancy myself among the Swiss mountains.
o.ru: Теперь я почти мог вообразить себя среди швейцарских гор.

o.en: The little patches of snow which yet lingered on the northern sides of the mountains, the lakes, and the dashing of the rocky streams were all familiar and dear sights to me.
o.ru: Небольшие пятна снега, ещё медлившие на северных склонах гор, озёра и плеск стремительных каменистых потоков — всё это были знакомые и милые мне картины.

o.en: Here also we made some acquaintances, who almost contrived to cheat me into happiness.
o.ru: Здесь мы также завели знакомства, которые почти сумели обманом вернуть мне счастье.

o.en: The delight of Clerval was proportionably greater than mine; his mind expanded in the company of men of talent, and he found in his own nature greater capacities and resources than he could have imagined himself to have possessed while he associated with his inferiors.
o.ru: Восторг Клерваля был соответственно больше моего; его ум расширялся в обществе талантливых людей, и он находил в своей натуре больше способностей и сил, чем мог бы вообразить в себе, пока водился с теми, кто стоял ниже его.

o.en: “I could pass my life here,” said he to me; “and among these mountains I should scarcely regret Switzerland and the Rhine.”
o.ru: «Я мог бы провести здесь всю жизнь, — сказал он мне, — и среди этих гор я едва ли жалел бы о Швейцарии и Рейне».

o.en: But he found that a traveller’s life is one that includes much pain amidst its enjoyments.
o.ru: Но он обнаружил, что жизнь путешественника заключает в себе много страданий среди радостей.

o.en: His feelings are for ever on the stretch; and when he begins to sink into repose, he finds himself obliged to quit that on which he rests in pleasure for something new, which again engages his attention, and which also he forsakes for other novelties.
o.ru: Его чувства вечно напряжены; и когда он начинает погружаться в покой, то оказывается вынужден покинуть то, на чём с удовольствием отдыхает, ради чего-то нового, что вновь занимает его внимание и что он тоже оставляет ради других новинок.

o.en: We had scarcely visited the various lakes of Cumberland and Westmorland and conceived an affection for some of the inhabitants when the period of our appointment with our Scotch friend approached, and we left them to travel on.
o.ru: Едва мы успели посетить разные озёра Камберленда и Уэстморленда и проникнуться привязанностью к некоторым из жителей, как приблизился срок нашей встречи с шотландским другом, и мы покинули их, чтобы ехать дальше.

o.en: For my own part I was not sorry.
o.ru: Что до меня, я не сожалел.

o.en: I had now neglected my promise for some time, and I feared the effects of the dæmon’s disappointment.
o.ru: Я уже некоторое время пренебрегал своим обещанием и страшился последствий разочарования демона.

o.en: He might remain in Switzerland and wreak his vengeance on my relatives.
o.ru: Он мог остаться в Швейцарии и обрушить свою месть на моих родных.

o.en: This idea pursued me and tormented me at every moment from which I might otherwise have snatched repose and peace.
o.ru: Эта мысль преследовала и терзала меня в каждый миг, когда иначе я мог бы урвать немного отдыха и покоя.

o.en: I waited for my letters with feverish impatience; if they were delayed I was miserable and overcome by a thousand fears; and when they arrived and I saw the superscription of Elizabeth or my father, I hardly dared to read and ascertain my fate.
o.ru: Я ждал писем с лихорадочным нетерпением; если они задерживались, я был несчастен и одолеваем тысячей страхов; а когда они приходили и я видел надпись рукою Элизабет или отца, я едва осмеливался читать, чтобы удостовериться в своей судьбе.

o.en: Sometimes I thought that the fiend followed me and might expedite my remissness by murdering my companion.
o.ru: Порой мне казалось, что злодей следует за мной и может поторопить моё промедление, убив моего спутника.

o.en: When these thoughts possessed me, I would not quit Henry for a moment, but followed him as his shadow, to protect him from the fancied rage of his destroyer.
o.ru: Когда эти мысли овладевали мной, я ни на миг не покидал Анри и следовал за ним, как тень, чтобы защитить его от воображаемой ярости его губителя.

o.en: I felt as if I had committed some great crime, the consciousness of which haunted me.
o.ru: Я чувствовал себя так, будто совершил какое-то великое преступление, сознание которого преследовало меня.

o.en: I was guiltless, but I had indeed drawn down a horrible curse upon my head, as mortal as that of crime.
o.ru: Я был невиновен, но воистину навлёк на свою голову ужасное проклятие, столь же смертоносное, как проклятие преступления.

o.en: I visited Edinburgh with languid eyes and mind; and yet that city might have interested the most unfortunate being.
o.ru: Я посетил Эдинбург с вялым взглядом и умом; а ведь этот город мог бы заинтересовать даже самое несчастное существо.

o.en: Clerval did not like it so well as Oxford, for the antiquity of the latter city was more pleasing to him.
o.ru: Клервалю он понравился не так, как Оксфорд, ибо древность последнего была ему приятнее.

o.en: But the beauty and regularity of the new town of Edinburgh, its romantic castle and its environs, the most delightful in the world, Arthur’s Seat, St. Bernard’s Well, and the Pentland Hills, compensated him for the change and filled him with cheerfulness and admiration.
o.ru: Но красота и правильность нового города Эдинбурга, его романтический замок и окрестности, прелестнейшие в мире, Трон Артура, Колодец святого Бернарда и Пентлендские холмы вознаградили его за перемену и наполнили весельем и восхищением.

o.en: But I was impatient to arrive at the termination of my journey.
o.ru: Я же нетерпеливо стремился к завершению своего путешествия.

o.en: We left Edinburgh in a week, passing through Coupar, St. Andrew’s, and along the banks of the Tay, to Perth, where our friend expected us.
o.ru: Через неделю мы покинули Эдинбург и, проехав через Купар, Сент-Эндрюс и вдоль берегов Тея, прибыли в Перт, где нас ждал наш друг.

o.en: But I was in no mood to laugh and talk with strangers or enter into their feelings or plans with the good humour expected from a guest; and accordingly I told Clerval that I wished to make the tour of Scotland alone.
o.ru: Но я был не в настроении смеяться и беседовать с незнакомцами или входить в их чувства и планы с тем добродушием, которого ждут от гостя; а потому я сказал Клервалю, что желаю совершить поездку по Шотландии один.

o.en: “Do you,” said I, “enjoy yourself, and let this be our rendezvous.
o.ru: «Ты же, — сказал я, — развлекайся, и пусть здесь будет место нашей встречи.

o.en: I may be absent a month or two; but do not interfere with my motions, I entreat you; leave me to peace and solitude for a short time; and when I return, I hope it will be with a lighter heart, more congenial to your own temper.”
o.ru: Я могу отсутствовать месяц или два; но не препятствуй моим передвижениям, заклинаю тебя; оставь меня ненадолго в покое и уединении; и когда я вернусь, надеюсь, это будет с более лёгким сердцем, более созвучным твоему нраву».

o.en: Henry wished to dissuade me, but seeing me bent on this plan, ceased to remonstrate.
o.ru: Анри хотел отговорить меня, но, видя, что я твёрдо решился на этот план, перестал возражать.

o.en: He entreated me to write often.

“I had rather be with you,” he said, “in your solitary rambles, than with these Scotch people, whom I do not know; hasten, then, my dear friend, to return, that I may again feel myself somewhat at home, which I cannot do in your absence.”
o.ru: «Я предпочёл бы быть с тобой, — сказал он, — в твоих одиноких странствиях, чем с этими шотландцами, которых я не знаю; так поспеши же, дорогой друг, вернуться, чтобы я снова почувствовал себя хоть немного как дома, чего я не могу в твоё отсутствие».

o.en: Having parted from my friend, I determined to visit some remote spot of Scotland and finish my work in solitude.
o.ru: Расставшись с другом, я решил посетить какой-нибудь отдалённый уголок Шотландии и закончить свою работу в уединении.

o.en: I did not doubt but that the monster followed me and would discover himself to me when I should have finished, that he might receive his companion.
o.ru: Я не сомневался, что чудовище следует за мной и явится мне, когда я закончу, чтобы получить свою подругу.

o.en: With this resolution I traversed the northern highlands and fixed on one of the remotest of the Orkneys as the scene of my labours.
o.ru: С этим намерением я пересёк северное нагорье и избрал местом своих трудов один из самых отдалённых Оркнейских островов.

o.en: It was a place fitted for such a work, being hardly more than a rock whose high sides were continually beaten upon by the waves.
o.ru: Это было место, пригодное для такой работы, ибо остров был едва ли больше скалы, чьи высокие склоны беспрестанно били волны.

o.en: The soil was barren, scarcely affording pasture for a few miserable cows, and oatmeal for its inhabitants, which consisted of five persons, whose gaunt and scraggy limbs gave tokens of their miserable fare.
o.ru: Почва была бесплодной и едва давала пастбище нескольким жалким коровам и овсяную муку жителям, которых было пятеро и чьи исхудалые, костлявые члены свидетельствовали о скудной пище.

o.en: Vegetables and bread, when they indulged in such luxuries, and even fresh water, was to be procured from the mainland, which was about five miles distant.
o.ru: Овощи и хлеб, когда они позволяли себе такую роскошь, и даже пресную воду приходилось добывать с большой земли, находившейся милях в пяти.

o.en: On the whole island there were but three miserable huts, and one of these was vacant when I arrived.
o.ru: На всём острове было лишь три жалкие хижины, и одна из них пустовала, когда я прибыл.

o.en: This I hired.
It contained but two rooms, and these exhibited all the squalidness of the most miserable penury.
o.ru: В ней было всего две комнаты, являвшие всё убожество самой жалкой нищеты.

o.en: The thatch had fallen in, the walls were unplastered, and the door was off its hinges.
o.ru: Соломенная кровля провалилась, стены были не оштукатурены, а дверь сорвана с петель.

o.en: I ordered it to be repaired, bought some furniture, and took possession, an incident which would doubtless have occasioned some surprise had not all the senses of the cottagers been benumbed by want and squalid poverty.
o.ru: Я велел её починить, купил кое-какую мебель и вступил во владение — событие, которое, несомненно, вызвало бы некоторое удивление, если бы все чувства обитателей хижин не были притуплены нуждой и убогой бедностью.

o.en: As it was, I lived ungazed at and unmolested, hardly thanked for the pittance of food and clothes which I gave, so much does suffering blunt even the coarsest sensations of men.
o.ru: А так я жил, никем не разглядываемый и никем не тревожимый, едва получая благодарность за ту малость пищи и одежды, что раздавал, — до того страдание притупляет даже самые грубые ощущения людей.

o.en: In this retreat I devoted the morning to labour; but in the evening, when the weather permitted, I walked on the stony beach of the sea to listen to the waves as they roared and dashed at my feet.
o.ru: В этом уединении я посвящал утро труду; а вечером, если позволяла погода, гулял по каменистому берегу моря, слушая, как волны ревут и разбиваются у моих ног.

o.en: It was a monotonous yet ever-changing scene.
o.ru: Это была однообразная и всё же вечно меняющаяся картина.

o.en: I thought of Switzerland; it was far different from this desolate and appalling landscape.
o.ru: Я думал о Швейцарии; как далека она была от этого пустынного и устрашающего пейзажа.

o.en: Its hills are covered with vines, and its cottages are scattered thickly in the plains.
o.ru: Её холмы покрыты виноградниками, а по равнинам густо рассыпаны домики.

o.en: Its fair lakes reflect a blue and gentle sky, and when troubled by the winds, their tumult is but as the play of a lively infant when compared to the roarings of the giant ocean.
o.ru: Её прекрасные озёра отражают голубое и кроткое небо, и когда их волнуют ветры, их смятение — лишь игра резвого младенца в сравнении с рёвом исполинского океана.

o.en: In this manner I distributed my occupations when I first arrived, but as I proceeded in my labour, it became every day more horrible and irksome to me.
o.ru: Так я распределял свои занятия поначалу, но по мере того, как я продвигался в работе, она становилась для меня с каждым днём всё ужаснее и тягостнее.

o.en: Sometimes I could not prevail on myself to enter my laboratory for several days, and at other times I toiled day and night in order to complete my work.
o.ru: Порой я по нескольку дней не мог заставить себя войти в лабораторию, а в другое время трудился день и ночь, чтобы завершить свою работу.

o.en: It was, indeed, a filthy process in which I was engaged.
o.ru: Это был поистине мерзкий процесс, которым я был занят.

o.en: During my first experiment, a kind of enthusiastic frenzy had blinded me to the horror of my employment; my mind was intently fixed on the consummation of my labour, and my eyes were shut to the horror of my proceedings.
o.ru: Во время первого опыта некое восторженное исступление ослепило меня и скрыло ужас моего занятия; мой ум был напряжённо устремлён к завершению труда, а глаза закрыты для ужаса моих действий.

o.en: But now I went to it in cold blood, and my heart often sickened at the work of my hands.
o.ru: Но теперь я приступал к нему хладнокровно, и сердце моё часто содрогалось от отвращения к делу моих рук.

o.en: Thus situated, employed in the most detestable occupation, immersed in a solitude where nothing could for an instant call my attention from the actual scene in which I was engaged, my spirits became unequal; I grew restless and nervous.
o.ru: В таком положении, занятый самым омерзительным делом, погружённый в одиночество, где ничто ни на миг не могло отвлечь моего внимания от того, чем я был занят, я утратил душевное равновесие; я стал беспокоен и нервен.

o.en: Every moment I feared to meet my persecutor.
o.ru: Каждую минуту я боялся встретить своего преследователя.

o.en: Sometimes I sat with my eyes fixed on the ground, fearing to raise them lest they should encounter the object which I so much dreaded to behold.
o.ru: Иногда я сидел, вперив глаза в землю, боясь поднять их, чтобы они не встретили того, кого я так страшился увидеть.

o.en: I feared to wander from the sight of my fellow creatures lest when alone he should come to claim his companion.
o.ru: Я боялся уходить из виду своих ближних, чтобы он не пришёл, когда я буду один, требовать свою подругу.

o.en: In the mean time I worked on, and my labour was already considerably advanced.
o.ru: Тем временем я продолжал работать, и мой труд уже значительно продвинулся.

o.en: I looked towards its completion with a tremulous and eager hope, which I dared not trust myself to question but which was intermixed with obscure forebodings of evil that made my heart sicken in my bosom.
o.ru: Я ожидал его завершения с трепетной и нетерпеливой надеждой, которую не смел подвергнуть сомнению, но к которой примешивались смутные предчувствия зла, отчего сердце моё изнывало в груди.

b2.en: London was where we stopped to rest for now; we decided to stay several months in this wonderful and famous city.
b2.ru: Лондон стал нашей нынешней остановкой; мы решили провести несколько месяцев в этом чудесном и знаменитом городе.

b2.en: Clerval wanted to meet the brilliant and talented men who were flourishing at that time, but for me this was of secondary importance.
b2.ru: Клерваль хотел общаться с блестящими и талантливыми людьми, которые процветали в то время, но для меня это было делом второстепенным.

b2.en: I was mainly concerned with finding the information I needed to fulfil my promise, and I quickly made use of the letters of introduction I had brought with me, addressed to the most distinguished scientists.
b2.ru: Я был главным образом занят тем, как добыть сведения, необходимые для выполнения моего обещания, и быстро воспользовался рекомендательными письмами, которые привёз с собой и которые были адресованы самым выдающимся естествоиспытателям.

b2.en: If this journey had taken place in my days of study and happiness, it would have given me indescribable pleasure.
b2.ru: Если бы это путешествие состоялось в дни моей учёбы и счастья, оно доставило бы мне невыразимое удовольствие.

b2.en: But a blight had fallen on my life, and I visited these people only for the information they might give me on the subject that concerned me so terribly deeply.
b2.ru: Но мою жизнь поразила порча, и я посещал этих людей лишь ради сведений, которые они могли мне дать о предмете, волновавшем меня так страшно глубоко.

b2.en: Company was tiresome to me; when I was alone, I could fill my mind with the sights of heaven and earth, and Henry’s voice soothed me, so I could trick myself into a brief peace.
b2.ru: Общество тяготило меня; наедине с собой я мог наполнить ум картинами неба и земли, голос Анри успокаивал меня, и так я мог обмануть себя, обретая мимолётный покой.

b2.en: But busy, dull, cheerful faces brought despair back into my heart.
b2.ru: Но деловитые, скучные, весёлые лица возвращали отчаяние в моё сердце.

b2.en: I saw an impassable barrier between me and other people; it was sealed with the blood of William and Justine, and thinking about the events linked to those names filled my soul with anguish.
b2.ru: Я видел непреодолимую преграду между собой и другими людьми; она была скреплена кровью Уильяма и Жюстины, и мысли о событиях, связанных с этими именами, наполняли мою душу мукой.

b2.en: But in Clerval I saw the image of my former self; he was curious and eager to gain experience and knowledge.
b2.ru: Но в Клервале я видел образ себя прежнего; он был любознателен и жаждал опыта и знаний.

b2.en: The different customs he observed were an endless source of learning and amusement for him.
b2.ru: Различия в обычаях, которые он наблюдал, были для него неиссякаемым источником знаний и развлечения.

b2.en: He was also pursuing a goal he had long had in mind.
b2.ru: Кроме того, он преследовал цель, которую давно наметил.

b2.en: He planned to go to India, believing that his knowledge of its languages and his understanding of its society would allow him to contribute significantly to the progress of European colonization and trade.
b2.ru: Он намеревался отправиться в Индию, полагая, что знание её языков и понимание её общества позволят ему существенно содействовать развитию европейской колонизации и торговли.

b2.en: Only in Britain could he move his plan forward.
b2.ru: Лишь в Британии мог он продвинуть осуществление своего плана.

b2.en: He was always busy, and the only thing that spoiled his enjoyment was my sad and gloomy state of mind.
b2.ru: Он всегда был занят, и единственное, что омрачало его радость, было моё печальное и подавленное настроение.

b2.en: I tried to hide this as much as I could, so as not to deprive him of the pleasures natural to someone starting a new chapter of life, untroubled by any worry or bitter memory.
b2.ru: Я старался скрывать это как можно лучше, чтобы не лишать его удовольствий, естественных для того, кто вступает в новую пору жизни, не омрачённую ни заботой, ни горьким воспоминанием.

b2.en: I often refused to go with him, pretending I had another appointment, so that I could stay alone.
b2.ru: Я часто отказывался сопровождать его, ссылаясь на другую встречу, чтобы остаться одному.
