sub: Victor destroys the half-made female creature; the monster vows revenge on his wedding night, and Victor, drifting at sea, lands in Ireland where he is arrested for a murder

o: I sat one evening in my laboratory; the sun had set, and the moon was just rising from the sea; I had not sufficient light for my employment, and I remained idle, in a pause of consideration of whether I should leave my labour for the night or hasten its conclusion by an unremitting attention to it. As I sat, a train of reflection occurred to me which led me to consider the effects of what I was now doing. Three years before, I was engaged in the same manner and had created a fiend whose unparalleled barbarity had desolated my heart and filled it for ever with the bitterest remorse. I was now about to form another being of whose dispositions I was alike ignorant; she might become ten thousand times more malignant than her mate and delight, for its own sake, in murder and wretchedness.

He had sworn to quit the neighbourhood of man and hide himself in deserts, but she had not; and she, who in all probability was to become a thinking and reasoning animal, might refuse to comply with a compact made before her creation. They might even hate each other; the creature who already lived loathed his own deformity, and might he not conceive a greater abhorrence for it when it came before his eyes in the female form? She also might turn with disgust from him to the superior beauty of man; she might quit him, and he be again alone, exasperated by the fresh provocation of being deserted by one of his own species.

Even if they were to leave Europe and inhabit the deserts of the new world, yet one of the first results of those sympathies for which the dæmon thirsted would be children, and a race of devils would be propagated upon the earth who might make the very existence of the species of man a condition precarious and full of terror. Had I right, for my own benefit, to inflict this curse upon everlasting generations? I had before been moved by the sophisms of the being I had created; I had been struck senseless by his fiendish threats; but now, for the first time, the wickedness of my promise burst upon me; I shuddered to think that future ages might curse me as their pest, whose selfishness had not hesitated to buy its own peace at the price, perhaps, of the existence of the whole human race.

I trembled and my heart failed within me, when, on looking up, I saw by the light of the moon the dæmon at the casement. A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips as he gazed on me, where I sat fulfilling the task which he had allotted to me. Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress and claim the fulfilment of my promise.

As I looked on him, his countenance expressed the utmost extent of malice and treachery. I thought with a sensation of madness on my promise of creating another like to him, and trembling with passion, tore to pieces the thing on which I was engaged. The wretch saw me destroy the creature on whose future existence he depended for happiness, and with a howl of devilish despair and revenge, withdrew.

I left the room, and locking the door, made a solemn vow in my own heart never to resume my labours; and then, with trembling steps, I sought my own apartment. I was alone; none were near me to dissipate the gloom and relieve me from the sickening oppression of the most terrible reveries.

Several hours passed, and I remained near my window gazing on the sea; it was almost motionless, for the winds were hushed, and all nature reposed under the eye of the quiet moon. A few fishing vessels alone specked the water, and now and then the gentle breeze wafted the sound of voices as the fishermen called to one another. I felt the silence, although I was hardly conscious of its extreme profundity, until my ear was suddenly arrested by the paddling of oars near the shore, and a person landed close to my house.

In a few minutes after, I heard the creaking of my door, as if some one endeavoured to open it softly. I trembled from head to foot; I felt a presentiment of who it was and wished to rouse one of the peasants who dwelt in a cottage not far from mine; but I was overcome by the sensation of helplessness, so often felt in frightful dreams, when you in vain endeavour to fly from an impending danger, and was rooted to the spot.

Presently I heard the sound of footsteps along the passage; the door opened, and the wretch whom I dreaded appeared. Shutting the door, he approached me and said in a smothered voice,

“You have destroyed the work which you began; what is it that you intend? Do you dare to break your promise? I have endured toil and misery; I left Switzerland with you; I crept along the shores of the Rhine, among its willow islands and over the summits of its hills. I have dwelt many months in the heaths of England and among the deserts of Scotland. I have endured incalculable fatigue, and cold, and hunger; do you dare destroy my hopes?”

“Begone! I do break my promise; never will I create another like yourself, equal in deformity and wickedness.”

“Slave, I before reasoned with you, but you have proved yourself unworthy of my condescension. Remember that I have power; you believe yourself miserable, but I can make you so wretched that the light of day will be hateful to you. You are my creator, but I am your master; obey!”

“The hour of my irresolution is past, and the period of your power is arrived. Your threats cannot move me to do an act of wickedness; but they confirm me in a determination of not creating you a companion in vice. Shall I, in cool blood, set loose upon the earth a dæmon whose delight is in death and wretchedness? Begone! I am firm, and your words will only exasperate my rage.”

The monster saw my determination in my face and gnashed his teeth in the impotence of anger. “Shall each man,” cried he, “find a wife for his bosom, and each beast have his mate, and I be alone? I had feelings of affection, and they were requited by detestation and scorn. Man! You may hate, but beware! Your hours will pass in dread and misery, and soon the bolt will fall which must ravish from you your happiness for ever.

Are you to be happy while I grovel in the intensity of my wretchedness? You can blast my other passions, but revenge remains—revenge, henceforth dearer than light or food! I may die, but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that gazes on your misery. Beware, for I am fearless and therefore powerful. I will watch with the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom. Man, you shall repent of the injuries you inflict.”

“Devil, cease; and do not poison the air with these sounds of malice. I have declared my resolution to you, and I am no coward to bend beneath words. Leave me; I am inexorable.”

“It is well. I go; but remember, I shall be with you on your wedding-night.”

I started forward and exclaimed, “Villain! Before you sign my death-warrant, be sure that you are yourself safe.”

I would have seized him, but he eluded me and quitted the house with precipitation. In a few moments I saw him in his boat, which shot across the waters with an arrowy swiftness and was soon lost amidst the waves.

All was again silent, but his words rang in my ears. I burned with rage to pursue the murderer of my peace and precipitate him into the ocean. I walked up and down my room hastily and perturbed, while my imagination conjured up a thousand images to torment and sting me. Why had I not followed him and closed with him in mortal strife? But I had suffered him to depart, and he had directed his course towards the mainland. I shuddered to think who might be the next victim sacrificed to his insatiate revenge.

And then I thought again of his words—“I will be with you on your wedding-night.” That, then, was the period fixed for the fulfilment of my destiny. In that hour I should die and at once satisfy and extinguish his malice. The prospect did not move me to fear; yet when I thought of my beloved Elizabeth, of her tears and endless sorrow, when she should find her lover so barbarously snatched from her, tears, the first I had shed for many months, streamed from my eyes, and I resolved not to fall before my enemy without a bitter struggle.

The night passed away, and the sun rose from the ocean; my feelings became calmer, if it may be called calmness when the violence of rage sinks into the depths of despair. I left the house, the horrid scene of the last night’s contention, and walked on the beach of the sea, which I almost regarded as an insuperable barrier between me and my fellow creatures; nay, a wish that such should prove the fact stole across me. I desired that I might pass my life on that barren rock, wearily, it is true, but uninterrupted by any sudden shock of misery. If I returned, it was to be sacrificed or to see those whom I most loved die under the grasp of a dæmon whom I had myself created.

I walked about the isle like a restless spectre, separated from all it loved and miserable in the separation. When it became noon, and the sun rose higher, I lay down on the grass and was overpowered by a deep sleep. I had been awake the whole of the preceding night, my nerves were agitated, and my eyes inflamed by watching and misery. The sleep into which I now sank refreshed me; and when I awoke, I again felt as if I belonged to a race of human beings like myself, and I began to reflect upon what had passed with greater composure; yet still the words of the fiend rang in my ears like a death-knell; they appeared like a dream, yet distinct and oppressive as a reality.

The sun had far descended, and I still sat on the shore, satisfying my appetite, which had become ravenous, with an oaten cake, when I saw a fishing-boat land close to me, and one of the men brought me a packet; it contained letters from Geneva, and one from Clerval entreating me to join him. He said that he was wearing away his time fruitlessly where he was, that letters from the friends he had formed in London desired his return to complete the negotiation they had entered into for his Indian enterprise.

He could not any longer delay his departure; but as his journey to London might be followed, even sooner than he now conjectured, by his longer voyage, he entreated me to bestow as much of my society on him as I could spare. He besought me, therefore, to leave my solitary isle and to meet him at Perth, that we might proceed southwards together. This letter in a degree recalled me to life, and I determined to quit my island at the expiration of two days.

Yet, before I departed, there was a task to perform, on which I shuddered to reflect; I must pack up my chemical instruments, and for that purpose I must enter the room which had been the scene of my odious work, and I must handle those utensils the sight of which was sickening to me. The next morning, at daybreak, I summoned sufficient courage and unlocked the door of my laboratory. The remains of the half-finished creature, whom I had destroyed, lay scattered on the floor, and I almost felt as if I had mangled the living flesh of a human being.

I paused to collect myself and then entered the chamber. With trembling hand I conveyed the instruments out of the room, but I reflected that I ought not to leave the relics of my work to excite the horror and suspicion of the peasants; and I accordingly put them into a basket, with a great quantity of stones, and laying them up, determined to throw them into the sea that very night; and in the meantime I sat upon the beach, employed in cleaning and arranging my chemical apparatus.

Nothing could be more complete than the alteration that had taken place in my feelings since the night of the appearance of the dæmon. I had before regarded my promise with a gloomy despair as a thing that, with whatever consequences, must be fulfilled; but I now felt as if a film had been taken from before my eyes and that I for the first time saw clearly. The idea of renewing my labours did not for one instant occur to me; the threat I had heard weighed on my thoughts, but I did not reflect that a voluntary act of mine could avert it. I had resolved in my own mind that to create another like the fiend I had first made would be an act of the basest and most atrocious selfishness, and I banished from my mind every thought that could lead to a different conclusion.

Between two and three in the morning the moon rose; and I then, putting my basket aboard a little skiff, sailed out about four miles from the shore. The scene was perfectly solitary; a few boats were returning towards land, but I sailed away from them. I felt as if I was about the commission of a dreadful crime and avoided with shuddering anxiety any encounter with my fellow creatures. At one time the moon, which had before been clear, was suddenly overspread by a thick cloud, and I took advantage of the moment of darkness and cast my basket into the sea; I listened to the gurgling sound as it sank and then sailed away from the spot.

The sky became clouded, but the air was pure, although chilled by the northeast breeze that was then rising. But it refreshed me and filled me with such agreeable sensations that I resolved to prolong my stay on the water, and fixing the rudder in a direct position, stretched myself at the bottom of the boat. Clouds hid the moon, everything was obscure, and I heard only the sound of the boat as its keel cut through the waves; the murmur lulled me, and in a short time I slept soundly.

I do not know how long I remained in this situation, but when I awoke I found that the sun had already mounted considerably. The wind was high, and the waves continually threatened the safety of my little skiff. I found that the wind was northeast and must have driven me far from the coast from which I had embarked. I endeavoured to change my course but quickly found that if I again made the attempt the boat would be instantly filled with water. Thus situated, my only resource was to drive before the wind. I confess that I felt a few sensations of terror.

I had no compass with me and was so slenderly acquainted with the geography of this part of the world that the sun was of little benefit to me. I might be driven into the wide Atlantic and feel all the tortures of starvation or be swallowed up in the immeasurable waters that roared and buffeted around me. I had already been out many hours and felt the torment of a burning thirst, a prelude to my other sufferings.

I looked on the heavens, which were covered by clouds that flew before the wind, only to be replaced by others; I looked upon the sea; it was to be my grave. “Fiend,” I exclaimed, “your task is already fulfilled!” I thought of Elizabeth, of my father, and of Clerval—all left behind, on whom the monster might satisfy his sanguinary and merciless passions. This idea plunged me into a reverie so despairing and frightful that even now, when the scene is on the point of closing before me for ever, I shudder to reflect on it.

Some hours passed thus; but by degrees, as the sun declined towards the horizon, the wind died away into a gentle breeze and the sea became free from breakers. But these gave place to a heavy swell; I felt sick and hardly able to hold the rudder, when suddenly I saw a line of high land towards the south.

Almost spent, as I was, by fatigue and the dreadful suspense I endured for several hours, this sudden certainty of life rushed like a flood of warm joy to my heart, and tears gushed from my eyes.

How mutable are our feelings, and how strange is that clinging love we have of life even in the excess of misery! I constructed another sail with a part of my dress and eagerly steered my course towards the land. It had a wild and rocky appearance, but as I approached nearer I easily perceived the traces of cultivation. I saw vessels near the shore and found myself suddenly transported back to the neighbourhood of civilised man.

I carefully traced the windings of the land and hailed a steeple which I at length saw issuing from behind a small promontory. As I was in a state of extreme debility, I resolved to sail directly towards the town, as a place where I could most easily procure nourishment. Fortunately I had money with me. As I turned the promontory I perceived a small neat town and a good harbour, which I entered, my heart bounding with joy at my unexpected escape.

As I was occupied in fixing the boat and arranging the sails, several people crowded towards the spot. They seemed much surprised at my appearance, but instead of offering me any assistance, whispered together with gestures that at any other time might have produced in me a slight sensation of alarm. As it was, I merely remarked that they spoke English, and I therefore addressed them in that language. “My good friends,” said I, “will you be so kind as to tell me the name of this town and inform me where I am?”

“You will know that soon enough,” replied a man with a hoarse voice. “Maybe you are come to a place that will not prove much to your taste, but you will not be consulted as to your quarters, I promise you.”

I was exceedingly surprised on receiving so rude an answer from a stranger, and I was also disconcerted on perceiving the frowning and angry countenances of his companions. “Why do you answer me so roughly?” I replied. “Surely it is not the custom of Englishmen to receive strangers so inhospitably.”

“I do not know,” said the man, “what the custom of the English may be, but it is the custom of the Irish to hate villains.”

While this strange dialogue continued, I perceived the crowd rapidly increase. Their faces expressed a mixture of curiosity and anger, which annoyed and in some degree alarmed me. I inquired the way to the inn, but no one replied. I then moved forward, and a murmuring sound arose from the crowd as they followed and surrounded me, when an ill-looking man approaching tapped me on the shoulder and said, “Come, sir, you must follow me to Mr. Kirwin’s to give an account of yourself.”

“Who is Mr. Kirwin? Why am I to give an account of myself? Is not this a free country?”

“Ay, sir, free enough for honest folks. Mr. Kirwin is a magistrate, and you are to give an account of the death of a gentleman who was found murdered here last night.”

This answer startled me, but I presently recovered myself. I was innocent; that could easily be proved; accordingly I followed my conductor in silence and was led to one of the best houses in the town. I was ready to sink from fatigue and hunger, but being surrounded by a crowd, I thought it politic to rouse all my strength, that no physical debility might be construed into apprehension or conscious guilt. Little did I then expect the calamity that was in a few moments to overwhelm me and extinguish in horror and despair all fear of ignominy or death.

I must pause here, for it requires all my fortitude to recall the memory of the frightful events which I am about to relate, in proper detail, to my recollection.

Three years earlier I had been engaged in the same work and had created a fiend whose unparalleled cruelty had devastated my heart and filled it for ever with the bitterest remorse. Now I was about to make another being whose character I knew just as little about; she might become ten thousand times more malicious than her mate and take pleasure in murder and misery for their own sake.

He had sworn to leave the world of men and hide in deserts, but she had not; and she, who would most probably be a thinking, reasoning creature, might refuse to keep an agreement made before she was even created. They might even hate each other; the creature who already lived loathed his own ugliness, and might he not feel even greater disgust for it when he saw it in female form? She, too, might turn away from him in disgust, preferring the greater beauty of human beings; she might leave him, and he would be alone again, made even more furious by being abandoned by one of his own kind.

Even if they left Europe and settled in the deserts of the New World, one of the first results of the companionship the demon longed for would be children, and a race of devils would spread across the earth, making the very existence of humankind uncertain and full of terror. Did I have the right, for my own sake, to bring this curse upon endless generations? Before, I had been swayed by the clever arguments of the being I had created and stunned by his fiendish threats; but now, for the first time, the wickedness of my promise struck me with full force. I shuddered to think that future ages might curse me as their plague, a man who had selfishly bought his own peace at the price, perhaps, of the whole human race.

I trembled and my heart sank when, looking up, I saw the demon at the window in the moonlight. A ghastly grin twisted his lips as he stared at me, sitting there carrying out the task he had given me. Yes, he had followed me on my travels; he had lingered in forests, hidden in caves or sheltered on wide, empty moors, and now he had come to check my progress and demand that I keep my promise.

Only a few fishing boats dotted the water, and now and then the gentle breeze carried the voices of the fishermen calling to each other. I felt the silence, though I was hardly aware of how deep it was, until my ear suddenly caught the splash of oars near the shore, and someone landed close to my house.

I trembled from head to foot; I sensed who it was and wanted to wake one of the peasants who lived in a cottage not far from mine. But I was overcome by that helplessness we so often feel in nightmares, when we try in vain to escape from a looming danger, and I was rooted to the spot.

He closed the door, came towards me and said in a muffled voice: “You have destroyed the work you began; what do you mean to do? Do you dare to break your promise? I have endured hardship and misery; I left Switzerland with you; I crept along the banks of the Rhine, among its willow islands and over the tops of its hills. For many months I have lived on the moors of England and in the wilds of Scotland. I have suffered endless exhaustion, cold and hunger; do you dare to destroy my hopes?”

“Go away! Yes, I am breaking my promise; I will never create another being like you, equal to you in ugliness and evil.” “Slave, I tried to reason with you before, but you have shown that you do not deserve my patience. Remember that I have power; you think you are miserable, but I can make you so wretched that daylight itself will become hateful to you. You are my creator, but I am your master; obey!”

“My time of weakness is over, and the time of your power has come to an end. Your threats cannot force me to do something wicked; they only strengthen my decision not to create a partner for you in evil. Should I, in cold blood, let loose on the earth a demon who delights in death and misery? Go away! I am determined, and your words will only make me angrier.”

The monster saw the determination in my face and ground his teeth in helpless fury. “Shall every man find a wife to hold close,” he cried, “and every animal have its mate, while I am left alone? I had loving feelings, and they were repaid with loathing and contempt. Man! You may hate, but beware! Your hours will be spent in dread and misery, and soon the blow will fall that will tear your happiness from you for ever.

Are you to be happy while I crawl in the depths of my misery? You can crush all my other passions, but revenge remains—revenge, from now on dearer to me than light or food! I may die, but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, will curse the sun that looks down on your misery. Beware, for I am fearless and therefore powerful. I will wait and watch with the cunning of a snake, so that I can strike with its venom. Man, you will regret the wrongs you are doing me.”

“Devil, stop; do not poison the air with such spiteful words. I have told you my decision, and I am not a coward who gives in to words. Leave me; nothing will change my mind.” “Very well. I will go; but remember, I will be with you on your wedding night.” I rushed forward and cried, “Villain! Before you sign my death warrant, make sure that you yourself are safe.” I would have grabbed him, but he slipped away from me and left the house in a great hurry. A few moments later I saw him in his boat, which shot across the water as fast as an arrow and was soon lost among the waves.

All was silent again, but his words kept ringing in my ears. I burned with rage and longed to chase the destroyer of my peace and hurl him into the ocean. I paced up and down my room, agitated, while my imagination conjured up a thousand images to torment me. Why had I not gone after him and fought him to the death? But I had let him leave, and he had set off towards the mainland. I shuddered to think who might be the next victim of his insatiable revenge.

And then I thought again of his words—“I will be with you on your wedding night.” So that was the moment fixed for my fate to be fulfilled. At that hour I would die, and my death would both satisfy and put out his hatred. The thought did not frighten me; yet when I thought of my beloved Elizabeth, of her tears and endless grief when she found her lover so brutally torn from her, tears, the first I had shed for many months, streamed from my eyes, and I resolved not to fall before my enemy without a bitter fight.

The night passed, and the sun rose from the ocean; my feelings grew calmer, if you can call it calm when violent rage sinks into deep despair. I left the house, the horrible scene of the night’s quarrel, and walked along the beach; I almost saw the sea as an impassable barrier between me and other people, and I even found myself wishing that it really were so. I wished I could spend my life on that barren rock, wearily, it is true, but free from any sudden shock of misery. If I went back, it would only be to be sacrificed, or to see those I loved most die in the grip of a demon I had created myself.

I wandered around the island like a restless ghost, cut off from everything it loved and miserable in its loneliness. At noon, when the sun had risen higher, I lay down on the grass and was overcome by a deep sleep. I had been awake the whole of the previous night; my nerves were on edge and my eyes were sore from sleeplessness and misery. The sleep refreshed me, and when I woke I felt once more that I belonged to the human race, and I began to think over what had happened more calmly. Even so, the fiend’s words still rang in my ears like a death knell; they seemed like a dream, yet as clear and oppressive as reality.

The sun was low in the sky, and I was still sitting on the shore, satisfying my ravenous hunger with an oatcake, when I saw a fishing boat land close by, and one of the men brought me a packet. It contained letters from Geneva, and one from Clerval begging me to join him. He said that he was wasting his time where he was, and that the friends he had made in London were writing to ask him to return and complete the negotiations they had begun for his Indian venture.

He could not put off his departure any longer; and since his trip to London might be followed, even sooner than he now expected, by his longer voyage, he begged me to give him as much of my company as I could spare. He therefore urged me to leave my lonely island and meet him in Perth, so that we could travel south together. This letter brought me back to life to some extent, and I decided to leave the island in two days’ time.

But before I left, there was a task I dreaded even to think about: I had to pack up my chemical instruments. To do that, I had to enter the room where I had done my hateful work and handle the equipment that made me feel sick just to look at. The next morning, at dawn, I gathered enough courage and unlocked the door of my laboratory. The remains of the half-finished creature I had destroyed lay scattered across the floor, and I almost felt as if I had torn apart the living flesh of a human being.

I paused to steady myself and then went into the room. With a trembling hand I carried the instruments out, but it occurred to me that I should not leave the remains of my work behind to arouse the horror and suspicion of the peasants. So I put them into a basket with a large number of stones, set it aside and decided to throw it into the sea that very night; meanwhile I sat on the beach, cleaning and sorting my chemical equipment.

Nothing could have been more complete than the change in my feelings since the night the demon appeared. Before, I had regarded my promise with gloomy despair, as something that had to be fulfilled whatever the consequences; but now I felt as if a veil had been lifted from my eyes and I was seeing clearly for the first time. The idea of starting my work again did not cross my mind for a single moment; the threat I had heard weighed on me, but it did not occur to me that I could prevent it by any choice of my own. I had made up my mind that creating another being like the first fiend would be an act of the lowest and most dreadful selfishness, and I drove from my mind every thought that might lead me to a different conclusion.

Between two and three in the morning the moon rose; I put my basket into a small boat and sailed out about four miles from the shore. The place was completely deserted; a few boats were heading back to land, but I sailed away from them. I felt as though I were about to commit a terrible crime, and I anxiously avoided meeting any other human being. At one point the moon, which had been clear, was suddenly covered by a thick cloud, and I took advantage of the darkness to throw my basket into the sea; I listened to the gurgling sound as it sank and then sailed away.

The sky clouded over, but the air was fresh, though chilled by the north-east wind that was beginning to rise. It refreshed me and gave me such pleasant sensations that I decided to stay out on the water longer, so I fixed the rudder in a straight position and stretched out in the bottom of the boat. Clouds hid the moon, everything was dark, and I could hear only the sound of the keel cutting through the waves; the murmur lulled me, and soon I was fast asleep.

I do not know how long I stayed like this, but when I woke up, the sun was already high in the sky. The wind was strong, and the waves constantly threatened my little boat. I realised that the wind was from the north-east and must have carried me far from the coast I had set out from. I tried to change course, but I soon saw that if I tried again the boat would instantly fill with water. In this situation, my only option was to let the wind drive me along. I admit that I felt a certain amount of terror.

I had no compass with me, and I knew so little about the geography of this part of the world that the sun was of little use to me. I might be driven out into the open Atlantic and suffer all the agonies of starvation, or be swallowed up by the vast waters that roared and battered me on every side. I had already been at sea for many hours and was tormented by a burning thirst, a foretaste of my other sufferings.

I looked at the sky, which was covered by clouds racing before the wind, only to be replaced by others; I looked at the sea; it was going to be my grave. “Fiend,” I cried, “your task is already done!” I thought of Elizabeth, of my father and of Clerval—all left behind, at the mercy of the monster’s bloodthirsty and merciless passions. This thought plunged me into such a despairing and frightful state of mind that even now, when my life is about to close for ever, I shudder to think of it.

Several hours passed in this way; but gradually, as the sun sank towards the horizon, the wind died down to a gentle breeze and the breaking waves disappeared. They were followed by a heavy swell; I felt sick and could barely hold the rudder, when suddenly I saw a line of high land to the south. Exhausted as I was by fatigue and the terrible suspense of those hours, this sudden certainty that I would live rushed into my heart like a flood of warm joy, and tears poured from my eyes.

How changeable our feelings are, and how strange is that stubborn love of life we cling to even in the depths of misery! I made another sail out of part of my clothes and eagerly steered towards the land. It looked wild and rocky, but as I came closer I could easily see signs of farming. I saw ships near the shore and suddenly found myself back in the world of civilised people.

I carefully followed the curves of the coast and greeted with joy a church spire that I finally saw rising from behind a small headland. As I was extremely weak, I decided to sail straight to the town, where I could most easily get food. Luckily, I had money with me. As I rounded the headland, I saw a small, tidy town and a good harbour, which I entered, my heart leaping with joy at my unexpected escape.

While I was busy tying up the boat and sorting out the sails, several people crowded towards the spot. They seemed very surprised by my appearance, but instead of offering to help, they whispered to each other with gestures that at any other time might have made me slightly alarmed. As it was, I merely noticed that they spoke English, so I spoke to them in that language. “My good friends,” I said, “would you be so kind as to tell me the name of this town and where I am?”

“You’ll find that out soon enough,” replied a man in a hoarse voice. “Maybe you’ve come to a place you won’t like much, but nobody will ask you where you’d like to stay, I promise you.” I was extremely surprised to get such a rude answer from a stranger, and I was also unsettled to see the scowling, angry faces of his companions. “Why do you answer me so rudely?” I replied. “Surely it is not the custom of the English to receive strangers so unkindly.” “I don’t know,” said the man, “what the custom of the English may be, but it is the custom of the Irish to hate villains.”

While this strange conversation went on, I noticed the crowd growing fast. Their faces showed a mixture of curiosity and anger, which annoyed me and, to some extent, alarmed me. I asked the way to the inn, but nobody answered. Then I moved forward, and a murmur rose from the crowd as they followed and surrounded me, until an unpleasant-looking man came up, tapped me on the shoulder and said, “Come, sir, you must come with me to Mr Kirwin’s to explain yourself.”

“Who is Mr Kirwin? Why should I have to explain myself? Isn’t this a free country?” “Yes, sir, free enough for honest people. Mr Kirwin is a magistrate, and you are to explain the death of a gentleman who was found murdered here last night.”

This answer startled me, but I soon recovered. I was innocent, and that could easily be proved, so I followed my guide in silence and was led to one of the best houses in the town. I was ready to collapse from exhaustion and hunger, but with a crowd around me, I thought it wise to summon all my strength, so that my physical weakness would not be taken for fear or a guilty conscience. Little did I know then of the disaster that was about to overwhelm me within moments and, in horror and despair, wipe out all fear of disgrace or death. I must stop here, for it takes all my strength of mind to recall in full detail the terrible events I am about to describe.
b1: One evening I was sitting in my laboratory. The sun had gone down, and the moon was rising from the sea. There was not enough light to work, so I sat and wondered whether to stop for the night or to work hard and finish quickly. As I sat there, I began to think about what I was doing and what might happen because of it. Three years before, I had done the same work and created a monster. His terrible cruelty had broken my heart and filled it with guilt for ever. Now I was going to make another creature, and again I did not know what she would be like. She might be ten thousand times more evil than him and enjoy killing and causing pain.

He had promised to leave people and hide in wild places, but she had made no promise. She would probably be able to think for herself, and she might refuse to keep an agreement made before she was born. They might even hate each other. He already hated his own ugly body, and he might hate it even more when he saw it in a woman. She might turn away from him because men were more beautiful. She might leave him, and then he would be alone again and even angrier, because one of his own kind had left him.

Even if they left Europe and lived in the empty lands of America, they would soon have children. A race of devils would spread over the earth, and people would live in danger and fear. Did I have the right to bring this curse on all future generations just to help myself? Before, the creature’s clever words had moved me, and his threats had frightened me. But now, for the first time, I saw how wicked my promise was. I shook when I thought that people in the future might curse me. They would say that I had bought my own peace at the price of the whole human race.

I trembled, and my heart went cold. When I looked up, I saw the monster at the window in the moonlight. A horrible smile twisted his lips as he watched me doing the work he had given me. Yes, he had followed me on my journey. He had hidden in forests and caves and on wide, empty hills, and now he had come to see how my work was going and to make me keep my promise.

As I looked at him, his face was full of evil and cruelty. I thought of my promise to make another creature like him, and I felt almost mad. Shaking with anger, I tore to pieces the body I was working on. The monster saw me destroy the creature that was his only hope of happiness. He gave a terrible howl of despair and anger and went away.

I left the room and locked the door. In my heart I made a serious promise never to start that work again. Then, with shaking legs, I went to my own room. I was alone, and there was nobody to help me forget my dark and terrible thoughts.

Several hours passed, and I stayed by my window, looking at the sea. The sea hardly moved, because there was no wind, and everything was quiet under the moon. There were only a few fishing boats on the water, and sometimes the wind brought the voices of fishermen calling to each other. I felt the deep silence. Then suddenly I heard oars near the shore, and someone got out of a boat close to my house.

A few minutes later I heard my door creak, as if someone was trying to open it quietly. I shook from head to foot. I felt I knew who it was, and I wanted to wake one of the farmers who lived in a cottage near mine. But I felt completely helpless, like in a bad dream when you try to run from danger but cannot, and I could not move.

Soon I heard footsteps in the passage. The door opened, and the monster that I feared came in. He closed the door, came up to me and said in a low voice: “You have destroyed the work that you started. What are you planning? Do you dare to break your promise? I have suffered a lot. I left Switzerland with you, and I secretly followed you along the river Rhine, past its islands and over its hills. For many months I have lived in the wild lands of England and Scotland. I have been terribly tired, cold and hungry. Do you dare to destroy my hopes?”

“Go away! Yes, I am breaking my promise. I will never make another creature like you, as ugly and as evil as you are.” “Slave, I talked to you calmly before, but you do not deserve it. Remember that I am strong. You think you are unhappy, but I can make you so miserable that you will hate the light of day. You made me, but I am your master. Obey!”

“I am not weak any more, and your power over me is finished. Your threats cannot make me do something evil. They only make me more sure that I must not create an evil partner for you. Shall I calmly let a demon loose on the earth, a demon who loves death and pain? Go away! I will not change my mind, and your words will only make me angrier.”

The monster saw in my face that I would not change my mind. He ground his teeth in helpless anger. “Every man can find a wife, and every animal has a mate,” he cried. “Must I be alone? I had feelings of love, and people answered them with hate. Man! You may hate me, but be careful! You will live in fear and misery, and soon a blow will fall that will take away your happiness for ever.

Will you be happy while I suffer in the dust? You can destroy my other hopes, but I still have revenge, and from now on revenge is more important to me than light or food! I may die, but first you, my cruel master, will curse the sun that shines on your pain. Be careful, because I am not afraid of anything, and so I am strong. I will watch you like a clever snake, and then I will bite you with its poison. Man, you will be sorry for the harm you do to me.”

“Devil, stop! Do not fill the air with such evil words. I have told you my decision, and I am not a coward. Words cannot make me change it. Leave me!” “All right. I am going; but remember, I will be with you on your wedding night.” I jumped forward and shouted, “You evil creature! Before you decide to kill me, make sure that you are safe yourself.” I wanted to catch him, but he escaped and left the house very quickly. A few moments later I saw him in his boat. It moved across the water as fast as an arrow and soon disappeared among the waves.

Everything was quiet again, but I could still hear his words. I was burning with anger, and I wanted to follow him and throw him into the sea. I walked quickly up and down my room, very upset, and I imagined a thousand terrible things. Why had I not followed him and fought him to the death? But I had let him go, and he had sailed towards the mainland. I shook when I wondered who would be the next victim of his endless revenge.

Then I remembered his words again: “I will be with you on your wedding night.” So that was the time he had chosen for my death. On that night I would die, and his hatred would be satisfied. I was not afraid of that. But then I thought of my dear Elizabeth, and of her tears and sadness when the man she loved was cruelly taken from her. For the first time in many months, I cried, and I decided that I would not die without a hard fight.

The night passed, and the sun came up from the ocean. I felt calmer, but it was not real calm: my anger had simply turned into deep despair. I left the house where the terrible meeting had happened and walked on the beach. The sea seemed to me like a wall between me and other people, and I almost wished it really was. I wanted to spend my life on that empty rock; it would be a sad life, but a quiet one, without any new shocks. If I went home, I would be killed, or I would see the people I loved most die at the hands of the monster I had made.

I walked around the island like a restless ghost, far from everyone I loved and very unhappy. At midday, when the sun was higher, I lay down on the grass and fell into a deep sleep. I had not slept at all the night before, my nerves were bad, and my eyes were red and painful. The sleep made me feel better. When I woke up, I felt like a normal human being again, and I could think about what had happened more calmly. But the monster’s words still sounded in my ears like a funeral bell; they seemed like a dream, but they were as clear and heavy as real life.

The sun was low, and I was still sitting on the shore, eating an oatcake because I was very hungry. Then a fishing boat landed near me, and one of the men gave me a packet. It had letters from Geneva in it, and one from Clerval, who asked me to come to him. He wrote that he was wasting his time where he was. His new friends in London wanted him to come back and finish the plans for his business in India.

He could not wait any longer. After London he might soon have to go on his long journey, maybe sooner than he thought, so he asked me to spend as much time with him as I could. He asked me to leave my lonely island and meet him in Perth, so that we could travel south together. This letter brought me back to life a little, and I decided to leave the island in two days.

But before I left, I had a job to do, and I hated to think about it. I had to pack my chemical instruments. For that, I had to go into the room where I had done my horrible work and touch the tools that made me feel sick. The next morning, at sunrise, I found enough courage and unlocked the door of my laboratory. The pieces of the half-finished creature lay all over the floor. I almost felt as if I had cut up the living body of a human being.

I stopped to calm myself and then went into the room. With a shaking hand I carried the instruments out. But I thought that I should not leave the remains of my work there, because the farmers would find them and feel horror and suspicion. So I put them into a basket with a lot of stones and decided to throw it into the sea that night. Meanwhile I sat on the beach and cleaned and packed my chemical equipment.

Since the night the monster had come, my feelings had changed completely. Before, I had thought, in dark despair, that I had to keep my promise, whatever happened. But now I felt as if something had been taken away from my eyes, and I could see clearly for the first time. I did not think even for a moment about starting my work again. His threat was always in my mind, but I did not think that I could stop it by doing what he wanted. I had decided that making another creature like the first one would be the most terrible and selfish act, and I did not let myself think anything different.

Between two and three in the morning the moon rose. I put my basket into a small boat and sailed about four miles away from the shore. There was nobody around; a few boats were going back to land, but I sailed away from them. I felt as if I was going to do a terrible crime, and I was afraid to meet anyone. Suddenly a thick cloud covered the moon. In the darkness I threw my basket into the sea. I listened to the sound of the water as it sank, and then I sailed away.

The sky was cloudy, but the air was clean and a little cold because of the north-east wind. The wind made me feel fresh and good, so I decided to stay on the water longer. I fixed the rudder so that it did not move, and I lay down at the bottom of the boat. Clouds covered the moon, everything was dark, and I heard only the sound of the boat going through the waves. The soft sound sent me to sleep, and soon I was sleeping deeply.

I do not know how long I slept, but when I woke up the sun was already high. The wind was strong, and the waves were dangerous for my little boat. The wind was from the north-east, and it must have carried me far from the coast. I tried to change direction, but I soon saw that if I tried again, water would fill the boat. So I could only let the wind carry me. I have to say that I felt quite frightened.

I had no compass, and I knew so little about that part of the world that the sun did not help me much. The wind might carry me into the wide Atlantic Ocean, where I would die of hunger, or the huge, roaring waves might swallow me. I had been on the sea for many hours, and I was already terribly thirsty. It was the beginning of my other sufferings.

I looked at the sky, where the wind drove clouds along and more clouds came after them. I looked at the sea; it was going to be my grave. “Monster,” I shouted, “your job is already done!” I thought of Elizabeth, my father and Clerval. They were all far away, and the monster could kill them in his cruel anger. This thought filled me with such despair and fear that even now, near the end of my life, I shake when I remember it.

Some hours passed like this. But slowly, as the sun went down towards the horizon, the wind became a gentle breeze and the big waves stopped. Instead, the sea rose and fell heavily; I felt sick and could hardly hold the rudder. Then suddenly I saw a line of high land to the south. I was very tired after those long hours of fear, but now I knew I would live, and warm joy filled my heart. Tears ran from my eyes.

How quickly our feelings change, and how strongly we love life, even when we are very unhappy! I made another sail from some of my clothes and steered eagerly towards the land. It looked wild and rocky, but as I came nearer I saw fields. I saw ships near the shore and suddenly I was back among civilised people.

I carefully followed the coast, and I was very happy to see a church tower behind a small point of land. I was very weak, so I decided to sail straight to the town, where I could easily get food. Luckily, I had money with me. When I came round the point, I saw a small, neat town and a good harbour. I sailed into it, and my heart jumped with joy because I had escaped.

While I was tying up the boat and putting the sails in order, several people came towards me. They looked very surprised to see me, but they did not offer to help. Instead they whispered to each other and made signs, which at another time might have worried me a little. But I only noticed that they spoke English, so I spoke to them in English. “My good friends,” I said, “could you please tell me the name of this town and where I am?”

“You’ll know that soon enough,” answered a man with a rough voice. “Perhaps you won’t like this place very much, but nobody will ask you where you want to stay, I promise you.” I was very surprised by such a rude answer from a stranger. I was also worried when I saw the angry faces of the people with him. “Why do you answer me so rudely?” I asked. “Surely Englishmen do not usually treat strangers so badly.” “I don’t know what the English usually do,” said the man, “but the Irish usually hate criminals.”

While we were having this strange conversation, the crowd quickly grew bigger. Their faces showed curiosity and anger, and this annoyed me and frightened me a little. I asked the way to the inn, but nobody answered. Then I started to walk, and the people murmured as they followed me and stood around me. An unpleasant-looking man came up, touched me on the shoulder and said, “Come, sir, you must come with me to Mr Kirwin and explain who you are.”

“Who is Mr Kirwin? Why must I explain who I am? Isn’t this a free country?” “Yes, sir, it’s free enough for honest people. Mr Kirwin is a judge, and you must explain the death of a gentleman who was found murdered here last night.”

This answer shocked me, but I soon felt calm again. I was innocent, and that was easy to prove. So I followed the man without a word, and he took me to one of the best houses in the town. I was almost falling down from tiredness and hunger, but with the crowd around me, I tried to look strong. I did not want them to think that I was weak because I was afraid or guilty. I did not know then that in a few moments a terrible disaster would fall on me, and I would forget all fear of shame or death in my horror and despair. I must stop here, because I need all my courage to remember the terrible things that I am going to tell you.
a2: One evening I was sitting in my laboratory. The sun went down, and the moon came up over the sea. It was too dark to work, so I sat and thought. Should I stop for the night, or should I work and finish quickly? Three years before, I made a monster. He was very cruel, and I was always sorry that I made him. Now I was making a second creature, a woman. I did not know what she was going to be like. Maybe she will be much worse than him, I thought, and she will love killing.

He promised to go far away from people, but she did not promise anything. She will think for herself, and maybe she will say no. Maybe they will hate each other. He hated his own ugly body. Maybe she will like beautiful men more than him and leave him. Then he will be alone again and even angrier.

Even if they went far away, they will have children. Soon there will be many monsters in the world, and people will live in fear. These monsters will be dangerous for everybody. Did I have the right to do this to the world? Before, the monster’s words and threats made me agree. But now I understood that my promise was very bad. People in the future will hate me, I thought. I wanted peace for myself, but all people may pay for it.

Then I looked up and I felt very afraid. In the moonlight I saw the monster at the window. He smiled a terrible smile and watched me at my work. He followed me all the way from Switzerland. He hid in forests and caves. Now he came to see my work. He wanted to see my promise come true.

His face was very evil. I thought about my promise, and I felt almost mad. I was shaking, and I tore the half-made woman to pieces. The monster saw it. She was his only hope. He screamed with pain and anger, and went away.
I left the room and locked the door. I promised myself: I will never do this work again. Then I went to my room. I was alone with my terrible thoughts.

For some hours I sat by the window and looked at the sea. There was no wind, and everything was quiet. The moon was quiet above the water. There were a few fishing boats on the water. Sometimes I heard the fishermen’s voices. Then I heard a boat near the shore. Someone got out of it near my house.

A few minutes later my door made a noise. Someone was opening it quietly. I was shaking all over, because I knew who it was. I wanted to call my neighbours, but I could not move. It was like a bad dream.

I heard steps, and then the monster came in. He closed the door and spoke quietly: “You destroyed your work. Why? Are you going to break your promise? I followed you from Switzerland. I walked along the river Rhine and over the hills. I lived for months in the wild places of England and Scotland. I was tired, cold and hungry. Do you want to kill my hopes?”

“Go away! Yes, I am breaking my promise. I will never make another monster like you.” “Slave! I was kind to you before, but now I will not be kind. I am strong. I can make your life terrible. You made me, but I am your master. Do what I say!”

“No. You have no power over me now. Your threats cannot make me do a bad thing. I will not make an evil woman for you. I will not send another killer into the world. Go away! I will not change my mind.”

The monster saw that I was serious. He was very angry. “Every man has a wife, and every animal has a partner,” he cried. “Why must I be alone? I wanted love, but people gave me only hate. Be careful! Soon something terrible will happen to you, and you will never be happy again.

Why should you be happy when I am so unhappy? Now I want only one thing: revenge! Maybe I will die, but first you will be very unhappy. I am not afraid of anything, so I am strong. I will watch you like a snake, and then I will bite. You will be sorry.”

“Stop, devil! I told you my answer, and I am not afraid of your words. Leave me!” “All right. I am going. But remember: I will be with you on your wedding night.” I jumped up and shouted, “You bad creature! You want to kill me, but be careful!” I tried to catch him, but he ran out of the house. A moment later I saw him in his boat. It went very fast and soon I could not see it. It went across the water like an arrow.

Everything was quiet again, but I could still hear his words. I was very angry, and I wanted to kill him. I walked up and down my room. Why did I not follow him and fight him? Now he was going to the mainland. But I let him go. Who is he going to kill next, I thought.

Then I remembered his words: “I will be with you on your wedding night.” So he was going to kill me on that night. I was not afraid to die. But then I thought of Elizabeth. She will cry, and she will be sad for ever. For the first time in many months, I cried. I decided to fight him.

The night ended, and the sun came up. I was calmer now, but I was very sad. I left the house and walked on the beach. The sea was like a wall between me and other people, and I almost liked that. I wanted to stay on that island for ever. Life there will be sad, but quiet, I thought. If I go home, I thought, the monster will kill me or the people I love.

I walked around the island like a ghost. At midday I lay down on the grass and fell asleep. I did not sleep the night before, and I was very tired. After the sleep I felt better. I could think more calmly. But I still heard the monster’s words in my head. They were like a dream, but they felt very real.

In the evening I was sitting on the beach and eating some bread. A fishing boat came, and a man gave me some letters. There were letters from Geneva and one from Clerval. Clerval wrote: “Please come to me.” His friends in London wanted him to come back and finish his plans for India.

He could not wait any longer. Soon he was going to go on a long journey, so he wanted to spend time with me. He asked me to meet him in Perth. This letter made me feel a little better. I decided to leave the island in two days.

But first I had to do a job that I hated. I had to pack my instruments. They were in my laboratory, and I did not want to go in there. I was afraid, but I found my courage. The next morning I opened the door. The pieces of the woman were all over the floor. I felt like a murderer.

I stopped for a moment and then went in. I carried my instruments out. I did not want the people of the island to find the pieces. So I put them in a basket with a lot of stones. I decided to throw it into the sea that night. Then I sat on the beach and cleaned my instruments.

My feelings were now completely different. Before, I thought I must keep my promise. Now I could see clearly for the first time. I never wanted to start the work again. I remembered the monster’s words, but I could not stop him. Making another monster was a very bad and selfish thing, and I knew it.

At about three o’clock in the morning the moon came up. I put my basket into a small boat and sailed away from the shore. I sailed about four miles out. There was nobody near me. I felt like a criminal, and I did not want to meet anybody. Then a big cloud covered the moon. In the dark I threw the basket into the sea. I heard it go down, and I sailed away.

The sky was cloudy, and a cold wind started. But I liked the fresh air, so I stayed on the water. The wind was cold, but it felt good. I lay down in the bottom of the boat. It was dark, and I heard only the waves. Soon I was asleep.

When I woke up, the sun was high. The wind was strong, and there were big waves. The wind carried me far from the island. I tried to turn the boat, but the water almost came in. So I had to go where the wind wanted. I was afraid.

I did not have a compass, and I did not know where I was. Maybe the wind will take me into the big ocean, I thought, and I will die there. Maybe the big waves will pull me down. I was on the sea for many hours, and I was very thirsty.

I looked at the sky and the clouds. I looked at the sea, and I thought: I will die here. “Monster,” I shouted, “you have won!” I thought of Elizabeth, my father and Clerval. The monster can kill them now, and I cannot help them. Even today I feel afraid when I remember it.

Some hours went by. In the evening the wind became softer, and the big waves stopped. I felt sick and very tired. Then suddenly I saw land in the south! I knew that I was going to live, and I cried with joy.

It is strange how much we love life, even when we are very unhappy! I made another sail from my clothes and sailed to the land. It was rocky, but there were fields too. It looked wild, but people lived there. I saw ships near the shore. I was back with people again.

I sailed along the coast and saw a church. I was very weak, so I went to the town to get food. Luckily, I had some money. I found a small, pretty town with a good harbour. I was very happy because I was safe.

When I was tying up my boat, some people came. They looked at me with surprise, but they did not help me. They whispered to each other. Their faces were not friendly. They spoke English, so I spoke English too. “Friends,” I said, “please tell me the name of this town.”

“You’ll know soon,” said a man. “Maybe you won’t like this place.” I was surprised because he was very rude. The other people looked angry too. “Why are you so rude?” I asked. “English people are usually kind to strangers.” “I don’t know about the English,” said the man, “but we Irish hate bad people.”

More and more people came. They looked at me with interest and anger, and I felt afraid. I asked the way to a hotel, but nobody answered. I started to walk, and the people followed me. Then a man touched my shoulder and said, “Come with me to Mr Kirwin.”
“Who is Mr Kirwin? Why must I go to him? Isn’t this a free country?” “Mr Kirwin is a judge. Last night someone killed a man here. You must answer questions about it.”

I was surprised, but I soon felt calm again. I did not do anything wrong, so I went with the man. I was very tired and hungry, but I tried to look strong. I did not know that something terrible was going to happen. In a few minutes my life was going to change again. I must stop here, because it is very hard for me to remember it.

o.en: I sat one evening in my laboratory; the sun had set, and the moon was just rising from the sea; I had not sufficient light for my employment, and I remained idle, in a pause of consideration of whether I should leave my labour for the night or hasten its conclusion by an unremitting attention to it.
o.ru: Однажды вечером я сидел в своей лаборатории; солнце уже село, и луна только поднималась из моря; света для работы мне не хватало, и я сидел без дела, раздумывая, оставить ли труд до утра или ускорить его завершение, не отрываясь от него ни на миг.

o.en: As I sat, a train of reflection occurred to me which led me to consider the effects of what I was now doing.
o.ru: Пока я так сидел, мне пришла на ум вереница мыслей, которая заставила меня задуматься о последствиях того, что я теперь делал.

o.en: Three years before, I was engaged in the same manner and had created a fiend whose unparalleled barbarity had desolated my heart and filled it for ever with the bitterest remorse.
o.ru: Тремя годами раньше я был занят тем же самым и создал демона, чья беспримерная жестокость опустошила моё сердце и навсегда наполнила его горчайшим раскаянием.

o.en: I was now about to form another being of whose dispositions I was alike ignorant; she might become ten thousand times more malignant than her mate and delight, for its own sake, in murder and wretchedness.
o.ru: Теперь я собирался создать другое существо, о нраве которого я так же ничего не знал; она могла стать в десять тысяч раз злобнее своего друга и находить удовольствие в убийстве и страданиях ради них самих.

o.en: He had sworn to quit the neighbourhood of man and hide himself in deserts, but she had not; and she, who in all probability was to become a thinking and reasoning animal, might refuse to comply with a compact made before her creation.
o.ru: Он поклялся покинуть жилища людей и скрыться в пустынях, но она не клялась; и она, которая, по всей вероятности, должна была стать мыслящим и рассуждающим существом, могла отказаться исполнять договор, заключённый до её сотворения.

o.en: They might even hate each other; the creature who already lived loathed his own deformity, and might he not conceive a greater abhorrence for it when it came before his eyes in the female form?
o.ru: Они могли даже возненавидеть друг друга; существо, которое уже жило, питало отвращение к собственному уродству — так не почувствует ли оно ещё большего омерзения, когда это уродство предстанет перед его глазами в женском облике?

o.en: She also might turn with disgust from him to the superior beauty of man; she might quit him, and he be again alone, exasperated by the fresh provocation of being deserted by one of his own species.
o.ru: Она тоже могла с отвращением отвернуться от него к превосходящей красоте человека; она могла покинуть его, и он снова остался бы один, озлобленный новой обидой — тем, что его бросило существо его же породы.

o.en: Even if they were to leave Europe and inhabit the deserts of the new world, yet one of the first results of those sympathies for which the dæmon thirsted would be children, and a race of devils would be propagated upon the earth who might make the very existence of the species of man a condition precarious and full of terror.
o.ru: Даже если бы они покинули Европу и поселились в пустынях Нового Света, одним из первых плодов той привязанности, которой так жаждал демон, стали бы дети, и по земле расплодилось бы племя дьяволов, способное сделать само существование рода человеческого шатким и полным ужаса.

o.en: Had I right, for my own benefit, to inflict this curse upon everlasting generations?
o.ru: Имел ли я право ради собственной выгоды навлечь это проклятие на бесконечные поколения?

o.en: I had before been moved by the sophisms of the being I had created; I had been struck senseless by his fiendish threats; but now, for the first time, the wickedness of my promise burst upon me; I shuddered to think that future ages might curse me as their pest, whose selfishness had not hesitated to buy its own peace at the price, perhaps, of the existence of the whole human race.
o.ru: Прежде меня тронули софизмы созданного мною существа, его дьявольские угрозы лишили меня рассудка; но теперь, впервые, вся порочность моего обещания открылась мне; я содрогался при мысли, что грядущие века, быть может, будут проклинать меня как свою чуму — того, чей эгоизм не поколебался купить собственный покой ценой, возможно, существования всего человечества.

o.en: I trembled and my heart failed within me, when, on looking up, I saw by the light of the moon the dæmon at the casement.
o.ru: Я задрожал, и сердце моё замерло, когда, подняв глаза, я увидел в лунном свете демона у окна.

o.en: A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips as he gazed on me, where I sat fulfilling the task which he had allotted to me.
o.ru: Жуткая усмешка кривила его губы, пока он смотрел на меня, сидевшего за исполнением задачи, которую он мне назначил.

o.en: Yes, he had followed me in my travels; he had loitered in forests, hid himself in caves, or taken refuge in wide and desert heaths; and he now came to mark my progress and claim the fulfilment of my promise.
o.ru: Да, он следовал за мной в моих странствиях; он бродил по лесам, прятался в пещерах или укрывался в широких пустынных вересковых пустошах; и теперь он пришёл проверить, как продвигается моя работа, и потребовать исполнения моего обещания.

o.en: As I looked on him, his countenance expressed the utmost extent of malice and treachery.
o.ru: Когда я взглянул на него, его лицо выражало крайнюю степень злобы и вероломства.

o.en: I thought with a sensation of madness on my promise of creating another like to him, and trembling with passion, tore to pieces the thing on which I was engaged.
o.ru: С чувством, похожим на безумие, я подумал о своём обещании создать другое существо, подобное ему, и, дрожа от ярости, разорвал на куски то, над чем работал.

o.en: The wretch saw me destroy the creature on whose future existence he depended for happiness, and with a howl of devilish despair and revenge, withdrew.
o.ru: Негодяй увидел, как я уничтожаю создание, от будущего существования которого зависело его счастье, и с воем дьявольского отчаяния и жажды мести удалился.

o.en: I left the room, and locking the door, made a solemn vow in my own heart never to resume my labours; and then, with trembling steps, I sought my own apartment.
o.ru: Я вышел из комнаты и, заперев дверь, дал в сердце торжественный обет никогда не возобновлять своих трудов; а затем дрожащими шагами направился в свою комнату.

o.en: I was alone; none were near me to dissipate the gloom and relieve me from the sickening oppression of the most terrible reveries.
o.ru: Я был один; рядом не было никого, кто рассеял бы мрак и избавил меня от тошнотворного гнёта самых страшных видений.

o.en: Several hours passed, and I remained near my window gazing on the sea; it was almost motionless, for the winds were hushed, and all nature reposed under the eye of the quiet moon.
o.ru: Прошло несколько часов, а я всё стоял у окна, глядя на море; оно было почти неподвижно, ибо ветры стихли, и вся природа покоилась под оком тихой луны.

o.en: A few fishing vessels alone specked the water, and now and then the gentle breeze wafted the sound of voices as the fishermen called to one another.
o.ru: Лишь несколько рыбачьих судёнышек пестрели на воде, и время от времени лёгкий ветерок доносил голоса перекликавшихся рыбаков.

o.en: I felt the silence, although I was hardly conscious of its extreme profundity, until my ear was suddenly arrested by the paddling of oars near the shore, and a person landed close to my house.
o.ru: Я ощущал тишину, хотя едва сознавал всю её глубину, как вдруг мой слух уловил плеск вёсел у берега, и какой-то человек высадился недалеко от моего дома.

o.en: In a few minutes after, I heard the creaking of my door, as if some one endeavoured to open it softly.
o.ru: Через несколько минут я услышал скрип двери, словно кто-то пытался тихонько её открыть.

o.en: I trembled from head to foot; I felt a presentiment of who it was and wished to rouse one of the peasants who dwelt in a cottage not far from mine; but I was overcome by the sensation of helplessness, so often felt in frightful dreams, when you in vain endeavour to fly from an impending danger, and was rooted to the spot.
o.ru: Я задрожал с головы до ног; я предчувствовал, кто это, и хотел разбудить кого-нибудь из крестьян, живших в хижине неподалёку от моей; но меня охватило чувство беспомощности, какое так часто испытываешь в страшных снах, когда тщетно пытаешься бежать от надвигающейся опасности, — и я словно прирос к месту.

o.en: Presently I heard the sound of footsteps along the passage; the door opened, and the wretch whom I dreaded appeared.
o.ru: Вскоре я услышал шаги в коридоре; дверь открылась, и появился негодяй, которого я так страшился.

o.en: Shutting the door, he approached me and said in a smothered voice,
o.ru: Закрыв дверь, он подошёл ко мне и сказал приглушённым голосом:

o.en: “You have destroyed the work which you began; what is it that you intend?
o.ru: «Ты уничтожил работу, которую начал; что ты задумал?

o.en: Do you dare to break your promise?
I have endured toil and misery; I left Switzerland with you; I crept along the shores of the Rhine, among its willow islands and over the summits of its hills.
o.ru: Я терпел лишения и муки; я покинул Швейцарию вместе с тобой; я крался по берегам Рейна, среди его ивовых островов и по вершинам его холмов.

o.en: I have dwelt many months in the heaths of England and among the deserts of Scotland.
o.ru: Много месяцев я жил на пустошах Англии и в пустынных краях Шотландии.

o.en: I have endured incalculable fatigue, and cold, and hunger; do you dare destroy my hopes?”
o.ru: Я вынес неисчислимую усталость, и холод, и голод; ты смеешь разрушить мои надежды?»

o.en: “Begone! I do break my promise; never will I create another like yourself, equal in deformity and wickedness.”
o.ru: «Прочь! Да, я нарушаю своё обещание; никогда я не создам другого, подобного тебе, равного тебе в уродстве и злобе».

o.en: “Slave, I before reasoned with you, but you have proved yourself unworthy of my condescension.
o.ru: «Раб, прежде я убеждал тебя доводами, но ты показал, что недостоин моей снисходительности.

o.en: Remember that I have power; you believe yourself miserable, but I can make you so wretched that the light of day will be hateful to you.
o.ru: Помни, что у меня есть сила; ты считаешь себя несчастным, но я могу сделать тебя таким жалким, что сам дневной свет станет тебе ненавистен.

o.en: You are my creator, but I am your master; obey!”
o.ru: Ты мой создатель, но я твой господин; повинуйся!»

o.en: “The hour of my irresolution is past, and the period of your power is arrived.
o.ru: «Час моей нерешительности прошёл, и время твоей власти окончилось.

o.en: Your threats cannot move me to do an act of wickedness; but they confirm me in a determination of not creating you a companion in vice.
o.ru: Твои угрозы не заставят меня совершить злодеяние; напротив, они укрепляют мою решимость не создавать тебе сообщницу в пороке.

o.en: Shall I, in cool blood, set loose upon the earth a dæmon whose delight is in death and wretchedness?
o.ru: Неужели я хладнокровно выпущу на землю демона, чья радость — в смерти и страданиях?

o.en: Begone!
I am firm, and your words will only exasperate my rage.”
o.ru: Я твёрд, и твои слова лишь распалят мой гнев».

o.en: The monster saw my determination in my face and gnashed his teeth in the impotence of anger.
o.ru: Чудовище увидело решимость на моём лице и заскрежетало зубами в бессильной ярости.

o.en: “Shall each man,” cried he, “find a wife for his bosom, and each beast have his mate, and I be alone?
o.ru: «Неужели у каждого человека, — вскричал он, — будет жена, которую он прижмёт к груди, у каждого зверя — своя пара, а я останусь один?

o.en: I had feelings of affection, and they were requited by detestation and scorn.
o.ru: Я питал чувства любви, а в ответ получил ненависть и презрение.

o.en: Man! You may hate, but beware!
o.ru: Человек! Ты можешь ненавидеть, но берегись!

o.en: Your hours will pass in dread and misery, and soon the bolt will fall which must ravish from you your happiness for ever.
o.ru: Твои часы пройдут в страхе и муках, и скоро грянет удар, который навсегда похитит у тебя твоё счастье.

o.en: Are you to be happy while I grovel in the intensity of my wretchedness?
o.ru: Неужели ты будешь счастлив, пока я пресмыкаюсь в бездне своих страданий?

o.en: You can blast my other passions, but revenge remains—revenge, henceforth dearer than light or food!
o.ru: Ты можешь уничтожить все мои другие страсти, но месть останется — месть, отныне дороже мне света и пищи!

o.en: I may die, but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that gazes on your misery.
o.ru: Я могу умереть, но прежде ты, мой тиран и мучитель, проклянёшь солнце, которое взирает на твоё горе.

o.en: Beware, for I am fearless and therefore powerful.
o.ru: Берегись, ибо я бесстрашен, а значит, могуществен.

o.en: I will watch with the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom.
o.ru: Я буду выжидать с хитростью змеи, чтобы ужалить её ядом.

o.en: Man, you shall repent of the injuries you inflict.”
o.ru: Человек, ты раскаешься в обидах, которые причиняешь».

o.en: “Devil, cease; and do not poison the air with these sounds of malice.
o.ru: «Дьявол, замолчи; не отравляй воздух этими злобными речами.

o.en: I have declared my resolution to you, and I am no coward to bend beneath words.
o.ru: Я объявил тебе своё решение, и я не трус, чтобы склониться перед словами.

o.en: Leave me; I am inexorable.”
“It is well. I go; but remember, I shall be with you on your wedding-night.”
o.ru: «Хорошо. Я ухожу; но помни: я буду с тобой в твою брачную ночь».

o.en: I started forward and exclaimed, “Villain! Before you sign my death-warrant, be sure that you are yourself safe.”
o.ru: Я бросился вперёд и воскликнул: «Злодей! Прежде чем подписать мне смертный приговор, убедись, что сам ты в безопасности».

o.en: I would have seized him, but he eluded me and quitted the house with precipitation.
o.ru: Я схватил бы его, но он ускользнул от меня и стремительно покинул дом.

o.en: In a few moments I saw him in his boat, which shot across the waters with an arrowy swiftness and was soon lost amidst the waves.
o.ru: Через несколько мгновений я увидел его в лодке, которая с быстротой стрелы понеслась по воде и вскоре скрылась среди волн.

o.en: All was again silent, but his words rang in my ears.
o.ru: Снова всё стихло, но его слова звенели у меня в ушах.

o.en: I burned with rage to pursue the murderer of my peace and precipitate him into the ocean.
o.ru: Я пылал яростью, желая догнать убийцу моего покоя и низвергнуть его в океан.

o.en: I walked up and down my room hastily and perturbed, while my imagination conjured up a thousand images to torment and sting me.
o.ru: Я торопливо и в смятении ходил взад и вперёд по комнате, а воображение рисовало мне тысячи образов, терзавших и жаливших меня.

o.en: Why had I not followed him and closed with him in mortal strife?
o.ru: Почему я не бросился за ним и не схватился с ним в смертельной борьбе?

o.en: But I had suffered him to depart, and he had directed his course towards the mainland.
o.ru: Но я позволил ему уйти, и он направился к большой земле.

o.en: I shuddered to think who might be the next victim sacrificed to his insatiate revenge.
o.ru: Я содрогался при мысли о том, кто станет следующей жертвой его ненасытной мести.

o.en: And then I thought again of his words—“I will be with you on your wedding-night.”
o.ru: И тут я снова вспомнил его слова: «Я буду с тобой в твою брачную ночь».

o.en: That, then, was the period fixed for the fulfilment of my destiny.
o.ru: Значит, именно тогда назначено исполниться моей судьбе.

o.en: In that hour I should die and at once satisfy and extinguish his malice.
o.ru: В тот час мне суждено умереть и тем самым одновременно насытить и погасить его злобу.

o.en: The prospect did not move me to fear; yet when I thought of my beloved Elizabeth, of her tears and endless sorrow, when she should find her lover so barbarously snatched from her, tears, the first I had shed for many months, streamed from my eyes, and I resolved not to fall before my enemy without a bitter struggle.
o.ru: Эта мысль не внушала мне страха; но когда я подумал о моей любимой Элизабет, о её слезах и бесконечном горе, когда она увидит, как её возлюбленного так жестоко вырвали у неё, слёзы — первые за много месяцев — хлынули из моих глаз, и я решил не пасть перед врагом без ожесточённой борьбы.

o.en: The night passed away, and the sun rose from the ocean; my feelings became calmer, if it may be called calmness when the violence of rage sinks into the depths of despair.
o.ru: Ночь прошла, и солнце поднялось из океана; мои чувства стали спокойнее, если можно назвать спокойствием то, что неистовство ярости погружается в глубины отчаяния.

o.en: I left the house, the horrid scene of the last night’s contention, and walked on the beach of the sea, which I almost regarded as an insuperable barrier between me and my fellow creatures; nay, a wish that such should prove the fact stole across me.
o.ru: Я покинул дом — страшное место ночной схватки — и пошёл по морскому берегу, почти видя в море непреодолимую преграду между мной и моими ближними; более того, во мне шевельнулось тайное желание, чтобы так оно и оказалось.

o.en: I desired that I might pass my life on that barren rock, wearily, it is true, but uninterrupted by any sudden shock of misery.
o.ru: Мне хотелось провести жизнь на этой бесплодной скале — пусть уныло, это правда, но без внезапных ударов несчастья.

o.en: If I returned, it was to be sacrificed or to see those whom I most loved die under the grasp of a dæmon whom I had myself created.
o.ru: Если бы я вернулся, то лишь затем, чтобы быть принесённым в жертву или увидеть, как те, кого я любил больше всего, гибнут в руках демона, которого я сам создал.

o.en: I walked about the isle like a restless spectre, separated from all it loved and miserable in the separation.
o.ru: Я бродил по острову, как беспокойный призрак, разлучённый со всем, что он любил, и несчастный в этой разлуке.

o.en: When it became noon, and the sun rose higher, I lay down on the grass and was overpowered by a deep sleep.
o.ru: Когда наступил полдень и солнце поднялось выше, я лёг на траву, и меня одолел глубокий сон.
