b1.en: I do not know how long I slept, but when I woke up the sun was already high.
b1.ru: Не знаю, сколько я спал, но когда проснулся, солнце уже было высоко.

b1.en: The wind was strong, and the waves were dangerous for my little boat.
b1.ru: Ветер был сильный, и волны были опасны для моей маленькой лодки.

b1.en: The wind was from the north-east, and it must have carried me far from the coast.
b1.ru: Ветер дул с северо-востока, и он, должно быть, унёс меня далеко от берега.

b1.en: I tried to change direction, but I soon saw that if I tried again, water would fill the boat.
b1.ru: Я попытался изменить направление, но скоро увидел, что при новой попытке лодку зальёт водой.

b1.en: So I could only let the wind carry me.
b1.ru: Поэтому я мог только позволить ветру нести меня.

b1.en: I have to say that I felt quite frightened.
b1.ru: Должен признаться, мне было довольно страшно.

b1.en: I had no compass, and I knew so little about that part of the world that the sun did not help me much.
b1.ru: У меня не было компаса, и я так мало знал об этой части света, что солнце мне почти не помогало.

b1.en: The wind might carry me into the wide Atlantic Ocean, where I would die of hunger, or the huge, roaring waves might swallow me.
b1.ru: Ветер мог унести меня в широкий Атлантический океан, где я умер бы от голода, или огромные ревущие волны могли поглотить меня.

b1.en: I had been on the sea for many hours, and I was already terribly thirsty.
b1.ru: Я пробыл в море много часов и уже страшно хотел пить.

b1.en: It was the beginning of my other sufferings.
b1.ru: Это было начало других моих страданий.

b1.en: I looked at the sky, where the wind drove clouds along and more clouds came after them.
b1.ru: Я смотрел на небо, где ветер гнал тучи, а за ними шли новые.

b1.en: I looked at the sea; it was going to be my grave.
b1.ru: Я смотрел на море; ему предстояло стать моей могилой.

b1.en: “Monster,” I shouted, “your job is already done!”
b1.ru: «Чудовище, — закричал я, — твоя работа уже сделана!»

b1.en: I thought of Elizabeth, my father and Clerval.
b1.ru: Я думал об Элизабет, об отце и о Клервале.

b1.en: They were all far away, and the monster could kill them in his cruel anger.
b1.ru: Все они были далеко, и чудовище могло убить их в своей жестокой злобе.

b1.en: This thought filled me with such despair and fear that even now, near the end of my life, I shake when I remember it.
b1.ru: Эта мысль наполнила меня таким отчаянием и страхом, что даже сейчас, в конце моей жизни, я дрожу, когда вспоминаю её.

b1.en: Some hours passed like this.
b1.ru: Так прошло несколько часов.

b1.en: But slowly, as the sun went down towards the horizon, the wind became a gentle breeze and the big waves stopped.
b1.ru: Но постепенно, когда солнце опускалось к горизонту, ветер стал лёгким бризом, и большие волны утихли.

b1.en: Instead, the sea rose and fell heavily; I felt sick and could hardly hold the rudder.
b1.ru: Вместо этого море тяжело поднималось и опускалось; меня тошнило, и я едва мог держать руль.

b1.en: Then suddenly I saw a line of high land to the south.
b1.ru: Тут вдруг я увидел на юге полосу высокой земли.

b1.en: I was very tired after those long hours of fear, but now I knew I would live, and warm joy filled my heart.
b1.ru: Я очень устал после долгих часов страха, но теперь я знал, что буду жить, и тёплая радость наполнила моё сердце.

b1.en: Tears ran from my eyes.
b1.ru: Слёзы текли из моих глаз.

b1.en: How quickly our feelings change, and how strongly we love life, even when we are very unhappy!
b1.ru: Как быстро меняются наши чувства и как сильно мы любим жизнь, даже когда очень несчастны!

b1.en: I made another sail from some of my clothes and steered eagerly towards the land.
b1.ru: Я сделал ещё один парус из части своей одежды и с нетерпением направил лодку к земле.

b1.en: It looked wild and rocky, but as I came nearer I saw fields.
b1.ru: Она выглядела дикой и скалистой, но, подплыв ближе, я увидел поля.

b1.en: I saw ships near the shore and suddenly I was back among civilised people.
b1.ru: Я увидел корабли у берега и вдруг снова оказался среди цивилизованных людей.

b1.en: I carefully followed the coast, and I was very happy to see a church tower behind a small point of land.
b1.ru: Я внимательно следовал вдоль берега и очень обрадовался, увидев церковную башню за небольшим мысом.

b1.en: I was very weak, so I decided to sail straight to the town, where I could easily get food.
b1.ru: Я был очень слаб, поэтому решил плыть прямо к городу, где можно было легко достать еду.

b1.en: Luckily, I had money with me.
b1.ru: К счастью, у меня были с собой деньги.

b1.en: When I came round the point, I saw a small, neat town and a good harbour.
b1.ru: Обогнув мыс, я увидел небольшой аккуратный городок и хорошую гавань.

b1.en: I sailed into it, and my heart jumped with joy because I had escaped.
b1.ru: Я вошёл в неё, и моё сердце прыгало от радости, потому что я спасся.

b1.en: While I was tying up the boat and putting the sails in order, several people came towards me.
b1.ru: Пока я привязывал лодку и приводил в порядок паруса, ко мне подошли несколько человек.

b1.en: They looked very surprised to see me, but they did not offer to help.
b1.ru: Они выглядели очень удивлёнными, увидев меня, но не предложили помощи.

b1.en: Instead they whispered to each other and made signs, which at another time might have worried me a little.
b1.ru: Вместо этого они шептались друг с другом и делали знаки, которые в другое время могли бы меня немного встревожить.

b1.en: But I only noticed that they spoke English, so I spoke to them in English.
b1.ru: Но я лишь заметил, что они говорят по-английски, и поэтому заговорил с ними по-английски.

b1.en: “My good friends,” I said, “could you please tell me the name of this town and where I am?”
b1.ru: «Друзья мои, — сказал я, — скажите, пожалуйста, как называется этот город и где я нахожусь?»

b1.en: “You’ll know that soon enough,” answered a man with a rough voice.
b1.ru: «Скоро узнаете», — ответил человек грубым голосом.

b1.en: “Perhaps you won’t like this place very much, but nobody will ask you where you want to stay, I promise you.”
b1.ru: «Может, вам здесь не очень понравится, но никто не спросит вас, где вы хотите жить, это я вам обещаю».

b1.en: I was very surprised by such a rude answer from a stranger.
b1.ru: Я был очень удивлён таким грубым ответом незнакомца.

b1.en: I was also worried when I saw the angry faces of the people with him.
b1.ru: Меня также встревожили сердитые лица людей рядом с ним.

b1.en: “Why do you answer me so rudely?” I asked.
b1.ru: «Почему вы отвечаете мне так грубо?» — спросил я.

b1.en: “Surely Englishmen do not usually treat strangers so badly.”
b1.ru: «Ведь англичане обычно не обращаются так плохо с чужими людьми».

b1.en: “I don’t know what the English usually do,” said the man, “but the Irish usually hate criminals.”
b1.ru: «Не знаю, что обычно делают англичане, — сказал человек, — но ирландцы обычно ненавидят преступников».

b1.en: While we were having this strange conversation, the crowd quickly grew bigger.
b1.ru: Пока шёл этот странный разговор, толпа быстро росла.

b1.en: Their faces showed curiosity and anger, and this annoyed me and frightened me a little.
b1.ru: Их лица выражали любопытство и гнев, и это раздражало меня и немного пугало.

b1.en: I asked the way to the inn, but nobody answered.
b1.ru: Я спросил дорогу к гостинице, но никто не ответил.

b1.en: Then I started to walk, and the people murmured as they followed me and stood around me.
b1.ru: Тогда я пошёл, а люди, шепчась, пошли за мной и окружили меня.

b1.en: An unpleasant-looking man came up, touched me on the shoulder and said, “Come, sir, you must come with me to Mr Kirwin and explain who you are.”
b1.ru: Подошёл человек неприятного вида, тронул меня за плечо и сказал: «Пойдёмте, сэр, вы должны пойти со мной к мистеру Кервину и объяснить, кто вы такой».

b1.en: “Who is Mr Kirwin?
b1.ru: «Кто такой мистер Кервин?

b1.en: Why must I explain who I am?
b1.ru: Почему я должен объяснять, кто я такой?

b1.en: Isn’t this a free country?”
b1.ru: Разве это не свободная страна?»

b1.en: “Yes, sir, it’s free enough for honest people.
b1.ru: «Да, сэр, она достаточно свободная для честных людей.

b1.en: Mr Kirwin is a judge, and you must explain the death of a gentleman who was found murdered here last night.”
b1.ru: Мистер Кервин — судья, и вы должны объяснить смерть джентльмена, которого нашли здесь убитым прошлой ночью».

b1.en: This answer shocked me, but I soon felt calm again.
b1.ru: Этот ответ потряс меня, но я скоро снова успокоился.

b1.en: I was innocent, and that was easy to prove.
b1.ru: Я был невиновен, и это было легко доказать.

b1.en: So I followed the man without a word, and he took me to one of the best houses in the town.
b1.ru: Поэтому я молча пошёл за этим человеком, и он привёл меня в один из лучших домов города.

b1.en: I was almost falling down from tiredness and hunger, but with the crowd around me, I tried to look strong.
b1.ru: Я почти падал от усталости и голода, но, окружённый толпой, старался выглядеть сильным.

b1.en: I did not want them to think that I was weak because I was afraid or guilty.
b1.ru: Я не хотел, чтобы они подумали, будто я слаб, потому что боюсь или виноват.

b1.en: I did not know then that in a few moments a terrible disaster would fall on me, and I would forget all fear of shame or death in my horror and despair.
b1.ru: Я тогда не знал, что через несколько мгновений на меня обрушится страшная беда и в ужасе и отчаянии я забуду всякий страх позора или смерти.

b1.en: I must stop here, because I need all my courage to remember the terrible things that I am going to tell you.
b1.ru: Здесь я должен остановиться, потому что мне нужно всё моё мужество, чтобы вспомнить те страшные события, о которых я собираюсь рассказать.

a2.en: One evening I was sitting in my laboratory.
a2.ru: Однажды вечером я сидел в своей лаборатории.

a2.en: The sun went down, and the moon came up over the sea.
a2.ru: Солнце село, и над морем поднялась луна.

a2.en: It was too dark to work, so I sat and thought.
a2.ru: Было слишком темно для работы, и я сидел и думал.

a2.en: Should I stop for the night, or should I work and finish quickly?
a2.ru: Остановиться ли мне на ночь или работать и быстро закончить?

a2.en: Three years before, I made a monster.
a2.ru: Три года назад я создал чудовище.

a2.en: He was very cruel, and I was always sorry that I made him.
a2.ru: Он был очень жестоким, и я всегда жалел, что создал его.

a2.en: Now I was making a second creature, a woman.
a2.ru: Теперь я делал второе существо — женщину.

a2.en: I did not know what she was going to be like.
a2.ru: Я не знал, какой она будет.

a2.en: Maybe she will be much worse than him, I thought, and she will love killing.
a2.ru: Может быть, она будет намного хуже его, думал я, и будет любить убивать.

a2.en: He promised to go far away from people, but she did not promise anything.
a2.ru: Он обещал уйти далеко от людей, но она ничего не обещала.

a2.en: She will think for herself, and maybe she will say no.
a2.ru: Она будет думать сама, и, может быть, она скажет «нет».

a2.en: Maybe they will hate each other.
a2.ru: Может быть, они возненавидят друг друга.

a2.en: He hated his own ugly body.
a2.ru: Он ненавидел своё уродливое тело.

a2.en: Maybe she will like beautiful men more than him and leave him.
a2.ru: Может быть, ей больше понравятся красивые люди, и она бросит его.

a2.en: Then he will be alone again and even angrier.
a2.ru: Тогда он снова останется один и станет ещё злее.

a2.en: Even if they went far away, they will have children.
a2.ru: Даже если они уедут далеко, у них будут дети.

a2.en: Soon there will be many monsters in the world, and people will live in fear.
a2.ru: Скоро в мире будет много чудовищ, и люди будут жить в страхе.

a2.en: These monsters will be dangerous for everybody.
a2.ru: Эти чудовища будут опасны для всех.

a2.en: Did I have the right to do this to the world?
a2.ru: Имел ли я право так поступить с миром?

a2.en: Before, the monster’s words and threats made me agree.
a2.ru: Раньше слова и угрозы чудовища заставили меня согласиться.

a2.en: But now I understood that my promise was very bad.
a2.ru: Но теперь я понял, что моё обещание было очень плохим.

a2.en: People in the future will hate me, I thought.
a2.ru: Люди в будущем будут ненавидеть меня, думал я.

a2.en: I wanted peace for myself, but all people may pay for it.
a2.ru: Я хотел покоя для себя, но за это могут заплатить все люди.

a2.en: Then I looked up and I felt very afraid.
a2.ru: Потом я поднял глаза, и мне стало очень страшно.

a2.en: In the moonlight I saw the monster at the window.
a2.ru: В лунном свете я увидел чудовище в окне.

a2.en: He smiled a terrible smile and watched me at my work.
a2.ru: Он улыбался страшной улыбкой и смотрел, как я работаю.

a2.en: He followed me all the way from Switzerland.
a2.ru: Он шёл за мной всю дорогу из Швейцарии.

a2.en: He hid in forests and caves.
a2.ru: Он прятался в лесах и пещерах.

a2.en: Now he came to see my work.
a2.ru: Теперь он пришёл посмотреть на мою работу.

a2.en: He wanted to see my promise come true.
a2.ru: Он хотел, чтобы моё обещание сбылось.

a2.en: His face was very evil.
a2.ru: Его лицо было очень злым.

a2.en: I thought about my promise, and I felt almost mad.
a2.ru: Я подумал о своём обещании, и почувствовал, что почти схожу с ума.

a2.en: I was shaking, and I tore the half-made woman to pieces.
a2.ru: Я дрожал и разорвал недоделанную женщину на куски.

a2.en: The monster saw it.
a2.ru: Чудовище увидело это.

a2.en: She was his only hope.
a2.ru: Она была его единственной надеждой.

a2.en: He screamed with pain and anger, and went away.
a2.ru: Он закричал от боли и гнева и ушёл.

a2.en: I left the room and locked the door.
a2.ru: Я вышел из комнаты и запер дверь.

a2.en: I promised myself: I will never do this work again.
a2.ru: Я пообещал себе: я никогда больше не буду делать эту работу.

a2.en: Then I went to my room.
a2.ru: Потом я пошёл в свою комнату.

a2.en: I was alone with my terrible thoughts.
a2.ru: Я был один со своими страшными мыслями.

a2.en: For some hours I sat by the window and looked at the sea.
a2.ru: Несколько часов я сидел у окна и смотрел на море.

a2.en: There was no wind, and everything was quiet.
a2.ru: Не было ветра, и всё было тихо.

a2.en: The moon was quiet above the water.
a2.ru: Над водой тихо светила луна.

a2.en: There were a few fishing boats on the water.
a2.ru: На воде было несколько рыбачьих лодок.

a2.en: Sometimes I heard the fishermen’s voices.
a2.ru: Иногда я слышал голоса рыбаков.

a2.en: Then I heard a boat near the shore.
a2.ru: Потом я услышал лодку у берега.

a2.en: Someone got out of it near my house.
a2.ru: Кто-то вышел из неё рядом с моим домом.

a2.en: A few minutes later my door made a noise.
a2.ru: Через несколько минут моя дверь скрипнула.

a2.en: Someone was opening it quietly.
a2.ru: Кто-то тихо её открывал.

a2.en: I was shaking all over, because I knew who it was.
a2.ru: Я весь дрожал, потому что знал, кто это.

a2.en: I wanted to call my neighbours, but I could not move.
a2.ru: Я хотел позвать соседей, но не мог пошевелиться.

a2.en: It was like a bad dream.
a2.ru: Это было как в страшном сне.

a2.en: I heard steps, and then the monster came in.
a2.ru: Я услышал шаги, и потом вошло чудовище.

a2.en: He closed the door and spoke quietly:
a2.ru: Он закрыл дверь и тихо заговорил:

a2.en: “You destroyed your work. Why?
a2.ru: «Ты уничтожил свою работу. Почему?

a2.en: Are you going to break your promise?
a2.ru: Ты собираешься нарушить обещание?

a2.en: I followed you from Switzerland.
a2.ru: Я шёл за тобой из Швейцарии.

a2.en: I walked along the river Rhine and over the hills.
a2.ru: Я шёл вдоль Рейна и через холмы.

a2.en: I lived for months in the wild places of England and Scotland.
a2.ru: Я месяцами жил в диких местах Англии и Шотландии.

a2.en: I was tired, cold and hungry. Do you want to kill my hopes?”
a2.ru: Я был усталым, замёрзшим и голодным. Ты хочешь убить мои надежды?»

a2.en: “Go away! Yes, I am breaking my promise.
a2.ru: «Уходи! Да, я нарушаю обещание.

a2.en: I will never make another monster like you.”
a2.ru: Я никогда не сделаю другое чудовище, как ты».

a2.en: “Slave! I was kind to you before, but now I will not be kind.
a2.ru: «Раб! Раньше я был добр к тебе, но теперь не буду.

a2.en: I am strong.
a2.ru: Я сильный.

a2.en: I can make your life terrible.
a2.ru: Я могу сделать твою жизнь ужасной.

a2.en: You made me, but I am your master. Do what I say!”
a2.ru: Ты создал меня, но я твой хозяин. Делай, что я говорю!»

a2.en: “No. You have no power over me now.
a2.ru: «Нет. Теперь у тебя нет власти надо мной.

a2.en: Your threats cannot make me do a bad thing.
a2.ru: Твои угрозы не заставят меня сделать плохое дело.

a2.en: I will not make an evil woman for you.
a2.ru: Я не сделаю для тебя злую женщину.

a2.en: I will not send another killer into the world.
a2.ru: Я не выпущу в мир ещё одного убийцу.

a2.en: Go away! I will not change my mind.”
a2.ru: Уходи! Я не передумаю».

a2.en: The monster saw that I was serious.
a2.ru: Чудовище увидело, что я говорю серьёзно.

a2.en: He was very angry.
a2.ru: Он очень разозлился.

a2.en: “Every man has a wife, and every animal has a partner,” he cried. “Why must I be alone?
a2.ru: «У каждого мужчины есть жена, и у каждого зверя есть пара, — закричал он. — Почему я должен быть один?

a2.en: I wanted love, but people gave me only hate.
a2.ru: Я хотел любви, но люди давали мне только ненависть.

a2.en: Be careful!
a2.ru: Берегись!

a2.en: Soon something terrible will happen to you, and you will never be happy again.
a2.ru: Скоро с тобой случится что-то страшное, и ты больше никогда не будешь счастлив.

a2.en: Why should you be happy when I am so unhappy?
a2.ru: Почему ты должен быть счастлив, когда я так несчастен?

a2.en: Now I want only one thing: revenge!
a2.ru: Теперь я хочу только одного — мести!

a2.en: Maybe I will die, but first you will be very unhappy.
a2.ru: Может быть, я умру, но сначала ты будешь очень несчастен.

a2.en: I am not afraid of anything, so I am strong.
a2.ru: Я ничего не боюсь, поэтому я сильный.

a2.en: I will watch you like a snake, and then I will bite.
a2.ru: Я буду следить за тобой, как змея, а потом укушу.

a2.en: You will be sorry.”
a2.ru: Ты пожалеешь».

a2.en: “Stop, devil!
a2.ru: «Замолчи, дьявол!

a2.en: I told you my answer, and I am not afraid of your words.
a2.ru: Я сказал тебе свой ответ, и я не боюсь твоих слов.

a2.en: Leave me!”
a2.ru: Оставь меня!»

a2.en: “All right. I am going. But remember: I will be with you on your wedding night.”
a2.ru: «Хорошо. Я ухожу. Но помни: я буду с тобой в твою брачную ночь».

a2.en: I jumped up and shouted, “You bad creature! You want to kill me, but be careful!”
a2.ru: Я вскочил и закричал: «Злодей! Ты хочешь убить меня, но берегись!»

a2.en: I tried to catch him, but he ran out of the house.
a2.ru: Я попытался схватить его, но он выбежал из дома.

a2.en: A moment later I saw him in his boat.
a2.ru: Через мгновение я увидел его в лодке.

a2.en: It went very fast and soon I could not see it.
a2.ru: Она плыла очень быстро, и скоро я перестал её видеть.

a2.en: It went across the water like an arrow.
a2.ru: Она неслась по воде, как стрела.

a2.en: Everything was quiet again, but I could still hear his words.
a2.ru: Всё снова стихло, но я всё ещё слышал его слова.

a2.en: I was very angry, and I wanted to kill him.
a2.ru: Я был очень зол и хотел убить его.

a2.en: I walked up and down my room.
a2.ru: Я ходил взад и вперёд по комнате.

a2.en: Why did I not follow him and fight him?
a2.ru: Почему я не погнался за ним и не сразился с ним?

a2.en: Now he was going to the mainland.
a2.ru: Теперь он плыл к большой земле.

a2.en: But I let him go.
a2.ru: Но я отпустил его.

a2.en: Who is he going to kill next, I thought.
a2.ru: Кого он убьёт следующим, думал я.

a2.en: Then I remembered his words: “I will be with you on your wedding night.”
a2.ru: Потом я вспомнил его слова: «Я буду с тобой в твою брачную ночь».

a2.en: So he was going to kill me on that night.
a2.ru: Значит, он собирался убить меня в ту ночь.

a2.en: I was not afraid to die.
a2.ru: Я не боялся умереть.

a2.en: But then I thought of Elizabeth.
a2.ru: Но потом я подумал об Элизабет.

a2.en: She will cry, and she will be sad for ever.
a2.ru: Она будет плакать и будет грустить всегда.

a2.en: For the first time in many months, I cried.
a2.ru: Впервые за много месяцев я заплакал.

a2.en: I decided to fight him.
a2.ru: Я решил бороться с ним.

a2.en: The night ended, and the sun came up.
a2.ru: Ночь закончилась, и взошло солнце.

a2.en: I was calmer now, but I was very sad.
a2.ru: Теперь я был спокойнее, но мне было очень грустно.

a2.en: I left the house and walked on the beach.
a2.ru: Я вышел из дома и пошёл по берегу.

a2.en: The sea was like a wall between me and other people, and I almost liked that.
a2.ru: Море было как стена между мной и другими людьми, и мне это почти нравилось.

a2.en: I wanted to stay on that island for ever.
a2.ru: Я хотел остаться на этом острове навсегда.

a2.en: Life there will be sad, but quiet, I thought.
a2.ru: Жизнь там будет грустной, но спокойной, думал я.

a2.en: If I go home, I thought, the monster will kill me or the people I love.
a2.ru: Если я поеду домой, думал я, чудовище убьёт меня или тех, кого я люблю.

a2.en: I walked around the island like a ghost.
a2.ru: Я бродил по острову, как призрак.

a2.en: At midday I lay down on the grass and fell asleep.
a2.ru: В полдень я лёг на траву и уснул.

a2.en: I did not sleep the night before, and I was very tired.
a2.ru: Прошлой ночью я не спал и очень устал.

a2.en: After the sleep I felt better.
a2.ru: После сна мне стало лучше.

a2.en: I could think more calmly.
a2.ru: Я мог думать спокойнее.

a2.en: But I still heard the monster’s words in my head.
a2.ru: Но я всё ещё слышал в голове слова чудовища.

a2.en: They were like a dream, but they felt very real.
a2.ru: Они были как сон, но казались очень настоящими.

a2.en: In the evening I was sitting on the beach and eating some bread.
a2.ru: Вечером я сидел на берегу и ел хлеб.

a2.en: A fishing boat came, and a man gave me some letters.
a2.ru: Пришла рыбачья лодка, и человек дал мне письма.

a2.en: There were letters from Geneva and one from Clerval.
a2.ru: Там были письма из Женевы и одно от Клерваля.

a2.en: Clerval wrote: “Please come to me.”
a2.ru: Клерваль писал: «Пожалуйста, приезжай ко мне».

a2.en: His friends in London wanted him to come back and finish his plans for India.
a2.ru: Его друзья в Лондоне хотели, чтобы он вернулся и закончил свои планы насчёт Индии.

a2.en: He could not wait any longer.
a2.ru: Он не мог больше ждать.

a2.en: Soon he was going to go on a long journey, so he wanted to spend time with me.
a2.ru: Скоро он собирался отправиться в долгое путешествие, поэтому хотел провести время со мной.

a2.en: He asked me to meet him in Perth.
a2.ru: Он попросил меня встретиться с ним в Перте.

a2.en: This letter made me feel a little better.
a2.ru: Это письмо помогло мне почувствовать себя немного лучше.

a2.en: I decided to leave the island in two days.
a2.ru: Я решил покинуть остров через два дня.

a2.en: But first I had to do a job that I hated.
a2.ru: Но сначала мне нужно было сделать работу, которую я ненавидел.

a2.en: I had to pack my instruments.
a2.ru: Мне нужно было упаковать свои инструменты.

a2.en: They were in my laboratory, and I did not want to go in there.
a2.ru: Они были в лаборатории, а я не хотел туда входить.

a2.en: I was afraid, but I found my courage.
a2.ru: Мне было страшно, но я нашёл в себе смелость.

a2.en: The next morning I opened the door.
a2.ru: На следующее утро я открыл дверь.

a2.en: The pieces of the woman were all over the floor.
a2.ru: Куски женщины лежали по всему полу.

a2.en: I felt like a murderer.
a2.ru: Я чувствовал себя убийцей.

a2.en: I stopped for a moment and then went in.
a2.ru: Я на минуту остановился, а потом вошёл.

a2.en: I carried my instruments out.
a2.ru: Я вынес свои инструменты.

a2.en: I did not want the people of the island to find the pieces.
a2.ru: Я не хотел, чтобы жители острова нашли куски.

a2.en: So I put them in a basket with a lot of stones.
a2.ru: Поэтому я положил их в корзину вместе с кучей камней.

a2.en: I decided to throw it into the sea that night.
a2.ru: Я решил бросить её в море той ночью.

a2.en: Then I sat on the beach and cleaned my instruments.
a2.ru: Потом я сидел на берегу и чистил инструменты.

a2.en: My feelings were now completely different.
a2.ru: Теперь мои чувства были совсем другими.

a2.en: Before, I thought I must keep my promise.
a2.ru: Раньше я думал, что должен сдержать обещание.

a2.en: Now I could see clearly for the first time.
a2.ru: Теперь я впервые видел всё ясно.

a2.en: I never wanted to start the work again.
a2.ru: Я никогда больше не хотел начинать эту работу.

a2.en: I remembered the monster’s words, but I could not stop him.
a2.ru: Я помнил слова чудовища, но не мог его остановить.

a2.en: Making another monster was a very bad and selfish thing, and I knew it.
a2.ru: Сделать ещё одно чудовище было очень плохим и эгоистичным поступком, и я это знал.

a2.en: At about three o’clock in the morning the moon came up.
a2.ru: Около трёх часов ночи взошла луна.

a2.en: I put my basket into a small boat and sailed away from the shore.
a2.ru: Я поставил корзину в маленькую лодку и отплыл от берега.

a2.en: I sailed about four miles out.
a2.ru: Я отплыл примерно на четыре мили.

a2.en: There was nobody near me.
a2.ru: Рядом со мной никого не было.

a2.en: I felt like a criminal, and I did not want to meet anybody.
a2.ru: Я чувствовал себя преступником и не хотел никого встречать.

a2.en: Then a big cloud covered the moon.
a2.ru: Потом большая туча закрыла луну.

a2.en: In the dark I threw the basket into the sea.
a2.ru: В темноте я бросил корзину в море.

a2.en: I heard it go down, and I sailed away.
a2.ru: Я слышал, как она пошла ко дну, и уплыл.

a2.en: The sky was cloudy, and a cold wind started.
a2.ru: Небо было облачным, и подул холодный ветер.

a2.en: But I liked the fresh air, so I stayed on the water.
a2.ru: Но мне нравился свежий воздух, поэтому я остался на воде.

a2.en: The wind was cold, but it felt good.
a2.ru: Ветер был холодным, но это было приятно.

a2.en: I lay down in the bottom of the boat.
a2.ru: Я лёг на дно лодки.

a2.en: It was dark, and I heard only the waves.
a2.ru: Было темно, и я слышал только волны.

a2.en: Soon I was asleep.
a2.ru: Скоро я уснул.

a2.en: When I woke up, the sun was high.
a2.ru: Когда я проснулся, солнце было высоко.

a2.en: The wind was strong, and there were big waves.
a2.ru: Ветер был сильный, и были большие волны.

a2.en: The wind carried me far from the island.
a2.ru: Ветер унёс меня далеко от острова.

a2.en: I tried to turn the boat, but the water almost came in.
a2.ru: Я попытался повернуть лодку, но вода чуть не залилась внутрь.

a2.en: So I had to go where the wind wanted.
a2.ru: Поэтому мне пришлось плыть туда, куда хотел ветер.

a2.en: I was afraid.
a2.ru: Мне было страшно.

a2.en: I did not have a compass, and I did not know where I was.
a2.ru: У меня не было компаса, и я не знал, где нахожусь.

a2.en: Maybe the wind will take me into the big ocean, I thought, and I will die there.
a2.ru: Может быть, ветер унесёт меня в большой океан, думал я, и я там умру.

a2.en: Maybe the big waves will pull me down.
a2.ru: Может быть, большие волны утянут меня на дно.

a2.en: I was on the sea for many hours, and I was very thirsty.
a2.ru: Я был в море много часов, и мне очень хотелось пить.

a2.en: I looked at the sky and the clouds.
a2.ru: Я смотрел на небо и тучи.

a2.en: I looked at the sea, and I thought: I will die here.
a2.ru: Я смотрел на море и думал: я умру здесь.

a2.en: “Monster,” I shouted, “you have won!”
a2.ru: «Чудовище, — закричал я, — ты победил!»

a2.en: I thought of Elizabeth, my father and Clerval.
a2.ru: Я думал об Элизабет, об отце и о Клервале.

a2.en: The monster can kill them now, and I cannot help them.
a2.ru: Теперь чудовище может убить их, а я не могу им помочь.

a2.en: Even today I feel afraid when I remember it.
a2.ru: Даже сегодня мне страшно, когда я вспоминаю это.

a2.en: Some hours went by.
a2.ru: Прошло несколько часов.

a2.en: In the evening the wind became softer, and the big waves stopped.
a2.ru: Вечером ветер стал тише, и большие волны утихли.

a2.en: I felt sick and very tired.
a2.ru: Меня тошнило, и я очень устал.

a2.en: Then suddenly I saw land in the south!
a2.ru: И вдруг я увидел землю на юге!

a2.en: I knew that I was going to live, and I cried with joy.
a2.ru: Я понял, что буду жить, и заплакал от радости.

a2.en: It is strange how much we love life, even when we are very unhappy!
a2.ru: Странно, как сильно мы любим жизнь, даже когда очень несчастны!

a2.en: I made another sail from my clothes and sailed to the land.
a2.ru: Я сделал ещё один парус из своей одежды и поплыл к земле.

a2.en: It was rocky, but there were fields too.
a2.ru: Она была скалистой, но там были и поля.

a2.en: It looked wild, but people lived there.
a2.ru: Она выглядела дикой, но там жили люди.

a2.en: I saw ships near the shore.
a2.ru: Я увидел корабли у берега.

a2.en: I was back with people again.
a2.ru: Я снова был среди людей.

a2.en: I sailed along the coast and saw a church.
a2.ru: Я плыл вдоль берега и увидел церковь.

a2.en: I was very weak, so I went to the town to get food.
a2.ru: Я был очень слаб, поэтому поплыл в город, чтобы добыть еду.

a2.en: Luckily, I had some money.
a2.ru: К счастью, у меня были деньги.

a2.en: I found a small, pretty town with a good harbour.
a2.ru: Я нашёл маленький красивый городок с хорошей гаванью.

a2.en: I was very happy because I was safe.
a2.ru: Я был очень счастлив, потому что был в безопасности.

a2.en: When I was tying up my boat, some people came.
a2.ru: Когда я привязывал лодку, пришли люди.

a2.en: They looked at me with surprise, but they did not help me.
a2.ru: Они с удивлением смотрели на меня, но не помогли мне.

a2.en: They whispered to each other.
a2.ru: Они шептались друг с другом.

a2.en: Their faces were not friendly.
a2.ru: Их лица были недружелюбными.

a2.en: They spoke English, so I spoke English too.
a2.ru: Они говорили по-английски, и я тоже заговорил по-английски.

a2.en: “Friends,” I said, “please tell me the name of this town.”
a2.ru: «Друзья, — сказал я, — пожалуйста, скажите мне, как называется этот город».

a2.en: “You’ll know soon,” said a man.
a2.ru: «Скоро узнаете», — сказал один человек.

a2.en: “Maybe you won’t like this place.”
a2.ru: «Может, вам здесь не понравится».

a2.en: I was surprised because he was very rude.
a2.ru: Я удивился, потому что он был очень груб.

a2.en: The other people looked angry too.
a2.ru: Другие люди тоже выглядели сердитыми.

a2.en: “Why are you so rude?” I asked. “English people are usually kind to strangers.”
a2.ru: «Почему вы так грубы? — спросил я. — Англичане обычно добры к чужим».

a2.en: “I don’t know about the English,” said the man, “but we Irish hate bad people.”
a2.ru: «Не знаю, как англичане, — сказал человек, — а мы, ирландцы, ненавидим плохих людей».

a2.en: More and more people came.
a2.ru: Приходило всё больше и больше людей.

a2.en: They looked at me with interest and anger, and I felt afraid.
a2.ru: Они смотрели на меня с интересом и гневом, и мне стало страшно.

a2.en: I asked the way to a hotel, but nobody answered.
a2.ru: Я спросил дорогу к гостинице, но никто не ответил.

a2.en: I started to walk, and the people followed me.
a2.ru: Я пошёл, и люди пошли за мной.

a2.en: Then a man touched my shoulder and said, “Come with me to Mr Kirwin.”
a2.ru: Потом один человек тронул меня за плечо и сказал: «Пойдёмте со мной к мистеру Кервину».

a2.en: “Who is Mr Kirwin?
a2.ru: «Кто такой мистер Кервин?

a2.en: Why must I go to him? Isn’t this a free country?”
a2.ru: Почему я должен идти к нему? Разве это не свободная страна?»

a2.en: “Mr Kirwin is a judge.
a2.ru: «Мистер Кервин — судья.

a2.en: Last night someone killed a man here.
a2.ru: Прошлой ночью здесь кто-то убил человека.

a2.en: You must answer questions about it.”
a2.ru: Вы должны ответить на вопросы об этом».

a2.en: I was surprised, but I soon felt calm again.
a2.ru: Я удивился, но скоро снова успокоился.

a2.en: I did not do anything wrong, so I went with the man.
a2.ru: Я не сделал ничего плохого, поэтому пошёл с этим человеком.

a2.en: I was very tired and hungry, but I tried to look strong.
a2.ru: Я очень устал и был голоден, но старался выглядеть сильным.

a2.en: I did not know that something terrible was going to happen.
a2.ru: Я не знал, что сейчас случится что-то ужасное.

a2.en: In a few minutes my life was going to change again.
a2.ru: Через несколько минут моя жизнь должна была снова измениться.

a2.en: I must stop here, because it is very hard for me to remember it.
a2.ru: Здесь я должен остановиться, потому что мне очень тяжело это вспоминать.

o.p: in a pause of consideration of whether I should

C2 · unparalleled = беспримерный; barbarity = варварство, жестокость (simpler: unequalled cruelty)

o.p: of whose dispositions I was alike ignorant

o.p: delight, for its own sake, in murder and wretchedness

o.p: a condition precarious and full of terror

o.tip: вопрос без do (устар.): Had I right…? = имел ли я право…?; inflict = навлечь, причинить

причастный оборот: trembling with passion = дрожа от ярости (passion здесь = гнев)

o.p: tore to pieces the thing on which I was engaged
o.tip: инверсия дополнения: tore to pieces the thing… (обычно: tore the thing to pieces); be engaged on = работать над

o.p: on whose future existence he depended for happiness
o.tip: предлог перед whose: от будущего существования которого зависело его счастье

o.tip: C2 · dissipate = рассеивать; gloom = мрак, уныние

o.p: the sickening oppression of the most terrible reveries
o.tip: C2 · oppression = гнёт; reverie = грёзы, (тут) мрачные видения
C1 · hushed = утихший, притихший

o.tip: олицетворение: природа покоилась под оком луны; repose = покоиться

o.p: I felt a presentiment of who it was
o.tip: C2 · presentiment = предчувствие

o.p: rouse one of the peasants who dwelt in a cottage
o.tip: rouse = будить, поднимать; dwell – dwelt = жить, обитать

o.p: so often felt in frightful dreams

C1 · wretch = негодяй, несчастный; dread = страшиться

o.tip: причастный оборот: Shutting the door = закрыв дверь
C1 · smothered = приглушённый, сдавленный

o.p: I have endured toil and misery
o.tip: C1 · endure = выносить; toil = тяжкий труд

o.tip: инверсия после never: never will I… = никогда я не…

o.tip: C2 · irresolution = нерешительность

o.p: the period of your power is arrived

o.tip: confirm sb in sth = утвердить кого-то в чём-то; companion in vice = сообщник в пороке

o.p: your words will only exasperate my rage
o.tip: C2 · exasperate = усиливать, распалять (гнев)

o.p: gnashed his teeth in the impotence of anger
o.tip: C2 · gnash one's teeth = скрежетать зубами; impotence = бессилие

o.p: the bolt will fall which must ravish from you your happiness
o.tip: bolt = удар молнии; ravish (устар.) = похитить, вырвать

o.p: Are you to be happy while I grovel

o.p: You can blast my other passions
o.tip: C1 · blast = губить, уничтожать (надежды, чувства)

o.tip: повтор (анадиплосис): revenge… revenge; henceforth = отныне

o.p: I am fearless and therefore powerful
o.tip: афористичная формула: бесстрашен, а потому могуществен

o.p: the wiliness of a snake, that I may sting with its venom
o.tip: wiliness = хитрость; that I may… = чтобы я мог… (цель); venom = яд

o.p: his words rang in my ears
o.tip: ring in one's ears = звучать в ушах

o.p: my imagination conjured up a thousand images
o.tip: C1 · conjure up = вызывать в воображении

o.p: closed with him in mortal strife
o.tip: close with = схватиться; mortal strife = смертельная борьба

o.p: I had suffered him to depart
o.tip: устар. suffer sb to do = позволить кому-то сделать
C2 · insatiate (= insatiable) = ненасытный

o.tip: вставное then = значит; причастие fixed = назначенный

o.tip: at once = одновременно; extinguish = погасить

o.p: distinct and oppressive as a reality

устар. порядок: far перед причастием = солнце опустилось низко

o.p: satisfying my appetite, which had become ravenous
o.tip: C2 · ravenous = зверски голодный

o.p: one from Clerval entreating me to join him
o.tip: C2 · entreat = умолять

o.p: he was wearing away his time fruitlessly
o.tip: wear away = растрачивать; fruitlessly = бесплодно, впустую

o.p: even sooner than he now conjectured

o.tip: придаточное цели: that we might… = чтобы мы могли…; proceed = продолжать путь
устар. in a degree = отчасти (сейчас: to some degree)

o.tip: expiration = истечение (срока): через два дня

o.p: the scene of my odious work

o.p: I conveyed the instruments out of the room

o.p: the relics of my work to excite the horror and suspicion

o.p: employed in cleaning and arranging my chemical apparatus

o.p: Nothing could be more complete than the alteration

o.tip: метафора: словно пелена спала с глаз

o.p: did not for one instant occur to me
o.tip: not for one instant = ни на миг; occur to = прийти в голову

o.p: although chilled by the northeast breeze

o.tip: such … that … = такие…, что…

o.p: fixing the rudder in a direct position
o.tip: причастный оборот: fixing the rudder = закрепив руль

o.p: its keel cut through the waves
o.tip: keel = киль
C1 · lull = убаюкать

o.p: the sun had already mounted considerably

o.p: must have driven me far from the coast

o.p: so slenderly acquainted with the geography

o.p: be swallowed up in the immeasurable waters

sub: Charged with a murder in Ireland, Victor is shown Henry Clerval's body, falls into a long fever in prison, is cleared of the crime and sails home with his father

o: I was soon introduced into the presence of the magistrate, an old benevolent man with calm and mild manners. He looked upon me, however, with some degree of severity, and then, turning towards my conductors, he asked who appeared as witnesses on this occasion.

About half a dozen men came forward; and, one being selected by the magistrate, he deposed that he had been out fishing the night before with his son and brother-in-law, Daniel Nugent, when, about ten o’clock, they observed a strong northerly blast rising, and they accordingly put in for port. It was a very dark night, as the moon had not yet risen; they did not land at the harbour, but, as they had been accustomed, at a creek about two miles below. He walked on first, carrying a part of the fishing tackle, and his companions followed him at some distance.

As he was proceeding along the sands, he struck his foot against something and fell at his length on the ground. His companions came up to assist him, and by the light of their lantern they found that he had fallen on the body of a man, who was to all appearance dead. Their first supposition was that it was the corpse of some person who had been drowned and was thrown on shore by the waves, but on examination they found that the clothes were not wet and even that the body was not then cold. They instantly carried it to the cottage of an old woman near the spot and endeavoured, but in vain, to restore it to life. It appeared to be a handsome young man, about five and twenty years of age. He had apparently been strangled, for there was no sign of any violence except the black mark of fingers on his neck.

The first part of this deposition did not in the least interest me, but when the mark of the fingers was mentioned I remembered the murder of my brother and felt myself extremely agitated; my limbs trembled, and a mist came over my eyes, which obliged me to lean on a chair for support. The magistrate observed me with a keen eye and of course drew an unfavourable augury from my manner.

The son confirmed his father’s account, but when Daniel Nugent was called he swore positively that just before the fall of his companion, he saw a boat, with a single man in it, at a short distance from the shore; and as far as he could judge by the light of a few stars, it was the same boat in which I had just landed.

A woman deposed that she lived near the beach and was standing at the door of her cottage, waiting for the return of the fishermen, about an hour before she heard of the discovery of the body, when she saw a boat with only one man in it push off from that part of the shore where the corpse was afterwards found.

Another woman confirmed the account of the fishermen having brought the body into her house; it was not cold. They put it into a bed and rubbed it, and Daniel went to the town for an apothecary, but life was quite gone.

Several other men were examined concerning my landing, and they agreed that, with the strong north wind that had arisen during the night, it was very probable that I had beaten about for many hours and had been obliged to return nearly to the same spot from which I had departed. Besides, they observed that it appeared that I had brought the body from another place, and it was likely that as I did not appear to know the shore, I might have put into the harbour ignorant of the distance of the town of —— from the place where I had deposited the corpse.

Mr. Kirwin, on hearing this evidence, desired that I should be taken into the room where the body lay for interment, that it might be observed what effect the sight of it would produce upon me. This idea was probably suggested by the extreme agitation I had exhibited when the mode of the murder had been described. I was accordingly conducted, by the magistrate and several other persons, to the inn. I could not help being struck by the strange coincidences that had taken place during this eventful night; but, knowing that I had been conversing with several persons in the island I had inhabited about the time that the body had been found, I was perfectly tranquil as to the consequences of the affair.

I entered the room where the corpse lay and was led up to the coffin. How can I describe my sensations on beholding it? I feel yet parched with horror, nor can I reflect on that terrible moment without shuddering and agony. The examination, the presence of the magistrate and witnesses, passed like a dream from my memory when I saw the lifeless form of Henry Clerval stretched before me. I gasped for breath, and throwing myself on the body, I exclaimed, “Have my murderous machinations deprived you also, my dearest Henry, of life? Two I have already destroyed; other victims await their destiny; but you, Clerval, my friend, my benefactor—”

The human frame could no longer support the agonies that I endured, and I was carried out of the room in strong convulsions.

A fever succeeded to this. I lay for two months on the point of death; my ravings, as I afterwards heard, were frightful; I called myself the murderer of William, of Justine, and of Clerval. Sometimes I entreated my attendants to assist me in the destruction of the fiend by whom I was tormented; and at others I felt the fingers of the monster already grasping my neck, and screamed aloud with agony and terror. Fortunately, as I spoke my native language, Mr. Kirwin alone understood me; but my gestures and bitter cries were sufficient to affright the other witnesses.

Why did I not die? More miserable than man ever was before, why did I not sink into forgetfulness and rest? Death snatches away many blooming children, the only hopes of their doting parents; how many brides and youthful lovers have been one day in the bloom of health and hope, and the next a prey for worms and the decay of the tomb! Of what materials was I made that I could thus resist so many shocks, which, like the turning of the wheel, continually renewed the torture?

But I was doomed to live and in two months found myself as awaking from a dream, in a prison, stretched on a wretched bed, surrounded by gaolers, turnkeys, bolts, and all the miserable apparatus of a dungeon. It was morning, I remember, when I thus awoke to understanding; I had forgotten the particulars of what had happened and only felt as if some great misfortune had suddenly overwhelmed me; but when I looked around and saw the barred windows and the squalidness of the room in which I was, all flashed across my memory and I groaned bitterly.

This sound disturbed an old woman who was sleeping in a chair beside me. She was a hired nurse, the wife of one of the turnkeys, and her countenance expressed all those bad qualities which often characterise that class. The lines of her face were hard and rude, like that of persons accustomed to see without sympathising in sights of misery. Her tone expressed her entire indifference; she addressed me in English, and the voice struck me as one that I had heard during my sufferings.

“Are you better now, sir?” said she.

I replied in the same language, with a feeble voice, “I believe I am; but if it be all true, if indeed I did not dream, I am sorry that I am still alive to feel this misery and horror.”

“For that matter,” replied the old woman, “if you mean about the gentleman you murdered, I believe that it were better for you if you were dead, for I fancy it will go hard with you! However, that’s none of my business; I am sent to nurse you and get you well; I do my duty with a safe conscience; it were well if everybody did the same.”

I turned with loathing from the woman who could utter so unfeeling a speech to a person just saved, on the very edge of death; but I felt languid and unable to reflect on all that had passed. The whole series of my life appeared to me as a dream; I sometimes doubted if indeed it were all true, for it never presented itself to my mind with the force of reality.

As the images that floated before me became more distinct, I grew feverish; a darkness pressed around me; no one was near me who soothed me with the gentle voice of love; no dear hand supported me. The physician came and prescribed medicines, and the old woman prepared them for me; but utter carelessness was visible in the first, and the expression of brutality was strongly marked in the visage of the second. Who could be interested in the fate of a murderer but the hangman who would gain his fee?

These were my first reflections, but I soon learned that Mr. Kirwin had shown me extreme kindness. He had caused the best room in the prison to be prepared for me (wretched indeed was the best); and it was he who had provided a physician and a nurse. It is true, he seldom came to see me, for although he ardently desired to relieve the sufferings of every human creature, he did not wish to be present at the agonies and miserable ravings of a murderer. He came, therefore, sometimes to see that I was not neglected, but his visits were short and with long intervals.

One day, while I was gradually recovering, I was seated in a chair, my eyes half open and my cheeks livid like those in death. I was overcome by gloom and misery and often reflected I had better seek death than desire to remain in a world which to me was replete with wretchedness. At one time I considered whether I should not declare myself guilty and suffer the penalty of the law, less innocent than poor Justine had been. Such were my thoughts when the door of my apartment was opened and Mr. Kirwin entered. His countenance expressed sympathy and compassion; he drew a chair close to mine and addressed me in French,

“I fear that this place is very shocking to you; can I do anything to make you more comfortable?”

“I thank you, but all that you mention is nothing to me; on the whole earth there is no comfort which I am capable of receiving.”

“I know that the sympathy of a stranger can be but of little relief to one borne down as you are by so strange a misfortune. But you will, I hope, soon quit this melancholy abode, for doubtless evidence can easily be brought to free you from the criminal charge.”

“That is my least concern; I am, by a course of strange events, become the most miserable of mortals. Persecuted and tortured as I am and have been, can death be any evil to me?”

“Nothing indeed could be more unfortunate and agonising than the strange chances that have lately occurred. You were thrown, by some surprising accident, on this shore, renowned for its hospitality, seized immediately, and charged with murder. The first sight that was presented to your eyes was the body of your friend, murdered in so unaccountable a manner and placed, as it were, by some fiend across your path.”

As Mr. Kirwin said this, notwithstanding the agitation I endured on this retrospect of my sufferings, I also felt considerable surprise at the knowledge he seemed to possess concerning me. I suppose some astonishment was exhibited in my countenance, for Mr. Kirwin hastened to say,

“Immediately upon your being taken ill, all the papers that were on your person were brought me, and I examined them that I might discover some trace by which I could send to your relations an account of your misfortune and illness. I found several letters, and, among others, one which I discovered from its commencement to be from your father. I instantly wrote to Geneva; nearly two months have elapsed since the departure of my letter. But you are ill; even now you tremble; you are unfit for agitation of any kind.”

“This suspense is a thousand times worse than the most horrible event; tell me what new scene of death has been acted, and whose murder I am now to lament?”

“Your family is perfectly well,” said Mr. Kirwin with gentleness; “and someone, a friend, is come to visit you.”

I know not by what chain of thought the idea presented itself, but it instantly darted into my mind that the murderer had come to mock at my misery and taunt me with the death of Clerval, as a new incitement for me to comply with his hellish desires. I put my hand before my eyes, and cried out in agony,

“Oh! Take him away! I cannot see him; for God’s sake, do not let him enter!”

Mr. Kirwin regarded me with a troubled countenance. He could not help regarding my exclamation as a presumption of my guilt and said in rather a severe tone,

“I should have thought, young man, that the presence of your father would have been welcome instead of inspiring such violent repugnance.”

“My father!” cried I, while every feature and every muscle was relaxed from anguish to pleasure. “Is my father indeed come? How kind, how very kind! But where is he, why does he not hasten to me?”

My change of manner surprised and pleased the magistrate; perhaps he thought that my former exclamation was a momentary return of delirium, and now he instantly resumed his former benevolence. He rose and quitted the room with my nurse, and in a moment my father entered it.

Nothing, at this moment, could have given me greater pleasure than the arrival of my father. I stretched out my hand to him and cried,

“Are you then safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father calmed me with assurances of their welfare and endeavoured, by dwelling on these subjects so interesting to my heart, to raise my desponding spirits; but he soon felt that a prison cannot be the abode of cheerfulness. “What a place is this that you inhabit, my son!” said he, looking mournfully at the barred windows and wretched appearance of the room. “You travelled to seek happiness, but a fatality seems to pursue you. And poor Clerval—”

The name of my unfortunate and murdered friend was an agitation too great to be endured in my weak state; I shed tears.

“Alas! Yes, my father,” replied I; “some destiny of the most horrible kind hangs over me, and I must live to fulfil it, or surely I should have died on the coffin of Henry.”

We were not allowed to converse for any length of time, for the precarious state of my health rendered every precaution necessary that could ensure tranquillity. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that my strength should not be exhausted by too much exertion. But the appearance of my father was to me like that of my good angel, and I gradually recovered my health.

As my sickness quitted me, I was absorbed by a gloomy and black melancholy that nothing could dissipate. The image of Clerval was for ever before me, ghastly and murdered. More than once the agitation into which these reflections threw me made my friends dread a dangerous relapse. Alas! Why did they preserve so miserable and detested a life? It was surely that I might fulfil my destiny, which is now drawing to a close. Soon, oh, very soon, will death extinguish these throbbings and relieve me from the mighty weight of anguish that bears me to the dust; and, in executing the award of justice, I shall also sink to rest. Then the appearance of death was distant, although the wish was ever present to my thoughts; and I often sat for hours motionless and speechless, wishing for some mighty revolution that might bury me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The season of the assizes approached. I had already been three months in prison, and although I was still weak and in continual danger of a relapse, I was obliged to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court was held. Mr. Kirwin charged himself with every care of collecting witnesses and arranging my defence. I was spared the disgrace of appearing publicly as a criminal, as the case was not brought before the court that decides on life and death. The grand jury rejected the bill, on its being proved that I was on the Orkney Islands at the hour the body of my friend was found; and a fortnight after my removal I was liberated from prison.

My father was enraptured on finding me freed from the vexations of a criminal charge, that I was again allowed to breathe the fresh atmosphere and permitted to return to my native country. I did not participate in these feelings, for to me the walls of a dungeon or a palace were alike hateful. The cup of life was poisoned for ever, and although the sun shone upon me, as upon the happy and gay of heart, I saw around me nothing but a dense and frightful darkness, penetrated by no light but the glimmer of two eyes that glared upon me. Sometimes they were the expressive eyes of Henry, languishing in death, the dark orbs nearly covered by the lids and the long black lashes that fringed them; sometimes it was the watery, clouded eyes of the monster, as I first saw them in my chamber at Ingolstadt.

My father tried to awaken in me the feelings of affection. He talked of Geneva, which I should soon visit, of Elizabeth and Ernest; but these words only drew deep groans from me. Sometimes, indeed, I felt a wish for happiness and thought with melancholy delight of my beloved cousin or longed, with a devouring maladie du pays, to see once more the blue lake and rapid Rhone, that had been so dear to me in early childhood; but my general state of feeling was a torpor in which a prison was as welcome a residence as the divinest scene in nature; and these fits were seldom interrupted but by paroxysms of anguish and despair. At these moments I often endeavoured to put an end to the existence I loathed, and it required unceasing attendance and vigilance to restrain me from committing some dreadful act of violence.

Yet one duty remained to me, the recollection of which finally triumphed over my selfish despair. It was necessary that I should return without delay to Geneva, there to watch over the lives of those I so fondly loved and to lie in wait for the murderer, that if any chance led me to the place of his concealment, or if he dared again to blast me by his presence, I might, with unfailing aim, put an end to the existence of the monstrous image which I had endued with the mockery of a soul still more monstrous. My father still desired to delay our departure, fearful that I could not sustain the fatigues of a journey, for I was a shattered wreck—the shadow of a human being. My strength was gone. I was a mere skeleton, and fever night and day preyed upon my wasted frame.

Still, as I urged our leaving Ireland with such inquietude and impatience, my father thought it best to yield. We took our passage on board a vessel bound for Havre-de-Grace and sailed with a fair wind from the Irish shores. It was midnight. I lay on the deck looking at the stars and listening to the dashing of the waves. I hailed the darkness that shut Ireland from my sight, and my pulse beat with a feverish joy when I reflected that I should soon see Geneva.

The past appeared to me in the light of a frightful dream; yet the vessel in which I was, the wind that blew me from the detested shore of Ireland, and the sea which surrounded me, told me too forcibly that I was deceived by no vision and that Clerval, my friend and dearest companion, had fallen a victim to me and the monster of my creation. I repassed, in my memory, my whole life; my quiet happiness while residing with my family in Geneva, the death of my mother, and my departure for Ingolstadt. I remembered, shuddering, the mad enthusiasm that hurried me on to the creation of my hideous enemy, and I called to mind the night in which he first lived. I was unable to pursue the train of thought; a thousand feelings pressed upon me, and I wept bitterly.

Ever since my recovery from the fever, I had been in the custom of taking every night a small quantity of laudanum, for it was by means of this drug only that I was enabled to gain the rest necessary for the preservation of life. Oppressed by the recollection of my various misfortunes, I now swallowed double my usual quantity and soon slept profoundly. But sleep did not afford me respite from thought and misery; my dreams presented a thousand objects that scared me.

Towards morning I was possessed by a kind of nightmare; I felt the fiend’s grasp in my neck and could not free myself from it; groans and cries rang in my ears. My father, who was watching over me, perceiving my restlessness, awoke me; the dashing waves were around, the cloudy sky above, the fiend was not here: a sense of security, a feeling that a truce was established between the present hour and the irresistible, disastrous future imparted to me a kind of calm forgetfulness, of which the human mind is by its structure peculiarly susceptible.
b2: I was soon brought before the magistrate, a kindly old man with a calm, gentle manner. Even so, he looked at me with a certain severity, and then, turning to the men who had brought me, he asked who was here as a witness.

About six men stepped forward, and the magistrate chose one of them. He stated that the night before he had been out fishing with his son and his brother-in-law, Daniel Nugent, when, at about ten o’clock, they noticed a strong north wind getting up, so they headed for land. The night was very dark, since the moon had not yet risen, and instead of landing at the harbour they came ashore, as they usually did, at a creek about two miles further down. He went ahead, carrying some of the fishing gear, and the others followed some way behind.

As he was making his way along the sand, he stumbled over something and fell flat on the ground. The others hurried up to help him, and by the light of their lantern they saw that he had fallen over the body of a man who seemed to be dead. At first they assumed it was someone who had drowned and been washed ashore, but when they looked more closely they found that the clothes were dry and the body was still warm. They carried it at once to an old woman’s cottage nearby and tried, without success, to bring the man back to life. He was a handsome young man of about twenty-five. He seemed to have been strangled, because there was no mark of violence on him except the black prints of fingers on his neck.

The first part of this evidence did not interest me at all, but when the finger marks were mentioned, I remembered my brother’s murder and became terribly agitated; my limbs shook, and a mist clouded my eyes, so that I had to lean on a chair to stay upright. The magistrate watched me closely and, naturally, drew a conclusion that did not favour me.

The son backed up his father’s story, but when Daniel Nugent was called, he swore firmly that just before his companion fell, he had seen a boat with a single man in it not far from the shore, and that, as far as he could tell by the light of a few stars, it was the very boat I had just landed in. A woman stated that she lived near the beach and had been standing at her cottage door, waiting for the fishermen to come home, about an hour before she heard that the body had been found. At that moment she saw a boat with only one man in it push off from the part of the shore where the corpse was later discovered.

Another woman confirmed that the fishermen had carried the body into her house, and that it was not cold. They laid it on a bed and rubbed it, and Daniel went into town to fetch an apothecary, but the man was already gone. Several other men were questioned about my landing, and they agreed that, with the strong north wind that had blown up in the night, I had very probably been tossed about for hours and forced back almost to the spot I had set out from. They also pointed out that I seemed to have brought the body from somewhere else, and that since I clearly did not know the coast, I might have put into the harbour without realising how close the town of —— was to the place where I had left the corpse.

After hearing this evidence, Mr. Kirwin ordered that I should be taken to the room where the body was laid out for burial, so that they could see what effect the sight of it had on me. The idea had probably come from the violent agitation I had shown when the manner of the murder was described. So the magistrate and several others led me to the inn. I could not help being struck by the strange coincidences of that eventful night, but since I knew that I had been talking to several people on the island where I lived at about the time the body was found, I felt entirely calm about how the affair would end.

I entered the room where the corpse lay and was led up to the coffin. How can I describe what I felt when I saw it? Even now my mouth goes dry with horror, and I cannot think of that terrible moment without shuddering in agony. The inquiry, the magistrate and the witnesses all vanished from my mind like a dream when I saw the lifeless body of Henry Clerval stretched out before me. I gasped for breath and, throwing myself on the body, cried out, “Have my deadly schemes robbed you of life too, my dearest Henry? I have already destroyed two; other victims are waiting for their fate; but you, Clerval, my friend, my benefactor—” My body could no longer bear such agony, and I was carried out of the room in violent convulsions.

A fever followed. For two months I lay close to death; my ravings, as I was told later, were dreadful: I called myself the murderer of William, of Justine and of Clerval. Sometimes I begged the people looking after me to help me destroy the fiend who was tormenting me; at other times I felt the monster’s fingers already gripping my throat, and I screamed aloud in agony and terror. Luckily, since I was speaking my own language, only Mr. Kirwin understood me, but my gestures and bitter cries were enough to frighten the other witnesses.

Why did I not die? More wretched than any man before me, why did I not sink into oblivion and rest? Death carries off so many children in full bloom, the only hope of their adoring parents; how many brides and young lovers are glowing with health and hope one day, and the next are food for worms and the decay of the grave! What was I made of, that I could withstand so many shocks, which, like the turning of a wheel, kept renewing the torture?

But I was fated to live, and two months later I found myself waking as if from a dream, in a prison, lying on a miserable bed, surrounded by jailers, turnkeys, bolts and all the grim equipment of a dungeon. It was morning, I remember, when I came back to my senses; I had forgotten the details of what had happened and felt only that some great disaster had suddenly crushed me. But when I looked round and saw the barred windows and the squalor of the room, everything came flooding back, and I groaned bitterly.

The sound woke an old woman who was asleep in a chair beside me. She was a hired nurse, the wife of one of the turnkeys, and her face showed all the bad qualities that are often found in people of her kind. Her features were hard and coarse, like those of people who are used to looking at suffering without feeling any sympathy. Her tone was completely indifferent; she spoke to me in English, and I felt that I had heard her voice during my illness. “Are you feeling better now, sir?” she asked. I answered in the same language, in a weak voice, “I think so; but if it is all true, if I really did not dream it, I am sorry I am still alive to feel such misery and horror.”

“As to that,” the old woman replied, “if you mean the gentleman you murdered, I think you’d be better off dead, because I reckon things will go badly for you! Still, that’s none of my business; I’ve been sent to nurse you and get you well; I do my duty with a clear conscience, and it would be a good thing if everyone did the same.” I turned away in disgust from a woman who could say something so heartless to a man who had only just been saved from the very edge of death; but I felt too weak and listless to think about everything that had happened. My whole life seemed like a dream to me; sometimes I doubted whether any of it was true, because it never struck my mind with the force of reality.

As the images drifting before me grew clearer, I became feverish; darkness closed in around me; there was no one near to comfort me with the gentle voice of love, no dear hand to support me. The doctor came and prescribed medicines, and the old woman prepared them for me; but the doctor showed complete indifference, and the nurse’s face bore a clear look of brutality. Who could care about the fate of a murderer except the hangman, who would earn his fee?

Those were my first thoughts, but I soon learned that Mr. Kirwin had shown me great kindness. He had arranged for the best room in the prison to be made ready for me (and the best was wretched enough), and it was he who had found me a doctor and a nurse. It is true that he rarely came to see me, for although he sincerely wished to ease the suffering of every human being, he did not want to witness the agonies and wild ravings of a murderer. So he came now and then to make sure I was not neglected, but his visits were short and far apart.

One day, as I was slowly recovering, I sat in a chair with my eyes half closed and my cheeks as pale and grey as a corpse’s. I was overwhelmed by gloom and misery, and I often thought that I had better seek death than wish to stay in a world that, for me, was full of wretchedness. At one point I wondered whether I should declare myself guilty and suffer the punishment of the law, since I was less innocent than poor Justine had been. I was thinking such thoughts when the door of my room opened and Mr. Kirwin came in. His face showed sympathy and compassion; he pulled a chair up close to mine and spoke to me in French.

“I’m afraid this place must be very distressing for you; is there anything I can do to make you more comfortable?” “Thank you, but nothing you mention matters to me; there is no comfort on the whole earth that I am able to receive.” “I know that a stranger’s sympathy can do little to relieve someone weighed down, as you are, by such a strange misfortune. But I hope you will soon leave this gloomy place, for surely evidence can easily be found to clear you of the criminal charge.” “That is the least of my worries; through a chain of strange events, I have become the most miserable of mortals. Hunted and tortured as I am and always have been, how can death be an evil to me?”

“Indeed, nothing could be more unlucky or more painful than the strange chances that have happened recently. Some astonishing accident threw you onto this shore, which is famous for its hospitality, and you were immediately arrested and charged with murder. The first thing you saw was the body of your friend, murdered in such a mysterious way and placed, as it were, in your path by some fiend.” As Mr. Kirwin said this, despite the distress that this review of my sufferings caused me, I was also rather surprised at how much he seemed to know about me. I suppose my face showed some astonishment, for Mr. Kirwin quickly added,

“As soon as you fell ill, all the papers you had on you were brought to me, and I went through them in the hope of finding some clue that would allow me to inform your relatives of your misfortune and illness. I found several letters, including one which, from its opening lines, I could tell was from your father. I wrote to Geneva at once; almost two months have passed since my letter was sent. But you are ill; even now you are trembling; you are in no state for any kind of excitement.” “This uncertainty is a thousand times worse than the most horrible news; tell me what new scene of death has taken place, and whose murder I must now mourn?” “Your family are all perfectly well,” Mr. Kirwin said gently, “and someone, a friend, has come to visit you.”

I do not know what chain of thought led me to it, but the idea suddenly flashed into my mind that the murderer had come to mock my misery and taunt me with Clerval’s death, to push me once more into obeying his hellish demands. I covered my eyes with my hand and cried out in agony, “Oh! Take him away! I cannot see him; for God’s sake, don’t let him in!” Mr. Kirwin looked at me with a troubled face. He could not help taking my outburst as a sign of my guilt, and he said in a rather stern voice, “I would have thought, young man, that your father’s arrival would be welcome to you rather than filling you with such violent disgust.”

“My father!” I cried, and every feature and every muscle of my face relaxed as anguish turned to joy. “Has my father really come? How kind, how very kind! But where is he? Why doesn’t he hurry to me?” My change of manner surprised and pleased the magistrate; perhaps he thought that my earlier outburst had been a passing return of delirium, and at once he became as kind as before. He got up and left the room with my nurse, and a moment later my father came in. Nothing at that moment could have given me greater joy than my father’s arrival. I held out my hand to him and cried, “Are you all safe, then—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father calmed me by assuring me that they were well, and he tried to lift my low spirits by talking about the things so dear to my heart; but he soon realised that a prison cannot be a cheerful home. “What a place you are living in, my son!” he said, gazing sadly at the barred windows and the wretched look of the room. “You went travelling to find happiness, but some fatal curse seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—” The name of my unhappy, murdered friend stirred up feelings too strong for me to bear in my weak state, and I burst into tears. “Alas, yes, Father,” I replied; “some destiny of the most horrible kind hangs over me, and I must live to fulfil it, or I would surely have died on Henry’s coffin.”

We were not allowed to talk for long, because my health was so fragile that every precaution had to be taken to keep me calm. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that I must not wear myself out with too much effort. But my father’s presence was like that of a guardian angel to me, and little by little my health returned.

As my illness left me, I sank into a dark, gloomy depression that nothing could lift. The image of Clerval, ghastly and murdered, was always before my eyes. More than once these thoughts threw me into such a state that my friends feared a dangerous relapse. Alas! Why did they save such a miserable and hated life? Surely it was so that I could fulfil my destiny, which is now nearing its end. Soon, oh, very soon, death will still this throbbing and free me from the huge weight of anguish that crushes me into the dust; and when justice has been done, I too shall sink to rest. Back then death still seemed far away, although I longed for it constantly; I often sat for hours without moving or speaking, wishing for some great upheaval that would bury me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The time of the assizes, the county court sessions, drew near. I had already spent three months in prison, and although I was still weak and in constant danger of a relapse, I had to travel nearly a hundred miles to the county town where the court sat. Mr. Kirwin took on all the work of gathering witnesses and preparing my defence. I was spared the shame of appearing in public as a criminal, because the case never came before the court that decides matters of life and death. The grand jury threw out the charge once it was proved that I had been in the Orkney Islands at the hour my friend’s body was found, and two weeks after my transfer I was released from prison.

My father was overjoyed to see me freed from the torment of a criminal charge, allowed to breathe fresh air again and to go back to my own country. I did not share his feelings, for to me the walls of a dungeon and those of a palace were equally hateful. The cup of life had been poisoned for ever, and although the sun shone on me as it did on the happy and light-hearted, all I saw around me was a thick and fearful darkness, pierced by no light except the gleam of two eyes staring at me. Sometimes they were Henry’s expressive eyes, fading in death, the dark pupils almost hidden by the lids and the long black lashes around them; sometimes they were the watery, clouded eyes of the monster, as I had first seen them in my room at Ingolstadt.

My father tried to reawaken my feelings of love. He talked about Geneva, which I would soon see again, and about Elizabeth and Ernest, but his words only drew deep groans from me. Sometimes, it is true, I felt a longing for happiness and thought with sad delight of my beloved cousin, or yearned, with a consuming homesickness, to see the blue lake and the swift Rhone again, which had been so dear to me as a child. But my usual state was a kind of numbness in which a prison seemed as good a home as the loveliest place in nature, and this was rarely broken except by fits of anguish and despair. At such moments I often tried to end the existence I hated, and I had to be watched constantly to stop me from doing something terribly violent.

Yet one duty remained, and the thought of it finally won out over my selfish despair. I had to return to Geneva without delay, to guard the lives of those I loved so dearly and to lie in wait for the murderer. If chance ever led me to his hiding place, or if he dared to curse me with his presence again, I would, with a steady aim, put an end to the monstrous being I had given a mocking imitation of a soul, one even more monstrous than its body. My father still wanted to put off our departure, afraid that I could not survive the strain of the journey, for I was a broken wreck—the shadow of a human being. My strength had gone. I was nothing but a skeleton, and day and night the fever ate away at my wasted body.

However, since I pressed so anxiously and impatiently for us to leave Ireland, my father decided it was best to give in. We boarded a ship bound for Havre-de-Grace and sailed from the Irish coast with a favourable wind. It was midnight. I lay on the deck, gazing at the stars and listening to the waves crashing. I welcomed the darkness that hid Ireland from view, and my pulse raced with feverish joy at the thought that I would soon see Geneva.

The past seemed to me like a terrible dream; yet the ship I was on, the wind that carried me away from the hated shore of Ireland and the sea all around me told me only too clearly that this was no illusion, and that Clerval, my friend and dearest companion, had fallen victim to me and to the monster I had created. I went back over my whole life in my memory: my quiet happiness living with my family in Geneva, my mother’s death and my departure for Ingolstadt. Shuddering, I remembered the wild enthusiasm that had driven me on to create my hideous enemy, and I recalled the night when he first came to life. I could not follow this train of thought any further; a thousand feelings overwhelmed me, and I wept bitterly.

Ever since I had recovered from the fever, I had been in the habit of taking a small dose of laudanum every night, as this drug was the only thing that allowed me to get the rest I needed to stay alive. Weighed down by the memory of all my misfortunes, I now swallowed twice my usual amount and soon fell into a deep sleep. But sleep gave me no relief from thought and misery; my dreams were full of a thousand things that terrified me.

Towards morning I was gripped by a kind of nightmare; I felt the fiend’s hands around my neck and could not break free; groans and cries rang in my ears. My father, who was watching over me, saw how restless I was and woke me. The waves were splashing all around, the cloudy sky was overhead, and the fiend was not there. A sense of safety, a feeling that a truce had been made between the present hour and the unstoppable, disastrous future, gave me a kind of calm forgetfulness, to which the human mind is, by its very nature, especially prone.
b1: Soon I was taken to the magistrate. He was a kind old man with calm, gentle manners. But he looked at me quite seriously, and then he asked the men who had brought me which of them were witnesses.

About six men came forward, and the magistrate chose one of them to speak. The man said that the night before he had been fishing with his son and his brother-in-law, Daniel Nugent. At about ten o’clock a strong north wind started to blow, so they went back to land. The night was very dark because the moon was not up yet. They did not land at the harbour but, as usual, at a small bay about two miles away. He walked in front, carrying some of the fishing things, and the others followed a little way behind.

As he was walking along the sand, his foot hit something and he fell down. The others came to help him, and with their lamp they saw that he had fallen over a man’s body. The man looked dead. At first they thought he had drowned in the sea and the waves had thrown him onto the beach. But then they saw that his clothes were not wet and his body was still warm. They carried him quickly to an old woman’s cottage nearby and tried to save him, but they could not. He was a good-looking young man of about twenty-five. It seemed that someone had strangled him, because the only mark on him was the black mark of fingers on his neck.

I was not interested in the first part of the story. But when the man spoke about the marks of fingers, I remembered my brother’s murder and became very upset. My arms and legs shook, and my eyes went cloudy, so I had to hold on to a chair. The magistrate watched me carefully, and of course he did not like what he saw.

The son agreed with his father’s story. Then Daniel Nugent was called, and he swore that just before his friend fell, he saw a boat with one man in it not far from the shore. There was only a little starlight, but he thought it was the same boat that I had just arrived in. A woman said that she lived near the beach. About an hour before she heard about the body, she was standing at the door of her cottage and waiting for the fishermen. Then she saw a boat with one man in it leave the part of the beach where the body was found later.

Another woman said that the fishermen had brought the body into her house, and that it was not cold.
