a2.ru: Мы не могли долго разговаривать, потому что я был ещё очень болен.

a2.en: Mr. Kirwin came in and said, “He must rest now.”
a2.ru: Вошёл мистер Кирвин и сказал: «Теперь ему нужно отдохнуть».

a2.en: But my father was like a good angel for me, and slowly I got better.
a2.ru: Но отец был для меня как добрый ангел, и понемногу я поправился.

a2.en: My illness went away, but I was very, very sad.
a2.ru: Болезнь прошла, но мне было очень-очень грустно.

a2.en: I saw Clerval’s dead face all the time.
a2.ru: Я всё время видел мёртвое лицо Клерваля.

a2.en: My family was often afraid that I was going to become ill again.
a2.ru: Родные часто боялись, что я снова заболею.

a2.en: Why did they save my unhappy life?
a2.ru: Зачем они спасли мою несчастную жизнь?

a2.en: I think it was because I had to finish my story.
a2.ru: Думаю, потому, что я должен был закончить свою историю.

a2.en: Now the end is near.
a2.ru: Теперь конец близок.

a2.en: Soon I will die, and I will be free from my pain.
a2.ru: Скоро я умру и освобожусь от своей боли.

a2.en: But at that time I often sat for hours and did not move or speak.
a2.ru: Но тогда я часто часами сидел, не двигаясь и не говоря.

a2.en: I wanted something very big to kill me and the monster together.
a2.ru: Я хотел, чтобы что-то огромное убило меня и чудовище вместе.

a2.en: The time for the big court came.
a2.ru: Пришло время большого суда.

a2.en: I was in prison for three months.
a2.ru: Я пробыл в тюрьме три месяца.

a2.en: I was still weak, but I had to travel a hundred miles to the court.
a2.ru: Я был ещё слаб, но мне пришлось проехать сто миль до суда.

a2.en: Mr. Kirwin found witnesses and helped me.
a2.ru: Мистер Кирвин нашёл свидетелей и помог мне.

a2.en: People could prove that I was on the Orkney Islands when they found my friend’s body.
a2.ru: Люди смогли доказать, что я был на Оркнейских островах, когда нашли тело моего друга.

a2.en: So there was no big trial.
a2.ru: Поэтому большого суда не было.

a2.en: Two weeks later I was free.
a2.ru: Через две недели я был свободен.

a2.en: My father was very happy because I was free and I could go home.
a2.ru: Отец был очень рад, потому что я был свободен и мог вернуться домой.

a2.en: But I was not happy.
a2.ru: Но я не радовался.

a2.en: A prison or a palace, it was all the same to me.
a2.ru: Тюрьма или дворец — мне было всё равно.

a2.en: My life was poisoned for ever.
a2.ru: Моя жизнь была отравлена навсегда.

a2.en: The sun was shining, but I saw only darkness.
a2.ru: Светило солнце, но я видел только тьму.

a2.en: In the darkness there were two eyes.
a2.ru: Во тьме были два глаза.

a2.en: Sometimes they were Henry’s dying eyes.
a2.ru: Иногда это были умирающие глаза Анри.

a2.en: Sometimes they were the monster’s eyes, as I first saw them in Ingolstadt.
a2.ru: Иногда это были глаза чудовища, какими я впервые увидел их в Ингольштадте.

a2.en: My father talked about Geneva, Elizabeth and Ernest.
a2.ru: Отец говорил о Женеве, об Элизабет и Эрнесте.

a2.en: But his words only made me groan.
a2.ru: Но от его слов я только стонал.

a2.en: Sometimes I thought about my dear Elizabeth.
a2.ru: Иногда я думал о моей дорогой Элизабет.

a2.en: Sometimes I wanted to see the blue lake and the river Rhone again.
a2.ru: Иногда мне хотелось снова увидеть синее озеро и реку Рону.

a2.en: But usually I felt nothing.
a2.ru: Но обычно я ничего не чувствовал.

a2.en: Sometimes I felt terrible pain, and I tried to kill myself.
a2.ru: Иногда я чувствовал страшную боль и пытался покончить с собой.

a2.en: People had to watch me all the time.
a2.ru: За мной всё время приходилось следить.

a2.en: But I had one important job.
a2.ru: Но у меня было одно важное дело.

a2.en: I had to go back to Geneva quickly.
a2.ru: Мне нужно было скорее вернуться в Женеву.

a2.en: I wanted to protect my family and wait for the monster.
a2.ru: Я хотел защитить свою семью и ждать чудовище.

a2.en: If I found him, I was going to kill him.
a2.ru: Если я найду его, я его убью.

a2.en: My father wanted to wait, because I was very weak.
a2.ru: Отец хотел подождать, потому что я был очень слаб.

a2.en: I was like a shadow of a man.
a2.ru: Я был как тень человека.

a2.en: I was very thin, like a skeleton, and I still had a fever.
a2.ru: Я был очень худой, как скелет, и у меня всё ещё была горячка.

a2.en: But I asked again and again, so my father agreed.
a2.ru: Но я просил снова и снова, и отец согласился.

a2.en: We got on a ship to Havre-de-Grace and left Ireland.
a2.ru: Мы сели на корабль до Гавр-де-Граса и покинули Ирландию.

a2.en: It was midnight.
a2.ru: Была полночь.

a2.en: I lay on the deck and looked at the stars.
a2.ru: Я лежал на палубе и смотрел на звёзды.

a2.en: I listened to the waves.
a2.ru: Я слушал волны.

a2.en: I was glad that I could not see Ireland any more.
a2.ru: Я был рад, что больше не вижу Ирландию.

a2.en: Soon I was going to see Geneva!
a2.ru: Скоро я увижу Женеву!

a2.en: The past was like a bad dream.
a2.ru: Прошлое было как дурной сон.

a2.en: But the ship, the wind and the sea were real.
a2.ru: Но корабль, ветер и море были настоящими.

a2.en: Clerval, my best friend, was really dead because of me and my monster.
a2.ru: Клерваль, мой лучший друг, действительно погиб из-за меня и моего чудовища.

a2.en: I remembered my happy life with my family in Geneva.
a2.ru: Я вспомнил свою счастливую жизнь с семьёй в Женеве.

a2.en: I remembered my mother’s death and my journey to Ingolstadt.
a2.ru: Я вспомнил смерть матери и поездку в Ингольштадт.

a2.en: I remembered the night when the monster first opened his eyes.
a2.ru: Я вспомнил ночь, когда чудовище впервые открыло глаза.

a2.en: I could not think any more, and I cried.
a2.ru: Я больше не мог думать и заплакал.

a2.en: After my fever, I took a little medicine called laudanum every night.
a2.ru: После горячки я каждую ночь принимал немного лекарства, которое называется лауданум.

a2.en: It helped me to sleep.
a2.ru: Оно помогало мне спать.

a2.en: That night I was very sad, so I took two times more than usual.
a2.ru: В ту ночь мне было очень грустно, поэтому я принял вдвое больше обычного.

a2.en: I fell asleep quickly.
a2.ru: Я быстро уснул.

a2.en: But I had terrible dreams.
a2.ru: Но мне снились ужасные сны.

a2.en: In the morning I had a nightmare.
a2.ru: Утром мне приснился кошмар.

a2.en: I felt the monster’s hand on my neck, and I could not get free.
a2.ru: Я чувствовал руку чудовища на своей шее и не мог вырваться.

a2.en: My father was next to me, and he woke me up.
a2.ru: Отец был рядом со мной и разбудил меня.

a2.en: I saw the waves and the grey sky.
a2.ru: Я увидел волны и серое небо.

a2.en: The monster was not there.
a2.ru: Чудовища не было.

a2.en: For a short time I felt safe and calm, and I forgot about the terrible future.
a2.ru: Ненадолго я почувствовал себя в безопасности и спокойно и забыл о страшном будущем.

sub: In Paris and Geneva Victor hides his secret, receives Elizabeth's letter, agrees to marry her despite the creature's threat, and sets off with her across the lake to Evian on their wedding day

o: The voyage came to an end. We landed, and proceeded to Paris. I soon found that I had overtaxed my strength and that I must repose before I could continue my journey. My father’s care and attentions were indefatigable, but he did not know the origin of my sufferings and sought erroneous methods to remedy the incurable ill.

He wished me to seek amusement in society. I abhorred the face of man. Oh, not abhorred! They were my brethren, my fellow beings, and I felt attracted even to the most repulsive among them, as to creatures of an angelic nature and celestial mechanism. But I felt that I had no right to share their intercourse. I had unchained an enemy among them whose joy it was to shed their blood and to revel in their groans. How they would, each and all, abhor me and hunt me from the world, did they know my unhallowed acts and the crimes which had their source in me!

My father yielded at length to my desire to avoid society and strove by various arguments to banish my despair. Sometimes he thought that I felt deeply the degradation of being obliged to answer a charge of murder, and he endeavoured to prove to me the futility of pride.

“Alas! My father,” said I, “how little do you know me. Human beings, their feelings and passions, would indeed be degraded if such a wretch as I felt pride. Justine, poor unhappy Justine, was as innocent as I, and she suffered the same charge; she died for it; and I am the cause of this—I murdered her. William, Justine, and Henry—they all died by my hands.”

My father had often, during my imprisonment, heard me make the same assertion; when I thus accused myself, he sometimes seemed to desire an explanation, and at others he appeared to consider it as the offspring of delirium, and that, during my illness, some idea of this kind had presented itself to my imagination, the remembrance of which I preserved in my convalescence.

I avoided explanation and maintained a continual silence concerning the wretch I had created. I had a persuasion that I should be supposed mad, and this in itself would for ever have chained my tongue. But, besides, I could not bring myself to disclose a secret which would fill my hearer with consternation and make fear and unnatural horror the inmates of his breast. I checked, therefore, my impatient thirst for sympathy and was silent when I would have given the world to have confided the fatal secret. Yet, still, words like those I have recorded would burst uncontrollably from me. I could offer no explanation of them, but their truth in part relieved the burden of my mysterious woe.

Upon this occasion my father said, with an expression of unbounded wonder, “My dearest Victor, what infatuation is this? My dear son, I entreat you never to make such an assertion again.”

“I am not mad,” I cried energetically; “the sun and the heavens, who have viewed my operations, can bear witness of my truth. I am the assassin of those most innocent victims; they died by my machinations. A thousand times would I have shed my own blood, drop by drop, to have saved their lives; but I could not, my father, indeed I could not sacrifice the whole human race.”

The conclusion of this speech convinced my father that my ideas were deranged, and he instantly changed the subject of our conversation and endeavoured to alter the course of my thoughts. He wished as much as possible to obliterate the memory of the scenes that had taken place in Ireland and never alluded to them or suffered me to speak of my misfortunes.

As time passed away I became more calm; misery had her dwelling in my heart, but I no longer talked in the same incoherent manner of my own crimes; sufficient for me was the consciousness of them. By the utmost self-violence I curbed the imperious voice of wretchedness, which sometimes desired to declare itself to the whole world, and my manners were calmer and more composed than they had ever been since my journey to the sea of ice.

A few days before we left Paris on our way to Switzerland, I received the following letter from Elizabeth:

“My dear Friend,

“It gave me the greatest pleasure to receive a letter from my uncle dated at Paris; you are no longer at a formidable distance, and I may hope to see you in less than a fortnight. My poor cousin, how much you must have suffered! I expect to see you looking even more ill than when you quitted Geneva. This winter has been passed most miserably, tortured as I have been by anxious suspense; yet I hope to see peace in your countenance and to find that your heart is not totally void of comfort and tranquillity.

“Yet I fear that the same feelings now exist that made you so miserable a year ago, even perhaps augmented by time. I would not disturb you at this period, when so many misfortunes weigh upon you, but a conversation that I had with my uncle previous to his departure renders some explanation necessary before we meet.

Explanation! You may possibly say, What can Elizabeth have to explain? If you really say this, my questions are answered and all my doubts satisfied. But you are distant from me, and it is possible that you may dread and yet be pleased with this explanation; and in a probability of this being the case, I dare not any longer postpone writing what, during your absence, I have often wished to express to you but have never had the courage to begin.

“You well know, Victor, that our union had been the favourite plan of your parents ever since our infancy. We were told this when young, and taught to look forward to it as an event that would certainly take place. We were affectionate playfellows during childhood, and, I believe, dear and valued friends to one another as we grew older. But as brother and sister often entertain a lively affection towards each other without desiring a more intimate union, may not such also be our case? Tell me, dearest Victor. Answer me, I conjure you by our mutual happiness, with simple truth—Do you not love another?

“You have travelled; you have spent several years of your life at Ingolstadt; and I confess to you, my friend, that when I saw you last autumn so unhappy, flying to solitude from the society of every creature, I could not help supposing that you might regret our connection and believe yourself bound in honour to fulfil the wishes of your parents, although they opposed themselves to your inclinations. But this is false reasoning. I confess to you, my friend, that I love you and that in my airy dreams of futurity you have been my constant friend and companion.

But it is your happiness I desire as well as my own when I declare to you that our marriage would render me eternally miserable unless it were the dictate of your own free choice. Even now I weep to think that, borne down as you are by the cruellest misfortunes, you may stifle, by the word honour, all hope of that love and happiness which would alone restore you to yourself. I, who have so disinterested an affection for you, may increase your miseries tenfold by being an obstacle to your wishes. Ah! Victor, be assured that your cousin and playmate has too sincere a love for you not to be made miserable by this supposition. Be happy, my friend; and if you obey me in this one request, remain satisfied that nothing on earth will have the power to interrupt my tranquillity.

“Do not let this letter disturb you; do not answer tomorrow, or the next day, or even until you come, if it will give you pain. My uncle will send me news of your health, and if I see but one smile on your lips when we meet, occasioned by this or any other exertion of mine, I shall need no other happiness.

“Elizabeth Lavenza.

“Geneva, May 18th, 17—”

This letter revived in my memory what I had before forgotten, the threat of the fiend—“I will be with you on your wedding-night!” Such was my sentence, and on that night would the dæmon employ every art to destroy me and tear me from the glimpse of happiness which promised partly to console my sufferings. On that night he had determined to consummate his crimes by my death.

Well, be it so; a deadly struggle would then assuredly take place, in which if he were victorious I should be at peace and his power over me be at an end. If he were vanquished, I should be a free man. Alas! What freedom? Such as the peasant enjoys when his family have been massacred before his eyes, his cottage burnt, his lands laid waste, and he is turned adrift, homeless, penniless, and alone, but free. Such would be my liberty except that in my Elizabeth I possessed a treasure, alas, balanced by those horrors of remorse and guilt which would pursue me until death.

Sweet and beloved Elizabeth! I read and reread her letter, and some softened feelings stole into my heart and dared to whisper paradisiacal dreams of love and joy; but the apple was already eaten, and the angel’s arm bared to drive me from all hope. Yet I would die to make her happy.

If the monster executed his threat, death was inevitable; yet, again, I considered whether my marriage would hasten my fate. My destruction might indeed arrive a few months sooner, but if my torturer should suspect that I postponed it, influenced by his menaces, he would surely find other and perhaps more dreadful means of revenge. He had vowed to be with me on my wedding-night, yet he did not consider that threat as binding him to peace in the meantime, for as if to show me that he was not yet satiated with blood, he had murdered Clerval immediately after the enunciation of his threats. I resolved, therefore, that if my immediate union with my cousin would conduce either to hers or my father’s happiness, my adversary’s designs against my life should not retard it a single hour.

In this state of mind I wrote to Elizabeth. My letter was calm and affectionate. “I fear, my beloved girl,” I said, “little happiness remains for us on earth; yet all that I may one day enjoy is centred in you. Chase away your idle fears; to you alone do I consecrate my life and my endeavours for contentment. I have one secret, Elizabeth, a dreadful one; when revealed to you, it will chill your frame with horror, and then, far from being surprised at my misery, you will only wonder that I survive what I have endured. I will confide this tale of misery and terror to you the day after our marriage shall take place, for, my sweet cousin, there must be perfect confidence between us. But until then, I conjure you, do not mention or allude to it. This I most earnestly entreat, and I know you will comply.”

In about a week after the arrival of Elizabeth’s letter we returned to Geneva. The sweet girl welcomed me with warm affection, yet tears were in her eyes as she beheld my emaciated frame and feverish cheeks. I saw a change in her also. She was thinner and had lost much of that heavenly vivacity that had before charmed me; but her gentleness and soft looks of compassion made her a more fit companion for one blasted and miserable as I was.

The tranquillity which I now enjoyed did not endure. Memory brought madness with it, and when I thought of what had passed, a real insanity possessed me; sometimes I was furious and burnt with rage, sometimes low and despondent. I neither spoke nor looked at anyone, but sat motionless, bewildered by the multitude of miseries that overcame me.

Elizabeth alone had the power to draw me from these fits; her gentle voice would soothe me when transported by passion and inspire me with human feelings when sunk in torpor. She wept with me and for me. When reason returned, she would remonstrate and endeavour to inspire me with resignation. Ah! It is well for the unfortunate to be resigned, but for the guilty there is no peace. The agonies of remorse poison the luxury there is otherwise sometimes found in indulging the excess of grief.

Soon after my arrival my father spoke of my immediate marriage with Elizabeth. I remained silent.

“Have you, then, some other attachment?”

“None on earth. I love Elizabeth and look forward to our union with delight. Let the day therefore be fixed; and on it I will consecrate myself, in life or death, to the happiness of my cousin.”

“My dear Victor, do not speak thus. Heavy misfortunes have befallen us, but let us only cling closer to what remains and transfer our love for those whom we have lost to those who yet live. Our circle will be small but bound close by the ties of affection and mutual misfortune. And when time shall have softened your despair, new and dear objects of care will be born to replace those of whom we have been so cruelly deprived.”

Such were the lessons of my father. But to me the remembrance of the threat returned; nor can you wonder that, omnipotent as the fiend had yet been in his deeds of blood, I should almost regard him as invincible, and that when he had pronounced the words “I shall be with you on your wedding-night,” I should regard the threatened fate as unavoidable. But death was no evil to me if the loss of Elizabeth were balanced with it, and I therefore, with a contented and even cheerful countenance, agreed with my father that if my cousin would consent, the ceremony should take place in ten days, and thus put, as I imagined, the seal to my fate.

Great God! If for one instant I had thought what might be the hellish intention of my fiendish adversary, I would rather have banished myself for ever from my native country and wandered a friendless outcast over the earth than have consented to this miserable marriage. But, as if possessed of magic powers, the monster had blinded me to his real intentions; and when I thought that I had prepared only my own death, I hastened that of a far dearer victim.

As the period fixed for our marriage drew nearer, whether from cowardice or a prophetic feeling, I felt my heart sink within me. But I concealed my feelings by an appearance of hilarity that brought smiles and joy to the countenance of my father, but hardly deceived the ever-watchful and nicer eye of Elizabeth. She looked forward to our union with placid contentment, not unmingled with a little fear, which past misfortunes had impressed, that what now appeared certain and tangible happiness might soon dissipate into an airy dream and leave no trace but deep and everlasting regret.

Preparations were made for the event, congratulatory visits were received, and all wore a smiling appearance. I shut up, as well as I could, in my own heart the anxiety that preyed there and entered with seeming earnestness into the plans of my father, although they might only serve as the decorations of my tragedy. Through my father’s exertions a part of the inheritance of Elizabeth had been restored to her by the Austrian government. A small possession on the shores of Como belonged to her. It was agreed that, immediately after our union, we should proceed to Villa Lavenza and spend our first days of happiness beside the beautiful lake near which it stood.

In the meantime I took every precaution to defend my person in case the fiend should openly attack me. I carried pistols and a dagger constantly about me and was ever on the watch to prevent artifice, and by these means gained a greater degree of tranquillity. Indeed, as the period approached, the threat appeared more as a delusion, not to be regarded as worthy to disturb my peace, while the happiness I hoped for in my marriage wore a greater appearance of certainty as the day fixed for its solemnisation drew nearer and I heard it continually spoken of as an occurrence which no accident could possibly prevent.

Elizabeth seemed happy; my tranquil demeanour contributed greatly to calm her mind. But on the day that was to fulfil my wishes and my destiny, she was melancholy, and a presentiment of evil pervaded her; and perhaps also she thought of the dreadful secret which I had promised to reveal to her on the following day. My father was in the meantime overjoyed, and, in the bustle of preparation, only recognised in the melancholy of his niece the diffidence of a bride.

After the ceremony was performed a large party assembled at my father’s, but it was agreed that Elizabeth and I should commence our journey by water, sleeping that night at Evian and continuing our voyage on the following day. The day was fair, the wind favourable; all smiled on our nuptial embarkation.

Those were the last moments of my life during which I enjoyed the feeling of happiness. We passed rapidly along; the sun was hot, but we were sheltered from its rays by a kind of canopy while we enjoyed the beauty of the scene, sometimes on one side of the lake, where we saw Mont Salêve, the pleasant banks of Montalègre, and at a distance, surmounting all, the beautiful Mont Blanc, and the assemblage of snowy mountains that in vain endeavour to emulate her; sometimes coasting the opposite banks, we saw the mighty Jura opposing its dark side to the ambition that would quit its native country, and an almost insurmountable barrier to the invader who should wish to enslave it.

I took the hand of Elizabeth. “You are sorrowful, my love. Ah! If you knew what I have suffered and what I may yet endure, you would endeavour to let me taste the quiet and freedom from despair that this one day at least permits me to enjoy.”

“Be happy, my dear Victor,” replied Elizabeth; “there is, I hope, nothing to distress you; and be assured that if a lively joy is not painted in my face, my heart is contented. Something whispers to me not to depend too much on the prospect that is opened before us, but I will not listen to such a sinister voice. Observe how fast we move along and how the clouds, which sometimes obscure and sometimes rise above the dome of Mont Blanc, render this scene of beauty still more interesting. Look also at the innumerable fish that are swimming in the clear waters, where we can distinguish every pebble that lies at the bottom. What a divine day! How happy and serene all nature appears!”

Thus Elizabeth endeavoured to divert her thoughts and mine from all reflection upon melancholy subjects. But her temper was fluctuating; joy for a few instants shone in her eyes, but it continually gave place to distraction and reverie.

The sun sank lower in the heavens; we passed the river Drance and observed its path through the chasms of the higher and the glens of the lower hills. The Alps here come closer to the lake, and we approached the amphitheatre of mountains which forms its eastern boundary. The spire of Evian shone under the woods that surrounded it and the range of mountain above mountain by which it was overhung.

The wind, which had hitherto carried us along with amazing rapidity, sank at sunset to a light breeze; the soft air just ruffled the water and caused a pleasant motion among the trees as we approached the shore, from which it wafted the most delightful scent of flowers and hay. The sun sank beneath the horizon as we landed, and as I touched the shore I felt those cares and fears revive which soon were to clasp me and cling to me for ever.
b2: The voyage came to an end. We landed and travelled on to Paris. I soon realised that I had overstrained my strength and needed to rest before I could go any further. My father looked after me tirelessly, but he did not know the true cause of my suffering, and he tried mistaken ways to cure an illness that could not be cured.

He wanted me to find some entertainment in society. I loathed the sight of other people. No, not loathed! They were my brothers, my fellow creatures, and I felt drawn even to the most repulsive of them, as if they were angelic beings of heavenly design. But I felt I had no right to share their company. I had set loose among them an enemy who delighted in shedding their blood and gloating over their groans. How every one of them would hate me and hunt me out of the world if they knew about my unholy deeds and the crimes that had sprung from me!

In the end my father gave in to my wish to avoid company, and he used all sorts of arguments to drive away my despair. Sometimes he thought I was deeply hurt by the humiliation of having had to answer a charge of murder, and he tried to show me that such pride was pointless. “Oh, father,” I said, “how little you know me. Human beings, with all their feelings and passions, would truly be degraded if a wretch like me felt pride. Justine, poor unhappy Justine, was as innocent as I was, and she faced the same charge; she died for it; and I am the cause of it—I murdered her. William, Justine and Henry—they all died by my hand.”

During my imprisonment my father had often heard me say the same thing. When I accused myself like this, he sometimes seemed to want an explanation, but at other times he appeared to think it was the product of fever: that during my illness some idea of this kind had come into my mind, and I had kept the memory of it while I was recovering.

I avoided explaining and kept a constant silence about the wretch I had created. I was convinced that people would think I was mad, and that alone would have silenced me for ever. Besides, I could not bring myself to reveal a secret that would fill my listener with dismay and plant fear and unnatural horror in his heart. So I held back my desperate longing for sympathy and stayed silent, even when I would have given anything to share my fatal secret. Even so, words like the ones I have just repeated would sometimes burst out of me uncontrollably. I could not explain them, but the fact that they were partly true lightened the burden of my mysterious grief.

On this occasion my father said, with a look of utter astonishment, “My dearest Victor, what madness is this? My dear son, I beg you never to say such a thing again.” “I am not mad,” I cried passionately; “the sun and the skies, which have seen what I did, can testify that I am telling the truth. I am the murderer of those completely innocent victims; they died because of my schemes. A thousand times I would have shed my own blood, drop by drop, to save their lives; but I could not, father, I really could not sacrifice the whole human race.”

The end of this speech convinced my father that my mind was disturbed, and he immediately changed the subject and tried to steer my thoughts in another direction. He wanted, as far as possible, to wipe out the memory of what had happened in Ireland, and he never mentioned those events or allowed me to talk about my misfortunes.

As time went by, I grew calmer. Misery still lived in my heart, but I no longer talked so wildly about my own crimes; it was enough for me to be aware of them. With the greatest self-control I silenced the commanding voice of my wretchedness, which sometimes wanted to announce itself to the whole world, and my behaviour was calmer and more composed than it had been at any time since my journey to the sea of ice.

A few days before we left Paris for Switzerland, I received this letter from Elizabeth: “My dear friend, “I was overjoyed to receive a letter from my uncle sent from Paris; you are no longer frighteningly far away, and I can hope to see you in less than two weeks. My poor cousin, how much you must have suffered! I expect you to look even more ill than when you left Geneva. This winter has been very miserable for me, tormented as I have been by anxious waiting; yet I hope to see peace in your face and to find that your heart is not completely empty of comfort and calm.

“Yet I fear that the same feelings that made you so unhappy a year ago still exist, perhaps even strengthened by time. I would not want to trouble you now, when so many misfortunes weigh on you, but a conversation I had with my uncle before he left makes some explanation necessary before we meet. Explanation! You may well ask, what can Elizabeth have to explain? If you really say this, my questions are answered and all my doubts are settled. But you are far away from me, and it is possible that you may dread this explanation and yet be glad of it; and since this may be the case, I dare not put off any longer writing what I have often wanted to tell you while you were away but never had the courage to begin.

“You know very well, Victor, that our marriage has been your parents’ dearest plan ever since we were babies. We were told about it when we were young and taught to look forward to it as something that would certainly happen. As children we were loving playmates, and, I believe, as we grew older we became dear and valued friends to each other. But just as a brother and sister often feel a warm affection for each other without wanting a closer union, might this not be our case too? Tell me, dearest Victor. Answer me, I beg you, for the sake of our happiness, with the simple truth—Do you love someone else?

“You have travelled; you have spent several years of your life at Ingolstadt; and I admit, my friend, that when I saw you so unhappy last autumn, fleeing into solitude away from everyone, I could not help thinking that you might regret our engagement and believe yourself bound in honour to carry out your parents’ wishes, even though they went against your own feelings. But this is false reasoning. I confess to you, my friend, that I love you, and that in my dreamy thoughts of the future you have always been my constant friend and companion.

But it is your happiness I want as well as my own when I tell you that our marriage would make me unhappy for ever unless it were your own free choice. Even now I cry to think that, weighed down as you are by the cruellest misfortunes, you might crush, for the sake of the word honour, all hope of the love and happiness that alone could make you yourself again. I, whose love for you is so unselfish, might multiply your sufferings tenfold by standing in the way of your wishes. Oh, Victor, be sure that your cousin and playmate loves you far too sincerely not to be made miserable by this thought. Be happy, my friend; and if you do this one thing I ask, you can rest assured that nothing on earth will be able to disturb my peace.

“Do not let this letter upset you; do not answer tomorrow, or the day after, or even until you arrive, if it will hurt you. My uncle will send me news of your health, and if I see just one smile on your lips when we meet, whether it comes from this or from any other effort of mine, I shall need no other happiness. “Elizabeth Lavenza. “Geneva, May 18th, 17—”

This letter brought back to my memory something I had forgotten: the fiend’s threat—“I will be with you on your wedding-night!” That was my sentence, and on that night the demon would use every trick to destroy me and tear me away from the glimpse of happiness that promised to ease my suffering a little. On that night he had resolved to complete his crimes with my death.

Well, so be it; a deadly struggle would then certainly take place, and if he won, I would be at peace and his power over me would be over. If he were defeated, I would be a free man. But what freedom? The kind a peasant has when his family has been slaughtered before his eyes, his cottage burnt, his fields ruined, and he is cast out, homeless, penniless and alone, but free. That would be my freedom, except that in Elizabeth I had a treasure, though one outweighed by the horrors of remorse and guilt that would haunt me until I died.

Sweet, beloved Elizabeth! I read her letter again and again, and some gentler feelings crept into my heart and dared to whisper heavenly dreams of love and joy; but the apple had already been eaten, and the angel’s arm was already raised to drive me out of all hope. Yet I would die to make her happy.

If the monster carried out his threat, my death was certain; yet I wondered whether my marriage would bring my fate any closer. My death might indeed come a few months earlier, but if my tormentor suspected that I was delaying the wedding because of his threats, he would surely find other, perhaps even more terrible, ways of taking revenge. He had sworn to be with me on my wedding-night, but he did not see that threat as binding him to keep the peace until then; as if to show me that his thirst for blood was not yet satisfied, he had murdered Clerval straight after making his threats. So I decided that if marrying my cousin at once would add to her happiness or my father’s, my enemy’s plans against my life should not delay it by a single hour.

In this frame of mind I wrote to Elizabeth. My letter was calm and loving. “I fear, my beloved girl,” I wrote, “that little happiness is left for us on earth; yet all the happiness I may one day enjoy is centred in you. Drive away your groundless fears; to you alone I devote my life and my efforts to be content. I have one secret, Elizabeth, a terrible one; when I reveal it to you, it will freeze you with horror, and then, far from being surprised at my misery, you will only wonder that I have survived what I have been through. I will tell you this tale of misery and terror the day after our wedding, because, my sweet cousin, there must be complete trust between us. But until then, I beg you, do not mention it or even hint at it. I ask this of you most earnestly, and I know you will agree.”

About a week after Elizabeth’s letter arrived, we returned to Geneva. The sweet girl welcomed me with warm affection, but there were tears in her eyes when she saw my wasted body and feverish cheeks. I saw a change in her too. She was thinner and had lost much of the heavenly liveliness that had once charmed me; but her gentleness and her soft, pitying looks made her a more suitable companion for someone as blighted and miserable as I was.

The calm I now enjoyed did not last. Memory brought madness with it, and when I thought of what had happened, a real insanity took hold of me; sometimes I was furious and burned with rage, sometimes I was low and hopeless. I neither spoke to anyone nor looked at anyone, but sat without moving, bewildered by the endless miseries that overwhelmed me.

Only Elizabeth had the power to bring me out of these fits; her gentle voice would calm me when I was carried away by passion and fill me with human feelings when I had sunk into numbness. She cried with me and for me. When I came to my senses, she would gently reproach me and try to teach me acceptance. Ah! It is fine for the unfortunate to accept their fate, but for the guilty there is no peace. The agonies of remorse poison even the strange comfort that can sometimes be found in giving way completely to grief.

Soon after I arrived, my father spoke about my marrying Elizabeth without delay. I said nothing. “Is there, then, someone else you love?” “No one on earth. I love Elizabeth and look forward to our marriage with delight. So let the day be set; and on that day I will devote myself, in life or death, to my cousin’s happiness.”

“My dear Victor, do not talk like that. Terrible misfortunes have struck us, but let us simply hold more tightly to what remains and give the love we had for those we have lost to those who are still alive. Our circle will be small, but it will be held tightly together by bonds of affection and shared misfortune. And when time has softened your despair, new and dear people to care for will be born to take the place of those who were so cruelly taken from us.”

Such was my father’s advice. But the memory of the threat came back to me; and you cannot be surprised that, since the fiend had so far been all-powerful in his bloody deeds, I almost considered him unbeatable, and that when he had spoken the words “I shall be with you on your wedding-night,” I saw the fate he threatened as unavoidable. But death did not frighten me as long as it did not also mean losing Elizabeth, and so, with a contented and even cheerful face, I agreed with my father that if my cousin consented, the wedding would take place in ten days, and so, as I imagined, I set the seal on my fate.

Great God! If I had thought for one moment what my fiendish enemy’s hellish intention might be, I would rather have exiled myself from my native land for ever and wandered the earth as a friendless outcast than agreed to this wretched marriage. But, as if he had magic powers, the monster had blinded me to his real plans; and when I thought I had arranged only my own death, I brought on the death of a far dearer victim.

As the day set for our wedding drew nearer, whether out of cowardice or a prophetic feeling, I felt my heart sink. But I hid my feelings behind a show of cheerfulness that brought smiles and joy to my father’s face but hardly fooled Elizabeth’s ever-watchful and sharper eye. She looked forward to our marriage with quiet contentment, mixed with a little fear, left by past misfortunes, that what now seemed certain and real happiness might soon melt away like a dream and leave nothing behind but deep and endless regret.

Preparations were made for the wedding, visitors came to congratulate us, and everything looked cheerful. As well as I could, I locked away in my own heart the anxiety that was eating at me, and I joined in my father’s plans with apparent enthusiasm, although they might only turn out to be the decorations for my tragedy. Thanks to my father’s efforts, the Austrian government had given back to Elizabeth part of her inheritance. A small property on the shores of Lake Como belonged to her. It was agreed that immediately after the wedding we would go to the Villa Lavenza and spend our first happy days beside the beautiful lake where it stood.

Meanwhile I took every precaution to protect myself in case the fiend attacked me openly. I always carried pistols and a dagger and was constantly on my guard against any trick, and in this way I became calmer. Indeed, as the day came closer, the threat seemed more like a delusion, not worth disturbing my peace, while the happiness I hoped to find in marriage seemed more and more certain as the wedding day approached and I heard everyone speak of it as an event that no accident could possibly prevent.

Elizabeth seemed happy; my calm manner did much to settle her mind. But on the day that was to fulfil my wishes and my destiny, she was sad, and a feeling that something evil was coming filled her; perhaps she was also thinking of the terrible secret I had promised to tell her the next day. My father, meanwhile, was overjoyed, and in the rush of preparations he saw in his niece’s sadness only the shyness of a bride.

After the ceremony a large party gathered at my father’s house, but it was agreed that Elizabeth and I would begin our journey by boat, spend that night at Evian and continue our voyage the next day. The day was fine and the wind was favourable; everything smiled on us as we set off after our wedding.

Those were the last moments of my life in which I felt happy. We moved along quickly; the sun was hot, but we were shaded from its rays by a sort of canopy while we enjoyed the beauty of the scenery. Sometimes we were on one side of the lake, where we saw Mont Salêve, the pleasant banks of Montalègre and, far away, towering above everything, the beautiful Mont Blanc and the group of snowy mountains that try in vain to rival her; sometimes we sailed along the opposite shore and saw the mighty Jura turning its dark side against anyone ambitious to leave their native country, and forming an almost impassable barrier to any invader who might wish to conquer it.

I took Elizabeth’s hand. “You are sad, my love. Oh! If you knew what I have suffered and what I may still have to bear, you would try to let me enjoy the quiet and the freedom from despair that this one day at least allows me.”

“Be happy, my dear Victor,” replied Elizabeth; “there is nothing, I hope, to trouble you; and rest assured that even if great joy is not written on my face, my heart is content. Something whispers to me not to rely too much on the future that lies open before us, but I will not listen to such a sinister voice. See how fast we are moving, and how the clouds, which sometimes hide the dome of Mont Blanc and sometimes rise above it, make this beautiful scene even more interesting. Look, too, at the countless fish swimming in the clear water, where we can make out every pebble lying on the bottom. What a heavenly day! How happy and peaceful all nature looks!”

In this way Elizabeth tried to turn her thoughts and mine away from sad subjects. But her mood kept changing; for a few moments joy shone in her eyes, but it kept giving way to absent-mindedness and daydreaming. The sun sank lower in the sky; we passed the river Drance and followed its course through the gorges of the higher hills and the valleys of the lower ones. Here the Alps come closer to the lake, and we approached the amphitheatre of mountains that forms its eastern edge. The church spire of Evian shone beneath the woods that surrounded it and the rows of mountains, one above another, that towered over it.

The wind, which until then had carried us along amazingly fast, dropped at sunset to a light breeze; the soft air barely rippled the water and gently stirred the trees as we approached the shore, from which it carried the most delightful scent of flowers and hay. The sun set below the horizon as we landed, and as I stepped onto the shore, I felt those worries and fears return which were soon to grip me and cling to me for ever.
b1: The journey by sea ended. We got off the ship and went to Paris. I soon saw that I was too weak to go on and that I had to rest first. My father took care of me all the time. But he did not know the real reason for my pain, so he tried the wrong ways to cure it. Nothing could cure it.

He wanted me to go out and meet people. I hated to see people’s faces. No, I did not really hate them! They were my brothers, and I loved even the ugliest of them, as if they were angels. But I felt that I had no right to be with them. I had let loose among them an enemy who loved to kill them and to hear them cry out in pain. If they knew what I had done, they would all hate me and chase me out of the world!

In the end my father agreed that I could stay away from people, and he tried in many ways to help me feel less hopeless. Sometimes he thought I felt ashamed because I had been accused of murder, and he tried to show me that pride was not important. “Oh, father,” I said, “you do not know me at all. A terrible man like me has no right to feel proud. Poor Justine was as innocent as I was, and people said the same thing about her; she died because of it; and it was my fault—I killed her. William, Justine and Henry—they all died because of me.”

When I was in prison, my father often heard me say the same thing. Sometimes he seemed to want me to explain. At other times he seemed to think that it was only a strange idea from my fever, and that I still remembered it now that I was getting better.

I did not explain, and I never said a word about the monster I had made. I was sure people would think I was mad, and that was enough to keep me quiet for ever. Also, I could not tell a secret that would fill anyone who heard it with fear and horror. So I stopped myself, although I badly wanted someone to understand me. I would have given anything to tell my terrible secret. But sometimes words like the ones above still burst out of me. I could not explain them, but because they were partly true, they made my heavy sadness a little lighter.

This time my father was very surprised and said, “My dearest Victor, what is this strange idea? My dear son, please never say such a thing again.” “I am not mad,” I cried strongly; “the sun and the sky saw what I did, and they know I am telling the truth. I am the killer of those innocent people; they died because of my plans. I would have given my own blood a thousand times to save them; but I could not, father, I really could not sacrifice all the people in the world.”

After these words my father was sure that my mind was ill. He changed the subject at once and tried to make me think about other things. He wanted me to forget what had happened in Ireland, so he never talked about it and never let me speak about my troubles.

As time passed, I became calmer. My heart was still full of pain, but I no longer talked wildly about my crimes; it was enough for me to know about them. With great effort I kept my misery inside, although sometimes it wanted to shout to the whole world. I was calmer than I had been at any time since my trip to the sea of ice.

A few days before we left Paris for Switzerland, I got this letter from Elizabeth: “My dear friend, “I was so glad to get a letter from my uncle from Paris. You are not so terribly far away now, and I hope to see you in less than two weeks. My poor cousin, how much you must have suffered! I think you will look even more ill than when you left Geneva. This winter was very unhappy for me because I was always waiting and worrying. But I hope to see peace in your face and to find some comfort and calm in your heart.

“But I am afraid that you still have the same feelings that made you so unhappy a year ago, and maybe they are even stronger now. I do not want to worry you now, when you have so many troubles, but I had a talk with my uncle before he left, and now I must explain something before we meet. Explain! Perhaps you will say, what does Elizabeth need to explain? If you really say this, then I have my answer and I have no more doubts. But you are far away, and perhaps you will be afraid of this explanation and also happy about it. So I cannot wait any longer to write what I have often wanted to tell you, but never had the courage to begin.

“You know, Victor, that since we were babies your parents always planned that we would marry. They told us this when we were young, and we learned to wait for it as something that would surely happen. As children we played together happily, and as we grew older, I think we became dear friends. But a brother and sister often love each other without wanting to marry. Could this be true for us too? Tell me, dearest Victor. Answer me honestly, I beg you, for the sake of our happiness—Do you love another girl?

“You have travelled, and you have spent several years in Ingolstadt. When I saw you so unhappy last autumn, running away from everyone to be alone, I could not help thinking that you were sorry about our engagement. I thought that perhaps you felt you had to do what your parents wanted, even if you did not want it yourself. But this is the wrong way to think. I must tell you, my friend, that I love you, and in my dreams about the future you have always been my friend and companion.

But I want you to be happy, not only me. So I tell you that our marriage would make me unhappy for ever if you did not choose it freely yourself. Even now I cry when I think that you, with all your terrible troubles, may give up all hope of love and happiness because of the word ‘honour’. Only love and happiness could make you yourself again. I love you without thinking of myself, but I could make your pain ten times worse if I stand in the way of what you want. Oh, Victor, believe me, I love you too much not to be unhappy at this thought. Be happy, my friend; if you do this one thing for me, nothing on earth will ever take away my peace.

“Do not let this letter upset you; do not answer tomorrow, or the day after, or even before you come, if it will hurt you. My uncle will tell me about your health, and if I see just one smile on your face when we meet, I will need no other happiness. “Elizabeth Lavenza. “Geneva, May 18th, 17—”

This letter made me remember something I had forgotten: the monster’s words—“I will be with you on your wedding-night!” That was my sentence. On that night the monster would try everything to kill me and take away the small hope of happiness that I had. He had decided to finish his crimes on that night with my death.

Well, let it be so. There would be a fight to the death. If he won, I would be at peace, and his power over me would end. If he lost, I would be free. But what kind of freedom? The freedom of a poor farmer whose family has been killed in front of him, whose house has been burnt and whose fields have been destroyed; he has no home, no money and no one, but he is free. My freedom would be like that, except that I had Elizabeth, my treasure. But my guilt and pain would follow me until I died.

Sweet, dear Elizabeth! I read her letter again and again, and some softer feelings came into my heart and let me dream of love and joy. But, like Adam, I had already eaten the apple, and the angel was ready to drive me away from all hope. Still, I was ready to die to make her happy.

If the monster did what he said, I would surely die; but I asked myself whether my marriage would make it come sooner. Perhaps I would die a few months earlier. But if he thought that I was waiting because I was afraid of him, he would surely find other, maybe worse, ways to take revenge. He had promised to be with me on my wedding-night, but that did not mean he would do nothing until then. To show me that he still wanted blood, he had killed Clerval right after he made his threats. So I decided that if a quick wedding would make Elizabeth or my father happier, my enemy’s plans would not stop it for even one hour.

Feeling like this, I wrote to Elizabeth. My letter was calm and loving. “I am afraid, my dear girl,” I wrote, “that we do not have much happiness left on earth; but all the happiness I may ever have is in you. Do not be afraid for no reason; I give my life only to you. I have one terrible secret, Elizabeth. When I tell you, you will go cold with horror. Then you will not be surprised that I am so unhappy; you will only be surprised that I am still alive after everything. I will tell you this terrible story the day after our wedding, because, my sweet cousin, we must trust each other completely. But until then, please do not talk about it at all. I ask you this very seriously, and I know you will agree.”

About a week after Elizabeth’s letter came, we went back to Geneva. The dear girl welcomed me warmly, but she had tears in her eyes when she saw how thin I was and how hot my cheeks were with fever. I saw that she had changed too. She was thinner, and she had lost much of the bright, happy spirit that I had loved before. But because she was so gentle and kind, she was a better companion for a broken, unhappy man like me.

But my calm did not last. My memories made me almost mad. When I thought about what had happened, I lost my mind; sometimes I was burning with anger, and sometimes I was sad and hopeless. I did not speak to anyone or look at anyone. I just sat without moving, lost in all my troubles.

Only Elizabeth could bring me out of these moods. Her soft voice calmed me when I was angry and made me feel human again when I was lost in a heavy sleep of the mind. She cried with me and for me. When I could think clearly again, she gently told me I was wrong and tried to help me accept my fate. Oh! It is good for unlucky people to accept their fate, but guilty people can never find peace. Guilt spoils even the small comfort that people sometimes find in crying freely.

Soon after I arrived, my father talked about my marrying Elizabeth soon. I said nothing. “Do you love someone else, then?” “No one in the world. I love Elizabeth, and I am happy to think of our marriage. So let us choose the day; and on that day I will give myself, in life or death, to making my cousin happy.”

“My dear Victor, do not talk like that. Terrible things have happened to us, but let us hold on to what we still have. Let us give the love we had for the dead to the people who are still alive. Our family will be small, but love and shared sadness will keep us close. And when time has made your pain softer, new dear little ones will be born to take the place of those we lost so cruelly.”

That was what my father told me. But I remembered the monster’s threat again. He had always been so powerful in his killings that I thought no one could beat him. So when he said, “I shall be with you on your wedding-night,” I was sure that this would really happen. But I was not afraid of death, as long as I did not lose Elizabeth too. So, with a happy and even cheerful face, I agreed with my father that, if Elizabeth said yes, the wedding would be in ten days. In this way, I thought, I decided my fate.

Oh God! If I had thought for one moment about the monster’s real evil plan, I would have left my country for ever and wandered the world alone, rather than agree to this terrible marriage. But it was as if the monster had magic powers and had made me blind to his real plans. I thought I was only preparing my own death, but I was bringing death much closer to someone far dearer to me.

As our wedding day came closer, I felt my heart grow heavy, perhaps because I was a coward, or perhaps because I felt what was coming. But I hid my feelings and pretended to be cheerful. This made my father smile, but it did not really fool Elizabeth, who always watched me closely. She waited for our wedding calmly and happily, but she was also a little afraid. After all our past troubles, she feared that this happiness, which now seemed so sure and real, might soon disappear like a dream and leave only deep sadness for ever.

Everyone got ready for the wedding, people came to congratulate us, and everything looked happy. I hid my worry deep in my heart as well as I could and joined in my father’s plans as if I was happy about them. But perhaps they were only the decorations for my tragedy. Thanks to my father’s help, the Austrian government gave back to Elizabeth part of her family’s money. She now owned a small house by Lake Como. We agreed that right after the wedding we would go to the Villa Lavenza and spend our first happy days by the beautiful lake.

Meanwhile, I did everything I could to protect myself in case the monster attacked me. I always carried pistols and a knife and was always watching for tricks, and this made me feel calmer. In fact, as the day came closer, the threat began to seem like a mistake of my imagination, not something to worry about. And my hope of happiness in marriage seemed more and more certain, because everyone kept talking about the wedding as something that nothing could stop.

Elizabeth seemed happy; my calm manner helped her to feel calm too. But on the wedding day she was sad, and she felt that something bad was going to happen. Perhaps she was also thinking about the terrible secret that I had promised to tell her the next day. My father, meanwhile, was full of joy, and he was so busy that he thought his niece was just a shy bride.

After the wedding many guests came to my father’s house. But we had agreed that Elizabeth and I would travel by boat, spend the night at Evian and go on the next day. The day was fine and the wind was good; everything smiled on us as we left.

Those were the last happy moments of my life. We moved quickly across the water; the sun was hot, but we sat under a cover and enjoyed the beautiful view. On one side of the lake we saw Mont Salêve, the lovely shores of Montalègre and, far away, above everything, beautiful Mont Blanc with the snowy mountains that try to be as great as it is. On the other side we saw the great Jura mountains. They stood dark and strong, like a wall against people who wanted to leave the country and against enemies who wanted to take it.
I took Elizabeth’s hand. “You are sad, my love. Oh! If you knew how much I have suffered and how much more I may suffer, you would let me enjoy the peace that this one day gives me.”

“Be happy, my dear Victor,” Elizabeth answered; “I hope nothing is worrying you. Even if you cannot see great joy on my face, believe me, my heart is happy. Something tells me not to trust too much in the future in front of us, but I will not listen to such a dark voice. Look how fast we are moving, and how the clouds sometimes cover the top of Mont Blanc and sometimes rise above it; they make this beautiful place even more interesting. Look at all the fish in the clear water, where we can see every little stone on the bottom. What a wonderful day! How happy and peaceful everything looks!”

In this way Elizabeth tried to stop us both from thinking about sad things. But her mood kept changing; sometimes her eyes shone with joy for a few moments, but then she became distant and lost in thought. The sun went lower in the sky. We passed the river Drance and saw how it ran through the deep valleys between the hills. Here the Alps come closer to the lake, and we came near the circle of mountains at its eastern end. The church tower of Evian shone among the trees, with mountains rising high above it.

The wind had carried us very fast all day, but at sunset it became a light breeze. The soft air moved the water a little and moved the trees as we came near the shore. It brought us the lovely smell of flowers and hay. The sun went down as we landed. As soon as I stepped on the shore, my worries and fears came back, and soon they were going to hold me and never let me go.
a2: The journey by sea ended. We arrived and went to Paris. Soon I understood that I was very weak. I needed to rest before we travelled again. My father took care of me every day. But he did not know why I was so ill. He tried many things to help me, but nothing worked.

He wanted me to meet people and have fun. I did not want to see anybody. But I did not hate people. They were my brothers, and I loved all of them, even the ugly ones. But I felt that I could not be with them. I made a monster, and now he was among them. He liked to kill people and to hear them cry. If people knew what I did, they would all hate me!

In the end my father let me stay away from people. He talked to me a lot and tried to make me feel better. He thought I felt bad because people said I was a murderer. “Oh, father,” I said, “you do not know me. A bad man like me cannot be proud. Poor Justine did nothing wrong, but she died. It was my fault—I killed her. William, Justine and Henry—they all died because of me.”
When I was in prison, my father often heard me say this. Sometimes he wanted to know more. But usually he thought it was only a bad dream from my illness.

I did not explain anything. I never talked about the monster. I knew that people would think I was mad. Also, my secret was too terrible. It would fill anyone with fear. So I said nothing, but I really wanted to tell someone. Sometimes the words came out, and I could not stop them. I did not explain them, but saying them helped me a little.

This time my father was very surprised. “My dear Victor, what are you saying? Please never say that again.” “I am not mad,” I cried. “The sun and the sky saw everything, and they know it is true. I killed those good people; they died because of my plans. I wanted to die to save them. But I could not, father. I could not put all the people in the world in danger.”

After this my father was sure that I was ill in my mind. He started talking about other things. He wanted me to forget what happened in Ireland. He never talked about it, and he did not let me talk about my problems.

Time passed, and I became calmer. I was still very sad, but I did not talk about my crimes any more. It was enough for me to know about them. Sometimes I wanted to tell the whole world, but I stopped myself. I was calmer than at any time since my trip to the ice.

A few days before we left Paris, I got a letter from Elizabeth: “My dear friend, “I was very happy to get a letter from my uncle in Paris. You are not very far now, and I hope to see you in two weeks. My poor cousin, you have suffered so much! I think you will look very ill. This winter was very hard for me because I was always worried. But I hope that you will be calm and a little happier.

“But I am afraid that you are still as sad as you were a year ago. I do not want to worry you now. But I talked with my uncle before he left, and now I must explain something. Explain! Maybe you will ask, what does Elizabeth want to explain? If you ask this, then I have my answer. But you are far away, so I must write. I wanted to say this for a long time, but I was afraid to start.

“Victor, you know that your parents always wanted us to marry. They told us this when we were small children. We played together as children, and later we became good friends. But a brother and sister can love each other and not want to marry. Maybe it is the same with us? Tell me the truth, dear Victor. Do you love another girl?

“You have travelled a lot, and you lived in Ingolstadt for some years. Last autumn you were very unhappy and did not want to see anybody. So I thought: maybe he does not want to marry me. Maybe he wants to marry me only because his parents want it. But I was wrong to think this. I love you, Victor. In my dreams about the future, you are always my friend.

But I want you to be happy too. If you do not really want to marry me, I will be unhappy for ever. You have many terrible problems. I do not want you to marry me only because you promised. Only love can make you happy again. I love you, and I do not want to make your life harder. Please be happy, my friend. If you are happy, I will be calm.
“Do not worry about this letter. You do not need to answer now. If I see just one smile on your face when we meet, I will be happy. “Elizabeth Lavenza. “Geneva, May 18th, 17—”

This letter helped me to remember something. It was the monster’s promise—“I will be with you on your wedding-night!” On that night the monster was going to try to kill me. He wanted to take my happiness away. He wanted to finish his crimes with my death.

Well, OK. We were going to fight. If he won, I would die and be at peace. If he lost, I would be free. But what kind of freedom was that? It was like the freedom of a poor farmer after enemies killed his family and burned his house. He has no home, no money and no friends, but he is free. I had Elizabeth, but I also had my guilt, and it was going to stay with me until I died.

Sweet, dear Elizabeth! I read her letter many times. I felt softer, and I began to dream about love and happiness. But it was too late for me. I could not hope any more. But I was ready to die for her happiness.

If the monster did what he promised, I was going to die. Would my wedding make my death come sooner? Perhaps a few months sooner. But if I waited because I was afraid, the monster would be angry. He would find other, worse ways to hurt me. He promised to come on my wedding-night, but he killed Clerval right after that promise. He still wanted more blood. So I decided: if the wedding would make Elizabeth and my father happy, I would not wait.

So I wrote to Elizabeth. My letter was calm and kind. “My dear,” I wrote, “I am afraid that we will not have much happiness in this life. But all my happiness is you. Do not be afraid. My life is only for you. I have a terrible secret, Elizabeth. When you hear it, you will be very frightened. Then you will understand why I am so sad. I will tell you everything the day after our wedding. We must not have secrets from each other. But until then, please do not ask me about it. I know you will do this for me.”

About a week later we went back to Geneva. Elizabeth was very happy to see me. But she cried because I was so thin and ill. She was different too. She was thinner and less cheerful than before. But she was very gentle and kind, and this was good for a sad man like me.
But I did not stay calm for long. My memories made me almost mad. Sometimes I was very angry, and sometimes I was very sad. I did not speak or look at anybody. I just sat and did not move.

Only Elizabeth could help me. Her soft voice made me calm when I was angry. She helped me to feel again when I felt nothing. She cried with me and for me. When I was better, she talked to me kindly and asked me to accept my life. But a guilty man can never be at peace. My guilt made my sadness even worse.

Soon my father talked about my wedding with Elizabeth. I did not answer. “Do you love another girl?” “No, nobody. I love Elizabeth, and I want to marry her. Let us choose the day. I will give my life to make her happy.”

“My dear Victor, do not talk like that. We lost many people we loved. But we must love the people who are still with us. Our family is small now, but we will be close. Later you will feel better, and you will have children. They will take the place of the people we lost.”

My father said these things. But I remembered the monster’s words again. He was very strong, and he always did what he wanted. He said, “I shall be with you on your wedding-night.” I was sure that this was going to happen. But I was not afraid to die, if I did not lose Elizabeth. So I smiled and agreed with my father. If Elizabeth agreed, the wedding would be in ten days.

Oh God! I did not understand the monster’s real plan. If I understood it, I would leave my country for ever. I would never agree to this wedding. But the monster made me blind. I thought that he wanted to kill only me. But he wanted to kill someone much dearer to me.

The wedding day came nearer, and my heart felt heavy. I hid my feelings and smiled. My father was happy, but Elizabeth saw that something was wrong. She was calm and happy, but also a little afraid. She had many sad times in the past. She was afraid that this happiness would go away like a dream.

Everyone was getting ready for the wedding. Friends visited us, and everybody smiled. I hid my worry and helped my father with his plans. My father helped Elizabeth to get back some of her family’s money from the Austrian government. Now she had a small house by Lake Como. After the wedding, we were going to go there, to the Villa Lavenza, and spend our first happy days by the lake.

I was ready to fight the monster. I always carried guns and a knife, and I was always careful. This made me calmer. As the wedding came nearer, the monster’s words seemed less real. Everyone talked about the wedding, and I began to believe that I would be happy.

Elizabeth seemed happy, and I was calm, so she was calm too. But on our wedding day she was sad. She felt that something bad was going to happen. Maybe she was also thinking about my terrible secret. My father was very happy. He thought that Elizabeth was just a shy bride.
After the wedding many people came to my father’s house. Elizabeth and I left by boat. We planned to sleep at Evian and travel on the next day. It was a beautiful day, and the wind was good.

Those were the last happy moments of my life. Our boat moved fast. The sun was hot, but we sat in the shade. We looked at the beautiful mountains: Mont Salêve, the hills of Montalègre and, far away, the great white Mont Blanc. On the other side were the dark Jura mountains. They were like a big wall that kept the country safe from enemies.
I took Elizabeth’s hand. “You are sad, my love. I have suffered so much. Today I feel a little calm and happy. Please help me to enjoy this day.”

“Be happy, my dear Victor,” Elizabeth answered. “I hope nothing is worrying you. Maybe my face does not look very happy, but my heart is happy. Something tells me to be careful about the future, but I will not listen to it. Look how fast we are going! Look at the clouds over Mont Blanc! Look at all the fish in the clear water! We can see every little stone on the bottom. What a beautiful day! Everything looks so happy and quiet!”

Elizabeth wanted us to stop thinking about sad things. But her feelings changed all the time. Sometimes she looked happy, but then she became quiet and thoughtful. The sun went down lower. We passed the river Drance. Here the mountains come very close to the lake. We saw the church of Evian among the trees, with high mountains behind it.

All day the wind was strong, but in the evening it became soft. The water moved a little, and the trees moved too. From the shore came the nice smell of flowers and grass. The sun went down when we arrived. When I stepped on the shore, all my fears came back. Soon they were going to hold me and never let me go.

o.en: The voyage came to an end.
We landed, and proceeded to Paris.
o.ru: Мы высадились на берег и направились в Париж.

o.en: I soon found that I had overtaxed my strength and that I must repose before I could continue my journey.
o.ru: Вскоре я обнаружил, что переутомил свои силы и что мне необходимо отдохнуть, прежде чем продолжать путь.

o.en: My father’s care and attentions were indefatigable, but he did not know the origin of my sufferings and sought erroneous methods to remedy the incurable ill.
o.ru: Заботы и внимание отца были неутомимы, но он не знал истоков моих страданий и искал ошибочных средств, чтобы излечить неизлечимый недуг.

o.en: He wished me to seek amusement in society.
o.ru: Он желал, чтобы я искал развлечений в обществе.

o.en: I abhorred the face of man.
Oh, not abhorred!
They were my brethren, my fellow beings, and I felt attracted even to the most repulsive among them, as to creatures of an angelic nature and celestial mechanism.
o.ru: Люди были моими братьями, моими ближними, и меня влекло даже к самым отталкивающим из них, как к созданиям ангельской природы и небесного устройства.

o.en: But I felt that I had no right to share their intercourse.
o.ru: Но я чувствовал, что не имею права разделять их общество.

o.en: I had unchained an enemy among them whose joy it was to shed their blood and to revel in their groans.
o.ru: Я спустил с цепи среди них врага, чьей радостью было проливать их кровь и упиваться их стонами.

o.en: How they would, each and all, abhor me and hunt me from the world, did they know my unhallowed acts and the crimes which had their source in me!
o.ru: Как бы все они, до единого, возненавидели меня и изгнали из мира, если бы знали о моих нечестивых деяниях и о преступлениях, источником которых был я!

o.en: My father yielded at length to my desire to avoid society and strove by various arguments to banish my despair.
o.ru: Отец в конце концов уступил моему желанию избегать общества и всевозможными доводами старался изгнать моё отчаяние.

o.en: Sometimes he thought that I felt deeply the degradation of being obliged to answer a charge of murder, and he endeavoured to prove to me the futility of pride.
o.ru: Порой он думал, что я глубоко переживаю унижение от того, что мне пришлось отвечать на обвинение в убийстве, и силился доказать мне тщетность гордости.

o.en: “Alas! My father,” said I, “how little do you know me.
o.ru: «Увы, отец мой, — сказал я, — как мало вы меня знаете.

o.en: Human beings, their feelings and passions, would indeed be degraded if such a wretch as I felt pride.
o.ru: Люди, их чувства и страсти, поистине были бы унижены, если бы такой негодяй, как я, испытывал гордость.

o.en: Justine, poor unhappy Justine, was as innocent as I, and she suffered the same charge; she died for it; and I am the cause of this—I murdered her.
o.ru: Жюстина, бедная несчастная Жюстина, была так же невинна, как я, и ей было предъявлено то же обвинение; она умерла за это; и причина тому я — я убил её.

o.en: William, Justine, and Henry—they all died by my hands.”
o.ru: Уильям, Жюстина и Анри — все они погибли от моей руки».

o.en: My father had often, during my imprisonment, heard me make the same assertion; when I thus accused myself, he sometimes seemed to desire an explanation, and at others he appeared to consider it as the offspring of delirium, and that, during my illness, some idea of this kind had presented itself to my imagination, the remembrance of which I preserved in my convalescence.
o.ru: Во время моего заключения отец часто слышал от меня то же утверждение; когда я так обвинял себя, он порой, казалось, желал объяснения, а порой, видимо, считал это порождением бреда: будто во время болезни подобная мысль представилась моему воображению и воспоминание о ней сохранилось у меня и в пору выздоровления.

o.en: I avoided explanation and maintained a continual silence concerning the wretch I had created.
o.ru: Я избегал объяснений и хранил постоянное молчание о негодяе, которого создал.

o.en: I had a persuasion that I should be supposed mad, and this in itself would for ever have chained my tongue.
o.ru: Я был убеждён, что меня сочтут безумным, и уже одно это навеки сковало бы мне язык.

o.en: But, besides, I could not bring myself to disclose a secret which would fill my hearer with consternation and make fear and unnatural horror the inmates of his breast.
o.ru: Но, кроме того, я не мог заставить себя открыть тайну, которая наполнила бы слушателя смятением и поселила бы в его груди страх и противоестественный ужас.

o.en: I checked, therefore, my impatient thirst for sympathy and was silent when I would have given the world to have confided the fatal secret.
o.ru: Поэтому я подавлял свою нетерпеливую жажду сочувствия и молчал, тогда как отдал бы весь мир, чтобы доверить кому-нибудь роковую тайну.

o.en: Yet, still, words like those I have recorded would burst uncontrollably from me.
o.ru: И всё же слова, подобные приведённым мною, порой неудержимо вырывались у меня.

o.en: I could offer no explanation of them, but their truth in part relieved the burden of my mysterious woe.
o.ru: Я не мог их объяснить, но то, что в них была доля правды, отчасти облегчало бремя моей таинственной скорби.

o.en: Upon this occasion my father said, with an expression of unbounded wonder, “My dearest Victor, what infatuation is this?
o.ru: В этот раз отец сказал с выражением безграничного изумления: «Мой дорогой Виктор, что это за наваждение?

o.en: My dear son, I entreat you never to make such an assertion again.”
o.ru: Сын мой, заклинаю тебя, никогда больше не говори подобного».

o.en: “I am not mad,” I cried energetically; “the sun and the heavens, who have viewed my operations, can bear witness of my truth.
o.ru: «Я не безумен, — горячо воскликнул я, — солнце и небеса, взиравшие на мои труды, могут засвидетельствовать мою правду.

o.en: I am the assassin of those most innocent victims; they died by my machinations.
o.ru: Я убийца этих ни в чём не повинных жертв; они погибли из-за моих козней.

o.en: A thousand times would I have shed my own blood, drop by drop, to have saved their lives; but I could not, my father, indeed I could not sacrifice the whole human race.”
o.ru: Тысячу раз я пролил бы собственную кровь, каплю за каплей, чтобы спасти их жизни; но я не мог, отец мой, поистине не мог принести в жертву весь род человеческий».

o.en: The conclusion of this speech convinced my father that my ideas were deranged, and he instantly changed the subject of our conversation and endeavoured to alter the course of my thoughts.
o.ru: Конец этой речи убедил отца, что мой рассудок помрачён, и он тотчас переменил предмет разговора и постарался изменить течение моих мыслей.

o.en: He wished as much as possible to obliterate the memory of the scenes that had taken place in Ireland and never alluded to them or suffered me to speak of my misfortunes.
o.ru: Он хотел, насколько возможно, изгладить память о событиях, происшедших в Ирландии, и никогда не упоминал о них и не позволял мне говорить о моих несчастьях.

o.en: As time passed away I became more calm; misery had her dwelling in my heart, but I no longer talked in the same incoherent manner of my own crimes; sufficient for me was the consciousness of them.
o.ru: С течением времени я стал спокойнее; страдание поселилось в моём сердце, но я больше не говорил так бессвязно о собственных преступлениях: мне было довольно сознавать их.

o.en: By the utmost self-violence I curbed the imperious voice of wretchedness, which sometimes desired to declare itself to the whole world, and my manners were calmer and more composed than they had ever been since my journey to the sea of ice.
o.ru: Величайшим насилием над собой я обуздывал властный голос несчастья, которому порой хотелось заявить о себе всему миру, и держался я спокойнее и сдержаннее, чем когда-либо со времени моего путешествия к ледяному морю.

o.en: A few days before we left Paris on our way to Switzerland, I received the following letter from Elizabeth:
o.ru: За несколько дней до того, как мы покинули Париж по пути в Швейцарию, я получил от Элизабет следующее письмо:

o.en: “My dear Friend,
“It gave me the greatest pleasure to receive a letter from my uncle dated at Paris; you are no longer at a formidable distance, and I may hope to see you in less than a fortnight.
o.ru: Величайшую радость доставило мне письмо дяди из Парижа; ты уже не так устрашающе далеко, и я могу надеяться увидеть тебя меньше чем через две недели.

o.en: My poor cousin, how much you must have suffered!
o.ru: Мой бедный кузен, как много ты, должно быть, выстрадал!

o.en: I expect to see you looking even more ill than when you quitted Geneva.
