b1.en: There were no horses, so I had to go back across the lake.
b1.ru: Лошадей не было, и мне пришлось возвращаться по озеру.

b1.en: But the wind was against us, and it was raining very hard.
b1.ru: Но ветер был встречный, и шёл очень сильный дождь.

b1.en: Still, it was early morning, so I hoped to arrive by night.
b1.ru: И всё же было раннее утро, и я надеялся добраться к ночи.

b1.en: I paid some men to row, and I took an oar too, because hard physical work always helped me when I suffered.
b1.ru: Я нанял гребцов и сам взялся за весло, потому что тяжёлый физический труд всегда помогал мне в страдании.

b1.en: But I was too unhappy and too upset to do anything.
b1.ru: Но я был слишком несчастен и расстроен, чтобы что-то делать.

b1.en: I threw down the oar, put my head in my hands and let all my dark thoughts come.
b1.ru: Я бросил весло, уронил голову на руки и отдался всем мрачным мыслям.

b1.en: When I looked up, I saw places that I knew from happier times.
b1.ru: Когда я поднимал глаза, я видел места, знакомые мне по более счастливым временам.

b1.en: Only the day before, I had looked at them with Elizabeth, and now she was only a shadow and a memory.
b1.ru: Только вчера я смотрел на них вместе с Элизабет, а теперь она была лишь тенью и воспоминанием.

b1.en: Tears ran from my eyes.
b1.ru: Слёзы текли из моих глаз.

b1.en: The rain stopped for a moment, and I saw fish playing in the water, just as they had done a few hours before, when Elizabeth watched them.
b1.ru: Дождь на минуту прекратился, и я видел, как в воде играют рыбы — так же, как несколько часов назад, когда на них смотрела Элизабет.

b1.en: Nothing hurts the human mind more than a great and sudden change.
b1.ru: Ничто так не ранит человеческий разум, как большая и внезапная перемена.

b1.en: The sun could shine or the sky could be dark, but nothing looked the same to me as it had the day before.
b1.ru: Могло светить солнце или хмуриться небо, но ничто уже не выглядело для меня так, как накануне.

b1.en: A monster had taken away all my hope of happiness.
b1.ru: Чудовище отняло у меня всю надежду на счастье.

b1.en: Nobody had ever been as unhappy as I was; nothing so terrible had ever happened to anyone.
b1.ru: Никто никогда не был так несчастен, как я; ни с кем не случалось ничего столь ужасного.

b1.en: But why should I tell you everything that happened after this terrible event?
b1.ru: Но зачем мне рассказывать вам обо всём, что случилось после этого страшного события?

b1.en: My story is a story of horrors, and I have reached the worst of them.
b1.ru: Моя история — история ужасов, и я дошёл до самого страшного.

b1.en: What I must tell now will only bore you.
b1.ru: То, что мне осталось рассказать, лишь утомит вас.

b1.en: My friends were taken from me one by one, and I was left alone.
b1.ru: Моих близких отнимали у меня одного за другим, и я остался один.

b1.en: I have no strength left, so I will tell the rest of my terrible story in a few words.
b1.ru: Сил у меня не осталось, поэтому я расскажу остаток своей страшной истории в нескольких словах.

b1.en: I arrived in Geneva.
b1.ru: Я приехал в Женеву.

b1.en: My father and Ernest were still alive, but my father could not bear the news that I brought.
b1.ru: Отец и Эрнест были ещё живы, но отец не вынес известий, которые я привёз.

b1.en: I can still see him now, that good and wise old man!
b1.ru: Я и сейчас вижу его, этого доброго и мудрого старика!

b1.en: His eyes looked at nothing, because he had lost his joy: his Elizabeth, who was more than a daughter to him.
b1.ru: Его глаза ни на что не смотрели, потому что он потерял свою радость — свою Элизабет, которая была ему больше чем дочерью.

b1.en: He loved her very much, as old men love the few people they have left.
b1.ru: Он очень любил её, как старики любят тех немногих, кто у них остался.

b1.en: I curse the monster who brought such pain to that old man!
b1.ru: Будь проклято чудовище, которое причинило такую боль этому старику!

b1.en: He could not live with all these horrors around him.
b1.ru: Он не мог жить среди всех этих ужасов.

b1.en: He could not get out of bed, and a few days later he died in my arms.
b1.ru: Он не мог встать с постели и через несколько дней умер у меня на руках.

b1.en: What happened to me then?
b1.ru: Что же случилось со мной потом?

b1.en: I do not know.
b1.ru: Я не знаю.

b1.en: I felt nothing, and I only knew chains and darkness.
b1.ru: Я ничего не чувствовал и знал только цепи и тьму.

b1.en: Sometimes I dreamed that I was walking in fields of flowers with the friends of my youth, but then I woke up in a prison.
b1.ru: Иногда мне снилось, что я гуляю по цветущим полям с друзьями юности, но потом я просыпался в тюрьме.

b1.en: I was very sad, but slowly I began to understand my situation clearly, and then they let me go.
b1.ru: Мне было очень тяжело, но постепенно я начал ясно понимать своё положение, и тогда меня отпустили.

b1.en: They had thought I was mad, and for many months I had lived alone in a small cell.
b1.ru: Меня считали сумасшедшим, и много месяцев я прожил один в маленькой камере.

b1.en: But freedom would be useless to me if I did not also want revenge.
b1.ru: Но свобода была бы мне бесполезна, если бы я не хотел и мести.

b1.en: When I remembered my past misfortunes, I thought about their cause: the monster I had made and sent out into the world to destroy me.
b1.ru: Вспоминая свои прошлые несчастья, я думал об их причине — о чудовище, которое я создал и выпустил в мир себе на погибель.

b1.en: When I thought of him, I felt a crazy anger.
b1.ru: Когда я думал о нём, меня охватывала безумная ярость.

b1.en: I prayed that I could catch him and take a terrible revenge on him.
b1.ru: Я молился, чтобы поймать его и страшно ему отомстить.

b1.en: And I did more than just wish.
b1.ru: И я не просто мечтал.

b1.en: I began to think about the best way to catch him.
b1.ru: Я начал думать, как лучше его поймать.

b1.en: About a month after I was freed, I went to a judge in the town.
b1.ru: Примерно через месяц после освобождения я пошёл к судье в городе.

b1.en: I told him that I wanted to accuse someone, that I knew who had killed my family, and that he must use all his power to catch the murderer.
b1.ru: Я сказал ему, что хочу кого-то обвинить, что знаю, кто убил мою семью, и что он должен употребить всю свою власть, чтобы поймать убийцу.

b1.en: The judge listened to me carefully and kindly.
b1.ru: Судья выслушал меня внимательно и доброжелательно.

b1.en: “Don’t worry, sir,” he said, “I will do everything I can to find the criminal.”
b1.ru: «Не беспокойтесь, сударь, — сказал он, — я сделаю всё возможное, чтобы найти преступника».

b1.en: “Thank you,” I answered. “So please listen to my story.
b1.ru: «Благодарю вас, — ответил я. — Тогда, пожалуйста, выслушайте мою историю.

b1.en: It is so strange that I am afraid you will not believe it, but the truth has a power that makes people believe.
b1.ru: Она так странна, что я боюсь, вы не поверите, но у правды есть сила, которая заставляет верить.

b1.en: My story is too clear to be a dream, and I have no reason to lie.”
b1.ru: Моя история слишком ясна, чтобы быть сном, и мне незачем лгать».

b1.en: I spoke seriously but calmly.
b1.ru: Я говорил серьёзно, но спокойно.

b1.en: In my heart I had decided to follow my enemy until he was dead, and this decision made my pain quieter and helped me to live for a while.
b1.ru: В душе я решил преследовать своего врага до его смерти, и это решение смягчило мою боль и на время помогло мне жить.

b1.en: I told my story briefly, clearly and exactly.
b1.ru: Я рассказал свою историю коротко, ясно и точно.

b1.en: I gave all the dates correctly, and I never shouted or became angry.
b1.ru: Я правильно называл все даты и ни разу не кричал и не злился.

b1.en: At first the judge did not believe me at all, but as I went on, he became more and more interested.
b1.ru: Сначала судья совсем мне не верил, но по мере рассказа ему становилось всё интереснее.

b1.en: Sometimes he shook with horror, and sometimes he looked very surprised.
b1.ru: Иногда он вздрагивал от ужаса, а иногда выглядел очень удивлённым.

b1.en: When I finished my story, I said, “This is the creature I accuse.
b1.ru: Закончив рассказ, я сказал: «Вот существо, которое я обвиняю.

b1.en: Please use all your power to catch him and punish him.
b1.ru: Прошу вас, употребите всю свою власть, чтобы поймать и наказать его.

b1.en: It is your duty as a judge, and I hope that as a man you will want to do it.”
b1.ru: Это ваш долг как судьи, и я надеюсь, что как человек вы захотите его исполнить».

b1.en: These words changed the judge’s face.
b1.ru: Эти слова изменили выражение лица судьи.

b1.en: He had half believed my story, as people half believe stories about ghosts.
b1.ru: Он наполовину поверил моей истории, как люди наполовину верят рассказам о призраках.

b1.en: But when I asked him to act, he stopped believing it again.
b1.ru: Но когда я попросил его действовать, он снова перестал верить.

b1.en: Still, he answered kindly, “I would like to help you, but this creature seems too strong for me.
b1.ru: Всё же он мягко ответил: «Я хотел бы вам помочь, но это существо, похоже, слишком сильно для меня.

b1.en: Who can follow an animal that can cross the sea of ice and live in caves where no man would go?
b1.ru: Кто может преследовать зверя, который переходит ледяное море и живёт в пещерах, куда не пойдёт ни один человек?

b1.en: Also, several months have passed since his crimes, and nobody can guess where he is now.”
b1.ru: К тому же с его преступлений прошло несколько месяцев, и никто не может угадать, где он сейчас».

b1.en: “I am sure that he stays near the place where I live.
b1.ru: «Я уверен, что он держится поблизости от места, где я живу.

b1.en: And if he is hiding in the Alps, we can hunt him like a wild animal and kill him.
b1.ru: А если он прячется в Альпах, мы можем охотиться на него, как на дикого зверя, и убить его.

b1.en: But I know what you are thinking.
b1.ru: Но я знаю, о чём вы думаете.

b1.en: You do not believe my story, and you do not plan to catch my enemy and punish him as he deserves.”
b1.ru: Вы не верите моей истории и не собираетесь ловить моего врага и наказывать его, как он того заслуживает».

b1.en: As I spoke, my eyes shone with anger, and the judge became afraid.
b1.ru: Пока я говорил, глаза мои горели гневом, и судья испугался.

b1.en: “You are wrong,” he said.
b1.ru: «Вы ошибаетесь», — сказал он.

b1.en: “I will try hard, and if I can catch the monster, I promise that he will be punished for his crimes.
b1.ru: «Я очень постараюсь, и если смогу поймать чудовище, обещаю, что он будет наказан за свои преступления.

b1.en: But from what you have told me about him, I am afraid it will be impossible.
b1.ru: Но, судя по тому, что вы мне о нём рассказали, боюсь, это будет невозможно.

b1.en: We will do everything we should, but you must be ready for disappointment.”
b1.ru: Мы сделаем всё, что положено, но вы должны быть готовы к разочарованию».

b1.en: “That cannot be, but there is no use in saying more.
b1.ru: «Этого не может быть, но говорить больше нет смысла.

b1.en: My revenge is not important to you.
b1.ru: Моя месть для вас не важна.

b1.en: I know that it is wrong, but it is the only strong feeling in my heart.
b1.ru: Я знаю, что это дурно, но это единственное сильное чувство в моём сердце.

b1.en: I am full of anger when I think that the murderer I made and let loose among people is still alive.
b1.ru: Я полон гнева, когда думаю, что убийца, которого я создал и выпустил к людям, всё ещё жив.

b1.en: You say no to my fair request, so I have only one choice: I will give my life, or my death, to destroying him.”
b1.ru: Вы отказываете мне в справедливой просьбе, поэтому у меня остаётся лишь один выход: я отдам жизнь или смерть тому, чтобы уничтожить его».

b1.en: I was shaking with emotion as I said this.
b1.ru: Я дрожал от волнения, говоря это.

b1.en: I was wild, and I think I had something of the proud fire of the old martyrs.
b1.ru: Я был вне себя, и, думаю, во мне было что-то от гордого огня древних мучеников.

b1.en: But the judge in Geneva was thinking about very different things, and to him I simply looked mad.
b1.ru: Но женевский судья думал совсем о другом, и ему я просто казался сумасшедшим.

b1.en: He tried to calm me down as a nurse calms a child, and he said my story came from an ill mind.
b1.ru: Он пытался успокоить меня, как няня успокаивает ребёнка, и сказал, что моя история — плод больного ума.

b1.en: “Man,” I cried, “you think you are wise, but you know nothing!
b1.ru: «Человек, — вскричал я, — ты думаешь, что мудр, но ничего не знаешь!

b1.en: Stop; you don’t understand what you are saying.”
b1.ru: Замолчи; ты не понимаешь, что говоришь».

b1.en: I left the house angry and upset and went away to think of another plan.
b1.ru: Я ушёл из дома, рассерженный и расстроенный, чтобы придумать другой план.

a2.en: We arrived at eight o’clock in the evening.
a2.ru: Мы приплыли в восемь часов вечера.

a2.en: We walked by the lake for a short time.
a2.ru: Мы немного погуляли у озера.

a2.en: Then we went to the hotel and looked at the water, the trees and the mountains.
a2.ru: Потом мы пошли в гостиницу и смотрели на воду, деревья и горы.

a2.en: It was dark, but we could still see them.
a2.ru: Было темно, но мы ещё видели их.

a2.en: Then a strong wind started to blow from the west.
a2.ru: Потом с запада подул сильный ветер.

a2.en: The moon was high in the sky.
a2.ru: Луна была высоко в небе.

a2.en: Clouds moved quickly across it and hid its light.
a2.ru: Облака быстро неслись по ней и закрывали её свет.

a2.en: The water in the lake was moving, and there were big waves.
a2.ru: Вода в озере волновалась, и поднимались большие волны.

a2.en: Suddenly it started to rain very hard.
a2.ru: Вдруг пошёл очень сильный дождь.

a2.en: I was calm in the day, but at night I felt very afraid.
a2.ru: Днём я был спокоен, но ночью мне стало очень страшно.

a2.en: I watched everything carefully.
a2.ru: Я внимательно следил за всем.

a2.en: I had a gun in my coat, and I held it in my right hand.
a2.ru: У меня под одеждой был пистолет, и я держал его в правой руке.

a2.en: Every sound frightened me.
a2.ru: Каждый звук пугал меня.

a2.en: But I was ready to fight until I or my enemy was dead.
a2.ru: Но я был готов сражаться, пока я или мой враг не умрёт.

a2.en: Elizabeth watched me quietly, and she was afraid too.
a2.ru: Элизабет молча смотрела на меня, и ей тоже было страшно.

a2.en: She was shaking.
a2.ru: Она дрожала.

a2.en: “What is wrong, Victor?” she asked. “What are you afraid of?”
a2.ru: «Что случилось, Виктор? — спросила она. — Чего ты боишься?»

a2.en: “Don’t worry, my love,” I said. “After tonight we will be safe. But this night is terrible.”
a2.ru: «Не волнуйся, любимая, — сказал я. — После этой ночи мы будем в безопасности. Но эта ночь ужасна».

a2.en: An hour passed.
a2.ru: Прошёл час.

a2.en: Then I thought, “It will be terrible for my wife to see the fight.”
a2.ru: Потом я подумал: «Жене будет страшно увидеть драку».

a2.en: So I asked her to go to bed.
a2.ru: Поэтому я попросил её лечь спать.

a2.en: I wanted to find my enemy first.
a2.ru: Я хотел сначала найти своего врага.

a2.en: She left, and I walked around the house.
a2.ru: Она ушла, а я ходил по дому.

a2.en: I looked in every corner, but I did not find him.
a2.ru: Я заглядывал в каждый угол, но не нашёл его.

a2.en: I started to think that maybe he was not coming.
a2.ru: Я начал думать, что, может быть, он не придёт.

a2.en: Then suddenly I heard a terrible scream.
a2.ru: И вдруг я услышал ужасный крик.

a2.en: It came from Elizabeth’s room.
a2.ru: Он донёсся из комнаты Элизабет.

a2.en: At once I understood everything.
a2.ru: Я сразу всё понял.

a2.en: For a moment I could not move.
a2.ru: На мгновение я не мог пошевелиться.

a2.en: I could feel the blood moving in my body.
a2.ru: Я чувствовал, как кровь движется по моему телу.

a2.en: Then I heard the scream again, and I ran into the room.
a2.ru: Потом я снова услышал крик и вбежал в комнату.

a2.en: Oh God! Why didn’t I die then?
a2.ru: О Боже! Почему я тогда не умер?

a2.en: Elizabeth was the best and kindest person in the world.
a2.ru: Элизабет была самым лучшим и добрым человеком на свете.

a2.en: She was lying across the bed, dead.
a2.ru: Она лежала поперёк кровати, мёртвая.

a2.en: Her head was hanging down, and her face was white.
a2.ru: Голова её свешивалась вниз, а лицо было белым.

a2.en: I still see her there every day.
a2.ru: Я до сих пор каждый день вижу её там.

a2.en: How could I see this and live?
a2.ru: Как я мог это увидеть и остаться жить?

a2.en: Life is strong, and it stays with us even when we hate it.
a2.ru: Жизнь сильна, и она остаётся с нами, даже когда мы её ненавидим.

a2.en: I fell to the floor.
a2.ru: Я упал на пол.

a2.en: When I opened my eyes, there were people from the hotel around me.
a2.ru: Когда я открыл глаза, вокруг меня стояли люди из гостиницы.

a2.en: They were very frightened, but my pain was much bigger than theirs.
a2.ru: Им было очень страшно, но моя боль была гораздо сильнее.

a2.en: I went back to Elizabeth’s room.
a2.ru: Я вернулся в комнату Элизабет.

a2.en: Someone had moved her.
a2.ru: Кто-то её переложил.

a2.en: Her head was on her arm, and there was a cloth over her face.
a2.ru: Её голова лежала на руке, а на лице был платок.

a2.en: She looked like she was sleeping.
a2.ru: Казалось, что она спит.

a2.en: I ran to her and held her.
a2.ru: Я подбежал к ней и обнял её.

a2.en: But she was cold, and I knew that she was gone.
a2.ru: Но она была холодной, и я понял, что её больше нет.

a2.en: She was not my Elizabeth any more.
a2.ru: Это уже была не моя Элизабет.

a2.en: There were marks of the monster’s hand on her neck.
a2.ru: На её шее были следы руки чудовища.

a2.en: She was not breathing.
a2.ru: Она не дышала.

a2.en: Then I looked up.
a2.ru: Потом я поднял глаза.

a2.en: The window was open, and the moon was shining into the room.
a2.ru: Окно было открыто, и в комнату светила луна.

a2.en: At the window I saw the monster!
a2.ru: В окне я увидел чудовище!

a2.en: He was smiling an evil smile and pointing at my dead wife.
a2.ru: Он злобно ухмылялся и показывал на мою мёртвую жену.

a2.en: I took out my gun and shot at him, but I missed.
a2.ru: Я выхватил пистолет и выстрелил в него, но промахнулся.

a2.en: He jumped down, ran very fast and jumped into the lake.
a2.ru: Он спрыгнул вниз, очень быстро побежал и прыгнул в озеро.

a2.en: Many people ran into the room when they heard the shot.
a2.ru: Услышав выстрел, в комнату вбежало много людей.

a2.en: I showed them where he went, and we looked for him in boats.
a2.ru: Я показал им, куда он ушёл, и мы искали его на лодках.

a2.en: After many hours we came back.
a2.ru: Через много часов мы вернулись.

a2.en: We did not find him.
a2.ru: Мы его не нашли.

a2.en: Most people thought that I only imagined him.
a2.ru: Большинство людей думали, что он мне просто привиделся.

a2.en: Then they looked for him in the woods and fields.
a2.ru: Потом они искали его в лесах и полях.

a2.en: I tried to go with them, but I felt ill.
a2.ru: Я пытался пойти с ними, но мне стало плохо.

a2.en: My head was going round, and I fell down.
a2.ru: Голова кружилась, и я упал.

a2.en: I was very hot and had a fever.
a2.ru: Мне было очень жарко, у меня был жар.

a2.en: They carried me back to a bed.
a2.ru: Меня отнесли обратно в постель.

a2.en: My eyes looked around the room, but I did not know what I was looking for.
a2.ru: Я оглядывал комнату, но не знал, что ищу.

a2.en: I did not really understand what happened.
a2.ru: Я толком не понимал, что случилось.

a2.en: Later I got up and went slowly to the room where Elizabeth was.
a2.ru: Позже я встал и медленно пошёл в комнату, где была Элизабет.

a2.en: Some women were crying there, and I cried with them.
a2.ru: Там плакали женщины, и я плакал вместе с ними.

a2.en: I could not think clearly.
a2.ru: Я не мог ясно думать.

a2.en: I was confused and afraid.
a2.ru: Я был растерян, и мне было страшно.

a2.en: William, Justine, Clerval and now my wife were all dead.
a2.ru: Уильям, Жюстина, Клерваль, а теперь и моя жена — все были мертвы.

a2.en: And my father and Ernest were alone.
a2.ru: А мой отец и Эрнест были одни.

a2.en: Maybe the monster was killing them now!
a2.ru: Может быть, чудовище убивало их прямо сейчас!

a2.en: I jumped up and decided to go home to Geneva quickly.
a2.ru: Я вскочил и решил поскорее ехать домой, в Женеву.

a2.en: There were no horses, so we went by boat.
a2.ru: Лошадей не было, поэтому мы поплыли на лодке.

a2.en: The wind was bad, and it was raining hard.
a2.ru: Ветер был плохой, и шёл сильный дождь.

a2.en: It was early in the morning, and I hoped to be home by night.
a2.ru: Было раннее утро, и я надеялся быть дома к ночи.

a2.en: I paid some men to row the boat, and I helped them.
a2.ru: Я заплатил людям, чтобы они гребли, и помогал им.

a2.en: But I was too sad and too weak.
a2.ru: Но я был слишком печален и слаб.

a2.en: I stopped and put my head in my hands.
a2.ru: Я остановился и уронил голову на руки.

a2.en: I saw places that I knew.
a2.ru: Я видел знакомые места.

a2.en: Only yesterday I was here with Elizabeth, and now she was dead.
a2.ru: Только вчера я был здесь с Элизабет, а теперь она была мертва.

a2.en: I cried.
a2.ru: Я плакал.

a2.en: When the rain stopped, I saw the fish in the water.
a2.ru: Когда дождь прекратился, я увидел рыб в воде.

a2.en: Elizabeth watched them only a few hours before.
a2.ru: Элизабет смотрела на них всего несколько часов назад.

a2.en: Now everything was different.
a2.ru: Теперь всё было по-другому.

a2.en: A big, sudden change is the most painful thing for people.
a2.ru: Большая внезапная перемена — самое тяжёлое для человека.

a2.en: Nothing looked the same to me now.
a2.ru: Теперь всё казалось мне другим.

a2.en: The monster took away all my hope.
a2.ru: Чудовище отняло у меня всю надежду.

a2.en: Nobody was ever as unhappy as I was.
a2.ru: Никто никогда не был так несчастен, как я.

a2.en: But I will not tell you everything that happened next.
a2.ru: Но я не буду рассказывать вам всё, что случилось дальше.

a2.en: My story is full of terrible things, and the rest will be boring for you.
a2.ru: Моя история полна ужасов, а остальное будет вам скучно.

a2.en: I lost my friends one by one, and I was alone.
a2.ru: Я терял друзей одного за другим и остался один.

a2.en: I am very tired now, so I will tell you the end quickly.
a2.ru: Я очень устал, поэтому быстро расскажу вам конец.

a2.en: I arrived in Geneva.
a2.ru: Я приехал в Женеву.

a2.en: My father and Ernest were alive, but the news was too much for my father.
a2.ru: Отец и Эрнест были живы, но эта новость оказалась слишком тяжёлой для отца.

a2.en: He loved Elizabeth like a daughter.
a2.ru: Он любил Элизабет как дочь.

a2.en: He was old, and she was his great joy.
a2.ru: Он был стар, а она была его большой радостью.

a2.en: His eyes looked at nothing.
a2.ru: Его глаза ни на что не смотрели.

a2.en: I hate the monster who brought him so much pain!
a2.ru: Я ненавижу чудовище, которое причинило ему столько боли!

a2.en: My father could not get out of bed, and a few days later he died in my arms.
a2.ru: Отец не мог встать с постели и через несколько дней умер у меня на руках.

a2.en: What happened to me after that?
a2.ru: Что случилось со мной после этого?

a2.en: I don’t know.
a2.ru: Я не знаю.

a2.en: I only remember chains and darkness.
a2.ru: Я помню только цепи и темноту.

a2.en: Sometimes I dreamed about beautiful fields and my old friends, but then I woke up in a prison.
a2.ru: Иногда мне снились красивые поля и старые друзья, но потом я просыпался в тюрьме.

a2.en: People thought I was mad, and I was in a small room alone for many months.
a2.ru: Люди думали, что я сошёл с ума, и много месяцев я провёл один в маленькой комнате.

a2.en: Slowly I got better, and they let me go.
a2.ru: Постепенно мне стало лучше, и меня отпустили.

a2.en: But now I wanted only one thing: revenge.
a2.ru: Но теперь я хотел только одного — мести.

a2.en: I thought about the monster that I made.
a2.ru: Я думал о чудовище, которое я создал.

a2.en: He was the cause of all my pain.
a2.ru: Оно было причиной всех моих страданий.

a2.en: I was very angry, and I wanted to catch him and punish him.
a2.ru: Я был в ярости и хотел поймать его и наказать.

a2.en: About a month after I left the prison, I went to a judge in the town.
a2.ru: Примерно через месяц после того, как я вышел из тюрьмы, я пошёл к судье в городе.

a2.en: I told him, “I know who killed my family.
a2.ru: Я сказал ему: «Я знаю, кто убил мою семью.

a2.en: Please help me to catch the murderer.”
a2.ru: Пожалуйста, помогите мне поймать убийцу».

a2.en: “You must use all your power,” I said.
a2.ru: «Вы должны употребить всю свою власть», — сказал я.

a2.en: The judge listened kindly.
a2.ru: Судья доброжелательно выслушал меня.

a2.en: “I will do everything to find him,” he said.
a2.ru: «Я сделаю всё, чтобы найти его», — сказал он.

a2.en: “Thank you,” I said. “Please listen to my story.
a2.ru: «Спасибо, — сказал я. — Пожалуйста, выслушайте мою историю.

a2.en: It is very strange, but it is true.
a2.ru: Она очень странная, но это правда.

a2.en: I am not lying.”
a2.ru: Я не лгу».

a2.en: I spoke calmly.
a2.ru: Я говорил спокойно.

a2.en: I wanted to follow my enemy until he was dead, and this plan helped me to live.
a2.ru: Я хотел преследовать своего врага до его смерти, и этот план помогал мне жить.

a2.en: I told my story clearly, with all the dates.
a2.ru: Я рассказал свою историю ясно, со всеми датами.

a2.en: At first the judge did not believe me, but then he became interested.
a2.ru: Сначала судья мне не верил, но потом ему стало интересно.

a2.en: Sometimes he looked afraid, and sometimes he looked surprised.
a2.ru: Иногда он выглядел испуганным, а иногда удивлённым.

a2.en: I never shouted.
a2.ru: Я ни разу не закричал.

a2.en: At the end I said, “This is the creature who did it.
a2.ru: В конце я сказал: «Вот существо, которое это сделало.

a2.en: You are a judge, so please catch him and punish him.”
a2.ru: Вы судья, поэтому, пожалуйста, поймайте и накажите его».

a2.en: The judge’s face changed.
a2.ru: Лицо судьи изменилось.

a2.en: He listened to my story like a ghost story, but now he did not believe it.
a2.ru: Он слушал мою историю как сказку о привидениях, но теперь он ей не верил.

a2.en: He answered kindly, “I want to help you, but this creature is too strong.
a2.ru: Он мягко ответил: «Я хочу вам помочь, но это существо слишком сильное.

a2.en: He can walk across ice and live in caves in the mountains.
a2.ru: Он может ходить по льду и жить в горных пещерах.

a2.en: Who can follow him?
a2.ru: Кто может его преследовать?

a2.en: And it is many months later now.
a2.ru: И с тех пор прошло много месяцев.

a2.en: Nobody knows where he is.”
a2.ru: Никто не знает, где он».

a2.en: “I am sure he is near me,” I said.
a2.ru: «Я уверен, что он рядом со мной», — сказал я.

a2.en: “If he is in the mountains, we can hunt him like an animal.
a2.ru: «Если он в горах, мы можем охотиться на него, как на зверя.

a2.en: But I know you don’t believe me.
a2.ru: Но я знаю, что вы мне не верите.

a2.en: You are not going to catch him.”
a2.ru: Вы не собираетесь его ловить».

a2.en: My eyes were full of anger, and the judge was afraid.
a2.ru: Мои глаза были полны гнева, и судья испугался.

a2.en: “No, you are wrong,” he said.
a2.ru: «Нет, вы ошибаетесь», — сказал он.

a2.en: “I will try, and if I catch him, he will be punished.
a2.ru: «Я постараюсь, и если я его поймаю, он будет наказан.

a2.en: But I think it will be impossible.
a2.ru: Но я думаю, что это будет невозможно.

a2.en: Please don’t hope for too much.”
a2.ru: Пожалуйста, не надейтесь на многое».

a2.en: “You are wrong,” I said. “But talking will not help.
a2.ru: «Вы не правы, — сказал я. — Но разговоры не помогут.

a2.en: My revenge is not important to you, but it is everything to me.
a2.ru: Моя месть для вас не важна, но для меня она — всё.

a2.en: I know that it is wrong, but I cannot stop.
a2.ru: Я знаю, что это дурно, но не могу остановиться.

a2.en: The murderer is still alive, and I made him!
a2.ru: Убийца всё ещё жив, и это я его создал!

a2.en: You will not help me, so I will do it alone.
a2.ru: Вы мне не поможете, поэтому я сделаю это сам.

a2.en: I will give my life to killing him.”
a2.ru: Я отдам свою жизнь, чтобы убить его».

a2.en: I was shaking as I said this.
a2.ru: Я дрожал, говоря это.

a2.en: I was wild and proud.
a2.ru: Я был вне себя и полон гордости.

a2.en: But to the judge I looked mad.
a2.ru: Но судье я казался сумасшедшим.

a2.en: He was not interested in heroes.
a2.ru: Героизм его не интересовал.

a2.en: He tried to calm me like a child.
a2.ru: Он пытался успокоить меня, как ребёнка.

a2.en: He thought my story came from an ill mind.
a2.ru: Он думал, что моя история — плод больного ума.

a2.en: “You think you are clever, but you know nothing!” I cried.
a2.ru: «Вы думаете, что умны, но ничего не знаете!» — закричал я.

a2.en: “Stop! You don’t understand anything.”
a2.ru: «Замолчите! Вы ничего не понимаете».

a2.en: I left the house angrily.
a2.ru: Я сердито ушёл из дома.

a2.en: I went away to make a new plan.
a2.ru: Я ушёл, чтобы придумать новый план.

sub: Victor swears revenge at his family's grave and pursues the creature across Europe, Russia and the frozen sea until Walton's ship rescues him, begging Walton to finish his task

o:
My present situation was one in which all voluntary thought was swallowed up and lost. I was hurried away by fury; revenge alone endowed me with strength and composure; it moulded my feelings and allowed me to be calculating and calm at periods when otherwise delirium or death would have been my portion.

My first resolution was to quit Geneva for ever; my country, which, when I was happy and beloved, was dear to me, now, in my adversity, became hateful. I provided myself with a sum of money, together with a few jewels which had belonged to my mother, and departed.

And now my wanderings began which are to cease but with life. I have traversed a vast portion of the earth and have endured all the hardships which travellers in deserts and barbarous countries are wont to meet. How I have lived I hardly know; many times have I stretched my failing limbs upon the sandy plain and prayed for death. But revenge kept me alive; I dared not die and leave my adversary in being.

When I quitted Geneva my first labour was to gain some clue by which I might trace the steps of my fiendish enemy. But my plan was unsettled, and I wandered many hours round the confines of the town, uncertain what path I should pursue. As night approached I found myself at the entrance of the cemetery where William, Elizabeth, and my father reposed. I entered it and approached the tomb which marked their graves. Everything was silent except the leaves of the trees, which were gently agitated by the wind; the night was nearly dark, and the scene would have been solemn and affecting even to an uninterested observer. The spirits of the departed seemed to flit around and to cast a shadow, which was felt but not seen, around the head of the mourner.

The deep grief which this scene had at first excited quickly gave way to rage and despair. They were dead, and I lived; their murderer also lived, and to destroy him I must drag out my weary existence. I knelt on the grass and kissed the earth and with quivering lips exclaimed, “By the sacred earth on which I kneel, by the shades that wander near me, by the deep and eternal grief that I feel, I swear; and by thee, O Night, and the spirits that preside over thee, to pursue the dæmon who caused this misery, until he or I shall perish in mortal conflict.

For this purpose I will preserve my life; to execute this dear revenge will I again behold the sun and tread the green herbage of earth, which otherwise should vanish from my eyes for ever. And I call on you, spirits of the dead, and on you, wandering ministers of vengeance, to aid and conduct me in my work. Let the cursed and hellish monster drink deep of agony; let him feel the despair that now torments me.”

I had begun my adjuration with solemnity and an awe which almost assured me that the shades of my murdered friends heard and approved my devotion, but the furies possessed me as I concluded, and rage choked my utterance.

I was answered through the stillness of night by a loud and fiendish laugh. It rang on my ears long and heavily; the mountains re-echoed it, and I felt as if all hell surrounded me with mockery and laughter. Surely in that moment I should have been possessed by frenzy and have destroyed my miserable existence but that my vow was heard and that I was reserved for vengeance. The laughter died away, when a well-known and abhorred voice, apparently close to my ear, addressed me in an audible whisper, “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have determined to live, and I am satisfied.”

I darted towards the spot from which the sound proceeded, but the devil eluded my grasp. Suddenly the broad disk of the moon arose and shone full upon his ghastly and distorted shape as he fled with more than mortal speed.

I pursued him, and for many months this has been my task. Guided by a slight clue, I followed the windings of the Rhone, but vainly. The blue Mediterranean appeared, and by a strange chance, I saw the fiend enter by night and hide himself in a vessel bound for the Black Sea. I took my passage in the same ship, but he escaped, I know not how.

Amidst the wilds of Tartary and Russia, although he still evaded me, I have ever followed in his track. Sometimes the peasants, scared by this horrid apparition, informed me of his path; sometimes he himself, who feared that if I lost all trace of him I should despair and die, left some mark to guide me. The snows descended on my head, and I saw the print of his huge step on the white plain. To you first entering on life, to whom care is new and agony unknown, how can you understand what I have felt and still feel?

Cold, want, and fatigue were the least pains which I was destined to endure; I was cursed by some devil and carried about with me my eternal hell; yet still a spirit of good followed and directed my steps and when I most murmured would suddenly extricate me from seemingly insurmountable difficulties. Sometimes, when nature, overcome by hunger, sank under the exhaustion, a repast was prepared for me in the desert that restored and inspirited me. The fare was, indeed, coarse, such as the peasants of the country ate, but I will not doubt that it was set there by the spirits that I had invoked to aid me. Often, when all was dry, the heavens cloudless, and I was parched by thirst, a slight cloud would bedim the sky, shed the few drops that revived me, and vanish.

I followed, when I could, the courses of the rivers; but the dæmon generally avoided these, as it was here that the population of the country chiefly collected. In other places human beings were seldom seen, and I generally subsisted on the wild animals that crossed my path. I had money with me and gained the friendship of the villagers by distributing it; or I brought with me some food that I had killed, which, after taking a small part, I always presented to those who had provided me with fire and utensils for cooking.

My life, as it passed thus, was indeed hateful to me, and it was during sleep alone that I could taste joy. O blessed sleep! Often, when most miserable, I sank to repose, and my dreams lulled me even to rapture. The spirits that guarded me had provided these moments, or rather hours, of happiness that I might retain strength to fulfil my pilgrimage. Deprived of this respite, I should have sunk under my hardships. During the day I was sustained and inspirited by the hope of night, for in sleep I saw my friends, my wife, and my beloved country; again I saw the benevolent countenance of my father, heard the silver tones of my Elizabeth’s voice, and beheld Clerval enjoying health and youth.

Often, when wearied by a toilsome march, I persuaded myself that I was dreaming until night should come and that I should then enjoy reality in the arms of my dearest friends. What agonising fondness did I feel for them! How did I cling to their dear forms, as sometimes they haunted even my waking hours, and persuade myself that they still lived! At such moments vengeance, that burned within me, died in my heart, and I pursued my path towards the destruction of the dæmon more as a task enjoined by heaven, as the mechanical impulse of some power of which I was unconscious, than as the ardent desire of my soul.

What his feelings were whom I pursued I cannot know. Sometimes, indeed, he left marks in writing on the barks of the trees or cut in stone that guided me and instigated my fury. “My reign is not yet over”—these words were legible in one of these inscriptions—“you live, and my power is complete. Follow me; I seek the everlasting ices of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, to which I am impassive. You will find near this place, if you follow not too tardily, a dead hare; eat and be refreshed. Come on, my enemy; we have yet to wrestle for our lives, but many hard and miserable hours must you endure until that period shall arrive.”

Scoffing devil! Again do I vow vengeance; again do I devote thee, miserable fiend, to torture and death. Never will I give up my search until he or I perish; and then with what ecstasy shall I join my Elizabeth and my departed friends, who even now prepare for me the reward of my tedious toil and horrible pilgrimage!

As I still pursued my journey to the northward, the snows thickened and the cold increased in a degree almost too severe to support. The peasants were shut up in their hovels, and only a few of the most hardy ventured forth to seize the animals whom starvation had forced from their hiding-places to seek for prey. The rivers were covered with ice, and no fish could be procured; and thus I was cut off from my chief article of maintenance.

The triumph of my enemy increased with the difficulty of my labours. One inscription that he left was in these words: “Prepare! Your toils only begin; wrap yourself in furs and provide food, for we shall soon enter upon a journey where your sufferings will satisfy my everlasting hatred.”

My courage and perseverance were invigorated by these scoffing words; I resolved not to fail in my purpose, and calling on Heaven to support me, I continued with unabated fervour to traverse immense deserts, until the ocean appeared at a distance and formed the utmost boundary of the horizon. Oh! How unlike it was to the blue seasons of the south! Covered with ice, it was only to be distinguished from land by its superior wildness and ruggedness. The Greeks wept for joy when they beheld the Mediterranean from the hills of Asia, and hailed with rapture the boundary of their toils. I did not weep, but I knelt down and with a full heart thanked my guiding spirit for conducting me in safety to the place where I hoped, notwithstanding my adversary’s gibe, to meet and grapple with him.

Some weeks before this period I had procured a sledge and dogs and thus traversed the snows with inconceivable speed. I know not whether the fiend possessed the same advantages, but I found that, as before I had daily lost ground in the pursuit, I now gained on him, so much so that when I first saw the ocean he was but one day’s journey in advance, and I hoped to intercept him before he should reach the beach. With new courage, therefore, I pressed on, and in two days arrived at a wretched hamlet on the seashore.

I inquired of the inhabitants concerning the fiend and gained accurate information. A gigantic monster, they said, had arrived the night before, armed with a gun and many pistols, putting to flight the inhabitants of a solitary cottage through fear of his terrific appearance. He had carried off their store of winter food, and placing it in a sledge, to draw which he had seized on a numerous drove of trained dogs, he had harnessed them, and the same night, to the joy of the horror-struck villagers, had pursued his journey across the sea in a direction that led to no land; and they conjectured that he must speedily be destroyed by the breaking of the ice or frozen by the eternal frosts.

On hearing this information I suffered a temporary access of despair. He had escaped me, and I must commence a destructive and almost endless journey across the mountainous ices of the ocean, amidst cold that few of the inhabitants could long endure and which I, the native of a genial and sunny climate, could not hope to survive. Yet at the idea that the fiend should live and be triumphant, my rage and vengeance returned, and like a mighty tide, overwhelmed every other feeling. After a slight repose, during which the spirits of the dead hovered round and instigated me to toil and revenge, I prepared for my journey.

I exchanged my land-sledge for one fashioned for the inequalities of the Frozen Ocean, and purchasing a plentiful stock of provisions, I departed from land.

I cannot guess how many days have passed since then, but I have endured misery which nothing but the eternal sentiment of a just retribution burning within my heart could have enabled me to support. Immense and rugged mountains of ice often barred up my passage, and I often heard the thunder of the ground sea, which threatened my destruction. But again the frost came and made the paths of the sea secure.

By the quantity of provision which I had consumed, I should guess that I had passed three weeks in this journey; and the continual protraction of hope, returning back upon the heart, often wrung bitter drops of despondency and grief from my eyes. Despair had indeed almost secured her prey, and I should soon have sunk beneath this misery.

Once, after the poor animals that conveyed me had with incredible toil gained the summit of a sloping ice mountain, and one, sinking under his fatigue, died, I viewed the expanse before me with anguish, when suddenly my eye caught a dark speck upon the dusky plain. I strained my sight to discover what it could be and uttered a wild cry of ecstasy when I distinguished a sledge and the distorted proportions of a well-known form within. Oh! With what a burning gush did hope revisit my heart! Warm tears filled my eyes, which I hastily wiped away, that they might not intercept the view I had of the dæmon; but still my sight was dimmed by the burning drops, until, giving way to the emotions that oppressed me, I wept aloud.

But this was not the time for delay; I disencumbered the dogs of their dead companion, gave them a plentiful portion of food, and after an hour’s rest, which was absolutely necessary, and yet which was bitterly irksome to me, I continued my route. The sledge was still visible, nor did I again lose sight of it except at the moments when for a short time some ice-rock concealed it with its intervening crags. I indeed perceptibly gained on it, and when, after nearly two days’ journey, I beheld my enemy at no more than a mile distant, my heart bounded within me.

But now, when I appeared almost within grasp of my foe, my hopes were suddenly extinguished, and I lost all trace of him more utterly than I had ever done before. A ground sea was heard; the thunder of its progress, as the waters rolled and swelled beneath me, became every moment more ominous and terrific. I pressed on, but in vain. The wind arose; the sea roared; and, as with the mighty shock of an earthquake, it split and cracked with a tremendous and overwhelming sound. The work was soon finished; in a few minutes a tumultuous sea rolled between me and my enemy, and I was left drifting on a scattered piece of ice that was continually lessening and thus preparing for me a hideous death.

In this manner many appalling hours passed; several of my dogs died, and I myself was about to sink under the accumulation of distress when I saw your vessel riding at anchor and holding forth to me hopes of succour and life. I had no conception that vessels ever came so far north and was astounded at the sight. I quickly destroyed part of my sledge to construct oars, and by these means was enabled, with infinite fatigue, to move my ice raft in the direction of your ship.

I had determined, if you were going southwards, still to trust myself to the mercy of the seas rather than abandon my purpose. I hoped to induce you to grant me a boat with which I could pursue my enemy. But your direction was northwards. You took me on board when my vigour was exhausted, and I should soon have sunk under my multiplied hardships into a death which I still dread, for my task is unfulfilled.

Oh! When will my guiding spirit, in conducting me to the dæmon, allow me the rest I so much desire; or must I die, and he yet live? If I do, swear to me, Walton, that he shall not escape, that you will seek him and satisfy my vengeance in his death. And do I dare to ask of you to undertake my pilgrimage, to endure the hardships that I have undergone? No; I am not so selfish.

Yet, when I am dead, if he should appear, if the ministers of vengeance should conduct him to you, swear that he shall not live—swear that he shall not triumph over my accumulated woes and survive to add to the list of his dark crimes. He is eloquent and persuasive, and once his words had even power over my heart; but trust him not. His soul is as hellish as his form, full of treachery and fiend-like malice. Hear him not; call on the names of William, Justine, Clerval, Elizabeth, my father, and of the wretched Victor, and thrust your sword into his heart. I will hover near and direct the steel aright.

The snow fell on my head, and I saw the prints of his huge feet on the white plain. You are only just starting out in life, and worry is new to you and agony unknown, so how can you understand what I have felt and still feel?

Cold, hunger and exhaustion were the least of the pains I was destined to suffer; I was cursed by some devil and carried my own eternal hell around with me; yet a good spirit still followed and guided my steps, and whenever I complained most bitterly, it would suddenly rescue me from difficulties that seemed impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when my body gave way under hunger and exhaustion, a meal was laid out for me in the wilderness that restored my strength and lifted my spirits. The food was plain, it is true, the kind the local peasants ate, but I will not doubt that it was left there by the spirits I had called on to help me. Often, when everything was dry, the sky was cloudless and I was parched with thirst, a small cloud would darken the sky, shed the few drops that revived me, and vanish.

When I could, I followed the courses of the rivers; but the demon usually avoided them, because that was where most of the country’s people lived. Elsewhere people were rarely seen, and I mostly lived on the wild animals that crossed my path. I had money with me and won the friendship of the villagers by handing it out; or I brought along some game I had killed and, after taking a small share, always gave the rest to those who had lent me fire and pots for cooking.

Living like this, I truly hated my life, and only in sleep could I taste any joy. O blessed sleep! Often, at my most miserable, I sank into rest, and my dreams soothed me until I was almost in raptures. The spirits that watched over me had given me these moments, or rather hours, of happiness so that I would keep the strength to complete my pilgrimage. Without this relief, I would have collapsed under my hardships. During the day I was kept going and cheered by the hope of night, for in my sleep I saw my friends, my wife and my beloved country; I saw my father’s kind face again, heard the silvery tones of my Elizabeth’s voice, and saw Clerval full of health and youth.

Often, worn out by a gruelling march, I convinced myself that I was dreaming until night came, and that then I would enjoy reality in the arms of my dearest friends. What painful tenderness I felt for them! How I clung to their dear figures when they sometimes haunted even my waking hours, and how I convinced myself that they were still alive! At such moments the vengeance burning inside me died in my heart, and I pursued my path towards the demon’s destruction more as a duty imposed by heaven, as the mechanical impulse of some power I was not aware of, than as the passionate desire of my soul.

I cannot know what the one I was hunting felt. Sometimes, in fact, he left written messages on the bark of trees or carved in stone that guided me and fuelled my fury. “My reign is not over yet”—these words could be read in one of these inscriptions—“you live, and my power is complete. Follow me; I am heading for the everlasting ice of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, which cannot touch me. If you do not follow too slowly, you will find a dead hare near this place; eat it and regain your strength. Come on, my enemy; we still have to wrestle for our lives, but you must endure many hard and miserable hours before that time comes.”

Mocking devil! Once again I vow vengeance; once again I condemn you, miserable fiend, to torture and death. I will never give up my search until he or I die; and then with what joy I will join my Elizabeth and my departed friends, who are even now preparing my reward for my long, weary labour and my terrible pilgrimage!

As I continued my journey northwards, the snow grew deeper and the cold became almost too severe to bear. The peasants stayed shut up in their huts, and only a few of the toughest dared to go out to catch the animals that starvation had driven from their hiding places in search of prey. The rivers were frozen over, and no fish could be caught; so I was cut off from my main source of food. My enemy’s triumph grew as my struggles became harder. One inscription he left read: “Prepare! Your hardships are only beginning; wrap yourself in furs and get food, for we will soon set out on a journey where your sufferings will satisfy my everlasting hatred.”

These mocking words strengthened my courage and determination; I resolved not to fail in my purpose and, calling on Heaven to support me, I went on with undiminished passion across immense wastelands, until the ocean appeared in the distance and formed the farthest edge of the horizon. Oh! How different it was from the blue seas of the south! Covered with ice, it could only be told apart from the land by its greater wildness and roughness. The Greeks wept for joy when they saw the Mediterranean from the hills of Asia, and greeted the end of their hardships with rapture. I did not weep, but I knelt down and, with a full heart, thanked my guiding spirit for leading me safely to the place where, despite my enemy’s taunt, I hoped to meet him and grapple with him.

A few weeks earlier I had obtained a sledge and dogs, and so I crossed the snow at astonishing speed. I do not know whether the fiend had the same advantages, but I found that, whereas before I had lost ground every day, I was now catching up with him, so much so that when I first saw the ocean he was only one day’s journey ahead, and I hoped to cut him off before he reached the shore. With fresh courage, therefore, I pushed on, and two days later I reached a miserable little village on the coast.

I asked the inhabitants about the fiend and received accurate information. A gigantic monster, they said, had arrived the night before, armed with a gun and several pistols, and had put to flight the people of a lonely cottage, who were terrified by his dreadful appearance. He had carried off their winter supply of food, put it on a sledge, seized a large team of trained dogs to pull it and harnessed them, and that same night, to the joy of the horror-struck villagers, he had set off across the sea in a direction that led to no land; they guessed that he would soon be killed when the ice broke up, or frozen to death by the eternal frosts.

When I heard this news, I was seized by a brief fit of despair. He had escaped me, and I now had to begin a deadly and almost endless journey across the mountainous ice of the ocean, in cold that few of the local people could bear for long and which I, born in a mild and sunny climate, could not hope to survive. Yet at the thought that the fiend might live and triumph, my rage and desire for vengeance came back and, like a mighty tide, swept away every other feeling. After a short rest, during which the spirits of the dead hovered around me and urged me on to toil and revenge, I got ready for my journey. I exchanged my land sledge for one built for the uneven surface of the Frozen Ocean, bought a generous stock of provisions and left the land behind.

I cannot guess how many days have passed since then, but I have endured misery that I could never have borne without the eternal sense of just retribution burning in my heart. Huge, jagged mountains of ice often blocked my way, and I often heard the thunder of the swell beneath the ice, which threatened to destroy me. But then the frost returned and made the paths across the sea safe again.

Judging by the amount of food I had eaten, I would guess that I had spent three weeks on this journey; and hope, constantly put off and then returning to my heart, often wrung bitter tears of gloom and grief from my eyes. Despair had almost claimed its prey, and I would soon have collapsed under this misery.

Once, after the poor animals pulling me had struggled with incredible effort to the top of a sloping ice mountain, and one of them had collapsed from exhaustion and died, I was gazing in anguish at the vast expanse in front of me, when suddenly I caught sight of a dark speck on the dim plain. I strained my eyes to make out what it could be, and let out a wild cry of joy when I recognised a sledge with the twisted outline of a familiar figure inside it. Oh! With what a burning rush hope returned to my heart! Warm tears filled my eyes, and I quickly wiped them away so that they would not block my view of the demon; but my sight was still blurred by the burning drops until, overcome by my emotions, I wept aloud.

But there was no time to lose; I freed the dogs from their dead companion, gave them a generous portion of food and, after an hour’s rest, which was absolutely necessary but bitterly frustrating for me, I continued on my way. The sledge was still visible, and I never lost sight of it again, except when some ice-rock briefly hid it behind its jagged peaks. I was clearly gaining on it, and when, after almost two days’ travel, I saw my enemy no more than a mile away, my heart leapt within me.

But now, when my foe seemed almost within my reach, my hopes were suddenly crushed, and I lost all trace of him more completely than ever before. I heard the swell of the sea beneath the ice; its thunder, as the waters rolled and heaved beneath me, grew more menacing and terrifying every moment. I pushed on, but in vain. The wind rose; the sea roared; and, as if struck by the mighty shock of an earthquake, the ice split and cracked with a tremendous, overwhelming noise. It was over quickly; within a few minutes a raging sea lay between me and my enemy, and I was left drifting on a broken piece of ice that kept getting smaller, preparing a hideous death for me.

Many dreadful hours passed like this; several of my dogs died, and I myself was about to give in under the weight of my suffering when I saw your ship lying at anchor, offering me hope of rescue and life. I had no idea that ships ever came so far north and was astonished at the sight. I quickly broke up part of my sledge to make oars, and in this way, with endless effort, I managed to move my ice raft towards your ship.

I had made up my mind that if you were sailing south, I would still trust myself to the mercy of the sea rather than give up my purpose. I hoped to persuade you to give me a boat in which I could chase my enemy. But you were heading north. You took me on board when my strength was exhausted, and I would soon have sunk under my many hardships into a death that I still dread, because my task is not yet done.

Oh! When will my guiding spirit lead me to the demon and grant me the rest I long for so much; or must I die while he lives on? If I do, swear to me, Walton, that he will not escape, that you will hunt him down and satisfy my vengeance with his death. But do I dare to ask you to take on my pilgrimage and endure the hardships I have gone through? No; I am not so selfish.

Yet when I am dead, if he should appear, if the agents of vengeance should bring him to you, swear that he will not live—swear that he will not triumph over my piled-up sorrows and survive to add to the list of his dark crimes. He is eloquent and persuasive, and once his words even had power over my heart; but do not trust him. His soul is as hellish as his body, full of treachery and devilish malice. Do not listen to him; call on the names of William, Justine, Clerval, Elizabeth, my father and the wretched Victor, and drive your sword into his heart. I will hover nearby and guide the blade straight.
b1: At that time I could not think clearly at all. I was carried along by anger, and only revenge gave me strength and calm. It controlled my feelings and helped me to stay cool and careful at times when I might otherwise have gone mad or died. First I decided to leave Geneva for ever. I had loved my country when I was happy, but now, in my misery, I hated it. I took some money and a few jewels that had belonged to my mother, and I left.

So my travels began, and they will only end when I die. I have crossed a large part of the world and suffered all the difficulties that travellers meet in deserts and wild countries. I hardly know how I have stayed alive. Many times I have lain down on the sand, too weak to go on, and prayed for death. But revenge kept me alive; I could not die and leave my enemy living.

When I left Geneva, I first needed to find some sign of where my terrible enemy had gone. But I had no clear plan, and for many hours I walked around the edges of the town, not knowing which way to go. When night came, I found myself at the gate of the cemetery where William, Elizabeth and my father were buried. I went in and walked up to their grave. Everything was quiet except for the leaves moving softly in the wind. It was nearly dark, and even a stranger would have found the place serious and sad. The spirits of the dead seemed to move around me and to put a shadow over my head that I could feel but not see.

At first I felt deep sadness, but it quickly turned into anger and despair. They were dead, and I was alive. Their murderer was alive too, and I had to go on living my tired life so that I could destroy him. I knelt on the grass, kissed the ground and cried out with shaking lips, “By the holy earth where I kneel, by the ghosts near me, by my deep and endless sadness, I swear. And by you, Night, and the spirits of the night, I swear to hunt the demon who caused this pain, until he or I die in a fight to the death.

For this reason I will stay alive. To take my revenge, I will see the sun again and walk on the green grass, which I would otherwise leave for ever. I call on you, spirits of the dead, and on all the spirits of revenge, to help me and lead me in my work. Let the evil monster feel terrible pain; let him feel the despair that I feel now.”

I began my promise seriously and with great respect, and I almost believed that the ghosts of my murdered friends could hear me and agreed with me. But by the end I was wild with anger, and I could hardly speak. In the silence of the night, a loud, evil laugh answered me. It went on ringing in my ears for a long time, and the mountains sent it back as an echo. I felt as if all of hell was laughing at me. At that moment I would surely have gone mad and killed myself, but my promise had been heard, and I had to live for revenge. The laughter stopped, and then a voice that I knew and hated whispered clearly, very close to my ear, “I am happy, you miserable man! You have decided to live, and I am happy.”

I ran towards the place where the voice had come from, but the devil got away from me. Suddenly the big round moon came up and lit his ugly, twisted body as he ran away, faster than any man. I followed him, and for many months that has been my job. I followed a small clue along the river Rhône, but it was no use. I came to the blue Mediterranean Sea, and by a strange chance I saw the monster get onto a ship going to the Black Sea at night and hide there. I got on the same ship, but somehow he escaped.

He was still getting away from me, but I followed him through the wild lands of Tartary and Russia. Sometimes the frightened peasants told me which way the horrible creature had gone. Sometimes he himself left a sign for me, because he was afraid that if I lost him completely, I would give up and die. Snow fell on my head, and I saw his huge footprints on the white ground. You are young, and you have not known worry or great pain, so how can you understand what I have felt and still feel?

Cold, hunger and tiredness were the smallest of my pains. Some devil had cursed me, and I carried my own hell with me everywhere. But a good spirit also followed me and guided me, and when I complained the most, it suddenly saved me from problems that seemed impossible. Sometimes, when I was so hungry and tired that I fell down, I found a meal waiting for me in the wild, and it gave me new strength. It was simple food, like the peasants ate, but I believe that the spirits I had called on had left it there. Often, when everything was dry and I was terribly thirsty, a small cloud came into the clear sky, dropped a little rain to help me, and disappeared.

When I could, I travelled along the rivers, but the demon usually stayed away from them, because most people lived there. In other places there were very few people, and I usually lived on the wild animals I found on my way. I had money, and I made friends with the villagers by giving it to them. Or I brought them animals I had killed, and after I took a small part, I always gave the rest to the people who had let me use their fire and pots.

I hated living like this, and I could only feel joy when I was asleep. Oh, wonderful sleep! Often, when I was most unhappy, I fell asleep, and my dreams made me almost wildly happy. The spirits that protected me gave me these moments, or really hours, of happiness, so that I would stay strong enough to finish my long journey. Without this rest, I would have died from my hardships. During the day, the hope of night kept me going, because in my dreams I saw my friends, my wife and my dear country. I saw my father’s kind face again, heard the sweet sound of Elizabeth’s voice, and saw Clerval young and healthy.

Often, when I was tired from a long, hard walk, I told myself that I was dreaming until night came, and that then I would live in reality with my dearest friends. I loved them so much that it hurt! Sometimes I saw them even when I was awake, and I held on to them and told myself that they were still alive. At these moments my burning need for revenge died in my heart. Then I followed the demon to destroy him more as a job that heaven had given me, or as if some unknown power was pushing me, than because my soul wanted it.

I cannot know what the creature I was following felt. Sometimes he wrote messages on the trees or cut them into stone, and they guided me and made me angrier. “My time as king is not over yet”—I could read these words in one of his messages—“you are alive, and my power is complete. Follow me; I am going to the endless ice of the north, where you will suffer from the cold, but I will not. If you are not too slow, you will find a dead hare near this place; eat it and get your strength back. Come on, my enemy; one day we will fight for our lives, but before then you must suffer many hard and unhappy hours.”

Laughing devil! Again I promise to get my revenge; again I promise you, evil monster, pain and death. I will never stop looking for him until he or I die. And then how happy I will be to join my Elizabeth and my dead friends, who are already preparing a reward for my long, hard work and my terrible journey!

As I went further north, the snow got deeper and the cold became almost too strong to bear. The peasants stayed inside their small huts. Only a few of the strongest went out to catch animals that hunger had forced out of their hiding places. The rivers were frozen, and it was impossible to catch fish, so I lost my main food. The harder my journey became, the happier my enemy was. One of his messages said, “Get ready! Your troubles are only beginning; put on furs and take food, because soon we will start a journey where your suffering will satisfy my endless hate.”

His cruel words only made me braver and more determined. I decided that I would not fail, and, asking Heaven to help me, I went on with the same strong feeling across huge empty lands. At last I saw the ocean far away, at the very edge of the sky. Oh, how different it was from the blue seas of the south! It was covered with ice, and it only looked different from the land because it was even wilder and rougher. The ancient Greeks cried with joy when they saw the Mediterranean from the hills of Asia, because it meant the end of their hard journey. I did not cry, but I knelt down and thanked my guiding spirit for bringing me safely to the place where I hoped to meet my enemy and fight him, even though he had laughed at me.

A few weeks before, I had got a sledge and some dogs, so I could travel across the snow very fast. I do not know if the monster had the same, but before I had been falling behind every day, and now I was catching up with him. When I first saw the ocean, he was only one day ahead of me, and I hoped to stop him before he reached the beach. So, feeling braver, I hurried on, and two days later I arrived at a poor little village by the sea.

I asked the people there about the monster, and they told me exactly what had happened. A giant monster, they said, had come the night before with a gun and many pistols. The people in a lonely cottage had run away because he looked so frightening. He had taken all their food for the winter and put it on a sledge. He had caught a big group of trained dogs to pull it, and that same night, to the joy of the terrified villagers, he had set off across the frozen sea towards no land at all. They thought that he would soon die when the ice broke, or freeze to death in the endless cold.

When I heard this, I lost hope for a while. He had escaped me, and now I had to begin a dangerous, almost endless journey over the ice mountains of the ocean. Few of the local people could stand that cold for long, and I, who came from a warm, sunny country, could not hope to survive it. But when I thought that the monster might live and win, my anger and need for revenge came back, and like a great wave, they washed away every other feeling. I rested a little, while the spirits of the dead flew around me and pushed me on to work and revenge, and then I got ready for my journey. I changed my sledge for one that was made for the rough ice of the Frozen Ocean, bought plenty of food, and left the land.

I cannot guess how many days have passed since then. I have suffered terribly, and only my endless wish for fair punishment, burning in my heart, has helped me to bear it. Huge, rough mountains of ice often blocked my way, and I often heard the thunder of the sea under the ice, which could kill me. But then the frost came again and made the ice safe.

From the amount of food I had eaten, I guess that I had spent three weeks on this journey. My hope kept going and coming back, and it often made me cry bitter tears of sadness. I had almost lost all hope, and soon this misery would have killed me.

Once, after my poor dogs had pulled me to the top of a sloping ice mountain with great effort, and one of them had died of tiredness, I looked sadly at the huge space in front of me. Suddenly I saw a dark spot on the grey plain. I looked hard to see what it was, and I gave a wild cry of joy when I saw a sledge with the strange, twisted shape of someone I knew well in it. Oh, how strongly hope came back into my heart! Warm tears filled my eyes, and I wiped them away quickly so that I could still see the demon. But my eyes kept filling with hot tears, and at last I could not control my feelings, and I cried out loud.

But there was no time to wait. I took the dead dog away from the others and gave them plenty of food. I rested for an hour, because I really had to, although waiting made me very impatient, and then I went on. I could still see the sledge, and I did not lose sight of it again, except when a rock of ice hid it for a short time. I was clearly getting closer, and when, after almost two days, I saw my enemy less than a mile away, my heart jumped.

But just when I was almost close enough to catch him, all my hopes suddenly died, and I lost him more completely than ever before. I heard the sea moving under the ice. As the water rolled and rose under me, its thunder became more and more frightening. I tried to go on, but it was no use. The wind got stronger and the sea roared, and then, as if there had been an earthquake, the ice broke apart with a terrible, enormous noise. It was all over quickly. In a few minutes there was wild water between me and my enemy, and I was floating on a piece of ice that was getting smaller all the time, and I knew I would soon die a horrible death.

Many terrible hours passed like this. Several of my dogs died, and I was almost ready to give up when I saw your ship at anchor, which gave me hope of help and life. I had no idea that ships ever came so far north, and I was amazed to see it. I quickly broke part of my sledge to make oars, and with them, after a huge effort, I moved my piece of ice towards your ship.

I had decided that if you were going south, I would stay on the sea and take my chances rather than give up my plan. I hoped to get a boat from you so that I could follow my enemy. But you were going north. You took me on board when I had no strength left. I would soon have died from all my hardships, and I am still afraid of death, because I have not finished my task.

Oh! When will my guiding spirit take me to the demon and let me have the rest I want so much? Or must I die while he lives? If I die, promise me, Walton, that he will not escape, that you will find him and kill him for my revenge. But can I really ask you to continue my journey and suffer what I have suffered? No, I am not so selfish.

But after I die, if he appears, if the spirits of revenge bring him to you, promise that he will not live. Promise that he will not win over all my sorrows and live on to do more terrible crimes. He speaks very well and can make people believe him, and once his words even touched my heart; but do not trust him. His soul is as evil as his body, full of lies and devilish hate. Do not listen to him; remember the names of William, Justine, Clerval, Elizabeth, my father and poor Victor, and push your sword into his heart. I will be near you and guide your sword.
a2: At that time I could not think clearly. I was full of anger. Only the wish for revenge made me strong and calm. Without it, I think I would go mad or die. First I decided to leave Geneva for ever. I loved my country when I was happy, but now I hated it. I took some money and some of my mother’s jewels, and I left.

So my travels began. They will only end when I die. I have travelled across a lot of the world. I have had all the problems of travellers in deserts and wild countries. I do not really know how I stayed alive. Many times I lay on the sand and asked God to let me die. But I wanted revenge, so I could not die and leave my enemy alive.

When I left Geneva, I needed to find the monster’s trail. But I had no plan, and I walked around the town for hours. In the evening I came to the cemetery. William, Elizabeth and my father were buried there. I went to their grave. Everything was quiet, and the wind moved the leaves softly. It was almost dark. I felt that the spirits of the dead were around me.

At first I was very sad, but then I became angry. They were dead, and I was alive. Their killer was alive too. I had to live to kill him. I knelt on the grass and kissed the ground. Then I said, “I promise this by the earth, by the dead and by the Night. I will follow the demon until he dies or I die.
I will stay alive for this reason. I will see the sun and walk on the green grass again only for my revenge. Spirits of the dead, please help me! Let the monster feel great pain, like me.”

When I started, I felt that my dead friends were listening to me. But at the end I was so angry that I could not speak. Then, in the quiet night, I heard a loud, evil laugh. The mountains sent it back again and again. It felt as if all of hell was laughing at me. I almost went mad, but I had to live for my revenge. The laugh stopped, and a voice that I knew and hated whispered near my ear, “I am happy, you poor man! You are going to live, and I am happy.”

I ran to the place, but the devil got away. Then the moon came out, and I saw his ugly body. He was running faster than any man. I followed him, and I have done this for many months. First I went along the river Rhône, but I did not find him. Then I came to the Mediterranean Sea. One night I saw him get on a ship to the Black Sea. I got on the same ship, but he escaped.

I followed him through the wild lands of Tartary and Russia. Sometimes frightened villagers told me where he went. Sometimes he left signs for me. He did not want me to lose him and die. Snow fell on me, and I saw his big footprints in the snow. You are young, Walton. How can you understand my pain?

Cold, hunger and tiredness were my smallest problems. I carried my own hell with me. But a good spirit helped me too. Sometimes, when I was too hungry to go on, I found food waiting for me. It was simple food, like the villagers’ food. I believe the spirits left it there for me. And when I was very thirsty, a small cloud sometimes came and gave me a little rain.

I usually travelled along rivers, but the monster did not like rivers, because many people lived there. In other places there were not many people, so I ate wild animals. I gave money to the villagers, and they were friendly to me. I also gave them meat when they let me use their fire.

I hated my life. I was only happy when I was asleep. Oh, wonderful sleep! When I was very sad, my dreams made me happy. The spirits gave me these happy hours so that I could stay strong. In the day, I waited for the night. In my dreams I saw my friends, my wife and my country. I saw my father’s kind face, heard Elizabeth’s sweet voice and saw Clerval young and well.

Sometimes, when I was very tired in the day, I told myself, “This is only a dream. At night I will be with my friends again.” I loved them so much! Sometimes I saw them when I was awake, and I believed they were alive. At those times I did not feel angry. I followed the monster only because heaven wanted me to do it.

I do not know what the monster felt. Sometimes he wrote messages on trees or stones, and they made me angry. One message said, “I am still the king. You are alive, and I have power over you. Follow me to the ice in the north. You will feel the cold, but I will not. There is a dead rabbit near here; eat it. One day we will fight, but first you will suffer a lot.”
Horrible devil! I promise again that I will kill you. I will never stop until he or I die. Then I will be happy with Elizabeth and my friends again.

I went further north. There was more snow, and it was terribly cold. The villagers stayed in their houses. The rivers were frozen, so I could not catch fish. The monster was happy because my journey was so hard. One of his messages said, “Get ready! Take warm clothes and food. Soon we will go on a journey, and you will suffer a lot.”

His words made me braver. I asked Heaven to help me, and I travelled across huge empty lands. At last I saw the ocean far away. It was not blue like the sea in the south. It was covered with ice and looked like wild land. I knelt down and thanked my spirit. I hoped to meet my enemy and fight him there.

A few weeks before, I had bought a sledge and dogs, so I travelled very fast. Now I was getting closer to the monster every day. When I saw the ocean, he was only one day in front of me. After two more days, I came to a small, poor village by the sea.

I asked the villagers about the monster. They said, “A giant came here last night with a gun and pistols. The people in one house ran away because they were afraid. He took all their winter food and some dogs. Then he drove his sledge onto the frozen sea. There is no land that way. He will probably die in the ice and cold.”

When I heard this, I lost hope for a short time. He was gone, and now I had to travel across the frozen ocean. I came from a warm country, and I did not think I could live in that cold. But then I thought, “The monster is going to live and win!” My anger came back, stronger than every other feeling. I rested a little and got ready. I got a new sledge for the ice, bought a lot of food and left the land.

I do not know how many days have passed since then. I suffered a lot, but my wish for revenge helped me. Big mountains of ice often stopped me. I heard the sea moving under the ice, and I was afraid. But then it got colder, and the ice was safe again.
I think I travelled like this for three weeks. I often cried because I was losing hope. I was almost ready to die.

One day my dogs pulled me to the top of an ice hill. One dog died because it was so tired. I looked sadly at the ice in front of me. Suddenly I saw a dark spot far away. It was a sledge, and the monster was in it! I shouted with joy. Tears filled my eyes, and I cried.

But I could not wait. I took the dead dog away and gave the other dogs food. We rested for one hour, and then we went on. I could see the sledge most of the time. After two days, my enemy was less than a mile away. My heart jumped!

But then I lost him again. I heard the sea under the ice. The noise got louder and more frightening. The wind blew hard, and the ice broke with a terrible sound. In a few minutes there was water between me and my enemy. I was on a small piece of ice. It was getting smaller, and I knew I was going to die.

Many terrible hours passed, and some of my dogs died. I was almost dead too when I saw your ship. I was very surprised, because I did not know that ships came so far north. I broke my sledge and made oars from it. It was very hard, but I moved my piece of ice to your ship.

If you were going south, I was not going to come with you. I wanted to ask you for a boat to follow my enemy. But you were going north. You took me on your ship when I had no strength. I am still afraid to die, because my work is not finished.
Oh! When will I find the demon and rest? Or will I die, and he will live? If I die, Walton, promise me that you will find him and kill him. But no, I cannot ask you to do my hard work.

But if he comes to you after I die, promise me that you will kill him. Do not let him win and do more bad things. He speaks very well, and once I believed his words. But do not trust him.
