b1.ru: Если ты не будешь слишком медленным, найдёшь недалеко отсюда мёртвого зайца; съешь его и восстанови силы.

b1.en: Come on, my enemy; one day we will fight for our lives, but before then you must suffer many hard and unhappy hours.”
b1.ru: Вперёд, мой враг; однажды мы будем биться за жизнь, но до того тебе придётся пережить много тяжёлых и несчастных часов».

b1.en: Laughing devil!
b1.ru: Насмешливый дьявол!

b1.en: Again I promise to get my revenge; again I promise you, evil monster, pain and death.
b1.ru: Снова я обещаю отомстить; снова я обещаю тебе, злое чудовище, муки и смерть.

b1.en: I will never stop looking for him until he or I die.
b1.ru: Я никогда не перестану искать его, пока он или я не умрём.

b1.en: And then how happy I will be to join my Elizabeth and my dead friends, who are already preparing a reward for my long, hard work and my terrible journey!
b1.ru: И тогда как я буду счастлив соединиться с моей Элизабет и умершими друзьями, которые уже готовят мне награду за мой долгий тяжкий труд и ужасное путешествие!

b1.en: As I went further north, the snow got deeper and the cold became almost too strong to bear.
b1.ru: Чем дальше я шёл на север, тем глубже становился снег, а холод становился почти невыносимым.

b1.en: The peasants stayed inside their small huts.
b1.ru: Крестьяне сидели в своих маленьких хижинах.

b1.en: Only a few of the strongest went out to catch animals that hunger had forced out of their hiding places.
b1.ru: Только немногие самые сильные выходили ловить животных, которых голод выгнал из укрытий.

b1.en: The rivers were frozen, and it was impossible to catch fish, so I lost my main food.
b1.ru: Реки замёрзли, и поймать рыбу было невозможно, так что я лишился своей главной еды.

b1.en: The harder my journey became, the happier my enemy was.
b1.ru: Чем труднее становился мой путь, тем больше радовался мой враг.

b1.en: One of his messages said, “Get ready!
b1.ru: В одном из его посланий было написано: «Готовься!

b1.en: Your troubles are only beginning; put on furs and take food, because soon we will start a journey where your suffering will satisfy my endless hate.”
b1.ru: Твои беды только начинаются; надень меха и возьми еды, потому что скоро мы начнём путь, где твои страдания утолят мою бесконечную ненависть».

b1.en: His cruel words only made me braver and more determined.
b1.ru: Его жестокие слова только сделали меня смелее и решительнее.

b1.en: I decided that I would not fail, and, asking Heaven to help me, I went on with the same strong feeling across huge empty lands.
b1.ru: Я решил, что не отступлю, и, прося Небо о помощи, с той же силой чувства шёл дальше через огромные пустые земли.

b1.en: At last I saw the ocean far away, at the very edge of the sky.
b1.ru: Наконец я увидел вдали океан, у самого края неба.

b1.en: Oh, how different it was from the blue seas of the south!
b1.ru: О, как он был не похож на синие моря юга!

b1.en: It was covered with ice, and it only looked different from the land because it was even wilder and rougher.
b1.ru: Он был покрыт льдом и отличался от суши только тем, что был ещё более диким и неровным.

b1.en: The ancient Greeks cried with joy when they saw the Mediterranean from the hills of Asia, because it meant the end of their hard journey.
b1.ru: Древние греки плакали от радости, когда увидели Средиземное море с холмов Азии, потому что это означало конец их трудного пути.

b1.en: I did not cry, but I knelt down and thanked my guiding spirit for bringing me safely to the place where I hoped to meet my enemy and fight him, even though he had laughed at me.
b1.ru: Я не плакал, но встал на колени и поблагодарил своего духа-хранителя за то, что он благополучно привёл меня туда, где я надеялся встретить врага и сразиться с ним, хотя он и смеялся надо мной.

b1.en: A few weeks before, I had got a sledge and some dogs, so I could travel across the snow very fast.
b1.ru: За несколько недель до этого я раздобыл сани и собак, так что мог очень быстро передвигаться по снегу.

b1.en: I do not know if the monster had the same, but before I had been falling behind every day, and now I was catching up with him.
b1.ru: Не знаю, было ли то же самое у чудовища, но раньше я каждый день отставал, а теперь догонял его.

b1.en: When I first saw the ocean, he was only one day ahead of me, and I hoped to stop him before he reached the beach.
b1.ru: Когда я впервые увидел океан, он был впереди меня всего на один день, и я надеялся остановить его, прежде чем он доберётся до берега.

b1.en: So, feeling braver, I hurried on, and two days later I arrived at a poor little village by the sea.
b1.ru: Итак, приободрившись, я поспешил вперёд и через два дня прибыл в бедную деревушку у моря.

b1.en: I asked the people there about the monster, and they told me exactly what had happened.
b1.ru: Я расспросил тамошних жителей о чудовище, и они точно рассказали мне, что произошло.

b1.en: A giant monster, they said, had come the night before with a gun and many pistols.
b1.ru: Огромное чудовище, сказали они, пришло накануне вечером с ружьём и множеством пистолетов.

b1.en: The people in a lonely cottage had run away because he looked so frightening.
b1.ru: Люди из одинокого домика убежали, потому что он выглядел так страшно.

b1.en: He had taken all their food for the winter and put it on a sledge.
b1.ru: Он забрал всю их еду на зиму и погрузил её на сани.

b1.en: He had caught a big group of trained dogs to pull it, and that same night, to the joy of the terrified villagers, he had set off across the frozen sea towards no land at all.
b1.ru: Он поймал большую упряжку обученных собак, чтобы тянуть сани, и в ту же ночь, к радости перепуганных жителей, отправился по замёрзшему морю туда, где не было никакой земли.

b1.en: They thought that he would soon die when the ice broke, or freeze to death in the endless cold.
b1.ru: Они думали, что он скоро погибнет, когда лёд проломится, или замёрзнет насмерть в бесконечном холоде.

b1.en: When I heard this, I lost hope for a while.
b1.ru: Услышав это, я на какое-то время потерял надежду.

b1.en: He had escaped me, and now I had to begin a dangerous, almost endless journey over the ice mountains of the ocean.
b1.ru: Он ускользнул от меня, и теперь мне предстояло начать опасное, почти бесконечное путешествие по ледяным горам океана.

b1.en: Few of the local people could stand that cold for long, and I, who came from a warm, sunny country, could not hope to survive it.
b1.ru: Немногие из местных жителей могли долго выносить такой холод, а я, выходец из тёплой солнечной страны, не мог надеяться его пережить.

b1.en: But when I thought that the monster might live and win, my anger and need for revenge came back, and like a great wave, they washed away every other feeling.
b1.ru: Но когда я подумал, что чудовище может остаться жить и победить, мои злость и жажда мести вернулись и, как огромная волна, смыли все другие чувства.

b1.en: I rested a little, while the spirits of the dead flew around me and pushed me on to work and revenge, and then I got ready for my journey.
b1.ru: Я немного отдохнул, пока духи умерших кружили вокруг меня и подталкивали к труду и мести, а потом приготовился в путь.

b1.en: I changed my sledge for one that was made for the rough ice of the Frozen Ocean, bought plenty of food, and left the land.
b1.ru: Я обменял свои сани на другие, сделанные для неровного льда Ледовитого океана, купил много еды и покинул землю.

b1.en: I cannot guess how many days have passed since then.
b1.ru: Не могу сказать, сколько дней прошло с тех пор.

b1.en: I have suffered terribly, and only my endless wish for fair punishment, burning in my heart, has helped me to bear it.
b1.ru: Я страшно страдал, и только бесконечное желание справедливого наказания, горящее в моём сердце, помогло мне это вынести.

b1.en: Huge, rough mountains of ice often blocked my way, and I often heard the thunder of the sea under the ice, which could kill me.
b1.ru: Огромные неровные ледяные горы часто преграждали мне путь, и я часто слышал грохот моря подо льдом, который мог меня погубить.

b1.en: But then the frost came again and made the ice safe.
b1.ru: Но потом снова ударил мороз и сделал лёд надёжным.

b1.en: From the amount of food I had eaten, I guess that I had spent three weeks on this journey.
b1.ru: По количеству съеденной еды я предполагаю, что провёл в этом пути три недели.

b1.en: My hope kept going and coming back, and it often made me cry bitter tears of sadness.
b1.ru: Моя надежда то уходила, то возвращалась, и часто это заставляло меня плакать горькими слезами печали.

b1.en: I had almost lost all hope, and soon this misery would have killed me.
b1.ru: Я почти потерял всякую надежду, и скоро эти страдания убили бы меня.

b1.en: Once, after my poor dogs had pulled me to the top of a sloping ice mountain with great effort, and one of them had died of tiredness, I looked sadly at the huge space in front of me.
b1.ru: Однажды, после того как мои бедные собаки с огромным трудом втащили меня на вершину покатой ледяной горы, а одна из них умерла от усталости, я с тоской посмотрел на огромное пространство передо мной.

b1.en: Suddenly I saw a dark spot on the grey plain.
b1.ru: Вдруг я увидел тёмное пятнышко на серой равнине.

b1.en: I looked hard to see what it was, and I gave a wild cry of joy when I saw a sledge with the strange, twisted shape of someone I knew well in it.
b1.ru: Я пристально вгляделся, чтобы понять, что это, и издал дикий крик радости, когда увидел сани, а в них странную, искривлённую фигуру того, кого я хорошо знал.

b1.en: Oh, how strongly hope came back into my heart!
b1.ru: О, как сильно вернулась надежда в моё сердце!

b1.en: Warm tears filled my eyes, and I wiped them away quickly so that I could still see the demon.
b1.ru: Тёплые слёзы наполнили мои глаза, и я быстро вытер их, чтобы по-прежнему видеть демона.

b1.en: But my eyes kept filling with hot tears, and at last I could not control my feelings, and I cried out loud.
b1.ru: Но глаза снова и снова наполнялись горячими слезами, и наконец я не смог справиться с чувствами и громко заплакал.

b1.en: But there was no time to wait.
b1.ru: Но ждать было некогда.

b1.en: I took the dead dog away from the others and gave them plenty of food.
b1.ru: Я отцепил мёртвую собаку от остальных и хорошо их накормил.

b1.en: I rested for an hour, because I really had to, although waiting made me very impatient, and then I went on.
b1.ru: Я отдохнул час, потому что это было действительно необходимо, хотя ожидание выводило меня из себя, а потом поехал дальше.

b1.en: I could still see the sledge, and I did not lose sight of it again, except when a rock of ice hid it for a short time.
b1.ru: Я всё ещё видел сани и больше не терял их из виду, кроме тех случаев, когда ненадолго их закрывала ледяная скала.

b1.en: I was clearly getting closer, and when, after almost two days, I saw my enemy less than a mile away, my heart jumped.
b1.ru: Я явно приближался, и когда почти через два дня увидел своего врага меньше чем в миле от себя, сердце моё подпрыгнуло.

b1.en: But just when I was almost close enough to catch him, all my hopes suddenly died, and I lost him more completely than ever before.
b1.ru: Но как раз когда я был почти достаточно близко, чтобы схватить его, все мои надежды вдруг погибли, и я потерял его окончательнее, чем когда-либо.

b1.en: I heard the sea moving under the ice.
b1.ru: Я услышал, как под льдом движется море.

b1.en: As the water rolled and rose under me, its thunder became more and more frightening.
b1.ru: Пока вода перекатывалась и поднималась подо мной, её грохот становился всё страшнее.

b1.en: I tried to go on, but it was no use.
b1.ru: Я пытался двигаться дальше, но это было бесполезно.

b1.en: The wind got stronger and the sea roared, and then, as if there had been an earthquake, the ice broke apart with a terrible, enormous noise.
b1.ru: Ветер усилился, море заревело, а потом, словно от землетрясения, лёд раскололся со страшным, оглушительным шумом.

b1.en: It was all over quickly.
b1.ru: Всё закончилось быстро.

b1.en: In a few minutes there was wild water between me and my enemy, and I was floating on a piece of ice that was getting smaller all the time, and I knew I would soon die a horrible death.
b1.ru: Через несколько минут между мной и врагом бушевала вода, а я плыл на куске льда, который всё время уменьшался, и я знал, что скоро умру ужасной смертью.

b1.en: Many terrible hours passed like this.
b1.ru: Так прошло много ужасных часов.

b1.en: Several of my dogs died, and I was almost ready to give up when I saw your ship at anchor, which gave me hope of help and life.
b1.ru: Несколько моих собак умерло, и я был почти готов сдаться, когда увидел ваш корабль на якоре, который дал мне надежду на помощь и жизнь.

b1.en: I had no idea that ships ever came so far north, and I was amazed to see it.
b1.ru: Я понятия не имел, что корабли заходят так далеко на север, и был поражён, увидев его.

b1.en: I quickly broke part of my sledge to make oars, and with them, after a huge effort, I moved my piece of ice towards your ship.
b1.ru: Я быстро разломал часть саней, чтобы сделать вёсла, и с их помощью, приложив огромные усилия, направил свою льдину к вашему кораблю.

b1.en: I had decided that if you were going south, I would stay on the sea and take my chances rather than give up my plan.
b1.ru: Я решил, что если вы идёте на юг, то я останусь в море и буду полагаться на удачу, но не откажусь от своего плана.

b1.en: I hoped to get a boat from you so that I could follow my enemy.
b1.ru: Я надеялся получить от вас лодку, чтобы преследовать своего врага.

b1.en: But you were going north.
b1.ru: Но вы шли на север.

b1.en: You took me on board when I had no strength left.
b1.ru: Вы взяли меня на борт, когда у меня не осталось сил.

b1.en: I would soon have died from all my hardships, and I am still afraid of death, because I have not finished my task.
b1.ru: Я скоро умер бы от всех лишений, и я всё ещё боюсь смерти, потому что не закончил свою задачу.

b1.en: Oh! When will my guiding spirit take me to the demon and let me have the rest I want so much?
b1.ru: О! Когда же мой дух-хранитель приведёт меня к демону и позволит мне обрести покой, которого я так хочу?

b1.en: Or must I die while he lives?
b1.ru: Или я должен умереть, а он будет жить?

b1.en: If I die, promise me, Walton, that he will not escape, that you will find him and kill him for my revenge.
b1.ru: Если я умру, пообещайте мне, Уолтон, что он не уйдёт, что вы найдёте его и убьёте ради моей мести.

b1.en: But can I really ask you to continue my journey and suffer what I have suffered?
b1.ru: Но могу ли я правда просить вас продолжить мой путь и пережить то, что пережил я?

b1.en: No, I am not so selfish.
b1.ru: Нет, я не настолько эгоистичен.

b1.en: But after I die, if he appears, if the spirits of revenge bring him to you, promise that he will not live.
b1.ru: Но после моей смерти, если он появится, если духи мести приведут его к вам, пообещайте, что он не останется в живых.

b1.en: Promise that he will not win over all my sorrows and live on to do more terrible crimes.
b1.ru: Пообещайте, что он не восторжествует над всеми моими горестями и не будет жить дальше, чтобы совершать новые ужасные преступления.

b1.en: He speaks very well and can make people believe him, and once his words even touched my heart; but do not trust him.
b1.ru: Он очень хорошо говорит и умеет заставить людей поверить ему, и когда-то его слова даже тронули моё сердце; но не верьте ему.

b1.en: His soul is as evil as his body, full of lies and devilish hate.
b1.ru: Его душа так же зла, как и его тело, полна лжи и дьявольской ненависти.

b1.en: Do not listen to him; remember the names of William, Justine, Clerval, Elizabeth, my father and poor Victor, and push your sword into his heart.
b1.ru: Не слушайте его; вспомните имена Уильяма, Жюстины, Клерваля, Элизабет, моего отца и несчастного Виктора — и вонзите меч ему в сердце.

b1.en: I will be near you and guide your sword.
b1.ru: Я буду рядом с вами и направлю ваш меч.

a2.en: At that time I could not think clearly.
a2.ru: В то время я не мог ясно думать.

a2.en: I was full of anger.
a2.ru: Я был полон злости.

a2.en: Only the wish for revenge made me strong and calm.
a2.ru: Только желание отомстить делало меня сильным и спокойным.

a2.en: Without it, I think I would go mad or die.
a2.ru: Думаю, без него я сошёл бы с ума или умер.

a2.en: First I decided to leave Geneva for ever.
a2.ru: Сначала я решил навсегда уехать из Женевы.

a2.en: I loved my country when I was happy, but now I hated it.
a2.ru: Я любил свою страну, когда был счастлив, но теперь я её ненавидел.

a2.en: I took some money and some of my mother’s jewels, and I left.
a2.ru: Я взял немного денег и несколько украшений моей матери и уехал.

a2.en: So my travels began.
a2.ru: Так начались мои путешествия.

a2.en: They will only end when I die.
a2.ru: Они закончатся только тогда, когда я умру.

a2.en: I have travelled across a lot of the world.
a2.ru: Я проехал большую часть мира.

a2.en: I have had all the problems of travellers in deserts and wild countries.
a2.ru: У меня были все трудности путешественников в пустынях и диких странах.

a2.en: I do not really know how I stayed alive.
a2.ru: Я точно не знаю, как я остался жив.

a2.en: Many times I lay on the sand and asked God to let me die.
a2.ru: Много раз я лежал на песке и просил Бога дать мне умереть.

a2.en: But I wanted revenge, so I could not die and leave my enemy alive.
a2.ru: Но я хотел мести, поэтому не мог умереть и оставить врага в живых.

a2.en: When I left Geneva, I needed to find the monster’s trail.
a2.ru: Когда я уехал из Женевы, мне нужно было найти след чудовища.

a2.en: But I had no plan, and I walked around the town for hours.
a2.ru: Но у меня не было плана, и я часами ходил вокруг города.

a2.en: In the evening I came to the cemetery.
a2.ru: Вечером я пришёл на кладбище.

a2.en: William, Elizabeth and my father were buried there.
a2.ru: Там были похоронены Уильям, Элизабет и мой отец.

a2.en: I went to their grave.
a2.ru: Я подошёл к их могиле.

a2.en: Everything was quiet, and the wind moved the leaves softly.
a2.ru: Всё было тихо, и ветер мягко шевелил листья.

a2.en: It was almost dark.
a2.ru: Было почти темно.

a2.en: I felt that the spirits of the dead were around me.
a2.ru: Я чувствовал, что духи мёртвых рядом со мной.

a2.en: At first I was very sad, but then I became angry.
a2.ru: Сначала мне было очень грустно, но потом я разозлился.

a2.en: They were dead, and I was alive.
a2.ru: Они были мертвы, а я был жив.

a2.en: Their killer was alive too.
a2.ru: Их убийца тоже был жив.

a2.en: I had to live to kill him.
a2.ru: Я должен был жить, чтобы убить его.

a2.en: I knelt on the grass and kissed the ground.
a2.ru: Я встал на колени на траву и поцеловал землю.

a2.en: Then I said, “I promise this by the earth, by the dead and by the Night.
a2.ru: Потом я сказал: «Клянусь землёй, мёртвыми и Ночью.

a2.en: I will follow the demon until he dies or I die.
a2.ru: Я буду преследовать демона, пока он не умрёт или я не умру.

a2.en: I will stay alive for this reason.
a2.ru: Я останусь жить ради этого.

a2.en: I will see the sun and walk on the green grass again only for my revenge.
a2.ru: Я снова буду видеть солнце и ходить по зелёной траве только ради мести.

a2.en: Spirits of the dead, please help me!
a2.ru: Духи мёртвых, помогите мне!

a2.en: Let the monster feel great pain, like me.”
a2.ru: Пусть чудовище почувствует сильную боль, как я».

a2.en: When I started, I felt that my dead friends were listening to me.
a2.ru: Когда я начал, я чувствовал, что мои мёртвые друзья слушают меня.

a2.en: But at the end I was so angry that I could not speak.
a2.ru: Но к концу я был так зол, что не мог говорить.

a2.en: Then, in the quiet night, I heard a loud, evil laugh.
a2.ru: Потом в тихой ночи я услышал громкий злой смех.

a2.en: The mountains sent it back again and again.
a2.ru: Горы повторяли его снова и снова.

a2.en: It felt as if all of hell was laughing at me.
a2.ru: Казалось, будто весь ад смеётся надо мной.

a2.en: I almost went mad, but I had to live for my revenge.
a2.ru: Я чуть не сошёл с ума, но я должен был жить ради мести.

a2.en: The laugh stopped, and a voice that I knew and hated whispered near my ear, “I am happy, you poor man!
a2.ru: Смех прекратился, и голос, который я знал и ненавидел, прошептал у моего уха: «Я доволен, бедняга!

a2.en: You are going to live, and I am happy.”
a2.ru: Ты будешь жить, и я доволен».

a2.en: I ran to the place, but the devil got away.
a2.ru: Я побежал к тому месту, но дьявол убежал.

a2.en: Then the moon came out, and I saw his ugly body.
a2.ru: Потом вышла луна, и я увидел его уродливое тело.

a2.en: He was running faster than any man.
a2.ru: Он бежал быстрее любого человека.

a2.en: I followed him, and I have done this for many months.
a2.ru: Я погнался за ним и делаю это уже много месяцев.

a2.en: First I went along the river Rhône, but I did not find him.
a2.ru: Сначала я пошёл вдоль реки Роны, но не нашёл его.

a2.en: Then I came to the Mediterranean Sea.
a2.ru: Потом я пришёл к Средиземному морю.

a2.en: One night I saw him get on a ship to the Black Sea.
a2.ru: Однажды ночью я увидел, как он сел на корабль, идущий в Чёрное море.

a2.en: I got on the same ship, but he escaped.
a2.ru: Я сел на тот же корабль, но он сбежал.

a2.en: I followed him through the wild lands of Tartary and Russia.
a2.ru: Я шёл за ним через дикие земли Татарии и России.

a2.en: Sometimes frightened villagers told me where he went.
a2.ru: Иногда испуганные крестьяне говорили мне, куда он пошёл.

a2.en: Sometimes he left signs for me.
a2.ru: Иногда он оставлял мне знаки.

a2.en: He did not want me to lose him and die.
a2.ru: Он не хотел, чтобы я потерял его и умер.

a2.en: Snow fell on me, and I saw his big footprints in the snow.
a2.ru: На меня падал снег, и я видел его большие следы на снегу.

a2.en: You are young, Walton.
a2.ru: Вы молоды, Уолтон.

a2.en: How can you understand my pain?
a2.ru: Как вы можете понять мою боль?

a2.en: Cold, hunger and tiredness were my smallest problems.
a2.ru: Холод, голод и усталость были моими самыми маленькими бедами.

a2.en: I carried my own hell with me.
a2.ru: Я носил свой ад с собой.

a2.en: But a good spirit helped me too.
a2.ru: Но и добрый дух помогал мне.

a2.en: Sometimes, when I was too hungry to go on, I found food waiting for me.
a2.ru: Иногда, когда я был слишком голоден, чтобы идти дальше, я находил ожидающую меня еду.

a2.en: It was simple food, like the villagers’ food.
a2.ru: Это была простая еда, как у крестьян.

a2.en: I believe the spirits left it there for me.
a2.ru: Я верю, что её оставили для меня духи.

a2.en: And when I was very thirsty, a small cloud sometimes came and gave me a little rain.
a2.ru: А когда меня мучила жажда, иногда приходило облачко и давало мне немного дождя.

a2.en: I usually travelled along rivers, but the monster did not like rivers, because many people lived there.
a2.ru: Обычно я шёл вдоль рек, но чудовище не любило реки, потому что там жило много людей.

a2.en: In other places there were not many people, so I ate wild animals.
a2.ru: В других местах людей было мало, поэтому я ел диких животных.

a2.en: I gave money to the villagers, and they were friendly to me.
a2.ru: Я давал крестьянам деньги, и они были ко мне дружелюбны.

a2.en: I also gave them meat when they let me use their fire.
a2.ru: Ещё я давал им мясо, когда они разрешали мне пользоваться их огнём.

a2.en: I hated my life.
a2.ru: Я ненавидел свою жизнь.

a2.en: I was only happy when I was asleep.
a2.ru: Я был счастлив, только когда спал.

a2.en: Oh, wonderful sleep!
a2.ru: О, чудесный сон!

a2.en: When I was very sad, my dreams made me happy.
a2.ru: Когда мне было очень грустно, сны делали меня счастливым.

a2.en: The spirits gave me these happy hours so that I could stay strong.
a2.ru: Духи дарили мне эти счастливые часы, чтобы я оставался сильным.

a2.en: In the day, I waited for the night.
a2.ru: Днём я ждал ночи.

a2.en: In my dreams I saw my friends, my wife and my country.
a2.ru: Во сне я видел своих друзей, жену и свою страну.

a2.en: I saw my father’s kind face, heard Elizabeth’s sweet voice and saw Clerval young and well.
a2.ru: Я видел доброе лицо отца, слышал нежный голос Элизабет и видел Клерваля молодым и здоровым.

a2.en: Sometimes, when I was very tired in the day, I told myself, “This is only a dream.
a2.ru: Иногда, когда днём я очень уставал, я говорил себе: «Это только сон.

a2.en: At night I will be with my friends again.”
a2.ru: Ночью я снова буду с друзьями».

a2.en: I loved them so much!
a2.ru: Я так сильно любил их!

a2.en: Sometimes I saw them when I was awake, and I believed they were alive.
a2.ru: Иногда я видел их наяву и верил, что они живы.

a2.en: At those times I did not feel angry.
a2.ru: В такие минуты я не чувствовал злости.

a2.en: I followed the monster only because heaven wanted me to do it.
a2.ru: Я преследовал чудовище только потому, что этого хотело небо.

a2.en: I do not know what the monster felt.
a2.ru: Я не знаю, что чувствовало чудовище.

a2.en: Sometimes he wrote messages on trees or stones, and they made me angry.
a2.ru: Иногда он писал послания на деревьях или камнях, и они меня злили.

a2.en: One message said, “I am still the king.
a2.ru: Одно послание гласило: «Я всё ещё король.

a2.en: You are alive, and I have power over you.
a2.ru: Ты жив, и у меня есть власть над тобой.

a2.en: Follow me to the ice in the north.
a2.ru: Иди за мной ко льдам на севере.

a2.en: You will feel the cold, but I will not.
a2.ru: Ты почувствуешь холод, а я нет.

a2.en: There is a dead rabbit near here; eat it.
a2.ru: Недалеко отсюда лежит мёртвый заяц; съешь его.

a2.en: One day we will fight, but first you will suffer a lot.”
a2.ru: Однажды мы будем драться, но сначала ты будешь много страдать».

a2.en: Horrible devil!
a2.ru: Ужасный дьявол!

a2.en: I promise again that I will kill you.
a2.ru: Я снова обещаю, что убью тебя.

a2.en: I will never stop until he or I die.
a2.ru: Я никогда не остановлюсь, пока он или я не умрём.

a2.en: Then I will be happy with Elizabeth and my friends again.
a2.ru: Тогда я снова буду счастлив с Элизабет и друзьями.

a2.en: I went further north.
a2.ru: Я пошёл дальше на север.

a2.en: There was more snow, and it was terribly cold.
a2.ru: Снега было больше, и было ужасно холодно.

a2.en: The villagers stayed in their houses.
a2.ru: Крестьяне сидели в своих домах.

a2.en: The rivers were frozen, so I could not catch fish.
a2.ru: Реки замёрзли, поэтому я не мог ловить рыбу.

a2.en: The monster was happy because my journey was so hard.
a2.ru: Чудовище радовалось, потому что мой путь был таким трудным.

a2.en: One of his messages said, “Get ready!
a2.ru: В одном из его посланий было написано: «Готовься!

a2.en: Take warm clothes and food.
a2.ru: Возьми тёплую одежду и еду.

a2.en: Soon we will go on a journey, and you will suffer a lot.”
a2.ru: Скоро мы отправимся в путь, и ты будешь много страдать».

a2.en: His words made me braver.
a2.ru: Его слова сделали меня смелее.

a2.en: I asked Heaven to help me, and I travelled across huge empty lands.
a2.ru: Я попросил Небо помочь мне и шёл через огромные пустые земли.

a2.en: At last I saw the ocean far away.
a2.ru: Наконец я увидел вдали океан.

a2.en: It was not blue like the sea in the south.
a2.ru: Он не был синим, как море на юге.

a2.en: It was covered with ice and looked like wild land.
a2.ru: Он был покрыт льдом и был похож на дикую землю.

a2.en: I knelt down and thanked my spirit.
a2.ru: Я встал на колени и поблагодарил своего духа.

a2.en: I hoped to meet my enemy and fight him there.
a2.ru: Я надеялся встретить там врага и сразиться с ним.

a2.en: A few weeks before, I had bought a sledge and dogs, so I travelled very fast.
a2.ru: За несколько недель до этого я купил сани и собак, поэтому ехал очень быстро.

a2.en: Now I was getting closer to the monster every day.
a2.ru: Теперь я каждый день приближался к чудовищу.

a2.en: When I saw the ocean, he was only one day in front of me.
a2.ru: Когда я увидел океан, он был всего на один день впереди меня.

a2.en: After two more days, I came to a small, poor village by the sea.
a2.ru: Ещё через два дня я пришёл в маленькую бедную деревню у моря.

a2.en: I asked the villagers about the monster.
a2.ru: Я спросил крестьян о чудовище.

a2.en: They said, “A giant came here last night with a gun and pistols.
a2.ru: Они сказали: «Вчера вечером сюда пришёл великан с ружьём и пистолетами.

a2.en: The people in one house ran away because they were afraid.
a2.ru: Люди из одного дома убежали, потому что испугались.

a2.en: He took all their winter food and some dogs.
a2.ru: Он забрал всю их зимнюю еду и несколько собак.

a2.en: Then he drove his sledge onto the frozen sea.
a2.ru: Потом он поехал на санях по замёрзшему морю.

a2.en: There is no land that way.
a2.ru: В той стороне нет земли.

a2.en: He will probably die in the ice and cold.”
a2.ru: Он, наверное, погибнет во льдах и холоде».

a2.en: When I heard this, I lost hope for a short time.
a2.ru: Услышав это, я ненадолго потерял надежду.

a2.en: He was gone, and now I had to travel across the frozen ocean.
a2.ru: Он ушёл, и теперь мне нужно было ехать через замёрзший океан.

a2.en: I came from a warm country, and I did not think I could live in that cold.
a2.ru: Я был из тёплой страны и не думал, что смогу выжить в таком холоде.

a2.en: But then I thought, “The monster is going to live and win!”
a2.ru: Но потом я подумал: «Чудовище будет жить и победит!»

a2.en: My anger came back, stronger than every other feeling.
a2.ru: Моя злость вернулась, сильнее всех других чувств.

a2.en: I rested a little and got ready.
a2.ru: Я немного отдохнул и приготовился.

a2.en: I got a new sledge for the ice, bought a lot of food and left the land.
a2.ru: Я взял новые сани для льда, купил много еды и покинул землю.

a2.en: I do not know how many days have passed since then.
a2.ru: Я не знаю, сколько дней прошло с тех пор.

a2.en: I suffered a lot, but my wish for revenge helped me.
a2.ru: Я очень страдал, но желание отомстить помогало мне.

a2.en: Big mountains of ice often stopped me.
a2.ru: Большие ледяные горы часто останавливали меня.

a2.en: I heard the sea moving under the ice, and I was afraid.
a2.ru: Я слышал, как под льдом движется море, и мне было страшно.

a2.en: But then it got colder, and the ice was safe again.
a2.ru: Но потом стало холоднее, и лёд снова стал надёжным.

a2.en: I think I travelled like this for three weeks.
a2.ru: Думаю, я ехал так три недели.

a2.en: I often cried because I was losing hope.
a2.ru: Я часто плакал, потому что терял надежду.

a2.en: I was almost ready to die.
a2.ru: Я был почти готов умереть.

a2.en: One day my dogs pulled me to the top of an ice hill.
a2.ru: Однажды мои собаки втащили меня на вершину ледяного холма.

a2.en: One dog died because it was so tired.
a2.ru: Одна собака умерла, потому что очень устала.

a2.en: I looked sadly at the ice in front of me.
a2.ru: Я грустно посмотрел на лёд впереди.

a2.en: Suddenly I saw a dark spot far away.
a2.ru: Вдруг я увидел вдали тёмное пятно.

a2.en: It was a sledge, and the monster was in it!
a2.ru: Это были сани, и в них было чудовище!

a2.en: I shouted with joy.
a2.ru: Я закричал от радости.

a2.en: Tears filled my eyes, and I cried.
a2.ru: Слёзы наполнили мои глаза, и я заплакал.

a2.en: But I could not wait.
a2.ru: Но я не мог ждать.

a2.en: I took the dead dog away and gave the other dogs food.
a2.ru: Я убрал мёртвую собаку и покормил остальных.

a2.en: We rested for one hour, and then we went on.
a2.ru: Мы отдохнули один час, а потом поехали дальше.

a2.en: I could see the sledge most of the time.
a2.ru: Большую часть времени я видел сани.

a2.en: After two days, my enemy was less than a mile away.
a2.ru: Через два дня мой враг был меньше чем в миле от меня.

a2.en: My heart jumped!
a2.ru: Моё сердце подпрыгнуло!

a2.en: But then I lost him again.
a2.ru: Но потом я снова его потерял.

a2.en: I heard the sea under the ice.
a2.ru: Я услышал море подо льдом.

a2.en: The noise got louder and more frightening.
a2.ru: Шум становился громче и страшнее.

a2.en: The wind blew hard, and the ice broke with a terrible sound.
a2.ru: Подул сильный ветер, и лёд раскололся со страшным звуком.

a2.en: In a few minutes there was water between me and my enemy.
a2.ru: Через несколько минут между мной и врагом была вода.

a2.en: I was on a small piece of ice.
a2.ru: Я был на маленьком куске льда.

a2.en: It was getting smaller, and I knew I was going to die.
a2.ru: Он становился всё меньше, и я знал, что скоро умру.

a2.en: Many terrible hours passed, and some of my dogs died.
a2.ru: Прошло много ужасных часов, и некоторые мои собаки умерли.

a2.en: I was almost dead too when I saw your ship.
a2.ru: Я тоже был почти мёртв, когда увидел ваш корабль.

a2.en: I was very surprised, because I did not know that ships came so far north.
a2.ru: Я очень удивился, потому что не знал, что корабли заходят так далеко на север.

a2.en: I broke my sledge and made oars from it.
a2.ru: Я разломал сани и сделал из них вёсла.

a2.en: It was very hard, but I moved my piece of ice to your ship.
a2.ru: Это было очень тяжело, но я довёл свою льдину до вашего корабля.

a2.en: If you were going south, I was not going to come with you.
a2.ru: Если бы вы шли на юг, я не собирался плыть с вами.

a2.en: I wanted to ask you for a boat to follow my enemy.
a2.ru: Я хотел попросить у вас лодку, чтобы преследовать врага.

a2.en: But you were going north.
a2.ru: Но вы шли на север.

a2.en: You took me on your ship when I had no strength.
a2.ru: Вы взяли меня на корабль, когда у меня не было сил.

a2.en: I am still afraid to die, because my work is not finished.
a2.ru: Я всё ещё боюсь умереть, потому что моя работа не закончена.

a2.en: Oh! When will I find the demon and rest?
a2.ru: О! Когда же я найду демона и отдохну?

a2.en: Or will I die, and he will live?
a2.ru: Или я умру, а он будет жить?

a2.en: If I die, Walton, promise me that you will find him and kill him.
a2.ru: Если я умру, Уолтон, пообещайте мне, что найдёте его и убьёте.

a2.en: But no, I cannot ask you to do my hard work.
a2.ru: Но нет, я не могу просить вас делать мою тяжёлую работу.

a2.en: But if he comes to you after I die, promise me that you will kill him.
a2.ru: Но если он придёт к вам после моей смерти, пообещайте, что убьёте его.

a2.en: Do not let him win and do more bad things.
a2.ru: Не дайте ему победить и совершить новые злые дела.

a2.en: He speaks very well, and once I believed his words.
a2.ru: Он очень хорошо говорит, и когда-то я поверил его словам.

a2.en: But do not trust him.
a2.ru: Но не верьте ему.

a2.en: His heart is as evil as his face.
a2.ru: Его сердце так же злое, как и его лицо.

a2.en: Do not listen to him.
a2.ru: Не слушайте его.

a2.en: Remember William, Justine, Clerval, Elizabeth, my father and me, Victor, and push your sword into his heart.
a2.ru: Вспомните Уильяма, Жюстину, Клерваля, Элизабет, моего отца и меня, Виктора, — и вонзите меч ему в сердце.

a2.en: I will be near you and help you.
a2.ru: Я буду рядом с вами и помогу вам.

sub: Trapped in the ice, Walton agrees to turn home; Victor dies, and the creature mourns over his body, tells Walton his remorse and leaves to die in the far north

o:
Walton, in continuation.
August 26th, 17—.

You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine? Sometimes, seized with sudden agony, he could not continue his tale; at others, his voice broken, yet piercing, uttered with difficulty the words so replete with anguish. His fine and lovely eyes were now lighted up with indignation, now subdued to downcast sorrow and quenched in infinite wretchedness. Sometimes he commanded his countenance and tones and related the most horrible incidents with a tranquil voice, suppressing every mark of agitation; then, like a volcano bursting forth, his face would suddenly change to an expression of the wildest rage as he shrieked out imprecations on his persecutor.

His tale is connected and told with an appearance of the simplest truth, yet I own to you that the letters of Felix and Safie, which he showed me, and the apparition of the monster seen from our ship, brought to me a greater conviction of the truth of his narrative than his asseverations, however earnest and connected. Such a monster has, then, really existence! I cannot doubt it, yet I am lost in surprise and admiration. Sometimes I endeavoured to gain from Frankenstein the particulars of his creature’s formation, but on this point he was impenetrable.

“Are you mad, my friend?” said he. “Or whither does your senseless curiosity lead you? Would you also create for yourself and the world a demoniacal enemy? Peace, peace! Learn my miseries and do not seek to increase your own.”

Frankenstein discovered that I made notes concerning his history; he asked to see them and then himself corrected and augmented them in many places, but principally in giving the life and spirit to the conversations he held with his enemy. “Since you have preserved my narration,” said he, “I would not that a mutilated one should go down to posterity.”

Thus has a week passed away, while I have listened to the strangest tale that ever imagination formed. My thoughts and every feeling of my soul have been drunk up by the interest for my guest which this tale and his own elevated and gentle manners have created. I wish to soothe him, yet can I counsel one so infinitely miserable, so destitute of every hope of consolation, to live? Oh, no! The only joy that he can now know will be when he composes his shattered spirit to peace and death.

Yet he enjoys one comfort, the offspring of solitude and delirium; he believes that when in dreams he holds converse with his friends and derives from that communion consolation for his miseries or excitements to his vengeance, that they are not the creations of his fancy, but the beings themselves who visit him from the regions of a remote world. This faith gives a solemnity to his reveries that render them to me almost as imposing and interesting as truth.

Our conversations are not always confined to his own history and misfortunes. On every point of general literature he displays unbounded knowledge and a quick and piercing apprehension. His eloquence is forcible and touching; nor can I hear him, when he relates a pathetic incident or endeavours to move the passions of pity or love, without tears. What a glorious creature must he have been in the days of his prosperity, when he is thus noble and godlike in ruin! He seems to feel his own worth and the greatness of his fall.

“When younger,” said he, “I believed myself destined for some great enterprise. My feelings are profound, but I possessed a coolness of judgment that fitted me for illustrious achievements. This sentiment of the worth of my nature supported me when others would have been oppressed, for I deemed it criminal to throw away in useless grief those talents that might be useful to my fellow creatures. When I reflected on the work I had completed, no less a one than the creation of a sensitive and rational animal, I could not rank myself with the herd of common projectors.

But this thought, which supported me in the commencement of my career, now serves only to plunge me lower in the dust. All my speculations and hopes are as nothing, and like the archangel who aspired to omnipotence, I am chained in an eternal hell. My imagination was vivid, yet my powers of analysis and application were intense; by the union of these qualities I conceived the idea and executed the creation of a man.

Even now I cannot recollect without passion my reveries while the work was incomplete. I trod heaven in my thoughts, now exulting in my powers, now burning with the idea of their effects. From my infancy I was imbued with high hopes and a lofty ambition; but how am I sunk! Oh! My friend, if you had known me as I once was, you would not recognise me in this state of degradation. Despondency rarely visited my heart; a high destiny seemed to bear me on, until I fell, never, never again to rise.”

Must I then lose this admirable being? I have longed for a friend; I have sought one who would sympathise with and love me. Behold, on these desert seas I have found such a one, but I fear I have gained him only to know his value and lose him. I would reconcile him to life, but he repulses the idea.

“I thank you, Walton,” he said, “for your kind intentions towards so miserable a wretch; but when you speak of new ties and fresh affections, think you that any can replace those who are gone? Can any man be to me as Clerval was, or any woman another Elizabeth? Even where the affections are not strongly moved by any superior excellence, the companions of our childhood always possess a certain power over our minds which hardly any later friend can obtain.

They know our infantine dispositions, which, however they may be afterwards modified, are never eradicated; and they can judge of our actions with more certain conclusions as to the integrity of our motives. A sister or a brother can never, unless indeed such symptoms have been shown early, suspect the other of fraud or false dealing, when another friend, however strongly he may be attached, may, in spite of himself, be contemplated with suspicion.

But I enjoyed friends, dear not only through habit and association, but from their own merits; and wherever I am, the soothing voice of my Elizabeth and the conversation of Clerval will be ever whispered in my ear. They are dead, and but one feeling in such a solitude can persuade me to preserve my life. If I were engaged in any high undertaking or design, fraught with extensive utility to my fellow creatures, then could I live to fulfil it. But such is not my destiny; I must pursue and destroy the being to whom I gave existence; then my lot on earth will be fulfilled and I may die.”

My beloved Sister,
September 2d.
I write to you, encompassed by peril and ignorant whether I am ever doomed to see again dear England and the dearer friends that inhabit it. I am surrounded by mountains of ice which admit of no escape and threaten every moment to crush my vessel. The brave fellows whom I have persuaded to be my companions look towards me for aid, but I have none to bestow. There is something terribly appalling in our situation, yet my courage and hopes do not desert me. Yet it is terrible to reflect that the lives of all these men are endangered through me. If we are lost, my mad schemes are the cause.

And what, Margaret, will be the state of your mind? You will not hear of my destruction, and you will anxiously await my return. Years will pass, and you will have visitings of despair and yet be tortured by hope. Oh! My beloved sister, the sickening failing of your heart-felt expectations is, in prospect, more terrible to me than my own death. But you have a husband and lovely children; you may be happy. Heaven bless you and make you so!

My unfortunate guest regards me with the tenderest compassion. He endeavours to fill me with hope and talks as if life were a possession which he valued. He reminds me how often the same accidents have happened to other navigators who have attempted this sea, and in spite of myself, he fills me with cheerful auguries. Even the sailors feel the power of his eloquence; when he speaks, they no longer despair; he rouses their energies, and while they hear his voice they believe these vast mountains of ice are mole-hills which will vanish before the resolutions of man. These feelings are transitory; each day of expectation delayed fills them with fear, and I almost dread a mutiny caused by this despair.

September 5th.
A scene has just passed of such uncommon interest that, although it is highly probable that these papers may never reach you, yet I cannot forbear recording it.

We are still surrounded by mountains of ice, still in imminent danger of being crushed in their conflict. The cold is excessive, and many of my unfortunate comrades have already found a grave amidst this scene of desolation. Frankenstein has daily declined in health; a feverish fire still glimmers in his eyes, but he is exhausted, and when suddenly roused to any exertion, he speedily sinks again into apparent lifelessness.

I mentioned in my last letter the fears I entertained of a mutiny. This morning, as I sat watching the wan countenance of my friend—his eyes half closed and his limbs hanging listlessly—I was roused by half a dozen of the sailors, who demanded admission into the cabin. They entered, and their leader addressed me.

He told me that he and his companions had been chosen by the other sailors to come in deputation to me to make me a requisition which, in justice, I could not refuse. We were immured in ice and should probably never escape, but they feared that if, as was possible, the ice should dissipate and a free passage be opened, I should be rash enough to continue my voyage and lead them into fresh dangers, after they might happily have surmounted this. They insisted, therefore, that I should engage with a solemn promise that if the vessel should be freed I would instantly direct my course southwards.

This speech troubled me. I had not despaired, nor had I yet conceived the idea of returning if set free. Yet could I, in justice, or even in possibility, refuse this demand? I hesitated before I answered, when Frankenstein, who had at first been silent, and indeed appeared hardly to have force enough to attend, now roused himself; his eyes sparkled, and his cheeks flushed with momentary vigour. Turning towards the men, he said,

“What do you mean? What do you demand of your captain? Are you, then, so easily turned from your design? Did you not call this a glorious expedition? “And wherefore was it glorious? Not because the way was smooth and placid as a southern sea, but because it was full of dangers and terror, because at every new incident your fortitude was to be called forth and your courage exhibited, because danger and death surrounded it, and these you were to brave and overcome. For this was it a glorious, for this was it an honourable undertaking.

You were hereafter to be hailed as the benefactors of your species, your names adored as belonging to brave men who encountered death for honour and the benefit of mankind. And now, behold, with the first imagination of danger, or, if you will, the first mighty and terrific trial of your courage, you shrink away and are content to be handed down as men who had not strength enough to endure cold and peril; and so, poor souls, they were chilly and returned to their warm firesides.

Why, that requires not this preparation; ye need not have come thus far and dragged your captain to the shame of a defeat merely to prove yourselves cowards. Oh! Be men, or be more than men. Be steady to your purposes and firm as a rock. This ice is not made of such stuff as your hearts may be; it is mutable and cannot withstand you if you say that it shall not. Do not return to your families with the stigma of disgrace marked on your brows. Return as heroes who have fought and conquered and who know not what it is to turn their backs on the foe.”

He spoke this with a voice so modulated to the different feelings expressed in his speech, with an eye so full of lofty design and heroism, that can you wonder that these men were moved? They looked at one another and were unable to reply. I spoke; I told them to retire and consider of what had been said, that I would not lead them farther north if they strenuously desired the contrary, but that I hoped that, with reflection, their courage would return.

They retired and I turned towards my friend, but he was sunk in languor and almost deprived of life.

How all this will terminate, I know not, but I had rather die than return shamefully, my purpose unfulfilled. Yet I fear such will be my fate; the men, unsupported by ideas of glory and honour, can never willingly continue to endure their present hardships.

September 7th.
The die is cast; I have consented to return if we are not destroyed. Thus are my hopes blasted by cowardice and indecision; I come back ignorant and disappointed. It requires more philosophy than I possess to bear this injustice with patience.

September 12th.
It is past; I am returning to England. I have lost my hopes of utility and glory; I have lost my friend. But I will endeavour to detail these bitter circumstances to you, my dear sister; and while I am wafted towards England and towards you, I will not despond.

September 9th, the ice began to move, and roarings like thunder were heard at a distance as the islands split and cracked in every direction. We were in the most imminent peril, but as we could only remain passive, my chief attention was occupied by my unfortunate guest whose illness increased in such a degree that he was entirely confined to his bed. The ice cracked behind us and was driven with force towards the north; a breeze sprang from the west, and on the 11th the passage towards the south became perfectly free.

When the sailors saw this and that their return to their native country was apparently assured, a shout of tumultuous joy broke from them, loud and long-continued. Frankenstein, who was dozing, awoke and asked the cause of the tumult. “They shout,” I said, “because they will soon return to England.”

“Do you, then, really return?”

“Alas! Yes; I cannot withstand their demands. I cannot lead them unwillingly to danger, and I must return.”

“Do so, if you will; but I will not. You may give up your purpose, but mine is assigned to me by Heaven, and I dare not. I am weak, but surely the spirits who assist my vengeance will endow me with sufficient strength.” Saying this, he endeavoured to spring from the bed, but the exertion was too great for him; he fell back and fainted.

It was long before he was restored, and I often thought that life was entirely extinct. At length he opened his eyes; he breathed with difficulty and was unable to speak. The surgeon gave him a composing draught and ordered us to leave him undisturbed. In the meantime he told me that my friend had certainly not many hours to live.

His sentence was pronounced, and I could only grieve and be patient. I sat by his bed, watching him; his eyes were closed, and I thought he slept; but presently he called to me in a feeble voice, and bidding me come near, said, “Alas! The strength I relied on is gone; I feel that I shall soon die, and he, my enemy and persecutor, may still be in being. Think not, Walton, that in the last moments of my existence I feel that burning hatred and ardent desire of revenge I once expressed; but I feel myself justified in desiring the death of my adversary. During these last days I have been occupied in examining my past conduct; nor do I find it blamable.

In a fit of enthusiastic madness I created a rational creature and was bound towards him to assure, as far as was in my power, his happiness and well-being. This was my duty, but there was another still paramount to that. My duties towards the beings of my own species had greater claims to my attention because they included a greater proportion of happiness or misery. Urged by this view, I refused, and I did right in refusing, to create a companion for the first creature.

He showed unparalleled malignity and selfishness in evil; he destroyed my friends; he devoted to destruction beings who possessed exquisite sensations, happiness, and wisdom; nor do I know where this thirst for vengeance may end. Miserable himself that he may render no other wretched, he ought to die. The task of his destruction was mine, but I have failed. When actuated by selfish and vicious motives, I asked you to undertake my unfinished work, and I renew this request now, when I am only induced by reason and virtue.

“Yet I cannot ask you to renounce your country and friends to fulfil this task; and now that you are returning to England, you will have little chance of meeting with him. But the consideration of these points, and the well balancing of what you may esteem your duties, I leave to you; my judgment and ideas are already disturbed by the near approach of death. I dare not ask you to do what I think right, for I may still be misled by passion.

“That he should live to be an instrument of mischief disturbs me; in other respects, this hour, when I momentarily expect my release, is the only happy one which I have enjoyed for several years. The forms of the beloved dead flit before me, and I hasten to their arms. Farewell, Walton! Seek happiness in tranquillity and avoid ambition, even if it be only the apparently innocent one of distinguishing yourself in science and discoveries. Yet why do I say this? I have myself been blasted in these hopes, yet another may succeed.”

His voice became fainter as he spoke, and at length, exhausted by his effort, he sank into silence. About half an hour afterwards he attempted again to speak but was unable; he pressed my hand feebly, and his eyes closed for ever, while the irradiation of a gentle smile passed away from his lips.

Margaret, what comment can I make on the untimely extinction of this glorious spirit? What can I say that will enable you to understand the depth of my sorrow? All that I should express would be inadequate and feeble. My tears flow; my mind is overshadowed by a cloud of disappointment. But I journey towards England, and I may there find consolation.

I am interrupted. What do these sounds portend? It is midnight; the breeze blows fairly, and the watch on deck scarcely stir. Again there is a sound as of a human voice, but hoarser; it comes from the cabin where the remains of Frankenstein still lie. I must arise and examine. Good night, my sister.

Great God! what a scene has just taken place! I am yet dizzy with the remembrance of it. I hardly know whether I shall have the power to detail it; yet the tale which I have recorded would be incomplete without this final and wonderful catastrophe.

I entered the cabin where lay the remains of my ill-fated and admirable friend. Over him hung a form which I cannot find words to describe—gigantic in stature, yet uncouth and distorted in its proportions. As he hung over the coffin, his face was concealed by long locks of ragged hair; but one vast hand was extended, in colour and apparent texture like that of a mummy. When he heard the sound of my approach, he ceased to utter exclamations of grief and horror and sprung towards the window. Never did I behold a vision so horrible as his face, of such loathsome yet appalling hideousness. I shut my eyes involuntarily and endeavoured to recollect what were my duties with regard to this destroyer. I called on him to stay.

He paused, looking on me with wonder, and again turning towards the lifeless form of his creator, he seemed to forget my presence, and every feature and gesture seemed instigated by the wildest rage of some uncontrollable passion.

“That is also my victim!” he exclaimed. “In his murder my crimes are consummated; the miserable series of my being is wound to its close! Oh, Frankenstein! Generous and self-devoted being! What does it avail that I now ask thee to pardon me? I, who irretrievably destroyed thee by destroying all thou lovedst. Alas! He is cold, he cannot answer me.”

His voice seemed suffocated, and my first impulses, which had suggested to me the duty of obeying the dying request of my friend in destroying his enemy, were now suspended by a mixture of curiosity and compassion. I approached this tremendous being; I dared not again raise my eyes to his face, there was something so scaring and unearthly in his ugliness. I attempted to speak, but the words died away on my lips. The monster continued to utter wild and incoherent self-reproaches. At length I gathered resolution to address him in a pause of the tempest of his passion.

“Your repentance,” I said, “is now superfluous. If you had listened to the voice of conscience and heeded the stings of remorse before you had urged your diabolical vengeance to this extremity, Frankenstein would yet have lived.”

“And do you dream?” said the dæmon. “Do you think that I was then dead to agony and remorse? He,” he continued, pointing to the corpse, “he suffered not in the consummation of the deed. Oh! Not the ten-thousandth portion of the anguish that was mine during the lingering detail of its execution. A frightful selfishness hurried me on, while my heart was poisoned with remorse. Think you that the groans of Clerval were music to my ears? My heart was fashioned to be susceptible of love and sympathy, and when wrenched by misery to vice and hatred, it did not endure the violence of the change without torture such as you cannot even imagine.

“After the murder of Clerval I returned to Switzerland, heart-broken and overcome. I pitied Frankenstein; my pity amounted to horror; I abhorred myself. But when I discovered that he, the author at once of my existence and of its unspeakable torments, dared to hope for happiness, that while he accumulated wretchedness and despair upon me he sought his own enjoyment in feelings and passions from the indulgence of which I was for ever barred, then impotent envy and bitter indignation filled me with an insatiable thirst for vengeance.

I recollected my threat and resolved that it should be accomplished. I knew that I was preparing for myself a deadly torture, but I was the slave, not the master, of an impulse which I detested yet could not disobey. Yet when she died! Nay, then I was not miserable. I had cast off all feeling, subdued all anguish, to riot in the excess of my despair. Evil thenceforth became my good. Urged thus far, I had no choice but to adapt my nature to an element which I had willingly chosen. The completion of my demoniacal design became an insatiable passion. And now it is ended; there is my last victim!”

I was at first touched by the expressions of his misery; yet, when I called to mind what Frankenstein had said of his powers of eloquence and persuasion, and when I again cast my eyes on the lifeless form of my friend, indignation was rekindled within me. “Wretch!” I said. “It is well that you come here to whine over the desolation that you have made. You throw a torch into a pile of buildings, and when they are consumed, you sit among the ruins and lament the fall. Hypocritical fiend! If he whom you mourn still lived, still would he be the object, again would he become the prey, of your accursed vengeance. It is not pity that you feel; you lament only because the victim of your malignity is withdrawn from your power.”

“Oh, it is not thus—not thus,” interrupted the being. “Yet such must be the impression conveyed to you by what appears to be the purport of my actions. Yet I seek not a fellow feeling in my misery. No sympathy may I ever find. When I first sought it, it was the love of virtue, the feelings of happiness and affection with which my whole being overflowed, that I wished to be participated. But now that virtue has become to me a shadow, and that happiness and affection are turned into bitter and loathing despair, in what should I seek for sympathy? I am content to suffer alone while my sufferings shall endure; when I die, I am well satisfied that abhorrence and opprobrium should load my memory.

Once my fancy was soothed with dreams of virtue, of fame, and of enjoyment. Once I falsely hoped to meet with beings who, pardoning my outward form, would love me for the excellent qualities which I was capable of unfolding. I was nourished with high thoughts of honour and devotion. But now crime has degraded me beneath the meanest animal. No guilt, no mischief, no malignity, no misery, can be found comparable to mine.

When I run over the frightful catalogue of my sins, I cannot believe that I am the same creature whose thoughts were once filled with sublime and transcendent visions of the beauty and the majesty of goodness. But it is even so; the fallen angel becomes a malignant devil. Yet even that enemy of God and man had friends and associates in his desolation; I am alone.

“You, who call Frankenstein your friend, seem to have a knowledge of my crimes and his misfortunes. But in the detail which he gave you of them he could not sum up the hours and months of misery which I endured wasting in impotent passions. For while I destroyed his hopes, I did not satisfy my own desires. They were for ever ardent and craving; still I desired love and fellowship, and I was still spurned. Was there no injustice in this? Am I to be thought the only criminal, when all humankind sinned against me?

Why do you not hate Felix, who drove his friend from his door with contumely? Why do you not execrate the rustic who sought to destroy the saviour of his child? Nay, these are virtuous and immaculate beings! I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion, to be spurned at, and kicked, and trampled on. Even now my blood boils at the recollection of this injustice.

“But it is true that I am a wretch. I have murdered the lovely and the helpless; I have strangled the innocent as they slept and grasped to death his throat who never injured me or any other living thing. I have devoted my creator, the select specimen of all that is worthy of love and admiration among men, to misery; I have pursued him even to that irremediable ruin. There he lies, white and cold in death. You hate me, but your abhorrence cannot equal that with which I regard myself. I look on the hands which executed the deed; I think on the heart in which the imagination of it was conceived and long for the moment when these hands will meet my eyes, when that imagination will haunt my thoughts no more.

“Fear not that I shall be the instrument of future mischief. My work is nearly complete. Neither yours nor any man’s death is needed to consummate the series of my being and accomplish that which must be done, but it requires my own. Do not think that I shall be slow to perform this sacrifice. I shall quit your vessel on the ice raft which brought me thither and shall seek the most northern extremity of the globe; I shall collect my funeral pile and consume to ashes this miserable frame, that its remains may afford no light to any curious and unhallowed wretch who would create such another as I have been.

I shall die. I shall no longer feel the agonies which now consume me or be the prey of feelings unsatisfied, yet unquenched. He is dead who called me into being; and when I shall be no more, the very remembrance of us both will speedily vanish. I shall no longer see the sun or stars or feel the winds play on my cheeks. Light, feeling, and sense will pass away; and in this condition must I find my happiness.

Some years ago, when the images which this world affords first opened upon me, when I felt the cheering warmth of summer and heard the rustling of the leaves and the warbling of the birds, and these were all to me, I should have wept to die; now it is my only consolation. Polluted by crimes and torn by the bitterest remorse, where can I find rest but in death?

“Farewell! I leave you, and in you the last of humankind whom these eyes will ever behold. Farewell, Frankenstein! If thou wert yet alive and yet cherished a desire of revenge against me, it would be better satiated in my life than in my destruction. But it was not so; thou didst seek my extinction, that I might not cause greater wretchedness; and if yet, in some mode unknown to me, thou hadst not ceased to think and feel, thou wouldst not desire against me a vengeance greater than that which I feel. Blasted as thou wert, my agony was still superior to thine, for the bitter sting of remorse will not cease to rankle in my wounds until death shall close them for ever.

“But soon,” he cried with sad and solemn enthusiasm, “I shall die, and what I now feel be no longer felt. Soon these burning miseries will be extinct. I shall ascend my funeral pile triumphantly and exult in the agony of the torturing flames. The light of that conflagration will fade away; my ashes will be swept into the sea by the winds. My spirit will sleep in peace, or if it thinks, it will not surely think thus. Farewell.”

He sprang from the cabin-window as he said this, upon the ice raft which lay close to the vessel. He was soon borne away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.
b2:
Walton, in continuation.
August 26th, 17—.

You have now read this strange and terrible story, Margaret; doesn’t your blood freeze with horror, just as mine still curdles even now? Sometimes, seized by sudden agony, he could not go on with his tale; at other times his voice, broken yet piercing, forced out with difficulty words so full of anguish. His fine, beautiful eyes were at one moment lit up with indignation, at the next sunk in downcast sorrow and extinguished by endless misery. Sometimes he controlled his face and voice and described the most horrible events calmly, hiding every sign of agitation; then, like an erupting volcano, his face would suddenly change to an expression of the wildest rage as he screamed curses at his persecutor.

His story is coherent and told with every appearance of plain truth, yet I confess that the letters of Felix and Safie, which he showed me, and the sight of the monster from our ship convinced me of its truth more than all his assurances, however earnest and consistent. So such a monster really exists! I cannot doubt it, yet I am lost in astonishment and wonder. Sometimes I tried to learn from Frankenstein the details of how he had made his creature, but on this point he would reveal nothing.

“Are you mad, my friend?” he said. “Where is your senseless curiosity leading you? Would you also create a demonic enemy for yourself and for the world? Enough, enough! Learn from my misery and do not try to add to your own.”

Frankenstein found out that I was making notes on his story; he asked to see them and then corrected and expanded them himself in many places, above all by giving life and spirit to the conversations he had held with his enemy. “Since you have kept a record of my story,” he said, “I would not like a distorted version to be handed down to future generations.”

So a week has gone by while I have listened to the strangest tale ever conceived by the imagination. My thoughts and every feeling of my soul have been absorbed by the interest in my guest that this story and his own refined, gentle manners have awakened. I want to comfort him, yet how can I advise someone so utterly wretched, so completely without hope of consolation, to go on living? Oh, no! The only joy he can know now will come when he calms his shattered spirit into peace and death.

Yet he has one comfort, born of solitude and delirium: he believes that when he talks with his friends in dreams and draws from them comfort for his sorrows or encouragement for his revenge, they are not figments of his imagination but the real beings themselves, visiting him from some distant world. This belief gives his daydreams a solemnity that makes them seem to me almost as impressive and interesting as the truth.

Our conversations are not always limited to his own history and misfortunes. On every subject of general literature he shows boundless knowledge and a quick, sharp understanding. His eloquence is powerful and moving; I cannot listen without tears when he describes a touching event or tries to stir feelings of pity or love. What a glorious creature he must have been in the days of his success, if he is so noble and godlike even in ruin! He seems to feel his own worth and how far he has fallen.

“When I was younger,” he said, “I believed I was destined for some great undertaking. My feelings run deep, but I had a clarity of judgement that suited me for remarkable achievements. This sense of my own worth sustained me when others would have been crushed, for I considered it a crime to waste in useless grief talents that might benefit my fellow men. When I thought about the work I had completed — nothing less than creating a feeling, reasoning being — I could not count myself among the crowd of ordinary inventors.

But this thought, which sustained me at the start of my career, now only drags me lower into the dust. All my theories and hopes have come to nothing, and like the archangel who aspired to be all-powerful, I am chained in an eternal hell. My imagination was vivid, and my powers of analysis and hard work were intense; by combining these qualities I conceived the idea of a man and brought it into being.

Even now I cannot recall without emotion my daydreams while the work was still unfinished. In my thoughts I walked in heaven, at one moment exulting in my powers, at the next burning with the idea of what they could achieve. From childhood I was filled with high hopes and lofty ambition; but how low I have sunk! Oh! My friend, if you had known me as I once was, you would not recognise me in this degraded state. Despair rarely entered my heart; a high destiny seemed to carry me forward, until I fell, never, never to rise again.”

Must I lose this admirable man, then? I have longed for a friend; I have searched for someone who would share my feelings and love me. And here, on these empty seas, I have found such a person, but I fear I have gained him only to learn his value and then lose him. I would like to reconcile him to life, but he rejects the idea.

“Thank you, Walton,” he said, “for your kind intentions towards such a miserable wretch; but when you talk of new ties and fresh affections, do you really think anyone can replace those who are gone? Can any man be to me what Clerval was, or any woman another Elizabeth? Even when our affections are not deeply stirred by any special merit, the companions of our childhood always keep a certain power over our minds that hardly any later friend can gain.

They know our childhood character, which, however it may change later, is never wiped out; and they can judge our actions with greater certainty about the honesty of our motives. A sister or brother can never suspect the other of deceit or dishonesty, unless such signs appeared early, whereas another friend, however devoted, may, in spite of himself, come under suspicion.

But my friends were dear to me not only through habit and shared memories but for their own merits; and wherever I am, the soothing voice of my Elizabeth and the conversation of Clerval will always be whispering in my ear. They are dead, and in such loneliness only one feeling can persuade me to stay alive. If I were involved in some great undertaking or plan, full of wide benefit to my fellow men, then I could live to complete it. But that is not my destiny; I must hunt down and destroy the being I brought to life; then my purpose on earth will be fulfilled and I may die.”

My beloved Sister,
September 2d.
I am writing to you surrounded by danger, not knowing whether I am fated ever to see dear England again and the still dearer friends who live there. I am hemmed in by mountains of ice which allow no escape and threaten at every moment to crush my ship. The brave men I persuaded to come with me look to me for help, but I have none to give. There is something truly appalling about our situation, yet my courage and hopes have not abandoned me. Still, it is dreadful to think that all these men’s lives are in danger because of me. If we die, my reckless plans will be to blame.

And what, Margaret, will become of your peace of mind? You will never hear of my death, and you will wait anxiously for my return. Years will pass, and you will have bouts of despair and yet still be tormented by hope. Oh! My beloved sister, the thought of your heartfelt hopes slowly and painfully fading is more terrible to me than my own death. But you have a husband and lovely children; you can be happy. May Heaven bless you and make you so!

My unfortunate guest looks on me with the tenderest compassion. He tries to fill me with hope and talks as if life were something he valued. He reminds me how often the same things have happened to other sailors who attempted this sea, and in spite of myself he fills me with cheerful hopes. Even the sailors feel the power of his eloquence; when he speaks, they stop despairing; he rouses their energy, and while they hear his voice they believe these huge mountains of ice are molehills that will vanish before human determination. These feelings do not last; each day of waiting fills them with fear, and I almost dread a mutiny caused by this despair.

September 5th.
Something has just happened of such unusual interest that, although it is very likely these papers will never reach you, I cannot help recording it.

We are still surrounded by mountains of ice, still in immediate danger of being crushed as they collide. The cold is extreme, and many of my unfortunate companions have already found a grave in this desolate place. Frankenstein’s health has worsened day by day; a feverish fire still glows in his eyes, but he is exhausted, and whenever he is suddenly stirred to any effort, he quickly sinks back into a seemingly lifeless state.

In my last letter I mentioned my fears of a mutiny. This morning, as I sat watching my friend’s pale face — his eyes half closed and his limbs hanging limply — I was disturbed by six of the sailors, who demanded to be let into the cabin. They came in, and their leader spoke to me.

He told me that he and his companions had been chosen by the rest of the crew to come to me as representatives and make a request which, in fairness, I could not refuse. We were trapped in the ice and would probably never escape, but they feared that if the ice did break up, as it might, and a clear passage opened, I would be reckless enough to continue the voyage and lead them into new dangers after they had luckily survived this one. They therefore insisted that I make a solemn promise that, if the ship were freed, I would immediately turn south.

This speech troubled me. I had not lost hope, nor had I even considered going back if we were freed. Yet could I, in fairness or even in practice, refuse this demand? I hesitated before answering, and then Frankenstein, who had been silent at first and indeed seemed hardly strong enough to follow, roused himself; his eyes sparkled and his cheeks flushed with sudden strength. Turning to the men, he said,

“What do you mean? What are you demanding of your captain? Are you so easily turned away from your purpose? Didn’t you call this a glorious expedition? And why was it glorious? Not because the way was smooth and calm like a southern sea, but because it was full of danger and terror, because at every new event your endurance would be tested and your courage displayed, because danger and death surrounded it, and you were to face them and overcome them. That is why it was a glorious and an honourable undertaking.

In the future you would have been hailed as benefactors of the human race, your names honoured as those of brave men who faced death for honour and the good of mankind. And now, at the first thought of danger — or, if you like, the first great and terrible test of your courage — you shrink back and are content to be remembered as men who were not strong enough to endure cold and danger; poor things, they felt chilly and went home to their warm firesides.

Well, that did not need all these preparations; you did not have to come this far and drag your captain into the shame of defeat just to prove you are cowards. Oh! Be men, or be more than men. Hold firm to your purpose and stand like a rock. This ice is not made of the same stuff as your hearts may be; it can change, and it cannot resist you if you say it shall not. Do not go back to your families with the mark of disgrace branded on your foreheads. Go back as heroes who have fought and won and who do not know what it is to turn their backs on the enemy.”

He said this in a voice so perfectly matched to each feeling in his speech, with eyes so full of noble purpose and heroism, that can you wonder the men were moved? They looked at one another and could not reply. I spoke; I told them to go away and think about what had been said, that I would not lead them further north if they strongly wished otherwise, but that I hoped their courage would return once they had reflected.

They left, and I turned to my friend, but he had sunk into exhaustion and seemed almost lifeless.

How all this will end I do not know, but I would rather die than return in shame with my purpose unfulfilled. Yet I fear that will be my fate; without the ideas of glory and honour to support them, the men will never willingly go on enduring their present hardships.

September 7th.
The die is cast; I have agreed to turn back if we are not destroyed. So my hopes are ruined by cowardice and indecision; I come home ignorant and disappointed. It takes more philosophy than I have to bear this injustice patiently.

September 12th.
It is over; I am returning to England. I have lost my hopes of being useful and winning glory; I have lost my friend. But I will try to describe these bitter events to you, my dear sister; and while I am carried towards England and towards you, I will not lose heart.

On September 9th the ice began to move, and roars like thunder were heard in the distance as the ice islands split and cracked in every direction. We were in the most immediate danger, but since we could do nothing except wait, I gave most of my attention to my unfortunate guest, whose illness had grown so much worse that he was completely confined to his bed. The ice cracked behind us and was driven forcefully northwards; a breeze sprang up from the west, and on the 11th the way south became completely clear.

When the sailors saw this and realised that their return home seemed certain, a shout of wild joy burst from them, loud and long. Frankenstein, who was dozing, woke up and asked the reason for the uproar. “They are shouting,” I said, “because they will soon be back in England.”

“So you are really going back?”

“Alas, yes; I cannot resist their demands. I cannot lead them into danger against their will, and I must return.”

“Do so, if you wish; but I will not. You may give up your purpose, but mine has been given to me by Heaven, and I dare not. I am weak, but surely the spirits who help my revenge will give me enough strength.” As he said this, he tried to leap out of bed, but the effort was too much for him; he fell back and fainted.

It was a long time before he came round, and I often thought that life had completely gone. At last he opened his eyes; he was breathing with difficulty and could not speak. The ship’s doctor gave him a calming draught and told us to leave him in peace. Meanwhile, he told me that my friend certainly had only a few hours to live.

His sentence had been passed, and I could only grieve and wait. I sat by his bed, watching him; his eyes were closed and I thought he was asleep; but soon he called me in a faint voice and, asking me to come closer, said, “Alas! The strength I relied on is gone; I feel that I shall soon die, while he, my enemy and persecutor, may still be alive. Do not think, Walton, that in the last moments of my life I feel the burning hatred and passionate desire for revenge that I once expressed; but I feel justified in wishing for the death of my enemy. During these last days I have been examining my past conduct, and I do not find it to blame.
