In a fit of passionate madness I created a reasoning creature and was bound to ensure, as far as I could, its happiness and well-being. That was my duty, but there was another duty that mattered even more. My duties towards my own kind had a greater claim on me because they involved a greater share of happiness or misery. Guided by this view, I refused — and I was right to refuse — to create a companion for the first creature.

He showed unequalled malice and selfishness in evil; he destroyed my friends; he doomed to destruction people of exquisite sensitivity, happiness and wisdom; and I do not know where this thirst for revenge may end. Wretched as he is, he ought to die so that he can make no one else wretched. The task of destroying him was mine, but I have failed. When I was driven by selfish and vicious motives, I asked you to take on my unfinished work, and I repeat this request now, when I am moved only by reason and virtue.

“Yet I cannot ask you to give up your country and friends to carry out this task; and now that you are going back to England, you will have little chance of meeting him. But I leave it to you to consider these points and to weigh carefully what you think your duties are; my judgement and ideas are already confused by the approach of death. I dare not ask you to do what I think is right, for I may still be led astray by passion.

“That he should live on to do more harm troubles me; otherwise, this hour, when I expect my release at any moment, is the only happy one I have known for several years. The figures of my beloved dead drift before me, and I hurry into their arms. Farewell, Walton! Seek happiness in a quiet life and avoid ambition, even the apparently harmless ambition of making a name for yourself in science and discovery. But why do I say this? My own hopes have been destroyed, yet another man may succeed.”

His voice grew fainter as he spoke, and at last, exhausted by the effort, he fell silent. About half an hour later he tried to speak again but could not; he pressed my hand weakly, and his eyes closed for ever, while the glow of a gentle smile faded from his lips.

Margaret, what can I say about the untimely end of this glorious spirit? What words can help you understand the depth of my sorrow? Anything I could say would be inadequate and weak. My tears flow; my mind is darkened by a cloud of disappointment. But I am travelling towards England, and there I may find comfort.

I have been interrupted. What do these sounds mean? It is midnight; the breeze is fair, and the men on watch on deck hardly move. Again there is a sound like a human voice, but rougher; it is coming from the cabin where Frankenstein’s body still lies. I must get up and see what it is. Good night, my sister.

Great God! What a scene has just taken place! I am still dizzy when I remember it. I hardly know if I shall have the strength to describe it; yet the story I have written down would be incomplete without this final, astonishing catastrophe.

I went into the cabin where the body of my ill-fated and admirable friend lay. Over him hung a figure I cannot find words to describe — gigantic in size, yet clumsy and distorted in its proportions. As he bent over the coffin, his face was hidden by long, tangled locks of hair; but one huge hand was stretched out, in colour and texture like that of a mummy. When he heard me approaching, he stopped his cries of grief and horror and leapt towards the window. Never have I seen anything as horrible as his face, so repulsive and so appallingly hideous. I shut my eyes without meaning to and tried to remember what my duty was towards this destroyer. I called on him to stay.

He stopped, looking at me in wonder, and then, turning again to the lifeless body of his creator, he seemed to forget I was there, and every feature and gesture seemed driven by the wildest fury of some uncontrollable passion.

“He too is my victim!” he cried. “With his murder my crimes are complete; the miserable story of my existence is wound up to its end! Oh, Frankenstein! Generous, self-sacrificing being! What use is it now to ask you to forgive me? I, who destroyed you beyond repair by destroying everyone you loved. Alas! He is cold; he cannot answer me.”

His voice seemed choked, and my first impulse, which had told me it was my duty to obey my friend’s dying request and destroy his enemy, was now held back by a mixture of curiosity and compassion. I came closer to this tremendous being; I did not dare to raise my eyes to his face again, there was something so frightening and unearthly in his ugliness. I tried to speak, but the words died on my lips. The monster went on pouring out wild, incoherent reproaches against himself. At last I summoned the resolve to speak to him during a lull in the storm of his emotion.

“Your repentance,” I said, “is useless now. If you had listened to the voice of conscience and paid attention to the stings of remorse before you drove your devilish revenge to this extreme, Frankenstein would still be alive.”

“Are you dreaming?” said the demon. “Do you think I felt no agony or remorse then? He,” he went on, pointing to the corpse, “he did not suffer in the moment the deed was done. Oh! Not a ten-thousandth part of the anguish that I felt through the long, drawn-out carrying out of it. A terrible selfishness drove me on, while my heart was poisoned with remorse. Do you think Clerval’s groans were music to my ears? My heart was made to be capable of love and sympathy, and when misery twisted it towards vice and hatred, it did not suffer the violence of that change without torture such as you cannot even imagine.

“After Clerval’s murder I went back to Switzerland, heartbroken and overwhelmed. I pitied Frankenstein; my pity grew into horror; I loathed myself. But when I discovered that he — the creator both of my existence and of its unspeakable torments — dared to hope for happiness, that while he heaped misery and despair on me he was seeking his own pleasure in feelings and passions from which I was shut out for ever, then helpless envy and bitter indignation filled me with an unquenchable thirst for revenge.

I remembered my threat and resolved that it would be carried out. I knew I was preparing a deadly torture for myself, but I was the slave, not the master, of an impulse that I hated yet could not disobey. And yet when she died! No, then I was not miserable. I had thrown off all feeling and crushed all anguish, so as to run riot in the excess of my despair. From then on evil became my good. Driven this far, I had no choice but to adapt my nature to the element I had willingly chosen. Completing my demonic plan became a passion I could never satisfy. And now it is over; there lies my last victim!”

At first I was touched by his expressions of misery; yet when I remembered what Frankenstein had said about his powers of eloquence and persuasion, and when I looked again at the lifeless body of my friend, my indignation flared up again. “Wretch!” I said. “How fitting that you come here to whine over the destruction you have caused. You throw a torch into a group of buildings, and when they have burnt down, you sit among the ruins and mourn their fall. Hypocritical fiend! If the man you mourn were still alive, he would still be the target, and once again the prey, of your cursed revenge. It is not pity that you feel; you grieve only because the victim of your malice has been taken out of your power.”

“Oh, it is not like that — not like that,” the being broke in. “Yet that must be the impression my actions give you, judging by what they seem to mean. But I do not look for sympathy in my misery. I shall never find any. When I first sought it, it was my love of virtue, the feelings of happiness and affection that filled my whole being, that I wanted to share. But now that virtue has become a mere shadow to me, and happiness and affection have turned into bitter, loathing despair, where should I look for sympathy? I am content to suffer alone for as long as my sufferings last; when I die, I am quite willing for hatred and disgrace to weigh on my memory.

Once my imagination was soothed by dreams of virtue, of fame and of joy. Once I wrongly hoped to meet beings who would forgive my outward appearance and love me for the fine qualities I was capable of revealing. I was nourished by high thoughts of honour and devotion. But now crime has dragged me lower than the lowest animal. No guilt, no harm, no malice, no misery can compare with mine.

When I go over the dreadful list of my sins, I cannot believe I am the same creature whose thoughts were once full of sublime, transcendent visions of the beauty and majesty of goodness. But it is so; the fallen angel becomes an evil devil. Yet even that enemy of God and man had friends and companions in his desolation; I am alone.

“You, who call Frankenstein your friend, seem to know about my crimes and his misfortunes. But in the account he gave you, he could not sum up the hours and months of misery I endured, wasting away in helpless passions. For while I destroyed his hopes, I did not satisfy my own desires. They were always burning and craving; I still longed for love and friendship, and I was still rejected. Was there no injustice in that? Am I to be seen as the only criminal, when all mankind sinned against me?

Why don’t you hate Felix, who drove his friend from his door with scorn? Why don’t you curse the peasant who tried to kill the man who saved his child? No, these are virtuous and spotless beings! I, the miserable and abandoned one, am a monstrosity, to be scorned and kicked and trampled on. Even now my blood boils when I remember this injustice.

“But it is true that I am a wretch. I have murdered the lovely and the helpless; I have strangled the innocent as they slept and choked to death one who never harmed me or any other living thing. I have doomed my creator, the finest example of all that is worthy of love and admiration among men, to misery; I have pursued him right to this irreparable ruin. There he lies, white and cold in death. You hate me, but your hatred cannot equal my hatred of myself. I look at the hands that carried out the deed; I think of the heart in which the idea of it was born, and I long for the moment when these hands will no longer meet my eyes and that idea will no longer haunt my thoughts.

“Do not fear that I will cause any more harm. My work is almost finished. Neither your death nor any other man’s is needed to complete the story of my existence and do what must be done, but it does require my own. Do not think I will be slow to make this sacrifice. I shall leave your ship on the ice raft that brought me here and go to the northernmost end of the earth; I shall build my funeral pyre and burn this miserable body to ashes, so that its remains may give no clue to any curious, unholy wretch who might create another like me.

I shall die. I shall no longer feel the agonies that now consume me or be the prey of feelings that are never satisfied, yet never extinguished. The one who gave me life is dead; and when I am gone, even the memory of us both will quickly vanish. I shall no longer see the sun or the stars or feel the wind play on my cheeks. Light, feeling and sense will pass away; and in this state I must find my happiness.

Some years ago, when the sights of this world first opened before me, when I felt the cheerful warmth of summer and heard the rustling of the leaves and the singing of the birds, and these were everything to me, I would have wept to die; now death is my only comfort. Stained by crimes and torn by the bitterest remorse, where can I find rest except in death?

“Farewell! I am leaving you, and in you the last human being these eyes will ever see. Farewell, Frankenstein! If you were still alive and still wished for revenge against me, it would be better satisfied by my living than by my death. But it was not so; you sought my destruction so that I could cause no greater misery; and if, in some way unknown to me, you have not stopped thinking and feeling, you would not wish on me a revenge greater than what I feel already. Ruined as you were, my agony was still greater than yours, for the bitter sting of remorse will not stop festering in my wounds until death closes them for ever.

“But soon,” he cried with sad and solemn fervour, “I shall die, and what I feel now will be felt no longer. Soon these burning miseries will be extinguished. I shall climb onto my funeral pyre in triumph and exult in the agony of the torturing flames. The light of that blaze will fade away; my ashes will be swept into the sea by the winds. My spirit will sleep in peace, or if it thinks, it will surely not think like this. Farewell.”

As he said this, he leapt from the cabin window onto the ice raft that lay close to the ship. He was soon carried away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.
b1:
Walton, in continuation.
August 26th, 17—.

You have read this strange and terrible story, Margaret. Doesn’t it make your blood go cold with horror, as mine still does? Sometimes a sudden pain stopped him, and he could not go on with his story. At other times his voice was broken but sharp, and he spoke his sad words with difficulty. His beautiful eyes were sometimes bright with anger and sometimes full of deep sadness and misery. Sometimes he controlled his face and voice and told the most horrible events calmly. Then, like a volcano, his face suddenly changed to a look of wild anger, and he screamed curses at his enemy.

His story is clear and sounds completely true. But I must say that the letters of Felix and Safie, which he showed me, and the monster we saw from our ship made me believe it more than all his words. So such a monster really exists! I cannot doubt it, but I am full of surprise and wonder. Sometimes I tried to find out from Frankenstein how he made his creature, but he never told me anything about it.

“Are you mad, my friend?” he said. “Where is your foolish curiosity taking you? Do you also want to make a terrible enemy for yourself and the world? Stop, stop! Learn from my pain and do not make more pain for yourself.”

Frankenstein learned that I was writing notes about his story. He asked to see them, and then he corrected them and added to them in many places, especially his conversations with his enemy. “You have kept my story,” he said, “so I do not want a wrong version to reach people in the future.”

A week has passed like this, while I listened to the strangest story ever imagined. This story and his kind, noble manners have filled all my thoughts and feelings with interest in my guest. I want to comfort him. But can I tell a man so unhappy, with no hope at all, to go on living? Oh, no! The only joy he can have now will come when he calms his broken spirit and finds peace in death.

But he has one comfort, which comes from loneliness and fever. In his dreams he talks with his friends, and they comfort him or make him want revenge. He believes that they are not just in his imagination, but that they really come to visit him from a distant world. This belief makes his dreams serious, and to me they seem almost as important and interesting as the truth.

We do not only talk about his own story and troubles. He knows a huge amount about books and literature, and he understands things quickly and deeply. He speaks powerfully and movingly. When he describes something sad or speaks about pity or love, I cannot listen without tears. What a wonderful man he must have been in his happy days, if he is so noble even now, in ruin! He seems to know his own value and how far he has fallen.

“When I was younger,” he said, “I believed that I would do something great. My feelings are deep, but I also had a clear mind, which made me able to achieve great things. This belief in my own worth helped me when other people would have given up. I thought it was wrong to waste my talents in useless sadness when they could help other people. When I thought about my work — the creation of a living, thinking being — I could not see myself as an ordinary inventor.

But this thought, which helped me at the start of my career, now only pushes me lower into the dust. All my ideas and hopes are nothing now. Like the angel who wanted to be as powerful as God, I am chained in hell for ever. I had a strong imagination, and I could also study and work very hard. Together, these qualities helped me to have the idea of making a man and to make him.

Even now I cannot remember my dreams from the time of that work without strong emotion. In my thoughts I walked in heaven. I was proud of my powers and excited about what they could do. Since I was a child, I was full of high hopes and great ambition; but how low I have fallen! Oh! My friend, if you had known me before, you would not recognise me now. I rarely felt hopeless; a great future seemed to carry me forward, until I fell, never, never to rise again.”

Must I lose this wonderful man? I have always wanted a friend who would understand me and love me. Here, on these empty seas, I have found one. But I am afraid that I have found him only to learn how good he is and then lose him. I want to make him love life again, but he does not accept the idea.

“Thank you, Walton,” he said, “for being so kind to such a miserable man. But when you talk about new friends and new love, do you think anyone can take the place of those who have died? Can any man be for me what Clerval was, or can any woman be another Elizabeth? The friends of our childhood always have a special power over us, even if they are not especially good people. Later friends can hardly ever have this power.

They know what we were like as children. Our character may change later, but it never disappears completely. So they can judge our actions better and know if our reasons are honest. A sister or a brother will never suspect the other of lying or cheating, unless there were signs of it very early. But another friend, even a very close one, may come under suspicion without meaning to.

But I loved my friends not only because I was used to them, but because they were good people. Wherever I am, I will always hear the gentle voice of my Elizabeth and the words of Clerval in my ear. They are dead, and in my loneliness only one feeling can make me want to stay alive. If I were working on some great plan that could help many people, then I could live to finish it. But that is not my future. I must follow and destroy the creature that I gave life to; then my work on earth will be done, and I can die.”

My beloved Sister,
September 2d.
I am writing to you in great danger. I do not know if I will ever see dear England again, or my even dearer friends there. Mountains of ice are all around us, and there is no way out. Every moment they threaten to crush my ship. The brave men who came with me look to me for help, but I have no help to give. Our situation is terrible, but I have not lost my courage and hope. But it is awful to think that all these men are in danger because of me. If we die, it will be because of my crazy plans.

And how will you feel, Margaret? You will not hear that I have died, and you will wait anxiously for me to come back. Years will pass. Sometimes you will feel despair, but hope will still torture you. Oh! My dear sister, the thought of your hopes slowly dying is more terrible to me than my own death. But you have a husband and lovely children; you can be happy. May God bless you and make you happy!

My poor guest looks at me with great kindness and pity. He tries to give me hope, and he talks as if he valued his life. He reminds me that the same things have often happened to other sailors on this sea, and he makes me feel more cheerful. Even the sailors feel the power of his words. When he speaks, they stop feeling hopeless and find new energy. While they listen to him, they believe that these huge mountains of ice are just small hills that will disappear before brave men. But these feelings do not last. Each day of waiting makes them more afraid, and I am almost afraid that they will rebel against me.

September 5th.
Something very interesting has just happened. It is very likely that these letters will never reach you, but I must write it down.

We are still surrounded by mountains of ice and are still in great danger of being crushed. It is extremely cold, and many of my poor men have already died in this empty, frozen place. Frankenstein gets weaker every day. There is still a feverish fire in his eyes, but he is exhausted. When he suddenly makes an effort, he soon falls back and looks almost lifeless.

In my last letter I told you that I was afraid of a mutiny. This morning I was sitting and watching my friend’s pale face. His eyes were half closed and his arms and legs hung weakly. Suddenly six sailors came and asked to come into the cabin. They came in, and their leader spoke to me.

He said that the other sailors had chosen him and his friends to come to me with a request. He said that, to be fair, I could not refuse it. We were trapped in the ice and would probably never escape. But if the ice broke up and the way was open, they were afraid that I would foolishly continue the journey. Then I would lead them into new dangers after they had luckily survived this one. So they wanted me to promise seriously that if the ship was freed, I would turn south at once.

This speech worried me. I had not lost hope, and I had not even thought of going back. But could I fairly refuse them, or was it even possible? I waited before I answered. Then Frankenstein, who had been silent and seemed too weak even to listen, suddenly lifted himself up. His eyes shone and his cheeks went red with sudden strength. He turned to the men and said,

“What do you mean? What are you asking your captain to do? Do you give up your plan so easily? Didn’t you call this a great and glorious journey? And why was it glorious? Not because the way was easy and calm like a southern sea. It was glorious because it was full of danger and terror. Every new event would test your strength and show your courage. Danger and death were all around, and you were going to face them and beat them. That is why it was a glorious and honourable journey.

In the future people would call you heroes who helped all mankind. They would honour your names as the names of brave men who faced death for honour and for the good of everyone. And now, at the first thought of danger, at the first big test of your courage, you run away. You are happy for people to remember you as men who were not strong enough to bear the cold and danger. People will say: “Poor things, they felt cold, so they went home to their warm fires.”

You did not need all this preparation for that. You did not need to come so far and bring shame on your captain just to show that you are cowards. Oh! Be men, or be more than men. Keep to your plans and be as strong as a rock. This ice is not like your hearts; it can change, and it cannot stop you if you decide that it will not. Do not go home to your families with shame on your faces. Go home as heroes who have fought and won, and who never turn their backs on the enemy.”

His voice changed with every feeling in his speech, and his eyes were full of noble plans and courage. Can you be surprised that the men were moved? They looked at each other and could not answer. Then I spoke. I told them to go and think about what they had heard. I said that I would not take them further north if they really did not want to go. But I hoped that, after some thought, their courage would come back.

They left, and I turned to my friend, but he was very weak and almost lifeless.

I do not know how all this will end, but I would rather die than go home in shame without reaching my goal. But I am afraid that this will happen. Without dreams of glory and honour, the men will never agree to suffer these hardships any longer.

September 7th.
The decision is made; I have agreed to go back if we are not killed. So cowardice and weakness have destroyed my hopes. I am coming back without new knowledge and full of disappointment. I am not wise enough to accept this injustice patiently.

September 12th.
It is over; I am going back to England. I have lost my hopes of being useful and famous; I have lost my friend. But I will try to tell you about these sad events, my dear sister. While the wind carries me towards England and towards you, I will not lose hope.

On September 9th the ice began to move. We heard noises like thunder far away as the ice islands broke and cracked everywhere. We were in great danger, but we could do nothing. So I spent most of my time with my poor guest. He had become so ill that he could not leave his bed at all. The ice broke behind us and was pushed hard towards the north. A wind began to blow from the west, and on the 11th the way to the south was completely open.

When the sailors saw this and understood that they would probably get home, they gave a long, loud shout of joy. Frankenstein, who was sleeping lightly, woke up and asked what the noise was. “They are shouting,” I said, “because they will soon go back to England.”

“So are you really going back?”

“Sadly, yes; I cannot say no to them. I cannot lead them into danger against their will, so I must go back.”

“Go back if you want to; but I will not. You can give up your goal, but Heaven has given me mine, and I dare not give it up. I am weak, but I am sure the spirits who help my revenge will give me enough strength.” As he said this, he tried to jump out of bed, but it was too much for him; he fell back and fainted.

He did not wake up for a long time, and I often thought that he was dead. At last he opened his eyes. He could hardly breathe and could not speak. The doctor gave him some medicine to calm him and told us to leave him alone. Then the doctor told me that my friend had only a few hours to live.

So his death was certain, and I could only be sad and wait. I sat by his bed and watched him. His eyes were closed, and I thought he was asleep. But soon he called me in a weak voice and asked me to come closer. “Alas!” he said. “My strength is gone; I feel that I will die soon, and my enemy may still be alive. Do not think, Walton, that in my last moments I still feel the burning hate and wish for revenge that I felt before. But I still think I am right to want my enemy to die. In these last days I have thought about what I did in the past, and I do not think I was wrong.

In a moment of wild madness I created a thinking creature. So I had to make him happy and well, as far as I could. That was my duty, but I had another duty that was even more important. My duty to other people was greater, because more happiness or pain depended on it. So I refused to make a wife for the first creature, and I was right to refuse.

He was cruel and selfish and evil beyond anything. He killed my friends; he destroyed good, wise and happy people; and I do not know where his hunger for revenge will end. He is unhappy himself, and he must die so that he cannot make anyone else unhappy. It was my job to destroy him, but I have failed. Before, when my reasons were selfish and bad, I asked you to finish my work. Now I ask you again, but now only reason and goodness guide me.

“But I cannot ask you to leave your country and friends to do this. And now that you are going back to England, you will probably never meet him. You must think about all this and decide for yourself what your duty is. Death is near, and my mind is no longer clear. I dare not ask you to do what I think is right, because my feelings may still be leading me wrong.

“It worries me that he will live and do more evil. But apart from that, this hour, when I am waiting to be free at any moment, is the only happy hour I have had for many years. I can see my dear dead friends in front of me, and I am hurrying to their arms. Goodbye, Walton! Look for happiness in a quiet life and do not be ambitious, even if you only want to become famous in science. But why do I say this? My own hopes were destroyed, but another man may succeed.”

His voice became weaker as he spoke, and at last, tired by the effort, he stopped talking. About half an hour later he tried to speak again, but he could not. He pressed my hand weakly, and his eyes closed for ever, while a gentle smile slowly disappeared from his lips.

Margaret, what can I say about the early death of this wonderful man? How can I help you to understand how deep my sadness is? Anything I say will be too weak. I am crying; a dark cloud of disappointment covers my mind. But I am travelling to England, and perhaps I will find comfort there.

Someone has interrupted me. What do these sounds mean? It is midnight; there is a good wind, and the sailors on watch on deck hardly move. Again I hear a sound like a human voice, but rougher. It is coming from the cabin where Frankenstein’s body still lies. I must get up and see. Good night, my sister.

Great God! What a scene has just happened! I still feel dizzy when I remember it. I am not sure I will have the strength to describe it. But my story would not be complete without this last, amazing and terrible event.

I went into the cabin where my poor, wonderful friend lay dead. A figure was bending over him, and I cannot find words to describe it. It was a giant, but its body was ugly and badly shaped. As he bent over the coffin, long, untidy hair hid his face. But one huge hand was stretched out, and its colour and skin were like a mummy’s. When he heard me coming, he stopped crying out in sadness and horror and jumped towards the window. I have never seen anything as horrible as his face; it was disgusting and terribly ugly. I closed my eyes without thinking and tried to remember what I had to do about this killer. I shouted to him to stay.

He stopped and looked at me in surprise. Then he turned again to the dead body of his creator and seemed to forget me. His whole face and every movement seemed full of wild, uncontrollable anger.

“He is my victim too!” he cried. “With his murder my crimes are complete; the sad story of my life has come to its end! Oh, Frankenstein! Kind and generous man! What is the use of asking you to forgive me now? I destroyed you completely by destroying everyone you loved. Alas! He is cold; he cannot answer me.”

His voice seemed to choke. My first idea had been to do what my dying friend had asked and to kill his enemy. But now curiosity and pity stopped me. I went closer to this enormous creature. I did not dare to look at his face again, because his ugliness was so frightening and strange. I tried to speak, but the words died on my lips. The monster went on blaming himself in a wild, confused way. At last, when his storm of feeling calmed for a moment, I found the courage to speak to him.

“It is too late to be sorry now,” I said. “If you had listened to your conscience and felt sorry before your terrible revenge went so far, Frankenstein would still be alive.”

“Are you dreaming?” said the demon. “Do you think I felt no pain or guilt then? He,” he went on, pointing to the body, “he did not suffer when it happened. Oh! He did not feel a tiny part of the pain I felt during all the long time that I was doing it. A terrible selfishness pushed me on, while guilt poisoned my heart. Do you think Clerval’s cries were music to me? My heart was made for love and kindness. When misery turned it to evil and hate, the change was so violent that it caused me pain you cannot even imagine.

“After I killed Clerval, I went back to Switzerland, broken-hearted and weak. I felt sorry for Frankenstein; my pity grew into horror; I hated myself. But then I found out that he, who made me and my terrible suffering, dared to hope for happiness. He gave me only misery and despair, but he looked for his own joy in love, which I could never have. Then helpless jealousy and bitter anger filled me with an endless hunger for revenge.

I remembered my threat and decided to carry it out. I knew that I was preparing a terrible pain for myself. But I was the slave of a feeling that I hated but could not disobey. And yet when she died! No, then I did not feel miserable. I had thrown away all feeling and pushed down all pain, and I went wild in my despair. From then on, evil became my good. I had gone so far that I had to change my nature to fit the evil path I had chosen. Finishing my terrible plan became a passion I could not stop. And now it is finished; there is my last victim!”

At first his words of misery touched me. But then I remembered what Frankenstein had said about his power to persuade people with words. I looked again at my dead friend, and I felt angry again. “You wretch!” I said. “So you come here to cry over the destruction you have caused! You throw fire into a group of houses, and when they have burnt down, you sit in the ruins and cry about it. You lying devil! If the man you are crying for were alive, he would still be the victim of your terrible revenge. You do not feel pity; you are sad only because your victim has escaped from your power.”

“Oh, it is not like that — not like that,” the creature interrupted. “But I understand that my actions must make you think so. I am not looking for anyone to share my misery. I will never find sympathy. When I first looked for it, I wanted to share my love of goodness and the happiness and love that filled me. But now goodness is only a shadow to me, and my happiness and love have turned into bitter, hateful despair. So why should I look for sympathy? I am happy to suffer alone while my suffering lasts. When I die, I am quite happy for people to hate me and remember me with shame.

Once I had sweet dreams of goodness, fame and joy. Once I wrongly hoped to meet people who would forgive my ugly body and love me for the good qualities I could show them. My mind was full of high thoughts of honour and love. But now crime has made me lower than the lowest animal. No one’s guilt, evil or misery can be compared with mine.

When I think about the terrible list of my sins, I cannot believe that I am the same creature who once had such beautiful dreams of goodness. But it is true; the fallen angel becomes an evil devil. But even that enemy of God and man had friends in his loneliness; I am alone.

“You call Frankenstein your friend, and you seem to know about my crimes and his troubles. But when he told you about them, he could not describe the hours and months of misery that I suffered, full of helpless feelings. While I destroyed his hopes, I did not get what I wanted myself. My wishes were always strong and hungry; I still wanted love and friendship, and people still pushed me away. Wasn’t that unfair? Am I the only criminal, when all people did wrong to me?

Why don’t you hate Felix, who rudely drove his friend away from his door? Why don’t you hate the country man who tried to kill the one who saved his child? Oh no, they are good and perfect people! But I, poor and alone, am a monster that people can hate, kick and walk on. Even now my blood boils when I remember this injustice.

“But it is true that I am a wicked creature. I have murdered the beautiful and the helpless. I have strangled innocent people in their sleep, and I killed a man who never hurt me or anyone else. I made my creator, the best of men, deeply unhappy, and I followed him until he was completely destroyed. There he lies, white and cold in death. You hate me, but you cannot hate me as much as I hate myself. I look at the hands that did these things, and I think of the heart where the idea was born. I long for the moment when I will not see these hands or think these thoughts any more.

“Do not be afraid that I will do more evil. My work is almost finished. Neither your death nor anyone else’s is needed to finish what I must do; only my own death is needed. Do not think that I will wait long to do it. I will leave your ship on the ice raft that brought me here and go to the furthest north of the world. There I will build a fire and burn this miserable body to ashes. Then nothing will be left to help any curious, wicked person who wants to make another creature like me.

I will die. I will no longer feel the terrible pain that eats me up now, or feelings that are never satisfied and never die. The man who gave me life is dead; and when I am gone, people will soon forget us both. I will no longer see the sun or the stars or feel the wind on my face. Light, feeling and sense will disappear, and in this state I must find my happiness.

Some years ago, when I first saw this world, felt the warm summer and heard the leaves and the birds, these things were everything to me. Then I would have cried at the idea of dying; now it is my only comfort. My crimes have made me dirty, and terrible guilt tears me apart; where can I find rest, if not in death?

“Goodbye! I am leaving you, and you are the last human being I will ever see. Goodbye, Frankenstein! If you were still alive and still wanted revenge on me, my life would punish me more than my death. But that was not how it was; you wanted to kill me so that I could not cause more misery. And if, in some way I do not know, you can still think and feel, you would not wish me a worse punishment than the one I already feel. Your life was destroyed, but my pain was even greater than yours, because the bitter pain of guilt will hurt my wounds until death closes them for ever.

“But soon,” he cried with sad and serious passion, “I will die, and I will not feel what I feel now. Soon these burning pains will end. I will climb onto my funeral fire proudly and be glad in the pain of the flames. The light of that fire will die away; the winds will carry my ashes into the sea. My spirit will sleep in peace, or if it thinks, it will certainly not think like this. Goodbye.”

As he said this, he jumped out of the cabin window onto the ice raft that was next to the ship. The waves soon carried him away, and he was lost in the darkness and the distance.
a2:
Walton, in continuation.
August 26th, 17—.

You have read this strange and terrible story, Margaret. Does it make you cold with fear? It still makes me cold. Sometimes the pain stopped him, and he could not go on. Sometimes his voice broke. His beautiful eyes were sometimes angry and sometimes very sad. Sometimes he told the most horrible things in a calm voice. Then suddenly his face became wild and angry, and he screamed at his enemy.

His story is clear, and it sounds true. But I believe it most because of two things. He showed me the letters of Felix and Safie, and we saw the monster from our ship. So the monster is real! I cannot doubt it, but I am very surprised. Sometimes I asked Frankenstein how he made his creature, but he never told me.

“Are you mad, my friend?” he said. “Do you want to make a terrible enemy too? Stop! Learn from my pain, and don’t make more pain for yourself.”

Frankenstein saw that I was writing notes about his story. He read them and changed and added many things, especially his talks with his enemy. “You have written my story,” he said, “so I want it to be correct for people in the future.”

A week has passed, and I have listened to the strangest story in the world. I think about my guest all the time. He is kind and gentle. I want to help him, but can I tell such an unhappy man to live? Oh, no! The only thing that can make him happy now is peace and death.

But he has one comfort. He is lonely and ill, and in his dreams he talks to his dead friends. He believes that they really come to him from another world. Because of this, his dreams seem almost true to me too.

We do not only talk about his sad story. He knows a lot about books, and he is very clever. He speaks beautifully, and when he talks about sad things or about love, I cry. He is great even now, when his life is broken. How great he was in his happy days! He knows that he has fallen very low.

“When I was young,” he said, “I believed that I would do something great. I had strong feelings and a clear mind. This helped me when other people would give up. I did not want to waste my talents on sadness. I made a living, thinking being, so I did not feel like an ordinary man.

But now this thought only makes me feel worse. All my hopes are nothing. Like the angel who wanted to be as strong as God, I am in hell for ever. I had a strong imagination, and I worked very hard. Because of this, I was able to make a man.

Even now I remember my dreams from that time with strong feeling. I felt that I was walking in heaven. From a child, I had big hopes; but look at me now! Oh! My friend, if you knew me before, you would not know me now. I was rarely sad, and I thought I had a great future, but then I fell, and I will never get up again.”

Must I lose this wonderful man? I always wanted a friend who would love me. Now, on these empty seas, I have found one. But I am afraid that I will lose him soon. I want him to love life again, but he says no.

“Thank you, Walton,” he said, “you are very kind to me. But you talk about new friends. Can anyone take the place of my dead friends? Can any man be like Clerval, or any woman like Elizabeth? The friends of our childhood always have a special power over us. New friends almost never have it.

They knew us when we were children. We change later, but not completely. So they understand us and know that we are honest. A brother or a sister will never think that the other is lying. But a new friend, even a good one, may not trust us.

But I loved my friends because they were good people too. I will always hear the gentle voice of Elizabeth and the words of Clerval. They are dead, and only one thing keeps me alive. If I had a great plan to help people, I could live for it. But I don’t. I must find and kill the creature that I made; then my work is done, and I can die.”

My beloved Sister,
September 2d.
I am writing to you in great danger. I don’t know if I will ever see England and my friends again. There are mountains of ice all around us. We cannot get out, and the ice can break my ship at any moment. My brave men want help from me, but I cannot help them. It is terrible, but I still have hope. But all these men are in danger because of me. If we die, it is my fault.

And what about you, Margaret? You will not know that I am dead, and you will wait for me. Years will pass, and you will be sad but still hope. Oh! My dear sister, this is worse for me than my own death. But you have a husband and lovely children; you can be happy. God bless you!

My poor guest is very kind to me. He tries to give me hope, and he talks as if he loves life. He tells me that the same things happened to other sailors on this sea. He makes me feel better. The sailors love to hear him too. When he speaks, they feel strong, and the ice mountains seem small. But this does not last. Every day they are more afraid, and I am afraid that they will fight against me.

September 5th.
Something very interesting has just happened. Maybe you will never get these letters, but I must write about it.

We are still in the ice, and we are still in danger. It is very cold, and many of my men have died here. Frankenstein is weaker every day. His eyes still burn with fever, but he is very tired. When he tries to move, he soon lies still again, almost like a dead man.

In my last letter I said I was afraid that my men would fight against me. This morning I was sitting with my friend. His face was pale, and his eyes were half closed. Six sailors came to the door and wanted to come in. They came in, and their leader spoke to me.

He said that the other sailors had sent them to me with a request. We were in the ice and probably could not escape. But if the ice opened, they were afraid that I would go on north into new dangers. So they wanted me to promise to go south at once if the ship was free.

This worried me. I had not lost hope, and I did not want to go back. But could I say no to them? I did not answer at once. Then Frankenstein, who was very weak, suddenly sat up. His eyes were bright and his face was red. He turned to the men and said,

“What do you want from your captain? Do you give up so easily? You said that this was a great journey. Why was it great? Not because it was easy. It was great because it was dangerous. You wanted to show your courage and fight danger and death. That is why it was great.

People were going to call you heroes and remember your names. And now, at the first danger, you run away. People will remember you as men who were not strong enough. They will say: “Poor men, they were cold, so they went home to their warm fires.”

You did not need to come so far just to show that you are cowards. Oh! Be men, or be more than men. Be strong like a rock. This ice is not as strong as your hearts; it cannot stop you if you do not want it to. Don’t go home to your families in shame. Go home as heroes who have fought and won.”

He spoke with so much feeling and courage. Of course the men were moved! They looked at each other and did not answer. Then I told them to go and think. I said that I would not take them north if they really did not want to go. But I hoped that they would be brave again.

They left, and I turned to my friend, but he was very weak, almost dead.

I don’t know how this will end, but I would rather die than go home in shame. But I am afraid that we will go home. The men do not care about glory, and they will not suffer any more.

September 7th.
I have decided; I have agreed to go back if we do not die. My hopes are gone because my men are afraid. I am going home with nothing, and I am very sad. It is hard for me to be patient.

September 12th.
It is over; I am going back to England. I have lost my hopes, and I have lost my friend. But I will tell you everything, my dear sister. I am going towards England and towards you, and I will not be too sad.

On September 9th the ice began to move. We heard loud noises like thunder as the ice broke. We were in great danger, but we could do nothing. I stayed with my poor guest. He was very ill and could not get out of bed. Then a wind came from the west, and on the 11th the way south was open.

The sailors saw that they could go home, and they shouted with joy. Frankenstein woke up and asked about the noise. “They are shouting,” I said, “because they will soon go back to England.”

“Are you really going back?”

“Yes, I am sorry; I cannot say no to them. I cannot take them into danger if they don’t want to go, so I must go back.”

“Go back if you want to, but I will not. Heaven gave me my work, and I must do it. I am weak, but the spirits will give me strength for my revenge.” He tried to jump out of bed, but he was too weak; he fell back and fainted.

For a long time he did not wake up, and I thought he was dead. At last he opened his eyes, but he could not speak. The doctor gave him some medicine and told us to leave him. He told me that my friend would die in a few hours.

I could only be sad and wait. I sat by his bed. His eyes were closed, and I thought he was asleep. But soon he called me in a weak voice. “My strength is gone,” he said. “I will die soon, and my enemy may still be alive. Walton, I do not hate him so much now, but I still want him to die. I have thought about my past, and I do not think I was wrong.
In a moment of madness I made a living creature. I had to try to make him happy. But I had a more important duty to other people. So I did not make a wife for him, and I was right.

He was very cruel and evil. He killed my friends, good and happy people. I don’t know when his revenge will end. He must die so that he cannot hurt anyone else. It was my job to kill him, but I have failed. Before, I asked you to finish my work for selfish reasons. Now I ask you again, but for good reasons.

“But I cannot ask you to leave your country and friends. You are going back to England, so you will probably not meet him. You must decide what to do. I am dying, and I cannot think clearly. My feelings may be wrong.

“I am worried that he will do more evil. But this hour is my only happy hour for many years. I can see my dead friends, and I am going to them. Goodbye, Walton! Look for happiness in a quiet life, and do not try to be famous in science. But why do I say this? I failed, but another man may succeed.”
His voice became weaker, and at last he stopped speaking. Half an hour later he tried to speak again, but he could not. He pressed my hand, and his eyes closed for ever. A gentle smile left his lips.
Margaret, what can I say about the death of this great man? I cannot tell you how sad I am. I am crying. But I am going to England, and maybe I will feel better there.

Someone has stopped me. What are these sounds? It is midnight, and the sailors on deck are quiet. I hear a sound like a human voice, but rougher. It comes from the room where Frankenstein’s body is. I must go and look. Good night, my sister.
Oh, God! What has just happened! I still feel dizzy. I don’t know if I can write about it, but my story must have this last terrible part.

I went into the room where my dead friend was lying. A huge, ugly figure was standing over him. Long, dirty hair covered its face. One big hand was out, and it looked like the hand of a mummy. When he heard me, he stopped crying out and jumped to the window. I have never seen a face so horrible. I closed my eyes and tried to think what to do. I told him to stay.

He stopped and looked at me in surprise. Then he turned to the body of his maker again and forgot me. He looked wild with anger.

“He is my victim too!” he cried. “Now my crimes are finished! Oh, Frankenstein! Kind, good man! Why do I ask you to forgive me now? I killed everyone you loved. He is cold; he cannot answer me.”

His voice broke. I wanted to kill him, as my friend had asked. But I felt curious and sorry for him. I went closer, but I could not look at his ugly face. I tried to speak, but I could not. The monster went on crying and blaming himself. At last, when he was quiet for a moment, I spoke to him.

“It is too late to be sorry,” I said. “If you had listened to your heart before, Frankenstein would still be alive.”

“Do you think I did not suffer?” said the monster. “He,” he said, pointing to the body, “he did not suffer much when he died. I suffered much more while I did all these terrible things. I was selfish, but my heart was full of pain. Do you think I enjoyed it when Clerval cried? My heart was made for love. When it turned to hate, the pain was terrible.

“After I killed Clerval, I went back to Switzerland. My heart was broken. I felt sorry for Frankenstein, and I hated myself. But then I learned that he wanted to be happy. He gave me only pain, but he wanted love for himself. I could never have love. So I became jealous and angry, and I wanted revenge.

I remembered my promise, and I decided to do it. I knew that it would hurt me too, but I could not stop. And when she died? Then I did not feel sad. I stopped feeling anything. From then on, evil was my good. I had to finish my terrible plan. And now it is finished; there is my last victim!”

At first I felt sorry for him. But then I remembered that Frankenstein said he was very good with words. I looked at my dead friend again, and I became angry. “You evil thing!” I said. “You come here to cry about what you did. You burn the houses, and then you sit and cry in the ruins. If he were alive, you would still want to kill him. You are not sorry; you are only sad because he has escaped from you.”

“Oh, no, it is not like that,” said the creature. “I know that it looks like that to you. But I do not want anyone to feel sorry for me now. Before, I wanted to share my love and happiness with people. But now there is no love or happiness in me, only hate. I will suffer alone. When I die, people can hate me.

Once I dreamed about goodness and happiness. Once I hoped to find people who would not look at my ugly body and would love me for my good heart. But now my crimes have made me worse than an animal. No one is as bad as I am.

When I think about all my crimes, I cannot believe that I am the same creature who once had beautiful dreams. But it is true; the good angel became a devil. But even the devil had friends; I am alone.

“Frankenstein is your friend, and he told you about my crimes. But he could not tell you about all my months of pain. I destroyed his hopes, but I did not get what I wanted. I still wanted love and friends, and people still hated me. Was that fair? Am I the only bad one, when all people were bad to me?

Why don’t you hate Felix, who sent his friend away? Why don’t you hate the man who shot me when I saved his child? Oh no, they are good people! But I am a monster, and people can kick me. I still get angry when I think about it.

“But it is true that I am evil. I have killed beautiful, helpless people. I have killed innocent people in their sleep. I made my creator, the best of men, very unhappy, and I followed him until he died. There he lies, white and cold. You hate me, but I hate myself more. I look at my hands, and I want to stop seeing them and stop thinking about what they did.

“Don’t be afraid that I will do more evil. My work is almost finished. I don’t need to kill you or anyone else; I only need to die myself. I will do it soon. I will leave your ship on my piece of ice and go to the far north. There I will make a big fire and burn my body. Then no one can use it to make another creature like me.

I will die. I will not feel this terrible pain any more. The man who made me is dead; when I die too, people will soon forget us both. I will not see the sun or the stars or feel the wind. I will find my happiness in this.

A few years ago, when I first saw the world, I loved the warm summer, the leaves and the birds. Then I did not want to die; now death is my only comfort. I have done terrible things, and I feel terrible pain; where can I find rest, if not in death?

“Goodbye! You are the last person I will ever see. Goodbye, Frankenstein! If you were alive and wanted revenge, my life would hurt me more than my death. But you wanted to kill me so that I could not hurt more people. You suffered, but my pain is greater than yours, and it will stop only when I die.

“But soon,” he cried sadly, “I will die, and I will not feel anything. Soon my pain will end. I will go up onto my fire, and I will be glad. The fire will go out, and the wind will carry my ashes into the sea. My spirit will sleep in peace. Goodbye.”

He jumped from the window onto the piece of ice next to the ship. The waves soon carried him away into the dark, and he was gone.

o.en: Walton, in continuation.
August 26th, 17—.
You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?
o.ru: Ты прочла эту странную и страшную повесть, Маргарет; не стынет ли и твоя кровь от ужаса, подобного тому, что и теперь леденит мою?

o.en: Sometimes, seized with sudden agony, he could not continue his tale; at others, his voice broken, yet piercing, uttered with difficulty the words so replete with anguish.
o.ru: Порою, охваченный внезапной мукой, он не мог продолжать рассказ; порою же его голос, прерывистый, но пронзительный, с трудом произносил слова, исполненные такой тоски.

o.en: His fine and lovely eyes were now lighted up with indignation, now subdued to downcast sorrow and quenched in infinite wretchedness.
o.ru: Его прекрасные глаза то загорались негодованием, то потуплялись в унылой скорби и гасли в безмерном горе.

o.en: Sometimes he commanded his countenance and tones and related the most horrible incidents with a tranquil voice, suppressing every mark of agitation; then, like a volcano bursting forth, his face would suddenly change to an expression of the wildest rage as he shrieked out imprecations on his persecutor.
o.ru: Иногда он овладевал своим лицом и голосом и спокойно повествовал о самых ужасных событиях, подавляя всякий признак волнения; а затем, подобно извергающемуся вулкану, лицо его вдруг искажалось неистовой яростью, и он выкрикивал проклятия своему преследователю.

o.en: His tale is connected and told with an appearance of the simplest truth, yet I own to you that the letters of Felix and Safie, which he showed me, and the apparition of the monster seen from our ship, brought to me a greater conviction of the truth of his narrative than his asseverations, however earnest and connected.
o.ru: Рассказ его связен и ведётся с видом простейшей правды, и всё же признаюсь тебе, что письма Феликса и Сафии, которые он мне показал, и появление чудовища, замеченного с нашего корабля, убедили меня в истинности его повести сильнее, чем его уверения, сколь бы горячими и последовательными они ни были.

o.en: Such a monster has, then, really existence!
o.ru: Итак, подобное чудовище и вправду существует!

o.en: I cannot doubt it, yet I am lost in surprise and admiration.
o.ru: Я не могу в этом сомневаться, и всё же теряюсь в изумлении и восхищении.

o.en: Sometimes I endeavoured to gain from Frankenstein the particulars of his creature’s formation, but on this point he was impenetrable.
o.ru: Порою я пытался выведать у Франкенштейна подробности того, как было создано его существо, но в этом он оставался непроницаем.

o.en: “Are you mad, my friend?” said he.
o.ru: «Вы с ума сошли, друг мой? — сказал он.

o.en: “Or whither does your senseless curiosity lead you?
o.ru: — Или куда влечёт вас ваше безрассудное любопытство?

o.en: Would you also create for yourself and the world a demoniacal enemy?
o.ru: Неужто и вы хотите создать себе и миру демонического врага?

o.en: Peace, peace!
Learn my miseries and do not seek to increase your own.”
o.ru: Узнайте мои несчастья и не стремитесь умножить свои».

o.en: Frankenstein discovered that I made notes concerning his history; he asked to see them and then himself corrected and augmented them in many places, but principally in giving the life and spirit to the conversations he held with his enemy.
o.ru: Франкенштейн обнаружил, что я делаю заметки о его истории; он пожелал их увидеть, а затем сам во многих местах исправил и дополнил их, главным образом придав жизнь и дух своим беседам с врагом.

o.en: “Since you have preserved my narration,” said he, “I would not that a mutilated one should go down to posterity.”
o.ru: «Коль скоро вы сохранили моё повествование, — сказал он, — я не хотел бы, чтобы к потомству дошло оно искажённым».

o.en: Thus has a week passed away, while I have listened to the strangest tale that ever imagination formed.
o.ru: Так прошла неделя, в течение которой я слушал самую странную повесть, какую когда-либо создавало воображение.

o.en: My thoughts and every feeling of my soul have been drunk up by the interest for my guest which this tale and his own elevated and gentle manners have created.
o.ru: Мои мысли и все чувства моей души поглощены участием к моему гостю, которое пробудили эта повесть и его собственные возвышенные и кроткие манеры.

o.en: I wish to soothe him, yet can I counsel one so infinitely miserable, so destitute of every hope of consolation, to live?
o.ru: Я желаю утешить его, но могу ли я советовать жить тому, кто так безмерно несчастен, так лишён всякой надежды на утешение?

o.en: Oh, no!
The only joy that he can now know will be when he composes his shattered spirit to peace and death.
o.ru: Единственная радость, доступная ему теперь, придёт тогда, когда он успокоит свой разбитый дух миром и смертью.

o.en: Yet he enjoys one comfort, the offspring of solitude and delirium; he believes that when in dreams he holds converse with his friends and derives from that communion consolation for his miseries or excitements to his vengeance, that they are not the creations of his fancy, but the beings themselves who visit him from the regions of a remote world.
o.ru: И всё же у него есть одно утешение, порождение одиночества и бреда: он верит, что когда во сне он беседует со своими друзьями и черпает в этом общении утешение в своих бедах или побуждение к мести, то это не создания его фантазии, а сами они, посещающие его из пределов далёкого мира.

o.en: This faith gives a solemnity to his reveries that render them to me almost as imposing and interesting as truth.
o.ru: Эта вера придаёт его грёзам торжественность, делающую их в моих глазах почти столь же внушительными и занимательными, как истина.

o.en: Our conversations are not always confined to his own history and misfortunes.
o.ru: Наши беседы не всегда ограничиваются его собственной историей и несчастьями.

o.en: On every point of general literature he displays unbounded knowledge and a quick and piercing apprehension.
o.ru: В любом предмете словесности он обнаруживает безграничные познания и быстрое, проницательное понимание.

o.en: His eloquence is forcible and touching; nor can I hear him, when he relates a pathetic incident or endeavours to move the passions of pity or love, without tears.
o.ru: Красноречие его сильно и трогательно; и я не могу без слёз слушать его, когда он рассказывает о чём-нибудь печальном или старается пробудить чувства жалости или любви.

o.en: What a glorious creature must he have been in the days of his prosperity, when he is thus noble and godlike in ruin!
o.ru: Каким же прекрасным созданием должен был он быть в дни своего благополучия, если и в крушении он так благороден и богоподобен!

o.en: He seems to feel his own worth and the greatness of his fall.
o.ru: Он, кажется, сознаёт собственную ценность и величие своего падения.

o.en: “When younger,” said he, “I believed myself destined for some great enterprise.
o.ru: «В юности, — сказал он, — я считал себя предназначенным для какого-то великого свершения.

o.en: My feelings are profound, but I possessed a coolness of judgment that fitted me for illustrious achievements.
o.ru: Чувства мои глубоки, но я обладал хладнокровием суждения, делавшим меня пригодным для славных деяний.

o.en: This sentiment of the worth of my nature supported me when others would have been oppressed, for I deemed it criminal to throw away in useless grief those talents that might be useful to my fellow creatures.
o.ru: Это сознание достоинства моей натуры поддерживало меня там, где другие были бы подавлены, ибо я почитал преступным растрачивать в бесполезной скорби таланты, которые могли бы послужить моим ближним.

o.en: When I reflected on the work I had completed, no less a one than the creation of a sensitive and rational animal, I could not rank myself with the herd of common projectors.
o.ru: Размышляя о завершённом мною труде — ни много ни мало о создании чувствующего и разумного существа, — я не мог причислить себя к толпе заурядных прожектёров.

o.en: But this thought, which supported me in the commencement of my career, now serves only to plunge me lower in the dust.
o.ru: Но эта мысль, поддерживавшая меня в начале моего поприща, теперь лишь глубже повергает меня в прах.

o.en: All my speculations and hopes are as nothing, and like the archangel who aspired to omnipotence, I am chained in an eternal hell.
o.ru: Все мои замыслы и надежды обратились в ничто, и, подобно архангелу, возжелавшему всемогущества, я прикован в вечном аду.

o.en: My imagination was vivid, yet my powers of analysis and application were intense; by the union of these qualities I conceived the idea and executed the creation of a man.
o.ru: Воображение моё было пылким, а способность к анализу и прилежанию — огромной; соединением этих качеств я задумал и осуществил сотворение человека.

o.en: Even now I cannot recollect without passion my reveries while the work was incomplete.
o.ru: Даже теперь я не могу без волнения вспоминать свои мечты в ту пору, когда труд ещё не был завершён.

o.en: I trod heaven in my thoughts, now exulting in my powers, now burning with the idea of their effects.
o.ru: В мыслях я ступал по небесам, то ликуя от своих сил, то пылая мыслью об их плодах.

o.en: From my infancy I was imbued with high hopes and a lofty ambition; but how am I sunk!
o.ru: С младенчества я был исполнен высоких надежд и гордого честолюбия; но как низко я пал!

o.en: Oh!
My friend, if you had known me as I once was, you would not recognise me in this state of degradation.
o.ru: Друг мой, если бы вы знали меня таким, каким я был когда-то, вы не узнали бы меня в этом унижении.

o.en: Despondency rarely visited my heart; a high destiny seemed to bear me on, until I fell, never, never again to rise.”
o.ru: Уныние редко посещало моё сердце; высокая судьба, казалось, несла меня вперёд, пока я не пал, чтобы никогда, никогда более не подняться».

o.en: Must I then lose this admirable being?
o.ru: Неужели же мне суждено потерять это восхитительное существо?

o.en: I have longed for a friend; I have sought one who would sympathise with and love me.
o.ru: Я так жаждал друга; я искал того, кто разделял бы мои чувства и любил меня.

o.en: Behold, on these desert seas I have found such a one, but I fear I have gained him only to know his value and lose him.
o.ru: И вот в этих пустынных морях я нашёл такого человека, но боюсь, что обрёл его лишь затем, чтобы узнать ему цену и лишиться его.

o.en: I would reconcile him to life, but he repulses the idea.
o.ru: Я хотел бы примирить его с жизнью, но он отвергает эту мысль.

o.en: “I thank you, Walton,” he said, “for your kind intentions towards so miserable a wretch; but when you speak of new ties and fresh affections, think you that any can replace those who are gone?
o.ru: «Благодарю вас, Уолтон, — сказал он, — за добрые намерения по отношению к столь жалкому несчастнику; но когда вы говорите о новых узах и свежих привязанностях, неужели вы думаете, что кто-то может заменить ушедших?

o.en: Can any man be to me as Clerval was, or any woman another Elizabeth?
o.ru: Может ли какой-нибудь мужчина стать для меня тем, чем был Клерваль, или какая-нибудь женщина — второй Элизабет?

o.en: Even where the affections are not strongly moved by any superior excellence, the companions of our childhood always possess a certain power over our minds which hardly any later friend can obtain.
o.ru: Даже там, где привязанность не вызвана особыми достоинствами, товарищи нашего детства всегда сохраняют над нашей душой некую власть, какой едва ли добьётся позднейший друг.

o.en: They know our infantine dispositions, which, however they may be afterwards modified, are never eradicated; and they can judge of our actions with more certain conclusions as to the integrity of our motives.
o.ru: Они знают наши детские склонности, которые, как бы ни видоизменялись впоследствии, никогда не искореняются; и они могут судить о наших поступках, с большей уверенностью заключая о чистоте наших побуждений.

o.en: A sister or a brother can never, unless indeed such symptoms have been shown early, suspect the other of fraud or false dealing, when another friend, however strongly he may be attached, may, in spite of himself, be contemplated with suspicion.
o.ru: Сестра или брат никогда не заподозрят друг друга в обмане или вероломстве, если только подобные признаки не обнаружились рано, тогда как на иного друга, как бы крепко он ни был привязан, помимо его воли может пасть подозрение.

o.en: But I enjoyed friends, dear not only through habit and association, but from their own merits; and wherever I am, the soothing voice of my Elizabeth and the conversation of Clerval will be ever whispered in my ear.
o.ru: Но у меня были друзья, дорогие мне не только в силу привычки и близости, но и по их собственным достоинствам; и где бы я ни был, успокаивающий голос моей Элизабет и беседы Клерваля вечно будут звучать шёпотом в моих ушах.

o.en: They are dead, and but one feeling in such a solitude can persuade me to preserve my life.
o.ru: Они мертвы, и в таком одиночестве лишь одно чувство может убедить меня сохранить жизнь.

o.en: If I were engaged in any high undertaking or design, fraught with extensive utility to my fellow creatures, then could I live to fulfil it.
o.ru: Будь я занят каким-нибудь высоким предприятием или замыслом, сулящим обширную пользу моим ближним, тогда я мог бы жить ради его свершения.

o.en: But such is not my destiny; I must pursue and destroy the being to whom I gave existence; then my lot on earth will be fulfilled and I may die.”
o.ru: Но не такова моя участь; я должен преследовать и уничтожить существо, которому дал жизнь; тогда мой жребий на земле исполнится, и я смогу умереть».

o.en: My beloved Sister,
September 2d.
I write to you, encompassed by peril and ignorant whether I am ever doomed to see again dear England and the dearer friends that inhabit it.
o.ru: Я пишу тебе, окружённый опасностями и не зная, суждено ли мне когда-нибудь вновь увидеть милую Англию и ещё более милых друзей, её населяющих.

o.en: I am surrounded by mountains of ice which admit of no escape and threaten every moment to crush my vessel.
o.ru: Меня окружают ледяные горы, не оставляющие выхода и каждую минуту грозящие раздавить моё судно.

o.en: The brave fellows whom I have persuaded to be my companions look towards me for aid, but I have none to bestow.
o.ru: Храбрецы, которых я уговорил стать моими спутниками, ждут от меня помощи, но мне нечего им дать.

o.en: There is something terribly appalling in our situation, yet my courage and hopes do not desert me.
o.ru: В нашем положении есть нечто поистине ужасающее, и всё же мужество и надежды меня не покидают.

o.en: Yet it is terrible to reflect that the lives of all these men are endangered through me.
o.ru: Но страшно думать, что жизнь всех этих людей подвергается опасности из-за меня.

o.en: If we are lost, my mad schemes are the cause.
o.ru: Если мы погибнем, причиной тому будут мои безумные замыслы.

o.en: And what, Margaret, will be the state of your mind?
o.ru: А каково будет, Маргарет, у тебя на душе?

o.en: You will not hear of my destruction, and you will anxiously await my return.
o.ru: Ты не услышишь о моей гибели и будешь с тревогой ждать моего возвращения.

o.en: Years will pass, and you will have visitings of despair and yet be tortured by hope.
o.ru: Пройдут годы, тебя будут посещать приступы отчаяния, и всё же тебя будет терзать надежда.

o.en: Oh!
My beloved sister, the sickening failing of your heart-felt expectations is, in prospect, more terrible to me than my own death.
o.ru: Моя любимая сестра, мысль о мучительном крушении твоих сердечных ожиданий страшнее для меня, чем собственная смерть.

o.en: But you have a husband and lovely children; you may be happy.
o.ru: Но у тебя есть муж и прелестные дети; ты можешь быть счастлива.

o.en: Heaven bless you and make you so!
o.ru: Да благословит тебя Небо и да сделает тебя счастливой!

o.en: My unfortunate guest regards me with the tenderest compassion.
o.ru: Мой несчастный гость смотрит на меня с нежнейшим состраданием.

o.en: He endeavours to fill me with hope and talks as if life were a possession which he valued.
o.ru: Он старается вселить в меня надежду и говорит так, будто жизнь — это достояние, которым он дорожит.

o.en: He reminds me how often the same accidents have happened to other navigators who have attempted this sea, and in spite of myself, he fills me with cheerful auguries.
o.ru: Он напоминает мне, как часто то же самое случалось с другими мореплавателями, пытавшимися пройти этим морем, и, помимо моей воли, наполняет меня отрадными предчувствиями.

o.en: Even the sailors feel the power of his eloquence; when he speaks, they no longer despair; he rouses their energies, and while they hear his voice they believe these vast mountains of ice are mole-hills which will vanish before the resolutions of man.
o.ru: Даже матросы чувствуют силу его красноречия; когда он говорит, они перестают отчаиваться; он пробуждает в них силы, и пока они слышат его голос, им верится, что эти громадные ледяные горы — лишь кротовые кучи, которые исчезнут перед решимостью человека.

o.en: These feelings are transitory; each day of expectation delayed fills them with fear, and I almost dread a mutiny caused by this despair.
o.ru: Эти чувства преходящи; каждый день обманутого ожидания наполняет их страхом, и я почти боюсь бунта, порождённого этим отчаянием.

o.en: September 5th.
A scene has just passed of such uncommon interest that, although it is highly probable that these papers may never reach you, yet I cannot forbear recording it.
o.ru: Только что произошла сцена столь необычайная, что, хотя весьма вероятно, эти бумаги никогда до тебя не дойдут, я не могу удержаться, чтобы не записать её.

o.en: We are still surrounded by mountains of ice, still in imminent danger of being crushed in their conflict.
o.ru: Мы всё ещё окружены ледяными горами, всё ещё в неминуемой опасности быть раздавленными при их столкновении.

o.en: The cold is excessive, and many of my unfortunate comrades have already found a grave amidst this scene of desolation.
o.ru: Холод чрезвычайный, и многие мои несчастные товарищи уже нашли могилу среди этой картины запустения.

o.en: Frankenstein has daily declined in health; a feverish fire still glimmers in his eyes, but he is exhausted, and when suddenly roused to any exertion, he speedily sinks again into apparent lifelessness.
o.ru: Здоровье Франкенштейна с каждым днём слабеет; в его глазах ещё тлеет лихорадочный огонь, но он изнурён и, внезапно пробуждённый к какому-либо усилию, вскоре вновь впадает в видимую безжизненность.

o.en: I mentioned in my last letter the fears I entertained of a mutiny.
o.ru: В последнем письме я упоминал о своих опасениях бунта.

o.en: This morning, as I sat watching the wan countenance of my friend—his eyes half closed and his limbs hanging listlessly—I was roused by half a dozen of the sailors, who demanded admission into the cabin.
o.ru: Сегодня утром, когда я сидел, глядя на бледное лицо моего друга — глаза его были полузакрыты, а члены бессильно свисали, — меня потревожили полдюжины матросов, потребовавших, чтобы их впустили в каюту.

o.en: They entered, and their leader addressed me.
o.ru: Они вошли, и их предводитель обратился ко мне.

o.en: He told me that he and his companions had been chosen by the other sailors to come in deputation to me to make me a requisition which, in justice, I could not refuse.
o.ru: Он сказал мне, что он и его товарищи избраны остальными матросами, чтобы явиться ко мне депутацией и предъявить требование, в котором я по справедливости не мог отказать.

o.en: We were immured in ice and should probably never escape, but they feared that if, as was possible, the ice should dissipate and a free passage be opened, I should be rash enough to continue my voyage and lead them into fresh dangers, after they might happily have surmounted this.
o.ru: Мы были замурованы во льдах и, вероятно, никогда бы не выбрались, но они опасались, что если, как это возможно, лёд разойдётся и откроется свободный проход, я окажусь достаточно безрассуден, чтобы продолжить плавание и повести их навстречу новым опасностям, после того как они, быть может, счастливо избегнут этой.

o.en: They insisted, therefore, that I should engage with a solemn promise that if the vessel should be freed I would instantly direct my course southwards.
o.ru: Поэтому они настаивали, чтобы я связал себя торжественным обещанием, что, если судно освободится, я немедленно направлю его на юг.

o.en: This speech troubled me.
I had not despaired, nor had I yet conceived the idea of returning if set free.
o.ru: Я не отчаивался и ещё даже не помышлял о возвращении в случае освобождения.

o.en: Yet could I, in justice, or even in possibility, refuse this demand?
o.ru: Но мог ли я по справедливости или хотя бы по возможности отказать в этом требовании?

o.en: I hesitated before I answered, when Frankenstein, who had at first been silent, and indeed appeared hardly to have force enough to attend, now roused himself; his eyes sparkled, and his cheeks flushed with momentary vigour.
o.ru: Я колебался с ответом, когда Франкенштейн, который сначала молчал и, казалось, едва имел силы следить за разговором, вдруг встрепенулся; глаза его засверкали, а щёки вспыхнули мгновенной силой.

o.en: Turning towards the men, he said,
“What do you mean?
What do you demand of your captain?
o.ru: Чего вы требуете от своего капитана?

o.en: Are you, then, so easily turned from your design?
o.ru: Неужели вас так легко отвратить от вашего замысла?

o.en: Did you not call this a glorious expedition?
o.ru: Разве не называли вы эту экспедицию славной?

o.en: “And wherefore was it glorious?
o.ru: А почему же она была славной?

o.en: Not because the way was smooth and placid as a southern sea, but because it was full of dangers and terror, because at every new incident your fortitude was to be called forth and your courage exhibited, because danger and death surrounded it, and these you were to brave and overcome.
o.ru: Не потому, что путь был гладким и спокойным, как южное море, а потому, что он был полон опасностей и ужаса, потому что при каждом новом испытании вам предстояло явить стойкость и выказать мужество, потому что его окружали опасность и смерть, а вам надлежало бросить им вызов и одолеть их.

o.en: For this was it a glorious, for this was it an honourable undertaking.
o.ru: Вот почему это было славное, вот почему это было почётное предприятие.

o.en: You were hereafter to be hailed as the benefactors of your species, your names adored as belonging to brave men who encountered death for honour and the benefit of mankind.
o.ru: Впоследствии вас приветствовали бы как благодетелей вашего рода, а ваши имена чтили бы как имена храбрецов, встретивших смерть ради чести и блага человечества.

o.en: And now, behold, with the first imagination of danger, or, if you will, the first mighty and terrific trial of your courage, you shrink away and are content to be handed down as men who had not strength enough to endure cold and peril; and so, poor souls, they were chilly and returned to their warm firesides.
o.ru: А теперь, при первой же мысли об опасности, или, если угодно, при первом великом и грозном испытании вашего мужества, вы отступаете и согласны войти в память потомков людьми, у которых не хватило сил вынести холод и опасность; бедняжки, им стало зябко, и они вернулись к своим тёплым очагам.

o.en: Why, that requires not this preparation; ye need not have come thus far and dragged your captain to the shame of a defeat merely to prove yourselves cowards.
o.ru: Да ведь для этого не нужны были такие приготовления; незачем было заходить так далеко и навлекать на своего капитана позор поражения лишь для того, чтобы доказать, что вы трусы.

o.en: Oh!
Be men, or be more than men.
o.ru: Будьте мужчинами — или больше чем мужчинами.

o.en: Be steady to your purposes and firm as a rock.
o.ru: Будьте верны своим целям и тверды, как скала.

o.en: This ice is not made of such stuff as your hearts may be; it is mutable and cannot withstand you if you say that it shall not.
o.ru: Этот лёд сделан не из того вещества, из какого, быть может, сделаны ваши сердца; он изменчив и не устоит перед вами, если вы скажете, что он не устоит.

o.en: Do not return to your families with the stigma of disgrace marked on your brows.
o.ru: Не возвращайтесь к своим семьям с клеймом бесчестья на челе.

o.en: Return as heroes who have fought and conquered and who know not what it is to turn their backs on the foe.”
o.ru: Возвращайтесь героями, которые сражались и победили и которым неведомо, что значит показать спину врагу».

o.en: He spoke this with a voice so modulated to the different feelings expressed in his speech, with an eye so full of lofty design and heroism, that can you wonder that these men were moved?
